PAPER 2 — P2_SET_01
UNIT: Paper 2 Case Study
====================================================================================================

--- MAIN STEM ---
Tasty Treats (TT) was established 10 years ago as a private limited company in Country X. TT currently operates a retail chain of 50 cafes specializing in premium handcrafted luxury desserts, including gourmet cakes and artisan gelato. To expand market reach, the board plans to open a new flag-ship cafe at an estimated capital expenditure of $500,000. Managing Director Frances must decide whether to finance this project using accumulated retained profits or by securing an additional 5-year bank loan. The expansion involves hiring 1 store manager and 10 full-time employees who require specialized training in dessert assembly, customer service, and inventory control. Weekly operations at each cafe incur fixed overheads of $1,000 and total variable costs of $20,000 while serving 5,000 desserts. TT aims to maintain an environmentally sustainable brand image by utilizing 100% recyclable packaging for take-home orders.

--- APPENDIX 1 — MARKETING/OPS ---
Advertisement Extract: 'Visit TT Cafes today to experience our individually crafted luxury desserts and organic artisan gelatos. Customize your own toppings or purchase take-home cakes packaged in 100% biodegradable and recyclable boxes, helping us eliminate single-use plastics.'

--- APPENDIX 2 — FINANCIAL DATA ---
Title: Extract from TT's Statement of Financial Position as at 31 March ($ millions)
Headers: ['Financial Metric', '2024 ($m)', '2025 ($m)']
Inventory | 10.0 | 8.0
Trade Receivables | 3.0 | 1.5
Cash & Bank Balances | 2.0 | 2.5
Trade Payables | 5.0 | 3.0
Bank Overdraft | 0.0 | 5.0
Bank Loan (Non-Current) | 2.0 | 3.0

--- APPENDIX 3 — EXTERNAL ENVIRONMENT ---
Government Economic Gazette (March 2025): 'The government of Country X announces a reduction in personal income tax rates from 25% to 20%, alongside an increase in corporate profits tax from 24% to 26%. Furthermore, central bank policy interest rates are scheduled to drop by 1.5% as the domestic economy enters a technical recession.'

--- QUESTIONS ---
  Q1(a) [8 marks]
    Question: Explain two advantages and two disadvantages to TT of operating as a private limited company.
    Answer: Advantage 1: Limited liability protects owners' personal assets if the 50 cafes incur major debts. Application: Shareholders only risk capital invested in the $500,000 expansion.
Advantage 2: Ability to raise capital by selling shares to friends and family. Application: Provides finance towards the $500,000 expansion budget without public flotation.
Disadvantage 1: Shares cannot be sold to the general public on a stock exchange. Application: Restricts access to large equity capital when funding 50 cafes.
Disadvantage 2: Financial accounts must be published annually. Application: Competitors selling luxury desserts can view TT's cost metrics and profit margins.
    Keywords: 50 cafes, $500,000, luxury desserts, 10 employees, 5,000 desserts, gelato, cakes
    Mark scheme: knowledge_max_2: 1 mark for each valid advantage/disadvantage identified (max 2 advantages, max 2 disadvantages). | application_analysis_max_6: Up to 3 marks per point for contextual explanation applied to business context.

  Q1(b) [12 marks]
    Question: Consider the following three market research methods TT could use before opening the new cafe: Competitors' websites, Focus groups, and Observation in rival cafes. Which method should TT use? Justify your recommendation.
    Answer: Competitors' websites allow TT to quickly view prices of luxury desserts and menu choices at minimal cost, though online data may not reflect local customer preferences near the new cafe site. Focus groups gather detailed qualitative feedback on gelato flavors and packaging from potential customers in the targeted location, though organizing them is expensive and time-consuming. Observation in rival cafes provides accurate behavioral data on customer order frequency and dessert selections without direct questioning bias, though it fails to explain the underlying reasons behind customer choices. Recommendation: Focus groups should be used because gathering direct qualitative feedback on specific luxury dessert preferences of local residents in the new area is vital to ensure high demand for the 5,000 weekly desserts target, outweighing higher initial research costs.
    Keywords: 5,000 desserts, gelato, $500,000, luxury desserts, 10 employees, 50 cafes, recyclable packaging
    Mark scheme: level_1_1_to_4: Outline of research methods with limited context. | level_2_5_to_8: Detailed discussion of advantages/disadvantages of at least two methods in context. | level_3_9_to_12: Detailed discussion of all three methods in context with a fully supported recommendation.

  Q2(a) [8 marks]
    Question: Explain two benefits to TT of providing formal employment contracts to the 10 new cafe employees.
    Answer: Benefit 1: Clearly defines job duties and working hours, minimizing misunderstandings. Application: Ensures the 10 employees clearly understand expectations regarding customer service and making luxury desserts.
Benefit 2: Provides legal security and specifies notice periods. Application: Prevents sudden staff turnover among cafe workers, ensuring operational continuity across the 50 cafes.
    Keywords: 10 employees, 50 cafes, luxury desserts, 5,000 desserts, store manager
    Mark scheme: knowledge_max_2: 1 mark for each relevant benefit identified (max 2). | application_analysis_max_6: Up to 3 marks per point for detailed contextual explanation.

  Q2(b) [12 marks]
    Question: Consider the following two motivation methods TT could use for its cafe staff: 'Employee of the Month' award with a $20 voucher, or Job Enrichment. Which method should TT choose? Justify your decision.
    Answer: An 'Employee of the Month' award offering a $20 dessert voucher creates low-cost competition among the 10 employees to deliver excellent customer service, but it may demotivate the remaining staff who feel their hard work is unrewarded. Job enrichment involves giving employees added responsibilities such as choosing ingredient suppliers or designing new artisan cake recipes, which satisfies higher-level esteem needs under Herzberg's theory and boosts productivity, though it requires extra training expenses. Recommendation: Job enrichment is preferred because giving staff genuine responsibility over dessert creation builds long-term commitment and maintains high service standards across the 50 cafes, whereas a $20 voucher offers negligible long-term motivation.
    Keywords: $20 voucher, 10 employees, 50 cafes, luxury desserts, ingredient suppliers, 5,000 desserts
    Mark scheme: level_1_1_to_4: Basic description of motivation techniques. | level_2_5_to_8: Detailed analysis of benefits/drawbacks of one or both methods in context. | level_3_9_to_12: Comprehensive evaluation of both options in context with a justified recommendation.

  Q3(a) [8 marks]
    Question: 
    Answer: 
    Mark scheme: working_marks: 1 mark for correct formula/method, 1 mark for correct final figure ($4.20 and $4.00). 1 mark per valid use of cost data.

  Q3(b) [12 marks]
    Question: Using Appendix 2, evaluate TT's financial position by calculating the current ratio and acid test ratio for 2024 and 2025. Has TT's financial position improved?
    Answer: Calculations: 2024 Current Ratio = ($10m + $3m + $2m) / $5m = $15m / $5m = 3.0:1. 2024 Acid Test Ratio = ($15m - $10m) / $5m = 1.0:1.
2025 Current Ratio = ($8m + $1.5m + $2.5m) / ($3m + $5m) = $12m / $8m = 1.5:1. 2025 Acid Test Ratio = ($12m - $8m) / $8m = 0.5:1.
Evaluation: TT's liquidity position deteriorated significantly in 2025. The current ratio dropped from a secure 3.0:1 to 1.5:1, while the acid test ratio fell from 1.0:1 to an alarming 0.5:1 due to a $5m bank overdraft. TT holds insufficient liquid assets to settle short-term debts without selling inventory. Conclusion: TT's financial position did not improve; high reliance on a $5m overdraft creates severe liquidity risks when funding the $500,000 expansion.
    Keywords: 3.0:1, 1.5:1, 1.0:1, 0.5:1, $5m overdraft, $8m inventory, $500,000, 50 cafes
    Mark scheme: level_1_1_to_4: States balance sheet changes or incorrect ratio calculations. | level_2_5_to_8: Accurately calculates liquidity ratios for both years with contextual analysis. | level_3_9_to_12: Accurate ratio calculations combined with detailed evaluation of liquidity trends and a justified conclusion.

  Q4(a) [8 marks]
    Question: Explain one advantage and one disadvantage to TT of using 100% recyclable packaging for its take-home desserts.
    Answer: Advantage: Enhances brand reputation among environmentally conscious consumers. Application: Attracts eco-friendly customers to the 50 cafes, boosting total dessert sales revenue.
Disadvantage: Recyclable paper packaging has higher unit purchasing costs than standard plastic. Application: Increases weekly variable costs above $20,000, lowering gross profit margins on take-home cakes.
    Keywords: 100% recyclable packaging, 50 cafes, $20,000 variable costs, take-home cakes, luxury desserts
    Mark scheme: knowledge_max_2: 1 mark for valid advantage, 1 mark for valid disadvantage. | application_analysis_max_6: Up to 3 marks per point for contextual development.

  Q4(b) [12 marks]
    Question: Using Appendix 3, evaluate how a decrease in income tax, an increase in corporate profit tax, and a reduction in interest rates will affect TT. Which change will have the greatest impact? Justify your answer.
    Answer: Income tax reduction (25% to 20%) increases consumers' disposable income, driving higher spending on luxury desserts across TT's 50 cafes, boosting overall sales revenue. Profit tax increase (24% to 26%) reduces retained profits available for reinvestment, making it harder to fund the $500,000 expansion internally. Interest rate reduction (1.5% fall) lowers interest expenses on existing $3m bank loans and reduces borrowing costs if TT takes out a $500,000 loan for the new cafe. Conclusion: The decrease in personal income tax will have the greatest impact because it directly stimulates consumer demand for non-essential luxury food items during an economic recession, generating the cash flow needed to offset higher corporate profit taxes.
    Keywords: 25% to 20%, 24% to 26%, 1.5% fall, $500,000, $3m bank loans, 50 cafes, luxury desserts
    Mark scheme: level_1_1_to_4: Identifies economic factors with limited business context. | level_2_5_to_8: Analyzes impact of at least two economic changes on TT in context. | level_3_9_to_12: Detailed evaluation of all three economic changes in context with a well-justified judgment of the greatest impact.

PAPER 2 — P2_SET_02
UNIT: Paper 2 Case Study
====================================================================================================

--- MAIN STEM ---
VeloCraft Bikes (VB) is a private limited company operating a single manufacturing factory with 40 skilled production workers. VB produces premium custom carbon-fiber bicycles for competitive cyclists. Management plans to expand operations by introducing a new line of mass-produced commuter electric bikes (e-bikes) costing $1,200,000 in capital machinery. The factory currently operates under batch production, incurring fixed costs of $12,000 per month and total variable costs of $48,000 while producing 200 custom bicycles monthly. Directors are debating whether to maintain batch assembly or transition to an automated flow line. Additionally, VB faces quality control challenges, as 5% of custom frames currently fail stress testing, incurring expensive rework costs.

--- APPENDIX 1 — MARKETING/OPS ---
Operations Extract: 'VeloCraft Custom Frame Build Workflow: Step 1: Carbon-fiber layering (3 hours/frame); Step 2: Oven Curing (6 hours); Step 3: Manual Painting & Branding (4 hours); Step 4: Component Fitting (2 hours). Current monthly batch capacity: 200 units.'

--- APPENDIX 2 — FINANCIAL DATA ---
Title: VeloCraft Bikes - Statement of Financial Position Extract as at 31 December ($ thousands)
Headers: ['Financial Metric', '2024 ($000)', '2025 ($000)']
Inventory | 300 | 350
Trade Receivables | 200 | 100
Cash & Cash Equivalents | 100 | 50
Trade Payables | 150 | 250
Bank Overdraft | 50 | 150
Long-Term Bank Loan | 400 | 600

--- APPENDIX 3 — EXTERNAL ENVIRONMENT ---
Industry Trade Report (2025): 'Government introduces a $200 eco-subsidy for citizens purchasing electric bicycles. Simultaneously, import tariffs on imported carbon-fiber raw materials increase by 8%, while central bank interest rates rise from 4% to 6%.'

--- QUESTIONS ---
  Q1(a) [8 marks]
    Question: Explain two advantages to VB of maintaining its current business legal structure as a private limited company during expansion.
    Answer: Advantage 1: Limited liability protects shareholders' personal assets if the $1,200,000 e-bike expansion project fails. Application: Investors only lose capital equity invested in the factory.
Advantage 2: Maintenance of operational control without risk of hostile takeover. Application: The original founders retain majority ownership while managing 40 production workers.
    Keywords: $1,200,000, 40 workers, carbon-fiber bicycles, e-bikes, 200 custom bicycles, batch production
    Mark scheme: knowledge_max_2: 1 mark for each valid advantage (max 2). | application_analysis_max_6: Up to 3 marks per point for applied contextual explanation.

  Q1(b) [12 marks]
    Question: Consider three growth strategies VB could use for the new commuter e-bike line: Internal growth (expanding existing factory), Horizontal integration (merging with a rival bike maker), or Joint Venture with a battery manufacturer. Which strategy should VB choose? Justify your recommendation.
    Answer: Internal growth allows VB to retain complete control over carbon-fiber quality standards, though building line capacity takes considerable time and requires financing the full $1,200,000 expenditure. Horizontal integration provides immediate access to established retail channels and manufacturing capacity, though integrating corporate cultures across 40 skilled workers creates conflict risks. A Joint Venture spreads investment risks and combines battery technology expertise directly with bike frame assembly, though profits must be shared. Recommendation: A Joint Venture is the best strategy because sharing the financial burden mitigates risk when entering the unfamiliar commuter e-bike market while accessing specialized battery tech.
    Keywords: $1,200,000, 40 workers, commuter e-bike, carbon-fiber, 200 custom bicycles
    Mark scheme: level_1_1_to_4: Identifies growth methods with general explanation. | level_2_5_to_8: Analyzes pros and cons of two or three growth options in context. | level_3_9_to_12: Detailed evaluation of all three growth strategies with a well-justified recommendation.

  Q2(a) [8 marks]
    Question: Explain two benefits to VB of providing off-the-job safety and technical training for its 40 production workers.
    Answer: Benefit 1: Reduces manufacturing defects during technical tasks. Application: Minimizes the 5% frame failure rate during carbon-fiber oven curing and manual painting.
Benefit 2: Improves worker motivation through skill development. Application: Encourages 40 skilled staff to operate high-tech automated machinery safely, boosting productivity.
    Keywords: 40 production workers, 5% frame failure, carbon-fiber, oven curing, 200 custom bicycles
    Mark scheme: knowledge_max_2: 1 mark per valid benefit (max 2). | application_analysis_max_6: Up to 3 marks for contextual explanation.

  Q2(b) [12 marks]
    Question: Consider the advantages and disadvantages of Batch Production versus Flow Production for VB's proposed commuter e-bike line. Which production method should VB adopt? Justify your answer.
    Answer: Batch production offers operational flexibility to modify frame geometry and color options for small groups, using existing factory space and skilled workers, but results in higher unit costs and substantial work-in-progress inventory. Flow production allows VB to achieve economies of scale, significantly lowering average unit costs through continuous automated assembly line output, but requires high setup capital ($1,200,000) and reduces customization flexibility. Recommendation: Flow production should be adopted for the commuter e-bike line because high-volume standardized production is necessary to capture mass market demand driven by government eco-subsidies.
    Keywords: $1,200,000, 200 custom bicycles, commuter e-bikes, 40 skilled workers, 5% failure rate
    Mark scheme: level_1_1_to_4: Outlines characteristics of batch and flow production. | level_2_5_to_8: Discusses advantages and disadvantages of both methods in business context. | level_3_9_to_12: Thorough comparative evaluation of production methods with a clear, justified choice.

  Q3(a) [8 marks]
    Question: 
    Answer: 
    Mark scheme: working_marks: 1 mark for correct formula/method, 1 mark for correct numerical answer ($300 and $240). 1 mark per valid management advantage.

  Q3(b) [12 marks]
    Question: Using Appendix 2, evaluate VB's liquidity position by calculating the current ratio and acid test ratio for 2024 and 2025. Do you think VB's financial health improved?
    Answer: Calculations: 2024 Current Ratio = ($300k + $200k + $100k) / ($150k + $50k) = $600k / $200k = 3.0:1. 2024 Acid Test Ratio = ($600k - $300k) / $200k = 1.5:1.
2025 Current Ratio = ($350k + $100k + $50k) / ($250k + $150k) = $500k / $400k = 1.25:1. 2025 Acid Test Ratio = ($500k - $350k) / $400k = $150k / $400k = 0.375:1.
Evaluation: Liquidity severely deteriorated in 2025. The current ratio fell from 3.0:1 to 1.25:1, while the acid test ratio dropped from a healthy 1.5:1 to 0.375:1. This decline is driven by cash reserves falling to $50k and bank overdrafts escalating to $150k alongside $350k tied up in inventory. Conclusion: VB's financial health did not improve; the business faces immediate liquidity risk and cannot cover short-term debts without selling bike inventory.
    Keywords: 3.0:1, 1.25:1, 1.5:1, 0.375:1, $150k overdraft, $350k inventory, $1,200,000
    Mark scheme: level_1_1_to_4: Identifies line item changes or incorrect ratio calculations. | level_2_5_to_8: Accurately calculates ratios for both years with contextual liquidity analysis. | level_3_9_to_12: Full ratio evaluation for both years with clear comparative analysis and a justified conclusion.

  Q4(a) [8 marks]
    Question: Explain one advantage and one disadvantage to VB of introducing Total Quality Management (TQM) in its bicycle factory.
    Answer: Advantage: Eliminates scrap costs by preventing defects during assembly. Application: Reduces the current 5% frame stress failure rate during carbon-fiber curing, saving raw material costs.
Disadvantage: High initial expenditure required for comprehensive employee training. Application: Training 40 skilled workers in TQM principles increases short-term overheads above $12,000 monthly.
    Keywords: 5% failure rate, carbon-fiber curing, 40 skilled workers, $12,000 monthly, 200 custom bicycles
    Mark scheme: knowledge_max_2: 1 mark for valid advantage, 1 mark for valid disadvantage. | application_analysis_max_6: Up to 3 marks per point for detailed context.

  Q4(b) [12 marks]
    Question: Using Appendix 3, evaluate how a $200 eco-subsidy on e-bikes, an 8% tariff on carbon-fiber imports, and an increase in interest rates to 6% will affect VB. Which change will have the greatest impact? Justify your choice.
    Answer: The $200 government eco-subsidy lowers the net price of commuter e-bikes for consumers, boosting sales volume and market demand. The 8% tariff on imported carbon fiber directly increases variable costs per bicycle frame above $240, squeezing gross profit margins. The interest rate increase from 4% to 6% raises annual finance charges on existing $600k long-term bank loans and elevates interest costs for securing $1,200,000 in expansion capital. Conclusion: The interest rate increase to 6% has the greatest impact because it simultaneously elevates borrowing expenses on existing debt and significantly increases the annual cost of financing the $1,200,000 capital expansion during liquidity constraint.
    Keywords: $200 eco-subsidy, 8% tariff, 4% to 6%, $600k bank loans, $1,200,000, $240 variable cost, carbon fiber
    Mark scheme: level_1_1_to_4: Briefly describes external factors without application. | level_2_5_to_8: Analyzes impact of two or three external changes on VB in context. | level_3_9_to_12: Detailed evaluation of all three factors in context with a well-justified selection of the greatest impact.

PAPER 2 — P2_SET_03
UNIT: Paper 2 Case Study
====================================================================================================

--- MAIN STEM ---
GreenGrocer Retail (GGR) is a public limited company operating a supermarket chain of 12 organic grocery stores. GGR specializes in selling locally sourced organic produce and pre-packaged meal hampers. To capitalize on e-commerce demand, GGR plans to launch a nationwide home-delivery service requiring an investment of $2,000,000 in temperature-controlled delivery vans and micro-fulfillment centers. Each retail store currently employs 25 store assistants under flat organizational structures. Monthly fixed costs per store average $40,000, with variable costs totaling $160,000 while processing 40,000 customer transactions. GGR faces fierce competition from discount supermarket chains and struggles with high food wastage rates, as 8% of fresh organic inventory spoils before sale.

--- APPENDIX 1 — MARKETING/OPS ---
Store Operations Extract: 'GreenGrocer Weekly Waste Log: Average inventory turnover: 5 days. Fresh produce shelf-life: 7 days. Monthly organic food waste across 12 stores totals 3,200 kg due to stock rotation inefficiencies.'

--- APPENDIX 2 — FINANCIAL DATA ---
Title: GreenGrocer Retail Plc - Financial Position Extract at 30 June ($ millions)
Headers: ['Financial Metric', '2024 ($m)', '2025 ($m)']
Inventory | 1.2 | 1.1
Trade Receivables | 0.5 | 0.4
Cash Balance | 0.3 | 0.3
Trade Payables | 0.6 | 0.8
Bank Overdraft | 0.2 | 0.4
Bank Loan (10-Year) | 1.5 | 2.2

--- APPENDIX 3 — EXTERNAL ENVIRONMENT ---
National Economic News (2025): 'Government enacts stricter waste management regulations, imposing a $100 per ton fine on commercial food waste. Concurrently, inflation falls to 2%, while national minimum wage rates increase by 6% across retail sectors.'

--- QUESTIONS ---
  Q1(a) [8 marks]
    Question: Explain one advantage and one disadvantage to GGR of being a public limited company.
    Answer: Advantage: Ability to raise substantial capital by issuing new shares on the stock exchange. Application: Facilitates securing $2,000,000 needed to fund delivery vans and micro-fulfillment hubs.
Disadvantage: Risk of hostile takeover as shares can be purchased freely by competitors. Application: Rivals could acquire controlling stakes across the 12 organic grocery store chain.
    Keywords: 12 organic grocery stores, $2,000,000, delivery vans, 25 store assistants, 40,000 transactions
    Mark scheme: knowledge_max_2: 1 mark per valid advantage/disadvantage (max 2). | application_analysis_max_6: Up to 3 marks per point for context-applied explanation.

  Q1(b) [12 marks]
    Question: Consider three extension strategies GGR could use to increase sales of organic meal hampers: Entering new geographic markets, Adapting hamper contents for budget consumers, or Increasing promotional advertising. Which strategy should GGR choose? Justify your recommendation.
    Answer: Entering new geographic markets expands GGR's customer base into untapped suburban regions, maximizing revenue potential from home-delivery van investments, though distribution setup costs are substantial. Adapting hamper contents for budget consumers appeals to price-sensitive shoppers facing inflation, though it risks diluting GGR's premium organic brand image. Increasing promotional advertising creates immediate awareness across social channels, boosting store visits, though advertising costs erode operating margins. Recommendation: Launching into new geographic markets via home delivery is the best strategy because it directly leverages the $2,000,000 infrastructure investment while safeguarding premium brand reputation.
    Keywords: 12 organic grocery stores, $2,000,000, organic meal hampers, delivery vans, 40,000 transactions
    Mark scheme: level_1_1_to_4: Outlines marketing extension strategies simply. | level_2_5_to_8: Analyzes benefits and drawbacks of two or three strategies in context. | level_3_9_to_12: Thorough evaluation of all three strategies with a fully justified recommendation.

  Q2(a) [8 marks]
    Question: Explain two benefits to GGR of operating a flat organizational structure with a wide span of control in each of its 12 stores.
    Answer: Benefit 1: Speeds up communication and decision-making between management and store floor. Application: Allows 25 store assistants to quickly report inventory shelf-life issues and stock rotation needs.
Benefit 2: Encourages delegation and staff empowerment. Application: Gives retail assistants authority to discount near-expiry organic produce, boosting job satisfaction under Maslow's esteem needs.
    Keywords: 12 stores, 25 store assistants, organic produce, flat organizational structure, stock rotation
    Mark scheme: knowledge_max_2: 1 mark per benefit identified (max 2). | application_analysis_max_6: Up to 3 marks per point for detailed context.

  Q2(b) [12 marks]
    Question: Consider the following two recruitment methods for hiring delivery drivers for the new home-delivery service: Internal recruitment from existing store staff, or External recruitment via online job agencies. Which method should GGR select? Justify your decision.
    Answer: Internal recruitment redeploys existing store assistants who are already familiar with organic product ranges and corporate culture, reducing recruitment costs and providing promotion opportunities that motivate staff, though it creates staff vacancies across the 12 retail stores. External recruitment through online agencies attracts experienced commercial delivery drivers with valid licenses and route knowledge, though agency placement fees elevate recruitment expenses. Recommendation: External recruitment should be selected because hiring drivers with established route experience and commercial licensing is critical for fleet safety and logistics efficiency.
    Keywords: 12 retail stores, 25 store assistants, delivery drivers, organic produce, $2,000,000
    Mark scheme: level_1_1_to_4: Basic identification of recruitment types. | level_2_5_to_8: Detailed examination of pros and cons of internal vs external recruitment in context. | level_3_9_to_12: Comprehensive evaluation of both recruitment sources leading to a well-supported recommendation.

  Q3(a) [8 marks]
    Question: 
    Answer: 
    Mark scheme: working_marks: 1 mark for correct method, 1 mark for correct final output ($5.00 and $4.00). 1 mark per valid managerial application.

  Q3(b) [12 marks]
    Question: Using Appendix 2, evaluate GGR's financial position by calculating the current ratio and acid test ratio for 2024 and 2025. Has GGR's financial position improved?
    Answer: Calculations: 2024 Current Ratio = ($1.2m + $0.5m + $0.3m) / ($0.6m + $0.2m) = $2.0m / $0.8m = 2.5:1. 2024 Acid Test Ratio = ($2.0m - $1.2m) / $0.8m = 1.0:1.
2025 Current Ratio = ($1.1m + $0.4m + $0.3m) / ($0.8m + $0.4m) = $1.8m / $1.2m = 1.5:1. 2025 Acid Test Ratio = ($1.8m - $1.1m) / $1.2m = 0.58:1.
Evaluation: GGR's liquidity worsened significantly in 2025. The current ratio dropped from 2.5:1 to 1.5:1, while the acid test ratio declined from 1.0:1 to 0.58:1 due to doubling bank overdrafts to $0.4m and expanding trade payables to $0.8m. Holding $1.1m in perishable inventory exposes GGR to severe liquidity strain if stock spoils.   Q4(a) [8 marks]
    Question: Explain one advantage and one disadvantage to GGR of adopting Just-In-Time (JIT) inventory control for its organic produce.
    Answer: Advantage: Minimizes inventory holding costs and food spoilage. Application: Reduces monthly organic food waste below 3,200 kg across the 12 stores, lowering storage expenses.
Disadvantage: High risk of stockouts if local farmers experience crop delays. Application: Empty produce shelves result in lost sales transactions and dissatisfied retail customers.
    Keywords: 3,200 kg waste, 12 stores, organic produce, stockouts, 40,000 transactions
    Mark scheme: knowledge_max_2: 1 mark per valid advantage/disadvantage (max 2). | application_analysis_max_6: Up to 3 marks per point for applied explanation.

  Q4(b) [12 marks]
    Question: Using Appendix 3, evaluate how a $100 per ton food waste fine, 2% inflation, and a 6% minimum wage increase will affect GGR. Which change will have the greatest impact? Justify your recommendation.
    Answer: The $100 per ton food waste fine directly increases operating expenses unless GGR cuts its 3,200 kg monthly organic waste. Inflation at 2% stabilizes raw food procurement costs, allowing stable retail pricing on meal hampers. A 6% minimum wage increase significantly inflates wage expenses across 300 store assistants (25 staff x 12 stores), increasing monthly variable costs above $160,000 per store. Conclusion: The 6% minimum wage increase will have the greatest impact because labor costs form a massive proportion of store operating expenses across 300 employees, creating a permanent financial burden compared to avoidable waste fines.
    Keywords: $100 per ton, 3,200 kg waste, 6% wage increase, 300 store assistants, $160,000 variable costs, 12 stores
    Mark scheme: level_1_1_to_4: Outlines macroeconomic changes with limited application. | level_2_5_to_8: Analyzes the business impact of two or three external changes in context. | level_3_9_to_12: Comprehensive evaluation of all three factors in context with a well-reasoned judgment on greatest impact.

PAPER 2 — P2_SET_04
UNIT: Paper 2 Case Study
====================================================================================================

--- MAIN STEM ---
Pulse Electronics (PE) is a private limited company manufacturing consumer audio equipment, primarily wireless noise-canceling earbuds. PE operates one main assembly factory employing 150 production line workers under flow production. To expand into overseas markets, PE plans to build a second assembly facility costing $5,000,000. Managing Director Alex is evaluating two potential factory locations: Site A (an industrial park with high government grants) and Site B (a port-adjacent site with lower logistics costs). Monthly fixed factory costs currently total $50,000, with variable costs reaching $150,000 while producing 10,000 earbud units. PE experiences high staff turnover due to repetitive assembly tasks and autocratic supervision, prompting HR to consider introducing financial bonuses or job rotation.

--- APPENDIX 1 — MARKETING/OPS ---
Product Range Extract: 'Pulse Pro Earbuds: Bluetooth 5.3, active noise cancellation, 30-hour battery life. Unit selling price: $40. Current monthly factory output: 10,000 units. Reject rate at final acoustic testing: 4%.'

--- APPENDIX 2 — FINANCIAL DATA ---
Title: Pulse Electronics Ltd - Statement of Financial Position Extract as at 31 December ($ millions)
Headers: ['Financial Metric', '2024 ($m)', '2025 ($m)']
Inventory | 2.0 | 2.2
Trade Receivables | 1.5 | 1.0
Cash Balance | 0.5 | 0.4

--- MAIN STEM ---
Urban Mobility Dynamics (UMD) is a private limited company that manufactures heavy-duty electric cargo bikes for urban courier fleets. UMD operates one assembly factory employing 40 skilled bike mechanics and welders. Management plans to expand into commercial electric municipal street sweepers, requiring an investment of $2,400,000 in robotic steel chassis welding and high-voltage lithium battery installation equipment. Managing Director Uriah is evaluating whether to finance this expansion via venture capital investment or a 10-year bank loan. Under batch production, UMD's monthly operations generate fixed overheads of $70,000 and total variable costs of $210,000 while producing 35 electric cargo vehicles. UMD faces quality challenges, as 4% of sweepers fail automated brake torque testing, requiring manual caliper alignment.

--- APPENDIX 1 — MARKETING/OPS ---
Factory Operations Summary: 'UMD Output Summary: Frame welding (15 hours); Battery pack fitting (10 hours); Brake & safety testing (5 hours). Monthly output: 35 units. Selling price: $10,000 per sweeper. Brake defect rate: 4% (1 boat/sweeper every 2.5 months).'

--- APPENDIX 2 — FINANCIAL DATA ---
Title: Urban Mobility Dynamics Ltd - Statement of Financial Position Extract at 31 December ($ millions)
Headers: ['Financial Metric', '2024 ($m)', '2025 ($m)']
Inventory | 1.6 | 1.8
Trade Receivables | 1.0 | 0.6
Cash & Bank Balances | 0.3 | 0.1
Trade Payables | 0.7 | 1.2
Bank Overdraft | 0.3 | 0.7
Long-Term Loan Debt | 1.5 | 2.6

--- APPENDIX 3 — EXTERNAL ENVIRONMENT ---
Municipal Transit Gazette (2025): 'Government enacts a 20% clean fleet grant for municipalities purchasing electric maintenance vehicles. Concurrently, import tariffs on foreign lithium battery cells increase by 8%, while central bank interest rates fall from 6% to 4%.'

--- QUESTIONS ---
  Q1(a) [8 marks]
    Question: Explain two advantages to UMD of securing venture capital to finance its $2,400,000 electric street sweeper expansion.
    Answer: Advantage 1: Venture capital involves equity funding without mandatory monthly interest repayments. Application: Avoids inflating UMD's monthly fixed overheads above $70,000.
Advantage 2: Venture capitalists bring commercial connections with municipal transport authorities. Application: Assists UMD in securing municipal procurement tenders for electric street sweepers.
    Keywords: $2,400,000 expansion, electric street sweepers, venture capital, $70,000 fixed costs, 35 electric cargo
    Mark scheme: knowledge_max_2: 1 mark per valid advantage (max 2). | application_analysis_max_6: Up to 3 marks per point for contextual explanation.

  Q1(b) [12 marks]
    Question: Consider three growth strategies UMD could use for its electric sweepers: Market penetration with municipal city councils, Product development of autonomous robotic sweepers, or Joint Venture with a municipal vehicle manufacturer. Which strategy should UMD choose? Justify your recommendation.
    Answer: Market penetration leverages established sales channels with municipal councils, capturing fleet electrification tenders, though public tender cycles are long. Product development of autonomous robotic sweepers creates an advanced driverless sweeper commanding prices above $10,000, though software development costs are high. A Joint Venture with a municipal vehicle maker combines chassis assembly with established municipal sales networks, sharing $2,400,000 expansion risks, though profits must be shared. Recommendation: A Joint Venture is best because sharing financial risks and accessing established municipal tender networks is vital when launching commercial street sweepers.
    Keywords: electric street sweepers, municipal vehicle maker, $2,400,000, $10,000 price, municipal councils
    Mark scheme: level_1_1_to_4: Outlines growth strategies simply. | level_2_5_to_8: Analyzes pros and cons of two or three growth options in context. | level_3_9_to_12: Comprehensive evaluation of all three strategies leading to a well-supported recommendation.

  Q2(a) [8 marks]
    Question: Explain two benefits to UMD's mechanics and welders of being represented by a trade union.
    Answer: Benefit 1: Collective bargaining power for improved hourly pay rates. Application: Negotiates fair wage increases for 40 mechanics and welders operating heavy chassis cutters and battery fitting tools.
Benefit 2: Health and safety enforcement in heavy vehicle manufacturing. Application: Ensures strict safety standards around robotic welding cells, high-voltage battery assembly, and heavy lifting gear.
    Keywords: 40 mechanics, welders, robotic welding, electric sweepers
    Mark scheme: knowledge_max_2: 1 mark per valid benefit (max 2). | application_analysis_max_6: Up to 3 marks per point for contextual explanation.

  Q2(b) [12 marks]
    Question: Consider whether UMD should implement Total Quality Management (TQM) or rely on end-of-line Quality Control to solve its 4% brake flaw issue. Which quality system should UMD select? Justify your decision.
    Answer: Quality Control relies on brake torque testers identifying defective calipers after assembly, requiring manual alignment and re-testing before delivery, but fails to prevent labor rework waste and delays vehicle delivery schedules. TQM instills quality responsibility across all 40 mechanics, optimizing brake caliper fitting and torque calibration during assembly, eliminating expensive rework waste and lowering unit costs ($8,000), though comprehensive staff training expenses occur. Recommendation: TQM is superior because stopping brake flaws during assembly eliminates costly mechanical rework and delivery delays on municipal vehicle tenders.
    Keywords: 4% brake flaw, 40 mechanics, brake testing, re-testing, $8,000 unit cost, electric sweepers
    Mark scheme: level_1_1_to_4: Defines quality control and TQM simply. | level_2_5_to_8: Analyzes advantages and disadvantages of both quality systems in context. | level_3_9_to_12: Comprehensive evaluation of both quality systems leading to a well-supported choice.

    Mark scheme: working_marks: 1 mark for correct method, 1 mark for correct numerical result ($8,000.00 and $6,000.00). 1 mark per valid management application.

  Q3(b) [12 marks]
    Question: Using Appendix 2, evaluate UMD's liquidity position by calculating the current ratio and acid test ratio for 2024 and 2025. Has UMD's financial position improved?
    Answer: Calculations: 2024 Current Ratio = ($1.6m + $1.0m + $0.3m) / ($0.7m + $0.3m) = $2.9m / $1.0m = 2.9:1. 2024 Acid Test Ratio = ($2.9m - $1.6m) / $1.0m = 1.3:1.
2025 Current Ratio = ($1.8m + $0.6m + $0.1m) / ($1.2m + $0.7m) = $2.5m / $1.9m = 1.32:1. 2025 Acid Test Ratio = ($2.5m - $1.8m) / $1.9m = 0.37:1.
Evaluation: UMD's liquidity position deteriorated significantly in 2025. The current ratio dropped from 2.9:1 to 1.32:1, while the acid test ratio plunged from 1.3:1 to an illiquid 0.37:1 due to bank overdrafts expanding to $0.7m and trade payables rising to $1.2m alongside $2.6m in long-term debt. UMD holds $1.8m tied up in inventory relative to $0.1m cash. Conclusion: Financial position did not improve; severe liquidity constraints restrict UMD's capacity to self-fund the $2,400,000 expansion.
    Keywords: 2.9:1, 1.32:1, 1.3:1, 0.37:1, $0.7m overdraft, $1.8m inventory, $2,400,000
    Mark scheme: level_1_1_to_4: Describes balance sheet line items without accurate ratio calculations. | level_2_5_to_8: Accurately calculates liquidity ratios for both years with contextual analysis. | level_3_9_to_12: Detailed evaluation of liquidity trends across both years with a supported conclusion.

  Q4(a) [8 marks]
    Question: Explain one advantage and one disadvantage to UMD of utilizing Computer-Aided Manufacturing (CAM) robotic welding in chassis assembly.
    Answer: Advantage: Delivers consistent structural weld integrity for heavy vehicle frames. Application: Lowers chassis stress failures and improves mechanical reliability on electric sweepers.
Disadvantage: High initial setup costs and specialized robotic programmer maintenance outlays. Application: Requires $2,400,000 capital outlay and technical training for 40 mechanics.
    Keywords: CAM robotic welding, chassis assembly, 40 mechanics, $2,400,000, electric sweepers
    Mark scheme: knowledge_max_2: 1 mark per valid advantage/disadvantage (max 2). | application_analysis_max_6: Up to 3 marks per point for contextual explanation.

  Q4(b) [12 marks]
    Question: Using Appendix 3, evaluate how a 20% clean fleet grant, an 8% lithium battery tariff, and an interest rate drop to 4.0% will affect UMD. Which change will have the greatest impact? Justify your choice.
    Answer: A 20% clean fleet grant lowers net acquisition costs for municipal city councils purchasing electric maintenance vehicles, driving high tender demand for UMD's sweepers. An 8% tariff on imported lithium battery cells directly increases battery pack procurement costs, elevating variable costs above $6,000.00 per vehicle. Interest rates falling from 6% to 4.0% lowers borrowing costs on existing $2.6m bank debt and significantly reduces annual interest expenses for securing an expansion loan. Conclusion: The 20% clean fleet grant will have the greatest impact because government funding directly stimulates municipal procurement of zero-emission utility vehicles, driving tender sales volume.
    Keywords: 20% clean fleet grant, 8% lithium tariff, 6% to 4.0%, $2.6m bank debt, $2,400,000 expansion, lithium battery cells, $6,000.00 variable cost
    Mark scheme: level_1_1_to_4: Outlines external factors simply. | level_2_5_to_8: Analyzes the business impact of two or three external changes in context. | level_3_9_to_12: Comprehensive evaluation of all three factors in context with a well-reasoned judgment on greatest impact.

Under batch production, CAS's monthly operations generate fixed overheads of $36,000 and total variable costs of $108,000 while producing 900 filtration units. CAS faces quality challenges, as 3% of purifiers fail cleanroom particle leakage testing, requiring manual filter resealing.

BSP faces quality challenges, as 4% of film rolls fail tensile strength integrity testing, incurring raw resin scrap losses.

--- MAIN STEM ---
QuantumTech Energy (QTE) is a private limited company that manufactures commercial redox flow batteries for grid energy storage. QTE operates one main manufacturing plant employing 50 chemical and electrical engineers. Management plans to expand into modular residential flow batteries, requiring an investment of $2,200,000 in automated electrolyte tank molding and membrane assembly machinery. Managing Director Quentin is evaluating whether to finance this expansion via venture capital investment or securing a 5-year bank loan. Under batch production, QTE's monthly operations generate fixed overheads of $60,000 and total variable costs of $180,000 while producing 600 flow battery units. QTE faces quality challenges, as 3% of battery units fail membrane leak pressure testing, requiring manual cell re-sealing.

--- APPENDIX 1 — MARKETING/OPS ---
Factory Operations Log: 'QTE Flow Battery Log: Electrolyte cell molding (3 hours); Membrane stack assembly (4 hours); Leak pressure testing (2 hours). Monthly output: 600 units. Wholesale price: $500 per unit. Membrane leak defect rate: 3% (18 units/month).'

--- APPENDIX 2 — FINANCIAL DATA ---
Title: QuantumTech Energy Ltd - Statement of Financial Position Extract at 31 December ($ millions)
Headers: ['Financial Metric', '2024 ($m)', '2025 ($m)']

Trade Receivables | 0.9 | 0.5
Cash & Bank Balances | 0.3 | 0.2
Trade Payables | 0.6 | 1.1
Bank Overdraft | 0.2 | 0.6
Long-Term Bank Loan | 1.4 | 2.5

--- APPENDIX 3 — EXTERNAL ENVIRONMENT ---
Energy Gazette (2025): 'Government enacts a 15% clean energy equipment grant for residential battery installations. Concurrently, import tariffs on foreign vanadium electrolyte materials increase by 7%, while central bank interest rates fall from 5.5% to 4.0%.'

--- QUESTIONS ---

Management plans to expand into heavy-payload industrial cobots, requiring an investment of $2,250,000 in harmonic drive machining centers and automated torque calibration rigs. Managing Director Peter is evaluating whether to finance this project by issuing new private shares to existing shareholders or securing a 5-year bank loan. Under batch production, PRT's monthly operations generate fixed overheads of $60,000 and total variable costs of $180,000 while producing 300 cobot units. PRT faces quality challenges, as 4% of cobots fail joint torque repeatability testing, requiring manual gear disassembly.

--- APPENDIX 1 — MARKETING/OPS ---
Factory Output Log: 'PRT Output Log: Arm casting machining (4 hours); Harmonic drive fitment (4 hours); Torque calibration testing (2 hours). Monthly output: 300 units. Selling price: $1,200 per cobot. Defect rate: 4% (12 units/month).'

Advantage 2: Permanent equity capital that does not increase debt gearing. Application: Provides long-term funding for harmonic drive machining equipment without elevating bank loan liabilities.

PAPER 2 — P2_SET_101
UNIT: Paper 2 Case Study

--- MAIN STEM ---
Amberhill Artisan Bakery (AAB) is a private limited company in the artisan bakery sector, employing a workforce of 38. Founded in 2011 by Leila Haddad, it supplies sourdough, wholegrain loaves and pastries to supermarket chains and independent cafes along the coast, operating a flat organisational structure with democratic leadership. AAB plans to invest $620,000 in a central production kitchen with an online pre-order platform, financed by a $400,000 ten-year bank loan and $220,000 retained profit. It has fixed costs of $225,000 a year, a variable cost of $4.40 a unit and a selling price of $8.00, and currently produces 100,000 units a year. AAB faces rising unsold-stock waste, now 7% of daily output, and absenteeism has climbed to 8%.

--- APPENDIX 1 — MARKETING/OPS ---
Operations and Waste Report — Q3 2026: The central bakery produced 24,800 units last quarter at a mis-bake defect rate of 2.6%, down from 4.1% a year ago. Unsold-stock waste fell from 11% to 7% of daily output, while customer complaints fell from 26 to 15 per month. A survey of 400 in-store customers found 58% would pre-order via a mobile app and 46% buy sourdough every week. Average delivery time to branch stores is 2.1 days. Off-the-job hygiene certification at the technical college costs $700 per employee; 18 of 38 staff need recertification, while on-the-job coaching on the new convection ovens continues.

--- APPENDIX 2 — FINANCIAL DATA ---
Title: Extract from the Statement of Financial Position of Amberhill Artisan Bakery as at 31 March 2025 ($ '000)
Headers: ['Financial Metric', '2024', '2025']
Inventories | 85 | 70
Trade receivables | 60 | 75
Cash and cash equivalents | 30 | 55
Current liabilities | 125 | 110
Non-current assets | 1,150 | 1,600
Capital employed | 1,750 | 1,950

--- APPENDIX 3 — EXTERNAL ENVIRONMENT ---
Economic and Business Bulletin (November 2026): (1) The central bank has raised the base interest rate from 4.5% to 5.25%, its third rise this year, increasing borrowing costs for businesses with variable-rate loans. (2) The national minimum wage will rise by 7.1% from $11.90 to $12.74 per hour from April 2026, increasing total wage bills. (3) Wheat flour and butter input costs have risen 9.6% year-on-year, food-price inflation is running at 7.2%, while consumer spending on premium bakery products grew 2.8% in the same period.

--- QUESTIONS ---
  Q1(a) [8 marks]
    Question: AAB plans to fund part of its central production kitchen with a ten-year bank loan. Explain two advantages for AAB of using retained profit to fund the expansion instead of the bank loan.
    Answer: Point 1: Retained profit costs AAB nothing in interest or repayments, protecting cash flow while the business already carries fixed costs of $225,000 a year and services a $400,000 bank loan. Every dollar not paid as financing cost can absorb the 9.6% rise in flour and butter input costs, keeping the $8.00 sourdough affordable for supermarket buyers and defending AAB's $3.60 contribution per unit at a time when margins are already being squeezed across the bakery sector.

Point 2: Retained profit avoids the collateral and default risk attached to the bank loan, so the $620,000 central kitchen and online pre-order platform are not at risk of repossession if pre-order demand from the 58% of surveyed app-users disappoints. It also keeps ownership with Leila Haddad and her family, so no lender can impose conditions on how the kitchen is run or on future price rises, and AAB keeps full flexibility to reinvest profits into further capacity once the online range proves itself.
    Keywords: retained profit, bank loan, $220,000, $400,000, $620,000, $225,000
    Mark scheme: knowledge_max_2: 1 mark for each valid advantage identified (max 2). | application_analysis_max_6: Up to 3 marks per point for detailed contextual analysis linked to AAB's expansion, costs and ownership.

  Q1(b) [12 marks]
    Question: AAB is launching its online pre-order sourdough range to supermarket customers. Consider print advertising in supermarket magazines, local radio sponsorship, or social media influencer marketing. Which should AAB choose to promote the launch? Justify your recommendation.
    Answer: Print advertising in supermarket magazines: Supermarket magazine ads appear exactly where AAB's target shoppers decide what to buy and can carry the eco-hygiene story of the new kitchen. However, print has long lead times, declining circulation, limited interactivity and no way to drive immediate pre-orders on the new app, so its cost per pre-order is likely to be high for a business investing $620,000 and producing 100,000 units a year.

Local radio sponsorship: Local radio is affordable, suits time-sensitive launch messages and reaches the coast-wide catchment where AAB already delivers in 2.1 days. Its reach is limited to one region, however, while AAB supplies supermarket chains beyond that catchment, and radio cannot show the sourdough itself or capture the 58% of surveyed shoppers who said they would pre-order via a mobile app.

Social media influencer marketing: Food and family-lifestyle influencers can show AAB's sourdough being baked, sliced and pre-ordered, targeted precisely at the 58% of the 400 surveyed customers willing to use the app and the 46% who buy sourdough weekly. Cost per reached shopper is low, results are measurable in clicks and pre-orders, and national supermarket listings can be supported at scale. Drawbacks are influencer credibility risk, slower compounding reach than broadcast media, and dependence on platform algorithms.

Recommendation: AAB should choose social media influencer marketing. It targets the exact segment identified in its own research, reinforces the pre-order platform, scales nationally and fits a $620,000 investment with a ten-year bank loan. Print advertising is rejected as too slow, too passive and too weak at driving app pre-orders, and local radio is rejected as too narrow for supermarket chains beyond the coast; AAB should add modest in-store tasting sessions in partner supermarkets to support the influencer campaign.
    Keywords: sourdough, supermarket, 58%, 46%, $620,000, 100,000
    Mark scheme: level_1_1_to_4: Limited knowledge or outline of the promotional options with minimal context. | level_2_5_to_8: Detailed discussion of the advantages and disadvantages of at least two options in the context of AAB with some judgement. | level_3_9_to_12: Detailed discussion of all three options in the context of AAB with a well-justified recommendation explaining why print advertising and local radio are rejected.

  Q2(a) [8 marks]
    Question: AAB's absenteeism has reached 8% and unsold-stock waste is still high. Explain two benefits for AAB of using democratic leadership to improve motivation in its bakery teams.
    Answer: Point 1: Democratic leadership gives AAB's 38 staff a genuine voice in rota planning, bake schedules and waste reduction, which satisfies esteem and social needs on Maslow's hierarchy and raises job satisfaction. Workers who help decide oven loading and delivery timetables are more likely to attend reliably, directly attacking the 8% absenteeism rate and reducing the disruption it causes to the 2.1-day branch delivery promise and the 100,000-unit output plan.

Point 2: Involving the bakers in decisions surfaces practical ideas from the people who handle dough and convection ovens daily, improving first-time bake quality and pushing the 2.6% mis-bake defect rate down further. Higher involvement raises commitment and lowers labour turnover, saving the $700 per employee off-the-job hygiene recertification cost at the technical college and protecting consistency for the 400 surveyed customers, 46% of whom buy sourdough weekly and expect reliable availability. Used together, these benefits give AAB the attendance reliability and the quality ownership it needs to hold the 100,000-unit plan while absenteeism sits at 8% and branch delivery stays at 2.1 days.
    Keywords: democratic leadership, absenteeism, workforce of 38, $700, 2.6%, 100,000
    Mark scheme: knowledge_max_2: 1 mark for each valid benefit identified (max 2). | application_analysis_max_6: Up to 3 marks per point for detailed contextual analysis linked to AAB's absenteeism, waste and quality.

  Q2(b) [12 marks]
    Question: AAB must upskill 18 production staff on the new convection ovens before the central kitchen opens. Consider on-the-job training or off-the-job training at the technical college. Which should AAB choose? Justify your decision.
    Answer: On-the-job training: Training on AAB's own convection ovens is directly relevant to the exact machines, bake programmes and quality standards used in the new kitchen, costs nothing in course fees and keeps the 18 staff productive during the run-up to launch, protecting the 2.1-day branch delivery promise and daily output. The course certificates hygiene only; it does not cover convection-oven operation, which the insert assigns to on-the-job coaching, so machine-specific coaching would still be required. However, the course removes 18 of 38 staff from the line during training weeks, cutting short-term capacity and risking delivery failures just before launch.

Decision: AAB should choose on-the-job training for the six weeks before the kitchen opens, adding short college sessions for the two lead bakers. On-the-job training is cheapest, machine-specific and avoids further strain while absenteeism is at 8%, and loss of capacity would be unacceptable just before launch. Full off-the-job training is rejected as too disruptive and too generic for the pre-launch period; AAB can add college visits later once the line stabilises, and will still need the $700 per employee hygiene recertification for all 18 staff to satisfy auditors. Keeping training in-house through the launch also lets the two lead bakers coach the rest, freeing the technical college budget for the remaining certification outside peak production.

  Q3(b) [12 marks]
    Question: Using Appendix 2, evaluate AAB's financial position by calculating the current ratio and the acid test ratio for 2024 and 2025. Has AAB's financial position improved? Which of the two ratios gives the stronger evidence, and why? Justify your answer.
    Answer: Calculations:
Current Ratio 2024 = 1.40 : 1
Current Ratio 2025 = 1.82 : 1
Acid Test Ratio 2024 = 0.72 : 1
Acid Test Ratio 2025 = 1.18 : 1

Detailed workings: 2024 current assets = $85,000 inventories + $60,000 trade receivables + $30,000 cash = $175,000; 2025 current assets = $70,000 + $75,000 + $55,000 = $200,000. CR 2024 = $175,000 ÷ $125,000 current liabilities = 1.40; CR 2025 = $200,000 ÷ $110,000 = 1.82. AT 2024 = ($175,000 − $85,000) ÷ $125,000 = $90,000 ÷ $125,000 = 0.72; AT 2025 = ($200,000 − $70,000) ÷ $110,000 = $130,000 ÷ $110,000 = 1.18.

Evaluation: Liquidity has clearly strengthened. Current assets rose from $175,000 to $200,000 while current liabilities fell from $125,000 to $110,000, so short-term coverage improved on both measures. The AT line, which excludes inventories, rose from 0.72 to 1.18, meaning AAB no longer depends on selling perishable stock to pay its immediate debts — vital while it services a $400,000 ten-year bank loan and builds the $620,000 central kitchen. Cash nearly doubled from $30,000 to $55,000 and inventories were cut from $85,000 to $70,000, showing tighter stock rotation of fresh sourdough. Which ratio gives the stronger evidence? The acid test is the stronger indicator of AAB's short-term solvency because it excludes inventories — perishable fresh bread that may need discounting or write-off to realise cash — and it rose from 0.72 to 1.18, confirming that the stronger liquidity rests on cash and receivables rather than on stock build-up. Two concerns remain: trade receivables climbed from $60,000 to $75,000, tying up cash that could fund the kitchen, and the inventory reduction must not undershoot fresh-bread demand from the 46% of weekly sourdough buyers.

Conclusion: AAB's financial position has improved. Both the CR (1.40 to 1.82) and the AT (0.72 to 1.18) show stronger short-term solvency, and the improvement does not depend on inventory. The main residual risk is the $75,000 of trade receivables, so AAB should tighten credit control with its supermarket customers while proceeding with the expansion.

  Q4(b) [12 marks]
    Question: Using Appendix 3, evaluate how the rise in the base interest rate to 5.25%, the 7.1% minimum wage increase and the 9.6% rise in flour and butter input costs will affect AAB. Which change will have the greatest impact? Justify your answer.
    Answer: Interest rate rise (4.5% to 5.25%): If AAB's $400,000 ten-year bank loan is variable-rate, the 0.75% rise adds about $3,000 a year to financing costs and raises the effective burden on top of the $225,000 fixed costs. Higher rates also make consumers more cautious about premium bakery products, which could slow the 2.8% growth in premium bakery spending, and raise the cost of any future borrowing for the $620,000 kitchen. The direct cost impact is modest, and AAB can partly shield itself by fixing the loan rate or negotiating with its bank.

Minimum wage increase (7.1%, to $12.74 per hour): The insert gives a 7.1% rise from $11.90 to $12.74 — a derived delta of $0.84 per hour ($12.74 − $11.90; check: 7.1% × $11.90 ≈ $0.84). Roles anchored to the floor become more expensive from April 2026, and pay bands above the floor typically shift as well. The insert does not state hours worked per worker, so the annual cash impact cannot be computed precisely; however, with 38 wage-dependent posts in a business producing 100,000 units a year, every hour worked becomes more expensive, so the annual impact would be material and democratic leadership and productivity gains (100,000 units ÷ 38 staff ≈ 2,632 units per worker) would need to offset it through lower absenteeism and waste.

Input cost inflation (9.6% flour and butter): The insert gives a $4.40 variable cost per unit and a 9.6% year-on-year rise in flour and butter input costs. Taking the entire variable cost as an upper bound: 9.6% × $4.40 = about $0.42 per unit; at 100,000 units a year that is roughly $42,000 a year (100,000 × $0.42, derivation shown; an upper bound since not all of the $4.40 is flour and butter). Even a fraction of that bound would directly erode the $3.60 contribution per unit and squeeze the margin that justifies the $620,000 expansion, though AAB can partially recover through the premium sourdough positioning and supermarket price talks, since consumer spending on premium bakery products still grew 2.8%.

Conclusion: The minimum wage increase will have the greatest impact on AAB overall. The insert gives no cap on the hours affected, so a $0.84-an-hour rise applies mechanically to every working hour across the 38-strong workforce, directly threatening the $620,000 expansion business case, while the 9.6% input-cost rise is bounded at roughly $42,000 a year (an upper bound) against which premium positioning and supermarket price talks offer some cover, and the interest-rate rise is the smallest risk at about $3,000 a year and can be fixed or hedged. AAB should therefore plan its April 2026 pay bands and productivity drive carefully, while managing input inflation daily through pricing and protecting cash for the pre-order launch.
    Keywords: 5.25%, 7.1%, 9.6%, $12.74, $11.90, 2.8%
    Mark scheme: level_1_1_to_4: Identifies the external factors with limited application to AAB. | level_2_5_to_8: Analyses the impact of at least two external changes on AAB's costs, revenue or financing in context. | level_3_9_to_12: Detailed evaluation of all three external changes in the context of AAB with a well-justified judgement that the minimum wage increase has the greatest impact and why the other two are smaller.

UNIT: Paper 2 Case Study

--- MAIN STEM ---
Greenvale Dairy Cooperative (GDC) is a cooperative in the dairy processing sector, employing a workforce of 120. Founded in 1998 by the Greenvale valley farmers' group and led by chairperson Rosa Delgado, it supplies cheese and fresh milk to regional supermarket chains across the valley, using a hierarchical structure with autocratic plant management. GDC plans to invest $1,400,000 in a new automated cheese-packing and cold-storage facility, financed by an $800,000 member share issue and a $600,000 bank loan. It has fixed costs of $420,000 a year, a variable cost of $7.70 a unit and a selling price of $14.70, and currently produces 150,000 units a year. GDC suffers repeated cold-chain failures and rising labour turnover on the packing floor.

--- APPENDIX 1 — MARKETING/OPS ---
Quality and Cold-chain Report — October 2026: The packing plant processed 37,500 units last quarter at a defect rate of 2.1%, down from 3.4% a year ago. Cold-chain failures caused 14 rejected consignments this year, down from 29 in 2025, and customer complaints fell from 33 to 19 per month. A survey of 150 farmer-members found 72% support the automated packing expansion and 55% want investment in renewable-energy solar panels. Average delivery time to regional distributors is 4.5 days. Off-the-job cold-chain certification at the food institute costs $850 per employee; 26 of 120 staff lack up-to-date certification, while on-the-job coaching on the new packers continues.

--- APPENDIX 2 — FINANCIAL DATA ---
Title: Extract from the Statement of Financial Position of Greenvale Dairy Cooperative as at 31 March 2025 ($ '000)

Trade receivables | 210 | 240
Cash and cash equivalents | 70 | 40
Current liabilities | 380 | 430
Non-current assets | 2,900 | 4,100
Capital employed | 3,600 | 4,400

--- APPENDIX 3 — EXTERNAL ENVIRONMENT ---
Economic and Business Bulletin (November 2026): (1) The central bank has raised the base interest rate from 4.0% to 4.75%, raising borrowing costs for businesses with variable-rate loans. (2) The national minimum wage will rise by 6.0% from $12.10 to $12.83 per hour from April 2026, increasing wage bills across agriculture and processing. (3) Feed and packaging input costs have risen 11.0% year-on-year, food-price inflation is running at 6.5%, while consumer spending on cheese grew 4.2% in the same period.

--- QUESTIONS ---
  Q1(a) [8 marks]
    Question: GDC plans to fund part of its new automated cheese-packing and cold-storage facility with a member share issue. Explain two advantages for GDC of using a member share issue to fund the expansion instead of a bank loan.
    Answer: Point 1: A member share issue raises permanent capital from the 150 surveyed farmer-members and other cooperative members without any repayment schedule or interest charge, unlike the alternative of a larger bank loan. This protects GDC's cash flow while it already services a $600,000 loan and carries fixed costs of $420,000 a year, and it avoids the risk of the bank imposing restrictive covenants on the new cold-storage facility or on how the farmer-members are paid for their milk.

Point 2: A member share issue strengthens member commitment and loyalty, since farmers who buy shares have a direct stake in the cooperative's success and are more likely to supply milk consistently and support the automated packing project. It also avoids pledging the new $1,400,000 facility as collateral, so member equity absorbs the risk instead of the bank doing so, and it keeps decision-making within the cooperative's own democratic governance rather than passing control to an external lender with fixed interest and principal demands.
    Keywords: member share issue, bank loan, $800,000, $600,000, $1,400,000, $420,000
    Mark scheme: knowledge_max_2: 1 mark for each valid advantage identified (max 2). | application_analysis_max_6: Up to 3 marks per point for detailed contextual analysis linked to GDC's cooperative structure and expansion.

  Q1(b) [12 marks]
    Question: GDC is launching its new vintage cheddar to regional supermarkets. Consider television advertising, in-store supermarket tasting promotions, or sponsorship of the annual Greenvale valley farmers' fair. Which should GDC choose to promote the launch? Justify your recommendation.
    Answer: Television advertising: A regional TV campaign would build fast awareness of GDC's vintage cheddar across all the supermarket chains it supplies and reach millions of households quickly. However, production and airtime are expensive for a cooperative, much of the audience would be outside the Greenvale valley catchment, and the message would be fleeting. For a member-owned business funding a $1,400,000 facility through an $800,000 share issue, heavy TV spend could strain cash flow before the new cheese has proven itself on shelf.

In-store supermarket tasting promotions: Tastings put the cheddar directly in front of shoppers at the moment of purchase, let staff explain the cooperative story and the 72% member support for the expansion, and generate immediate trial and sales data per store. Costs are moderate and targeted, though reach is limited to participating stores and the effect fades once the promotion ends.

Sponsorship of the Greenvale valley farmers' fair: Sponsoring the fair reinforces GDC's local farmer-heritage brand, delights the 150 farmer-members, and reaches a loyal regional audience cheaply with strong goodwill and media coverage. Its weakness is scale: the fair reaches a few thousand people once a year, which cannot move the volume needed to justify a $1,400,000 automated packing facility supplying national supermarket chains, and non-attendees never see the product.

Recommendation: GDC should choose in-store supermarket tasting promotions. They convert shoppers at the point of sale where the cheese is stocked, cost far less than television, target precisely the consumers buying in the partner supermarkets, and generate measurable sales uplift and feedback. Television is rejected as unaffordable and untargeted for a cooperative with a $600,000 bank loan to service, and the farmers' fair is rejected as too small and too occasional to build the volumes the new facility requires; GDC can keep the fair sponsorship as low-cost community goodwill alongside the tastings.
    Keywords: supermarket, cheese, 72%, $1,400,000, 150,000, $14.70
    Mark scheme: level_1_1_to_4: Limited knowledge or outline of the promotional options with minimal context. | level_2_5_to_8: Detailed discussion of the advantages and disadvantages of at least two options in the context of GDC with some judgement. | level_3_9_to_12: Detailed discussion of all three options in the context of GDC with a well-justified recommendation explaining why television and the farmers' fair are rejected.

  Q2(a) [8 marks]
    Question: GDC faces rising labour turnover on the packing floor and repeated cold-chain failures. Explain two benefits for GDC of introducing democratic participation in its packing department.
    Answer: Point 1: Democratic participation, such as worker briefings and suggestion schemes on the packing floor, gives the 120 staff a voice in how shifts, cold-chain checks and machine loading are organised. This satisfies esteem and belonging needs, raises job satisfaction and can directly reduce labour turnover, cutting the cost of recruiting and retraining packers and reducing disruption to the 4.5-day delivery promise to regional distributors.

Point 2: Involving operators surfaces practical fixes from the people who run the cold chain daily, such as earlier temperature checks and faster fault reporting. This lowers the 2.1% defect rate further and prevents rejected consignments like the 14 cold-chain failures this year, protecting GDC's reputation with 72% of farmer-members who support the expansion and preserving the flow of 37,500 units per quarter through the plant. In combination, the two benefits attack both the attendance problem behind labour turnover and the process problem behind consignment rejections.

  Q2(b) [12 marks]
    Question: GDC wants to motivate its packing-floor workers and cut labour turnover. Consider introducing piece-rate bonus pay or a profit-sharing scheme across the cooperative. Which should GDC choose? Justify your decision.
    Answer: Piece-rate bonus pay: Paying packers per unit packed rewards individual effort directly and links pay to the 37,500 units processed per quarter, which can raise output speed and lower unit labour costs. It suits measurable, repetitive packing work and is easy to administer. However, it can push packers to rush, raising the 2.1% defect rate and worsening cold-chain handling, it can create friction between fast and careful workers, and it ignores quality, safety and teamwork — dangerous in a cold-storage environment handling dairy products with strict hygiene rules.

Profit-sharing scheme: Distributing a share of cooperative profits to all 120 staff rewards collective performance, aligns workers with member and customer interests, and reinforces the cooperative ethos that defines GDC. It encourages teamwork, quality and careful handling, which would protect the falling defect rate and the 4.5-day delivery record. Drawbacks are that individual effort is diluted across 120 people, payouts depend on annual profits rather than daily behaviour, and poor years (for example after 14 rejected consignments) could demotivate if nothing is paid.

Decision: GDC should choose the profit-sharing scheme. It fits the cooperative model, promotes the teamwork and care needed to eliminate cold-chain failures and the 2.1% defect rate, and benefits all 120 staff rather than penalising slower, careful workers. Piece-rate pay is rejected as too narrow and too likely to inflate defects and rejections, which would cost far more than the bonuses paid; GDC can review piece-rate elements only after certification is complete and quality stabilises. A clear communication plan and termly profit statements will be essential so all 120 staff understand how the scheme works.
    Keywords: labour turnover, 37,500, workforce of 120, 2.1%, 72%, cold-chain
    Mark scheme: level_1_1_to_4: Basic description of the two motivators with limited application to GDC. | level_2_5_to_8: Detailed analysis of the benefits and drawbacks of one or both motivators in the context of GDC. | level_3_9_to_12: Comprehensive evaluation of both motivators in the context of GDC with a well-justified decision covering quality, turnover, cooperative structure and cost.

    Question: Using Appendix 2, evaluate GDC's financial position by calculating the current ratio and the acid test ratio for 2024 and 2025. Has GDC's financial position improved? Which of the two ratios gives the stronger evidence, and why? Justify your answer.

Current Ratio 2024 = 1.42 : 1
Current Ratio 2025 = 1.37 : 1
Acid Test Ratio 2024 = 0.74 : 1
Acid Test Ratio 2025 = 0.65 : 1

Which ratio gives the stronger evidence? The acid test is the stronger indicator of GDC's short-term solvency because it excludes inventories — perishable dairy stock that may need to be discounted or scrapped to realise cash — and it fell from 0.74 to 0.65, confirming that the weakening is driven by rising liabilities and falling cash rather than by any improvement in stock quality.

Conclusion: GDC's financial position has not improved. Both the CR (1.42 to 1.37) and the AT (0.74 to 0.65) show weaker short-term solvency, with cash falling to just $40,000. Before the expansion proceeds, GDC should tighten credit control on its $240,000 of receivables, cut perishable inventories, and agree staged drawdown of the member share issue rather than upfront spending.

  Q4(b) [12 marks]
    Question: Using Appendix 3, evaluate how the rise in the base interest rate to 4.75%, the 6.0% minimum wage increase and the 11.0% rise in feed and packaging input costs will affect GDC. Which change will have the greatest impact? Justify your answer.
    Answer: Interest rate rise (4.0% to 4.75%): If GDC's $600,000 bank loan is variable-rate, the 0.75% rise adds about $4,500 a year in interest, a modest sum against fixed costs of $420,000 and the $1,400,000 facility budget. Higher rates would, however, raise the cost of any further borrowing and may encourage the cooperative to delay drawdown of the loan, and they could dampen consumer spending growth on cheese beyond the current 4.2%. The direct cash impact is small and can be managed by fixing the rate.

Minimum wage increase (6.0%, to $12.83 per hour): The insert gives a 6.0% rise from $12.10 to $12.83 — a derived delta of $0.73 per hour ($12.83 − $12.10; check: 6.0% × $12.10 ≈ $0.73). Many of the 120 staff hold production and packing roles whose pay is anchored to the floor, and bands above the floor typically shift too. The insert does not state hours worked, so the annual cash impact cannot be computed precisely; however, every hour worked becomes more expensive from April 2026, making this a direct hit to the operating margin that would pressure the pay of farmer-members relative to staff, and would require productivity gains — such as the automation in the new facility, which should cut labour demand per unit — to offset it without raising the $14.70 selling price.

Input cost inflation (11.0% feed and packaging): Feed drives the milk price GDC pays its farmer-members and packaging covers the new facility's output. The insert gives a $7.70 variable cost per unit and an 11.0% year-on-year rise in these inputs. Taking the entire variable cost as an upper bound: 11.0% × $7.70 = about $0.85 per unit; at 150,000 units a year that is roughly $127,500 a year (150,000 × $0.85, derivation shown; an upper bound since not all of the $7.70 is feed and packaging). Even a fraction of that bound would erode the $7.00 contribution per unit and squeeze the margin available to pay members for their milk, so feed and packaging contracts should be renegotiated before the new facility comes online.

Conclusion: The minimum wage increase will have the greatest impact. It is a mechanical $0.73-per-hour ($12.83 − $12.10) rise with no cap on the hours worked across the 120-strong workforce, whereas the input-cost rise is bounded at roughly $127,500 a year as an explicit upper bound (in practice far less), and vastly more than the $4,500 interest increase. It directly pressures the cooperative's ability to retain and motivate 120 staff while turnover is already rising. GDC must therefore prioritise productivity from automation, careful shift planning and, only if needed, modest cheese price rises, while fixing the loan rate and renegotiating feed contracts to contain the smaller input and interest-rate risks.
    Keywords: 4.75%, 6.0%, 11.0%, $12.83, $12.10, 4.2%

--- MAIN STEM ---
Ironpine Craft Brewery (ICB) is a private limited company in the craft brewing sector, employing a workforce of 52. Founded in 2014 by Dan Whitmore and Elena Ruiz, it brews hop-forward ales sold to bars, bottle shops and supermarket chains nationwide, using a flat organisational structure with laissez-faire leadership that prizes brewer creativity. ICB plans to invest $540,000 in a canning line to launch a low-alcohol craft lager, financed by a $150,000 bank overdraft and $390,000 retained profit. It has fixed costs of $180,000 a year, a variable cost of $12.00 a unit and a selling price of $16.00, and currently produces 72,000 units a year. ICB faces a defect rate of 3.2% on test cans and a widening skills gap among canning-line operators.

--- APPENDIX 1 — MARKETING/OPS ---
Brewing Quality Report — October 2026: Trial runs of the new canning line produced 18,400 units last quarter at a defect rate of 3.2%, down from 5.6% a year ago. Customer quality complaints fell from 24 to 12 per month. A survey of 500 customers across 30 bars found 61% would buy a low-alcohol craft lager and 49% prefer cans over bottles. Average delivery time to distributors is 2.8 days. Taste-panel testing costs $1,100 per recipe iteration, and 14 of 52 staff have completed advanced brewing certification, while on-the-job coaching on the canning line continues.

--- APPENDIX 2 — FINANCIAL DATA ---
Title: Extract from the Statement of Financial Position of Ironpine Craft Brewery as at 31 March 2025 ($ '000)
Headers: ['Financial Metric', '2024', '2025']
Inventories | 150 | 185
Trade receivables | 95 | 120
Cash and cash equivalents | 25 | 35
Current liabilities | 190 | 230
Non-current assets | 980 | 1,320
Capital employed | 1,480 | 1,720

--- APPENDIX 3 — EXTERNAL ENVIRONMENT ---
Economic and Business Bulletin (November 2026): (1) The central bank has raised the base interest rate from 4.25% to 5.0%, increasing costs for businesses using overdrafts. (2) The national minimum wage will rise by 5.5% from $12.30 to $12.98 per hour from April 2026, increasing wage bills. (3) Barley, hops and aluminium can input costs have risen 13.2% year-on-year, brewing input inflation is running at 9.8%, while consumer spending on premium craft beer grew 5.1% in the same period.
