--- MAIN STEM ---
Sole Ledger (SL) is a private limited company operating an online sneaker resale marketplace in the capital city of Dunmoor, employing a workforce of 62. Founded in 2016 by DeShawn Carter, the business authenticates and resells limited-edition trainers through a hierarchical structure with autocratic leadership. SL plans to invest $950,000 in a national authentication hub and a verified-seller onboarding programme for 300 new sellers, financed by a $600,000 bank loan and $350,000 from a share issue. It has fixed costs of $480,000 a year, a variable cost of $9.00 a unit and a selling price of $21.00, and currently produces 55,000 units a year. SL faces a serious operational problem: returns abuse has reached 6.8% of orders, driven by worn or switched pairs sent back for refunds.

--- APPENDIX 1 — MARKETING/OPS ---
Operations Log — Q3 2026: The Dunmoor authentication hub processed 9,400 pairs last quarter, rejecting 3.1% as counterfeit or unverifiable. Returns were 11% of orders, with 480 cases of suspected switched-item fraud referred for review. The average consigned sale price was $210, and average delivery time is 2.6 days. A survey of 350 buyers found 78% would pay a $19 authentication fee for guaranteed genuine stock, and 61% discovered SL through social media. Seller verification takes 6 working days, and 72% of new sellers fail the first audit.

--- APPENDIX 2 — FINANCIAL DATA ---
Title: Extract from the Statement of Financial Position of Sole Ledger as at 31 March 2025 ($ '000)
Headers: ['Financial Metric', '2024', '2025']
Inventories | 410 | 455
Trade receivables | 310 | 380
Cash and cash equivalents | 150 | 60
Current liabilities | 430 | 505
Non-current assets | 2,600 | 3,150
Capital employed | 3,040 | 3,410

--- APPENDIX 3 — EXTERNAL ENVIRONMENT ---
Economic and Business Bulletin (November 2026): (1) The central bank has raised the base interest rate from 4.5% to 5.25%, the third rise this year, lifting variable-rate borrowing costs. (2) The national minimum wage will rise by 4.9% from $12.66 to $13.28 per hour from April 2026, raising wage bills for authentication and packing teams. (3) Logistics and resale input costs (delivery, authentication and payment processing) have risen 10.6% year-on-year, and consumer spending on second-hand sneakers grew 14.2% in the same period.

--- QUESTIONS ---
  Q1(a) [8 marks]
    Question: SL must choose how to fund the national authentication hub. Explain two advantages for SL of using a share issue to raise $350,000 instead of increasing the $600,000 bank loan.
    Answer: Point 1: A share issue carries no repayment schedule and no interest charge, so SL avoids adding further fixed obligations while it absorbs a 10.6% rise in logistics and authentication input costs and a 4.9% minimum wage increase. This protects cash for the $950,000 hub build, when Appendix 2 already shows cash fell from $150,000 to $60,000 and current liabilities rose to $505,000 during expansion.

Point 2: Equity funding does not require the hub itself as collateral, so if launch yields slower seller sign-ups than the 300-seller target, the authentication hub is not at risk of repossession. It also strengthens SL's balance sheet and lender confidence, making the remaining $600,000 bank loan easier to service and assuring consigned sellers that a well-capitalised platform will honour their stock and payouts.
    Keywords: share issue, $600,000, bank loan, $950,000, workforce of 62, returns abuse
    Mark scheme: knowledge_max_2: 1 mark for each valid advantage identified (max 2). | application_analysis_max_6: Up to 3 marks per point for contextual explanation and analysis applied to Sole Ledger, its expansion decision and its financial position.

  Q1(b) [12 marks]
    Question: SL is onboarding 300 new verified sellers to its marketplace. Consider a social media influencer campaign, advertising in sneaker culture magazines, or sponsorship of a sneaker trade convention. Which should SL choose to promote seller onboarding? Justify your recommendation.
    Answer: Social media influencer campaign: Sneaker and streetwear creators could showcase the authentication process to both buyers and aspiring sellers. With 61% of buyers already discovering SL through social media and 78% willing to pay a $19 authentication fee, the channel directly reaches the exact audience and can onboard sellers with referral codes, live authentication demos and seller-spotlight series. Magazine print is rejected as unmeasurable and declining, and convention sponsorship is rejected as episodic and location-bound; SL can layer a single flagship convention appearance on top of the influencer programme rather than anchor the whole launch to it.
    Keywords: 61%, 78%, authentication hub, verified-seller, $19, 9,400
    Mark scheme: level_1_1_to_4: Limited knowledge or outline of the promotional options with minimal application to SL. | level_2_5_to_8: Detailed discussion of the advantages and disadvantages of at least two options in the context of SL with some judgement. | level_3_9_to_12: Detailed discussion of all three options in the context of SL with a well-justified recommendation explaining why magazine print and convention sponsorship are rejected.

  Q2(a) [8 marks]
    Question: SL's autocratic leadership has drawn criticism from authentication staff. Explain two benefits for SL of autocratic leadership when running seller verification and order authentication.

    Question: SL wants to cut fraudulent returns running at 6.8% of orders. Consider retraining its authentication staff on-the-job or hiring temporary auditors during peak releases. Which should SL choose? Justify your decision.
    Answer: On-the-job retraining: Senior authenticators train every packer and grader on the exact checks used in the Dunmoor hub — stitching, box labels, SKU matching and weight checks — so learning maps directly onto live consignments. It keeps all 62 staff productive, costs no course fees, and builds a permanent checking culture that outlasts any scheme; weaknesses are that production staff who train lose output time, bad habits can be copied, and there is no external certificate if SL faces disputes with major sellers.

Decision: SL should choose on-the-job retraining as its core response, reserving temporary auditors only for the two biggest release weekends. Retraining is cheaper, machine- and process-specific, raises long-term accuracy rather than patching peaks, and supports Carter's autocratic standard-setting with a skilled internal team. Hiring temps as the main solution is rejected because it treats symptoms, never builds internal capability, and erodes margins on every $210 sale while the 480 switched-item cases keep growing; permanent upskilling plus spot audits is the sustainable route.
    Keywords: returns abuse, 6.8%, authentication, 9,400, 480, 2.6 days
    Mark scheme: level_1_1_to_4: Basic description of the two options with limited application to SL. | level_2_5_to_8: Detailed analysis of the benefits and drawbacks of one or both options in the context of SL. | level_3_9_to_12: Comprehensive evaluation of both options in the context of SL with a well-justified decision covering cost, disruption, fraud prevention and long-term capability.

  Q3(a) [8 marks]
    Question: Calculate and explain how SL's management can use its cost, break-even and productivity data.

  Q3(b) [12 marks]
    Question: Using Appendix 2, evaluate SL's financial position by calculating the current ratio and the acid test ratio for 2024 and 2025. Has SL's financial position improved? Justify your answer.
    Answer: Calculations:
Current Ratio 2024 = 2.02 : 1
Current Ratio 2025 = 1.77 : 1
Acid Test Ratio 2024 = 1.07 : 1
Acid Test Ratio 2025 = 0.87 : 1

Detailed workings: 2024 current assets = $410,000 inventories + $310,000 trade receivables + $150,000 cash = $870,000; 2025 current assets = $455,000 + $380,000 + $60,000 = $895,000. 2024 cover = $870,000 ÷ $430,000 current liabilities = 2.02; 2025 cover = $895,000 ÷ $505,000 = 1.77. 2024 liquid cover = ($870,000 − $410,000) ÷ $430,000 = $460,000 ÷ $430,000 = 1.07; 2025 liquid cover = ($895,000 − $455,000) ÷ $505,000 = $440,000 ÷ $505,000 = 0.87.

Evaluation: SL's liquidity has deteriorated even though the business is growing. Non-current assets rose from $2,600,000 to $3,150,000 as the authentication hub and onboarding programme were built, but cash fell from $150,000 to $60,000 and current liabilities climbed from $430,000 to $505,000, so overall cover slipped from 2.02 to 1.77. The liquid cover slid from 1.07 to 0.87, meaning SL can no longer meet short-term debts without realising stock, an uncomfortable position for a platform holding $455,000 of unsold consigned inventory and $380,000 of trade receivables from sellers on settlement terms. Growing receivables suggest some sellers are slow to remit, and if the 300-seller onboarding accelerates cash absorption further, SL could face a squeeze precisely when the $600,000 bank loan repayments bite and interest costs rise with the base rate.

Conclusion: SL's financial position has not improved. Both measures fell — cover from 2.02 to 1.77 and liquid cover from 1.07 to 0.87 — because expansion consumed working capital faster than it generated it. SL should tighten seller settlement terms, stage the onboarding of the 300 sellers in cohorts, and pause further borrowing until cash recovers, even though the hub will strengthen long-term competitiveness and support premium authentication fees.

    Question: Using Appendix 3, evaluate how the interest rate rise to 5.25%, the 4.9% minimum wage increase and the 10.6% rise in resale input costs will affect SL. Which change will have the greatest impact? Justify your answer.
    Answer: Interest rate rise (from 4.5% to 5.25%): The 0.75% increase adds roughly $4,500 a year to repayments on a $600,000 variable-rate bank loan, and raises any top-up funding for the authentication hub. Minimum wage increase (4.9% rise to $13.28 per hour from April 2026): Authentication, packing and customer-support teams in a 62-person workforce are heavily hourly-paid. An average wage bill of around $1.6 million (about $26,000 per worker) rises by roughly $78,000 a year, concentrated at peak release weekends when overtime demand spikes. SL cannot fully automate grading yet, so this lands directly on operating costs and squeezes the $12.00 contribution per unit unless productivity rises or the $19 authentication fee is increased.

Input-cost inflation (10.6% rise in logistics, authentication and payment processing): SL's $9.00 variable cost per unit is dominated by these fees. Assuming about 70% of it ($6.30) is exposed to the 10.6% rise, that adds roughly $0.67 per pair, or about $37,000 a year on 55,000 units, before knock-on effects on the 14.2% growth in consumer spending which otherwise supports demand. SL could recover part through a modest sellers' fee rise given buyers' 78% willingness to pay for authentication.

Conclusion: The 4.9% minimum wage increase will have the greatest impact on SL, adding roughly $78,000 a year against about $37,000 for input costs and only around $4,500 for interest. It is unavoidable, recurring and concentrated on the authentication capability that differentiates SL from casual resale apps. SL should respond with a small, clearly signposted $19 authentication fee increase, tighter peak-release rostering and productivity incentives, while fixing its loan rate and renegotiating courier and payment-processing contracts to contain the other two threats.

--- MAIN STEM ---
Greenbasket Organics (GBO) is a cooperative in the organic food retail sector, employing a workforce of 34. Founded in 2010 by Hannah Okafor, the members' cooperative runs two organic shops and a farm-box scheme in Riverton, operating a flat structure with democratic leadership. GBO plans to invest $640,000 in a third organic store with a home-delivery depot, financed by $400,000 member share capital and $240,000 bank loan. It has fixed costs of $198,000 a year, a variable cost of $2.20 a unit and a selling price of $5.50, and currently produces 78,000 units a year. GBO faces twin operational problems: seasonal staffing shortages run 28% above roster in the December peak and organic waste is running at 7.5% of stock.

--- APPENDIX 1 — MARKETING/OPS ---
Quality and Waste Report — Q3 2026: GBO recorded 7.5% organic waste worth $36,000 over the year, with 240 kg of unsold produce donated each week. The farm-box scheme delivered 6,800 boxes last quarter at a 98.2% on-time rate. A member survey of 350 respondents found 66% would join an expanded home-delivery scheme and 71% prefer local farms within 50 km. Average basket value is $28.40, breakage complaints fell from 24 to 11 per month, and the December peak requires 28 seasonal hires above roster.

--- APPENDIX 2 — FINANCIAL DATA ---

(2) The national minimum wage will rise by 5.2% from $12.75 to $13.41 per hour from April 2026, lifting seasonal and part-time wage bills. (3) Organic produce input costs (grain, dairy and fresh vegetables) have risen 11.2% year-on-year, organic food inflation is 7.4%, and consumer spending on organic products grew 6.1% in the same period.

  Q1(a) [8 marks]
    Question: GBO must finance part of the third store and home-delivery depot. Explain two advantages for GBO of using member share capital instead of the $240,000 bank loan.
    Answer: Point 1: Member share capital carries no fixed interest or repayment, which matters when GBO's margins are tight — variable cost is $2.20 against a $5.50 selling price and organic waste already costs $36,000 a year. Avoiding loan repayments protects the cash needed for the $640,000 depot build and keeps the price of weekly farm boxes stable for price-sensitive member households.

Point 2: Raising money from members deepens the cooperative's democratic ethos and loyalty: the same members who invest are the 71% who prefer local farms within 50 km and the 66% who would join an expanded home-delivery scheme. Members who hold share capital are more likely to stay, shop and volunteer at the depot, strengthening GBO's local roots and making the launch less dependent on bank goodwill than the $240,000 bank loan alone would allow.
    Keywords: member share capital, bank loan, $240,000, $640,000, cooperative, farm-box

    Question: GBO is opening its third organic store with a home-delivery depot. Consider in-store tastings and farm open days, a local radio campaign, or social media food-blogger promotion. Which should GBO choose to promote the opening? Justify your recommendation.
    Answer: In-store tastings and farm open days: Face-to-face events let Riverton members taste organic produce, meet the 50 km-radius farmers GBO buys from, and sign up for the expanded home-delivery scheme on the spot, directly converting the 71% local-farm preference and the 66% who would join delivery into sales. Events build the cooperative community spirit that differentiates GBO from supermarkets, and costs are mainly staff time and free samples; the limit is reach — only those who attend are persuaded, so coverage is slower and more manual than media.

Local radio campaign: Radio reaches car commuters and farm-box households across Riverton quickly and repeatedly, suits opening-week announcements and delivery-route launches, and a cooperative message about local sourcing can feel authentic on air. However, it is one-way, cannot demonstrate freshness or taste, and spend is wasted on non-organic households; measuring response beyond a generic mention is difficult.

Social media food-blogger promotion: Food and farm bloggers could show recipes, box contents and farm visits to health-conscious followers, with trackable links to sign up for delivery. It is inexpensive and measurable, but GBO's members skew toward families and older buyers who may not follow bloggers daily, and blogger endorsement can backfire if a post overlooks the 7.5% waste problem GBO is trying to fix.

Recommendation: GBO should choose in-store tastings and farm open days as the anchor promotion, supported by a light social media schedule. It converts local trust into subscriptions exactly where the 71% and 66% research points, costs little beyond produce already in store, and embodies cooperative values better than broadcast or influencer marketing. Radio is rejected as one-way and wasteful outside the organic segment, and blogger-first promotion is rejected as too narrow and fragile for a weekly grocery habit; a small influencer budget can amplify the open days rather than replace them.

  Q2(b) [12 marks]
    Question: GBO wants to motivate seasonal checkout and packing staff for the December peak. Consider a seasonal attendance bonus or a profit-sharing scheme for all staff. Which should GBO choose? Justify your decision.
    Answer: Seasonal attendance bonus: A fixed cash bonus for any seasonal worker achieving near-perfect attendance across the four-week peak directly attacks the roster crisis, since the December shortfall of 28 hires is partly driven by unpredictable absences. It is simple to administer for short contracts, immediately salient, easy to budget against the $198,000 fixed cost base, and needs no annual profit data. It suits GBO's cooperative identity, rewards results not just showing up, and could lift retention so seasonal staff return each December. However, the reward is delayed until accounts close, weak for casuals on four-week contracts, may feel unfair if a bad weather week erases the surplus, and requires transparent surplus reporting GBO must prepare for every member.

Decision: GBO should choose a seasonal attendance bonus for the December cohort, keeping its existing profit-sharing for permanent members. The bonus targets the exact failure point — no-shows at peak when 28 extra hires are needed — is affordable, instant and easy to communicate to casuals, and can include a quality hurdle (breakage below a set rate) to blunt the careless-attendance weakness. A profit-sharing rollout now is rejected because it cannot motivate four-week seasonal staff whose contract may end before any payout, and because its administration cost outweighs gains in a peak crisis; GBO can extend it to high-performing seasonal staff next year once the depot opens.

PAPER 2 — P2_SET_114
UNIT: Paper 2 Case Study

--- MAIN STEM ---
Hartwell Homewares (HHW) is a public limited company in the homeware retail sector, employing a workforce of 210. Founded in 1994 by Gregory Hartwell, the chain operates twelve out-of-town stores across the Alderney region under a hierarchical structure with democratic leadership. HHW plans to invest $1,850,000 in three new out-of-town homeware stores, financed by a $1,200,000 share issue and $650,000 bank loan. It has fixed costs of $1,050,000 a year, a variable cost of $13 a unit and a selling price of $25.50, and currently produces 108,000 units a year. HHW faces a serious human resources problem: labour turnover has reached 41% a year across its stores and seasonal shelf-stacking gaps widen every Christmas.

--- APPENDIX 1 — MARKETING/OPS ---
Market Research Summary — October 2026: Across its twelve stores, HHW serves average monthly footfall of 92,000 shoppers with an average basket value of $46. A survey of 800 shoppers found 57% would buy furniture online for home delivery and 43% chose HHW for low prices; 66% were satisfied with in-store service, and 12% complained about checkout queues over 10 minutes. Online sales are 19% of revenue, up from 14% a year ago, and the three proposed stores scored an average 8.1 out of 10 on catchment research for visibility, parking and local spending.

--- APPENDIX 2 — FINANCIAL DATA ---
Title: Extract from the Statement of Financial Position of Hartwell Homewares as at 31 March 2025 ($ '000)
Headers: ['Financial Metric', '2024', '2025']
Inventories | 520 | 640
Trade receivables | 380 | 430
Cash and cash equivalents | 230 | 380
Current liabilities | 640 | 760
Non-current assets | 6,800 | 8,400
Capital employed | 7,290 | 8,990

--- APPENDIX 3 — EXTERNAL ENVIRONMENT ---
Economic and Business Bulletin (November 2026): (1) The central bank has raised the base interest rate from 4.25% to 5.0%, raising the cost of variable-rate borrowing for large retailers. (2) The national minimum wage will rise by 6.1% from $12.90 to $13.69 per hour from April 2026, increasing wage bills across stores and warehouses. (3) Furniture and homeware input costs (timber, steel and textiles) have risen 9.6% year-on-year, retail inflation is 5.8%, and consumer spending on homewares fell 2.4% in the same period.

--- QUESTIONS ---
  Q1(a) [8 marks]
    Question: HHW intends to fund part of the three-store expansion by share issue. Explain two advantages for HHW of financing the expansion with a $1,200,000 share issue instead of the $650,000 bank loan.
    Answer: Point 1: A share issue carries no interest and no fixed repayment dates, which is vital when HHW already faces fixed costs of $1,050,000 a year and a variable-rate bank loan element rising with the base rate. Avoiding further debt service protects HHW's cash headroom — important with labour turnover at 41% and wage inflation approaching — and leaves the $650,000 bank loan manageable alongside the share-issue proceeds.

Point 2: Selling shares spreads the ownership risk of three unproven out-of-town sites across many public investors rather than loading it onto HHW's property assets as security. It also strengthens the balance sheet and makes HHW more credible to landlords, suppliers and local authorities during catchment negotiations, supporting the 8.1 out of 10 catchment scores the three sites achieved, and preserving the freedom to stage openings rather than commit to aggressive early repayments.
    Keywords: share issue, bank loan, $1,200,000, $650,000, $1,850,000, labour turnover
    Mark scheme: knowledge_max_2: 1 mark for each valid advantage identified (max 2). | application_analysis_max_6: Up to 3 marks per point for contextual explanation and analysis applied to Hartwell Homewares, its expansion decision and its finances.

  Q1(b) [12 marks]
    Question: HHW is opening three new out-of-town homeware stores. Consider a national television campaign, local radio sponsorship in the three catchment areas, or social media marketing with home-lifestyle influencers. Which should HHW choose to promote the launch? Justify your recommendation.
    Answer: National television campaign: Television would reach millions across the whole Alderney region and build instant national awareness of the new stores, reinforcing HHW's twelve-store reputation. However, production and airtime are extremely expensive, much of the audience lives far outside the three catchments, and for a public limited company raising $1,200,000 in new equity, the wastage is hard to justify when only three stores open, and television cannot tell viewers exactly where to park or what opening offers apply locally.

Local radio sponsorship in the three catchment areas: Radio reaches commuters and local householders precisely where the stores will trade, suits opening-weekend messaging, price announcements and loyalty-card drives, and is far cheaper than television. Its weakness is audio-only communication — homewares is visual, so sofa styles and kitchen ranges cannot be shown — and frequency of spots is needed before recall builds, with no interactive click-through to HHW's website.

Social media marketing with home-lifestyle influencers: Influencers could tour showroom kitchens, style living rooms with HHW furniture and post discount codes, measurable through clicks and redemptions, suiting the 57% of shoppers willing to buy online. It is inexpensive and visual, but skew toward younger audiences under-represents HHW's core family furniture buyers, and quality control across many influencers is harder for a hierarchical, democratically governed chain.

Recommendation: HHW should choose local radio sponsorship anchored in the three catchment areas. It concentrates spend exactly where stores open, suits price-led homeware messages for family buyers, and costs a fraction of television and more targeting than untargeted social reach. National television is rejected as unaffordable and untargeted for three stores, and influencer-first social marketing is rejected as too young-skewing and hard to police for a 210-person chain; HHW should add in-store events and local press leaflets to convert radio listeners into opening-weekend footfall.
    Keywords: share issue, $1,850,000, 57%, workforce of 210, 8.1, footfall
    Mark scheme: level_1_1_to_4: Limited knowledge or outline of the promotional options with minimal application to HHW. | level_2_5_to_8: Detailed discussion of the advantages and disadvantages of at least two options in the context of HHW with some judgement. | level_3_9_to_12: Detailed discussion of all three options in the context of HHW with a well-justified recommendation explaining why television and influencer-first social marketing are rejected.

  Q2(a) [8 marks]
    Question: HHW operates a hierarchical structure with democratic leadership. Explain two benefits for HHW of its hierarchical structure when managing 210 staff across fifteen stores.
    Answer: Point 1: A hierarchical structure gives HHW clear levels of authority — store managers, department leads, shelf teams — so every one of the 210 staff knows who to report to and who makes pricing, returns and safety decisions. This clarity is essential for training new starters fast, cutting the disruption caused when labour turnover hits 41% a year, and keeping service consistent across twelve stores while three more open.

Point 2: Defined chains of command speed up escalation when problems arise, for example stock shortages or the 12% of shoppers complaining about checkout queues over 10 minutes; democratic leadership then lets employees contribute ideas through team briefings and worker forums before decisions are finalised, combining tight control with genuine staff buy-in from departments that understand homewares operations best.
    Keywords: hierarchical structure, democratic leadership, workforce of 210, labour turnover, 41%, twelve
    Mark scheme: knowledge_max_2: 1 mark for each valid benefit identified (max 2). | application_analysis_max_6: Up to 3 marks per point for detailed contextual development linked to HHW's scale, turnover problem and structure.

  Q2(b) [12 marks]
    Question: HHW wants to reduce its 41% annual labour turnover. Consider performance-related bonuses or job enrichment for store staff. Which should HHW choose? Justify your decision.
    Answer: Performance-related bonuses: Linking a monthly bonus to individual or team sales targets, mystery-shop scores and queue times would reward results directly — the $46 average basket value and 66% satisfaction with in-store service are measurable, and bonuses are easy to understand. They are particularly useful for checkout and sales-floor staff whose effort varies by shift. But bonuses narrow attention to measured metrics, can fuel unhealthy competition between the twelve stores, may reward selling over genuine advice, and do nothing for workers demotivated by repetitive stacking tasks; they also ratchet up the wage bill at a time when the minimum wage rises 6.1%.

Job enrichment: Redesigning roles so shelf stackers and cashiers take ownership of stock rotation, customer help, display refreshes and simple team budgets gives variety, responsibility and growth — the Herzberg hygiene-and-motivator insight that removing monotony beats adding cash. Enrichment costs little in cash, builds skills HHW needs for three new stores, and directly addresses boredom-driven quitting among younger shelf teams. Its limits are slower to show results, requires careful training and supervision, and cannot satisfy staff purely motivated by take-home pay.

Decision: HHW should choose job enrichment as its primary remedy, wrapped in targeted team bonuses only for new-store opening teams. Enrichment attacks the root cause of the 41% turnover — monotony and lack of progression in shelf and till roles — costs far less than adding bonus pay on top of a 6.1% minimum-wage rise, and builds the versatile staff the expansion needs. Performance-related bonuses alone are rejected because they pay more for output without fixing why people leave, risk worsening stock shrinkage and corner-cutting at busy periods, and would be repeated indefinitely; enrichment with recognition is the sustainable fix.
    Keywords: labour turnover, 41%, $46, workforce of 210, democratic leadership, minimum wage
    Mark scheme: level_1_1_to_4: Basic description of the two motivation methods with limited application to HHW. | level_2_5_to_8: Detailed analysis of the benefits and drawbacks of one or both methods in the context of HHW. | level_3_9_to_12: Comprehensive evaluation of both methods in the context of HHW with a well-justified decision explaining why performance-related bonuses are rejected as the sole remedy and job enrichment is preferred.

  Q3(a) [8 marks]
    Question: Calculate and explain how HHW's management can use its cost, break-even and productivity data.

  Q3(b) [12 marks]
    Question: Using Appendix 2, evaluate HHW's financial position by calculating the current ratio and the acid test ratio for 2024 and 2025. Has HHW's financial position improved? Justify your answer.
    Answer: Calculations:
Current Ratio 2024 = 1.77 : 1
Current Ratio 2025 = 1.91 : 1
Acid Test Ratio 2024 = 0.95 : 1
Acid Test Ratio 2025 = 1.07 : 1

Detailed workings: 2024 current assets = $520,000 inventories + $380,000 trade receivables + $230,000 cash = $1,130,000; 2025 current assets = $640,000 + $430,000 + $380,000 = $1,450,000. 2024 cover = $1,130,000 ÷ $640,000 current liabilities = 1.77; 2025 cover = $1,450,000 ÷ $760,000 = 1.91. 2024 liquid cover = ($1,130,000 − $520,000) ÷ $640,000 = $610,000 ÷ $640,000 = 0.95; 2025 liquid cover = ($1,450,000 − $640,000) ÷ $760,000 = $810,000 ÷ $760,000 = 1.07.

Evaluation: HHW's liquidity has improved modestly but genuinely. Cash and cash equivalents rose from $230,000 to $380,000, and non-current assets expanded from $6,800,000 to $8,400,000 as the three-store build-up progressed, yet current liabilities also grew from $640,000 to $760,000 as HHW financed stock timber, steel and textiles ahead of opening. Inventories rose from $520,000 to $640,000, reasonable for a stock-led retailer preparing launch inventory, while trade receivables climbed from $380,000 to $430,000, so HHW should tighten payment terms with its timber and steel suppliers' trade-credit arrangements to avoid over-reliance on supplier finance. The liquid cover crossing 1.00 in 2025 (1.07) is a positive signal for a retailer paying weekly wages to 210 staff.

Conclusion: HHW's financial position has improved. Overall cover strengthened from 1.77 to 1.91 and liquid cover from 0.95 to 1.07, giving headroom to absorb opening costs. However, inventories and receivables both rose faster than sales momentum, and consumer spending on homewares fell 2.4%, so HHW should clear slow stock before opening and keep the $650,000 bank loan fixed-rate to protect this improved flexibility.

  Q4(a) [8 marks]
    Question: Explain one advantage and one disadvantage for HHW of selling more homewares online through its website and allowing online ordering with store collection.
    Answer: Advantage: Online sales already represent 19% of revenue, up from 14% a year ago, and 57% of surveyed shoppers would buy furniture for home delivery, so extending the website with store-collection options would capture that demand without paying to build extra showroom space. HHW could reach beyond its twelve Alderney stores, reduce reliance on the $46 average basket's in-store dependence, gather customer data for targeted promotions, and smooth seasonal wage peaks by shifting discovery and payment online before collection.

Disadvantage: Selling higher-ticket furniture online raises the stakes on delivery, damage and returns — particularly timber and steel frames that cost more to move than the 12% checkout-queue complainants ever see. HHW would need drivers, packaging and insurance capacity, web photography and stock accuracy across twelve stores plus three new ones, and margin would be squeezed if the 5.8% retail inflation and 9.6% input-cost rise are passed through slowly, risking online price mismatches with store displays under its hierarchical pricing approvals.

  Q4(b) [12 marks]
    Question: Using Appendix 3, evaluate how the interest rate rise to 5.0%, the 6.1% minimum wage increase and the 9.6% rise in homeware input costs will affect HHW. Which change will have the greatest impact? Justify your answer.
    Answer: Interest rate rise (from 4.25% to 5.0%): The 0.75% increase adds roughly $4,875 a year to interest on a $650,000 variable-rate bank loan, and slightly raises the discount rate HHW and its investors apply to the three new stores' future cash flows. Higher rates also cool housing transactions and big-ticket furniture demand; with consumer spending on homewares already down 2.4%, the demand effect may matter more than the $4,875. HHW can fix the loan and negotiate terms, making this the smallest direct cash impact, but a real strategic headwind.

Minimum wage increase (6.1% rise to $13.69 per hour from April 2026): HHW's 210 staff — shelf teams, checkout, warehouse and new-store hires — are predominantly hourly. A wage bill of roughly $4.4 million a year rises by about $269,000 after the 6.1% increase, with extra pressure from overtime at Christmas shelf-stacking. For a retailer with $46 baskets, recovering $269,000 requires roughly 5,850 extra baskets a year (at $46) or a targeted price increase across top sellers; productivity, rostering and the 41% labour-turnover fix become urgent financial priorities, not just HR ones.

Input-cost inflation (9.6% rise in timber, steel and textiles): These inputs dominate HHW's $13 variable cost per unit, roughly $9.75 of it. A 9.6% rise adds close to $0.94 a unit, or about $101,000 a year on 108,000 units, squeezing the $12.50 contribution to about $11.56 unless prices rise or suppliers are renegotiated. Because retail inflation is only 5.8%, HHW cannot pass it all through quickly, but its $25.50 price point and 43% low-price positioning give some room.

Conclusion: The 6.1% minimum wage increase will have the greatest impact on HHW. At roughly $269,000 a year it dwarfs the $101,000 input-cost rise and the $4,875 interest addition, and it hits every hour of trading across all stores. HHW should accelerate job enrichment and multi-skilling to lift output per worker, re-tender cleaning and logistics contracts, introduce opening-weekend staffing flexibility, and take a modest, phased price rise on inelastic lines, while fixing the loan and pressuring timber and steel suppliers to contain the second-largest threat.
    Keywords: 5.0%, 6.1%, 9.6%, interest rate, $13.69, $650,000
    Mark scheme: level_1_1_to_4: Identifies the external factors with limited application to HHW. | level_2_5_to_8: Analyses the impact of at least two external changes on HHW's costs, revenue or financing in context. | level_3_9_to_12: Detailed evaluation of all three external changes in the context of HHW with a well-justified judgement that the minimum wage increase has the greatest impact and why the other two are smaller.

--- MAIN STEM ---
Velvette Beauty (VB) is a private limited company in the beauty and cosmetics retail sector, employing a workforce of 38. Founded in 2019 by Amara Osei, the pure-player brand sells skincare and cosmetics online from its Norwood fulfilment centre under a flat structure with autocratic leadership. VB plans to invest $920,000 in its first physical flagship store in the Norwood shopping district, financed by $480,000 venture capital and $440,000 retained profit. It has fixed costs of $270,000 a year, a variable cost of $7.00 a unit and a selling price of $16.00, and currently produces 44,000 units a year. VB faces a growing operational problem: returns abuse has reached 13% of online orders, with buyers ordering multiple shades and sending almost all of them back.

--- APPENDIX 1 — MARKETING/OPS ---
Advertisement Extract — Q3 2026 Campaign: Velvette Beauty's social media campaign generated 2.4 million impressions, 58,000 clicks and a 2.9% conversion rate. 46 influencer posts averaged 310,000 views each. Average order value was $34.60, with 31,500 units sold online last quarter. The campaign cost $21,000, and 54% of buyers were aged 18-34. A retargeting email series achieved a 6.4% open-to-purchase rate, and 72% of new customers discovered VB through influencer content. The flagship store launch target is 900 first-month visitors a day.

--- APPENDIX 2 — FINANCIAL DATA ---
Title: Extract from the Statement of Financial Position of Velvette Beauty as at 31 March 2025 ($ '000)
Headers: ['Financial Metric', '2024', '2025']
Inventories | 150 | 210
Trade receivables | 45 | 60
Cash and cash equivalents | 90 | 175
Current liabilities | 180 | 230
Non-current assets | 1,300 | 1,720
Capital employed | 1,405 | 1,725

--- APPENDIX 3 — EXTERNAL ENVIRONMENT ---
Economic and Business Bulletin (November 2026): (1) The central bank has raised the base interest rate from 4.1% to 4.9%, raising borrowing costs across the economy. (2) The national minimum wage will rise by 6.3% from $13.05 to $13.87 per hour from April 2026, increasing fulfilment and store-staff wage bills. (3) Botanical and packaging input costs have risen 10.8% year-on-year, cosmetics-price inflation is 6.6%, and consumer spending on online beauty grew 9.3% in the same period.

--- QUESTIONS ---
  Q1(a) [8 marks]
    Question: VB intends to fund part of the flagship store launch with venture capital. Explain two advantages for VB of using venture capital instead of its $440,000 retained profit to fund the store.
    Answer: Point 1: Venture capital brings more than money: VB gains an investor with beauty and retail expertise, supplier contacts and board-level guidance on site selection in Norwood, lease negotiation and store design — knowledge a 38-person pure-player brand may lack as it opens its first physical shop. The money arrives without interest or repayment dates, protecting VB's cash while the $920,000 build is on site.

Point 2: Keeping the $440,000 retained profit inside the business preserves a working-capital buffer for the online operation that still drives 31,500 units a quarter, absorbing the 10.8% rise in botanical and packaging input costs and the 13% returns abuse before the store pays for itself. VB's backers also back the brand publicly, boosting credibility with landlords and landlords' lenders, and patient venture capital is more flexible than a bank if opening weekends underperform targets. It also strengthens the balance sheet with new equity, making VB more credible to the Norwood shopping district's letting agents and their lenders.
    Keywords: venture capital, retained profit, $440,000, $920,000, $480,000, flagship store
    Mark scheme: knowledge_max_2: 1 mark for each valid advantage identified (max 2). | application_analysis_max_6: Up to 3 marks per point for contextual explanation and analysis applied to Velvette Beauty, its store launch and its finances.

  Q1(b) [12 marks]
    Question: VB is launching its first physical flagship store. Consider an influencer-led opening event, a national television campaign, or local radio sponsorship. Which should VB choose to promote the launch? Justify your recommendation.
    Answer: Influencer-led opening event: VB's entire brand is built on influencer discovery — 46 posts averaged 310,000 views and 72% of new customers find VB through creators, with 54% of buyers aged 18-34. An in-store event with skincare demos, shade-matching and limited edition bundles would fill the 900 first-month visitor target, generate genuine user content from the venue itself, and convert online fans into walk-in buyers for the price of appearances and samples rather than airtime.

National television campaign: Television would deliver mass reach across the whole country and legitimise the brand as a mainstream beauty retailer, suiting VB's ambition beyond Norwood. But production and airtime are far beyond a brand spending $21,000 on a whole digital quarter, most of the audience cannot visit one Norwood store, and measuring sales response is weak — an unjustifiable spend for a launch of this scale.

Local radio sponsorship: Radio would speak directly to Norwood listeners with opening offers, parking directions and loyalty-card sign-ups, cheap and frequent. However, VB's core 18-34 audience streams rather than listens to radio, beauty is visual, and radio cannot demonstrate texture, shade and scent — the very attributes that close beauty sales in store.

Recommendation: VB should choose an influencer-led opening event. It speaks directly to the 18-34 creator-fuelled audience that already drives the webstore, costs a small fraction of television, is measurable through redemptions and online mentions, and showcases the omni-channel story — try in store, reorder online. Television is rejected as unaffordable and geographically wasteful for a single flagship, and radio is rejected as unvisual and off-audience; VB can layer low-cost local PR and in-store sampling on top of the influencer anchor.
    Keywords: influencer, 72%, 54%, $21,000, flagship store, 900
    Mark scheme: level_1_1_to_4: Limited knowledge or outline of the promotional options with minimal application to VB. | level_2_5_to_8: Detailed discussion of the advantages and disadvantages of at least two options in the context of VB with some judgement. | level_3_9_to_12: Detailed discussion of all three options in the context of VB with a well-justified recommendation explaining why television and radio are rejected.

  Q2(a) [8 marks]
    Question: VB operates a flat structure with autocratic leadership. Explain two benefits for VB of autocratic leadership while launching its first physical store.
    Answer: Point 1: Autocratic leadership gives Amara Osei a single, decisive chain of command at a moment when hundreds of launch decisions — store layout, pricing, opening hours, staff contracts and merchandising — must align quickly for a fixed $920,000 budget. Clear directives prevent paralysis, keep the fulfilment centre and store teams coordinated, and ensure brand standards are met from day one without lengthy consultation committees.

Point 2: A flat hierarchy means the 38 staff already answer directly to the founder, so the opening store inherits a culture of fast execution and no filtering of bad news. Autocratic direction is especially valuable in beauty retail, where opening week must deliver consistent service, shade matching and till accuracy instantly; problems flagged in the morning can be fixed by the afternoon, protecting the $34.60 average order value as the brand pivots from web-only to physical trading.

  Q2(b) [12 marks]
    Question: VB wants to cut picking errors and returns abuse running at 13% of orders. Consider a picking-accuracy bonus or profit sharing for its fulfilment staff. Which should VB choose? Justify your decision.
    Answer: Picking-accuracy bonus: A measurable weekly bonus — for example, docked for mis-picked orders, wrong shades or wrong quantities — would directly attack the packing errors that drive the 13% returns rate, since VB can log every return against the picker and order. It is transparent, immediate, cheap to administer and highly visible to the fulfilment team; it concentrates minds on exactly the behaviour causing the problem. Its limits are that it narrowly rewards accuracy, not speed or customer care, and could make staff rush less — or game the metric by rejecting borderline orders, shifting work rather than eliminating mistakes.

Profit sharing: Sharing a percentage of quarterly online profit with all staff would lift morale across the whole business, reward everyone from packers to customer service, and motivate effort in areas tracking cannot capture — friendliness with customers, suggesting bundle alternatives, or flagging systemic stock issues. However, payouts reward total profit rather than the 13% returns defect specifically, are delayed and unpredictable (a bad quarter pays nothing), are small per head in a $16.00-unit model, and dilute VB's already-stretched $440,000 retained profit if margins are thin.

Decision: VB should choose a picking-accuracy bonus for fulfilment staff, reviewed quarterly, rather than across-the-board profit sharing. The returns problem is specific and measurable; a targeted bonus hits it directly, costs less than splitting profits, and fits the flat, autocratically led culture with clear targets and instant feedback. Profit sharing is rejected as the primary lever because it rewards diffuse outcomes, pays out for drivers VB cannot attribute to individuals, and weakens the urgent focus needed before the flagship store doubles order volume; VB can add a modest annual profit-sharing payout later, once the returns rate falls below 8%.
    Keywords: 13%, returns abuse, workforce of 38, $34.60, flat structure, autocratic leadership
    Mark scheme: level_1_1_to_4: Basic description of the two motivation methods with limited application to VB. | level_2_5_to_8: Detailed analysis of the benefits and drawbacks of one or both methods in the context of VB. | level_3_9_to_12: Comprehensive evaluation of both methods in the context of VB with a well-justified decision explaining why profit sharing is rejected as the primary lever and a picking-accuracy bonus is preferred.

  Q3(b) [12 marks]
    Question: Using Appendix 2, evaluate VB's financial position by calculating the current ratio and the acid test ratio for 2024 and 2025. Has VB's financial position improved? Justify your answer.
    Answer: Calculations:

  Q4(a) [8 marks]
    Question: Explain one advantage and one disadvantage for VB of introducing refillable skincare packaging for its core moisturiser range.

    Answer: Interest rate rise (from 4.1% to 4.9%): VB carries no variable-rate bank debt — the $480,000 venture capital is equity and the $440,000 retained profit is free — so the direct interest impact is negligible. The rise instead makes later borrowing (for stock lines or store expansion) pricier and may cool consumers' willingness to use credit for premium beauty, though online beauty spending still grew 9.3%. Minimum wage increase (6.3% rise to $13.87 per hour from April 2026): VB's 38 staff span fulfilment packers, customer service and, from opening day, store advisors and till staff on hourly contracts. Only a minority of the team is salaried; the fulfilment and store floor is largely hourly. Input-cost inflation (10.8% rise in botanicals and packaging): botanical extracts and active ingredients dominate VB's $7.00 variable cost per unit — roughly $4.60 of it is spent on raw ingredients and jars. A 10.8% rise adds close to $0.50 per unit, or about $22,000 a year on 44,000 units, and squeezes the $9.00 contribution per unit toward $8.50. Worse, cosmetics-price inflation is 6.6%, so VB cannot fully pass the increase on without breaking its mid-market positioning against cheaper supermarket skincare.

Conclusion: The 10.8% rise in botanical input costs will have the greatest impact on VB. At roughly $22,000 a year it exceeds the $16,400 wage rise and the negligible interest effect, it is inseparable from product quality (the core of VB's reputation), and it compounds with every unit sold online and in-store. VB should respond by locking 12-month botanical supply contracts, introducing a small, phased price increase concentrated on hero products, launching a refill programme where consumers accept higher value per pump, and expanding margin-accretive accessories — while fixing store rosters efficiently so the wage increase stays a manageable second threat.

--- MAIN STEM ---
Seabrook Coastal Hotels (SCH) is a private limited company in the hospitality and hotel sector, employing a workforce of 160. Founded in 2004 by Dana Whitmore, the group operates three coastal hotels along the shoreline and uses a flat organisational structure with autocratic leadership from Dana Whitmore. SCH plans to invest $1,200,000 in refurbishing its flagship cliff-top hotel and adding a new wedding and events wing, financed by a $750,000 twelve-year bank loan and $450,000 retained profit. It has fixed costs of $2,490,000 a year, a variable cost of $62 a unit and a selling price of $145, and currently produces 58,000 units a year (one unit is one occupied room-night). SCH faces two problems: seasonal staff turnover has reached 34% and absenteeism stands at 10%, and wedding enquiries are being lost to a rival events venue.

--- APPENDIX 1 — MARKETING/OPS ---
Operations Log — Q3 2026: SCH's hotels sold 15,080 room-nights at an average occupancy of 71%, up from 63% a year ago. Wedding and events bookings reached 46 this quarter, up from 29 a year ago. Guest complaints fell from 34 to 19 per month, and average check-in time is 6 minutes. Market research of 800 guests found 58% would pay up to $25 more per night for a refurbished sea-view room, and review scores average 8.4 out of 10 across 2,300 reviews. Training needs analysis shows 28 of 160 staff have not completed on-the-job training on the new wedding catering systems; college courses cost $1,100 per employee.

  Q1(a) [8 marks]
    Question: SCH plans to finance part of its refurbishment and wedding wing with a twelve-year bank loan. Explain two advantages for SCH of using retained profit to fund the expansion instead of the bank loan.
    Answer: Point 1: Using retained profit avoids all interest charges on the $750,000 bank loan, so the twelve-year commitment does not add to SCH's $2,490,000 fixed costs at a time when food and energy costs have already risen 9.8%. Every dollar SCH saves on interest can be redirected to the refurbishment and to absorbing the 5.9% rise in the minimum wage to $12.85, protecting the group's $83 contribution ($145 − $62) on each occupied room-night and keeping room rates at $145 competitive for domestic coastal tourists, whose spending grew 4.2% this year.

Point 2: Retained profit involves no collateral, so Dana Whitmore does not risk losing the flagship cliff-top hotel or its new wedding and events wing if trading becomes difficult during quieter winter months. It also preserves complete ownership and control for SCH's existing shareholders, avoids the lender imposing conditions on how the wing is run, and leaves the option of a bank loan open later if wedding bookings exceed the 46 already recorded in Q3 2026.

Local newspaper advertising: Local newspapers are cheap, reach the regional audience most likely to book sea-view weekend breaks and local weddings, and suit a grand-opening offer for the wing. Their limitation is narrow circulation and an ageing readership, so they would do little for the 58% of researched guests willing to pay more for sea-view rooms who live further afield, and they cannot showcase the wing visually in a competitive events market.

Social media influencer marketing: Partnering with wedding-planner influencers and coastal-lifestyle creators targets exactly the couples researching venues online, reaches a national audience for far less than TV, and provides measurable engagement, booking enquiries and review traction; the 8.4 average review score and rising occupancy of 71% give influencers strong proof to share. It depends on influencer authenticity and takes longer to compound than TV, but the cost per engaged couple is low.

Recommendation: SCH should choose social media influencer marketing. It speaks directly to wedding planners and couples nationally at a cost SCH can afford alongside its bank loan, reinforces the review-driven reputation (8.4/10), and shows the wing visually. Television is rejected as unaffordable and untargeted for a $1,200,000 project financed partly by debt; local newspapers are rejected as too narrow for a tiered national events market, though SCH can add low-cost local print for community weddings once the launch quietens.

Point 2: Training away from the hotel — for example in wedding catering systems and customer service — means the 28 staff who have not completed on-the-job training can learn without disrupting guests in the refurbished rooms.   Q2(b) [12 marks]
    Question: SCH is opening its wedding and events wing and needs staff for it. Consider recruiting more seasonal temporary staff or training and promoting existing permanent staff to lead the wing. Which should SCH choose? Justify your decision.
    Answer: Seasonal temporary staff: Hiring seasonal workers matches SCH's existing summer-peak pattern and keeps immediate wage costs low, which suits a wing that will be busiest at weekends and during wedding season. Promote and train existing permanent staff: Promoting from within rewards loyalty, fills the 28-person training gap identified in the needs analysis, and retains SCH's service culture and 8.4 review score for critical events. Promotion satisfies esteem needs (Maslow) and reduces labour turnover by giving staff a career path into events management.   Q3(a) [8 marks]
    Question: Calculate and explain how SCH's management can use its cost, break-even and productivity data.
    Answer: (i) Break-even output = 30,000 units a year, computed as $2,490,000 fixed costs divided by $83 contribution per room-night (selling price $145 less variable cost $62). At the current 58,000-unit output, SCH operates a margin of safety of 28,000 units, so room-night revenue comfortably covers both fixed and variable costs. (ii) Contribution per unit = $83 per occupied room-night, which is what every sold room-night contributes toward fixed costs and, after that, profit. (iii) Four applied uses: first, tracking the margin of safety ahead of the $750,000 bank loan repayments for the flagship refurbishment; second, modelling weekday coastal-holiday discounts where each $15 price cut reduces contribution to $68 ($130 − $62); third, setting rate and package targets for the new wedding and events wing so packages cover fixed costs after interest at 5.75%; fourth, unit-cost benchmarking at $104.93 ($2,490,000 ÷ 58,000 + $62) to locate food and energy overspends behind the 9.8% input-cost rise. Together these uses let Dana Whitmore test whether the hotel and wing stay above break-even through the quieter winter months while the $1,200,000 refurbishment is delivered.

  Q3(b) [12 marks]
    Question: Using Appendix 2, evaluate SCH's financial position by calculating the current ratio and the acid test ratio for 2024 and 2025. Has SCH's financial position improved? Justify your answer.
    Answer: Calculations:
Current Ratio 2024 = 1.53 : 1
Current Ratio 2025 = 1.83 : 1
Acid Test Ratio 2024 = 0.97 : 1
Acid Test Ratio 2025 = 1.36 : 1

Detailed workings: 2024 current assets = $210,000 inventories + $240,000 trade receivables + $130,000 cash = $580,000; 2025 current assets = $165,000 + $285,000 + $190,000 = $640,000. Current liabilities were $380,000 in 2024 and fell to $350,000 in 2025. 2024: $580,000 ÷ $380,000 = 1.53; 2025: $640,000 ÷ $350,000 = 1.83. The stricter measure excluding inventories: 2024 = ($580,000 − $210,000) ÷ $380,000 = $370,000 ÷ $380,000 = 0.97; 2025 = ($640,000 − $165,000) ÷ $350,000 = $475,000 ÷ $350,000 = 1.36.

Evaluation: Liquidity has strengthened considerably. Current assets cover short-term debts much more comfortably, aided by inventories falling from $210,000 to $165,000 and cash rising to $190,000, showing tighter stock control in hotel kitchens and stronger room-revenue collection. The stricter measure improved from below 1.0 to 1.36, meaning SCH can now meet short-term debts without selling food and beverage stock — important while it services a $750,000 twelve-year bank loan at a base rate of 5.75%. Two cautions remain: trade receivables rose from $240,000 to $285,000, so corporate wedding and events deposits must be collected promptly, and current liabilities of $350,000 still exceed cash alone.

Conclusion: SCH's financial position has improved. Both measures show stronger short-term solvency in 2025 and the improvement is not reliant on inventory. SCH should maintain the gain by tightening credit control on events deposits and preserving cash to fund the $1,200,000 refurbishment, which protects the occupancy and wedding bookings underpinning it.

  Q4(a) [8 marks]
    Question: Explain one advantage and one disadvantage for SCH of refurbishing with sustainable eco-friendly materials for its flagship cliff-top hotel.
    Answer: Advantage: Sustainable refurbishment matches the 58% of researched guests willing to pay up to $25 more per night for a refurbished sea-view room, many of whom actively choose hotels with credible environmental credentials. SCH can therefore hold or raise its $145 room rate, protecting the $83 contribution ($145 − $62) per occupied room-night even as food and energy costs rose 9.8%, and the eco-story strengthens the 8.4 review score and SCH's bid to win premium coastal wedding contracts over rival venues.

Disadvantage: Eco-materials such as certified timber, low-energy glazing and water-saving systems typically cost more than conventional fittings, so part of the $1,200,000 budget — already stretched by the $750,000 bank loan — would be consumed before the wing opens. If sustainable fittings fail early or deliver poorer soundproofing or durability, SCH's complaints (already down, but still 19 per month) could rise again, damaging the guest experience precisely when it is trying to convert the 71% occupancy into a higher sea-view price and fill the wedding and events wing with premium bookings.

  Q4(b) [12 marks]
    Question: Using Appendix 3, evaluate how the interest rate rise to 5.75%, the 5.9% minimum wage increase to $12.85 and the 9.8% rise in food and energy input costs will affect SCH. Which change will have the greatest impact? Justify your answer.
    Answer: Interest rate rise (5.0% to 5.75%): If SCH's $750,000 twelve-year bank loan is variable-rate, the 0.75 percentage-point rise adds about $5,625 a year in interest ($750,000 × 0.75% = $5,625), lifting the fixed-cost burden above $2,490,000. Higher rates also make premium coastal breaks less tempting for cautious visitors and raise the cost of any further borrowing for the refurbishment. The direct cash impact is modest, can be capped by fixing the loan rate, and is fully computable from insert figures — unlike the other two factors, it does not erode the $83 contribution ($145 − $62) per room-night.

Minimum wage increase (5.9%, to $12.85 per hour from April 2026): Appendix 3 gives both the old and new rates, so the hourly delta is exactly $0.70 ($12.85 − $12.15 = $0.70). The exact annual cost cannot be computed from the insert, because the headcount and hours paid at the minimum wage are not stated; what can be shown is the threshold at which this factor overtakes the interest rise — it does so once SCH pays more than roughly 8,036 minimum-wage hours a year ($5,625 ÷ $0.70 ≈ 8,036), a level plainly exceeded by a seasonal 160-employee hotel across a full trading year. In Maslow's terms, financial reward helps but does not cure the 10% absenteeism driven by motivation or the 34% seasonal staff turnover, so the rise is real but manageable through engagement and productivity.

Food and energy input costs (up 9.8% year-on-year): Appendix 3 names wholesale food and energy explicitly, and SCH's $62 variable cost per room-night will include ingredients, utilities and catering. No component share is given anywhere in the insert, so the honest bound runs from $0 (if no named input applied — implausible for a full-service hotel) to a labelled upper bound of applying the whole 9.8% to the entire $62: at most about $6.08 per room-night ($62 × 9.8% = $6.08), which over the current 58,000 room-nights would cap the damage at roughly $352,640 a year (58,000 × $6.08). The true figure lies between these bounds and cannot be pinned further without inventing a share; what is certain is that every matching input rises together for every room-night sold, that SCH cannot refinance this away the way it can fix the loan rate, and that it lands precisely when the $1,200,000 refurbishment pressure is highest.

Conclusion: The 9.8% rise in food and energy input costs will have the greatest impact. Unlike the interest rise, which is exactly $5,625 a year and fixable, and unlike the wage floor, whose exposure is limited to minimum-wage hours, input inflation applies continuously to every one of the 58,000 room-nights sold and to every offer SCH makes in the domestic coastal-holiday market where consumer spending grew 4.2%. Quantifying it precisely is impossible from the insert, but even a partially exposed $62 variable cost dwarfs $5,625, and the 9.8% figure is the steepest of the two percentage rises SCH can act on for all sales volumes. SCH should respond with supplier renegotiation, waste reduction in kitchens, selective sea-view price rises (58% of researched guests accept up to $25 more) and menu engineering, while treating the minimum-wage increase — significant but smaller — as second priority and the interest-rate motion as the smallest of the three.
    Keywords: 5.75%, 5.9%, 9.8%, $12.85, $750,000, $1,200,000
    Mark scheme: level_1_1_to_4: Identifies the external factors with limited application to SCH. | level_2_5_to_8: Analyses the impact of at least two external changes on SCH's costs, revenue or financing in context. | level_3_9_to_12: Detailed evaluation of all three external changes in the context of SCH with a well-justified judgement that input-cost inflation has the greatest impact and why the other two are smaller.

--- MAIN STEM ---
Acacia Trails Safari Lodge (ATSL) is a cooperative in the hospitality and tourism sector, employing a workforce of 85. Founded in 2011 by Sipho Dlamini, the lodge is owned and run by its staff-members and uses a flat organisational structure with democratic leadership, where staff vote on major decisions at monthly meetings. ATSL plans to invest $980,000 in a new tented eco-camp on adjacent land, financed by a $600,000 ten-year bank loan and a $380,000 member share issue. It has fixed costs of $4,970,000 a year, a variable cost of $88 a unit and a selling price of $230, and currently produces 46,000 units a year (one unit is one occupied guest-night). ATSL faces two problems: experienced safari guides are being poached by rival lodges, and absenteeism stands at 8%.

--- APPENDIX 1 — MARKETING/OPS ---
Market Research Summary (October 2026): ATSL surveyed 540 recent guests; 71% would pay up to $30 more per guest-night for a tented eco-camp stay, and 84% named the guided wildlife experience as the lodge's strongest feature. Average occupancy is 66% against a target of 75%. Review scores average 8.8 out of 10 across 1,240 online reviews, and repeat guests generate 44% of annual bookings. Direct bookings via the lodge website rose 27% after a site relaunch. The worst-rated aspect was breakfast variety, mentioned in 18% of comments.

--- APPENDIX 2 — FINANCIAL DATA ---
Title: Extract from the Statement of Financial Position of Acacia Trails Safari Lodge as at 31 March 2025 ($ '000)
Headers: ['Financial Metric', '2024', '2025']
Inventories | 140 | 120
Trade receivables | 160 | 150
Cash and cash equivalents | 220 | 260
Current liabilities | 310 | 300
Non-current assets | 3,900 | 4,700
Capital employed | 5,300 | 5,950

--- APPENDIX 3 — EXTERNAL ENVIRONMENT ---
Economic and Business Bulletin (November 2026): (1) The central bank has raised the base interest rate from 5.25% to 6.0%, raising borrowing costs for the lodge's variable-rate ten-year bank loan. (2) The national minimum wage will rise by 7.5% from $9.25 to $9.60 per hour from May 2026, lifting pay for lodge, catering and maintenance staff. (3) Diesel, park permit and laundry input costs have risen 11.2% year-on-year, while eco-tourism consumer spending in the region grew 6.8% in the same period.

--- QUESTIONS ---
  Q1(a) [8 marks]
    Question: ATSL plans to finance part of its tented eco-camp expansion with a member share issue. Explain two advantages for ATSL of using a member share issue instead of a ten-year bank loan.
    Answer: Point 1: A member share issue raises $380,000 from the staff-owners themselves, with no interest to pay and no fixed repayment timetable, unlike the $600,000 ten-year bank loan. This protects ATSL's $4,970,000 fixed costs — already stretched by the 11.2% rise in diesel, park permit and laundry input costs and the 7.5% minimum wage increase — and means the cooperative is never at risk of default if tented eco-camp bookings start slowly at the 66% occupancy level.

Point 2: Share capital from members deepens commitment: staff-owners who buy in financially have a direct stake in the new camp's success, supporting the democratic culture at monthly meetings and reducing the risk of guides being poached, because leaving would mean giving up member status. No bank can seize ATSL's land or lodge if times are hard, and democratic control stays fully with members rather than passing to an outside lender imposing covenants.
    Keywords: member share issue, bank loan, $380,000, $600,000, tented eco-camp, 66%
    Mark scheme: knowledge_max_2: 1 mark for each valid advantage identified (max 2). | application_analysis_max_6: Up to 3 marks per point for contextual explanation and analysis applied to Acacia Trails Safari Lodge and its expansion decision.

  Q1(b) [12 marks]
    Question: ATSL is launching its new tented eco-camp. Consider national newspaper advertising, social media influencer marketing, or exhibiting at a regional travel trade show. Which should ATSL choose to promote the launch? Justify your recommendation.
    Answer: National newspaper advertising: Major national papers would give ATSL broad awareness among potential eco-tourists across the country and suit a grand-opening story with beautiful photography of the tented camp. However, full-page colour rates are high for a cooperative with 85 employees funding $980,000 of expansion partly by bank loan, and papers reach a broad, untargeted audience including many people who will never book a safari; measured response rates for print advertising are weak.

Social media influencer marketing: Working with eco-travel and safari influencers targets exactly the 71% of surveyed past guests willing to pay up to $30 more per guest-night, uses the lodge's 8.8 review score and 1,240 reviews as persuasive proof, and produces measurable enquiries at low cost per reached viewer. It suits repeat and younger eco-tourists and amplifies the website's 27% direct-booking growth. Risks are influencer credibility and slower trust-building for luxury-price segments.

Travel trade show exhibition: A regional trade show puts ATSL directly in front of tour operators, corporate travel buyers and travel agents who package safari holidays, potentially securing group bookings and shoulder-season volume. Costs of stand space, travel and samples are moderate, and leads can be converted by follow-up. However, shows are episodic, reach a trade rather than consumer audience, and do little for direct repeat-guest marketing.

Recommendation: ATSL should choose social media influencer marketing. It reaches the precise eco-conscious segment identified in its research at the lowest cost per enquiry, leverages its 8.8/10 ratings and 44% repeat-guest base, and compounds with the website's direct bookings. Newspapers are rejected as too broad and expensive for the budget; the trade show is rejected as too narrow and episodic to fill the camp alone, though ATSL should attend one show a year to win operator contracts once the influencer campaign is live.
    Keywords: tented eco-camp, 71%, 8.8, 44%, $30, eco-tourism
    Mark scheme: level_1_1_to_4: Limited knowledge or outline of the promotional options with minimal context. | level_2_5_to_8: Detailed discussion of the advantages and disadvantages of at least two options in the context of ATSL with some judgement. | level_3_9_to_12: Detailed discussion of all three options in the context of ATSL with a well-justified recommendation explaining why newspaper advertising and the trade show are rejected.

  Q2(a) [8 marks]
    Question: ATSL's experienced safari guides are being poached by rival lodges and absenteeism stands at 8%. Explain two benefits for ATSL of using job enrichment for its safari guides.
    Answer: Point 1: Job enrichment gives guides greater responsibility — designing their own game-drive routes, leading guest safety briefings and mentoring junior staff — which satisfies their esteem and self-actualisation needs (Maslow) and raises the meaning of the work. Guides who feel trusted and challenged are far less likely to accept offers from rival lodges, directly reducing the poaching problem and the $4,970,000 cost pressure of repeatedly recruiting and certifying replacement guides.

Point 2: Enriched guides become more committed and proactive, improving the quality of the wildlife experience that 84% of surveyed guests rated as ATSL's strongest feature. They spot maintenance issues earlier, upsell the tented eco-camp and handle guest problems without escalation, supporting the 8.8 review score and 66% occupancy rate. Better motivation also tackles the 8% absenteeism directly, since staff with ownership over their role call in sick far less often than those doing repetitive, low-autonomy work. Enrichment is cheaper than across-the-board pay rises while the 7.5% minimum wage increase phases in, and it strengthens the cooperative's democratic culture, because empowered guides gain real influence rather than token consultation at monthly meetings.
    Keywords: safari guides, absenteeism, 8%, 8.8, 66%, poached
    Mark scheme: knowledge_max_2: 1 mark for each valid benefit identified (max 2). | application_analysis_max_6: Up to 3 marks per point for detailed contextual development linked to ATSL's poaching problem, absenteeism and guest experience.

  Q2(b) [12 marks]
    Question: ATSL must recruit two senior head guides for the new tented eco-camp. Consider recruiting externally from rival lodges or promoting and training existing junior guides from within the cooperative. Which should ATSL choose? Justify your decision.
    Answer: External recruitment from rival lodges: Hiring already-proven head guides would bring immediate expertise, fresh ideas and established guest-handling skills, and could lift the tented camp's credibility from opening day; it also avoids the temporary productivity dip of internal promotion. However, rival-poached guides may carry rivals' habits rather than ATSL's democratic, community-owned values, would demand head-guide salaries well above existing internal rates, and — having been poached once themselves — may be poached again, recreating the exact instability ATSL is trying to solve.

Promoting and training existing junior guides: Internal promotion rewards the loyalty of members who built the lodge since 2011, costs less in salary shocks, and firmly strengthens democratic commitment and retention — the key defence against rival poaching. Training gaps can be closed with off-the-job courses, and the flat structure means promoted guides can genuinely influence tented-camp operations. The risks are a slower capability build-up, internal jealousy if the selection is not transparent, and the need to backfill the vacated junior roles.

Decision: ATSL should choose promoting and training existing junior guides. It directly counters the poaching problem, preserves cooperative culture and member trust at monthly meetings, and is far cheaper than market-rate external salaries at a time when the bank loan and share issue already commit $980,000. External recruitment is rejected because it imports flight risk and pay inflation; wholesale external hiring is only justified if no internal candidate meets the camp's guiding certification standard, which the interview data should be checked against first. A phased internal promotion, benchmarked against external salaries, keeps pay fair, transparent and defensible at the monthly members' meeting and signals to every junior guide that the cooperative invests in its own people.
    Keywords: tented eco-camp, poached, democratic, $980,000, member, cooperative
    Mark scheme: level_1_1_to_4: Basic description of the two recruitment approaches with limited application to ATSL. | level_2_5_to_8: Detailed analysis of the benefits and drawbacks of one or both recruitment options in the context of ATSL. | level_3_9_to_12: Comprehensive evaluation of both options in the context of ATSL with a well-justified decision covering cost, culture, retention and capability.

  Q3(b) [12 marks]
    Question: Using Appendix 2, evaluate ATSL's financial position by calculating the current ratio and the acid test ratio for 2024 and 2025. Has ATSL's financial position improved? Justify your answer.
    Answer: Calculations:

Current Ratio 2025 = 1.77 : 1
