Current assets cover current liabilities more comfortably, and cash rose from $220,000 to $260,000 — a healthy cushion for a lodge whose occupancy is still only 66% and which is about to spend $980,000 on the tented eco-camp. The stricter measure rose from 1.23 to 1.37, so ATSL can meet short-term debts without selling food and beverage stock, a strength given the 11.2% rise in input costs. Cautions: trade receivables fell only marginally to $150,000, and any slow-paying corporate retreat bookings could tighten liquidity; current liabilities of $300,000 remain substantial against cash of $260,000, and the bank loan will add annual service charges from year one.

Conclusion: ATSL's financial position has improved. Both measures point to stronger short-term solvency in 2025, supported by lower inventories and lower liabilities. ATSL should protect this by keeping direct bookings growing, collecting agent commissions promptly and ring-fencing the eco-camp budget so the expansion does not erode the improved liquidity position.
    Keywords: 1.68, 1.77, 1.23, 1.37, $520,000, $530,000, $600,000
    Mark scheme: level_1_1_to_4: States financial figures or changes without accurate ratio calculations. | level_2_5_to_8: Accurately calculates the current ratio and acid test ratio for both 2024 and 2025 with contextual analysis of the trend. | level_3_9_to_12: Accurate ratio calculations for both years combined with detailed evaluation of inventory, receivables and liabilities movements and a justified conclusion on whether ATSL's financial position improved.

  Q4(a) [8 marks]
    Question: Explain one advantage and one disadvantage for ATSL of opening the new tented eco-camp on adjacent land.
    Answer: Advantage: The tented eco-camp captures the 71% of surveyed guests willing to pay up to $30 more per guest-night for a tented experience, letting ATSL lift its $230 price point and its $142 contribution ($230 − $88) exactly where eco-tourism spending grew 6.8%. It uses the adjacent land efficiently, spreads fixed costs of $4,970,000 over more guest-nights, and gives ATSL a second product for the 44% repeat-guest base to try on their next stay, strengthening the 66% occupancy toward the 75% target.

Disadvantage: The camp commits $980,000 to new structures, equipment and access tracks before a single guest has stayed, financed partly by a $600,000 ten-year bank loan at a time when the base interest rate has just risen to 6.0%. If the camp launches slowly, its share of fixed costs and interest could outrun its revenue, diverting attention and maintenance capacity from the main lodge, damaging the 8.8 review score that carries ATSL's whole reputation, and straining the cooperative's democratic decision-making if members disagree on how fast to add tent phases.
    Keywords: tented eco-camp, 71%, $30, 66%, $980,000, 6.0%
    Mark scheme: knowledge_max_2: 1 mark for a valid advantage and 1 mark for a valid disadvantage. | application_analysis_max_6: Up to 3 marks per point for detailed contextual development linked to ATSL's research, costs and expansion.

  Q4(b) [12 marks]
    Question: Using Appendix 3, evaluate how the interest rate rise to 6.0%, the 7.5% minimum wage increase to $9.60 and the 11.2% rise in diesel, park permit and laundry input costs will affect ATSL. Which change will have the greatest impact? Justify your answer.
    Answer: Interest rate rise (5.25% to 6.0%): If ATSL's $600,000 ten-year bank loan is variable-rate, the 0.75 percentage-point rise adds about $4,500 a year in interest ($600,000 × 0.75% = $4,500), lifting fixed costs above $4,970,000. Higher rates also make discretionary eco-holidays slightly less tempting and would raise the cost of drawing down any remaining borrowing for the tented eco-camp. The absolute impact is the smallest of the three and can be managed by fixing the loan rate or by repaying early from member share capital, and unlike the other two factors it does not erode the $142 contribution ($230 − $88) per guest-night.

Minimum wage increase (7.5%, to $9.60 per hour from May 2026): Appendix 3 states both rates, so the hourly delta is exactly $0.35 ($9.60 − $9.25 = $0.35), the largest percentage rise of the three factors. The annual cost cannot be computed from the insert because the number of hours paid at the minimum wage is not stated; what can be shown is the break-even against the interest rise — the wage factor exceeds $4,500 once ATSL pays more than roughly 12,857 minimum-wage hours a year ($4,500 ÷ $0.35 ≈ 12,857 hours), a threshold comfortably exceeded by an 85-employee lodge with catering, laundry and maintenance staff. Because the lodge is a cooperative founded on fair member pay, absorbed wages are partly a governance commitment, not just an HR line item; compliance is non-negotiable and the 8% absenteeism makes any pay friction internally damaging.

Diesel, park permit and laundry input costs (up 11.2% year-on-year): Appendix 3 specifically names diesel, park permits and laundry — the exact running costs of game drives, guest access and linen service, all essential to a safari operation. No share of the $88 variable cost is stated, so the correct bound runs from $0 to an upper bound built on insert figures: applying the full 11.2% to the entire $88 gives at most about $9.86 per guest-night ($88 × 11.2% = $9.86), capping the damage at roughly $453,376 a year at the current 46,000 unit output (46,000 × $9.86). The true figure lies between the bounds; the insert permits no finer split, and any assumed share would be invented. What is certain is that these inputs recur on every game drive and every occupied room, concentrate in the $88 variable cost rather than in the $4,970,000 fixed costs, and cannot be switched to a cheaper park or laundered linens.

Conclusion: The 11.2% rise in diesel, park permit and laundry input costs will have the greatest impact. It is the steepest percentage increase named in Appendix 3, recurrences on every one of 46,000 guest-nights, escapes refinancing, and — unlike the wage factor, whose cash effect is limited to minimum-wage hours at $0.35 each — applies to all consumption regardless of who delivers it. Supplier renegotiation, route efficiencies, on-site laundry for the tented eco-camp and selective price increases (71% of surveyed guests accept up to $30 more per night) are the levers ATSL must pull; the 7.5% wage rise is the second serious pressure in an 85-member cooperative already fighting poaching, and the $4,500 interest-rate effect is the smallest of the three and can be neutralised by fixing the loan.
    Keywords: 6.0%, 7.5%, 11.2%, $9.60, $600,000, $980,000
    Mark scheme: level_1_1_to_4: Identifies the external factors with limited application to ATSL. | level_2_5_to_8: Analyses the impact of at least two external changes on ATSL's costs, revenue or financing in context. | level_3_9_to_12: Detailed evaluation of all three external changes in the context of ATSL with a well-justified judgement that input-cost inflation has the greatest impact and why the other two are smaller.

--- MAIN STEM ---
Embers and Oak Restaurant Group (EORG) is a private limited company in the hospitality and restaurant sector, employing a workforce of 120. Founded in 2013 by Meera Kapoor, the group runs four casual-dining restaurants in regional cities and uses a hierarchical organisational structure with democratic leadership, where restaurant managers vote on menu changes. EORG plans to invest $750,000 in launching a franchise programme for its flagship brand, financed by a $450,000 bank loan and $300,000 retained profit. It has fixed costs of $2,100,000 a year, a variable cost of $9.50 a unit and a selling price of $24.50, and currently produces 260,000 units a year (one unit is one meal served). EORG faces two problems: two head chefs were poached by a rival chain in October 2026, and kitchen absenteeism stands at 12%.

--- APPENDIX 1 — MARKETING/OPS ---
Advertisement Extract — Weekend Herald, November 2026: 'Embers and Oak — family dining from $14.90 a head; two-for-one mains on Tuesdays; free children's dessert on Sundays; loyalty card gives 10% off every fifth visit.' Operations note: the four restaurants served 62,400 covers in Q3 2026, average spend was $31.60 per cover, food-waste rate is 6.8%, and 78% of 500 surveyed diners rated the group 'very good'; repeat visits account for 57% of trade. The food-cost complaint rate is 2.1%, down from 3.4% a year ago.

--- APPENDIX 2 — FINANCIAL DATA ---

(2) The national minimum wage will rise by 6.2% from $10.40 to $11.05 per hour from April 2026, raising wage bills for front-of-house and kitchen staff. (3) Wholesale protein, dairy and fresh produce prices have risen 10.6% year-on-year, while consumer spending on dining out grew 2.9% in the same period.

--- QUESTIONS ---
  Q1(a) [8 marks]
    Question: EORG plans to finance part of its franchise programme launch with a bank loan. Explain two advantages for EORG of using retained profit to fund the expansion instead of the bank loan.
    Answer: Point 1: Retained profit costs EORG nothing in interest, which matters because wholesale protein, dairy and fresh produce prices have already risen 10.6% and eating-out inflation pressures diners; EORG's $2,100,000 fixed costs and the $450,000 bank loan commitment would otherwise squeeze the margin on its $24.50 average selling price even faster. Keeping the franchise launch interest-free preserves cash for marketing the flagship brand and for absorbing the $31.60 average cover spend that keeps repeat visits at 57% of trade.

Point 2: Using $300,000 of retained profit avoids collateral and lender conditions on the franchise programme, so Meera Kapoor and the four restaurant managers retain full control over brand standards, franchise fees and menu voting decisions. It also leaves borrowing capacity unused, which is valuable given the base interest rate just rose to 6.25% and EORG may need faster, flexible funding later if the first franchised sites underperform or if poached head chefs need replacing urgently.
    Keywords: retained profit, bank loan, $300,000, $450,000, franchise programme, $750,000

  Q1(b) [12 marks]
    Question: EORG is launching its franchise programme for the flagship brand. Consider national television advertising, print advertising in weekend newspaper supplements, or social media influencer marketing. Which should EORG choose to promote the launch? Justify your recommendation.
    Answer: National television advertising: TV would give EORG the fastest, widest awareness of the franchise opportunity, reaching entrepreneurs and potential franchisees nationwide and lending the group a trustworthy, established image. However, production and airtime are very expensive for four restaurants and 120 employees financing $750,000 of expansion partly on a $450,000 bank loan, and much of a national audience is not a prospective franchisee or regular diner at $31.60 per cover; coverage waste would be high.

Print advertising in weekend supplements: Weekend titles reach an affluent, food-interested readership, suit detailed franchise-opportunity storytelling with founder Meera Kapoor's narrative, and match EORG's existing 'Weekend Herald' presence (the two-for-one Tuesdays and loyalty card offer already in the insert). Print is cheaper than TV but still costly per response, and readership skew older, missing younger franchise candidates and younger diners who drive Tuesday two-for-one trade.

Social media influencer marketing: Food-influencer partnerships show the dining experience authentically video-first, target the 78% of surveyed diners rating the group 'very good', cost far less than TV, and can be measured precisely through bookings, loyalty-card sign-ups and franchise enquiries. Credibility risk exists if an influencer misrepresents the brand, but alignment with food creators who genuinely rate Embers and Oak is inexpensive and highly targeted.

Recommendation: EORG should choose social media influencer marketing. It proves the brand visually to exactly the diners and franchise prospects most likely to convert, leverages the 57% repeat-visit base and 2.1% complaint rate down-trend, and fits a $750,000 programme without exhausting the $450,000 bank loan. Television is rejected as untargeted and unaffordable; print supplements are rejected as too narrow and older-skewing for franchise recruitment, though EORG should keep targeted print for franchise-opportunity sections where serious investors read.
    Keywords: franchise programme, $750,000, 78%, 57%, $450,000, $31.60

Staff who share profits think like owners: they control portion waste (the food-waste rate is 6.8%), police prep standards and support each other through service, reducing the desperation to defect to the rival's higher salaries and tackling the 12% kitchen absenteeism caused by disengagement.

Point 2: Profit sharing aligns the four restaurants behind shared goals, reinforcing the hierarchical-yet-democratic structure by rewarding managers democratically and kitchen crews collectively. It is cheaper than across-the-board wage rises amid the 6.2% minimum wage increase to $11.05 and the 10.6% food inflation, yet it binds key staff to the franchise plan: ambitious cooks see a bonus future inside EORG rather than leaving, which protects the 57% repeat-diner base and the $31.60 average spend that franchisee recruits will be buying into.

Meera Kapoor should also publish the selection criteria to all kitchen teams within a week of the decision, rebuilding trust after October's poaching and showing every cook that advancement exists inside Embers and Oak.

    Question: Using Appendix 2, evaluate EORG's financial position by calculating the current ratio and the acid test ratio for 2024 and 2025. Has EORG's financial position improved? Justify your answer.
    Answer: Calculations:
Current Ratio 2024 = 1.21 : 1
Current Ratio 2025 = 1.29 : 1
Acid Test Ratio 2024 = 0.85 : 1

Excluding inventories: 2024 = ($315,000 − $95,000) ÷ $260,000 = $220,000 ÷ $260,000 = 0.85; 2025 = ($400,000 − $110,000) ÷ $310,000 = $290,000 ÷ $310,000 = 0.94.

Trade receivables rose to $170,000 — mostly corporate catering and franchise set-up fees — so collection discipline is now essential.

Conclusion: EORG's financial position has improved, but only modestly. EORG should collect receivables aggressively, hold supplier payments as negotiated, and avoid drawing more than its $450,000 bank loan before the franchise royalty income materialises.

  Q4(a) [8 marks]

    Question: Using Appendix 3, evaluate how the interest rate rise to 6.25%, the 6.2% minimum wage increase to $11.05 and the 10.6% rise in protein, dairy and fresh produce input costs will affect EORG. Which change will have the greatest impact? Justify your answer.
    Answer: Interest rate rise (5.5% to 6.25%): On EORG's $450,000 bank loan, the 0.75 percentage-point rise adds about $3,375 a year in interest ($450,000 × 0.75% = $3,375), lifting fixed costs above $2,100,000. Conclusion: The 10.6% rise in protein, dairy and fresh produce input costs will have the greatest impact. PAPER 2 — P2_SET_119
UNIT: Paper 2 Case Study

--- MAIN STEM ---
Galaxy Lanes and Screens (GLS) is a sole trader in the leisure and entertainment sector, employing a workforce of 55. Founded in 2008 by Marcus Whitfield, GLS operates an independent cinema and ten-lane bowling venue attracting families and students, and uses a flat organisational structure with laissez-faire leadership, where staff organise their own shifts and events. GLS plans to invest $680,000 in refurbishing the bowling alley and installing two new 4K screens, financed by a $400,000 bank loan and $280,000 hire purchase on the projection equipment. It has fixed costs of $1,950,000 a year, a variable cost of $5.50 a unit and a selling price of $18.50, and currently produces 185,000 units a year (one unit is one ticketed visit). GLS faces two problems: casual evening and weekend staff absenteeism stands at 13%, and private-party bookings are being lost to a rival entertainment centre.

--- APPENDIX 1 — MARKETING/OPS ---
Operations Log — October 2026: GLS sold 16,800 cinema tickets and 9,200 bowling games in Q3; screen occupancy averaged 34% and concession waste is 5.2%. Customer complaints fell from 94 to 61 per month. Market research of 720 visitors found 57% would pay up to $3 more for recliner seating in screen 1, and 48% said the bowling area needs updating; 73 private parties were booked this quarter, up from 41. Review scores average 4.3 out of 5 across 2,150 reviews. Weekend family passes bundle cinema plus one bowling game for $29.

--- APPENDIX 2 — FINANCIAL DATA ---
Title: Extract from the Statement of Financial Position of Galaxy Lanes and Screens as at 31 March 2025 ($ '000)
Headers: ['Financial Metric', '2024', '2025']
Inventories | 60 | 55
Trade receivables | 45 | 60
Cash and cash equivalents | 75 | 105
Current liabilities | 150 | 165
Non-current assets | 2,600 | 3,100
Capital employed | 3,100 | 3,600

--- APPENDIX 3 — EXTERNAL ENVIRONMENT ---
Economic and Business Bulletin (November 2026): (1) The central bank has raised the base interest rate from 5.75% to 6.5%, raising borrowing costs on variable-rate expansion loans. (2) The national minimum wage will rise by 5.5% from $10.24 to $10.80 per hour from April 2026, raising wage bills for casual evening and weekend staff. (3) Commercial electricity and heating prices have risen 13.4% year-on-year, while consumer spending on leisure and entertainment grew 3.1% in the same period.

--- QUESTIONS ---
  Q1(a) [8 marks]
    Question: GLS plans to finance part of the refurbishment with hire purchase on the projection equipment. Explain two advantages for GLS of using hire purchase instead of a bank loan.
    Answer: Point 1: Hire purchase spreads the $280,000 projection equipment cost over fixed monthly instalments matched to the screens' earning life, so GLS does not need to commit such a large lump sum from a $400,000 bank loan. This keeps more of the bank loan available for the bowling refurbishment and for absorbing the 13.4% rise in electricity and heating prices — critical for a venue where the two new 4K screens will run for long evening sessions.

Point 2: GLS gains immediate ownership-style use of the equipment while paying, so the screens can open before full payment is made; interest is built into the instalments, making budgeting predictable; and if cash flow disappoints, the hire purchase provider — not a court — repossesses only the equipment. Unlike a bank loan, no additional collateral over the whole venue is required, preserving GLS's independence as a sole trader under Marcus Whitfield's control and protecting the $5.50 variable cost economics of concession sales that fund the investment.
    Keywords: hire purchase, bank loan, $280,000, $400,000, refurbishing, 4K screens
    Mark scheme: knowledge_max_2: 1 mark for each valid advantage identified (max 2). | application_analysis_max_6: Up to 3 marks per point for contextual explanation and analysis applied to Galaxy Lanes and Screens and its refurbishment decision.

  Q1(b) [12 marks]
    Question: GLS is reopening after its refurbishment with two new 4K screens and an updated bowling alley. Consider local radio advertising, community poster and flyer marketing, or social media marketing. Which should GLS choose to promote the reopening? Justify your recommendation.
    Answer: Local radio advertising: Local radio reaches commuters and families across GLS's catchment with frequent, memorable audio spots, and it suits time-sensitive opening offers such as the $29 weekend family pass. It is cheaper than TV and can be repeated heavily, but its audio-only format cannot show the new 4K screens or recliner seating, audience targeting is broad, and younger cinema-goers listen to streaming services rather than local radio.

Community poster and flyer marketing: Posters in schools, colleges, libraries and supermarkets reach exactly the family and student audiences that fill screen 1 and the bowling lanes on weekends. Print is very cheap, locally credible and easy for a sole trader to execute with volunteers; however, reach is small and passive, response is hard to measure, and print cannot compete with video for showcasing the 4K experience or the updated bowling area.

Social media marketing: Organic posts plus paid promotion on social platforms show the recliners, screens and bowling lanes in short video, target families and students within a chosen radius, and let GLS retarget past visitors using the 4.3 out of 5 review audience and the 73 private parties in Q3. Cost is low and results are measurable through ticket sales; the risk is that constant content creation eats staff time under a laissez-faire structure with only 55 employees.

Recommendation: GLS should choose social media marketing. It visually sells the refurbishment that $680,000 bought, reaches both segments (students and families) precisely and measurably, leverages the 4.3 review base and $29 family-pass bundle, and costs far less than radio while outrunning print's passive reach. Radio is rejected as too broad and unable to show the venue; community print is rejected as too passive and unmeasurable, though GLS should pin posters in schools alongside social ads to capture the primary-school birthday-party market where 73 Q3 parties came from.

    Question: Using Appendix 2, evaluate GLS's financial position by calculating the current ratio and the acid test ratio for 2024 and 2025. Has GLS's financial position improved? Justify your answer.
    Answer: Calculations:

Current Ratio 2025 = 1.33 : 1
Acid Test Ratio 2024 = 0.80 : 1

Conclusion: GLS's financial position has improved. Both measures rose and the stricter measure reached break-even parity at 1.00, so short solvency is no longer dependent on stock.   Q4(b) [12 marks]
    Question: Using Appendix 3, evaluate how the interest rate rise to 6.5%, the 5.5% minimum wage increase to $10.80 and the 13.4% rise in electricity and heating prices will affect GLS. Which change will have the greatest impact? Justify your answer.
    Answer: Interest rate rise (5.75% to 6.5%): On GLS's $400,000 variable-rate bank loan, the 0.75 percentage-point rise adds about $3,000 a year in interest ($400,000 × 0.75% = $3,000), lifting fixed costs above $1,950,000. Higher rates also make consumers more cautious about discretionary entertainment spending, though leisure spending grew 3.1%. The direct impact is the smallest of the three, is fully computable from insert figures, can be neutralised by fixing part of the loan, and unlike input costs does not compound with every hour the venue operates.

Minimum wage increase (5.5%, to $10.80 per hour from April 2026): Appendix 3 gives both rates, so the hourly delta is exactly $0.56 ($10.80 − $10.24 = $0.56). The annual cost cannot be computed because the insert does not state the number of minimum-wage hours; what can be shown is the threshold at which this factor exceeds the interest rise — it does so once GLS pays more than roughly 5,357 minimum-wage hours a year ($3,000 ÷ $0.56 ≈ 5,357), which a 55-employee venue with evening and weekend peaks will comfortably surpass. The rise lands hardest on the casual evening and weekend workforce already at 13% absenteeism, so pay policy, rostering and engagement all matter to contain the true cost.

Electricity and heating prices (up 13.4% year-on-year): Appendix 3 names commercial electricity and heating, the lifeblood of a cinema and ten-lane bowling alley — projectors, 4K screens, pinsetters, lane lighting, fryers and heating for long evening sessions. The insert does not state utilities' share of costs, so any precise total would be invented; even a bound built purely on insert figures favours a heavy impact: applying 13.4% to the entire $5.50 variable cost gives an extreme upper bound of about $0.74 per visit ($5.50 × 13.4% = $0.74), i.e. roughly $136,345 a year if every visit's variable cost were utility — an absolute ceiling, not a forecast. The honest judgement is directional and unavoidable: 13.4% is the steepest percentage rise in Appendix 3, recurs every operating hour, cannot be fixed or refinanced away the way the loan rate can, and cannot be spread over more visits quickly — screen occupancy is only 34%, and Marcus Whitfield's visitors told him they will pay at most $3 more for recliner seating.

Conclusion: The 13.4% rise in electricity and heating prices will have the greatest impact. It is the steepest percentage increase named, recurs continuously across every show and every lane hour, and offers no financing-style fix; it also undermines the refurbished two-4K-screen model precisely when GLS is trying to lift occupancy above the 34% base and justify the $680,000 investment. The 5.5% minimum wage rise to $10.80 is the second serious pressure on the 55-employee casual workforce and interacts with the 13% absenteeism problem, while the 0.75 point interest rise costs exactly $3,000 a year and can be managed by fixing part of the loan — the smallest of the three. GLS should respond with LED and high-efficiency projection, thermostat and lane-lighting schedules, renegotiating its energy contract, lifting screen occupancy via the recliner premium (57% of visitors would pay up to $3 more), and bundling the $29 weekend family pass — attacking energy use directly rather than passing costs to price-sensitive students and families.
    Keywords: 6.5%, 5.5%, 13.4%, $10.80, $400,000, 34%
    Mark scheme: level_1_1_to_4: Identifies the external factors with limited application to GLS. | level_2_5_to_8: Analyses the impact of at least two external changes on GLS's costs, revenue or financing in context. | level_3_9_to_12: Detailed evaluation of all three external changes in the context of GLS with a well-justified judgement that energy-cost inflation has the greatest impact and why the other two are smaller.

--- MAIN STEM ---
Harbourlink City Breaks (HCB) is a partnership in the travel and tourism sector, employing a workforce of 40. Founded in 2015 by Elena Vasquez, the partnership designs short-break packages across European capital cities and uses a hierarchical organisational structure with autocratic leadership from the managing partner. HCB plans to invest $900,000 in launching a premium '48-hour signature city break' programme with exclusive hotel partnerships, financed by a $600,000 bank loan and $300,000 of new partner capital. It has fixed costs of $3,050,000 a year, a variable cost of $1,240 a unit and a selling price of $1,850, and currently produces 10,800 units a year (one unit is one city-break package sold). HCB faces two problems: labour turnover among customer service staff has reached 29%, and seasonal operations absenteeism stands at 14% during the summer peak.

--- APPENDIX 1 — MARKETING/OPS ---
Market Research Summary (September 2026): HCB surveyed 900 recent customers; 67% prefer the planned '48-hour signature city break' concept, and the average booking value last year was $1,710. Booking satisfaction averaged 8.6 out of 10, and review scores average 4.6 out of 5 across 3,400 online reviews. Last-minute bookings (within 14 days of departure) now account for 31% of sales, and the cancellation rate is 4.2%. Online direct bookings grew 38% after a website relaunch, and average travel agent commission paid is 12%.

--- APPENDIX 2 — FINANCIAL DATA ---
Title: Extract from the Statement of Financial Position of Harbourlink City Breaks as at 31 March 2025 ($ '000)
Headers: ['Financial Metric', '2024', '2025']
Inventories | 80 | 95
Trade receivables | 520 | 610
Cash and cash equivalents | 160 | 140
Current liabilities | 480 | 620
Non-current assets | 1,750 | 2,200
Capital employed | 2,600 | 3,150

--- APPENDIX 3 — EXTERNAL ENVIRONMENT ---
Economic and Business Bulletin (November 2026): (1) The central bank has raised the base interest rate from 6.0% to 6.75%, raising borrowing costs on variable-rate expansion loans. (2) The national minimum wage will rise by 6.0% from $11.42 to $12.10 per hour from April 2026, lifting wage bills for customer service and operations staff. (3) Short-haul flight prices and hotel contracted rates have risen 9.4% year-on-year, while consumer spending on city breaks grew 5.6% in the same period.

  Q1(a) [8 marks]

    Answer: Point 1: New partner capital of $300,000 carries no interest and no fixed repayment schedule, unlike the $600,000 bank loan at a time when the base interest rate has risen to 6.75%. That protects HCB's $3,050,000 fixed costs from an immediate lift in debt service, and preserves cash for the signature programme's launch marketing and contracted flight and hotel rates, which have already risen 9.4% year-on-year.

Point 2: Partner capital strengthens the partnership's unity and commitment: partners who invest more capital have a direct financial stake in the signature programme's success, reinforcing autocratic decision-making with aligned incentives and reducing pressure for short-term distributions. The bank loan stays unused or partially drawn, protecting HCB's credit line for later expansion phases, avoiding lender covenants on how the programme is marketed, and keeping ownership and control fully with Elena Vasquez and her fellow partners. The downside is scale: partner capital is finite, so if the signature programme outgrows plan, the partnership may still need the bank loan later — but it would then negotiate from a position of strength, with bookings of 10,800 units already proven and fixed costs unchanged.

  Q4(b) [12 marks]
    Question: Using Appendix 3, evaluate how the interest rate rise to 6.75%, the 6.0% minimum wage increase to $12.10 and the 9.4% rise in short-haul flight prices and hotel contracted rates will affect HCB. Which change will have the greatest impact? Justify your answer.
    Answer: Interest rate rise (6.0% to 6.75%): On HCB's $600,000 variable-rate bank loan, the 0.75 percentage-point rise adds about $4,500 a year in interest ($600,000 × 0.75% = $4,500), lifting fixed costs above $3,050,000. Higher rates may also cool discretionary city-break demand at the margin, and could raise the cost of drawing the $900,000 signature-programme funding. The direct impact is the smallest of the three, is fully computable from insert figures, can be capped by fixing the loan rate, and does not erode the $610 contribution ($1,850 − $1,240) per package.

Minimum wage increase (6.0%, to $12.10 per hour from April 2026): Appendix 3 gives both rates, so the hourly delta is exactly $0.68 ($12.10 − $11.42 = $0.68). The annual cost cannot be computed from the insert because the number of minimum-wage hours is not stated; what can be shown is the threshold at which this factor exceeds the interest rise — it does so once HCB pays more than roughly 6,618 minimum-wage hours a year ($4,500 ÷ $0.68 ≈ 6,618), a level comfortably exceeded by a 40-employee operator with customer service, operations and support staff. This lands on a team already carrying 29% labour turnover and 14% summer absenteeism, so the award must be matched with engagement, flexible rostering and Herzberg-style responsibility if it is not to widen churn alongside cost.

Short-haul flight prices and hotel contracted rates (up 9.4% year-on-year): Appendix 3 names the two largest cost components of almost any short-haul city-break package — airfares and hotels. No share of the $1,240 variable cost is stated, so no legitimate total exists in the insert; anything precise would be invented. What can be shown is an upper bound built only on insert figures: applying the full 9.4% to the entire $1,240 gives at most about $116.56 per package ($1,240 × 9.4% = $116.56), i.e. roughly $1,258,848 a year across the current 10,800 packages as an absolute ceiling — real exposure will be lower but can only be lower by the fare/hotel share, which the insert does not disclose. What is certain is that flight and hotel costs scale with every unit sold, that they are contracted wholesale rather than discretionary, and that HCB cannot refinance them — it must renegotiate, re-time or re-route them before the $900,000 signature launch hard-wires new exclusivity clauses.

Conclusion: The 9.4% rise in short-haul flight prices and hotel contracted rates will have the greatest impact. It attaches to the two largest structural components of every one of the 10,800 packages sold, sits inside the $1,240 variable cost, exceeds the wage floor's per-hour exposure of $0.68 on typical annual totals by a clear margin in any plausible reading, and dwarfs the exactly computable $4,500 interest rise. The 6.0% minimum wage increase to $12.10 is second — real, unavoidable, and risky given 29% turnover and 14% absenteeism — while the 0.75 point interest rise is the smallest and can be fixed away. HCB must renegotiate contracted rates now, shift marketing to the direct channel (online direct bookings grew 38% after the website relaunch) to keep the full $610 contribution, time departures around fare cycles, and reserve any signature-price rises for the 67% of surveyed customers who prefer the concept, protecting contribution while the $900,000 programme proves itself.
    Keywords: 6.75%, 6.0%, 9.4%, $12.10, $600,000, 10,800
    Mark scheme: level_1_1_to_4: Identifies the external factors with limited application to HCB. | level_2_5_to_8: Analyses the impact of at least two external changes on HCB's costs, revenue or financing in context. | level_3_9_to_12: Detailed evaluation of all three external changes in the context of HCB with a well-justified judgement that flight and hotel input-cost inflation has the greatest impact and why the other two are smaller.

    Answer: Interest rate rise (5.0% to 5.75%): If CLF's $400,000 seven-year bank loan is variable-rate, the 0.75% increase adds roughly $3,000 a year to financing costs, slightly deepening the rise in interest payable from $54,000 to $66,000 seen in 2025. Minimum wage increase (5.9%, to $12.50 per hour from April 2027): CLF's 52-strong workforce is concentrated in driving and depot work. The insert gives the new floor at $12.50 per hour, up $0.70 from $11.80, so every employee paid at the minimum gains about $0.70 an hour; on top of 14% overtime this squeezes the $5.50 contribution unless the 4% carbon-neutral surcharge and route repricing are passed through. The hours worked are not stated in the insert, so the exact annual addition cannot be quantified precisely — but the rise falls broadly across the workforce and will recur every year. However, CLF can offset much of it through productivity and scheduling gains as the electric depot comes on line, and it partly protects morale, aiding the retention-bonus fight against the driver shortage.

Diesel and AdBlue input cost inflation (15.2%): Fuel is embedded in the $7.20 variable cost of every one of the 65,000 contracts CLF produces. The insert does not decompose the variable cost, so the exact annual addition cannot be quantified precisely; for illustration only, if the fuel-linked portion were $0.50 per unit, a 15.2% rise on it would add about $0.08 per unit, and at 65,000 units that is roughly $5,000 a year — illustrative only. Even so, the rise compounds on every unit and damages the 96.2% on-time economics of every route, striking precisely the margin that justifies the $640,000 expansion.

Conclusion: The 15.2% rise in diesel and AdBlue input costs will have the greatest impact. It compounds on every unit CLF produces, feeds straight into the $7.20 variable cost and the $5.50 contribution, and cannot be fully recovered without risking contracts in a competitive market. The wage increase is significant but more manageable through productivity and surcharges, and the interest-rate rise is the smallest cash impact and can be fixed. --- MAIN STEM ---
Portwyn Container Services (PCS) is a public limited company in the port handling and shipping sector, employing a workforce of 190 at the Port of Dunmere. Founded in 1996, the company is led by chief executive Devika Menon and operates a hierarchical structure with democratic leadership, handling import and export containers for international shipping lines. PCS plans to invest $1,250,000 in two ship-to-shore gantry cranes and a six-acre yard expansion, financed by a $750,000 share issue and a $500,000 bank loan. It has fixed costs of $480,000 a year, a variable cost of $18.50 a unit and a selling price of $26.50, and produces 95,000 units a year (each unit being one container lifted). PCS faces rising crane operator fatigue, with near-miss safety incidents reaching 7 last quarter.

--- APPENDIX 1 — MARKETING/OPS ---
Quality and Safety Report — Q3 2026: The terminal lifted 24,800 containers last quarter with a crane defect rate of 2.3%, down from 3.6% a year ago. Customer complaints fell from 41 to 26 per month. Average gate-to-gate turnaround time is 3.1 hours. A survey of 280 shipping line clients found that 67% would commit to longer contracts if dwell time fell below 48 hours, and 61% rated yard automation as their top priority. Fatigue monitoring shows 18 of 190 staff regularly work over 60 hours a week. Off-the-job crane simulator courses cost $1,100 per operator.

--- APPENDIX 2 — FINANCIAL DATA ---

--- APPENDIX 3 — EXTERNAL ENVIRONMENT ---

(2) The national minimum wage will rise by 6.2% from $13.10 to $13.91 per hour from April 2027, raising terminal labour costs. (3) Steel and container-handling equipment costs have risen 14.8% year-on-year, while import volumes through the Port of Dunmere grew 3.4% and congestion surcharges fell 5.5%.

  Q1(a) [8 marks]
    Question: PCS plans to finance its $1,250,000 crane and yard expansion partly with a $750,000 share issue. Explain two advantages for PCS of using a share issue to fund the expansion instead of the $500,000 bank loan.
    Answer: Point 1: A share issue brings in $750,000 of finance that never has to be repaid and carries no mandatory interest, which is ideal while PCS already pays interest payable of $70,000–$84,000 a year and has just taken on a $500,000 bank loan. Unlike a loan, share proceeds strengthen the equity base that supports the two new $1,250,000 gantry cranes, improving solvency and giving lenders confidence, and leaving PCS headroom to borrow again if a third crane or further yard automation becomes attractive.

Point 2: Selling new shares spreads ownership rather than concentrating risk with Devika Menon and existing shareholders, and public investors in a public limited company are usually comfortable funding infrastructure that earns returns over a long horizon. Crucially, a share issue avoids fixed repayment pressure during the years the cranes are being commissioned, when lift volumes and the 2.3% defect rate are still stabilising — the exact period when a $500,000 loan with interest already stretching to $84,000 could bite. No collateral is pledged against the yard, and the democratic board can present the issue as a growth story tied to the 67% of clients willing to sign longer contracts if dwell time improves.
    Keywords: share issue, bank loan, $750,000, $500,000, $1,250,000, gantry cranes
    Mark scheme: knowledge_max_2: 1 mark for each valid advantage identified (max 2). | application_analysis_max_6: Up to 3 marks per point for detailed contextual development linked to PCS's financing, expansion and crane commissioning.

    Question: PCS is promoting its expanded handling capacity and faster gate-to-gate turnaround to international shipping lines. Consider sponsoring a major ports industry conference, a series of trade-press adverts in shipping publications, or hosting open-house tours of the new yard for 280 client contacts.     Answer: Ports industry conference sponsorship: Sponsoring a major ports conference puts PCS in front of hundreds of shipping executives at once and confers prestige beside national competitors.     Question: PCS must cut crane operator fatigue and eliminate near-miss safety incidents. Consider introducing team working with quality circles for crane and yard crews, or a bonus scheme paying crews for every verified zero near-miss week. Which should PCS choose? Justify your decision.
    Answer: Team working with quality circles: Quality circles would bring crane operators, yard planners and supervisors together weekly to identify fatigue risks — shift patterns, cabin ergonomics, spreader signals — and propose solutions democratically. This fits PCS's democratic leadership under Devika Menon, empowers the 190 staff who actually run the cranes, and builds lasting safety habits rather than short-term compliance. Limitations: meetings take paid time out of already stretched shifts, quieter staff may not speak up, and benefits arrive gradually rather than stopping the next near-miss tomorrow.

Zero near-miss bonus scheme: A team bonus for each verified zero near-miss week is simple, immediately motivating and directly targets the 7 incidents recorded last quarter. Bonuses are highly visible and focus behaviour on safe lifting. However, cash bonuses alone can encourage under-reporting of incidents to keep payments flowing, do nothing about root causes such as fatigue from 60-hour weeks, and set an expensive precedent if every crew expects payment for ordinary safe work.

Decision: PCS should choose team working with quality circles, with a modest recognition element layered on top. It attacks the root causes of fatigue and near-misses, suits democratic leadership, involves the 18 over-worked staff in fixing their own shift design, and builds a durable safety culture as the new cranes arrive. A pure bonus scheme is rejected as the main tool because it risks silencing incident reporting and leaves exhausting 60-hour weeks untouched — the very conditions causing the 7 near-misses. Bonuses can remain a small supplement once reporting culture is trusted.
    Keywords: near-miss, fatigue, 7, 18 of 190, democratic leadership
    Mark scheme: level_1_1_to_4: Basic description of the two options with limited application to PCS. | level_2_5_to_8: Detailed analysis of the benefits and drawbacks of one or both options in the context of PCS. | level_3_9_to_12: Comprehensive evaluation of both options in the context of PCS with a well-justified decision covering motivation, reporting culture and fatigue root causes.

  Q4(a) [8 marks]

    Answer: Interest rate rise (4.5% to 5.0%): A 0.5% rise on PCS's $500,000 bank loan adds about $2,500 a year to financing costs, slightly steepening the increase in interest payable from $70,000 to $84,000 recorded in 2025. --- MAIN STEM ---
Brightroute Delivery Co-operative (BRD) is a workers' cooperative in the last-mile urban delivery sector, employing a workforce of 40. Founded in 2015 by Tunde Okafor and member couriers, the business delivers parcels for e-commerce retailers across the city using a flat structure with democratic leadership, where member couriers vote on major decisions. BRD plans to invest $520,000 in 25 electric cargo vans for its city-centre routes, financed by a $320,000 bank loan and a $200,000 member share issue. It has fixed costs of $184,000 a year, a variable cost of $4.60 a unit and a selling price of $9.20, and produces 58,000 units a year (each unit being one parcel delivered). BRD faces labour turnover of 31% among its couriers.

--- APPENDIX 1 — MARKETING/OPS ---
Market Research Summary — September 2026: BRD delivered 9,800 parcels last month, with 92.5% arriving within next-day windows, down from 95.0% in May. A survey of 420 online shoppers found that 73% prefer delivery firms using electric vehicles, and 66% would pay $1 extra per parcel for same-day evening slots. Social media mentions of BRD grew 38% this quarter. The repeat purchase rate from partner retailers is 84%. Courier absenteeism reached 8% in August. Members voted to trial Sunday delivery shifts.

In a co-operative, shares bought by members deepen their commitment to the fleet, align the owners with the vans they will drive, and avoid the risk of the bank seizing vehicles if a trading quarter disappoints — protecting the democratic model and the 40 members' livelihoods.

Point 2: Raising shares from members widens the co-op's capital base without diluting external ownership or ceding any say to a lender, so members retain full democratic control of route policy and working conditions as the 25 vans arrive. The issue also signals member confidence to partner retailers, helping win the same-day evening contracts that 66% of shoppers said they would pay $1 extra for, and it leaves the co-op headroom to borrow again later rather than exhausting its credit line on the $520,000 purchase.

--- MAIN STEM ---
Cinderhill Solar (CHS) is a private limited company in the solar energy sector, employing a workforce of 56. Founded in 2018 by Elena Vasquez, the business develops and operates solar farms selling electricity to the regional grid, using a flat structure with laissez-faire leadership across its project teams. CHS plans to invest $975,000 in a 12-megawatt extension of its Alder Meadow solar farm including a grid connection, financed by $600,000 venture capital and $375,000 retained profit. It has fixed costs of $348,000 a year, a variable cost of $9.80 a unit and a selling price of $15.60, and produces 84,000 units a year (each unit being one megawatt-hour of electricity). CHS faces a skills gap in grid-connection engineering.

--- APPENDIX 1 — MARKETING/OPS ---
Operations Log — Q3 2026: The Alder Meadow farm generated 21,500 megawatt-hours last quarter with availability of 97.2%, down from 98.4% a year ago. Two inverter failures caused 6,200 megawatt-hour-hours of lost output. A survey of 150 commercial energy buyers found that 69% would sign ten-year green power purchase agreements at current prices, and 55% prefer local suppliers. Grid connection waiting time is 14 months. Installer vacancies take 19 weeks to fill. Maintenance response time averages 2.6 hours.

--- APPENDIX 2 — FINANCIAL DATA ---
Title: Extract from the Statement of Profit or Loss and Capital employed data of Cinderhill Solar for the year ended 31 March 2025 ($ '000)
Headers: ['Financial Metric', '2024', '2025']
Revenue | 3,200 | 3,600
Cost of sales | 1,760 | 1,872
Gross profit | 1,440 | 1,728
Operating profit | 384 | 504
Capital employed | 2,400 | 2,800
Interest payable | 48 | 56

--- APPENDIX 3 — EXTERNAL ENVIRONMENT ---
Economic and Business Bulletin (November 2026): (1) The central bank raised the base interest rate from 4.0% to 4.5%, increasing project financing costs. (2) The national minimum wage will rise by 6.0% from $12.10 to $12.83 per hour from April 2027, lifting site maintenance wages. (3) Polysilicon panel and steel mounting costs have risen 13.6% year-on-year, while wholesale electricity prices rose 7.9% and feed-in tariff support for new solar capacity increased by 4.5%.

--- QUESTIONS ---
  Q1(a) [8 marks]
    Question: CHS plans to finance its $975,000 solar extension partly with $600,000 venture capital. Explain two advantages for CHS of using venture capital to fund the expansion instead of the $375,000 retained profit.
    Answer: Point 1: Venture capital brings in $600,000 in one injection rather than draining the $375,000 retained profit that CHS may want for grid deposits, inverter replacements or working capital. The investors accept high-risk, unconventional renewable projects that banks often avoid, so CHS can commission the 12-megawatt extension and the grid connection on schedule instead of waiting years to save from profits, protecting its first-mover position in the regional green-power market.

Point 2: Beyond cash, venture capital partners typically contribute technical expertise, grid-connection contacts and commercial discipline that a 56-person developer needs to negotiate ten-year power purchase agreements with the 69% of commercial buyers ready to sign.     Question: Using Appendix 3, evaluate how the rise in the base interest rate to 4.5%, the 6.0% increase in the minimum wage to $12.83 and the 13.6% rise in polysilicon panel and steel mounting costs will affect CHS. Which change will have the greatest impact? Justify your answer.
    Answer: Interest rate rise (4.0% to 4.5%): CHS is funded by $600,000 venture capital and $375,000 retained profit — equity and internal funds, not bank debt — so no existing repayments rise automatically with the base rate. However, a higher rate raises the cost of any future borrowing CHS may need for the 12-megawatt extension and grid connection, makes new venture-capital rounds harder to price, and can cool investor appetite by increasing the discount applied to future solar cash flows, potentially lowering valuations exactly when CHS most needs support. The immediate cash impact is therefore limited, and CHS can stage expenditure to match its equity funding, so this is the mildest of the three changes.

Minimum wage increase (6.0%, to $12.83 from April 2027): With 56 staff concentrated in maintenance and site operations, the insert gives the new floor at $12.83 per hour, up $0.73 from $12.10, so every employee paid at the minimum gains about $0.73 an hour and the site wage bill rises broadly across the workforce from April 2027. The hours worked are not stated in the insert, so the exact annual addition cannot be quantified precisely — partly recoverable through the 7.9% rise in wholesale electricity prices (which lifts revenue) and disciplined maintenance scheduling, the wage rise is manageable but real, and well above what the 4.5% feed-in uplift alone would fund.

Polysilicon panel and steel mounting cost inflation (13.6%): The 12-megawatt extension and its grid connection depend on panels, steel frames and import logistics. A 13.6% rise on the $975,000 extension could add roughly $132,600 to project cost — forcing either more venture capital, deeper retained-profit use, or a cheaper specification — and the same inflation raises maintenance spend embedded in the $348,000 fixed costs. Meanwhile wholesale electricity prices rose 7.9% and feed-in support increased 4.5%, which soften but do not erase the squeeze on the 45%–48% trading margin.

Conclusion: The 13.6% rise in polysilicon panel and steel mounting costs will have the greatest impact. It strikes the $975,000 expansion itself, the largest single commitment CHS has made, and every maintenance cycle thereafter, directly threatening the 48.0% margin and the return that justifies the venture capital. The wage rise is significant but absorbable through pricing and productivity, and the interest increase has no immediate repayment effect on CHS's equity-funded build. CHS should lock supplier prices, renegotiate the build contract and prioritise the extension's energisation before further cost creep.

--- MAIN STEM ---
Frostmere Cold Chain (FCC) is a partnership between Sofia and Marco Benedetti in the cold-storage logistics sector, employing a workforce of 50. Founded in 2012, the business stores and distributes frozen food for supermarkets and food manufacturers across the Breymore region, using a hierarchical structure with autocratic leadership from Sofia as managing partner. FCC plans to invest $780,000 in a new automated sub-zero depot with robotic picking, financed by a $480,000 bank loan and $300,000 from the partners' capital. It has fixed costs of $315,000 a year, a variable cost of $11.25 a unit and a selling price of $18.75, and produces 70,000 units a year (each unit being one pallet handled). FCC faces labour turnover of 26% among its forklift operators and two recent safety incidents.

--- APPENDIX 1 — MARKETING/OPS ---
Quality and Temperature Report — Q3 2026: The depot handled 17,300 pallets last quarter with temperature compliance of 98.6%, down from 99.4% in June after a refrigeration fault. Customer complaints fell from 29 to 17 per month. Energy use was 41,000 kWh for the quarter. A survey of 120 supermarket and manufacturer clients found that 74% would renew contracts if temperature compliance stayed above 99%, and 63% rank automated picking as the key factor in renewals. Labour turnover among forklift operators is 26%. Off-site forklift recertification costs $520 per operator.

--- APPENDIX 2 — FINANCIAL DATA ---
Title: Extract from the Statement of Profit or Loss and Capital employed data of Frostmere Cold Chain for the year ended 31 March 2025 ($ '000)
Headers: ['Financial Metric', '2024', '2025']
Revenue | 1,800 | 2,100
Cost of sales | 1,224 | 1,344
Gross profit | 576 | 756
Operating profit | 198 | 273
Capital employed | 1,800 | 2,100
Interest payable | 30 | 36

--- APPENDIX 3 — EXTERNAL ENVIRONMENT ---
Economic and Business Bulletin (November 2026): (1) The central bank raised the base interest rate from 4.75% to 5.25%, increasing repayments on variable-rate overdrafts and loans. (2) The national minimum wage will rise by 6.1% from $11.40 to $12.10 per hour from April 2027, lifting depot wage bills. (3) Commercial electricity and refrigerant costs have risen 16.8% year-on-year, while frozen food demand grew 4.2% and cold-chain diesel costs rose 7.4%.

The business already pays interest payable that rose from $30,000 to $36,000 in 2025, and adding $480,000 of bank debt would deepen that further; funding $300,000 of the cost internally keeps the partnership's distributions and working capital intact.

Unlike a bank loan, no collateral is pledged against the existing cold stores, and the partners avoid covenant risk while robotic picking is bedded in and the 26% forklift-operator turnover is being fixed.

Real but small, and largely avoidable by fixing the loan rate, this is the mildest of the three changes.

Minimum wage increase (6.1%, to $12.10 from April 2027): With 50 staff concentrated in forklift, picking and cleaning roles, the insert gives the new floor at $12.10 per hour, up $0.70 from $11.40, so every employee paid at the minimum gains about $0.70 an hour and the depot wage bill rises broadly from April 2027. The hours worked are not stated in the insert, so the exact annual addition cannot be quantified precisely; partly offset by the frozen food demand growth of 4.2% and by the incentive structure around the 99% compliance target, the rise is material but can be absorbed if renewal pricing improves.

Electricity and refrigerant cost inflation (16.8%): Energy is the lifeblood of a cold-storage facility — the depot drew 41,000 kWh in one quarter and refrigeration runs continuously. A 16.8% rise feeds straight into the $11.25 variable cost of every pallet handled across 70,000 units a year. The insert does not split the variable cost by input, so the exact annual addition cannot be quantified precisely — for illustration only, if the energy-linked portion were $1.00 per pallet, a 16.8% rise on it would add $0.168 per pallet, or about $11,760 a year across 70,000 pallets — illustrative only. Meanwhile diesel costs only rose 7.4%, so FCC's energy bill is inflating far faster than transport fuel, striking precisely the cost base behind its margins.

Conclusion: The 16.8% rise in commercial electricity and refrigerant costs will have the greatest impact. It strikes FCC's single most relentless operating cost, scales with every pallet handled (41,000 kWh drawn in one quarter and refrigeration that runs continuously), and directly threatens the margins already squeezed to 32%–36%. The wage rise is significant but manageable through compliance bonuses and price increases, and the interest-rate rise is small and fixable. FCC should secure fixed electricity tariffs, audit the new depot's refrigerant efficiency and pass energy surcharges into contract renewals immediately.
    Keywords: 5.25%, 6.1%, 16.8%, $12.10, interest rate, $480,000
    Mark scheme: level_1_1_to_4: Identifies the external changes with limited application to FCC. | level_2_5_to_8: Analyses the impact of at least two external changes on FCC's costs, revenue or financing in context. | level_3_9_to_12: Detailed evaluation of all three external changes in the context of FCC with a well-justified judgement that electricity and refrigerant inflation has the greatest impact.

--- MAIN STEM ---
Hartley Digital Payroll (HDP) is a private limited company in the payroll software sector, employing a workforce of 38. Founded in 2011 by Ananya Iyer, the business sells cloud payroll and HR compliance subscriptions to small and medium employers nationwide and operates a flat organisational structure with democratic leadership. It has fixed costs of $220,000 a year, a variable cost of $7.20 a unit and a selling price of $12.70, and currently produces 60,000 units a year. HDP faces an acute people problem: developer poaching by rival firms has pushed labour turnover to 14%, and remote engineers report communication breakdowns across the team.

--- APPENDIX 1 — MARKETING/OPS ---
Market Research Summary — October 2026: A survey of 520 payroll managers in client firms found 68% would upgrade to the v2 platform within 12 months, and 57% cited automated compliance as the main reason. 41% first heard of HDP through LinkedIn posts. Support tickets fell from 1,520 to 1,140 last quarter; average first-response time is 4.1 hours and platform uptime was 99.2%. The bug-report rate is 2.3% of releases. 22 of 38 staff are product engineers; on-the-job training on the v2 codebase runs weekly, while off-the-job cloud-certification courses at the tech college cost $1,150 per employee.

Every dollar saved in interest charges can absorb the 9.6% rise in cloud infrastructure costs and keep the $12.70 selling price competitive, defending the $5.50 contribution per unit across the 60,000 units sold each year.

Point 2: Using $270,000 of retained profit avoids the collateral risk attached to the loan, so the v2 platform and its AI compliance checking cannot be repossessed if launch uptake disappoints. It also preserves Ananya Iyer's ownership and the flat, democratic structure, since no external lender can impose conditions on how the roadmap or the engineering team is run, and signals financial strength to the 520 payroll managers surveyed, who want reliable compliance automation before switching. With fixed costs of $220,000 already committed and interest payable set to rise from $16,000 in 2024 to $27,000 in 2025, keeping debt service low defends the launch-year profit margin.

Profit Margin 2024 = 15.0%

ROCE 2024 = 10.0%
ROCE 2025 = 13.1%

    Question: Using Appendix 3, evaluate how the base interest rate rise to 5.25%, the 5.9% minimum wage increase and the 9.6% rise in cloud infrastructure costs will affect HDP. Which change will have the greatest impact? Justify your answer.
    Answer: Base interest rate rise (4.5% to 5.25%): If HDP's $450,000 ten-year bank loan carries a variable rate, annual interest rises by 0.75%, adding roughly $3,375 a year to financing costs and nudging fixed costs above $220,000. The cash impact is real but modest, and HDP can partly shield itself by fixing the loan rate before the next review.

Minimum wage increase (5.9% to $12.66): HDP's support and administration staff — roughly 9 of the 38 employees — work near the minimum wage. An annual wage bill near $240,000 for that group would rise by about $14,100 from April 2026. Engineers are unaffected directly, but pay-compression pressure may push HDP to review banded salaries for mid-level developers, already scarce given developer poaching, raising the total people-cost further.

Cloud infrastructure cost inflation (9.6%): Hosting is the backbone of the product and the main driver of the $7.20 variable cost. If infrastructure accounts for roughly $210,000 of annual spend (an estimate based on hosting fees within the cost base), a 9.6% rise adds about $20,160 every year, recurring against every one of the 60,000 units sold and cutting the $5.50 contribution per unit by roughly $0.34 a unit unless HDP renegotiates multi-year rates or lifts the $12.70 price.

Conclusion: The 9.6% cloud infrastructure cost rise will have the greatest impact. The wage rise is the second-largest pressure and can be offset by planning and modest price rises, while the interest rate increase is the smallest cash impact and can be fixed — both still require disciplined cost control and premium pricing while the v2 platform ramps up.

  Q4(a) [8 marks]
    Question: Explain one advantage and one disadvantage for VMS of switching ticket closure from a final quality-control inspection to built-in quality assurance checks.

    Question: Using Appendix 3, evaluate how the base interest rate rise to 5.75%, the 6.2% minimum wage increase and the 14.8% rise in cyber-insurance premiums will affect VMS. Which change will have the greatest impact? Justify your answer.

Cyber-insurance premium rise (14.8%): MSSP cover is already expensive; if VMS pays roughly $120,000 a year in premiums, a 14.8% rise adds about $17,800. Premiums can be shared in client contract pricing and demand for certified managed detection is rising, so this cost is partly recoverable and signals a market growing 8.6% this year — a genuine tailwind wrapped around a cost.

While the sales team ramps up and the offline mobile mode is built, cash peaks and troughs month to month; an overdraft covers the dips without the fixed monthly repayments of a long-term bank loan, protecting the $360,000 retained profit for genuine expansion spend.

Point 2: An overdraft provides fast, negotiable short-term finance without tying up collateral on long terms, ideal for a two-partner business that wants to keep total fixed costs near $180,000 a year. It can be cancelled or repaid once subscriber revenue covers the launch, unlike a ten-year loan that commits CEP regardless of how churn of 9% develops, and it avoids the formal appraisal, security and fees a full bank loan on $540,000 would entail. With interest payable of $19,000 in 2025 and the overdraft costing money only while drawn, CEP preserves cash for tutors and the offline mobile mode build instead of paying fixed loan interest from day one.

--- MAIN STEM ---
Sentinel Gate Cyber (SGC) is a public limited company in the cybersecurity managed services sector, employing a workforce of 88.   Q1(a) [8 marks]
    Question: SGC plans to finance its $900,000 energy-sector expansion with a $500,000 share issue. Explain two advantages for SGC of raising finance through a share issue instead of a bank loan.
    Answer: Point 1: A share issue raises $500,000 without creating fixed monthly repayments, so SGC's cash flow stays protected while the energy-sector control hub is built and before new client contracts ramp up. Interest and capital repayments on a comparable bank loan would add heavily to fixed costs already at $540,000 a year and would be especially painful with analyst burnout pushing absenteeism to 8%.

Point 2: Share capital is permanent finance — it never has to be repaid — which strengthens SGC's capital employed (already $3,750,000) and gives the plc more headroom for future borrowing at a lower rate. Stronger capital employed also lifts investor confidence ahead of the energy-sector launch and supports the credit rating that any future facilities will be priced against.

    Question: SGC is launching its energy-sector control hub. Consider national business-press advertising, sponsorship of the Energy Security Summit, or direct outreach to utility boards. Which should SGC choose to promote the launch? Justify your recommendation.

However, print is expensive, diffuse and difficult to attribute; much readership lies outside energy buyers, and a plc funding a $900,000 expansion needs measurable pipeline rather than vanity reach.

  Q2(a) [8 marks]
    Question: SGC faces analyst burnout from night shifts, absenteeism of 8% and widening cloud-defence skill gaps. Explain two benefits for SGC of using democratic leadership to rebuild morale in the SOC.
    Answer: Point 1: Democratic leadership gives SOC analysts a voice in rota design, shift length and escalation protocols, directly attacking the root cause of night-shift burnout and the 8% absenteeism. Analysts who help shape fatigue controls feel respected (Maslow's esteem needs), take ownership of attendance, and surface fatigue risks early — protecting the 103 alerts a day triage rhythm and the 14-minute mean time to detect that clients pay for.

Point 2: Involving analysts in decisions surfaces practical fixes — smarter alert-tuning to cut the 12,400-alert volume, peer handover notes for night shifts, and targeted CISSP study time for the 12 staff needing cloud-defence upskilling. The premium rise is second and partly recoverable through pricing and demand; the interest-rate rise is the smallest near-term effect for an equity-funded plc, though SGC should fix any overdraft and stress-test client signing timelines. --- MAIN STEM ---
Mosaic App Studio (MAS) is a cooperative in the mobile app development sector, employing a workforce of 24. Founded in 2018 by Lena Duarte, the studio designs and builds iOS and Android apps for retail, hospitality and public-sector clients and operates a flat structure with democratic leadership. MAS plans to invest $600,000 in opening a second studio in a coastal innovation hub, financed by $250,000 hire purchase for workstations and servers and $350,000 retained profit. It has fixed costs of $175,000 a year, a variable cost of $8.50 a unit and a selling price of $18.50, and currently produces 25,000 units a year. MAS faces a quality problem: defect rates on store submissions have risen and client complaints about release delays are climbing, straining the small delivery team.

--- APPENDIX 1 — MARKETING/OPS ---
Market Research Summary — October 2026: A survey of 700 app owners and digital leads found 59% want faster release cycles and 46% would pay a 15% premium for accessibility-compliant builds. The average project cycle is 9.5 weeks; 78% of annual-maintenance clients renew; client rating averages 4.6/5. 14 active contracts cover retail and hospitality apps; 3 of 24 studio members are UX designers.

  Q1(a) [8 marks]
    Question: MAS plans to finance its $600,000 second studio with $250,000 hire purchase. Explain two advantages for MAS of using hire purchase instead of paying cash from retained profit.

Keeping cash in the business protects day-to-day payroll for 24 cooperative members while the second studio ramps up and client revenue from the new site begins to flow.

Point 2: Fixed monthly instalments make budgeting predictable and the equipment becomes MAS's property at the end of the agreement, unlike leasing. It avoids draining reserves before the hub proves demand, and because the assets are essential production tools, hire purchase aligns payments with the revenue the machines help generate — far safer than committing the whole $600,000 up front from retained profit when defect rates on store submissions are already rising.

However, radio is audio-only — MAS cannot show its app portfolio — listening is fragmented across many stations, and reach does not map neatly onto the retail, hospitality and public-sector buyers who commission builds; spend is hard to attribute to signed contracts.

Regional social-media campaign: A targeted campaign on Instagram, LinkedIn and app-store showcases can display MAS's work, client ratings (4.6/5) and before-and-after release-cycle stories directly, reaching app owners and digital leads across the whole region, not just one town. Drawbacks: organic reach needs constant content, and paid ads demand weekly optimisation.

Print advertising in business magazines: Magazine ads signal credibility and prestige and reach senior hospitality and retail executives, but they are expensive, slow to produce, untargeted at the digital level and impossible to attribute; a 24-member cooperative funding a $600,000 launch cannot afford vanity reach.

Recommendation: MAS should choose the regional social-media campaign. It fits the audience 59% of whom want faster release cycles, showcases accessibility-compliant builds (46% would pay a 15% premium), is measurable and affordable alongside the $350,000 retained profit element, and converts directly into demo requests for the second studio. Local radio is rejected as audibly broad but visually empty for a portfolio-driven craft business, and print advertising is rejected as costly, slow and unaccountable — one targeted sponsorship at a regional tech event can be layered on once the social pipeline matures.

    Question: MAS must choose how the second studio will produce app feature modules. Consider batch production or flow production. Which should MAS choose? Justify your decision.
    Answer: Batch production: Building feature modules in batches suits MAS's varied order book — 14 active contracts across retail, hospitality and public-sector clients, each with distinct brand rules, accessibility requirements and release windows. Batches allow code reuse within a client family (for example, booking modules for hospitality), quality checks between batches, and flexibility to switch features when priorities change; setup cost per batch is modest and fits the 9.5-week average project cycle. Drawbacks: stockpiling of unused module variants, some changeover downtime, and less extreme efficiency than a fully standardised line.

Flow production: A flow line would push near-identical modules through standardised stages at very high speed with minimal changeover — ideal only if MAS were shipping one standard product at huge volume, like a commodity app. MAS's 25,000 units a year may sound high, but they split across 14 varied contracts; flow production would demand heavy capital equipment, rigid scheduling, and sacrifice the customisation that justifies MAS's $18.50 unit price, and any defect would cascade down the line before detection.

Decision: MAS should choose batch production, supported by a shared component library so repeated modules (logins, payments, analytics) move faster with each release. Batch production matches bespoke client work, contains defects before they spread, and preserves the craft quality behind the 4.6/5 rating and the 46% accessibility-premium opportunity. Flow production is rejected: its capital cost, inflexibility and defect-cascade risk are wrong for low-volume, high-variety contract work, and MAS's hire-purchase budget is better spent on reliable workstations and QA tooling for the second studio.

--- MAIN STEM ---
Alderney Dental Group (ADG) is a private limited company in the dental care sector, employing a workforce of 84. Founded in 2007 by Dr Ngozi Eze, ADG operates four general dental practices across the Alderney region and uses a hierarchical structure with autocratic leadership. It plans to invest $1,200,000 in a second branch in Millbrook, financed by a $700,000 ten-year bank loan and $500,000 retained profit. It has fixed costs of $384,000 a year, a variable cost of $28.00 a unit and a selling price of $60.00, and currently produces 96,000 units a year. ADG faces dentist and dental-nurse turnover of 24%, patient waiting lists averaging 11 days, and growing complaints about appointment delays.

--- APPENDIX 1 — MARKETING/OPS ---
Operations and Patient Report — Q3 2025: The four practices delivered 24,000 treatment units last quarter at a rework rate of 1.6%, down from 2.9% a year ago. Patient complaints fell from 31 to 19 per month. Market research of 750 patients found 62% would travel to the Millbrook branch and 48% would pay up to $12 more per visit for extended evening opening hours. Average waiting time is 11 days. Off-the-job training for the new digital imaging equipment costs $950 per employee at the regional college, and 21 of 84 staff have not completed it.

--- APPENDIX 2 — FINANCIAL DATA ---
Title: Extract from the Statement of Profit or Loss and Capital employed data of Alderney Dental Group for the year ended 31 March 2025 ($ '000)
Headers: ['Financial Metric', '2024', '2025']

Cost of sales | 3,000 | 3,168
Gross profit | 2,000 | 2,592
Operating profit | 750 | 1,152
Capital employed | 5,000 | 6,400
Interest payable | 35 | 44

--- APPENDIX 3 — EXTERNAL ENVIRONMENT ---
Economic and Business Bulletin (November 2026): (1) The central bank has raised the base interest rate from 4.5% to 5.25%, increasing borrowing costs for businesses with variable-rate loans. (2) The national minimum wage will rise by 6.9% from $12.60 to $13.47 per hour from April 2026, raising wage bills. (3) Dental materials and laboratory costs have risen 9.6% year-on-year, healthcare inflation is running at 7.4%, and consumer spending on private dental care grew 3.8% in the same period.

--- QUESTIONS ---
  Q1(a) [8 marks]
    Question: ADG plans to finance part of its Millbrook branch with a ten-year bank loan. Explain two advantages for ADG of using retained profit to fund the expansion instead of the bank loan.
    Answer: Point 1: Using retained profit costs ADG nothing in repayments or interest, protecting its cash flow at a time when it already carries fixed costs of $384,000 a year and a proposed $700,000 ten-year bank loan commitment. Every dollar not paid as interest can absorb the 9.6% rise in dental materials and laboratory costs and help ADG keep its average $60.00 price competitive, without stretching the 11-day waiting lists that are already generating complaints about appointment delays across the four practices.

Point 2: Retained profit avoids the collateral risk of borrowing against the new $1,200,000 Millbrook branch, so the $500,000 is available without risking the branch if demand disappoints or consumer spending growth of 3.8% stalls. Minimum wage increase (6.9%, to $13.47 per hour): The national minimum wage rises by 6.9%, from $12.60 to $13.47 per hour — an extra $0.87 an hour on every minimum-wage hour worked across ADG's workforce of 84. Input cost inflation (9.6% materials and laboratory): Dental materials and laboratory costs have risen 9.6% year-on-year. Conclusion: The 9.6% rise in dental materials and laboratory costs will have the greatest impact. It strikes every one of the 96,000 units sold at a 9.6% rate on the materials and laboratory element of the $28.00 variable cost, whereas the interest rise is capped at about $5,250 a year on the planned $700,000 loan even if it is variable-rate, and the wage rise — though permanent and spread across every minimum-wage hour worked — cannot be quantified from the data given and can be partly offset through democratic scheduling and imaging-driven productivity. It also directly threatens the fall in cost of sales as a share of revenue (60.0% to 55.0%) and the margin that justifies the Millbrook investment. --- MAIN STEM ---
Brightwood Nursery Group (BNG) is a private limited company in the early-years education sector, employing a workforce of 132. Founded in 2011 by Hannah Whitmore, BNG operates three nursery and preschool sites across the Brightwood region and uses a hierarchical structure with democratic leadership. It plans to invest $750,000 in a fourth nursery in Riverside and gain national early-years quality accreditation, financed by a $450,000 ten-year bank loan and $300,000 retained profit. It has fixed costs of $528,000 a year, a variable cost of $9.00 a unit and a selling price of $16.50, and currently produces 90,000 units a year. BNG faces difficult recruitment of qualified childcare practitioners, staff turnover of 27%, and a waiting list of 145 children.

--- APPENDIX 1 — MARKETING/OPS ---
Operations and Quality Report — Q3 2025: The three sites delivered 22,500 nursery session units last quarter at an incident rate of 0.9%, down from 1.7% a year ago. Parent complaints fell from 26 to 14 per month. A survey of 800 parents found 71% rated staff friendliness excellent and 57% want the Riverside site to offer forest-school sessions; 44% would pay up to $14 more per week for places. Off-the-job training at the local college costs $820 per practitioner. A waiting list of 145 children covers all three sites, and 33 of 132 staff are on fixed-term contracts.

--- APPENDIX 2 — FINANCIAL DATA ---
Title: Extract from the Statement of Profit or Loss and Capital employed data of Brightwood Nursery Group for the year ended 31 March 2025 ($ '000)
Headers: ['Financial Metric', '2024', '2025']
Revenue | 1,300 | 1,485
Cost of sales | 845 | 891
Gross profit | 455 | 594
Operating profit | 195 | 297
Capital employed | 1,560 | 1,980
Interest payable | 22 | 30

--- APPENDIX 3 — EXTERNAL ENVIRONMENT ---
Economic and Business Bulletin (November 2026): (1) The central bank has raised the base interest rate from 4.25% to 5.0%, increasing borrowing costs for businesses with variable-rate loans. (2) The national minimum wage will rise by 7.1% from $12.15 to $13.01 per hour from April 2026, raising childcare wage bills. (3) Nursery consumables and food costs have risen 10.8% year-on-year, education-services inflation is running at 6.5%, and consumer spending on early-years places grew 4.6% in the same period.

    Answer: Point 1: Using retained profit costs BNG nothing in interest or arrangement fees, protecting its cash flow at a time when it already carries fixed costs of $528,000 a year and a proposed $450,000 ten-year bank loan commitment. Every dollar not paid as interest can absorb the 10.8% rise in consumables and food costs and helps BNG keep its $16.50 average session price accessible while it bids for national early-years quality accreditation and fills Riverside places amid a waiting list of 145 children.

It also preserves Hannah Whitmore's ownership and control, since no lender can dictate staffing ratios, the curriculum mix such as the forest-school sessions wanted by 57% of surveyed parents, or the pace at which BNG integrates the fourth site.

Across 90,000 units the variable-cost spend pools to $810,000 ($9.00 × 90,000, computable from the insert). The extract does not split consumables from other variable costs, so the precise annual impact cannot be computed, but a 10.8% rise raises the cost of every session and threatens the fall in cost of sales as a share of revenue from 65.0% to 60.0% that drove gross profit from $455,000 to $594,000 — the gain underpinning the accreditation story parents were shown.

Conclusion: The 7.1% minimum wage increase will have the greatest impact. Unlike the interest rise — quantifiable at about $3,375 a year on the planned $450,000 loan even if it is variable-rate — and unlike the consumables rise, whose share of the $810,000 variable-cost pool is not given in the insert, the wage rise recurs on every hour of the labour-intensive early-years workforce, raising recruitment and retention costs precisely when recruitment is difficult and 27% turnover persists. It also squeezes the occupancy-led profit BNG needs to service the $450,000 loan. Consumable inflation is the second most serious risk; the interest rise is the smallest quantifiable impact and can be fixed, but both still demand tighter rota planning, fee reviews and occupancy discipline.
