--- MAIN STEM ---
Riverbend Veterinary Hospital (RVH) is a public limited company in the veterinary care sector, employing a workforce of 156. Founded in 1998 by Dr Marcus Ellison, RVH is listed on the regional stock exchange and operates a specialist referral hospital using a hierarchical structure with laissez-faire leadership. It plans to invest $2,400,000 in a 24-hour emergency and diagnostic service line, financed by a $1,500,000 share issue and $900,000 retained profit. It has fixed costs of $720,000 a year, a variable cost of $12.00 a unit and a selling price of $22.00, and currently produces 80,000 units a year. RVH faces routine-appointment waiting lists averaging 18 days, difficult recruitment of qualified veterinary staff, and nurse turnover of 29%.

--- APPENDIX 1 — MARKETING/OPS ---
Operations and Quality Report — Q3 2025: The hospital delivered 20,000 procedure units last quarter at a clinical rework rate of 1.1%, down from 2.4% a year ago. Client complaints fell from 44 to 27 per month. A survey of 900 pet owners found 66% would use a 24-hour emergency service and 39% would pay a monthly health-plan subscription of $24; 52% chose RVH because of its specialist teams. Average waiting time for routine consultations is 18 days, and 28 of 156 staff have not completed training on the new diagnostic imaging suite. Off-the-job training at the veterinary college costs $1,150 per employee.

--- APPENDIX 2 — FINANCIAL DATA ---

Every dollar of spare profit kept inside the company can absorb the 11.2% rise in pet-food and pharmaceutical costs and the upcoming 6.5% minimum wage rise, helping keep the $22.00 average price sustainable while the emergency line beds in.

Point 2: Retained profit avoids diluting existing shareholders' ownership and control, which matters to founder Dr Marcus Ellison and to a regional-exchange investor base watching RVH's reported revenue and operating profit, both shown growing in Appendix 2. It keeps funding internally available without market flotation risk or signalling worries, so the $900,000 stays committed to the service line even if pet-insurance growth of 5.2% plateaus or the 66% of owners willing to use a 24-hour emergency service take longer to convert into bookings, and no new shareholders can demand higher dividends instead of reinvesting in the imaging suite and recruitment.

    Answer: National press campaign: A national press campaign would build strong credibility for RVH's brand and reach pet owners across the country, reinforcing the specialist referral positioning that 52% of surveyed owners value. However, circulation is expensive, much of the readership lies far outside RVH's catchment, and print is poor at reaching owners at the moment of an emergency, so wastage would be large for an 80,000-unit business funding a $2,400,000 expansion partly with a $1,500,000 share issue.

Results are measurable per click and booking, budgets are controllable, and the approach suits the diagnostic-suite story; however, it depends on rapid response and good ad quality rather than deep editorial credibility.

Recommendation: RVH should choose online search and social media advertising. Each $1,000,000 of variable-rate borrowing would cost about $7,500 more per year (0.75% × $1,000,000, computable), so if any element of its banking were variable-rate the charge would rise above the $36,000 interest payable shown in 2025. Minimum wage increase (6.5%, to $13.26 per hour): The rise is $0.81 an hour ($13.26 − $12.45, both insert figures) on every minimum-wage hour worked. Senior vets and nurses earn well above the minimum wage, so the increase falls only on entry-level duties; the insert gives no wage-bill total or hours worked, so the exact annual cost cannot be quantified from the figures provided. Conclusion: The 11.2% rise in pet-food and pharmaceutical costs will have the greatest impact. It strikes every one of the 80,000 units at about $67,000 a year of lost contribution — exceeding the roughly $43,000 wage impact and dwarfing the modest interest-rate effect on RVH's share-funded expansion. --- MAIN STEM ---
Meadowlark Community Care (MCC) is a cooperative in the domiciliary care sector, employing a workforce of 210. Founded in 2004 by Anita Deshmukh, MCC is a member-owned home-care cooperative covering five districts and uses a flat structure with democratic leadership. It plans to invest $640,000 in a new regional care hub in Eastvale and national home-care accreditation, financed by a $400,000 ten-year bank loan and $240,000 retained profit. It has fixed costs of $765,000 a year, a variable cost of $8.50 a unit and a selling price of $17.00, and currently produces 120,000 units a year. MCC faces carer turnover of 34%, difficult recruitment of qualified carers, complaints about late visits, and a waiting list of new clients.

--- APPENDIX 1 — MARKETING/OPS ---
Operations and Quality Report — Q3 2025: The five care districts delivered 30,000 home-visit units last quarter; 93.2% of visits arrived within the scheduled 30-minute window, down from 95.1% a quarter earlier. Client complaints fell from 29 to 17 per month. A survey of 700 clients and families found 74% rated carer kindness excellent and 41% would use a dementia-care service line; 58% would pay up to $6 more per visit for weekend cover. Staff turnover is 34%, and 39 of 210 carers have not completed the new medication-awareness training. Off-the-job training at the community college costs $680 per carer.

--- MAIN STEM ---
Brightpath Tuition Partners (BTP) is a partnership in the private tutoring sector, employing a workforce of 36. Founded in 2014 by Kwame Mensah and Lena Fischer, BTP operates one city-centre institute offering after-school tuition and exam preparation, using a flat structure with autocratic leadership. It has fixed costs of $120,000 a year, a variable cost of $4.00 a unit and a selling price of $14.00, and currently produces 25,000 units a year. BTP faces difficult recruitment of qualified tutors, tutor turnover of 21%, complaints about timetable clashes, and a waiting list of 210 places for maths and sciences.

--- APPENDIX 1 — MARKETING/OPS ---
Operations and Quality Report — Q3 2025: The institute delivered 6,250 tuition units last quarter at an on-time rate of 94.5%, up from 91.2% a year ago. Student complaints fell from 18 to 11 per month. A survey of 600 parents found 69% reported mock-exam score improvement, 54% want an admissions-test programme and 46% would pay up to $45 more per month for small-group science classes. A waiting list of 210 places covers maths and sciences; 9 of 36 tutors have not completed the new online marking system training. Off-the-job training at the professional institute costs $540 per tutor.

It also keeps Kwame Mensah and Lena Fischer's shared ownership and direct, autocratic direction intact, since no finance company can dictate tuition methods, class sizes or the small-group science classes that 46% of the 600 parents surveyed would pay up to $45 more per month for.

--- MAIN STEM ---
Calder Vale Aggregates (CVA) is a private limited company in the quarrying and aggregates sector, employing a workforce of 140. Founded in 2003 by Derek Maddox, the business supplies crushed stone and rail ballast to regional road contractors and operates a hierarchical organisational structure with autocratic leadership. CVA plans to invest $1,450,000 in a new automated crushing and screening plant, financed by a $950,000 ten-year bank loan and $500,000 retained profit. It has fixed costs of $1,600,000 a year, a variable cost of $10.00 a unit and a selling price of $18.00, and currently produces 300,000 units a year. CVA faces two operational problems: dust levels at the crushing plant have breached safety limits, and absenteeism has reached 8%.

--- APPENDIX 1 — MARKETING/OPS ---
Quality and Safety Report — Q3 2026: The crushing plant processed 74,500 units last quarter at an off-spec rate of 2.2%, down from 3.5% a year ago. Dust monitoring recorded 6 readings above the safe limit in August, and 11 near-miss incidents were logged. Absenteeism has reached 8%; 34 of 140 staff have not completed dust and respirator refresher training, and the trade college course costs $750 per employee. Output per worker stands at 2,143 units a year.

--- APPENDIX 2 — FINANCIAL DATA ---
Title: Extract from the Statement of Profit or Loss and Capital employed data of Calder Vale Aggregates for the year ended 31 March 2025 ($ '000)
Headers: ['Financial Metric', '2024', '2025']
Revenue | 4,680 | 5,400
Cost of sales | 3,042 | 3,240
Gross profit | 1,638 | 2,160
Operating profit | 702 | 1,080
Capital employed | 3,900 | 4,800
Interest payable | 140 | 180

--- APPENDIX 3 — EXTERNAL ENVIRONMENT ---
Economic and Business Bulletin (November 2026): (1) The central bank raised the base interest rate from 4.75% to 5.5% in October 2026, increasing borrowing costs for businesses with variable-rate loans. (2) The national minimum wage will rise by 5.2% from $12.40 to $13.04 per hour from April 2027, raising wage bills. (3) Diesel, explosives and haulage input costs have risen 9.6% year-on-year, while aggregates demand from road contractors grew 2.8% in the same period.

--- QUESTIONS ---
  Q1(a) [8 marks]
    Question: CVA plans to finance part of the crushing plant investment with a ten-year bank loan. Explain two advantages for CVA of using retained profit to fund $500,000 of the expansion instead of borrowing more.
    Answer: Point 1: Using retained profit costs CVA nothing in repayments or interest, which protects cash flow at a time when the business already carries fixed costs of $1,600,000 a year and is committing to a $950,000 ten-year bank loan for the remaining $950,000-worth of the $1,450,000 project. Every dollar not paid as interest can offset the 9.6% rise in diesel and haulage input costs, helping CVA hold its $18.00 selling price against contractors who push for discounts and protecting the margin on 300,000 units a year.

Point 2: Retained profit carries no collateral or repossession risk, so the $500,000 is not at risk if contractor demand disappoints or near-miss stoppages intensify. It keeps the automated crushing and screening plant free from lender covenants that might restrict Maddox's control over hiring, wage settlements and safety investment, which is valuable for a private limited company with a hierarchical, autocratic structure that depends on decisive leadership from Derek Maddox and his directors.
    Keywords: retained profit, bank loan, $500,000, $950,000, $1,450,000, $1,600,000
    Mark scheme: knowledge_max_2: 1 mark for each valid advantage identified (max 2). | application_analysis_max_6: Up to 3 marks per point for contextual explanation and analysis applied to Calder Vale Aggregates and its expansion decision.

  Q1(b) [12 marks]
    Question: CVA is launching its new rail ballast supply contract for regional road contractors. Consider a national television campaign, trade-magazine advertising, or sponsorship of a regional construction expo. Which should CVA choose to promote the launch? Justify your recommendation.
    Answer: Trade-magazine advertising: Civil-engineering and aggregates trade press are read directly by the procurement managers and engineers who specify rail ballast and crushed stone. A full-page advert costs a small fraction of television and can carry CVA's $18.00 price and 2.2% off-spec performance data, and can be timed to contractors' budget-setting seasons. Its weakness is passive reach — it informs but cannot demonstrate the new automated plant's capacity or safety record.

Sponsorship of a regional construction expo: A stand would put buyers face to face with CVA, allow samples of rail ballast to be inspected and generate enquiries within days, and the 2.8% demand growth suggests contractors are actively specifying. However, stand fees, staffing the stand for three days and lost output make it expensive per qualified lead, and it reaches only visitors who attend that one event.

National television campaign: Television would build broad national awareness quickly and could launch CVA's brand publicly. But production and airtime costs are enormous for a private limited company with 140 employees, and the audience would be overwhelmingly outside CVA's regional catchment; householders do not order rail ballast, so awareness would not convert into contractor orders for a bulk supplier producing 300,000 units a year.

Recommendation: CVA should choose trade-magazine advertising. It targets exactly the buyers who specify aggregates, costs a fraction of television, recurs across the buying cycle unlike a one-off expo, and can feature the 2.2% off-spec rate and the new plant's throughput. Television is rejected as unaffordable and untargeted for a regional B2B supplier; the expo is rejected as a useful supporting tactic but too narrow and infrequent to carry the launch alone.
    Keywords: rail ballast, regional road contractors, $18.00, 2.2%, 300,000, 2.8%
    Mark scheme: level_1_1_to_4: Limited knowledge or outline of the promotional options with minimal context. | level_2_5_to_8: Detailed discussion of the advantages and disadvantages of at least two options in the context of CVA with some judgement. | level_3_9_to_12: Detailed discussion of all three options in the context of CVA with a well-justified recommendation explaining why television and the expo sponsorship are rejected.

  Q2(a) [8 marks]
    Question: CVA's absenteeism has reached 8% and 34 of 140 staff have not completed dust and respirator refresher training. Explain two benefits for CVA of its hierarchical organisational structure with autocratic leadership.
    Answer: Point 1: Autocratic leadership suits a safety-critical quarry where dust levels have already breached limits and 11 near-miss incidents were logged. Derek Maddox's supervisors can issue immediate, unambiguous instructions — stop work, fit respirators, isolate the crusher — without waiting for committee agreement, which is vital when seconds matter around crushing machinery and improvisation could kill. Fast, decisive orders reduce injury risk and the disruption that inflates the 8% absenteeism.

Point 2: A hierarchical structure gives every one of the 140 employees a clear line manager, defined chain of command and named accountability for safety and quality. Dust protocols and the 2.2% off-spec target cannot be ignored without consequence, and crew supervisors can report absence and quality figures weekly, escalate chronic cases to Maddox early, and schedule the 34 outstanding refresher courses before output per worker (2,143 units a year) slips further. Scheduling and accountability sit with named tiers rather than informal understandings, so nothing is lost as the automated plant comes online.
    Keywords: hierarchical organisational structure, autocratic leadership, absenteeism, 8%, 34 of 140 staff, 11 near-miss

  Q2(b) [12 marks]
    Question: CVA must certify 34 production staff in dust safety and machine operation before the new plant starts. Consider on-the-job training or off-the-job training at the trade college. Which should CVA choose? Justify your decision.
    Answer: Off-the-job training: The trade college course at $750 per employee would give all 34 staff structured, certificated teaching on dust control, respirator fit and crusher isolation. Total cost is $25,500 (34 × $750), affordable against fixed costs of $1,600,000 and the $1,450,000 investment already committed. Certification matters because road contractors and safety auditors increasingly require documented proof of training, and the fee also buys a recognised qualification beyond CVA. Drawbacks: staff leave production, courses are generic, and respirator fit varies by face shape, so classroom teaching cannot replace supervised practice at the actual crusher.

On-the-job training: Coaching by experienced crew at the plant is machine-specific, costs nothing in fees, keeps output flowing toward 300,000 units a year and corrects bad habits in context with signed-off competency cards crew by crew. However, uncertified trainers may pass on shortcuts, training records may not satisfy external safety auditors, and learning beside an active crushing face carries exactly the near-miss risk CVA is trying to eliminate — 11 incidents were logged last quarter.

Decision: CVA should choose off-the-job training at the trade college, followed by one day of machine-side verification per employee. Safety-critical certification cannot be guaranteed in-house, and $25,500 is trivial against the legal and human cost of another dust-related injury. On-the-job training alone is rejected because it produces no certificated evidence of competence, risks entrenching unsafe habits, and would leave CVA exposed in any subsequent dust-related claim; the college course without machine-side follow-up is rejected because respirator fit and crusher controls must be checked on site.
    Keywords: $750, 34 of 140 staff, $1,450,000, dust and respirator refresher training, absenteeism, 11 near-miss
    Mark scheme: level_1_1_to_4: Basic description of the two training methods with limited application to CVA. | level_2_5_to_8: Detailed analysis of the benefits and drawbacks of one or both training methods in the context of CVA. | level_3_9_to_12: Comprehensive evaluation of both training methods in the context of CVA with a well-justified decision covering cost, safety certification and machine relevance.

  Q3(a) [8 marks]
    Question: Calculate and explain how CVA's management can use its cost, break-even and productivity data.

  Q3(b) [12 marks]
    Question: Using Appendix 2, evaluate CVA's financial performance by calculating the gross profit margin, the profit margin and ROCE for 2024 and 2025. Has CVA's financial performance improved? Justify your answer.
    Answer: Calculations:
Gross Profit Margin 2024 = 35.0%

Profit Margin 2024 = 15.0%
Profit Margin 2025 = 20.0%

ROCE 2025 = 22.5%

Detailed workings: 2024 gross profit = $4,680,000 revenue − $3,042,000 cost of sales = $1,638,000; 2025 gross profit = $5,400,000 − $3,240,000 = $2,160,000. Capital employed rose from $3,900,000 to $4,800,000. 2024: $1,638,000 ÷ $4,680,000 = 35.0%; $702,000 ÷ $4,680,000 = 15.0%; $702,000 ÷ $3,900,000 = 18.0%. 2025: $2,160,000 ÷ $5,400,000 = 40.0%; $1,080,000 ÷ $5,400,000 = 20.0%; $1,080,000 ÷ $4,800,000 = 22.5%.

Evaluation: Profitability has clearly strengthened. Operating profit rose by $378,000 (+$378,000 ÷ $702,000 × 100 = 53.8%) even after interest payable increased from $140,000 to $180,000, so the gain is not borrowed or hollow. Capital employed grew by $900,000 to $4,800,000 yet returns on it still rose, showing the new plant is generating returns ahead of its cost. Conclusion: CVA's financial performance has improved. Both the absolute profit ($1,638,000 to $2,160,000 gross; $702,000 to $1,080,000 operating) and every return measure (35.0% to 40.0%, 15.0% to 20.0%, 18.0% to 22.5%) moved decisively in the right direction.   Q4(a) [8 marks]
    Question: Explain one advantage and one disadvantage for CVA of installing dust-suppression equipment and electric haul trucks at its quarry.
    Answer: Advantage: Dust suppression and electric haul trucks attack CVA's two worst safety indicators directly — 6 dust readings above the safe limit in August and 11 near-miss incidents — protecting workers and helping cut the 8% absenteeism that is draining output per worker of 2,143 units. Electrification also hedges the 9.6% diesel and haulage cost rise flagged in Appendix 3, because trucks run on charged batteries rather than imported fuel, which supports CVA's $18.00 selling price and improves the case for the $1,450,000 crushing plant investment.

Disadvantage: The retrofit is expensive: suppression misting systems, filtered cabs, chargers and new trucks could consume a six-figure sum on top of the $1,450,000 already committed, straining cash while a $950,000 loan is serviced and pushing capital employed beyond $4,800,000 before safety and quality gains (moving the off-spec rate further below its current 2.2%) materialise — risky if aggregates demand grows no faster than the 2.8% seen last period and contractors resist price rises.

  Q4(b) [12 marks]
    Question: Using Appendix 3, evaluate how the interest rate rise to 5.5%, the 5.2% minimum wage increase and the 9.6% rise in input costs will affect CVA. Which change will have the greatest impact? Justify your answer.
    Answer: Interest rate rise (4.75% to 5.5%): If CVA's $950,000 ten-year bank loan is variable-rate, the 0.75-point rise adds about $7,125 a year to interest, lifting financing costs above the $180,000 interest payable seen in 2025. Higher rates also cool contractor borrowing, so road and rail projects may be deferred, trimming the 2.8% demand growth. The impact is real but modest: CVA can fix the rate at renewal and the sum is small beside fixed costs of $1,600,000 a year.

Minimum wage rise (5.2%, to $13.04 per hour from April 2027): The award adds exactly $0.64 per hour for each minimum-wage worker ($13.04 − $12.40). The insert does not state per-worker hours, so the annual total cannot be fixed precisely, but the effect scales across the 140 staff; illustratively, if half the workforce (70 staff) averaged 1,000 minimum-wage hours each a year, the award would add 70 × 1,000 × $0.64 = $44,800 a year to the payroll — a meaningful increase beside fixed costs of $1,600,000 a year, and one the automated plant should help CVA absorb through higher labour productivity.

Input-cost inflation (9.6% diesel, explosives and haulage): CVA's $10.00 variable cost per unit includes diesel for haul trucks and mobile plant, but the insert does not split it by fuel share, so the exact per-unit effect cannot be isolated. What can be quantified: every $0.10 by which these components rise across 300,000 units totals $30,000 a year (300,000 × $0.10); an increase of $0.30 per unit would total $90,000 a year. Because it compounds at volume and strikes before the new plant's efficiency gains arrive, it erodes the $8.00 contribution per unit from day one, at a flat selling price of $18.00.

Conclusion: The 9.6% rise in input costs will have the greatest impact. Unlike the rate rise, it scales with every unit of the 300,000 CVA produces, compounds the wage bill, and lands immediately on the crushing plant's economics before efficiency gains arrive. The wage increase is second (bounded by the $0.64 per hour and by which staff are on minimum wage), and the interest-rate rise is smallest in cash terms (about $7,125 a year if the loan is variable). All three require CVA to fix the loan rate, automate to cut labour hours, index contract prices and renegotiate diesel supply urgently.
    Keywords: 5.5%, 5.2%, $13.04, 9.6%, interest rate, $10.00
    Mark scheme: level_1_1_to_4: Identifies the external factors with limited application to CVA. | level_2_5_to_8: Analyses the impact of at least two external changes on CVA's costs, revenue or financing in context. | level_3_9_to_12: Detailed evaluation of all three external changes in the context of CVA with a well-justified judgement that input-cost inflation has the greatest impact and why the other two are smaller.

--- MAIN STEM ---
Hartwell Modular Homes (HMH) is a public limited company in the construction sector, employing a workforce of 120. Founded in 2011 by Owen Hartwell, the business designs, manufactures and installs timber-frame modular houses for housing associations and private developers, and operates a flat organisational structure with democratic leadership. HMH plans to invest $2,300,000 in acquiring the assets of Fenwick Timber Frame, an insolvent modular rival in administration, financed by a $1,600,000 share issue and a $700,000 bank loan. It has fixed costs of $1,620,000 a year, a variable cost of $96,000 a unit and a selling price of $150,000, and currently produces 60 units a year. HMH faces two problems: a skills shortage, with 22 of 120 staff needing erector certification, and absenteeism has reached 7%.

--- APPENDIX 1 — MARKETING/OPS ---
Operations Log — Q3 2026: HMH completed 15 timber-frame house assemblies last quarter; the remedial-work (defect) rate fell to 2.7% from 4.2% a year ago. Average foundation-to-handover time fell from 9.5 to 7.5 weeks. Market research of 320 housing-association buyers found 58% prioritise modular speed and 46% want a net-zero specification. Erector certification costs $1,200 per person; 22 of 120 staff need it. HMH's order book covers 48 houses to be delivered by March 2027.

--- APPENDIX 2 — FINANCIAL DATA ---
Title: Extract from the Statement of Profit or Loss and Capital employed data of Hartwell Modular Homes for the year ended 31 March 2025 ($ '000)
Headers: ['Financial Metric', '2024', '2025']

Cost of sales | 5,460 | 6,120
Gross profit | 2,340 | 2,880
Operating profit | 1,170 | 1,440
Capital employed | 6,500 | 7,200
Interest payable | 340 | 410

--- APPENDIX 3 — EXTERNAL ENVIRONMENT ---
Economic and Business Bulletin (November 2026): (1) The central bank raised the base interest rate from 5.25% to 6.0%, its third rise this year, increasing mortgage and development-finance costs. (2) The national minimum wage will rise by 5.9% from $12.60 to $13.34 per hour from April 2027, raising assembly payroll costs. (3) Structural timber and panel import costs have risen 10.8% year-on-year, while planning approvals for new homes grew 4.6% in the same period.

  Q1(a) [8 marks]
    Question: HMH plans to finance part of the Fenwick Timber Frame acquisition with a $1,600,000 share issue. Explain two advantages for HMH of using a share issue rather than relying solely on a bank loan for the $2,300,000 acquisition.
    Answer: Point 1: A share issue raises permanent capital with no fixed interest or repayment schedule, so HMH is not committed to servicing a $2,300,000 bank loan on top of its existing $1,620,000 fixed costs and $410,000 interest payable. That keeps cash flow flexible while the insolvent Fenwick Timber Frame is integrated, protects the 48-house order book to March 2027, and guarantees the capital stays in the business indefinitely rather than being repaid at an inconvenient time.

Point 2: A larger share issue reduces default risk and spreads the acquisition's risk across new investors instead of loading it onto HMH's existing lenders. Unlike a bigger loan, it cannot trigger default, covenant breaches or a forced sale of Fenwick's assets if house completions slip, and it preserves borrowing capacity for a later overdraft or development finance needed to deliver the net-zero specification that 46% of surveyed housing-association buyers want — at a moment when planning approvals are growing only 4.6% and caution is prudent.
    Keywords: share issue, bank loan, $1,600,000, $2,300,000, $700,000, Fenwick Timber Frame
    Mark scheme: knowledge_max_2: 1 mark for each valid advantage identified (max 2). | application_analysis_max_6: Up to 3 marks per point for contextual explanation and analysis applied to Hartwell Modular Homes and its acquisition decision.

  Q1(b) [12 marks]
    Question: HMH is launching its net-zero timber-frame modular range to housing associations. Consider a national television campaign, sponsorship of a regional housing expo, or a targeted social-media campaign using home-tour case-study videos. Which should HMH choose to promote the launch? Justify your recommendation.
    Answer: National television campaign: Television would reach millions quickly and make HMH a household name, which could impress prospective buyers and council planners. However, a plc of 120 employees cannot easily justify production and national airtime of hundreds of thousands of dollars, most viewers are not housing-association decision-makers, and the message cannot be targeted to the 58% of buyers prioritising modular speed or the 46% wanting net-zero specification.

Sponsorship of a regional housing expo: A branded stand at the Expo would put HMH face to face with housing-association procurement officers, let them walk through a finished module, and generate qualified leads in two days. Drawbacks: high stand and staffing cost, one-off reach, and rival exhibitors competing for the same 320-survey audience, so awareness decays fast after the event.

Targeted social-media campaign: Short home-tour videos on LinkedIn and Instagram aimed at housing associations and developers can show 7.5-week handover times, the 2.7% defect rate and net-zero features, cost far less than television, and be measured click by click. Risks: slower to build reach, dependent on content quality, and may under-reach older procurement officers who do not use social media heavily.

Recommendation: HMH should choose the targeted social-media campaign. It matches the B2B audience identified in HMH's research, costs a fraction of television, scales nationally unlike a one-off expo, and directly showcases the speed and net-zero differentiators. Television is rejected as unaffordable and untargeted for HMH's budget; the expo is rejected as a useful supporting event but cannot sustain awareness or reach beyond its two days, so social media should lead with the expo as a complement.
    Keywords: housing associations, net-zero, 58%, 46%, $2,300,000, modular speed
    Mark scheme: level_1_1_to_4: Limited knowledge or outline of the promotional options with minimal context. | level_2_5_to_8: Detailed discussion of the advantages and disadvantages of at least two options in the context of HMH with some judgement. | level_3_9_to_12: Detailed discussion of all three options in the context of HMH with a well-justified recommendation explaining why television and the expo sponsorship are rejected as sole channels.

--- MAIN STEM ---
Rivermead Recycling Co-operative (RRC) is a cooperative in the recycling and waste-to-resource sector, employing a workforce of 60. Founded in 2015 by Ana Whitmore, the business turns council and commercial waste into biomass pellets and recycled aggregates, and operates a flat organisational structure with democratic leadership. RRC plans to invest $980,000 in a second pelletizing line at its Rivermead site, financed by $400,000 hire purchase of machinery and $580,000 retained profit. It has fixed costs of $640,000 a year, a variable cost of $12.00 a unit and a selling price of $20.00, and currently produces 110,000 units a year. RRC faces two operational problems: contamination of incoming sorted waste has averaged 6.4%, and absenteeism has reached 11%.

--- APPENDIX 1 — MARKETING/OPS ---
Quality and Waste Report — Q3 2026: The plant processed 27,500 units last quarter; contamination averaged 6.4%, down from 7.9% a year ago. Complaints from council customers fell from 17 to 9 per month. Average waste-to-pellet turnaround is 2.8 days. Fourteen near-miss incidents were logged; 18 of 60 staff have not completed machine-safety refresher training at $650 per employee. The household recycling rate in RRC's catchment stands at 44%, up from 39%.

  Q1(a) [8 marks]
    Question: RRC plans to finance part of the second pelletizing line with hire purchase and retained profit. Explain two advantages for RRC of using hire purchase rather than a bank loan to buy the new machinery.
    Answer: Point 1: Hire purchase lets RRC spread the $400,000 cost of the pelletizing machinery over its working life in fixed monthly instalments instead of drawing a lump-sum bank loan, protecting cash flow for the $580,000 retained-profit slice and everyday operations such as council gate-fee billing and waste haulage. Payments are known in advance, which makes budgeting for the 110,000-unit output and the 11% absenteeism problem far easier than variable loan repayments.

Point 2: With hire purchase the machinery is used from day one and ownership transfers after the final payment, so RRC acquires a productive second line without the collateral demands, early-repayment penalties or personal guarantees a bank might impose on a cooperative whose members trade with limited capital. If council contracts win, the machine pays for itself out of revenue; if not, RRC has limited its exposure to the instalments paid plus the machine itself, rather than a secured loan against the whole site.

    Answer: Local radio sponsorship: A sponsorship of the morning traffic show on regional stations would build name recognition among households (the 44% household recycling rate up from 39% shows growing public interest), but listeners are mostly private individuals, not tender-evaluating procurement officers, and coverage cannot be bought for only the two districts where RRC's customers operate. Cost per qualified B2B lead is poor.

Trade newsletter to council procurement officers: A targeted slot in a council procurement newsletter reaches exactly the people who sign waste-to-resource contracts, can feature the 6.4% contamination improvement, the 2.8-day turnaround and complaints falling from 17 to 9 per month, and costs only a few hundred dollars per insertion with measurable response. Reach is narrow and frequency limited, so awareness among the wider builder market would remain low.

Community social-media campaign: A zero-waste campaign on community Facebook groups and Instagram would build public goodwill, pressure councils to award RRC contracts, and appeal to environmentally conscious builders for its recycled aggregates. It is nearly free but results are indirect and slow; it rarely produces contract signatures within a quarter and needs constant content production.

Recommendation: RRC should choose the trade newsletter to council procurement officers. Waste-to-resource revenue comes from council and commercial contracts, so reaching decision-makers directly yields the fastest, cheapest route to orders; radio and social media build awareness but not tenders. Radio is rejected as untargeted and cost-ineffective for B2B; the social campaign is rejected as too slow and indirect to carry a commercial launch, though it should continue as a supporting activity for community goodwill.

  Q2(a) [8 marks]
    Question: RRC's absenteeism has reached 11% and contamination of incoming sorted waste has averaged 6.4%. Explain two benefits for RRC of its democratic leadership and flat structure.
    Answer: Point 1: Democratic leadership gives the 60 member-employees a genuine voice in how the sorting line is organised — shift patterns, contamination checks and safety briefings — which satisfies social and esteem needs (Maslow) and strengthens Herzberg's motivation factors of involvement and recognition. Workers who helped design the new contamination-flagging routine are more likely to follow it consistently, directly attacking the 6.4% average that forces reject loads, rework cost and extra $650 refresher training for 18 uncertified staff.

Point 2: A flat structure shortens the chain of command, so an absence spike reaches Ana Whitmore's management group the same shift and cover can be rearranged without a management layer; informal peer communication also means safety near-misses are flagged quickly. It reinforces cooperative values of equality and shared responsibility, lowering the turnover and disengagement that typically drive 11% absenteeism, and it keeps overhead inside the $640,000 fixed costs while the $980,000 second pelletizing line beds in.

  Q2(b) [12 marks]
    Question: RRC wants to improve productivity on the sorting line without raising contamination. Consider performance-related piece-rate pay or team working for its sorters. Which should RRC choose? Justify your decision.
    Answer: Piece-rate pay: Paying sorters per tonne processed would directly reward output, suiting Taylor-style scientific management, and could lift volumes toward what the new $980,000 pelletizing line needs to run at capacity. It is simple to administer and feels immediately rewarding. However, sorters rushing for money will miss contaminants, the 6.4% contamination rate would likely rise, reject loads would cost councils' trust (complaints fell from 17 to 9 per month), and safety near-misses (14 were logged) would increase as speed trumps care. It also conflicts with RRC's cooperative ethos of equal sharing.

Team working: Grouping sorters into small teams with shared quality and safety targets builds social belonging and shared ownership — the very motivators that sit behind RRC's democratic leadership and cooperative ethos — satisfying esteem needs and tapping Herzberg's motivators of teamwork and responsibility. Teams can run quality circles to attack contamination at its source, watch each other's near-misses and cover absences mutually — crucial with absenteeism at 11%. Drawbacks: pay is not immediately tied to output, some strong performers may resent free-riders, and team bonus administration is more complex.

Decision: RRC should choose team working. It directly supports the two problems identified — 6.4% contamination (through shared quality ownership and peer checking of loads) and 11% absenteeism (through peer support and belonging) — while fitting cooperative culture and protecting the council contracts that took years to win; team meetings can be slotted into shift changeovers so output is protected. Piece-rate pay is rejected because it incentivises raw speed over quality and safety, would likely push contamination and injuries upward, disadvantages newer sorters, and conflicts with the cooperative's equal-share principles; crucially, it does nothing to address why people are absent.

    Question: Using Appendix 3, evaluate how the interest rate rise to 5.25%, the 6.5% minimum wage increase and the landfill tax rise to $126 a tonne will affect RRC. Which change will have the greatest impact? Justify your answer.
    Answer: Interest rate rise (4.5% to 5.25%): RRC's hire-purchase instalments are usually fixed, so the immediate cash effect is small — about $3,000 a year if any variable borrowing exists. But the 0.75-point rise increases the cost of future borrowing for the Rivermead expansion, may cool construction activity that generates RRC's feedstock, and lifts council budgeting stress, indirectly tightening gate-fee negotiations. The direct financial hit is the smallest of the three.

Minimum wage rise (6.5%, to $13.10 per hour from April 2027): With 60 mainly sorting and pelletizing staff on hourly pay, the award adds about $0.80 per hour; at around 2,000 hours a year that is roughly $1,600 per worker or about $96,000 a year — close to 20% of operating profit. Combined with 11% absenteeism already forcing overtime, the payroll pressure is substantial, though mechanisation of the new line should claw some back through labour productivity.

Landfill tax rise (14.0%, to $126 a tonne from April 2027): This is market-shaping rather than cost-side. Every tonne diverted from landfill to RRC strengthens its pipeline at zero marketing cost; councils facing a $126-per-tonne alternative will pay RRC's gate fees, directly supporting the 3.4% growth in business waste collections and RRC's 44% catchment recycling rate. It also enables RRC to renegotiate multi-year council contracts at better prices. The risk is contamination rising with volumes.

Conclusion: The landfill tax rise will have the greatest impact. It is the only one of the three that expands RRC's market and revenue, not merely its costs; it reshapes council behaviour in RRC's favour for years, outweighing the ~$96,000 wage award and the negligible rate effect. The wage increase is second in cash terms, the interest rise is smallest and can be managed by fixing HP terms; all three still require RRC to invest in contamination control and mechanisation.
    Keywords: 5.25%, 6.5%, $13.10, $126 a tonne, 14.0%, interest rate

--- MAIN STEM ---
ThermaWool Industries (TWI) is a private limited company in the insulation and eco-materials manufacturing sector, employing a workforce of 85. Founded in 2016 by Lena Pettersson, the business makes recycled-denim and sheep's-wool insulation boards for the construction industry, and operates a hierarchical organisational structure with laissez-faire leadership at senior level. TWI plans to invest $1,100,000 in a second automated recycled-denim line, financed by a $600,000 bank loan and $500,000 hire purchase of machinery. It has fixed costs of $1,150,000 a year, a variable cost of $13.50 a unit and a selling price of $25.00, and currently produces 166,000 units a year. TWI faces two problems: a skills gap, with 28 of 85 staff not certified for the new line, and a defect rate of 2.9%.

--- APPENDIX 1 — MARKETING/OPS ---
Market Research Summary — October 2026: A survey of 450 building merchants and housing associations found 71% would stock TWI insulation, and 63% would pay a premium of up to 8% for recycled-denim boards. The current defect rate is 2.9%, down from 4.1% a year ago; complaints fell from 26 to 15 per month; average delivery time is 4.2 days. Certification for the new line costs $800 per employee.

--- APPENDIX 2 — FINANCIAL DATA ---

Headers: ['Financial Metric', '2024', '2025']

(2) The national minimum wage will rise by 5.9% from $12.25 to $12.97 per hour from April 2027, raising production payroll costs. (3) Gas and electricity costs have risen 15.3% year-on-year, while construction demand for eco-materials grew 6.2% in the same period.

  Q1(a) [8 marks]
    Question: TWI plans to finance part of the second recycled-denim line with a $600,000 bank loan. Explain two advantages for TWI of using a bank loan rather than hiring the machinery for the full $1,100,000.
    Answer: Point 1: A bank loan gives TWI immediate ownership of the $600,000 machinery with no hire-purchase premium or hidden interest embedded in instalments, so total financing cost is transparent and usually cheaper than machinery hire over the same term, and TWI can claim the line as its own asset for its whole life. The fixed monthly repayment also simplifies budgeting against the $1,150,000 fixed costs, useful while 28 of 85 staff await certification.

Point 2: Unlike hire, a bank loan can be renegotiated or refinanced if interest rates ease, rather than locking TWI into a fixed hire contract at a rate set today. Ownership also lets TWI modify the line and use it as collateral for future borrowing — valuable given the defect rate (2.9%, down from 4.1%) still has room to fall as output scales toward 166,000 units a year, and given energy costs rose 15.3% year-on-year.
    Keywords: bank loan, $600,000, $1,100,000, hire purchase, $1,150,000, 166,000

Justify your recommendation.
    Answer: Television advertising: Television would make TWI a familiar name to householders and could build demand for eco-insulation generally. But airtime production and placement run into hundreds of thousands of dollars, the mass audience is mostly irrelevant to TWI — building merchants and housing associations, not DIY viewers, specify insulation — and the message cannot feature the technical performance data (thermal values, fire rating, 63% premium acceptance of up to 8%) that wins B2B orders.

Sponsorship of a green-building trade expo: A stand at an eco-materials expo would put TWI in front of exactly the buyers in its survey of 450 merchants (71% would stock the product), allow live demonstrations of recycled-denim batts, and generate qualifying leads within days. Drawbacks: one-off reach, high stand and staff time away from the line, and competitors exhibiting alongside TWI diluting attention.

Social media with renovator influencers: Visible, low-cost, strong for sustainability storytelling — the sheep's-wool and recycled-denim angles would resonate with green-home audiences and support the 63% premium-tolerance finding — but renovation influencers reach homeowners, while TWI's volume sits with merchants and housing associations; consumer pull is indirect and slow to convert into pallet orders.

Recommendation: TWI should choose sponsorship of a green-building trade expo. It reaches the verified B2B decision-makers in TWI's 450-buyer research, supports hands-on product demonstration and specification discussions, and produces measurable leads within days. Television is rejected as untargeted and unaffordable for TWI's budget; influencer social media is rejected as aimed at the wrong audience for bulk insulation sales, though it should continue at low cost to reinforce the eco story.

    Question: TWI's skills gap means 28 of 85 staff are not certified for the new line, and the defect rate is 2.9%. Explain two benefits for TWI of laissez-faire leadership at senior level.

  Q2(b) [12 marks]
    Question: TWI must reduce its 2.9% defect rate on the new recycled-denim line. Consider quality control or quality assurance for the new line. Which should TWI choose? Justify your decision.
    Answer: Quality control: QC inspects finished boards at the end of the line, catching defects before dispatch — straightforward, familiar, and requires only the existing inspection station. It would hold the current 2.9% rate or push it marginally lower by weeding failures. However, QC detects problems after cost has been sunk into faulty boards, rework and scrap eat margin at the $25.00 price point, and it does nothing to prevent recurring faults or build the certified capability the new line needs.

Quality assurance: QA builds prevention into every stage — supplier checks on recycled denim and binders, calibrated die settings, in-process inspection checks, quality circles for operators, TQM-style ownership — targeting the defect rate's root causes. It costs more upfront in training ($800 per head × 28 pending = $22,400) and process redesign, and gains take longer to show. But it matches the premium positioning TWI is selling to the 63% of merchants who will pay up to 8% more for defect-free boards, and it dovetails with the certification programme.

Decision: TWI should choose quality assurance. Prevention beats detection when variable cost is $13.50 and boards are reworked at full material cost; QA addresses why defects occur, supports the certification rollout laissez-faire engineers can lead, and protects the eco-brand that wins the 71% stocking commitment. Quality control alone is rejected because it weeds out defects after value is destroyed, permits drift back above 2.9%, and cannot support a premium-price strategy on its own; a final inspection layer should complement, not replace, QA.

  Q4(a) [8 marks]
    Question: Explain one advantage and one disadvantage for TWI of using recycled denim and sheep's-wool as feedstock for its insulation boards.
    Answer: Advantage: Recycled-denim and sheep's-wool feedstock is the heart of TWI's eco-positioning, which its Market Research Summary shows buyers will pay for: 71% of 450 surveyed building merchants and housing associations would stock the boards and 63% would pay a premium of up to 8%, so the eco-feedstock underpins the $25.00 price and the $11.50 contribution per unit. It also satisfies rising green-building regulation and lets TWI qualify for public and housing-association frameworks that demand recycled content.

Disadvantage: Recycled feedstock supply is volatile — denim bales arrive irregularly and sheep's wool quality varies by season — so intake scheduling and a $800-per-person certification regime for 28 uncertified staff become harder to plan; any feedstock contamination (denim bales failing density or cleanliness checks) raises the 2.9% defect rate and rework cost on top of a $13.50 variable cost per unit, and sheep's-wool prices could spike if farming margins squeeze TWI's feedstock budget.
    Keywords: recycled-denim, sheep's-wool, 71%, 63%, $25.00, 2.9%
    Mark scheme: knowledge_max_2: 1 mark for a valid advantage and 1 mark for a valid disadvantage. | application_analysis_max_6: Up to 3 marks per point for detailed contextual development linked to TWI's feedstock strategy and costs.

  Q4(b) [12 marks]
    Question: Using Appendix 3, evaluate how the interest rate rise to 5.75%, the 5.9% minimum wage increase and the 15.3% rise in gas and electricity costs will affect TWI. Which change will have the greatest impact? Justify your answer.
    Answer: Interest rate rise (5.0% to 5.75%): On the $600,000 bank loan, 0.75 points adds about $4,500 a year, and the $175,000 interest payable will edge higher still on renewal. Greater is the demand-side signal: at 5.75%, builders and housing associations face costlier development finance, which can delay specification decisions and the 6.2% eco-materials demand growth TWI is counting on. Modest direct cost, noticeable strategic risk; TWI can fix the loan at renewal.

Minimum wage rise (5.9%, to $12.97 per hour from April 2027): With 85 staff, mainly line operators and packers on hourly pay, the award adds roughly $0.72 per hour; at around 2,000 hours a year that is about $1,440 per worker or roughly $122,000 a year — around 13% of operating profit. Combined with the certification programme ($800 each for 28 staff), payroll pressure is real but mechanisation on the new automated line will offset part of it through labour productivity.

Gas and electricity costs (+15.3% year-on-year): Insulation manufacture is energy-intensive — drying ovens, die heating and compressed systems run continuously. If energy is even one-quarter of the $13.50 variable cost (about $3.38), a 15.3% rise adds about $0.52 per unit; across 166,000 units that is roughly $86,000 a year, compounding every quarter with no volume offset. TWI can hedge with fixed-term contracts and solar but must renegotiate before margins erode further.

Conclusion: The 15.3% gas and electricity rise will have the greatest impact. Unlike the rate rise, it scales with every unit produced, exceeds the rate rise in annual cash terms and — critically — outruns the 6.2% demand growth that was meant to absorb it, squeezing both contribution and the energy-hungry commissioning of the new line. The wage increase is second (large but mechanisable); the interest-rate rise is smallest. TWI must lock in energy contracts, fit sub-metering on the new line and reprice contracts with an energy surcharge.
    Keywords: 5.75%, 5.9%, $12.97, 15.3%, interest rate, $13.50
    Mark scheme: level_1_1_to_4: Identifies the external factors with limited application to TWI. | level_2_5_to_8: Analyses the impact of at least two external changes on TWI's costs, revenue or financing in context. | level_3_9_to_12: Detailed evaluation of all three external changes in the context of TWI with a well-justified judgement that the gas and electricity rise has the greatest impact and why the other two are smaller.

--- MAIN STEM ---
VerdeMix Concrete (VMC) is a public limited company in the green concrete sector, employing a workforce of 110. Founded in 2014 by Maria Doyle, the business produces low-carbon precast blocks made with GGBS and recycled aggregates for infrastructure and housing projects, and operates a flat organisational structure with autocratic leadership. VMC plans to invest $1,750,000 in acquiring a recycled aggregate washing and batching facility, financed by a $1,000,000 share issue and $750,000 retained profit. It has fixed costs of $1,350,000 a year, a variable cost of $45.00 a unit and a selling price of $75.00, and currently produces 104,000 units a year. VMC faces two operational problems: two lost-time injuries in 2026 and absenteeism has reached 9%.

--- APPENDIX 1 — MARKETING/OPS ---
Operations Log — October 2026: The batching plant produced 19,500 units last quarter; the defect rate fell to 1.6% from 2.7% a year ago. Two lost-time injuries were recorded this year and absenteeism stands at 9%. Average order-to-delivery time is 2.1 days against a 1.5-day target. 34 of 110 staff have not completed silica-dust refresher training; the course costs $700 per employee. A new rail-depot contract is worth $2.1 million over two years.

It also avoids underwriting fees and the placing discount typically demanded by institutional buyers, stretching the $1,000,000 issue further and keeping the acquisition fully funded.

Point 2: Retained profit carries no interest, dividend or repayment obligation of any kind, unlike the $1,000,000 share issue alternative of deeper equity or any loan, so VMC keeps flexibility to fund the recycled aggregate washing facility's silica-dust safety upgrades for 34 uncertified staff or additional batching capacity if the $2.1 million rail-depot contract extends. It also signals genuine cash generation to the market, supporting the share price that enabled the issue and reassuring infrastructure clients of VMC's financial stability.

Recommendation: VMC should choose trade-magazine advertising.     Question: VMC must certify 34 staff in silica-dust safety and forklift operation before the new facility starts. Consider on-the-job training or off-the-job training at an external safety academy. Which should VMC choose? Justify your decision.
    Answer: Off-the-job training: An accredited safety academy would give all 34 staff certificated teaching on silica-dust control, respirator fit and forklift licensing, producing audit-ready documentation for inspectors and rail-depot clients. Decision: VMC should choose on-the-job training for the silica and forklift modules, supplemented by one short off-the-job awareness day for compliance and certification anchoring. The machine-side context is where silica exposure and forklift movements actually occur, output and rail-depot deadlines cannot pause, and the flat structure lets Maria Doyle monitor competency personally; $23,800 in fees would also divert cash from the $750,000 retained-profit leg of the acquisition. Pure off-the-job training is rejected because generic classroom content cannot certify competence on VMC's actual machines and would stop the line against a live order book.

    Answer: Interest rate rise (5.5% to 6.25%): VMC is an ex-dividend public limited company funded mainly by equity (the $1,000,000 share issue) and retained profit ($750,000), so direct interest exposure is limited — roughly $285,000 interest payable in 2025, a 0.75-point rise adding little on current borrowing. The bigger effect is demand: at 6.25% mortgage and development-finance costs squeeze housing approvals (+5.4% recently), delaying order decisions and pressure-testing the $2.1 million rail-depot timetable. Manageable, but strategically not ignorable.

Minimum wage rise (6.8%, to $13.35 per hour from April 2027): With 110 mainly plant and batching staff on hourly pay, the award adds about $0.85 per hour; at around 2,000 hours a year per employee, that is roughly $1,700 per worker or about $187,000 a year — around 13% of operating profit. The two lost-time injuries and 9% absenteeism already inflate overtime coverage; the certified forklift and silica roles will command above-minimum rates anyway. Mechanisation of the new wash plant will offset part of this.

Input-cost inflation (13.6% GGBS, cement and aggregate): VMC's $45.00 variable cost is dominated by binders and aggregates. If materials are 60% of variable cost (about $27.00), a 13.6% rise adds roughly $3.67 per unit; across 104,000 units that is about $382,000 a year — two to three times the wage award and many times the interest effect, directly eroding the $30.00 contribution per unit unless passed through in tender repricing.

Conclusion: The 13.6% input-cost rise will have the greatest impact. It scales with every one of the 104,000 units produced, outweighs the wage and interest effects several times over, and challenges the $75.00 price point directly before the recycled-aggregates plant delivers input savings. The wage increase is second (large but mechanisable); the interest-rate rise is smallest in cash but the greatest demand risk. VMC must lock GGBS supply contracts, renegotiate depot tenders with energy/material surcharges, and commission the wash plant on schedule to claw back input dependence.

PAPER 2 — P2_SET_141
UNIT: Paper 2 Case Study

--- MAIN STEM ---
Wexford Vale Creamery Cooperative (WVC) is a cooperative in the dairy processing and farming sector, owned by 64 member farms and employing a workforce of 38. Founded in 2004 and led by general manager Celia Brannigan, the business supplies farmhouse cheese and butter to regional and national supermarket chains, and operates a flat organisational structure with democratic leadership. WVC plans to invest $720,000 in a new cheese maturation and packing facility, financed by $300,000 member capital contributions, $280,000 retained profit and $140,000 bank loan. It has fixed costs of $225,000 a year, a variable cost of $9.50 a unit and a selling price of $14.00, and currently produces 64,000 units a year. WVC faces two problems: absenteeism has reached 7% and a skills gap has opened in cheese grading, with 14 of 38 staff not yet trained on the new grading line.

--- APPENDIX 1 — MARKETING/OPS ---
Quality and Waste Report — Q3 2026: The maturation facility processed 16,200 cheese wheels last quarter, with the defect rate falling to 2.4% from 3.6% a year ago. Customer complaints fell from 27 to 14 per month. Average order fulfilment time is 2.8 days. Waste from trimmings and brine wash fell to 4.7% of output. A survey of 500 supermarket shoppers found that 58% would pay up to $0.60 more for eco-packaging on locally produced cheese, and 47% read origin labels before buying. A training needs analysis shows 14 of 38 staff have not completed on-the-job training on the new grading line; off-the-job courses at the agricultural college cost $750 per employee.

--- APPENDIX 2 — FINANCIAL DATA ---
Title: Extract from the Statement of Financial Position of Wexford Vale Creamery Cooperative as at 31 March 2025 ($ '000)
Headers: ['Financial Metric', '2024', '2025']
Inventories | 160 | 145
Trade receivables | 130 | 155
Cash and cash equivalents | 35 | 50
Current liabilities | 250 | 225
Non-current assets | 1,600 | 2,050
Capital employed | 1,875 | 2,180

--- APPENDIX 3 — EXTERNAL ENVIRONMENT ---
Economic and Business Bulletin (November 2026): (1) The central bank has raised the base interest rate from 5.0% to 5.75%, the third rise this year, increasing borrowing costs for businesses with variable-rate loans. (2) The national minimum wage will rise by 5.5% from $12.00 to $12.66 per hour from April 2026, raising total wage bills. (3) Dairy feed and energy input costs have risen 9.8% year-on-year, and food-price inflation is running at 7.2%, while consumer spending on locally produced cheese grew 4.1% in the same period.

--- QUESTIONS ---
  Q1(a) [8 marks]
    Question: WVC plans to finance part of its new cheese maturation and packing facility through $300,000 of member capital contributions rather than relying entirely on a bank loan. Explain two advantages for WVC of using member capital contributions instead of a larger bank loan.
    Answer: Point 1: Member capital contributions cost WVC nothing in interest or arrangement fees, which protects the cooperative's cash flow at a time when it already carries fixed costs of $225,000 a year and a $140,000 bank loan commitment on the new $720,000 facility. Every dollar not paid as interest can absorb the 9.8% rise in dairy feed and energy input costs, helping WVC keep its $14.00 selling price stable for supermarket contracts rather than passing increases on to shoppers who are already cautious about food-price inflation at 7.2%.

Point 2: Because WVC is a cooperative owned by 64 member farms, raising $300,000 from members deepens their financial stake and loyalty, reducing the risk that they sell milk elsewhere when prices are tight. It also preserves the democratic control of the cooperative, since no external lender can attach covenants over how the maturation facility is run or veto the hiring of the 14 untrained graders. Contributions strengthen the balance sheet without forcing members to surrender ownership, unlike a share issue by an investor-owned firm, and they signal commitment to the 4.1% growth in locally produced cheese that the members' milk depends on.
    Keywords: member capital contributions, bank loan, $300,000, $720,000, cooperative, $140,000
    Mark scheme: knowledge_max_2: 1 mark for each valid advantage identified (max 2). | application_analysis_max_6: Up to 3 marks per point for contextual explanation and analysis applied to Wexford Vale Creamery Cooperative, its cooperative ownership and its expansion decision.

  Q1(b) [12 marks]
    Question: WVC is launching its locally produced farmhouse cheese range to national supermarkets. Consider a national television campaign, regional press and farmers' market sponsorship, or social media influencer marketing. Which should WVC choose to promote the launch? Justify your recommendation.
    Answer: National television campaign: A national TV campaign would reach millions of viewers very quickly and would build awareness of the WVC brand in the supermarket chains it supplies. However, production and airtime costs run into hundreds of thousands of dollars, and much of the audience sits outside WVC's supermarket distribution or does not buy premium locally produced cheese, so the spend would be poorly targeted for a 38-person cooperative carrying a $720,000 expansion and a $140,000 bank loan.

Regional press and farmers' market sponsorship: This is far cheaper and reaches the exact regional catchment where the 58% of surveyed shoppers willing to pay up to $0.60 more for eco-packaging and locally produced cheese live. Sampling at farmers' markets builds trust and direct feedback at low cost. Its limitation is reach: the new national supermarket listings need national awareness, so regional press alone cannot generate the volume required to fill the maturation facility or justify the $720,000 investment.

Social media influencer marketing: Food and lifestyle influencers can demonstrate the eco-packaging story to the 47% of shoppers who read origin labels, generate measurable engagement, and scale cheaply from regional to national coverage. Cost per reached shopper is low, and campaigns can be timed to supermarket launch windows. Results compound more slowly than television and depend on influencer credibility, but WVC can test messages with the 500 surveyed shoppers before committing.

Recommendation: WVC should choose social media influencer marketing, layered with small regional press adverts rather than a stand-alone buy. It is affordable, targeted at the eco-conscious segment, and nationally scalable. Television is rejected as unaffordable and untargeted for a cooperative funding an expansion largely with member money; regional press and farmers' markets are rejected as the sole launch channel because its reach is regional only, insufficient for national supermarket listings.
    Keywords: locally produced cheese, eco-packaging, $0.60, 58%, 47%, supermarket, $720,000
    Mark scheme: level_1_1_to_4: Limited knowledge or outline of the promotional options with minimal context. | level_2_5_to_8: Detailed discussion of the advantages and disadvantages of at least two options in the context of WVC with some judgement. | level_3_9_to_12: Detailed discussion of all three options in the context of WVC with a well-justified recommendation explaining why the national television campaign and regional press sponsorship are rejected.

  Q2(a) [8 marks]
    Question: WVC operates a flat organisational structure with democratic leadership. Explain two ways for WVC to apply Maslow's hierarchy of needs to motivate its 38 employees on the maturation and grading lines.
    Answer: Point 1: WVC can satisfy esteem and self-actualisation needs by giving grading-line staff responsibility for cheese quality sign-off and involving them in democratic decisions about maturation routines and shift patterns. Workers whose judgement is trusted, and who chair the quality circles that cut the defect rate from 3.6% to 2.4%, feel respected and fulfilled, which raises commitment and directly attacks the 7% absenteeism rate on the grading line.

Point 2: WVC can satisfy social needs by building team working between member-farm liaison staff and packing crews, for example celebrating member visits with shared tastings of the farmhouse cheese. Visible cooperation with the 64 member farms gives employees a sense of belonging to the cooperative's shared purpose, which is especially motivating for a members' business where profit is distributed according to each farm's milk supply. Recognising strong attendance with team rewards, rather than punishing absence, should reduce labour turnover, protect the 64,000-unit annual output and help the 14 untrained graders feel supported through the $750 agricultural college course.
    Keywords: 64 member farms, workforce of 38, democratic leadership, absenteeism, flat organisational structure, $750
    Mark scheme: knowledge_max_2: 1 mark for each valid motivational application of Maslow's hierarchy identified (max 2). | application_analysis_max_6: Up to 3 marks per point for detailed contextual development linked to WVC's flat democratic structure, its cooperative identity and its 7% absenteeism.

  Q2(b) [12 marks]
    Question: WVC must improve motivation on the maturation line. Consider introducing performance-related bonus payments or a profit-sharing scheme for its 38 employees. Which should WVC choose? Justify your decision.
    Answer: Performance-related bonus payments: Bonuses tied to individual or team output targets give immediate, visible rewards for above-standard effort, for example hitting packing targets as the facility ramps up to serve national supermarket orders. They are simple to administer and can be targeted at the 14 untrained graders who complete the on-the-job grading certification. The drawbacks are that individual bonuses can encourage corner-cutting on quality — risking a rise from the current 2.4% defect rate — and they can create resentment between elected democratic team leaders and other staff in a cooperative that prides itself on equality among 64 member farms and 38 employees.

Profit-sharing scheme: Profit sharing distributes a share of the cooperative's surplus to all 38 employees, reinforcing the democratic, collective ethos of a member-owned business. It rewards overall performance, aligns everyone with the supermarket growth that funds the $720,000 facility, and costs nothing in lean years — the scheme simply pays less. However, payouts are annual and distant from daily effort, individual contribution is invisible, and weak individual performers free-ride on team effort, which can frustrate high performers on the grading line.

Decision: WVC should choose profit sharing, possibly with a small recognition element rather than a pure performance bonus. Profit sharing matches the cooperative identity, rewards everyone for the supermarket growth that makes the $720,000 expansion viable, and avoids the quality risks and internal divisions that individual bonuses can create — critical while absenteeism is 7% and grading skills are being rebuilt. Performance-related bonuses are rejected as the main scheme because they can undermine quality culture and equality in a member-owned flat structure, though WVC can layer spot recognition for safety and quality suggestions on top of the profit-sharing pot.
    Keywords: cooperative, workforce of 38, democratic leadership, $720,000, absenteeism, 64 member farms
    Mark scheme: level_1_1_to_4: Basic description of bonus payments and profit sharing with limited application to WVC. | level_2_5_to_8: Detailed analysis of the benefits and drawbacks of both options in the context of WVC and its cooperative structure. | level_3_9_to_12: Comprehensive evaluation of both options in the context of WVC with a well-justified decision explaining why performance-related bonus payments are rejected as the main scheme.

  Q3(a) [8 marks]
    Question: Calculate and explain how WVC's management can use its cost, break-even and productivity data.
    Answer: (i) Break-even output = 50,000 units. Working: contribution per unit is $14.00 − $9.50 = $4.50, and $225,000 ÷ $4.50 = 50,000 units. (ii) Contribution per unit = $4.50. This is the revenue each unit of farmhouse cheese and butter contributes toward fixed costs after variable costs are covered. (iii) Four contextual uses explained: First, WVC's managers can set the supermarket sales budget with confidence because current output of 64,000 units clears the 50,000-unit break-even with a margin of safety of 14,000 units, so the maturation facility can absorb softer demand before losses begin. Second, the $4.50 contribution lets managers test any price negotiated with supermarket chains molecule by molecule: a $0.60 price cut would still leave $3.90 per unit, so a volume uplift above 58,000 units would keep total contribution above the $225,000 fixed costs. Third, break-even knowledge supports the $720,000 expansion appraisal: the second phase only proceeds once contracted volumes push output comfortably beyond 50,000 units, protecting the $140,000 bank loan repayment and the interests of the 64 member farms. Fourth, unit-cost analysis ($225,000 ÷ 64,000 units + $9.50 = $13.02) gives WVC a benchmark to attack the 4.7% trimmings waste, identify whether the $9.50 variable cost should be renegotiated against the 9.8% input-cost inflation, and decide whether to keep grading in-house or outsource during the 14-person skills gap.

  Q3(b) [12 marks]
    Question: Using Appendix 2, evaluate WVC's financial position by calculating the current ratio and the acid test ratio for 2024 and 2025. Has WVC's financial position improved? Justify your answer.
    Answer: Calculations:
Current Ratio 2024 = 1.30 : 1
Current Ratio 2025 = 1.56 : 1
Acid Test Ratio 2024 = 0.66 : 1
Acid Test Ratio 2025 = 0.91 : 1

Detailed workings: 2024 current assets = $160,000 inventories + $130,000 trade receivables + $35,000 cash = $325,000; 2025 current assets = $145,000 + $155,000 + $50,000 = $350,000. 2024 = $325,000 ÷ $250,000 = 1.30; 2025 = $350,000 ÷ $225,000 = 1.56. Excluding inventories, 2024 = ($325,000 − $160,000) ÷ $250,000 = $165,000 ÷ $250,000 = 0.66; 2025 = ($350,000 − $145,000) ÷ $225,000 = $205,000 ÷ $225,000 = 0.91.

Evaluation: WVC's liquidity has strengthened. The improvement in coverage of short-term obligations is helped by current liabilities falling from $250,000 to $225,000 while current assets rose from $325,000 to $350,000, partly reflecting the $50,000 cash build-up as supermarket contracts converted to receivables. The acid test, which strips out inventories of cheese wheels in maturation, moved from 0.66 to 0.91, so WVC now almost covers short-term debts without selling stock — essential while it services the $140,000 bank loan and stages the $720,000 facility. However, trade receivables rose from $130,000 to $155,000, meaning more cash is tied up with supermarket customers; if they stretch payment terms, the stronger position could deteriorate. Inventories fell from $160,000 to $145,000, so stock availability for peak Christmas cheese demand should be monitored rather than assumed.

Conclusion: WVC's financial position has improved. Both liquidity measures show clearer coverage of current liabilities, and the improvement does not rely on inventories, which actually fell. The main residual risk is rising trade receivables, so WVC should tighten supermarket credit terms and monitor collection while proceeding with the facility build-out and continuing to serve its 64 member farms.

    Question: Using Appendix 3, evaluate how the interest rate rise to 5.75%, the 5.5% minimum wage increase and the 9.8% rise in dairy feed and energy input costs will affect WVC. Which change will have the greatest impact? Justify your answer.
    Answer: Interest rate rise (5.0% to 5.75%): With a $140,000 bank loan attached to the $720,000 facility, if WVC's loan is variable-rate, annual interest rises by 0.75%, adding roughly $1,050 a year to financing costs — real but modest against fixed costs of $225,000. Higher rates also cool consumer appetite for premium locally produced cheese and raise the cost of any future borrowing to complete the facility. The direct cash impact is the smallest of the three changes and can be partly managed by fixing the loan rate or accelerating member contributions.

Minimum wage increase (5.5%, to $12.66 per hour from April 2026): WVC's workforce of 38, weighted toward grading, maturation and packing, faces a materially higher wage bill. If average hourly pay moves from about $12.00 to $12.66, the annual cost of one full-time employee rises by roughly $1,400, adding perhaps $53,000 a year across 38 staff — a significant burden for a cooperative whose member farms also face rising feed costs, though higher productivity on the new grading line (64,000 units ÷ 38 employees ≈ 1,684 units per worker) can offset part of it.

Input cost inflation (9.8% dairy feed and energy): WVC's $9.50 variable cost is dominated by milk, feed and energy. A 9.8% rise on even the feed-and-energy component adds roughly $0.55–$0.93 per unit; at 64,000 units that is about $35,000–$60,000 a year, cutting contribution from $4.50 toward $3.60–$3.95 and undermining the margin that justifies the maturation facility — though WVC can recover part through the $0.60 eco-packaging premium and supermarket price negotiations.

Conclusion: The 9.8% rise in dairy feed and energy input costs will have the greatest impact. It compresses the $4.50 contribution on every one of the 64,000 units WVC sells and feeds straight into member farmers' own costs, threatening the whole cooperative model. The wage rise is the second most serious pressure, while the interest rate increase is the smallest in cash terms and can be managed by fixing rates — but WVC must act on all three, prioritising input-cost control, premium pricing and productivity gains.

--- MAIN STEM ---
Rio Sol Fruit Juices (RSFJ) is a public limited company in the fruit juice manufacturing sector, employing a workforce of 240. Founded in 1991 by brothers Luis and Marco Herrera, the business bottles premium cold-pressed juice for national supermarkets and operates a hierarchical organisational structure with autocratic leadership at head office. RSFJ plans to invest $1,850,000 in a new aseptic bottling plant, financed by a $1,100,000 share issue and $750,000 retained profit. It has fixed costs of $510,000 a year, a variable cost of $4.10 a unit and a selling price of $7.50, and currently produces 210,000 units a year. RSFJ faces two problems: labour turnover has reached 16% among production staff and its warehouse reports a rising defect rate on capped bottles.

--- APPENDIX 1 — MARKETING/OPS ---
Market Research Summary — October 2026: A survey of 1,200 supermarket shoppers across five regions found that 61% prefer cold-pressed juice to from-concentrate, 55% would pay up to $0.80 more per bottle for premium juice, 49% associate the Rio Sol brand with freshness and 18% have bought juice through e-commerce in the past year. Weekly production is 4,300 units, and the defect rate is 1.5%, down from 2.7% a year ago. Average delivery lead time is 2.5 days. Customer complaints fell from 45 to 28 per month. 34 of 240 staff have not completed on-the-job training on the new capping machines; off-the-job courses at the technical college cost $950 per employee.

--- APPENDIX 2 — FINANCIAL DATA ---

Trade receivables | 520 | 610
Cash and cash equivalents | 90 | 150
Current liabilities | 700 | 760
Non-current assets | 4,200 | 5,500
Capital employed | 4,530 | 5,880

--- APPENDIX 3 — EXTERNAL ENVIRONMENT ---
Economic and Business Bulletin (November 2026): (1) The central bank has raised the base interest rate from 5.5% to 6.25%, the fourth rise this year, increasing borrowing costs for businesses carrying variable-rate debt. (2) The national minimum wage will rise by 7.0% from $13.00 to $13.91 per hour from April 2026, raising total wage bills. (3) Orange, mango and guava input costs have risen 14.2% year-on-year, juice-price inflation is running at 9.3%, while consumer spending on premium beverages grew 5.2% in the same period.
