    Question: Using Appendix 3, evaluate how the interest rate rise to 5.75%, the 5.6% minimum wage increase and the 32.0% rise in gas and electricity costs will affect MRT. Which change will have the greatest impact? Justify your answer.
    Answer: Interest rate rise to 5.75%: MRT's funding mix is deliberately interest-light — a $600,000 member share issue and $350,000 retained profit, with no bank loan — so the direct pass-through of the base rate moving from 5.00% to 5.75% is limited to any short-term working-capital costs, which will be minimal. The real risk is indirect: merchants holding lower cash balances may delay tile orders, and housing developers may slow project starts.

Minimum wage increase of 5.6% to $13.52: MRT's 48 staff — 30 of them members paid at or near the minimum plus member surplus — face a wage bill up roughly 5.6%. At average earnings near $13.52 an hour for 2,080 hours, each worker adds about $1,490 a year, or around $71,500 across the workforce. For a co-op, though, members vote on how to absorb this, for instance via smaller member surplus distributions rather than cuts.

Gas and electricity cost inflation of 32.0%: Clay tiles need firing; energy is the largest single component of MRT's $3.60 variable cost, roughly $1.45 per unit (about 40%). A 32.0% rise adds about $0.46 per tile. Across 171,000 units that is roughly $79,000 a year, compressing contribution per unit from $4.00 toward $3.54, narrowing margin of safety, and directly threatening the return behind the $950,000 extrusion and kiln line.

Conclusion: The 32.0% rise in gas and electricity costs will have the greatest impact. It recurs on every unit fired, outweighs the wage rise (~$71,500) and swamps the interest-rate effect (minimal). Unlike wages, energy cannot be re-spread by improving attendance, and unlike the 1.9% growth in housing starts it cannot be forecast away. MRT should hedge biomass/dual-fuel contracts, press for a 5% local-premium price increase across its merchant base, and evaluate the biomass conversion in Q4 before the next member dividends are declared.

--- MAIN STEM ---
Sentinel Flow Systems (SFS) is a public limited company in the plastics manufacturing sector, producing high-density polyethylene pipe and fittings for water utilities and drainage contractors, with a workforce of 95. Founded in 1997 by Helena Voss and led by chief executive Marcus Bell since 2015, SFS operates a hierarchical structure with democratic leadership. SFS plans to invest $1,450,000 in a twin-screw extrusion line for large-diameter pipe, financed by a $900,000 new share issue and $550,000 retained profit. It has fixed costs of $405,000 a year, a variable cost of $19.00 a unit and a selling price of $28.00, and produces 90,000 units a year. SFS faces a skills gap in CNC programming and labour turnover of 19%.

--- APPENDIX 1 — MARKETING/OPS ---
Quality and Waste Report — Q3 2025: The extrusion line produced 22,500 pipe lengths last quarter at a defect rate of 1.9%, down from 3.6% a year ago; regrind waste fell from 7.2% to 4.8% of resin throughput. Customer complaints fell from 31 to 17 per month. Average extrusion set-up time improved to 1.6 hours. A survey of 260 utility specifiers found that 54% would adopt larger-diameter pipe for new mains contracts and 41% prioritise lead-free certification. 22 of 95 staff need CNC programming upskilling; the off-the-job automation course costs $1,050 per employee.

--- APPENDIX 2 — FINANCIAL DATA ---

Current liabilities | 400 | 380

Capital employed | 3,400 | 3,750

(2) The national minimum wage will rise by 7.1% from $13.70 to $14.67 per hour from April 2026, squeezing manufacturers' labour costs. (3) HDPE resin input costs have risen 14.6% year-on-year and input-cost inflation in plastics is running at 7.8%, while water-utility capital expenditure grew 4.8% in the same period.

  Q1(a) [8 marks]
    Question: SFS plans to finance part of its large-diameter pipe line with a $900,000 new share issue. Explain two advantages for SFS of using retained profit instead of the share issue.
    Answer: Point 1: Retained profit is free of issue costs and carries no expectation of dividends, so SFS keeps more cash to fund the $1,450,000 twin-screw extrusion line without diluting ordinary shareholders. Existing shareholders would see their stake diluted if the new issue is large, whereas retained profit rewards them directly through the capital growth the new line will generate.

Point 2: Retained profit avoids signalling. Announcing a big share issue can be read by the market as SFS struggling to fund itself internally, knocking the share price and raising the cost of future capital before the pipe line proves itself. Using the $550,000 retained profit — built from years of supplying water utilities — demonstrates that SFS self-funds expansions, protects Helena Voss's and Marcus Bell's credibility with institutional holders, and keeps control squarely with current owners rather than new subscribers who might demand board influence or strategy changes.
    Keywords: retained profit, new share issue, $550,000, $900,000, $1,450,000, polyethylene
    Mark scheme: knowledge_max_2: 1 mark for each valid advantage identified (max 2). | application_analysis_max_6: Up to 3 marks per point for detailed contextual explanation and analysis applied to Sentinel Flow Systems and its extrusion-line expansion.

  Q1(b) [12 marks]
    Question: SFS is launching its large-diameter pipe to water utilities. Consider exhibiting at the International Water Infrastructure Exhibition, advertising in the Utilities Weekly trade press, or a targeted LinkedIn campaign aimed at procurement engineers. Which should SFS choose to promote the launch? Justify your recommendation.
    Answer: International Water Infrastructure Exhibition: A stand at the industry's flagship expo, absorbing a sizeable slice of the $1,450,000 line's budget, puts SFS in front of the exact 54% of utility specifiers who told its survey they would adopt larger-diameter pipe for new mains. Live flow and pressure demonstrations and EN-certified samples are persuasive for capital purchases, and one framework agreement with a regional utility could book out the twin-screw line's first-year capacity. Cost and staff-time are the drawbacks, plus a long tail of low-quality leads.

Utilities Weekly trade press: Quarter-page adverts costing only a few thousand dollars an issue reach engineers and procurement officers nationwide between buying cycles, reinforce the 41% lead-free-certification message with technical detail, and cost far less than an expo stand. However, print readership is shrinking, response is hard to attribute, and a single ad will not close a multi-year mains framework contract.

Targeted LinkedIn campaign for procurement engineers: Promoted content segmented by job title (procurement, network engineering, asset management) costs a modest five-figure sum each quarter, delivers measurable click-throughs to SFS's technical datasheet pack, and keeps SFS visible through long tender cycles. Engagement is opt-in and measurable, but conversion to signed frameworks is slow and depends on follow-up by the technical sales team.

Recommendation: SFS should choose the International Water Infrastructure Exhibition. Capital purchases of mains pipe are relationship and specification decisions made face-to-face between utility engineers and credible manufacturers; the expo is the only channel where all target specifiers converge in one place. Utilities Weekly is rejected as too passive and hard to measure for a launch; LinkedIn is rejected as an inadequate sole channel for a considered, committee-approved mains contract, though it is the ideal low-cost nurture channel between exhibitions and tender deadlines.
    Keywords: large-diameter, 54%, 41%, utility specifiers, $1,450,000, water utilities

    Question: SFS must end the manual bottleneck at the finishing bays. Consider replacing the manual end-facing and drilling stations with three automated CAM cells, or retaining the finishing crews and upskilling them in CNC programming. Which should SFS choose? Justify your decision.

Drawbacks are slower output growth, continued exposure to human error, and a risk that upskilled staff immediately resign for higher CAM-lab salaries elsewhere.

Decision: SFS should retain the finishing crews and fund the CNC upskilling now, while piloting one automated CAM cell alongside the extrusion line. This sequence attacks the skills gap at its root for $23,100, halves defect risk on the sensitive end-facing operation, and honours the democratic compact with employees before automation is layered in. Installing three CAM cells immediately is rejected because the 22-person programming gap would leave the machines underrun, morale would collapse under visible redundancy risk, and the $1,450,000 share-issue-funded extrusion line already stretches capital commitments. One pilot cell is the measured middle step SFS needs before scaling automation fully.

--- MAIN STEM ---
Northgate Formalwear (NGF) is a private limited company in the formal menswear retail sector, based in Columbus, Ohio, employing a workforce of 60. Founded in 2011 by David Okafor, it sells suits and office wear through three stores and a growing online shop, operating a hierarchical structure with democratic leadership. NGF plans to invest $720,000 in a new automated e-commerce fulfilment centre with computer stock control, financed by a $450,000 ten-year bank loan and $270,000 retained profit. The business has fixed costs of $310,000 a year, a variable cost of $14.50 a unit and a selling price of $24.50, and currently produces 55,000 units a year. NGF faces an online returns problem, with 13.5% of units returned and rising quality complaints.

--- APPENDIX 1 — MARKETING/OPS ---
Market Research Summary — October 2026: A survey of 800 online shoppers found that 58% would buy formalwear online at least once a year and 46% say free returns are the main reason they choose an online retailer. Fulfilment currently averages 3.5 days per order, and the returns rate stands at 13.5%, compared with 8.2% for in-store purchases. Of 1,200 orders shipped last quarter, 163 were returned. The survey also found that 61% of respondents say online sizing guides would increase their confidence to purchase, and 39% of returns cited 'item too large' or 'item too small' as the reason.

--- APPENDIX 2 — FINANCIAL DATA ---
Title: Extract from the Statement of Financial Position of Northgate Formalwear as at 31 March 2025 ($ '000)
Headers: ['Financial Metric', '2024', '2025']
Inventories | 260 | 210
Trade receivables | 140 | 175
Cash and cash equivalents | 30 | 55
Current liabilities | 300 | 270
Non-current assets | 1,400 | 2,100
Capital employed | 1,900 | 2,250

--- APPENDIX 3 — EXTERNAL ENVIRONMENT ---
Economic and Business Bulletin (November 2026): (1) The central bank has raised the base interest rate from 4.5% to 5.75%, the fifth rise this year, increasing borrowing costs for businesses with variable-rate loans. (2) The national minimum wage will rise by 6.2% from $13.42 to $14.25 per hour from April 2027, raising wage bills across retail. (3) Parcel carrier fuel surcharges have risen 8.0% year-on-year and clothing input costs are up 5.4%, although consumer online apparel spending grew 6.8%.

--- QUESTIONS ---
  Q1(a) [8 marks]
    Question: NGF plans to fund the new e-commerce fulfilment centre with a ten-year bank loan and retained profit. Explain two advantages for NGF of using retained profit to fund the expansion instead of increasing the bank loan.
    Answer: Point 1: Using retained profit costs NGF no interest and creates no new repayment commitments, so the $270,000 is invested without stretching cash flow at a time when fixed costs already stand at $310,000 a year and the business must service a $450,000 ten-year bank loan. Every dollar not paid in interest protects NGF's ability to absorb the 5.4% rise in clothing input costs and the 8.0% parcel carrier fuel surcharge while holding the $24.50 selling price against rival online retailers.

Point 2: Retained profit requires no collateral or guarantee, so the automated fulfilment centre is not at risk of repossession if online demand disappoints — a real possibility when 13.5% of units are already returned. Unlike increasing the bank loan, using its own profits also preserves David Okafor's ownership and control, since no lender can attach conditions on how the centre is run, what staff are hired or how quickly the loan must be repaid. Finally, avoiding extra debt strengthens NGF's relationship with its bank, keeping the $450,000 facility available for working capital while the expansion ramps up and the 6.8% growth in online apparel spending is pursued.
    Keywords: retained profit, $270,000, $450,000, $310,000, 5.4%, 13.5%
    Mark scheme: knowledge_max_2: 1 mark for each valid advantage identified (max 2). | application_analysis_max_6: Up to 3 marks per point for contextual explanation and analysis applied to NGF's expansion, costs, returns problem and financing decision.

  Q1(b) [12 marks]
    Question: NGF is launching the online range that will be fulfilled from the new centre. Consider paid search advertising, social media influencer marketing or email marketing to NGF's existing customers. Which should NGF choose to promote the launch? Justify your recommendation.
    Answer: Paid search advertising: Paid search places NGF at the top of results when shoppers search for terms such as 'buy suit online', capturing high-intent buyers exactly when they are ready to purchase. Spend is measurable through click-through and conversion data and NGF can cap the daily budget. However, bids for retail keywords are highly competitive, and every click costs money even without a sale, straining NGF's resources after committing $720,000 to the centre.

Social media influencer marketing: Fashion and lifestyle influencers could showcase NGF's suits to younger professionals, generating aspirational content and quick traffic surges. Its weaknesses are that results compound slowly, influencer credibility varies, and NGF's formalwear buyers skew older than typical influencer audiences, so much of the spend may not convert to the 55,000-unit target.

Email marketing: Emailing existing customers costs very little per message and reaches people who already trust NGF's stores. NGF can promote the launch, free returns and the online sizing guides that 61% of surveyed shoppers say would raise their confidence to buy, and track orders against the 1,200-orders-per-quarter benchmark. Its limitation is reach: it cannot win first-time customers, so awareness growth is capped.

Recommendation: NGF should choose email marketing as the lead channel, supported later by modest paid search. Email is the cheapest, most measurable and best-targeted route to announce the launch to a warm audience and to highlight the free returns valued by 46% of shoppers. Paid search alone is rejected as too expensive against national rivals for a business funding $720,000 of investment, influencer marketing is rejected as poorly matched to formalwear's buyer profile, and neither suits a launch better than a direct message to loyal customers.

  Q2(a) [8 marks]
    Question: NGF's returns rate has reached 13.5% and quality complaints are rising. Explain two benefits for NGF of using democratic leadership to tackle this problem with its fulfilment team.
    Answer: Point 1: Democratic leadership gives NGF's fulfilment employees a voice in how picking, packing and quality checks are organised, satisfying their esteem needs and raising commitment. Workers who help design the size-check and packing routines are more likely to follow them consistently, cutting the error rate that is driving the 13.5% returns rate and the 163 units sent back last quarter.

  Q2(b) [12 marks]
    Question: NGF needs a returns-quality supervisor for the fulfilment centre. Consider internal recruitment or external recruitment. Which should NGF choose? Justify your decision.
    Answer: Internal recruitment: Promoting an experienced picker or packer to returns-quality supervisor is fast and inexpensive, and NGF already knows the candidate's attendance, pace and attitude. The appointee understands the computer stock control system and the layout of the new centre, needs little induction, and the promotion signals to the 60 employees that effort is rewarded, aiding retention in a warehouse role. The drawbacks are that NGF may choose from a small pool, the promoted worker still needs supervisory training, and an internal hire may lack the fresh ideas or formal quality qualifications an external candidate could bring.

External recruitment: Advertising externally widens the pool to trained quality supervisors with formal credentials and experience of other retailers' returns operations, which could inject new standards and audit rigour into a business fighting a 13.5% returns rate with 163 units returned last quarter. However, external recruitment is slower and costlier — advertising, interviewing and induction while the centre is being commissioned — and a newcomer may misread NGF's flat, team-based ways of working or the specifics of its computer stock control system, risking an early mis-hire.

Decision: NGF should choose internal recruitment. The priority is speed and cultural fit during the $720,000 expansion: an internal appointee can be in post before the centre opens, understands the workforce and costs almost nothing in fees. External recruitment is rejected because the $450,000 bank loan is already committed to the investment itself, NGF's most urgent need is someone who knows its e-commerce returns flow from day one, and any gaps in quality-audit skills can be closed later with a short off-the-job course.

This personalises recommendations, supports the online sizing guides 61% of shoppers want, and lifts sales without the rent, fittings and staffing cost of a fourth store while the $720,000 fulfilment centre comes online and the 6.8% growth in online apparel spending is pursued.

  Q4(b) [12 marks]
    Question: Using Appendix 3, evaluate how the rise in the base interest rate to 5.75%, the 6.2% minimum wage increase to $14.25 and the combined 8.0% carrier fuel surcharge and 5.4% clothing input cost rise will affect NGF. Which change will have the greatest impact? Justify your answer.
    Answer: Interest rate rise (from 4.5% to 5.75%): NGF's $450,000 ten-year bank loan, if variable-rate, will cost roughly 1.25% more a year, adding about $5,600 of annual interest and marginally raising the cost of any future equipment borrowing. Higher rates may also dampen discretionary spending on suits. The direct effect is real but modest, and NGF could fix the loan rate or renegotiate terms to cap the exposure.

Minimum wage increase (6.2%, to $14.25 per hour): The national minimum wage rises from $13.42 to $14.25 per hour. That is a certain, recurring cost across NGF's wage bill — it hits every shift, every store and the fulfilment centre simultaneously, and democratic leadership, training and the productivity gains from automated fulfilment must offset it. NGF may need to review staffing levels or selective prices, and the wage rise may squeeze cash flow even as it builds the $720,000 automation investment.

Carrier fuel surcharge (+8.0%) and clothing input costs (+5.4%): A 5.4% rise on the $14.50 variable cost is about $0.78 per unit ($14.50 × 5.4% = $0.78), so the variable cost per unit rises and the $10.00 contribution absorbs some of it; the 8.0% fuel surcharge adds to delivery charges as well. Both are partly recoverable through sizing guides, carrier renegotiation and modest price increases.

Conclusion: The 6.2% minimum wage increase will have the greatest impact. It is a certain, recurring, unavoidable cost on the whole workforce, while the input and carrier increases are partly controllable through supplier negotiation and lower returns, and the interest-rate increase can be fixed. NGF must prioritise productivity gains, scheduling efficiency and selective price rises alongside its $720,000 automation investment.
    Keywords: 5.75%, 6.2%, $14.25, 5.4%, 8.0%, $450,000
    Mark scheme: level_1_1_to_4: Identifies the external factors with limited application to NGF. | level_2_5_to_8: Analyses the impact of at least two external changes on NGF's costs, revenue or financing in context. | level_3_9_to_12: Detailed evaluation of all three external changes in the context of NGF with a well-justified judgment that the minimum wage increase has the greatest impact and why the other two are smaller.

--- MAIN STEM ---
Paloma Rose Boutique (PRB) is a private limited company in the occasionwear retail sector, based in San Antonio, Texas, employing a workforce of 48. PRB plans to invest $650,000 in a fourth boutique in Austin with an online style-advice service, financed by $400,000 venture capital and $250,000 retained profit. The business has fixed costs of $420,000 a year, a variable cost of $17.00 a unit and a selling price of $38.00, and currently produces 32,000 units a year. PRB faces high labour turnover, with 22% of seasonal staff leaving before the festive season.

--- APPENDIX 1 — MARKETING/OPS ---

  Q1(a) [8 marks]
    Question: PRB plans to fund the Austin boutique with venture capital and retained profit. Explain two advantages for PRB of using venture capital to fund the expansion instead of a bank loan.

This protects the cash flow needed for the festive peak, avoids the risk of default that a loan would carry, and leaves the $250,000 retained profit untouched as a cushion against the 22% labour turnover and the 9.4% rent increase quoted for the premises.

Point 2: Venture capital investors in retail typically bring more than money: site-selection experience, supplier introductions and marketing know-how that can accelerate the Austin launch and the online style-advice service, shortening the time before the new boutique contributes towards the $420,000 annual fixed costs. Unlike a bank, which is indifferent to success beyond repayment, the investor's return depends on growth, so both parties are aligned. Crucially, PRB is not exposed to the 6.0% base rate on this capital, which keeps financing costs predictable while occasionwear consumer spending grows 4.8% a year and competition for the Austin site intensifies.

    Question: PRB is opening its fourth boutique in Austin. Consider billboard hoardings across Austin, local radio sponsorship or social media influencer marketing to promote the opening. Which should PRB choose to promote the launch? Justify your recommendation.
    Answer: Billboard hoardings: Large hoardings on Austin commuter routes would give the new boutique broad local visibility with repeated daily impressions. They suit a single catchment and build recognition fast. However, they are expensive to rent and print, cannot be targeted to occasionwear buyers specifically, and provide no direct response data — unlike the voucher code that tracked 1,320 store visits and 640 redemptions in the spring campaign — so PRB cannot tell whether the spend drives footfall or merely awareness.

Local radio sponsorship: Sponsoring an Austin drive-time or lifestyle show reaches exactly the car-commuting, style-conscious audience most likely to visit, and the station can voice a repeating opening offer with voucher code mechanics for measurement at a fraction of hoarding cost. It suits a flat, laissez-faire boutique where the creative team can script the spots. Weaknesses are limited reach beyond the metro area and no visual presence for fashion, though window displays and in-store styling can carry the visual side.

Social media influencer marketing: Austin fashion and lifestyle influencers could model occasionwear to younger followers, extending the 4.0% click-through behaviour of the spring campaign. However, influencer fees are paid regardless of results, audiences skew to followers living outside Austin, and attribution for a single-store opening is murky at best.

Recommendation: PRB should choose local radio sponsorship. It is the cheapest option delivering repeated, measurable, locally concentrated exposure carrying a redemption code, it fits a launch that must fill a new boutique quickly, and it avoids heavy fixed costs on a business whose fixed costs already run at $420,000 a year. Billboards are rejected as costly and unmeasurable for a data-driven business with proven voucher redemption, influencer marketing is rejected as untargeted for a single-city opening, with social promotion kept only as a supporting tactic.

    Answer: Point 1: Laissez-faire leadership gives experienced occasionwear consultants genuine autonomy over styling, merchandising and clienteling, satisfying their esteem and self-actualisation needs (Maslow). Staff who feel trusted are more loyal and engaged, which directly attacks the 22% seasonal labour turnover that leaves boutiques short-staffed in the festive peak when occasionwear demand is highest.

Creative freedom also produces fresher window displays, stronger social content and better-themed rails for the three boutiques, lifting footfall without extra cost. However, rotation during the busiest trading weeks of the year risks confusion and slower service, demands training time PRB does not have in late November, and weakens individual accountability for transactions and average order value.

Decision: PRB should choose the individual sales bonus for the festive period. It is fast to introduce, measurable from till data, directly tied to the revenue PRB must generate before Christmas and it motivates exactly the temporary workers most at risk of disengaging during the busiest six weeks of the year. Job rotation is rejected for now because reshuffling inexperienced temporary staff across departments in peak weeks would damage service, erode the average value per order and overload permanent staff who must re-train colleagues; PRB can rotate its permanent team between seasons once the December rush has passed and use rotation as next year's retention lever instead.

--- APPENDIX 1 — MARKETING/OPS ---

--- APPENDIX 2 — FINANCIAL DATA ---

Economic and Business Bulletin (November 2026): (1) The central bank raised the base interest rate to 5.25%, increasing the cost of variable-rate borrowing such as overdrafts. (2) The national minimum wage will rise by just 2.0% to $12.60 per hour from April 2027, the smallest rise in a decade. (3) Technical textile and ripstop fabric costs rose 9.6% year-on-year and diesel prices rose 11.0%, while consumer spending on outdoor recreation grew 4.2%.

  Q1(a) [8 marks]
    Question: TRO plans to fund the distribution centre automation with hire purchase and a bank overdraft. Explain two advantages for TRO of using hire purchase to fund the expansion instead of increasing the overdraft.
    Answer: Point 1: Hire purchase spreads the $540,000 cost of the conveyor and sorting machinery across fixed monthly instalments, making payments predictable and easy to budget against the $385,000 annual fixed costs. An overdraft, by contrast, is repayable on demand and its interest rate moves with the base rate — now 5.25% — so overdraft costs could escalate unpredictably and the bank could withdraw the facility exactly when TRO needs working capital most.

Point 2: Once TRO completes the instalments it will own the automated technology, turning a planned acquisition into a structured purchase without ever paying the full $920,000 at once. The overdraft remains free as a buffer for stock and payroll, and the hire purchase charge matches the long, productive life of the automation. An overdraft would add no ownership, would sit as a permanent short-term liability and would deepen cash-flow strain while the centre is commissioned and picking errors take time to fall below 4.6%.

  Q1(b) [12 marks]
    Question: TRO is launching next-day delivery for outdoor gear ordered online. Consider sponsorship of national hiking events, advertising in outdoor magazines or a national television campaign. Which should TRO choose? Justify your recommendation.
    Answer: Sponsorship of national hiking events: Sponsoring marked trails or entry packs at the national hiking festival places TRO directly in front of exactly the people who buy hiking and camping gear, creates hands-on product experience and generates social media content from participants. It is measurable via event promo codes, far cheaper than television, and the 4.2% growth in outdoor recreation spending shows the audience is expanding. Its limits are seasonal timing and modest reach beyond the participants.

Outdoor magazine advertising: Print ads in hiking and camping titles reach a defined enthusiast audience with high dwell time and editorial credibility, at moderate cost. However, circulation is small and static, frequency is limited to issue dates, and responses are hard to measure — better for reinforcing brand awareness than for a launch-time sales surge tied to the next-day delivery promise.

National television campaign: Television would build the widest national awareness of next-day delivery very quickly and give TRO the perceived national scale of larger chains. But production and airtime costs are very high for a single distribution centre rollout, much of the audience lies outside TRO's six-store catchment or does not buy outdoor gear online, and the wasted impressions would be hard to justify while $920,000 is still being invested and picking errors run at 4.6%.

Recommendation: TRO should choose sponsorship of national hiking events. It is the only option that reaches the exact target market at the moment of maximum receptivity, at a cost TRO can afford, with measurable promo-code responses and rich content for social media. Outdoor magazines are rejected as too narrow and slow for a launch, national television is rejected as unaffordable and untargeted for a distributor still commissioning $920,000 of automation rather than rolling out nationally.

Drawbacks are that trainers are removed from their own duties at a time when overtime is already up 18%, bad habits can transfer, and there is no formal certificate — a problem for insurers once $920,000 of automated equipment is running at full speed.

Off-the-job training: An accredited college course teaches conveyor mechanics, software diagnostics and machinery safety in a distraction-free environment and ends with a recognised certificate for all 22 operators, valuable evidence for insurers and for compliance around automated machinery. Drawbacks are tuition fees (roughly $1,250 per employee, about $27,500 in total), time away from the distribution centre during the festive peak, and content generic to the industry rather than TRO's exact configuration.

Decision: TRO should choose off-the-job training first, followed by brief on-the-job consolidation. The $920,000 investment is too valuable and the safety stakes too high to rely on informal learning around live conveyors; a certificate also protects TRO commercially and with its insurers. On-the-job training alone is rejected because it embeds unverified habits around dangerous, expensive machinery and leaves TRO unable to evidence operator competence. Once the core course is complete, short on-the-job sessions tailored to TRO's warehouse can follow at minimal extra cost.

Acid Test Ratio 2024 = 0.91 : 1

Conclusion: TRO's financial position has improved.     Answer: Interest rate rise (to 5.25%): TRO draws on a $380,000 overdraft, so a rise in the base rate increases its interest charge proportionally — perhaps an extra $1,500 to $3,000 a year depending on average drawn balance. Hire purchase instalments are fixed, limiting further exposure, but carrying trade receivables and stock for longer becomes more expensive, and delaying repayment of the overdraft is costlier than before.

Minimum wage increase (2.0%, to $12.60 per hour): With 85 employees, the 2.0% rise is the smallest in a decade; staffing costs remain manageable, though the longest-serving warehouse staff may still expect progression as they master the new technology.

Technical textile and ripstop fabric costs (+9.6%) and diesel prices (+11.0%): A 9.6% rise on TRO's $27.50 variable cost is about $2.64 per unit ($27.50 × 9.6% = $2.64), squeezing the $17.50 contribution on each of the 40,000 units a year sold; diesel price rises are material but small relative to textile costs and can be passed to carriers through fuel surcharges. TRO must renegotiate fabric contracts, tighten cutting waste and review pricing to defend the $17.50 contribution and the next-day delivery promise.

Conclusion: The 9.6% increase in technical textile costs will have the greatest impact. It erodes the $17.50 contribution on every unit sold and directly threatens the economics of the $920,000 automation investment, while the 11.0% diesel rise is small and passable to carriers and the 2.0% minimum wage rise is the mildest in a decade with manageable staffing costs. TRO must renegotiate fabric contracts, tighten cutting waste, audit carrier surcharges and review pricing to defend margins and the next-day delivery promise.

--- MAIN STEM ---
Fleetline Fashion (FLF) is a public limited company in the value fashion retail sector, based in New York, employing a workforce of 90. Founded in 2016 by Renee Caldwell, it sells affordable clothing through 14 stores and a growing website, operating a hierarchical structure with democratic leadership. FLF plans to invest $1,200,000 in a new automated distribution centre dedicated to its online own-label range, financed by an $800,000 share issue and a $400,000 bank loan. The business has fixed costs of $540,000 a year, a variable cost of $5.00 a unit and a selling price of $9.50, and currently produces 160,000 units a year. FLF faces rising unsold seasonal stock, now 18% of inventory, forcing deeper mark-downs.

--- APPENDIX 1 — MARKETING/OPS ---
Quality and Waste Report — Autumn/Winter 2026: Inspection rejected 3.1% of the 160,000 units (4,960 units), up from 2.4% last year. Unsold seasonal stock reached 18% of inventory value, and 24% of units were sold at discounted mark-down prices, up from 15% a year ago; the average mark-down was 35%. Fabric waste rose to 6.5% of cutting-room input, and 12% of purchase orders arrived late against an 11-week supplier lead time, driving over-ordering for the peak season.

--- APPENDIX 2 — FINANCIAL DATA ---
Title: Extract from the Statement of Financial Position of Fleetline Fashion as at 31 March 2025 ($ '000)
Headers: ['Financial Metric', '2024', '2025']
Inventories | 420 | 520
Trade receivables | 260 | 270
Cash and cash equivalents | 85 | 45
Current liabilities | 380 | 470
Non-current assets | 2,600 | 3,300
Capital employed | 3,300 | 3,700

--- APPENDIX 3 — EXTERNAL ENVIRONMENT ---
Economic and Business Bulletin (November 2026): (1) The central bank raised the base interest rate to 6.25%, its highest level in a decade. (2) Cotton and synthetic fabric costs rose 14.0% year-on-year, squeezing value-fashion margins. (3) Consumer spending on clothing grew just 1.8%, well below inflation of 6.5%, with value retailers reporting falling footfall and heavier price reductions.

  Q1(a) [8 marks]
    Question: FLF plans to fund the distribution centre with a share issue and a bank loan. Explain two advantages for FLF of using a share issue to fund the expansion instead of the bank loan.
    Answer: Point 1: A share issue raises the $800,000 with no interest charges and no fixed repayment schedule, which protects FLF at a time when its current ratio has already fallen from 2.01 to 1.78 and cash dropped from $85,000 to $45,000. Unlike the $400,000 bank loan, shareholders' capital cannot be called in on a set date, so FLF keeps maximum flexibility while the distribution centre ramps up.

Point 2: Issuing shares spreads the risk of a large, unproven $1,200,000 investment across many owners rather than concentrating it in debt. If the online own-label range underperforms, FLF owes shareholders no fixed interest — unlike a lender, they simply share in higher or lower returns. Financing two-thirds of the project with equity also preserves FLF's borrowing capacity for future trade finance or acquisitions, and avoids encumbering assets just as current liabilities have risen to $470,000.

However, production plus airtime would consume the $400,000 loan and far more, while much of the audience is not buying FLF at a $9.50 average price online, creating huge waste for a business already applying price reductions to 24% of its units.

Short-video influencer marketing: Short-video creators on the dominant social platforms can style, try on and price-compare the own-label range directly to price-sensitive younger shoppers, with spend tracked through views, clicks and redemption codes and fees flexible to performance. It matches FLF's margin structure, funnels traffic straight to the new website and distribution centre, and builds the kind of social proof that suits own-label discovery at low cost.

Billboard advertising in retail parks: Hoardings beside retail parks reach shoppers already in a buying mood and reinforce the own-label name locally.     Answer: Interest rate rise (to 6.25%): FLF's $400,000 bank loan would carry roughly an extra $25,000 a year of interest at the new rate, and future borrowing for the distribution centre will be pricier still. Unlike the interest rise (bounded and largely pre-funded) or fabric inflation (about $67,000 a year, quantifiable and partly recoverable through pricing and waste reduction), falling real demand attacks FLF's revenue, its stock clearance and the viability of the distribution centre simultaneously — a compounding, revenue-side risk that should drive FLF's response: sharper buying against the 11-week lead time, aggressive full-price conversion of the 18% overstock, and phased investment milestones tied to measured online sales growth.
    Keywords: 6.25%, 14.0%, 1.8%, 6.5%, $400,000, $800,000
    Mark scheme: level_1_1_to_4: Identifies the external factors with limited application to FLF. | level_2_5_to_8: Analyses the impact of at least two external changes on FLF's costs, revenue or financing in context. | level_3_9_to_12: Detailed evaluation of all three external changes in the context of FLF with a well-justified judgment that weak consumer spending has the greatest impact and why the other two are smaller.

--- MAIN STEM ---
Little Sprout Clothing Cooperative (LSP) is a cooperative in the childrenswear retail sector, based in Portland, Oregon, employing a workforce of 28. Founded in 2019 by Sophie and Dan Whitmore, it sells new and refurbished children's clothing through one shop and online, operating a flat structure with democratic leadership. LSP plans to invest $350,000 in a pre-loved childrenswear e-commerce platform with a garment repair workshop, financed by a $220,000 bank loan and $130,000 retained profit. The business has fixed costs of $210,000 a year, a variable cost of $5.50 a unit and a selling price of $12.00, and currently produces 40,000 units a year. LSP faces a skills gap, with only 6 of 28 staff trained in garment repair and refurbishment.

--- APPENDIX 1 — MARKETING/OPS ---
Market Research Summary — September 2026: A survey of 500 parents found that 71% would buy pre-loved children's clothing online and 64% already resell items informally. Among parents aged 25-40, 57% cited sustainability as their main reason to buy resale, and the average saving versus new was $14 per garment. Current repair turnaround averages 5 days.

Every dollar not paid as interest can fund repair workshop equipment and keep refurbished garments affordable for parents, which is central to LSP's cooperative mission.

Point 2: Retained profit keeps ownership and decision-making entirely with the worker-members, consistent with cooperative principles.     Question: Using Appendix 2, evaluate LSP's financial position by calculating the current ratio and the acid test ratio for 2024 and 2025. Has LSP's financial position improved? Justify your answer.
    Answer: Calculations:
Current Ratio 2024 = 1.16 : 1
Current Ratio 2025 = 1.37 : 1
Acid Test Ratio 2024 = 0.59 : 1
Acid Test Ratio 2025 = 0.90 : 1

Detailed workings: Current assets 2024 = $90,000 inventories + $60,000 trade receivables + $35,000 cash = $185,000. Current assets 2025 = $70,000 + $85,000 + $50,000 = $205,000. Stricter measure 2024 = ($185,000 − $90,000) ÷ $160,000 = $95,000 ÷ $160,000 = 0.59; 2025 = ($205,000 − $70,000) ÷ $150,000 = $135,000 ÷ $150,000 = 0.90.

The stricter measure improved from 0.59 to 0.90, the strongest single-year gain, so LSP no longer depends on selling inventory to pay short-term debts — a vital milestone before launching the platform and taking on a $220,000 bank loan. Cautions: trade receivables climbed from $60,000 to $85,000 (platform sales on account) and should be collected promptly, and cash of $50,000 remains thin against a $350,000 project, leaving little room for cost overruns or slippage in launch revenue.

Conclusion: LSP's financial position has improved. Both measures strengthened (1.16 to 1.37 and 0.59 to 0.90), and the improvement does not rest on inventories, which actually fell from $90,000 to $70,000 as refurbished stock turned faster. LSP should collect receivables faster and phase platform spending carefully to protect cash during the launch so the stronger position endures.

    Question: Using Appendix 3, evaluate how the base interest rate rise to 5.5%, the 6.0% minimum wage increase to $13.60 and the 18.5% online resale market growth and 15.0% forecast expansion will affect LSP. Which change will have the greatest impact? Justify your answer.
    Answer: Interest rate rise (to 5.5%): LSP's $220,000 bank loan, if variable-rate, will cost roughly an extra $1,100 to $2,000 a year — small alongside fixed costs of $210,000. LSP can fix the rate and shield itself. Higher rates may slightly reduce consumers' willingness to borrow for discretionary purchases, though resale's saving positioning ($14 per garment versus new) is relatively resilient when household budgets are tight.

Minimum wage increase (6.0%, to $13.60 per hour): For 28 mainly retail and workshop staff, the 6.0% rise is noticeable for a cooperative on modest margins. It strengthens the case for the repair upskilling programme because higher productivity per hour is the natural offset, and schedulers must be smarter about peak-hour cover to absorb it.

Online resale market growth (18.5% last year, forecast to expand a further 15.0% in 2027): This is a direct, measurable expansion of LSP's addressable market exactly as the platform launches. Capturing even a modest share of that growth would add thousands of orders, lift throughput beyond 40,000 units, fully utilise the repair workshop and push contribution well above current levels — dwarfing the interest-rate effect and offsetting the wage rise. The risk is failing to scale people and process fast enough to meet demand.

Conclusion: The 18.5% online resale market growth will have the greatest impact. It is strategic, not merely financial: it can determine whether the $350,000 platform creates step-change value or merely digitises a small shop. The wage rise is real and may be noticeable for the 28-person cooperative, but it is manageable through upskilling and peak-hour scheduling, and interest at 5.5% is minor and fixable. LSP should move quickly to train the 22 untrained members, lock supplier and freight deals and launch the platform while the window of 15.0% forecast growth is open — missing it forfeits the first-mover advantage in its home market.

--- MAIN STEM ---
Carrowdale Hall (CDH) is a private limited company in the hospitality and events sector, employing a workforce of 64. Founded in 2009 by Elena Carrow, the business operates a heritage wedding and conference venue on the shores of Lake Carrow and uses a hierarchical organisational structure with autocratic leadership. CDH plans to invest $1,450,000 in a new lakeside events pavilion with 400 covers, financed by an $800,000 ten-year bank loan and $650,000 retained profit. It has fixed costs of $216,000 a year, a variable cost of $46 a unit and a selling price of $70, and currently produces 15,000 units a year. CDH faces two operational problems: labour turnover in the banqueting team has reached 17% and food waste from events is rising.

--- APPENDIX 1 — MARKETING/OPS ---
Market Research Summary — August 2026: A survey of 480 couples and corporate clients found 73% prefer all-inclusive event packages, 61% would pay up to $12 extra per guest for locally sourced catering, and 48% say on-site accommodation influenced their venue choice. Carrowdale Hall staged 132 events last year at an average spend of $14,500 per wedding and $6,200 per conference. Complaints fell from 29 to 17 per quarter, and the lead time from enquiry to signed contract is 5.5 weeks. A skills audit found 22 of 64 banqueting staff have not completed on-the-job training on the pavilion catering equipment; off-the-job courses at the regional college cost $850 per employee.

--- APPENDIX 2 — FINANCIAL DATA ---
Title: Extract from the Statement of Financial Position of Carrowdale Hall as at 31 March 2025 ($ '000)
Headers: ['Financial Metric', '2024', '2025']
Inventories | 150 | 110
Trade receivables | 260 | 340
Cash and cash equivalents | 55 | 90
Current liabilities | 310 | 350
Non-current assets | 3,100 | 4,250
Capital employed | 3,700 | 4,450

--- APPENDIX 3 — EXTERNAL ENVIRONMENT ---
Economic and Business Bulletin (November 2026): (1) The central bank raised the base interest rate from 4.5% to 5.25%, its third rise this year, increasing costs for businesses servicing variable-rate loans. (2) The national minimum wage will rise by 5.9% from $11.85 to $12.55 per hour from April 2026, lifting hospitality staffing costs. (3) Wholesale catering input costs have risen 9.6% year-on-year and food inflation stands at 7.0%, while consumer spending on weddings and conferences grew 4.8% over the same period.

With the base rate now at 5.25%, interest on an even larger loan would absorb more of the $24 contribution earned on every $70 cover, so retained profit keeps more of the 15,000 units' revenue available to fund the pavilion build and to absorb the 9.6% rise in catering input costs.

Point 2: Retained profit avoids the collateral and condition risk attached to a bigger bank loan. If wedding and conference demand softens (the wider market grew only 4.8% last year), CDH would not face repossession of the lakeside pavilion or Lake Carrow assets, and Elena Carrow retains full ownership and control without lender conditions on how the pavilion and its 400 covers are run. The $650,000 retained profit is also available immediately without application delays, letting CDH lock in the 132-events pipeline and the 5.5-week contract lead time while rivals wait for credit approval.

    Question: CDH is launching its new lakeside events pavilion. Consider a national television campaign, local radio sponsorship, or social media influencer marketing. Which should CDH choose to promote the launch? Justify your recommendation.

    Answer: Calculations:
Current Ratio 2024 = 1.50 : 1
Current Ratio 2025 = 1.54 : 1
Acid Test Ratio 2024 = 1.02 : 1
Acid Test Ratio 2025 = 1.23 : 1

Detailed workings: 2024 current assets = $150,000 inventories + $260,000 trade receivables + $55,000 cash = $465,000; 2025 current assets = $110,000 + $340,000 + $90,000 = $540,000. 2024 = $465,000 ÷ $310,000 = 1.50 : 1; 2025 = $540,000 ÷ $350,000 = 1.54 : 1.     Question: Using Appendix 3, evaluate how the interest rate rise to 5.25%, the 5.9% minimum wage increase and the 9.6% rise in catering input costs will affect CDH. Which change will have the greatest impact? Justify your answer.
    Answer: Interest rate rise (4.5% to 5.25%): If CDH's $800,000 ten-year bank loan, or any portion refinanced at today's rates, carries a variable rate, the 0.75 percentage point rise adds roughly $6,000 a year — meaningful against $216,000 fixed costs but absorbable. Higher rates also cool household discretionary spending on weddings, although CDH's corporate conference pipeline (conferences average $6,200 per event) is less rate-sensitive.

Minimum wage increase (5.9%, to $12.55): Hospitality is labour-intensive, and banqueting, kitchen and housekeeping roles concentrate near the minimum. If, for illustration, 40 of the 64 staff are near the minimum, the extra $0.70 per hour costs about $56,000 a year — a recurring hit equal to roughly a quarter of fixed costs, landing exactly when the pavilion opens and new staff are hired.

Catering input-cost inflation (9.6%): Food is the dominant element of the $46 unit cost. If, for illustration, ingredients are around half the unit cost (about $23), a 9.6% rise adds about $2.20 per cover; across 15,000 units that is roughly $33,000 a year, dragging contribution from $24 toward $21.80 at the worst moment, and it recurs on every cover rather than once a year.

Conclusion: The 9.6% rise in catering input costs will have the greatest impact. Unlike the wage rise, it cannot be avoided by hiring decisions or rota design; unlike the interest rise (about $6,000 a year, hedgeable by fixing the loan), it compounds on every one of the 15,000 units sold and cannot be fully recovered — clients sign all-inclusive budgets 5.5 weeks in advance, leaving CDH stuck with pre-agreed prices. The wage rise is the second most serious pressure; the interest rise is smallest and manageable. CDH should lock input-price contracts with lake-district suppliers, re-price packages from 2027, and fix its loan rate before April 2026.

--- MAIN STEM ---
Sorrel Bay Apart-Hotels (SBA) is a public limited company in the hospitality and apart-hotel sector, employing a workforce of 120. Founded in 2004 by Farah Qureshi, the group operates serviced apartments around the Sorrel Bay marina and uses a flat organisational structure with democratic leadership. It has fixed costs of $480,000 a year, a variable cost of $28 a unit and a selling price of $52, and currently produces 38,000 units a year. SBA faces two operational problems: labour turnover among housekeeping staff has reached 22% and guest complaints about maintenance delays have risen.

--- APPENDIX 1 — MARKETING/OPS ---
Operations Log — Q3 2026: The 148 serviced apartments recorded 33,200 guest-nights last quarter, up from 29,400 a year ago, at an average occupancy of 78%. Maintenance requests averaged 140 per month with an average resolution time of 2.6 days, down from 3.4 days a year ago. Guest complaints fell from 64 to 41 per month. A survey of 750 guests found 66% prefer contactless check-in and 57% rate housekeeping consistency their top priority. A skills audit found 26 of 120 staff have not completed on-the-job training on the contactless check-in system; off-the-job training at the maritime college costs $750 per employee.

Unlike a share issue, it does not dilute existing shareholders or create market pressure to maintain payouts, which matters for a public limited company answerable to investors who will scrutinise every $2,400,000 the marina build consumes.

Point 2: Retained profit involves no issue costs, no underwriting fees and no roadshow marketing, and it is deployed immediately without waiting for shareholder approval or subscription. SBA can lock in the 30-apartment construction slot before material costs climb further, keeps Farah Qureshi's control undiluted, and signals financial strength to the market without the discount often applied to new share issues, protecting the $52 average rate economics across the 38,000 units sold this year and reassuring the 750-strong guest base that SBA is building from profit, not from fragile balance-sheet stretch.

Brackenfell Adventure Co (BAC) is a partnership in the activity tourism sector, employing a workforce of 28. It has fixed costs of $126,000 a year, a variable cost of $18 a unit and a selling price of $33, and currently produces 14,000 units a year. It also demonstrates personal commitment from the founders, reassuring local suppliers and the regional bank on the retained $400,000 portion, protects the partnership's negotiating position, strengthens BAC's credit file for any future tranche, and keeps long-term plans for the climbing centre fully in Brackenfell hands.

    Question: BAC must recertify 7 of 28 guides in advanced swift-water rescue. Consider on-the-job coaching by lead guides or off-the-job recertification at the regional centre. Which should BAC choose? Justify your decision.

--- MAIN STEM ---
Copperbowl Food Hall (CFH) is a worker cooperative in the hospitality and food hall sector, employing a workforce of 52. Founded in 2016 by Rosa Delgado, CFH runs a 14-stall food hall in the dockside quarter and uses a flat organisational structure with democratic leadership. The co-op plans to invest $950,000 in a second food hall at the Old Market, financed by a $550,000 community share issue and $400,000 retained profit. It has fixed costs of $180,000 a year, a variable cost of $9 a unit and a selling price of $15, and currently produces 45,000 units a year. CFH faces two operational problems: food waste running at 13.6% of ingredients and rising quality complaints across its 14 stalls.

--- APPENDIX 1 — MARKETING/OPS ---
Quality/Waste Report — October 2026: Copperbowl served 41,000 meals last quarter across 14 stalls at an average transaction value of $12.60. Food waste ran at 13.6% of ingredients by value, down from 15.2% a year ago; customer complaints fell from 52 to 33 per month; the defect rate on prepared dishes is 2.1%. Footfall counters recorded 210,000 visits last quarter. A survey of 800 shoppers found 69% cite local sourcing as a priority and 62% would pay $1.00 extra for low-waste meals. On-the-job training in portion control is proposed for stallholders; off-the-job workshops at the culinary college cost $700 per stallholder.

--- APPENDIX 2 — FINANCIAL DATA ---

Unlike a share issue, it keeps member voting power undiluted — every member retains an equal stake in how the Old Market site is run, which protects Rosa Delgado's democratic leadership model.

Point 2: Retained profit costs nothing in issue administration, member communications or return-of-capital expectations, and is available immediately — important while the base rate of 5.3% raises the hurdle for external finance and share-investor expectations. Using profit the co-op already earned demonstrates prudence to members, building support for the second food hall ahead of the member vote, keeps member returns steady, and avoids pressure on stallholders to slash portion quality or local-sourcing standards to fund new distributions or service any new obligations or member-return expectations this year.

Engagement is measurable (footfall, sales per stall, premium uptake), costs are low, and the content reinforces the co-op's community narrative better than any advertisement.

It targets the exact ethical-food segment CFH's own research identified, preserves the margin needed to fund the Old Market build, and builds durable community loyalty. --- MAIN STEM ---
Thornwick Grange Inn (TGI) is a sole trader in the heritage inn and hospitality sector, employing a workforce of 23. Founded in 1998 by Margaret Thornwick, the business is a 16th-century coaching inn with restaurant and bar, and uses a flat organisational structure with laissez-faire leadership. TGI plans to invest $720,000 to restore the coach house into 10 en-suite guest rooms, financed by a $450,000 bank loan and $270,000 of personal savings. It has fixed costs of $150,000 a year, a variable cost of $22 a unit and a selling price of $37, and currently produces 16,000 units a year. TGI faces two operational problems: service-quality complaints have risen and absenteeism among kitchen staff is 8%.

--- APPENDIX 1 — MARKETING/OPS ---
Market Research Summary — September 2026: A survey of 650 visitors found 72% chose Thornwick Grange for its historic character, 65% would pay a $18 premium for a coach-house room, and 54% dine in the inn restaurant during every stay. Average room rate last quarter was $88 with occupancy of 61%, up from 54% a year ago. Service complaints rose from 12 to 19 per month. Lead time for the coach-house booking diary is 8.5 weeks. A skills audit found 9 of 23 staff have not completed on-the-job training on the refurbished kitchen equipment; off-the-job courses at the culinary college cost $650 per employee.

--- APPENDIX 2 — FINANCIAL DATA ---
Title: Extract from the Statement of Financial Position of Thornwick Grange Inn as at 31 March 2025 ($ '000)
Headers: ['Financial Metric', '2024', '2025']

Trade receivables | 20 | 25

Current liabilities | 105 | 120
Non-current assets | 1,150 | 1,750
Capital employed | 1,325 | 1,970

--- APPENDIX 3 — EXTERNAL ENVIRONMENT ---
Economic and Business Bulletin (November 2026): (1) The central bank raised the base interest rate from 4.8% to 5.5%, increasing mortgage and small-business loan costs. (2) The national minimum wage will rise by 5.5% from $12.00 to $12.66 per hour from April 2026. (3) Utilities and energy costs have risen 13.1% year-on-year and hospitality food-cost inflation stands at 8.8%, while heritage-tourism visits grew 4.4% and domestic weekend-break demand rose 6.1%.

--- QUESTIONS ---
  Q1(a) [8 marks]
    Question: TGI plans to finance part of the coach-house restoration with a $450,000 bank loan. Explain two advantages for TGI of using personal savings to fund the expansion instead of a larger bank loan.
    Answer: Point 1: Personal savings carry no interest or repayment schedule, protecting the inn's cash flow while the coach house is restored and before the ten new rooms generate their share of revenue. With the base rate now at 5.5%, enlarging the loan would add interest on top of fixed costs of $150,000 a year and squeeze the $15 contribution earned on each of the 16,000 units sold — one-third of which are restaurant covers already priced against tight 8.8% food-cost inflation.

Point 2: Personal savings keep Margaret Thornwick fully in control without lender covenants over a historic listed building — no repossession risk hanging over the 16th-century coaching inn, and no conditions on materials, room count or opening dates. Savings are also immediately available without application delays or arrangement fees, letting TGI lock in heritage craftspeople before utilities (up 13.1%) and food-cost inflation climb further, and without diluting the family's sole right to manage the Grange.
    Keywords: personal savings, $270,000, bank loan, $450,000, $720,000, 5.5%
    Mark scheme: knowledge_max_2: 1 mark for each valid advantage identified (max 2). | application_analysis_max_6: Up to 3 marks per point for detailed contextual development applied to TGI's financing decision and restoration.

  Q1(b) [12 marks]
    Question: TGI is launching the 10 coach-house rooms. Consider a national food and travel magazine feature, local newspaper and radio advertising, or social media heritage-travel influencer marketing. Which should TGI choose to promote the launch? Justify your recommendation.
    Answer: National magazine feature: A glossy feature in a food and travel magazine would suit TGI's historic brand and reach aspirational heritage travellers nationwide. However, leads take weeks, print readership is shrinking, and the audience is untargeted — most readers will never book one inn in one county; the $18-premium coach-house rooms are better sold with moving visuals than text, and the cost competes directly with the $720,000 restoration budget.

Local newspaper and radio: Cheap and immediate, reaching the regional weekend-break market exactly where domestic weekend-break demand rose 6.1%. But reach is capped at the county, frequency depends on budget, and it cannot show the restored rooms; local residents already fill the 61% occupancy, so the 10 new premium rooms must draw guests from farther afield to pay back.

Social media heritage-travel influencer marketing: Heritage-travel creators can film the timber-framed restoration, the coach-house dining room and the $88 average room rate, reaching the 72% who choose character properties and the 65% willing to pay a premium — precisely the coach-house segment. 8.5-week diary bookings are directly trackable from links and codes, and costs are low against the build.

Recommendation: TGI should choose social media heritage-travel influencer marketing. It reaches the exact premium heritage segment at a fraction of magazine advertising cost, outruns local print in geographic reach, and turns restoration progress into a booking diary filled 8.5 weeks ahead of opening. --- MAIN STEM ---
Meridian Rail Freight (MRF) is a private limited company in the rail freight industry, operating container and bulk trains between the coast port and inland terminals across the country. Founded in 2009 by Idris Bakare, it employs a workforce of 120 and operates a hierarchical structure with democratic leadership. MRF plans to invest $1,150,000 in two new electric locomotives and an upgraded inland freight terminal on the port-Midlands corridor, financed by a $650,000 ten-year bank loan and $500,000 retained profit. It has fixed costs of $420,000 a year, a variable cost of $34 a unit and a selling price of $58, and currently produces 30,000 units a year. MRF faces one operational problem: absenteeism among train drivers has reached 8% and is disrupting schedule reliability.

--- APPENDIX 1 — MARKETING/OPS ---
Operations Log — Q3 2026: MRF's intermodal services achieved 91.2% on-time performance in Q3 2026, up from 84.6% a year earlier. Average turnaround at the port terminal was 5.4 hours, down from 6.8 hours. Customer complaints fell from 24 to 15 per month. Market research of 480 freight buyers found that 58% would switch providers for guaranteed sub-6-hour terminal turnaround and 61% require rail carbon reporting in supplier selection. A driver training needs analysis shows 18 of 120 drivers have not completed simulator refresher training; courses at the national rail academy cost $750 per driver. A training needs analysis found that 18 drivers need on-the-job training on the new locomotive diagrams and off-the-job training at the national rail academy before the full service launch.

--- APPENDIX 2 — FINANCIAL DATA ---
Title: Extract from the Statement of Profit or Loss and Capital employed data of Meridian Rail Freight for the year ended 31 March 2025 ($ '000)
Headers: ['Financial Metric', '2024', '2025']

Cost of sales | 2,160 | 2,310
Gross profit | 1,440 | 1,890
Operating profit | 360 | 630
Capital employed | 2,400 | 3,000
Interest payable | 84 | 112

--- APPENDIX 3 — EXTERNAL ENVIRONMENT ---
Economic and Business Bulletin (November 2026): (1) The central bank has raised the base interest rate from 5.25% to 6.0%, the third rise this year, increasing borrowing costs for businesses with variable-rate loans. (2) The national minimum wage will rise by 5.9% from $13.10 to $13.87 per hour from April 2027, raising wage bills in transport and warehousing. (3) Commercial electricity and wholesale diesel costs have risen 14.2% year-on-year, while rail freight volumes grew 2.8% as retailers shifted goods from road to rail.

  Q1(a) [8 marks]
    Question: MRF plans to fund part of its electric locomotive investment with a $650,000 ten-year bank loan. Explain two advantages for MRF of using retained profit to fund the expansion rather than the bank loan.
    Answer: Point 1: Using retained profit costs MRF nothing in interest, which protects the business at a time when commercial electricity has risen 14.2% and its fixed costs already stand at $420,000 a year. Every dollar not paid to the bank can be retained to absorb the input-cost inflation in traction energy, helping MRF hold its $58 selling price and its 91.2% on-time performance standard while the port-Midlands corridor ramps up.

Point 2: Retained profit avoids the risk attached to borrowing at a time when the base interest rate has risen from 5.25% to 6.0% and may rise again. If MRF funds the $1,150,000 expansion from its own reserves, Idris Bakare and the existing shareholders keep full control of when the two electric locomotives enter service, with no lender covenant restricting how the inland terminal upgrade is phased. It also preserves borrowing headroom for future wagon purchases that self-funding would consume.

    Answer: Trade press advertising: Advertising in logistics magazines would reach freight buyers and fleet managers with detailed copy about the electric locomotives' emissions credentials and the 5.4-hour terminal turnaround. It is credible among industry readers and relatively affordable, but readership is broad and largely uncontracted; many readers work for rival carriers or road hauliers, so wastage of spend is high for a single-corridor launch backed by a $1,150,000 commitment, and it generates enquiries, not signed volume.

Sponsorship of the national rail industry conference: Sponsorship would position MRF strongly with the exact firms that specify rail contracts, generate face-to-face leads, and reinforce its attendance at a time when 61% of surveyed buyers require rail carbon reporting. However, conference sponsorship is expensive for one or two days a year, coverage ends when the event closes, and competitors exhibit alongside MRF, diluting exclusivity.

Dedicated contracts team: A small contracts team calling on freight forwarders directly converts the 58% of 480 surveyed buyers ready to switch providers for guaranteed sub-6-hour turnaround into written agreements, tailoring capacity commitments to each forwarder's volumes. It is slower to scale than advertising and carries salary costs, but it targets the highest-intent buyers and matches the B2B nature of rail freight.

Recommendation: MRF should choose the dedicated contracts team. Rail freight is bought through negotiated contracts, not spot purchases, so direct selling captures the switching-intent segment that advertising can only reach passively; the conference is rejected as too brief and shared with rivals, and trade press alone is rejected as too untargeted and non-binding to secure corridor volumes. MRF can use the 91.2% on-time rate and 5.4-hour turnaround as the team's proof points, adding modest conference presence only as supporting credibility.

--- MAIN STEM ---
Harborlight Bunkering (HBK) is a private limited company in the marine fuel bunkering sector, supplying low-sulphur fuel oil and LNG-blended bunker fuel to container ships and tankers calling at the harbour. Founded in 2013 by Lena Marchetti, it employs a workforce of 38 and operates a flat structure with autocratic leadership. HBK plans to invest $2,400,000 in a new LNG-fuelled bunker barge to serve the harbour's growing fleet, financed by a $1,500,000 seven-year bank loan and $900,000 retained profit. It has fixed costs of $280,000 a year, a variable cost of $42 a unit and a selling price of $50, and currently produces 55,000 units a year of marine fuel. HBK faces one operational problem: labour turnover among barge crew has reached 14% and is putting safety compliance at risk.

--- APPENDIX 1 — MARKETING/OPS ---
Quality and Safety Report — October 2026: HBK's bunker barge completed 1,240 fuel deliveries in the last 12 months at a near-miss rate of 0.9 per 1,000 tonnes, down from 1.7.     Answer: Marine fuel price rise (18.6%): Fuel is the dominant component of HBK's $42 variable cost per unit. A 18.6% rise on a fuel component of, say, $30 adds roughly $5.60 per unit — about $308,000 a year at 55,000 units — and slashes contribution per unit from $8 toward $2.40 unless HBK reprices. HBK can pass some of this to agents through the 3% green premium and emissions-certificate pricing, but competitive pressure from rival bunker suppliers caps the pass-through; procurement hedging and tighter supplier contracts become essential.

Minimum wage increase (7.1%, to $13.82 per hour): With 38 crew and office staff, HBK's wage bill rises by roughly 7.1%. If average hourly pay is around $13.82, one full-time employee costs roughly $28,700 a year, so a 7.1% rise adds about $1,910 per worker — roughly $72,600 across the workforce. Interest rate rise (5.0% to 5.75%): If the $1,500,000 seven-year bank loan is variable-rate, the 0.75% increase adds about $11,250 a year in interest. That is manageable and partly offsettable by holding profit before the LNG fleet ramps, and HBK could negotiate a fixed rate at renewal; the risk is small relative to fuel or payroll but does tighten cash while the barge is underperforming early volumes.

Conclusion: The 18.6% rise in marine fuel prices will have the greatest impact. It is by far the largest cash exposure, roughly $300,000 a year before mitigation, it directly compresses the $8 contribution that underpins the $2,400,000 barge investment, and it cannot be absorbed without repricing — whereas the wage rise is painful but absorbable through productivity, and the interest increase is the smallest in cash terms. HBK should respond with supplier hedging, premium invoicing to the 72% of agents willing to pay more, and strict fuel-stock controls before committing to the barge schedule.

--- MAIN STEM ---
Crossport Shuttle Logistics (CSL) is a partnership in the port shuttle trucking sector, running container shuttles between the container port, an inland rail yard and regional distribution depots. Founded in 2016 by Nadia Karim and Tom Whitmore, it employs a workforce of 64 and operates a flat structure with democratic leadership. CSL plans to invest $780,000 in 12 new electric port-shuttle trucks for its busiest container routes, financed by $480,000 hire purchase and $300,000 retained profit. It has fixed costs of $390,000 a year, a variable cost of $69 a unit and a selling price of $95, and currently produces 24,000 units a year. CSL faces one operational problem: labour turnover among shuttle drivers has reached 12%, undermining terminal turnaround times.

--- APPENDIX 1 — MARKETING/OPS ---
Operations Log — Q3 2026: CSL's fleet completed 6,100 port runs in the quarter at an on-time rate of 93.5%, up from 88.0% a year earlier. Average turnaround at the container terminal fell to 41 minutes from 55 minutes. Empty running dropped from 22% to 14% of total miles. Market research of 320 freight forwarders found that 63% would pay more for zero-emission shuttle capacity and 57% require electric-delivery certificates for port contracts. A training needs analysis shows 9 of 64 drivers have not completed electric-truck familiarisation; courses at the haulage training centre cost $800 per driver. A training needs analysis found that drivers need on-the-job training in electric-truck handling and off-the-job training at the freight college before the new trucks enter service.

--- APPENDIX 2 — FINANCIAL DATA ---

--- APPENDIX 3 — EXTERNAL ENVIRONMENT ---

(2) The national minimum wage will rise by 6.3% from $13.20 to $14.03 per hour from April 2027, raising wage bills across road freight. (3) The central bank has raised the base interest rate from 4.75% to 5.5%, increasing the cost of new vehicle finance for logistics businesses.

  Q1(a) [8 marks]
    Question: CSL plans to fund the 12 new electric port-shuttle trucks with $480,000 hire purchase. Explain two advantages for CSL of using hire purchase to fund the expansion rather than a bank loan.
    Answer: Point 1: Hire purchase matches the repayment profile to the trucks' earnings, with fixed monthly instalments that CSL can budget against a $69 variable cost and a $95 selling price. Unlike a bank loan, which typically requires a lump-sum principal and interest schedule and may demand blanket security over the partnership's assets, hire purchase keeps each truck self-funding from the $26 contribution each container move generates, so the $780,000 investment does not strain the $390,000 fixed-cost base.

Point 2: At the end of the hire purchase term the trucks become partnership property with no further capital outlay, whereas early-settled bank finance on new vehicles can leave asset and debt mismatched on the books. CSL also retains its $300,000 retained profit as a working-capital cushion against the 16.4% diesel-price rise, driver recruitment at 12% labour turnover, and the $800 per driver electric-truck courses, while the hire purchase provider carries the residual-value risk if electric battery technology improves faster than expected.

    Answer: Roadside billboards: Billboards near the port gate, rail yard and distribution depots would build brand recognition among drivers, port workers and passing commuters at low cost per impression. They suit simple visuals of the new electric trucks, but they cannot explain zero-emission certification, emissions reporting or contracted capacity, and the people who see them are overwhelmingly not the decision-makers at the 320 freight forwarders CSL researched — so awareness grows faster than contracts.

Radio advertising: Local radio would deliver a catchy launch message, reach thousands of commuters in the port city, and fit a tight tactical budget for a few weeks around the first 6,100 port runs of the electric fleet. However, the audience is fragmented across drivers, office workers and retirees rather than logistics buyers, complex messages are lost in short slots, and response is hard to attribute to specific contracts.

Targeted LinkedIn campaign: LinkedIn places CSL in front of the exact 320 freight forwarders and shipping-line procurement managers who sign port shuttle contracts, lets CSL showcase the 93.5% on-time rate, 41-minute turnaround and the zero-emission certificates demanded by 57% of forwarders, and generates measurable enquiries with cost per lead tracked post by post. It is slower and narrower than broadcast media and requires good content, but it targets switch-ready buyers directly.

    Question: Explain one advantage and one disadvantage for CSL of introducing electric port-shuttle trucks on its container routes.
    Answer: Advantage: Electric trucks cut fuel and maintenance costs per port run, helping CSL hold its $95 selling price even as wholesale diesel rose 16.4%, and let it issue the zero-emission delivery certificates that 57% of the 320 surveyed forwarders now require for port contracts. Winning those certified lanes protects the 93.5% on-time rate reputation, lifts the 24,000 units a year toward the 12 trucks' combined capacity, and positions CSL as the default electric shuttle.

Disadvantage: The $780,000 investment plus $480,000 hire purchase commits CSL to fixed instalments regardless of volumes, and the 12 trucks lose productivity to battery charging and turnaround at the depot exactly when the terminal expects 41-minute container moves. Battery technology is also improving quickly, so the new fleet risks partial obsolescence, and 9 drivers still need $800 familiarisation while the 12% labour turnover makes retaining certified electric-truck drivers genuinely hard.

  Q4(b) [12 marks]
    Question: Using Appendix 3, evaluate how the 16.4% rise in diesel prices, the 6.3% minimum wage increase and the base interest rate rise to 5.5% will affect CSL. Which change will have the greatest impact? Justify your answer.
    Answer: Diesel price rise (16.4%): Fuel dominates the $69 variable cost of diesel runs. A 16.4% rise on a fuel component of roughly $30 adds about $4.92 per diesel unit — over $118,000 a year across the diesel share of 24,000 units. Margins compress toward $21 contribution unless CSL reprices or surcharges forwarders, but the rise also validates the $780,000 electric truck investment, because each additional electric lane permanently removes diesel exposure from the P&L.

Minimum wage increase (6.3%, to $14.03 per hour): With 64 staff — drivers, yard hands and admin — CSL's wage bill rises by roughly 6.3%. If average hourly pay is around $14.03, one full-time employee costs roughly $29,200 a year, so a 6.3% rise adds about $1,840 per worker — roughly $117,800 across the workforce. That rivals the diesel increase in cash terms and lands as the 12% driver labour turnover peak bites, lifting recruitment and overtime costs alongside the base pay rise.

Interest rate rise (4.75% to 5.5%): The hire purchase instalments are largely fixed, so the 0.75% rise directly affects only new or floating finance CSL might arrange for further trucks or depot charging equipment — perhaps $3,000 to $6,000 a year. It is the least damaging of the three in immediate cash terms and can be managed by fixing finance at negotiation, though it makes further expansion borrowing costlier.

Conclusion: The 16.4% diesel price rise will have the greatest impact. It is the largest single cost exposure in the diesel operation, roughly $118,000 a year at current volumes, it recurs on every future litre, and it cannot be passed through instantly without risking forwarder contracts — while the electric truck rollout both shields CSL and monetises the zero-emission premium. The wage rise is the second most serious threat and demands rostering discipline and profit sharing to retain drivers, while the interest rate move is manageable, though both still require tighter cost control and firmer contract pricing.
    Keywords: 16.4%, 6.3%, 5.5%, interest rate, $14.03, $69
    Mark scheme: level_1_1_to_4: Identifies the external changes with limited application to CSL. | level_2_5_to_8: Analyses the impact of at least two external changes on CSL's costs, revenue or financing in context. | level_3_9_to_12: Detailed evaluation of all three external changes in the context of CSL with a well-justified judgement that the diesel price rise has the greatest impact and why the other two are smaller.

--- MAIN STEM ---
Aurora Hydrogen (AHY) is a public limited company in the hydrogen refuelling sector, operating a green-hydrogen truck refuelling station on the national industrial corridor. Founded in 2021 by Dr Elena Vasquez, it employs a workforce of 22 and operates a flat structure with laissez-faire leadership among its engineers. AHY plans to invest $640,000 in a second high-pressure dispenser and a mobile refuelling trailer for HGV fleet trials, financed by a $340,000 share issue and $300,000 bank loan. It has fixed costs of $176,000 a year, a variable cost of $6.30 a unit and a selling price of $9.50, and currently produces 78,000 units a year. AHY faces one operational problem: a skills gap, as 16 of its 22 staff have not completed high-pressure hydrogen safety certification.

--- APPENDIX 1 — MARKETING/OPS ---
Market Research Summary — October 2026 (n = 210 HGV fleet managers): 68% would trial hydrogen trucks within 24 months if corridor refuelling is reliable; 54% would pay up to $0.60 more per kg for guaranteed green hydrogen; 47% cite lack of refuelling infrastructure as the main barrier. Pilot operations ran 1,380 kg of hydrogen through the dispenser in Q3 2026 with zero customer complaints and an average refuelling time of 11 minutes. 16 of 22 staff have not completed high-pressure hydrogen safety certification; courses at the energy skills centre cost $950 per employee. A training needs analysis found that drivers and dispenser technicians need on-the-job training on hydrogen safety and off-the-job training on high-pressure refuelling certification before the corridor depot opens.
