--- MAIN STEM ---
Greywater Slate Quarry (GSQ) is a private limited company in the primary extraction and construction-materials sector, quarrying and dressing roofing slate for builders, roofers and heritage restoration contractors. Founded in 2013 by Mared Llewelyn, it employs a workforce of 46 and operates a flat organisational structure with democratic leadership. GSQ plans to invest $700,000 in a diamond-wire sawing and computerised sorting line to cut waste and lift output, financed by a $450,000 ten-year bank loan and $250,000 retained profit. It has fixed costs of $225,000 a year, a variable cost of $5.10 a unit and a selling price of $9.60, and currently produces 75,000 units a year. --- APPENDIX 1 — MARKETING/OPS ---

  Q1(a) [8 marks]
    Question: GSQ plans to finance part of its diamond-wire sawing and computerised sorting line with a ten-year bank loan. Explain two advantages for GSQ of using retained profit to fund the expansion instead of the bank loan.
    Answer: Point 1: Retained profit costs GSQ no interest or arrangement fees, protecting cash at a time when fixed costs already run at $225,000 a year. The central bank has raised its base rate from 4.5% to 5.0%, so every variable-rate dollar borrowed becomes more expensive; funding $250,000 internally avoids that exposure, preserves the $5.10 variable-cost cushion on 75,000 units, and avoids weakening the $9.60 selling price that roofers and heritage contractors currently accept for certified matched-size slate. Point 2: Retained profit keeps full ownership and control with Mared Llewelyn and the existing shareholders. No lender can impose covenants on how the sawing line is operated, on staffing levels across the flat democratic structure, or on future investment; GSQ can time installation around the 3.8% growth in public-building repair spending. It also avoids collateral risk against the $700,000 plant itself, which could be repossessed under the bank loan if 6.3% defect rates persisted and heritage orders slipped past the expected monthly delivery guarantee.

Quality of finance: Using $250,000 retained profit for part of the $700,000 line means the bank loan covers only $450,000, keeping repayments well inside the cash flow generated at the current 75,000 units of output and matched against the premium-pricing upside identified in the market research.

Decision: GSQ should choose on-the-job training, supplemented by one external safety audit day for the whole saw crew. On-the-job training costs nothing in fees, keeps dressing output stable while the new sorting line beds in, and passes on machine-specific fault detection faster than a generic college syllabus; the single external audit day satisfies insurers without the $10,920 fee.   Q4(a) [8 marks]
    Question: Explain one advantage and one disadvantage for GSQ of introducing a reclaimed-slate takeback scheme with its heritage customers.
    Answer: Advantage: A takeback scheme lets GSQ collect reusable slate off restoration sites, grade and redress it, and resell matched-size reclaimed pieces to the 57% of surveyed contractors willing to pay a 6% premium. Disadvantage: Returned slate arrives mixed with lime mortar, nails and battens, so grading and dressing reclaimed pieces consumes scarce skilled labour and warehouse space, and contaminated batches may be unsaleable — worsening the waste position that already sends 6.3% of current production to low-value aggregate. Handling and re-certifying reclaimed matched-size pieces also adds quality-assurance cost and could delay dispatch of new orders, jeopardising the 4 days fulfilment promise valued by the 68% of contractors who rank delivery reliability as decisive.

  Q4(b) [12 marks]
    Question: Using Appendix 3, evaluate how the rise in the base interest rate to 5.0%, the 5.5% minimum wage increase and the 8.6% rise in diesel, blasting and haulage costs will affect GSQ. Which change will have the greatest impact? Justify your answer.
    Answer: Interest rate rise (4.5% to 5.0%): If GSQ's $450,000 ten-year bank loan is variable-rate, a 0.5 percentage-point rise adds about $2,250 a year of interest — modest against fixed costs of $225,000 — though it also discourages new construction borrowing and could slow the 3.8% growth in public-building repair spending that drives roofing-slate demand. GSQ can shield itself by fixing the loan rate; the direct cash impact is small and containable.

Minimum wage increase (5.5% to $12.10): Quarry dressing is labour-intensive. If around 30 of GSQ's 46 staff earn near the current minimum, the 5.5% rise adds roughly $39,900 a year (30 × $11.47 × 2,000 hours × 5.5% ≈ $37,850, plus supervisory knock-ons), on top of fixed costs and with no equivalent productivity gain guaranteed. Democratic leadership and the new sorting line should absorb part of this through fewer rejections and rehandling, but the cash hit is material.

Input-cost inflation (8.6% diesel, blasting and haulage): Fuel, explosives and haulage sit inside the $5.10 variable cost of every unit GSQ produces. Even if they represent about 45% of that cost (≈ $2.30), an 8.6% rise adds about $0.20 per unit, or roughly $14,900 a year on 75,000 units, compounding with the 6.3% defect rate that already forces expensive reprocessing.

Conclusion: The 5.5% minimum wage increase will have the greatest impact. Unlike the interest-rate rise (about $2,250 a year and fixable through the loan terms) and the fuel increase (roughly $14,900 a year, partly recoverable through the 6% matched-size premium), the wage bill lands directly on GSQ's core dressing workforce — its scarcest resource — adding nearly $38,000–$40,000 a year before any productivity offset, and squeezing the $5.10 variable-cost cushion from day one. GSQ must raise dressing-crew productivity through the new sorting line, renegotiate merchant price lists to pass on part of the increase, and prioritise hiring retentions over expansion until the margin recovers.
    Keywords: 5.0%, 5.5%, 8.6%, $12.10, interest rate, $5.10
    Mark scheme: level_1_1_to_4: Identifies the external factors with limited application to GSQ. | level_2_5_to_8: Analyses the impact of at least two external changes on GSQ's costs, revenue or financing in context. | level_3_9_to_12: Detailed evaluation of all three external changes in the context of GSQ with a well-justified judgement that the minimum wage increase has the greatest impact and why the other two are smaller.

--- MAIN STEM ---
Caldbeck Lime Works (CLW) is a partnership in the eco-materials and construction-materials sector, burning high-calcium lime for conservation mortars, plasters and limewash used by restoration contractors. Founded in 2009 by Harriet and Joe Callis, it employs a workforce of 33 and operates a flat organisational structure with laissez-faire leadership that trusts its experienced kiln burners. CLW plans to invest $520,000 in a new kiln with waste-heat recovery to cut fuel use and emissions, financed by a $320,000 bank loan and $200,000 retained profit. It has fixed costs of $168,000 a year, a variable cost of $8.40 a unit and a selling price of $14.40, and currently produces 40,000 units a year. Its kiln batch defect rate has reached 4.7%, wasting fuel and forcing expensive reburning.

--- APPENDIX 1 — MARKETING/OPS ---
Operations Log — October 2025: The kiln produced 10,000 units of quicklime and hot-mix mortar last quarter; 4.7% of batches failed calcium-purity testing, up from 3.2% a year ago, and reburning consumed an extra 61 tonnes of gas. Average order fulfilment is 6 days. Market research of 280 conservation contractors found that 62% would pay a 5% premium for certified high-calcium lime with chain-of-custody paperwork, and 54% rank consistent batch purity as decisive. A loader breakdown log shows 7 stoppages last quarter; off-the-job training courses at the local college cost $850 per employee, while on-the-job training relies on senior burners and is uncertified, and 11 of 33 staff lack hot-mix handling certification.

--- APPENDIX 2 — FINANCIAL DATA ---
Title: Extract from the Statement of Profit or Loss and Capital employed data of Caldbeck Lime Works for the year ended 31 March 2025 ($ '000)
Headers: ['Financial Metric', '2024', '2025']

Cost of sales | 2,464 | 2,640
Gross profit | 1,386 | 1,760
Operating profit | 308 | 528
Capital employed | 2,800 | 3,520
Interest payable | 140 | 165

--- APPENDIX 3 — EXTERNAL ENVIRONMENT ---
Economic and Business Bulletin (November 2026): (1) The central bank has raised the base interest rate from 4.75% to 5.25%, its third rise this year, increasing variable-rate loan costs. (2) Industrial gas prices paid by medium manufacturers rose 14.9% year-on-year, the fourth consecutive quarterly increase, while home insulation retrofit grants for older buildings rose by $1,000. (3) The national minimum wage will rise by 1.5% to $11.70 per hour from April 2026, and construction-sector input inflation stands at 5.2%.

  Q1(a) [8 marks]
    Question: CLW plans to finance part of its waste-heat recovery kiln with a ten-year bank loan. Explain two advantages for CLW of using retained profit to fund the kiln instead of the bank loan.
    Answer: Point 1: Retained profit costs CLW no interest or arrangement fees, protecting cash when fixed costs already run at $168,000 a year. The central bank has raised its base rate from 4.75% to 5.25%, so variable-rate borrowing keeps getting more expensive; funding $200,000 internally avoids that exposure and preserves the $8.40 variable-cost cushion on 40,000 units of lime. Every dollar not paid as interest can absorb the 14.9% rise in industrial gas prices without weakening the $14.40 selling price that conservation contractors accept for certified high-calcium lime.

Point 2: Retained profit keeps full ownership and control with Harriet and Joe Callis as the two partners. No lender can impose covenants on kiln scheduling, staffing across the flat laissez-faire structure, or how the new kiln is commissioned. It also avoids collateral risk against the kiln itself if the 4.7% batch defect rate persisted and reburning kept consuming an extra 61 tonnes of gas, and it avoids diluting the partnership's simple structure — no share issue, no community investors, no outside shareholder expectations for dividends if a quarter's profits are retained to weather fuel-price volatility.

Quality of finance: Using $200,000 retained profit for part of the $520,000 package means the bank loan covers only $320,000, keeping annual repayments well within the cash generated at 40,000 units of output and matched against the 5% premium the 62% of surveyed contractors already signal.

Operating profit moved from $308,000 on sales of $3,850,000 to $528,000 on sales of $4,400,000. Capital employed grew from $2,800,000 to $3,520,000 as the kiln project was funded, and interest payable rose from $140,000 to $165,000.

Evaluation: Performance strengthened across every measure. The share of revenue kept after production costs widened from 36.0% to 40.0%, reflecting better high-calcium certified mixes, tighter batch discipline and chain-of-custody paperwork that qualifies the 5% premium the 62% of contractors accept. The surplus after operating costs improved from $308,000 to $528,000, and the return earned on the enlarged capital base rose from 11.0% to 15.0%, so the kiln investment is already out-earning its funding cost. Caution is warranted: capital employed grew by $720,000, reburning still consumed an extra 61 tonnes of gas, and interest payable rose to $165,000 alongside the $320,000 loan — so any slip in the 4.7% defect rate would compress returns quickly in a year of 14.9% gas inflation.

Conclusion: CLW's financial position has improved. Trading margins and returns on the capital base all moved favourably, and the improvement is rooted in genuine premium pricing and waste reduction rather than accounting effects. The partners should commission the new waste-heat recovery kiln promptly, protect the certified batch discipline that underpins the 40.0% surplus share, and refinance the bank loan if rates rise further.
    Keywords: Gross Profit Margin, Profit Margin, ROCE, 36.0%, 40.0%, $528,000, $4,400,000
    Mark scheme: level_1_1_to_4: States financial figures or changes without accurate ratio calculations. | level_2_5_to_8: Accurately calculates the gross profit margin, profit margin and ROCE for both 2024 and 2025 with contextual analysis of the trend. | level_3_9_to_12: Accurate ratio calculations for both years combined with detailed evaluation of revenue, cost and capital movements and a justified conclusion on whether CLW's financial position improved.

  Q4(a) [8 marks]
    Question: Explain one advantage and one disadvantage for CLW of adopting the waste-heat recovery kiln to produce lower-carbon lime.
    Answer: Advantage: Waste-heat recovery recaptures exhaust heat to pre-dry and pre-heat incoming limestone, cutting the fuel burned per unit of lime and directly reducing exposure to the 14.9% rise in industrial gas prices. It also cuts CLW's emissions per unit, letting the partners claim verified lower-carbon lime — a claim the 62% of surveyed contractors willing to pay a 5% premium for certified product would value, and one that strengthens chain-of-custody paperwork demanded by heritage bodies specifying for listed buildings.

Disadvantage: The $520,000 kiln is a large capital commitment for a $3,520,000-capital-employed partnership, and installation requires weeks of shutdown. During installation, average order fulfilment slips beyond the current 6 days, jeopardising the 54% of contractors who rank consistent supply as decisive and risking contract penalties on scheduled restoration scaffolding. If the heat-recovery system underperforms, fuel savings may be lower than modelled, squeezing the $8.40 variable cost exactly when gas prices have risen 14.9%.
    Keywords: waste-heat recovery, $520,000, 62%, 6 days, 14.9%, chain-of-custody paperwork
    Mark scheme: knowledge_max_2: 1 mark for a valid advantage and 1 mark for a valid disadvantage. | application_analysis_max_6: Up to 3 marks per point for detailed contextual development linked to CLW's research data, fuel costs and expansion.

  Q4(b) [12 marks]
    Question: Using Appendix 3, evaluate how the rise in the base interest rate to 5.25%, the 14.9% rise in industrial gas prices and the 1.5% minimum wage increase will affect CLW. Which change will have the greatest impact? Justify your answer.
    Answer: Interest rate rise (4.75% to 5.25%): If CLW's $320,000 ten-year bank loan is variable-rate, the 0.5 percentage-point rise adds about $1,600 a year of interest — modest against fixed costs of $168,000. Higher rates also cool construction lending, which could slow the wider restoration pipeline that drives demand for conservation lime, and raise the cost of refinancing when the loan is renewed. CLW can fix or hedge; the direct cash impact is small.

Minimum wage increase (1.5% to $11.70): With 33 staff, mainly kiln burners, loader drivers and mill crew, a 1.5% rise adds roughly $11,400 a year if all staff earn near the current rate (33 × $23,050 × 1.5% ≈ $11,400) — meaningful but absorbable through batch discipline gains and the 5% certified premium. It ranks behind the fuel problem in urgency.

Industrial gas price rise (14.9%): The kiln is CLW's biggest cost engine. Gas already forced reburning of an extra 61 tonnes last quarter at a 4.7% defect rate. If fuel is roughly 30% of the $8.40 variable cost (≈ $2.52), a 14.9% rise adds about $0.38 per unit — roughly $15,100 a year on 40,000 units, before any reburning multiplier on faulty batches. Unlike wages and interest, this cost scales with every unit produced and cannot be renegotiated away without the waste-heat recovery kiln.

Conclusion: The 14.9% rise in industrial gas prices will have the greatest impact. It is the largest percentage increase on CLW's biggest production cost, it compounds with the 4.7% defect rate into reburning waste, and it applies to every one of the 40,000 units sold — totalling roughly $15,000 a year before reburning, several times the interest-rate impact ($1,600) and comfortably above the 1.5% wage rise (around $11,400). CLW must commission the waste-heat recovery kiln quickly, lock fuel contracts with suppliers, and pass part of the increase into the certified 5% premium before taking on new restoration orders.
    Keywords: 5.25%, 14.9%, 1.5%, $11.70, interest rate, gas prices

--- MAIN STEM ---
Montagu Cork Flooring Co-operative (MCFC) is a cooperative in the eco-materials and construction-materials sector, laminating cork-bark granules into floating floor tiles and acoustic underlay for low-energy housing. Founded in 2016 by 21 members led by general manager Rosa Inglis, it employs a workforce of 29 and operates a flat organisational structure with democratic, member-elected leadership. MCFC plans to invest $480,000 in an automated lamination and edge-sealing press, financed by a $280,000 bank loan and a $200,000 community share issue. It has fixed costs of $180,000 a year, a variable cost of $9.00 a unit and a selling price of $15.00, and currently produces 45,000 units a year. Its offcut dust contamination rate has reached 5.8%, wasting premium cork and slowing lines.

--- APPENDIX 1 — MARKETING/OPS ---
Market Research and Production Summary — October 2025: MCFC laminated and edge-sealed 11,250 units last quarter; 5.8% of tiles failed adhesion and thickness testing, up from 3.6% a year ago; customer complaints fell from 16 to 10 per month. Average order fulfilment is 5 days. Market research of 340 eco-home builders and homeowners found that 64% would pay a 7% premium for certified renewable-bark flooring, and 59% rank fast, reliable supply as decisive. A maintenance log shows the press stopped 8 times last quarter; off-the-job training courses at the technical college cost $700 per employee, while on-the-job training lacks certification, and 7 of 29 staff lack lamination-press lockout certification.

With the base rate raised to 5.25%, every variable-rate dollar of the alternative $280,000 bank loan adds interest MCFC cannot pass on easily; community shares instead carry flexible, patient capital that members understand and rarely rush.

Point 2: Member investors are customers too — likely builders, homeowners and housing co-ops — so the issue strengthens the local market for certified renewable-bark flooring exactly where the 64% of surveyed buyers willing to pay a 7% premium live. They campaign for MCFC, recommend it in community groups, and stay patient on returns. It also avoids the bank's covenants over the flat democratic structure, preserving member control of pressing schedules, hires and the eco-housing tender pipeline rather than subordinating the co-op to lender conditions.

Quality of finance: Using a $200,000 community issue for part of the $480,000 package means the bank loan covers only $280,000, keeping annual repayments within cash flow at 45,000 units of output and matched against the 7% premium opportunity.

    Question: MCFC is launching its certified renewable-bark flooring for low-energy housing. Consider eco-home exhibitions, social media influencer marketing, or sponsorship of a DIY home improvement programme. Which should MCFC choose to promote the flooring? Justify your recommendation.

--- MAIN STEM ---
Vulcan Structural Steel (VSS) is a public limited company in the construction-materials and fabrication sector, cutting, drilling and welding structural steel portal frames for commercial buildings and stadiums. Founded in 1998 by engineers Marcus and Lena Vale, it employs a workforce of 120 and operates a hierarchical organisational structure with autocratic leadership. VSS plans to invest $1,500,000 in a computer-controlled plasma-cutting and robotic welding cell, financed by a $900,000 bank loan and a $600,000 share issue. It has fixed costs of $840,000 a year, a variable cost of $28.50 a unit and a selling price of $38.50, and currently produces 120,000 units a year. Its weld defect rate has reached 3.1%, causing rework and delivery delays for major contractors.

--- APPENDIX 1 — MARKETING/OPS ---
Quality and Waste Report — November 2025: The fabrication shop delivered 30,000 units of cut and welded structural steel last quarter. The weld defect rate reached 3.1%, up from 2.2% a year ago, and two reworked bridge beams cost $38,000 in extra labour and re-inspection. Average order fulfilment is 7 days. Market research of 280 commercial contractors found that 69% would pay a 3% premium for certified zero-defect steel, and 57% rank on-time delivery as decisive. A certification audit shows only 9 of 120 staff hold robotic-welding tickets; off-the-job training courses at the technical college cost $1,100 per employee, while on-the-job training is available but uncertified.

--- APPENDIX 2 — FINANCIAL DATA ---
Title: Extract from the Statement of Profit or Loss and Capital employed data of Vulcan Structural Steel for the year ended 31 March 2025 ($ '000)
Headers: ['Financial Metric', '2024', '2025']
Revenue | 12,400 | 13,600
Cost of sales | 8,370 | 8,840
Gross profit | 4,030 | 4,760
Operating profit | 868 | 1,020
Capital employed | 6,200 | 6,800
Interest payable | 380 | 420

--- APPENDIX 3 — EXTERNAL ENVIRONMENT ---
Economic and Business Bulletin (December 2026): (1) The central bank has raised the base interest rate from 4.75% to 5.25%, its third rise this year, increasing variable-rate loan costs. (2) Structural steel and scrap input costs rose 10.2% year-on-year, and producer-price inflation in fabricated metals stands at 8.3%. (3) The national minimum wage will rise by 5.5% to $13.10 per hour from April 2027, while public infrastructure spending grew 6.1% year-on-year.

--- QUESTIONS ---
  Q1(a) [8 marks]
    Question: VSS plans to finance part of its plasma-cutting and robotic welding cell with a share issue. Explain two advantages for VSS of using a share issue to fund the cell instead of the bank loan.
    Answer: Point 1: A share issue raises permanent capital with no repayment schedule and no interest. VSS has already committed to a $900,000 bank loan, the central bank has just pushed its base rate to 5.25%, and interest payable reached $420,000 last year. Financing the $600,000 balance with shares instead of a larger loan keeps annual debt service fixed, protects the cash buffer against the 10.2% steel-price shock, and removes any risk that the lender calls in collateral — the $1,500,000 cell — if welding defects of 3.1% delay the contractor payments it was bought to win.

Point 2: Share capital is permanent and uninsured in maturity — it never falls due for repayment, unlike the ten-year loan tenor staring down the income statement. That lets VSS plan for the slow ramp of the plasma-cutting cell and the robotic line, build the 9 certified robotic-welding leads, absorb the $38,000 bridge-beam rework without covenant stress, and fund further certification without scrambling for overdraft headroom. Dividends remain discretionary, so in a weak quarter VSS can retain cash for loan paydown instead of being forced to service fixed interest.

Quality of finance: Using the $600,000 share issue for part of the $1,500,000 cell means the $900,000 bank loan remains a fixed, knowable liability — permanent capital now covers the long-life half of the asset while the loan funds the quick-returning half.
    Keywords: share issue, bank loan, $600,000, $900,000, $1,500,000, 3.1%, 5.25%
    Mark scheme: knowledge_max_2: 1 mark for each valid advantage identified (max 2). | application_analysis_max_6: Up to 3 marks per point for contextual explanation and analysis applied to Vulcan Structural Steel and its expansion decision.

  Q1(b) [12 marks]
    Question: VSS is promoting its certified zero-defect structural steel to commercial contractors. Consider construction awards sponsorship, trade journal case-study advertising, or targeted LinkedIn marketing. Which should VSS choose to promote the steel? Justify your recommendation.
    Answer: Construction awards sponsorship: Sponsoring a regional construction or engineering awards dinner buys gala-night visibility, trophy-table networking with chief estimators and developers, and halo credibility when VSS wins or sponsors the zero-defect prize. Drawbacks: costs are high (table, branding, tickets) relative to a 120-person fabricator mid-investment; the audience is hundreds, not the thousands of contractors who specify steel nationwide; and attribution back to qualified quote requests is almost impossible to prove.

Trade journal case-study advertising: Detailed case studies in fabricated-metals and construction trade journals carry technical weight with the 280 contractors surveyed — showing how the plasma-cutting and robotic welding cell delivered two bridge beams, zero rework and 7 days fulfilment — and suits buyers who research before tendering. Drawbacks: print readership is shrinking, lead times are long, copy cannot be tested or rotated quickly, and the format reaches only existing journal subscribers rather than the full contractor market.

Targeted LinkedIn marketing: LinkedIn allows VSS to target by job title and company — procurement managers, project directors and chief estimators at the exact contractors surveyed — with short project-completion videos, weld-quality metrics and certified zero-defect certificates, then measure every click, connection and quote request. Cost per qualified enquiry is low, creative can be rotated weekly, and the 69% premium-acceptors can be re-targeted with the 3% premium justification. Drawbacks: it demands consistent content, sales follow-through and is powerless against buyers who ignore social media entirely.

Recommendation: VSS should choose targeted LinkedIn marketing. It is the only option that reaches the precise 280-contractor segment with measurable, improvable spend, fits a company financing a $900,000 bank loan, and directly showcases the zero-defect credentials that win the 57% of contractors who rank on-time delivery as decisive. Trade journal case studies are rejected as too slow and too quiet to shift a 120-person order book; construction awards sponsorship is rejected as costly, unmeasurable and too narrow in reach for a national fabrication launch.   Q2(a) [8 marks]
    Question: VSS's weld defect rate has reached 3.1%. Explain two benefits for VSS of its hierarchical structure with a clear chain of command for meeting contractor deadlines.

Clear chains also enforce consistent safety briefings on the cutting-cell floor, reduce contradictory instructions, and keep the two reworked bridge beams ($38,000) from recurring as the cell commissions.

Certified leads satisfy contractors' audits immediately, anchor the quality system the 3% premium depends on, and can then train the rest internally against recognised procedure-qualification records. Full on-the-job training is rejected as the primary route because it produces no certification for the auditors of the 280 contractors surveyed, and certification is the precondition of VSS's zero-defect marketing claim — without it, neither the premium nor the tender pipeline is real.   Q4(a) [8 marks]
    Question: Explain one advantage and one disadvantage for VSS of introducing a scrap-steel recycling loop inside its new robotic welding cell.
    Answer: Advantage: A closed scrap loop captures offcuts and reject weldments from the cutting cell and returns them directly to the steel mill for credit towards VSS's next delivery, cutting effective raw-material cost per unit and shrinking the 10.2% steel-input inflation shock on the $28.50 variable cost. It also strengthens VSS's tender narrative for public infrastructure work — government buyers increasingly score suppliers on recycled content — and reduces the environmental cost of sending 3.1% weld-rework scrap to landfill.

Disadvantage: Scrap handling needs dedicated skip space, segregation discipline and transport slots, raising fixed costs above $840,000 and adding admin for a 120-person hierarchy whose supervisory layers already slow decisions. Scrap credits are also volatile — mill prices swing quarter to quarter — so the loop's cash saving may disappoint precisely when rework volumes peak, and any contamination of scrap grades (mixed alloys, paints, oils) forfeits the credit entirely, turning the loop into a pure cost rather than the margin protector VSS needs.

    Answer: Interest rate rise (4.75% to 5.25%): If VSS's $900,000 bank loan is variable-rate, the 0.5 percentage-point rise adds about $4,500 a year of interest — modest against interest payable of $420,000, though it also weighs on contractors' capital budgets broadly and could soften the 6.1% government infrastructure spending momentum that feeds VSS's order pipeline. The impact is real but second-order, and VSS can fix or refinance the loan independently of the $600,000 share issue.

Minimum wage increase (5.5% to $13.10): With 120 staff, mainly cutting-cell and welding-bay crew, a 5.5% rise costs materially — if 60 staff earn near the current minimum, roughly $82,000 a year before knock-ons, and it lands on top of certification overtime already stretching the plasma-cutting shift pattern. However, rising output and the 3% zero-defect premium should absorb much of it.

Steel and scrap input-cost inflation (10.2%): Steel dominates VSS's $28.50 variable cost — typically 55–65% of it. A 10.2% rise on even a $17 steel-and-scrap share adds about $1.73 per unit; at 120,000 units that is roughly $208,000 a year before any hedging, equivalent to over 20% of operating profit. It applies to every unit cut and welded, compounds with the 3.1% defect rate's rework demands, and cannot be renegotiated with mills already quoting extended lead times.

Conclusion: The 10.2% rise in structural steel and scrap costs will have the greatest impact. It is roughly twice the cash impact of the wage rise and nearly fifty times the interest-rate effect, it strikes at the dominant input of every unit VSS fabricates, and it directly threatens the 3% zero-defect premium the 69% of contractors accept. The wage increase (≈ $82,000) ranks second and needs productivity offset from the new cell; the interest-rate rise (≈ $4,500) is trivial by comparison. VSS must negotiate mill contracts in bulk, qualify a second scrap source, enforce the certification programme to cut rework, and pass the smallest viable increase into contract price lists before taking on further infrastructure tenders.
    Keywords: 5.25%, 10.2%, 5.5%, $13.10, interest rate, steel
    Mark scheme: level_1_1_to_4: Identifies the external factors with limited application to VSS. | level_2_5_to_8: Analyses the impact of at least two external changes on VSS's costs, revenue or financing in context. | level_3_9_to_12: Detailed evaluation of all three external changes in the context of VSS with a well-justified judgement that the steel input-cost rise has the greatest impact and why the other two are smaller.

--- MAIN STEM ---
Bower Formwork Systems (BFS) is a sole trader in the construction-materials and building-services sector, manufacturing reusable steel formwork panels and support props for concrete contractors and formwork hire firms. Founded in 2018 by Rosa Bower, it employs a workforce of 21 and operates a flat organisational structure with autocratic leadership. BFS plans to invest $240,000 in a CNC press-brake and robotic welding bay to cut panel distortion, financed by a $150,000 hire purchase agreement and $90,000 retained profit. It has fixed costs of $160,000 a year, a variable cost of $10.50 a unit and a selling price of $15.50, and currently produces 40,000 units a year. Absenteeism in the fabrication workshop has reached 6%, stretching delivery deadlines on fixed-price contracts.

--- APPENDIX 1 — MARKETING/OPS ---
Market Research Summary — October 2025: BFS delivered 10,000 units of formwork panels and props last quarter; 1.9% of panels were miscut or rejected, down from 2.7% a year ago, and customer complaints fell from 17 to 9 per month. Average order fulfilment is 5 days. Market research of 300 commercial contractors and formwork hire firms found that 58% would pay a 5% premium for panels with a certified 500-use life, and 61% rank local lead time as decisive. A workshop audit shows CNC spindle replacement is due within 6 months, quoted at $2,800; the repair path extends spindle life but risks inaccurate bends. A training review shows 6 of 21 staff need CNC refresher training; off-the-job training courses at the technical college cost $900 per employee, while on-the-job training is available but uncertified. Absenteeism has reached 6% and is concentrated in the cutting bay.

--- APPENDIX 2 — FINANCIAL DATA ---
Title: Extract from the Statement of Profit or Loss and Capital employed data of Bower Formwork Systems for the year ended 31 March 2025 ($ '000)
Headers: ['Financial Metric', '2024', '2025']
Revenue | 1,700 | 1,900
Cost of sales | 986 | 1,045
Gross profit | 714 | 855
Operating profit | 170 | 228
Capital employed | 1,700 | 1,900
Interest payable | 70 | 80

--- APPENDIX 3 — EXTERNAL ENVIRONMENT ---
Economic and Business Bulletin (November 2026): (1) The central bank has raised the base interest rate from 5.0% to 5.5%, its second rise this year, increasing variable-rate borrowing costs. (2) The national minimum wage will rise by 4.0% to $11.20 per hour from April 2026, raising payroll costs for workshop staff. (3) Consumer spending on home renovation and extension work fell 3.4% year-on-year as household budgets tightened, cutting orders for smaller residential pours.

--- QUESTIONS ---
  Q1(a) [8 marks]
    Question: BFS plans to finance part of its CNC press-brake and robotic welding bay with hire purchase. Explain two advantages for BFS of using retained profit to fund the bay instead of hire purchase.
    Answer: Point 1: Retained profit buys the press-brake outright, so BFS owns it from day one and never faces hire-purchase interest or arrangement fees. A $150,000 hire purchase agreement typically adds thousands of dollars in charges over its life and, crucially, the HP company retains legal ownership until the final instalment — if BFS missed payments during a slow quarter, the machine would be repossessed and the fabrication workshop, and its delivery of 10,000 units a quarter, would stop immediately.

Point 2: Retained profit keeps Rosa Bower completely free to modify, resell or relocate the CNC asset — no HP restrictions on usage, no mileage-style conditions on operation hours, and no consent needed for a spindle upgrade at $2,800. It also keeps the workshop's credit lines clean: a young sole trader with fixed-price contracts cannot afford to have finance houses rejecting a materials overdraft application because HP instalments are consuming the headroom.

Quality of finance: Using $90,000 retained profit for part of the $240,000 bay means the hire purchase agreement underwrites only $150,000, trimming total interest charges and keeping ownership risk minimal while the machine pays for itself through certified 500-use panel demand.
    Keywords: retained profit, hire purchase, $90,000, $150,000, $240,000, CNC press-brake, 5.5%
    Mark scheme: knowledge_max_2: 1 mark for each valid advantage identified (max 2). | application_analysis_max_6: Up to 3 marks per point for contextual explanation and analysis applied to Bower Formwork Systems and its expansion decision.

  Q1(b) [12 marks]
    Question: BFS is promoting its certified 500-use formwork panels to concrete contractors. Consider design-build expo sponsorship, a referral and reward scheme for contractors, or industry magazine print advertising. Which should BFS choose to promote the panels? Justify your recommendation.
    Answer: Design-build expo sponsorship: A regional expo puts BFS's panels, props and walers in front of commercial contractors and formwork hire firms in one weekend, with live bend-quality demonstrations on a CNC-accurate sample rack. It suits the 61% of the 300 surveyed contractors who rank local lead time as decisive, and builds face-to-face relationships. Drawbacks: one-off events, costs of a branded stand and demo material, and limited reach beyond one city — the strongest leads still need months of follow-up quoting.

Referral and reward scheme: A structured scheme paying existing contractors a reward for every qualified referral turned into a panel order converts BFS's strongest asset — its on-time, complaint-free delivery record — into a marketing channel. Contractors trust peer recommendations, the cost is paid only on results, and the 58% willing to pay a 5% premium for certified 500-use panels can be rewarded in material credit. Drawbacks: rewards must be funded, tracking referrals honestly takes admin discipline, and rewards can be abused if loosely policed.

Industry magazine print advertising: Print in construction magazines reaches quantity surveyors and project managers who specify formwork, and suits a considered, specification-led purchase. Drawbacks: slow response, shrinking readership among younger buyers, and no guarantee the phone rings — measuring return is nearly impossible for a sole trader spending $240,000 capital on new equipment.

Recommendation: BFS should choose the referral and reward scheme. It converts existing customer trust into measurable, low-cost orders at a moment when BFS's HP instalments already squeeze cash; cost is payable only on signed business; and it reinforces the 5 days lead-time advantage that 61% of contractors rank decisive. The design-build expo is rejected as a single weekend spike with weak follow-through; magazine print advertising is rejected as passive, slow and unmeasurable for a 21-person sole trader. BFS can revisit expo sponsorship later, funded from scheme-generated margin.
    Keywords: formwork panels, 58%, 61%, 300, 500-use, $240,000, 5 days

  Q2(a) [8 marks]
    Question: BFS's absenteeism in the cutting bay has reached 6%. Explain two benefits for BFS of its flat organisational structure for communicating with its fabrication crew.
    Answer: Point 1: A flat structure puts the owner — Rosa Bower — in direct, daily contact with the 21 cutting-bay workers who bend and weld every panel. Problems surface in minutes, not through a chain of supervisors: a worker struggling with a CNC programme or a difficult bend pattern gets an immediate answer, morale rises because people feel heard, and absenteeism of 6% can be discussed face-to-face — shift root causes (fatigue, machine faults, transport) rather than guessed at.

Point 2: Flat communication cuts distortion between what the workshop decides and what actually happens. When the new press-brake arrives, Bower can brief all 21 staff herself, demo the bend quality targets and the 500-use certification goal in one sitting, and collect instant feedback on guarding and workflow. Fewer layers also mean fewer meetings, faster decisions and lower overhead — vital for a sole trader holding fixed costs at $160,000 a year while maximising margin on 40,000 units.

Drawbacks: 6 staff leave for two days, the syllabus is generic rather than matched to BFS's specific panel jigs, and wages continue during absence while output stalls.

Decision: BFS should choose on-the-job training with a college assessor visiting to certify competency on site. It preserves scarce cutting-bay hours — essential while absenteeism already stretches fixed-price delivery schedules — targets the exact machine and jigs BFS uses, and keeps the $5,400 course fees available for the $2,800 spindle replacement. Full off-the-job training is rejected as the primary route because generic machines cannot teach BFS's panel tolerances, and cost and disruption outweigh the marginal benefit over assessor-verified on-site training; if any QA auditor later demands paper certificates, BFS can send one lead operator on the college course as a backstop.

BFS should diversify into hire-firm framework contracts, which are less homeowner-seasonal, before cutting prices to chase smaller residential pours.

--- MAIN STEM ---
Valle Dorado Olive Oil (VDO) is a private limited company in the olive oil production and bottling sector, employing a workforce of 64. Founded in 2007 by Catalina Reyes, the business presses and bottles single-estate extra virgin olive oil for supermarket supply across three export markets and operates a hierarchical structure with autocratic leadership. VDO plans to invest $1,200,000 in an automated bottling and filtration line with eco-friendly glass packaging, financed by a $650,000 share issue and $550,000 retained profit. It has fixed costs of $288,000 a year, a variable cost of $8.20 a unit and a selling price of $14.60, and currently produces 95,000 units a year. VDO faces two problems: quality complaints about sediment in unfiltered bottles have reached 26 per month, and its warehouse has reported rising spillage waste.

--- APPENDIX 1 — MARKETING/OPS ---
Quality and Operations Report — Q3 2026: The bottling line filled 23,750 units last quarter with a defect rate of 2.4% (faulty seals and sediment), down from 3.7% a year ago. Customer complaints about cloudy oil fell from 34 to 26 per month. Average order fulfilment time is 4.3 days. Market research of 750 specialty-food shoppers found that 58% would pay up to $0.50 more for certified single-estate oil, and 47% check origin traceability before buying. 18 of 64 staff have not completed on-the-job training on the new filtration unit; off-the-job certification courses at the technical college cost $750 per employee.

--- APPENDIX 2 — FINANCIAL DATA ---

(2) The national minimum wage will rise by 5.9% from $12.85 to $13.61 per hour from April 2027, raising wage bills. (3) Olive harvest prices and bottle-glass costs have risen 9.8% year-on-year, and food inflation is running at 7.2%, while consumer spending on premium cooking oils grew 4.1% in the same period.

    Question: VDO plans to fund part of its bottling-line expansion with a $650,000 share issue. Explain two advantages for VDO of using retained profit to fund the expansion instead of the share issue.
    Answer: Point 1: Using retained profit costs VDO nothing in interest or dividend payments, protecting cash flow while it already carries fixed costs of $288,000 a year and is committing $1,200,000 to the automated bottling and filtration line. Every dollar not paid to new shareholders stays inside the company to absorb the 9.8% rise in olive harvest and bottle-glass costs, so VDO can hold its $14.60 selling price instead of raising it for supermarket customers.

Point 2: Retained profit avoids issuing new shares, so Catalina Reyes keeps full ownership and control of VDO and no external shareholder can influence how the automated line is run or demand higher dividends. It also signals financial strength to supermarkets considering the three export contracts, and preserves the $650,000 share issue as a standby funding source if the filtration unit costs overrun or the spillage waste problem proves more expensive to fix than budgeted, and it avoids revealing commercial terms to new shareholders while VDO is still negotiating its third export market.

    Question: VDO is launching its certified single-estate range to supermarket shoppers. Consider a national television campaign, food-magazine advertising, or social media influencer marketing. Which should VDO choose to promote the launch? Justify your recommendation.
    Answer: National television campaign: A national TV slot would reach millions of viewers quickly and give the new single-estate range mass brand awareness across all three export markets. However, production and airtime costs would absorb a large share of the $1,200,000 expansion budget, and much of the audience buys value vegetable oil rather than premium extra virgin products, so wastage would be very high for a 64-employee business financing the line through a share issue and retained profit.

Food-magazine advertising: Specialist food and lifestyle magazines reach readers who actively seek premium cooking oils, and full-page features can explain single-estate origin and certification in depth, matching the 47% of 750 surveyed shoppers who check origin traceability. The drawbacks are narrow circulation, monthly frequency, and no direct way to show younger supermarket buyers the packaging story at the point of purchase, so awareness builds slowly against well-funded rival brands.

Results depend on influencer credibility and are slower to compound than TV, and a share of spend is lost to follower fraud, but cost per genuinely interested shopper is far lower than television.

Recommendation: VDO should choose social media influencer marketing. It reaches the precise premium segment already proven in its research, costs a fraction of television, scales across all three export markets unlike local print editions, and reinforces the origin story that 47% of shoppers check.   Q2(b) [12 marks]
    Question: VDO must train 18 staff who have not completed filtration-unit certification. Consider on-the-job training on the line or off-the-job certification at the technical college. Which should VDO choose? Justify your decision.
    Answer: On-the-job training: Training beside experienced operators on VDO's own filtration unit is directly relevant to the exact machine settings, bottle types and eco-friendly glass packaging used in production, costs nothing in course fees, and keeps the 18 staff productive while they learn, protecting the 23,750-unit quarterly output and the push to cut complaints below 26 per month. Off-the-job certification: Courses at the technical college cost $750 per employee, so 18 staff cost $13,500 in total; this is minor beside the $1,200,000 investment. Staff learn current best practice away from production pressure, gain a recognised certificate that supports ISO-style audits and export-market credibility, and return with knowledge of the science behind sediment removal rather than just machine routines. However, it removes them from the line, reducing short-term output, and the generic syllabus will not match every VDO-specific seal and filtration setting, so follow-up coaching would still be needed.

Decision: VDO should choose off-the-job certification for the 18 staff, followed by short on-the-job coaching on the actual filtration unit. The $13,500 cost is trivial against $1,200,000 and against the commercial damage of 26 monthly complaints and a 2.4% defect rate on export contracts; VDO's autocratic hierarchy can schedule the two-week absence with minimal disruption, and the certificate strengthens supermarket negotiations. On-the-job training alone is rejected because it cannot produce documented externally benchmarked competence, risks inconsistent standards across three export markets, and would leave VDO unable to prove to auditors that sediment defects are systematically controlled.

Current Ratio 2025 = 1.98 : 1
Acid Test Ratio 2024 = 0.88 : 1
Acid Test Ratio 2025 = 1.21 : 1

  Q4(a) [8 marks]

  Q4(b) [12 marks]
    Question: Using Appendix 3, evaluate how the interest rate rise to 5.0%, the 5.9% minimum wage increase and the 9.8% rise in input costs will affect VDO. Which change will have the greatest impact? Justify your answer.
    Answer: Interest rate rise (4.25% to 5.0%): VDO is financed by a $650,000 share issue and $550,000 retained profit rather than a new variable-rate loan, so the direct cash hit is limited; however, higher interest raises the cost of any overdraft used for working capital while receivables stand at $190,000, and could temper supermarket and export buyers' appetite for premium orders if consumer credit tightens. The effect is real but modest, and VDO can shield itself further by avoiding variable-rate borrowing until the expansion pays back.

Minimum wage increase (5.9%, to $13.61 per hour): VDO employs 64 staff, many in low-paid bottling and warehouse roles. If average hourly pay is near $13, the annual cost of one full-time worker is roughly $27,000, so a 5.9% rise adds about $1,600 per worker, or roughly $100,000 a year across the workforce — far larger than the interest-rate effect. Democratic involvement is not available under its autocratic style, so VDO must recover this through productivity on the automated line, reduced spillage waste and tighter supervision rather than through staff consultation.

Input cost inflation (9.8% olive harvest and bottle glass): VDO's variable cost of $8.20 per unit is dominated by raw materials and packaging. A 9.8% rise on those components adds roughly $0.60 to $0.80 per unit; at 95,000 units a year that is about $57,000 to $76,000 a year, cutting contribution per unit from $6.40 toward $5.60 to $5.80 before any price rise, and eroding the margin that justifies the $1,200,000 investment unless VDO secures the $0.50 premium from supermarkets and renegotiates supplier contracts.

Conclusion: The 9.8% input cost inflation will have the greatest impact. It strikes every one of the 95,000 units VDO sells and removes an estimated $57,000 to $76,000 a year directly from contribution, threatening exactly the margin that services the expansion; even selling the premium range at full price, supermarket contracts may resist passing on the full increase. The minimum wage rise is the second most serious threat, adding roughly $100,000 to payroll unless automation absorbs it, while the interest-rate increase is the smallest cash impact because VDO avoided new variable-rate debt — all three, though, require VDO to prioritise cost control, price recovery and waste reduction before the April 2027 wage change.
    Keywords: 5.0%, 5.9%, 9.8%, $13.61, interest rate, $8.20
    Mark scheme: level_1_1_to_4: Identifies the external factors with limited application to VDO. | level_2_5_to_8: Analyses the impact of at least two external changes on VDO's costs, revenue or financing in context. | level_3_9_to_12: Detailed evaluation of all three external changes in the context of VDO with a well-justified judgement that input-cost inflation has the greatest impact and why the other two are smaller.

--- MAIN STEM ---
Bramblewick Free-Range Eggs (BRE) is a partnership between siblings Dan and Meg Bramble in the free-range egg farming and packing sector, employing a workforce of 35. Founded in 2013, the business runs two free-range laying units and a grading and packing shed supplying cafés, farm shops and independent grocers across the region, operating a flat structure with democratic leadership. BRE plans to invest $600,000 in a second 12,000-bird free-range laying barn and upgraded packing shed, financed by a $420,000 ten-year bank loan and $180,000 hire purchase for the grading machinery. It has fixed costs of $216,000 a year, a variable cost of $4.70 a unit and a selling price of $9.50, and currently produces 105,000 units a year. BRE faces two problems: the rejection rate for cracked or blood-spot eggs has reached 6.5%, and labour turnover among weekend packers is rising.

--- APPENDIX 1 — MARKETING/OPS ---
Grading and Waste Report — Q3 2026: The grading line packed 27,300 boxes last quarter; the rejection rate for cracked and blood-spot eggs was 6.5%, up from 4.9% a year ago. Customer complaints about stale eggs fell from 24 to 11 per month. Average order fulfilment time is 2.4 days. A survey of 500 café and farm-shop buyers found that 61% would pay up to $0.30 more per box for free-range certified eggs, and 44% want QR-code traceability printed on boxes. The shed currently relies on quality control inspection at the end of the line, and the partners are considering quality assurance methods to prevent defects earlier. 9 of 35 staff have not completed manual egg-grading training; on-the-job coaching is available on the line, and on-site refresher courses cost $320 per employee. A quotation for a solar-powered laying barn (panels and fittings) is $48,000; grid electricity costs have risen 8.9% year-on-year.

--- APPENDIX 2 — FINANCIAL DATA ---
Title: Extract from the Statement of Financial Position of Bramblewick Free-Range Eggs as at 31 March 2025 ($ '000)
Headers: ['Financial Metric', '2024', '2025']
Inventories | 140 | 170
Trade receivables | 90 | 75
Cash and cash equivalents | 35 | 50
Current liabilities | 180 | 150
Non-current assets | 950 | 1,480
Capital employed | 1,035 | 1,625

--- APPENDIX 3 — EXTERNAL ENVIRONMENT ---
Economic and Business Bulletin (November 2026): (1) The central bank has raised the base interest rate from 4.5% to 5.25%, the fourth rise this year, increasing borrowing costs for businesses with variable-rate bank facilities. (2) The national minimum wage will rise by 6.2% from $13.10 to $13.91 per hour from April 2027, raising wage bills for weekend packing staff. (3) Grain and soya feed costs have risen 11.6% year-on-year, and egg-price inflation is running at 7.8%, while consumer spending on free-range eggs grew 4.6% in the same period.

--- QUESTIONS ---
  Q1(a) [8 marks]
    Question: BRE plans to fund the grading machinery with $180,000 hire purchase. Explain two advantages for BRE of hire purchase instead of funding the machinery entirely with the $420,000 bank loan.
    Answer: Point 1: Hire purchase spreads the $180,000 cost of the grading machinery over fixed monthly instalments, so BRE keeps more of its $420,000 bank loan free for the laying barn, feed stores and wage costs during the expensive construction phase. The machinery secures its own finance, useful for a partnership whose combined borrowing is already stretched by the $600,000 expansion.

Point 2: Payments under hire purchase are matched to the useful life of the grading machinery, which is exactly how the asset generates revenue — graded boxes of 27,300 per quarter at a 6.5% rejection rate BRE badly needs to cut. BRE gets immediate use of the machine without a single large outflow, protects working capital while feed costs rise 11.6%, and gains ownership outright once the final instalment is paid, unlike an overdraft that could be called in at short notice; it also keeps the partners' personal credit untouched ahead of any future barn refinancing, and avoids pressure from the bank to shorten the $420,000 loan term once the new shed is trading.
    Keywords: hire purchase, $180,000, $420,000, $600,000, grading machinery, 27,300
    Mark scheme: knowledge_max_2: 1 mark for each valid advantage identified (max 2). | application_analysis_max_6: Up to 3 marks per point for contextual explanation and analysis applied to Bramblewick Free-Range Eggs and its expansion decision.

  Q1(b) [12 marks]
    Question: BRE is launching its free-range certified box range to farm shops and cafés. Consider national television advertising, sponsorship of a regional food festival, or social media marketing aimed at local buyers. Which should BRE choose to promote the launch? Justify your recommendation.
    Answer: National television advertising: A national TV campaign would give BRE's free-range boxes instant mass awareness and could shift national attitudes toward free-range certification. However, production and airtime costs would consume a large part of the $600,000 expansion budget, and most viewers live outside BRE's delivery region, where cafés and farm shops cannot receive boxes; for a 35-employee partnership funded by a bank loan and hire purchase, the wasted reach would be unaffordable and unmeasurable.

Sponsorship of a regional food festival: A weekend festival stall with egg cookery demonstrations reaches exactly BRE's farm-shop and café customer base face to face, lets buyers taste egg dishes, and builds the personal relationships that independent grocers value; the 61% of 500 surveyed buyers willing to pay up to $0.30 more per box can be converted on the spot with samples and QR sign-ups for traceability. The drawback is very short exposure — one weekend a year — and no scale beyond the regional catchment, so sales lift fades quickly without follow-up.

Social media marketing aimed at local buyers: Targeted posts and short videos aimed at local cafés, farm shops and conscious consumers cost little, can showcase the 6.5%-to-4.9% quality drive, the QR-code traceability that 44% of buyers want, and the $0.30 price premium story, and they reach exactly the regional catchment BRE serves, with measurable clicks to an order form. Its weakness is that reach builds slowly and depends on consistent content, and some café owners still prefer print tasting notes over social feeds.

Recommendation: BRE should choose social media marketing aimed at local buyers. It is the only option that is low-cost, targeted to the exact regional customer base, aligned with the 61% premium-willing segment and the 44% wanting QR traceability, and measurable weekly; television is rejected as too costly and geographically wasteful for a regional supplier, and festival sponsorship is rejected as a one-weekend tactic with no lasting reach, though BRE should keep a single festival stall as a complement rather than the lead promotion.
    Keywords: free-range, $600,000, 105,000, 61%, 44%, farm shops
    Mark scheme: level_1_1_to_4: Limited knowledge or outline of the promotional options with minimal context. | level_2_5_to_8: Detailed discussion of the advantages and disadvantages of at least two options in the context of BRE with some judgement. | level_3_9_to_12: Detailed discussion of all three options in the context of BRE with a well-justified recommendation explaining why television and festival sponsorship are rejected.

    Question: BRE's egg rejection rate has reached 6.5%. Explain two benefits for BRE of using democratic leadership to involve packing-shed staff in reducing cracked and blood-spot eggs.
    Answer: Point 1: Democratic leadership lets the 35 employees suggest grading-line improvements — for example better light positioning at inspection tables or gentler handling of the 27,300 boxes packed last quarter — because the packers themselves see which tray positions crack the most shells. Involving them satisfies esteem needs, raises their commitment to the fix, and attacks the rejection rate directly rather than relying on end-of-line inspection alone.

  Q2(b) [12 marks]
    Question: BRE must cut the 6.5% rejection rate. Consider quality control (end-of-line inspection) or quality assurance (prevention built into the grading process). Which should BRE choose? Justify your decision.
    Answer: Quality control: End-of-line inspection means trained graders checking every box after packing and downgrading cracked or blood-spot eggs before dispatch. It is simple to introduce, needs no process redesign, and matches BRE's existing routine, so stale-complaint numbers can keep falling from the current 11 per month. However, it is a detection method, not prevention: eggs are already cracked by the time they are caught, so the 4.9%-to-6.5% slide continues upstream, rejected boxes are pure cost at a $4.70 variable cost, and inspection labour is duplicated if rejections keep rising.

Quality assurance: Quality assurance builds prevention into each stage — calibrated grading machines, on-the-job coaching for the 9 untrained staff at $320 each, gentler conveyors, tray audits at the feeder and egg-quality sampling at the laying barn. It costs more up front in training, machine settings and documentation time, but it attacks root causes, so rejections fall before eggs reach the box, waste and rework disappear, and café and farm-shop customers receive consistent graded product that protects the $9.50 price and the $0.30 certification premium that 61% of buyers would pay.

Decision: BRE should adopt quality assurance as its primary approach, keeping a light end-of-line quality control check as a safety net. Prevention is the only route to reversing the 6.5% rejection rate rather than merely containing it, it fits the democratic flat structure where staff propose fixes, and its up-front cost is repaid through less waste, fewer complaints than the peak of 24 per month and stronger certification credibility for the new barn. Quality control alone is rejected because it leaves root causes untouched, locks in avoidable waste on every box packed, and would force BRE to hire more weekend graders at rising wage rates instead of solving the problem once.
    Keywords: quality control, quality assurance, 6.5%, 4.9%, 27,300, $4.70
    Mark scheme: level_1_1_to_4: Basic description of quality control and quality assurance with limited application to BRE. | level_2_5_to_8: Detailed analysis of both approaches in the context of BRE's rejection rate and complaints. | level_3_9_to_12: Comprehensive evaluation of both approaches in the context of BRE with a well-justified decision covering cost, waste, complaint trends and certification credibility.

The quick coverage rose from 0.69 to 0.83, so BRE needs stock less to meet short-term claims, although 0.83 is still below 1.0, meaning the business remains dependent on selling those 170,000 units of feed and boxed eggs to bridge any shock. Inventories rose from $140,000 to $170,000, sensible ahead of the new barn but cash-intensive, and the $420,000 bank loan plus $180,000 hire purchase will add fixed commitments that make the stronger liquidity position essential, not optional.

Conclusion: BRE's financial position has improved. Both the current ratio (1.47 to 1.97) and the acid test ratio (0.69 to 0.83) show better short-term solvency, receivables management has tightened, and the improvement is genuine rather than depending solely on inventory. The residual concern is the sub-1.0 quick coverage and rising stock, so BRE should continue tighter credit terms with cafés and farm shops and stage the barn build to protect cash before the hire-purchase instalments begin.
    Keywords: 1.47, 1.97, 0.69, 0.83, $265,000, $295,000, $600,000
    Mark scheme: level_1_1_to_4: States financial figures or changes without accurate ratio calculations. | level_2_5_to_8: Accurately calculates the current ratio and acid test ratio for both 2024 and 2025 with contextual analysis of the trend. | level_3_9_to_12: Accurate ratio calculations for both years combined with detailed evaluation of inventory, receivables and liabilities movements and a justified conclusion on whether BRE's financial position improved.

  Q4(a) [8 marks]
    Question: Explain one advantage and one disadvantage for BRE of introducing a solar-powered laying barn for the new 12,000-bird unit.
    Answer: Advantage: A solar-powered laying barn quoting at $48,000 cuts BRE's grid electricity bill just as electricity costs have risen 8.9% year-on-year, directly protecting the $9.50 selling price and the $4.80 contribution per unit on 105,000 units a year. It also strengthens BRE's free-range and certification credentials with the 61% of surveyed buyers willing to pay up to $0.30 more per box, and the green image can be featured in the QR-code traceability material the 44% of buyers want, supporting premium farm-shop listings.

Disadvantage: The $48,000 panel cost is an extra outflow on top of the $600,000 barn budget that is already financed by a $420,000 bank loan and $180,000 hire purchase, stretching cash flow before the new unit produces a single box. Solar generation is also weather-dependent, so feed augers and lighting still need grid backup in winter months, meaning the panels will not eliminate electricity costs, and upfront maintenance or roof repairs could disrupt the 12,000-bird unit during its critical first laying cycle if panel fitting delays the barn's completion date.
    Keywords: solar-powered laying barn, 61%, 44%, $0.30, 8.9%, $48,000, 12,000-bird
    Mark scheme: knowledge_max_2: 1 mark for a valid advantage and 1 mark for a valid disadvantage. | application_analysis_max_6: Up to 3 marks per point for detailed contextual development linked to BRE's research data, costs and expansion.

  Q4(b) [12 marks]
    Question: Using Appendix 3, evaluate how the interest rate rise to 5.25%, the 6.2% minimum wage increase and the 11.6% rise in feed costs will affect BRE. Which change will have the greatest impact? Justify your answer.
    Answer: Interest rate rise (4.5% to 5.25%): BRE's $420,000 ten-year bank loan may carry a variable or repriced element, so a 0.75-point rise adds roughly $3,150 a year in interest, while the $180,000 hire purchase is fixed-rate and unaffected. Higher rates may also cool consumer spending on premium free-range boxes as households cut back, and any refinancing of the barn would now be pricier. The direct cash impact is modest but persistent, and BRE can manage part of it by fixing loan pricing early with its bank.

Minimum wage increase (6.2%, to $13.91 per hour): BRE employs 35 staff, many in weekend grading and packing roles paid near minimum wage. A 6.2% rise adds roughly $1,700 per full-time worker per year; across a workforce of 35, with weekend casuals on top, the total payroll increase is on the order of $60,000 a year — a major pressure for a partnership whose contribution per unit is only $4.80. Democratic leadership can capture staff efficiency suggestions to offset this, but BRE must raise throughput per packer or prices to absorb the extra cost.

Input cost inflation (11.6% grain and soya feed): Feed is BRE's largest variable cost within the $4.70 per box. An 11.6% rise on the feed component adds roughly $0.35–$0.45 per box; at 105,000 boxes that is about $37,000 to $47,000 a year, cutting contribution toward $4.25–$4.35 and squeezing the margin that must service the barn loan, at exactly the moment feed volumes will rise with 12,000 more birds.

Conclusion: The 6.2% minimum wage increase will have the greatest impact. It adds on the order of $60,000 a year to BRE's payroll across 35 staff, it cannot be avoided by reformulation or supplier switching, and it lands in the same year as the green-barn launch and grading training drive. The 11.6% feed rise is the second most serious pressure at roughly $37,000–$47,000 a year but can be partly offset by reformulating rations with nutritionists and renegotiating feed contracts; the interest-rate increase is the smallest in cash terms at a few thousand dollars and can be capped by fixing loan pricing — so BRE must respond to the wage rise first, through productivity, modest price recovery and staff retention, before defending its margin on the new barn.
    Keywords: 5.25%, 6.2%, 11.6%, $13.91, interest rate, $4.70
    Mark scheme: level_1_1_to_4: Identifies the external factors with limited application to BRE. | level_2_5_to_8: Analyses the impact of at least two external changes on BRE's costs, revenue or financing in context. | level_3_9_to_12: Detailed evaluation of all three external changes in the context of BRE with a well-justified judgement that the minimum wage increase has the greatest impact and why the other two are smaller.

--- MAIN STEM ---
Stonebarrow Vineyard & Wine Co-operative (SBV) is a cooperative owned by 31 member grape-growing families in the wine production sector, employing a workforce of 58. Founded in 1994 and led by chairperson Tessa Vidal, the cooperative vinifies member grapes into single-vineyard still and sparkling wines sold to independent wine merchants and its cellar door, operating a flat structure with laissez-faire leadership among member growers. SBV plans to invest $950,000 in a temperature-controlled fermentation and barrel-maturation hall with an extended cellar door and online shop, financed by a $400,000 community share issue and $550,000 retained profit. It has fixed costs of $360,000 a year, a variable cost of $9.60 a unit and a selling price of $16.80, and currently produces 120,000 units a year. SBV faces two problems: labour turnover among casual harvest pickers reached 28% this season, and barrel-fault defect rates are rising.

--- APPENDIX 1 — MARKETING/OPS ---
Cellar Operations Log — Q3 2026: The winery crushed 310 tonnes of member grapes last vintage. Bottle-fault inspections found a defect rate of 2.1% (cork taint and fill faults), down from 3.0% a year ago. Complaints from wine merchants fell from 19 to 9 per month. Average dispatch time is 5.5 days. A survey of 800 wine buyers found that 59% would pay up to $1.20 more for single-vineyard co-op wine, and 51% check sustainable viticulture certification before buying. The board is weighing a $0.40-per-tonne harvest bonus to retain casual harvest pickers, and it is deciding between permanent cellar positions and seasonal casual contracts for the coming vintage; casual pickers averaged 34 hours a week this year.

--- APPENDIX 2 — FINANCIAL DATA ---
Title: Extract from the Statement of Financial Position of Stonebarrow Vineyard & Wine Co-operative as at 31 March 2025 ($ '000)
Headers: ['Financial Metric', '2024', '2025']
Inventories | 320 | 290
Trade receivables | 210 | 240
Cash and cash equivalents | 60 | 85
Current liabilities | 300 | 275
Non-current assets | 2,900 | 3,700
Capital employed | 3,190 | 4,040

--- APPENDIX 3 — EXTERNAL ENVIRONMENT ---
Economic and Business Bulletin (November 2026): (1) The central bank has raised the base interest rate from 4.0% to 4.75%, the third rise this year, increasing borrowing costs for vineyard equipment finance. (2) The national minimum wage will rise by 6.9% from $13.45 to $14.38 per hour from April 2027, raising wage bills for casual harvest staff working 34 hours a week. (3) Bottle glass and cork costs have risen 13.2% year-on-year, and wine inflation is running at 8.3%, while consumer spending on premium wine grew 3.8% in the same period.

--- QUESTIONS ---
  Q1(a) [8 marks]
    Question: SBV plans to fund the fermentation hall with $550,000 retained profit and a $400,000 community share issue. Explain two advantages for SBV of using retained profit instead of relying entirely on the community share issue.
    Answer: Point 1: Retained profit costs SBV nothing in dividends, interest or issue administration, protecting the cash flow of a cooperative whose 31 member families already expect stable grape payments while it funds a $950,000 hall. Avoiding sole reliance on the community share issue reduces the risk that member appetite for shares falls short of the target, which would leave the fermentation hall underfunded or push SBV toward expensive unplanned borrowing from a bank that knows nothing of wine cycles — damaging member confidence in the cooperative model itself.

Point 2: Using retained profit first signals to members and wine merchants that SBV is financially disciplined and self-reliant, strengthening confidence in the single-vineyard expansion and in the 59% premium-willing segment identified in its research. It also preserves the $400,000 community share issue as a buffer for cost overruns on the temperature-controlled hall — significant because barrel-fault defects and 13.2% bottle-glass inflation could both squeeze the project's budget before the 2027 vintage, and because member appetites for further share calls would fade if the hall overran its cost.
    Keywords: retained profit, community share issue, $400,000, $550,000, $950,000, single-vineyard
    Mark scheme: knowledge_max_2: 1 mark for each valid advantage identified (max 2). | application_analysis_max_6: Up to 3 marks per point for contextual explanation and analysis applied to Stonebarrow Vineyard & Wine Co-operative and its expansion decision.

  Q1(b) [12 marks]
    Question: SBV is launching its single-vineyard co-op range of still and sparkling wines. Consider cellar-door wine-tasting events, targeted social media advertising, or local radio sponsorship. Which should SBV choose to promote the launch? Justify your recommendation.
    Answer: Cellar-door wine-tasting events: Tasting events at the cellar door let visitors sample the single-vineyard range, meet the member growers and buy direct, deepening loyalty and supporting the $16.80 price point without wine-merchant margin. They showcase the 51% of buyers who check sustainable viticulture certification with face-to-face storytelling. The limitation is capacity: the cellar door already serves visitors while handling dispatch in 5.5 days, so tastings can never reach buyers beyond the local region, and each event sells limited volume relative to a 120,000-unit annual output target.

Targeted social media advertising: Targeted campaigns on food, wine and lifestyle channels can reach precisely the 59% of 800 surveyed buyers willing to pay up to $1.20 more for single-vineyard co-op wine, across every region and export market the online shop serves, with measurable click-through to the shop and retargeting of engagers. It costs a fraction of mass media, fits SBV's cooperative, low-overheads ethos, and can feature member-grower stories and certification badges — though it demands regular content and results build over weeks rather than instantly.

Local radio sponsorship: Local radio delivers frequency and name recall in the immediate region at low cost, and a harvest-time sponsorship slot would reach loyal local wine drinkers effectively. However, radio cannot target premium wine buyers specifically, much of its audience neither visits the cellar door nor orders online, and coverage stops at the transmitter boundary while SBV ships to independent merchants across multiple regions.

Recommendation: SBV should choose targeted social media advertising. It alone combines precise targeting of the 59% premium-willing segment and the 51% certification-checkers, national scalability for the online shop, measurable returns on the $950,000 investment, and low cost suited to a cooperative without large marketing reserves. Cellar-door tastings are rejected as the lead strategy because their limited local reach cannot move 120,000 units a year; local radio is rejected as untargeted and geographically capped, though one monthly tasting evening should continue as a complement rather than the anchor of the launch campaign.
    Keywords: single-vineyard, 59%, 51%, 120,000, $950,000, cellar door

  Q2(a) [8 marks]
    Question: SBV's labour turnover among casual harvest pickers reached 28% this season. Explain two benefits for SBV of using a harvest bonus to motivate pickers during the vintage.
    Answer: Point 1: A harvest bonus tied to tonnes picked gives casual pickers a direct financial incentive to stay for the whole crush rather than leave mid-vintage, directly attacking the 28% turnover. Because the bonus scales with output, SBV pays only for results — crucial when pickers work 34 hours a week and the winery crushed 310 tonnes of member grapes that must be processed within days of picking.

Point 2: A completion bonus at the end of harvest raises morale and loyalty beyond the picking rows, making pickers more willing to return next year and to handle fruit carefully — which supports the 2.1% bottle-fault defect target and the falling complaints from 19 to 9 per month. Retaining experienced pickers also cuts re-recruitment and induction costs and protects member growers' fruit quality, reinforcing the cooperative's democratic values and member confidence in Tessa Vidal's leadership — while giving seasonal workers a tangible reason to return for the 2027 vintage.
    Keywords: harvest bonus, labour turnover, 28%, casual harvest, 2.1%, 310 tonnes

  Q2(b) [12 marks]
    Question: SBV needs reliable workers for the coming vintage. Consider offering permanent cellar positions or seasonal casual contracts. Which should SBV choose? Justify your decision.
    Answer: Permanent cellar positions: Permanent contracts would end the 28% labour turnover among pickers, give the winery a skilled core team that knows the temperature-controlled fermentation hall, barrel handling and bottle-fault standards, and support long-horizon quality gains such as pushing the 2.1% defect rate below 2%. Permanent staff also justify off-the-job training investment, answer member growers' demands for consistency, and are easier to brief on the sustainable viticulture certification that 51% of buyers check. The downsides are higher fixed wage costs through quiet months — pickers work only seasonally on current 34-hour weeks — plus redundancy risk if a vintage fails, and permanent employment law obligations such as employment contracts and redundancy processes that a small cooperative must administer.

Seasonal casual contracts: Seasonal contracts scale labour to the crush exactly when it is needed, keep fixed costs low, preserve flexibility in lean years, and suit pickers who only want vintage work; they also protect cash ahead of the $950,000 hall investment and match the proposed $0.40-per-tonne harvest bonus. However, they entrench the 28% turnover, require retraining every season, risk inconsistent fruit handling and higher defects, and undermine the certification credibility and merchant relationships SBV is building for its single-vineyard range.

Decision: SBV should offer permanent cellar positions for a core team of cellar and bottling staff, keeping seasonal casual contracts only for the peak crush weeks with the harvest bonus attached. Permanent contracts solve the root cause — 28% turnover — protect quality in the new hall, and are affordable against $950,000-expansion economics since cellar work continues year-round; pure seasonal contracting is rejected because it recreates the very churn, defect and retraining costs SBV must eliminate to supply premium merchants, would weaken the certification story, and would leave member growers' fruit handling expertise walking away every autumn.
    Keywords: permanent cellar positions, seasonal casual, 28%, $0.40-per-tonne harvest bonus, 2.1%, vintage
    Mark scheme: level_1_1_to_4: Basic description of permanent and seasonal employment with limited application to SBV. | level_2_5_to_8: Detailed analysis of both options in the context of SBV's labour turnover and vintage workload. | level_3_9_to_12: Comprehensive evaluation of both options in the context of SBV with a well-justified decision covering cost, quality, retention and certification credibility.

    Answer: Interest rate rise (4.0% to 4.75%): SBV's $950,000 expansion is funded by a $400,000 community share issue and $550,000 retained profit, not new variable-rate debt, so the direct hit is small — it applies mainly to any equipment finance and overdraft margins; a 0.75-point rise on modest borrowing adds at most a few thousand dollars a year. The minimum wage increase is the second most serious pressure and can be partly absorbed by the harvest-bonus retention saving on re-recruitment, while the interest-rate change is minor given SBV's equity-funded expansion; SBV should nevertheless lock in a bottle and cork supply contract or forward purchase before April 2027 to defend its margin.

PAPER 2 — P2_SET_184
