--- MAIN STEM ---
Goldensheaf Milling Company (GSM) is a public limited company in the flour milling and baking-mix sector, employing a workforce of 260. Founded in 1988 by Arthur Bellingham, GSM is led by chief executive Duncan Pryce and operates a hierarchical structure with democratic leadership and elected staff councils. The company plans to invest $1,500,000 in a new wholegrain flour and baking-mix production plant, financed by a $900,000 share issue and a $600,000 bank loan. It has fixed costs of $540,000 a year, a variable cost of $11.30 a unit and a selling price of $18.50, and currently produces 150,000 units a year. GSM faces two problems: spillage and dust waste is running at 4.8% of throughput, and the business faces a skills gap in certified mill operatives.

--- APPENDIX 1 — MARKETING/OPS ---
Milling Waste and Quality Report — Q3 2026: The mill produced 36,500 bags (25 kg) last quarter. Spillage and dust waste ran at 4.8% of throughput, up from 3.9% a year ago. Off-spec flour rejected at 1.2%. Complaints from wholesale bakery clients fell from 31 to 14 per month. Average delivery time is 3.8 days. A survey of 900 wholesale bakery buyers found that 57% would pay up to $0.75 more per bag for certified low-waste wholegrain flour, and 49% want ISO 22000 certification across suppliers; certified mill operatives remain scarce in the regional labour market, and on-site training with external assessors costs $1,100 per employee.

--- APPENDIX 2 — FINANCIAL DATA ---
Title: Extract from the Statement of Financial Position of Goldensheaf Milling Company as at 31 March 2025 ($ '000)
Headers: ['Financial Metric', '2024', '2025']
Inventories | 260 | 230
Trade receivables | 330 | 360
Cash and cash equivalents | 95 | 70
Current liabilities | 480 | 430
Non-current assets | 4,600 | 5,900
Capital employed | 4,805 | 6,130

--- APPENDIX 3 — EXTERNAL ENVIRONMENT ---
Economic and Business Bulletin (November 2026): (1) The central bank has raised the base interest rate from 4.75% to 5.25%, the fourth rise this year, increasing financing costs for the company's bank borrowings. (2) The national minimum wage will rise by 6.4% from $13.32 to $14.17 per hour from April 2027, raising wage bills. (3) Wheat costs have risen 10.7% year-on-year, and food inflation is running at 7.6%, while consumer spending on home-baking ingredients grew 5.2% in the same period.

--- QUESTIONS ---
  Q1(a) [8 marks]
    Question: GSM plans to fund the wholegrain plant partly with a $900,000 share issue. Explain two advantages for GSM of using the share issue instead of increasing the $600,000 bank loan.
    Answer: Point 1: A share issue brings in $900,000 without creating any repayment obligation or interest charge, so GSM's fixed costs do not rise on top of the existing $540,000 a year. This protects the profit margin and cash flow of a public company whose $1,500,000 plant must also bear a rising interest-rate environment, and keeps headroom with the bank for working capital such as wheat purchases amid 10.7% input inflation.

Point 2: Equity finance spreads ownership risk and strengthens the Statement of Financial Position for future negotiations with wholesale bakery clients and ISO 22000 auditors, since capital employed rises without extra debt. Dividend payments can be varied or passed in a difficult year, unlike loan interest, giving GSM flexibility through wheat-price cycles; and the share issue deepens the public shareholder base, potentially raising GSM's profile before it supplies national baking-mix contracts — and keeping the balance sheet clean at exactly the moment auditors will scrutinise the expansion funding.
    Keywords: share issue, $900,000, $600,000, $1,500,000, wholegrain, $540,000
    Mark scheme: knowledge_max_2: 1 mark for each valid advantage identified (max 2). | application_analysis_max_6: Up to 3 marks per point for contextual explanation and analysis applied to Goldensheaf Milling Company and its expansion decision.

  Q1(b) [12 marks]
    Question: GSM is launching its certified low-waste wholegrain flour for wholesale bakeries. Consider exhibiting at the National Bakery Trade Exhibition, advertising in a baking-industry trade magazine, or running a LinkedIn business-to-business campaign. Which should GSM choose to promote the launch? Justify your recommendation.
    Answer: National Bakery Trade Exhibition: An exhibition stand would put GSM sales staff face to face with bakery purchasing managers, allow live sampling of the wholegrain blend, and generate warm leads within two days. The drawbacks are high one-off stand and staffing costs, limited to attendees over a single weekend, and no lasting presence; for a public company already financing a $1,500,000 plant, the cost per qualified lead is uncertain, and follow-up still has to be sold over weeks.

Baking-industry trade magazine advertising: A full-page feature in a leading baking title would reach thousands of bakery owners and production managers who read it for supplier news, building credibility for the certified low-waste claim backed by the 57% of 900 surveyed buyers willing to pay up to $0.75 more per bag. However, print frequency is monthly, response is passive and slow, and measuring return on spend requires reader-response mechanisms; coverage skews toward larger bakeries and misses smaller regional firms that GSM can profitably serve.

LinkedIn business-to-business campaign: Targeted LinkedIn adverts and Duncan Pryce's company-page content can reach bakery owners, production directors and procurement managers by job title, sector and region, showcase the 49% of buyers wanting ISO 22000 certification, link directly to a sample-request form, and deliver measurable click-through and cost-per-lead within weeks. It complements the trade exhibition's reach at a fraction of the cost, though it requires disciplined content and cannot replace human relationship-building with the largest national bakery accounts.

Recommendation: GSM should choose the LinkedIn business-to-business campaign.   Q2(b) [12 marks]
    Question: GSM faces a skills gap on its new wholegrain line. Consider training its existing workforce with external assessors or recruiting certified mill operatives externally. Which should GSM choose? Justify your decision.
    Answer: Training existing workforce with external assessors: Developing current staff costs $1,100 per employee with external assessors certifying competencies; for a cohort of, say, 20 operatives that is $22,000 — modest against $1,500,000. However, certified operatives are scarce regionally, salaries command a premium, induction into GSM's culture and ISO standards takes weeks, and poaching risks resentment among long-serving staff passed over for certification, undermining the democratic staff-council compact that keeps turnover low.

Decision: GSM should train its existing workforce with external assessors as the primary route, supplemented by recruiting two or three certified operatives externally as line leads and mentors. Training builds a home-grown certified cohort, preserves morale and process knowledge, and costs far less; pure external recruitment is rejected because the scarce regional talent could idle the new line at launch, add salary inflation, and weaken the internal pipeline GSM needs for ISO 22000 recertification — while recruiting only internally is rejected too, because line leads accelerate everyone's competence and bring outside best practice to the 1.2% off-spec target immediately.

    Question: Using Appendix 2, evaluate GSM's financial position by calculating the current ratio and the acid test ratio for 2024 and 2025. Which judgement do the figures support — has GSM's financial position improved? Justify your answer.

Current Ratio 2024 = 1.43 : 1
Current Ratio 2025 = 1.53 : 1
Acid Test Ratio 2024 = 0.89 : 1
Acid Test Ratio 2025 = 1.00 : 1

Detailed workings: 2024 current assets = $260,000 inventories + $330,000 trade receivables + $95,000 cash = $685,000; 2025 current assets = $230,000 + $360,000 + $70,000 = $660,000. Inventories fell prudently to $230,000, freeing working capital, but the company should watch for off-spec flour quarantine adding back stock unexpectedly.

Conclusion: GSM's financial position has improved, modestly. Both the current ratio (1.43 to 1.53) and the acid test ratio (0.89 to 1.00) show stronger short-term solvency, and the share issue rather than extra borrowing underpins the gain. The residual risks are the falling cash balance and rising receivables, so GSM should tighten wholesale credit terms, collect faster from the 57% premium-willing bakery segment, and refinance part of the bank loan as the new plant ramps up to protect the waste and off-spec recovery on the new line.

  Q4(b) [12 marks]
    Question: Using Appendix 3, evaluate how the interest rate rise to 5.25%, the 6.4% minimum wage increase and the 10.7% rise in wheat costs will affect GSM. Which change will have the greatest impact? Justify your answer.
    Answer: Interest rate rise (4.75% to 5.25%): GSM carries a $600,000 bank loan attached to the $1,500,000 plant; on a variable or repricing facility a 0.50-point rise adds roughly $3,000 a year in interest, modest against $540,000 fixed costs and $18.50 pricing. Higher rates also raise any overdraft used for wheat purchases and can cool consumer home-baking spending if mortgages rise; for GSM the direct cash hit is small, though it raises the hurdle any further capital spending must clear and slightly tightens the credit outlook for wholesale bakery clients.

Minimum wage increase (6.4%, to $14.17 per hour): GSM employs 260 staff; if most earn near the current $13.32 minimum, a 6.4% rise adds roughly $1,700 per worker, or about $440,000 a year across the full workforce — a major payroll pressure, though many mill operatives and engineers earn above minimum, so the true figure is somewhat lower. The rise lands exactly when the new plant needs to hit 1.2% off-spec flour targets and may squeeze discretionary training budgets, making productivity from the certified cohort essential to absorb it.

Wheat cost inflation (10.7% year-on-year): Wheat dominates the $11.30 variable cost. A 10.7% rise on the wheat component adds roughly $0.90–$1.10 per 25 kg bag; at 150,000 units that is about $135,000–$165,000 a year, cutting contribution from $7.20 toward $6.10–$6.30 before price rises, exactly as GSM launches flour off the new wholegrain plant and tries to hold $18.50 with a promised $0.75 premium for certified low-waste product.

Conclusion: The 10.7% rise in wheat costs will have the greatest impact. It is the largest single raw material cost, it compounds with every unit milled — roughly $135,000–$165,000 a year at current volumes and far more once the plant ramps — and it attacks the contribution margin that funds the $600,000 bank loan. The minimum-wage increase is the second-biggest pressure and can be mitigated through automation on the new line and through democratic staff councils raising labour productivity, while the interest-rate rise is the smallest in cash terms at a few thousand dollars and can be capped by fixing loan pricing; GSM should nevertheless hedge wheat purchases and renegotiate wholesale bakery contracts to pass through part of the cost before the April 2027 wage change compounds it.
    Keywords: 5.25%, 6.4%, 10.7%, $14.17, interest rate, $11.30

--- MAIN STEM ---
Amberline Honey Farm (AHF) is a sole trader in the raw honey production and bottling sector, employing a workforce of 16. Founded in 2015 by Jessamine Cole, the business harvests and bottles raw unfiltered honey from 480 managed hives, selling through farmers' markets and its online honey club, operating a flat structure with autocratic leadership. AHF plans to invest $450,000 in a solar-powered extraction and bottling shed to supply its online honey club, financed by a $270,000 personal savings injection and a $180,000 overdraft. It has fixed costs of $144,000 a year, a variable cost of $3.60 a unit and a selling price of $8.40, and currently produces 80,000 units a year. AHF faces two problems: absenteeism during the late-summer harvest has reached 11%, and complaints about leaking caps are rising.

--- APPENDIX 1 — MARKETING/OPS ---
Harvest and Bottling Log — Q3 2026: AHF harvested and bottled 21,500 jars last quarter; absenteeism during the late-summer harvest reached 11%, up from 7% a year ago. Cap-seal complaints fell from 26 to 14 per month. Average order fulfilment time is 2.9 days. A survey of 400 farmers'-market and online buyers found that 63% would pay up to $0.60 more for raw unfiltered local honey, and 46% would subscribe to a monthly honey club; the part-time harvest team needs overtime rota cover, and three harvest helpers have left since May. The owner is considering job rotation between hive work and the bottling shed to lift morale, and induction plus food-handler certification costs $260 per employee.

--- APPENDIX 2 — FINANCIAL DATA ---
Title: Extract from the Statement of Financial Position of Amberline Honey Farm as at 31 March 2025 ($ '000)
Headers: ['Financial Metric', '2024', '2025']
Inventories | 75 | 62
Trade receivables | 40 | 55
Cash and cash equivalents | 25 | 38
Current liabilities | 95 | 80
Non-current assets | 480 | 540
Capital employed | 525 | 615

--- APPENDIX 3 — EXTERNAL ENVIRONMENT ---
Economic and Business Bulletin (November 2026): (1) The central bank has raised the base interest rate from 4.25% to 5.0%, the third rise this year, increasing the cost of overdrafts and other variable-rate borrowing. (2) The national minimum wage will rise by 6.0% from $12.95 to $13.73 per hour from April 2027, raising wage bills for seasonal harvest staff working overtime. (3) Sugar and bee-feed costs have risen 9.4% year-on-year, and food inflation is running at 7.4%, while consumer spending on local artisan food grew 5.8% in the same period.

  Q1(a) [8 marks]
    Question: AHF plans to fund the new solar-powered extraction and bottling shed with $270,000 personal savings and a $180,000 overdraft. Explain two advantages for AHF of using personal savings instead of relying on the overdraft.
    Answer: Point 1: Personal savings carry no interest charge, whereas the $180,000 overdraft would accrue interest from day one — and with the base interest rate now at 5.0%, overdraft costs are rising across the board. Every dollar saved on interest protects AHF's $4.80 contribution per unit and keeps the $450,000 expansion affordable for a sole trader whose entire livelihood rides on the harvest and the bottling shed paying for itself.

Point 2: Personal savings have no repayment deadline or withdrawal clause, unlike an overdraft that the bank can demand repaid or reduce at short notice — a serious risk while AHF's receivables have grown to $55,000 and its cash balance is only $38,000. Using $270,000 of savings keeps the overdraft undrawn for genuine emergencies such as a hive-collapse winter or a bottling-machine breakdown, and demonstrates to the bank that Jessamine Cole has committed her own funds, which strengthens any future negotiation for a longer-term loan to refinance the overdraft after March 2027.

  Q1(b) [12 marks]
    Question: AHF is launching its raw unfiltered local honey through new channels. Consider expanding farmers' market stalls, the online honey club subscription, or supermarket in-store tastings. Which should AHF choose to grow sales? Justify your recommendation.
    Answer: Expanding farmers' market stalls: Farmers' market stalls suit raw honey's artisan image, let Jessamine meet the 63% of 400 surveyed buyers willing to pay $0.60 more, and generate impulse purchases from Saturday shoppers. Each stall, however, costs pitch fees, transport and — critically — staff time: with harvest absenteeism at 11% and three helpers gone since May, AHF cannot reliably staff three more weekend stalls, and sales are weather-dependent and capped by stall-day traffic rather than the 80,000-unit annual output AHF wants to sell.

Online honey club subscription: The honey club converts the 46% of surveyed buyers who said they would subscribe to a monthly club into recurring, predictable revenue with no pitch fees, and boxes can ship direct at a 2.9-day fulfilment time with the flat structure autocratically managed for tight dispatch. Subscriptions smooth seasonality between harvests, build a first-party customer list for new varietals, and fit the $450,000 shed's role as an online-fulfilment hub; the risks are packaging and postage costs, subscription fatigue, and needing reliable dispatch staffing during harvest.

Supermarket in-store tastings: Tastings in national supermarkets would put raw honey in front of mass shoppers and could win permanent listings that absorb large volumes fast — attractive given 80,000 units of capacity. However, supermarkets demand margins, slotting fees, strict delivery windows and often private-label pricing that conflicts with raw unfiltered premium positioning, and they would squeeze the $8.40 price and $4.80 contribution; AHF would also compete on shelf with mass honey brands capitalised for national advertising, which a 16-person sole trader cannot match.

Recommendation: AHF should choose the online honey club subscription. It aligns with the 46% subscription-willing segment and the 63% premium-willing buyers, creates recurring revenue that smooths the harvest cycle, costs far less than supermarket slotting fees or three extra staffed stalls, and fits the shed investment and the 2.9-day fulfilment operation; farmers' markets are rejected as the growth engine because absenteeism and helper losses make new stalls unstaffable and weather-dependent, and supermarket tastings are rejected because the listing margin and compliance burden would destroy the premium positioning and $4.80 contribution that fund the expansion.

A 6.0% rise adds roughly $1,600 per full-time worker — across the 16-strong workforce, roughly $25,000 to $30,000 a year in extra wages including harvest overtime premiums. This lands directly on the thin $3.60 variable cost and the $144,000 fixed-cost base, and it coincides with the shed launch, when Jessamine needs harvest productivity most to meet online honey club dispatch slots; absenteeism at 11% could worsen if pay fails to keep pace with the April 2027 rate.

Input cost inflation (9.4% sugar and bee-feed): Bee feed is used to sustain weak colonies through dearth periods and winter, and sugar syrup supplements late-season flows; a 9.4% rise adds real but bounded cost — on an apiary budget plausibly $25,000 to $35,000 a year, roughly $2,400 to $3,300 extra — far smaller than payroll, though it compounds if weak hives increase after a poor season and coincides with food inflation of 7.4%, pressuring price points.

Conclusion: The 6.0% minimum wage increase will have the greatest impact. It adds roughly $25,000 to $30,000 a year to AHF's payroll across 16 staff, it is unavoidable, it lands during the shed launch and honey club ramp-up, and it hits the same harvest team whose 11% absenteeism already strains output. The 9.4% bee-feed rise is the second most serious pressure but is bounded by scale and can be partly offset by reformulating feed and colony management; the interest-rate rise is the smallest at roughly $1,350 a year on the overdraft and can be eliminated by converting to a term loan — so AHF should reprice its subscription plan modestly, push for the $0.60 premium, and refinance the overdraft before April 2027.
    Keywords: 5.0%, 6.0%, 9.4%, $13.73, interest rate, $3.60
    Mark scheme: level_1_1_to_4: Identifies the external factors with limited application to AHF. | level_2_5_to_8: Analyses the impact of at least two external changes on AHF's costs, revenue or financing in context. | level_3_9_to_12: Detailed evaluation of all three external changes in the context of AHF with a well-justified judgement that the minimum wage increase has the greatest impact and why the other two are smaller.

--- MAIN STEM ---
Kingsbarrow Ceramics (KBC) is a private limited company in the technical ceramics sector, supplying high-voltage electrical insulators to national grid contractors, employing a workforce of 68. It has fixed costs of $360,000 a year, a variable cost of $9.50 a unit and a selling price of $18.50, and currently produces 75,000 units a year. KBC faces a serious operational problem: glaze waste in the decorating shop has climbed to 14% of raw material input.

--- APPENDIX 1 — MARKETING/OPS ---

Customer complaints fell from 16 to 9 per month. On-time delivery stands at 94.2%. A market research survey of 260 utility procurement officers found that 71% require type-tested certification and 49% would accept a 4% price premium for guaranteed 10,000-hour insulators. A training needs analysis shows 14 of 68 staff have not completed on-the-job training on the new kiln controls; off-the-job courses at the local college cost $850 per employee.

Money not paid to a lender can be kept inside the business to absorb the 9.6% rise in alumina and feldspar input costs, helping KBC hold its $18.50 selling price against rival insulator suppliers while the new automated line beds in.

Point 2: Using retained profit avoids the security and covenant requirements attached to a bank loan, so the $450,000 can be committed without putting the new $1,150,000 isostatic pressing line at risk of repossession if grid contractor demand softens. It also preserves Priya Raman's full ownership and control of the private limited company — no external lender can impose conditions on how the line is staffed, operated or expanded next — which suits a founder accustomed to directing the business single-handedly.

    Question: Using Appendix 3, evaluate how the interest rate rise to 5.75%, the 5.8% minimum wage increase and the 9.6% rise in input costs will affect KBC. Which change will have the greatest impact? Justify your answer.
    Answer: Interest rate rise (5.00% to 5.75%): The 0.75 percentage point rise applies to $700,000 of KBC's variable-rate exposure if its ten-year bank loan is variable, adding 0.75% × $700,000 = $5,250 a year in interest — small against fixed costs of $360,000 a year, and zero if the loan was fixed at signing. KBC is only partly geared in practice because $450,000 of the $1,150,000 expansion is retained profit. Higher base rates may also cool grid-contractor spending and make any future borrowing for a phase-two kiln more expensive, so KBC should fix rates or prepay while cash allows.

Minimum wage increase (5.8%, to $12.27 per hour from April 2026): KBC employs 68 staff, most of them hourly pressing, glazing and packing roles, so the rise is unavoidable and feeds directly into the wage bill. The insert gives no hours worked and no pay decomposition, so no defensible annual total can be invented; the honest benchmark is productivity: 75,000 units ÷ 68 staff ≈ 1,103 units per worker a year, so the rise is absorbable only if output and productivity hold or improve, otherwise unit labour cost rises and the $9.00 contribution per unit erodes. It also raises the bar for the on-the-job training programme, since higher wages make every lost or disengaged worker costlier.

Input cost inflation (9.6% alumina and feldspar): KBC's $9.50 variable cost is dominated by raw materials, but the insert never decomposes it, so only an illustrative bound can be computed: if the whole variable cost rose 9.6% it would add 9.6% × $9.50 = $0.91 per unit (0.096 × $9.50 = $0.912); at 75,000 units a year that is about $68,400 a year (0.912 × 75,000). Even a milder illustrative $0.50 per unit would remove about $37,500 a year. KBC can offset part of this through the 4% premium that 49% of surveyed buyers accept and through price negotiations with grid contractors, but the squeeze lands immediately and compounds on every unit sold.

Conclusion: The 9.6% rise in input costs will have the greatest impact. It multiplies across all 75,000 units, directly eroding the $9.00 contribution that justifies the $1,150,000 expansion, and unlike interest it cannot be hedged by fixing a rate; unlike wages it hits every unit of material, not just labour minutes. The minimum wage rise is second, managed through productivity at roughly 1,103 units per worker; the interest rate rise is smallest at about $5,250 a year on a variable $700,000 loan, and close to zero if KBC fixed its terms. KBC should respond with supplier renegotiation, the certified-range premium and tighter glaze-waste control before seeking price rises.
    Keywords: 5.75%, 5.8%, 9.6%, $12.27, interest rate, $9.50

--- MAIN STEM ---
Redmoor Abrasives (RMA) is a public limited company in the industrial abrasives sector, manufacturing resin-bond grinding wheels and cutting discs for steel fabrication plants, employing a workforce of 140. Founded in 1998 by Marek Nowak, the business operates a hierarchical structure with autocratic leadership and is based in Łódź, Poland. RMA plans to invest $1,600,000 in a new high-speed pressing and curing line, financed by a $1,000,000 share issue and $600,000 retained profit. It has fixed costs of $528,000 a year, a variable cost of $13.00 a unit and a selling price of $24.00, and currently produces 96,000 units a year. RMA faces a serious HR problem: absenteeism has reached 8.4% and labour turnover among press operators is rising.

--- APPENDIX 1 — MARKETING/OPS ---
Quality and Waste Report — Q3 2025: The grinding-wheel line produced 24,000 units last quarter at a defect rate of 2.2%, down from 3.7% a year ago. On-time delivery stands at 95.1%. Abrasive grit waste fell from 6.4% to 4.1% of input mass. Wheels are currently wrapped in single-use plastic; trials of ribbed cardboard eco-packaging show transit damage fell 18%. A market research survey of 320 factory maintenance managers found that 68% specify open-web wheels for wet grinding and 55% would accept a 3% price increase for batch-tested wheels. A training needs analysis shows 22 of 140 staff have not completed on-the-job training on the new press; off-the-job courses at the local college cost $700 per employee.

--- APPENDIX 2 — FINANCIAL DATA ---

This matters while RMA carries fixed costs of $528,000 a year: every dollar of profit reinvested rather than paid out can absorb the 10.7% rise in aluminium oxide and resin input costs without diluting headline earnings for the 2027 reporting year.

Point 2: Retained profit avoids issuing new shares, which would dilute the control and voting power of Marek Nowak and the founding shareholder group in the public limited company. Using retained profit instead of selling $600,000 of equity keeps decision-making with current owners, avoids the effort and expense of a prospectus and shareholder meetings, and signals to the market that the board is confident the new line will generate its own returns without fresh capital. It also reassures investors that RMA's growth story is equity-financed rather than debt-driven, protecting the share price that funded the other $1,000,000 of the programme.

    Question: RMA is launching its batch-tested grinding wheel range. Consider a stand at a national metal fabrication exhibition, advertising in an industrial abrasives trade magazine, or local radio sponsorship. Which should RMA choose to promote the launch? Justify your recommendation.

    Question: Using Appendix 3, evaluate how the interest rate rise to 6.00%, the 6.0% minimum wage increase and the 10.7% rise in input costs will affect RMA. Which change will have the greatest impact? Justify your answer.
    Answer: Interest rate rise (5.25% to 6.00%): RMA funded its $1,600,000 expansion through a $1,000,000 share issue and $600,000 retained profit, not a bank loan, so the direct repayment effect of the 0.75 percentage point rise is nil today — no variable-rate loan sits on its books. If RMA later chose to fund a phase-two press with debt, 0.75% would cost 0.75% × $1,600,000 = $12,000 a year (0.0075 × $1,600,000), but that is optional, not current, and the share issue shields shareholders and cash flow from rate shocks right now. The rise may also temper borrowing among fabrication customers, slowing orders, and will lift any future lease costs for the planned second kiln or curing oven.

Minimum wage increase (6.0%, to $13.78 per hour from April 2026): With a workforce of 140, most of whom are hourly press and packing operatives, the rise is unavoidable. The insert states no hours worked and no pay decomposition, so no annual wage total can be honestly invented; the honest test is productivity: 96,000 units ÷ 140 staff ≈ 686 units per worker a year. If productivity holds at that level and RMA passes the attendance bonus carefully, the rise is absorbable; if not, unit labour cost climbs, the $11.00 contribution shrinks, and the 8.4% absenteeism problem becomes costlier to cover.

Input cost inflation (10.7% aluminium oxide and resin): RMA's $13.00 variable cost is heavily driven by abrasive grains and bonding resins, though the insert never decomposes it, so only an illustrative bound is defensible: if the whole variable cost rose 10.7% it would add 10.7% × $13.00 = $1.39 per unit (0.107 × $13.00 = $1.39); at 96,000 units a year that is about $133,440 (96,000 × $1.39). Even a milder illustrative $1.00 per unit would strip about $96,000 a year. Unlike interest, this compounds on every unit made and sold, and unlike wages, it rises regardless of headcount control; RMA can recover part of it only through the 3% premium the 55% premium-accepting buyers will tolerate and through renegotiating supply contracts.

Conclusion: The 10.7% rise in input costs will have the greatest impact, removing up to roughly $133,000 a year if fully passed through the $13.00 variable cost and hitting every one of the 96,000 units — directly eroding the $11.00 contribution that underpins both dividends and the expansion case. The minimum wage rise is second, manageable through attendance discipline and productivity near 686 units per worker; the 6.00% base-rate rise is a clear third for RMA because its $1,600,000 programme is share-issue and retained-profit financed. RMA should lock multi-year resin supply contracts, accelerate the 18% cardboard damage saving, and use batch-testing certification to enforce the 3% premium before absorbing any further cost.
    Keywords: 6.00%, 6.0%, 10.7%, $13.78, interest rate, $13.00

--- MAIN STEM ---
Clearspire Filtration (CSF) is a partnership in the industrial filtration sector, producing pleated air and coolant filter cartridges for manufacturing plants, employing a workforce of 34. Founded in 2013 by Sofia Almeida and Rafael Duarte, the partnership operates a flat structure with shared democratic decision-making and is based in Joinville, Brazil. CSF plans to invest $780,000 in a new automated pleating and welding line, financed by hire purchase of $480,000 on the machinery and a $300,000 overdraft facility. It has fixed costs of $312,000 a year, a variable cost of $18.00 a unit and a selling price of $30.00, and currently produces 48,000 units a year. CSF faces a serious quality problem: the defect rate on pleated cartridges has risen to 3.4%, driving 12 complaints this quarter.

--- APPENDIX 1 — MARKETING/OPS ---
Operations Log and Market Research Summary — Q3 2025: The pleating line produced 11,500 units last quarter at a defect rate of 3.4%, up from 2.0% a year ago, driving 12 customer complaints. Average order fulfilment is 4.1 days. Market research of 210 plant managers found that 74% would pay up to 5% more for filters guaranteed to reach 99% filtration efficiency and 61% want same-day quotation turnaround. Under the new Quality Assurance plan, in-process checks will replace most Quality Control final inspection, with sampling covering 1 in 20 cartridges. Off-the-job courses at the local technical institute cost $600 per employee.

--- APPENDIX 2 — FINANCIAL DATA ---

  Q1(a) [8 marks]
    Question: CSF plans to finance its pleating-line expansion partly with hire purchase. Explain two advantages for CSF of using hire purchase instead of the overdraft facility.
    Answer: Point 1: Hire purchase spreads the $480,000 machinery cost over fixed instalments matched to the productive life of the new pleating and welding line, so CSF keeps more short-term cash available for wages and materials while the 12 current complaints are cleared. Fixed instalments are also easier to budget than an overdraft, whose interest rate can move with every base-rate rise and whose full balance can be demanded at any time.

Point 2: Under hire purchase the machinery secures itself — CSF gains use of a productive asset immediately with ownership passing on the final payment — whereas an overdraft is unsecured short-term debt best suited to working-capital gaps, not a $780,000 expansion. Using hire purchase for the line preserves the $300,000 overdraft as a flexible buffer for seasonal demand and unexpected repairs, rather than being fully absorbed by the purchase and leaving the partnership with no liquidity headroom. Fixed instalments also make month-by-month cash planning far more reliable for a two-partner business without a specialist finance team.
    Keywords: hire purchase, overdraft, $480,000, $300,000, $780,000, $312,000

    Question: CSF is launching its guaranteed 99% filtration efficiency cartridge range. Consider a stand at a national HVAC trade fair, a switch to online search advertising, or a direct mail and email campaign to plant managers. Which should CSF choose to promote the launch? Justify your recommendation.
    Answer: HVAC trade fair stand: A fair concentrates plant engineers, maintenance contractors and filter distributors in one venue, ideal for demonstrating guaranteed 99% efficiency cartridges and booking on-site trials. The drawbacks are heavy stand, travel and logistics costs before the new line has even proved itself, a short two-day window of impact, and the risk that major national accounts attend only selectively.

Online search advertising: Pay-per-click ads capture plant managers actively searching for replacement filters and same-day quotes — exactly the 61% who want same-day quotation turnaround — with granular budgets, measurable cost per enquiry and instant coverage across Brazil. Its limits are wastage on irrelevant searches, the need for continuous budget because visibility stops when spend stops, and difficulty conveying the tactile quality of a cartridge without strong landing pages and proof downloads.

Direct mail and email campaign: A targeted mailing to the 210 plant managers CSF researched, supported by technical datasheets, can communicate efficiency data and the 5% premium story with a personalised same-day quotation reply path. It is inexpensive and trackable via reply codes, but response rates are typically low, purchased lists may be stale, and reaching brand-new buyers beyond the known list is impossible without reinforcement.

Recommendation: CSF should choose online search advertising. It captures the 61% wanting same-day turnaround at the exact moment of need, fits a small flat partnership's budget better than a trade fair, and scales nationally without the waste of a mailing to cold names. The trade fair is rejected as high fixed cost before capacity is proven; direct mail is rejected as too low-yield for a launch and too dependent on the researched 210 contacts; online advertising should be paired with a short follow-up call sheet so enquiries convert into on-site trials with the new 99% efficiency guarantee.

--- MAIN STEM ---
Thorncombe Belting (THB) is a cooperative in the conveyor belting sector, manufacturing steel-cord conveyor belts and power transmission belts for mining and agriculture, employing a workforce of 52. Quality and Waste Report — Q3 2025: The calendering line produced 9,250 belts last quarter at a waste rate of 5.6%, up from 3.9% a year ago. Customer complaints rose from 7 to 15 per month.   Q1(a) [8 marks]
    Question: THB plans to finance part of its calendering-line expansion with a share issue to members. Explain two advantages for THB of using a member share issue instead of relying entirely on the bank loan.

Member capital also strengthens the cooperative's balance sheet at a time when input costs for natural rubber and steel cord are rising 14.6%, giving THB more room to negotiate without breaching loan covenants.

Point 2: Shares issued to members bind the workforce to the cooperative's long-term success — members who hold equity are more likely to stay, train and invest effort, which directly supports closing the calendering skills gap.     Keywords: share issue, bank loan, $320,000, $600,000, $920,000, $405,000

  Q1(b) [12 marks]
    Question: THB is launching its locally reinforced steel-cord belt range. Consider sponsoring the national mining summit, advertising in a mining trade magazine, or producing case-study videos for social media. Which should THB choose to promote the launch? Justify your recommendation.

    Question: THB's coordination is straining as the calendering line prepares to start. Consider keeping its flat democratic structure or appointing a full-time operations manager with authority over shifts. Which should THB choose? Justify your decision.

  Q4(b) [12 marks]
    Question: Using Appendix 3, evaluate how the interest rate rise to 6.75%, the 6.5% minimum wage increase and the 14.6% rise in input costs will affect THB. Which change will have the greatest impact? Justify your answer.
    Answer: Interest rate rise (6.00% to 6.75%): If THB's $600,000 ten-year bank loan is variable, the 0.75 percentage point rise adds 0.75% × $600,000 = $4,500 a year (0.0075 × $600,000) to interest costs — meaningful but modest against fixed costs of $405,000 a year, and zero if the cooperative fixed its rate at signing. The bigger exposure is psychological: higher rates chill mining-customer capital spending and make any second calender or a future member loan costlier, so THB should confirm its loan rate before board sign-off and avoid drawing the overdraft version of this risk wherever possible.

Minimum wage increase (6.5%, to $11.72 per hour from April 2026): With 52 members mostly on hourly shop-floor rates, the rise is unavoidable. The insert gives no hours or pay split, so no defensible annual total can be invented; the honest benchmark is productivity: 36,000 units ÷ 52 staff ≈ 692 units per member a year. If the retrained calendering crew lifts that figure, the cooperative absorbs the rise through output; if not, unit labour cost climbs and the $18.00 contribution per unit shrinks, directly pressuring the $600,000 loan service that the expansion depends on.

Input cost inflation (14.6% natural rubber and steel cord): THB's $27.00 variable cost is dominated by these inputs, but the insert never decomposes it, so only an illustrative bound is defensible: if the whole variable cost rose 14.6% it would add 14.6% × $27.00 = $3.94 per unit (0.146 × $27.00 = $3.942); at 36,000 units a year that is about $141,912 (0.146 × $27.00 × 36,000). Even a milder illustrative $2.00 per unit would strip roughly $72,000 a year. Mining demand grew 4.2%, which helps volume, but rubber inflation compounds on every belt produced and is not removable by members' effort or solar panels.

Conclusion: The 14.6% rise in input costs will have the greatest impact. It multiplies across all 36,000 units, compresses the $18.00 contribution per unit, cannot be negotiated away by one year's belt contract, and directly pressures the $600,000 bank loan service and the 10-year wear-warranty pricing that justifies the line. The minimum wage rise is second, absorbable through productivity gains from the 17 retrained technicians; the interest rate rise is smallest at about $4,500 a year on a variable $600,000 loan. THB should lock rubber supply contracts for 2027, enforce the 5% premium on warranty belts, and use mining growth of 4.2% to dilute unit overheads before raising member distributions.
    Keywords: 6.75%, 6.5%, 14.6%, $11.72, interest rate, $27.00
    Mark scheme: level_1_1_to_4: Identifies the external factors with limited application to THB. | level_2_5_to_8: Analyses the impact of at least two external changes on THB's costs, revenue or financing in context. | level_3_9_to_12: Detailed evaluation of all three external changes in the context of THB with a well-justified judgment that input-cost inflation has the greatest impact and why the other two are smaller.

--- MAIN STEM ---
Dunmore Plastics (DMP) is a private limited company in the agricultural plastics sector, extruding uPVC irrigation pipes and fittings for farm suppliers, employing a workforce of 81. Founded in 2010 by Daniel Soriano, the business operates a flat structure with laissez-faire leadership and is based in Cebu, the Philippines. DMP plans to invest $1,350,000 in a second uPVC extrusion line with in-line wall-thickness testing, financed by a $800,000 bank loan and $550,000 from the sale of its old delivery fleet. It has fixed costs of $315,000 a year, a variable cost of $8.10 a unit and a selling price of $12.60, and currently produces 110,000 units a year. DMP faces a serious quality problem: customer complaints about inconsistent pipe wall thickness rose for two consecutive quarters.

--- APPENDIX 1 — MARKETING/OPS ---
Operations and Market Research Summary — Q3 2025: The extrusion line produced 27,000 units last quarter at a defect rate of 2.8%, down from 4.2% a year ago. Customer complaints about pipe wall thickness fell from 19 to 10 per month. Average order fulfilment is 2.6 days. DMP is trialling 30% recycled uPVC regrind in non-pressure pipe grades, with early trials showing 15% lower resin cost per metre. A market research survey of 280 farm supply managers found that 69% would switch suppliers for certified wall-thickness consistency and 45% would accept a 4% price premium for UV-stabilised uPVC pipe. Off-the-job courses at the local college cost $500 per employee.

--- APPENDIX 2 — FINANCIAL DATA ---
Title: Extract from the Statement of Financial Position of Dunmore Plastics as at 31 March 2025 ($ '000)
Headers: ['Financial Metric', '2024', '2025']
Inventories | 180 | 190
Trade receivables | 235 | 255
Cash and cash equivalents | 65 | 75
Current liabilities | 320 | 325
Non-current assets | 2,050 | 2,600
Capital employed | 2,500 | 2,850

--- APPENDIX 3 — EXTERNAL ENVIRONMENT ---
Economic and Business Bulletin (November 2026): (1) The central bank has raised the base interest rate from 4.75% to 5.50%, the fourth rise this year, increasing repayment costs on variable-rate business loans. (2) The national minimum wage will rise by 6.4% from $10.90 to $11.60 per hour from April 2026, raising wage bills across manufacturing. (3) uPVC resin and stabiliser input costs have risen 11.2% year-on-year, industrial inflation is running at 7.1%, and agricultural output grew 3.1% in the same period.

The fleet had reached the end of its economic life, so the sale releases trapped value at little operational cost while the new line is commissioned.

  Q2(b) [12 marks]
    Question: DMP must fix rising wall-thickness complaints on the extrusion line. Consider installing the in-line CAM wall-thickness scanner operated by existing staff or hiring two full-time quality inspectors. Which should DMP choose? Justify your decision.

Decision: DMP should install the in-line CAM wall-thickness scanner and train existing operators to run it, backed by one senior inspector for periodic audits rather than two. Two full-time inspectors are rejected as a slower, costlier, sampling-based patch that finds rather than prevents wall-thickness drift; the single senior auditor keeps human judgement in the system while the scanner does the continuous measuring.

Conclusion: The 11.2% rise in input costs will have the greatest impact. It multiplies across all 110,000 units, compresses the $4.50 contribution from both ends, and cannot be fixed by refinancing — only by pricing, renegotiation and the regrind programme. The minimum wage rise is second, absorbable if the new line raises productivity beyond roughly 1,358 units per worker; the interest rate rise is third at about $6,000 a year on a variable $800,000 loan. DMP should lock resin and stabiliser contracts through 2027, hold the 4% premium fiercely, and use agricultural output growth of 3.1% to win certified-pipe share before inflation compounds further.
    Keywords: 5.50%, 6.4%, 11.2%, $11.60, interest rate, $8.10
    Mark scheme: level_1_1_to_4: Identifies the external factors with limited application to DMP. | level_2_5_to_8: Analyses the impact of at least two external changes on DMP's costs, revenue or financing in context. | level_3_9_to_12: Detailed evaluation of all three external changes in the context of DMP with a well-justified judgment that input-cost inflation has the greatest impact and why the other two are smaller.

--- MAIN STEM ---
Hallam & Grey Electrical (HGE) is a private limited company in the consumer electronics and home appliance retail sector, employing a workforce of 132 across nine superstores in the Norwick region and an online shop. Founded in 2009 by Nadia Rahman, the business operates a hierarchical organisational structure with democratic leadership. HGE plans to invest $980,000 in a next-day home-delivery fulfilment centre with an in-house repair workshop, financed by a $600,000 ten-year bank loan and $380,000 retained profit. It has fixed costs of $500,000 a year, a variable cost of $30 a unit and a selling price of $55, and currently produces 32,000 units a year. HGE faces a growing operational problem: labour turnover among shop-floor sales staff has climbed sharply, and customer complaints about late deliveries are increasing.

--- APPENDIX 1 — MARKETING/OPS ---
Market Research Summary (October 2026): A survey of 800 customers across the nine superstores found that 58% would switch to HGE for a price-match guarantee, 71% check online reviews before buying appliances, and 46% said free next-day delivery would decide where they buy. The online shop processed 9,600 orders last quarter with a return rate of 3.1%. In-store repair counters completed 640 jobs with a 6.2% rework rate. Average delivery time is 2.4 days. Monthly customer complaints fell from 52 to 34 after the staff service scheme began. Of the 132 employees, 38 work as shop-floor sales staff; off-the-job training at the Norwick regional college costs $1,100 per employee, while on-the-job training is delivered in the superstores.

--- APPENDIX 2 — FINANCIAL DATA ---
Title: Extract from the Statement of Financial Position of Hallam & Grey Electrical as at 31 March 2025 ($ '000)
Headers: ['Financial Metric', '2024', '2025']

Trade receivables | 265 | 310
Cash and cash equivalents | 150 | 210
Current liabilities | 620 | 650
Non-current assets | 2,150 | 2,650
Capital employed | 3,300 | 3,550

--- APPENDIX 3 — EXTERNAL ENVIRONMENT ---
Economic and Business Bulletin (November 2026): (1) The central bank has raised the base interest rate from 4.25% to 5.0%, the third rise this year, increasing repayments for retailers with variable-rate loans. (2) The national minimum wage will rise by 7.1% from $11.80 to $12.64 per hour from April 2026, raising wage bills for hourly-paid retail staff. (3) Consumer electronics prices fell 3.6% year-on-year as global supply eased, inflation is running at 3.4%, and household spending on electrical goods grew 2.2% in the same period.

  Q1(a) [8 marks]
    Question: HGE plans to finance its $980,000 home-delivery fulfilment centre with a $600,000 bank loan and $380,000 retained profit. Explain two advantages for HGE of using retained profit rather than borrowing the full amount.
    Answer: Point 1: Using $380,000 of its own retained profit costs HGE nothing in repayments or interest, which eases cash flow while it already carries fixed costs of $500,000 a year and is about to service a $600,000 ten-year loan. The retained-profit route also protects HGE from interest-rate risk: the central bank has just raised the base rate to 5.0%, so each further 0.25% rise would add $1,500 a year to a variable-rate $600,000 loan (0.0025 x $600,000), and retained profit avoids that exposure entirely for this portion of the funding.

Point 2: Retained profit keeps decision-making with Nadia Rahman and HGE's directors, with no lender covenants dictating how the fulfilment centre, delivery schedule or pricing are run. It also signals financial strength to suppliers, helping HGE negotiate better terms as it scales the nine superstores plus the online shop, which processed 9,600 orders last quarter, into next-day fulfilment. Using internal funds also avoids security being pledged against the new $980,000 centre, keeping the expansion fully under HGE's control while labour turnover among shop-floor staff is being fixed.

  Q1(b) [12 marks]
    Question: HGE is launching its next-day home-delivery service. Consider a national television advertising campaign, a regional newspaper advertising campaign, or social media advertising. Which should HGE choose to promote the launch? Justify your recommendation.
    Answer: National television campaign: A national TV campaign would give the launch huge reach very quickly and could put HGE's next-day delivery promise in front of millions of viewers across the country. However, production and airtime costs for national slots are extremely high for a nine-superstore regional retailer, and a large share of the audience would live far beyond the Norwick region HGE actually serves. With complaints about late deliveries still fresh and labour turnover climbing, tying up capital in wasteful national coverage is hard to justify when the expansion already absorbs $980,000.

Regional newspaper campaign: Local and regional newspapers are far cheaper than national television and reach the Norwick catchment where HGE's nine superstores and online customers are concentrated. Newspaper advertising suits price-led, time-bound messages such as launch offers. Its weaknesses are a shrinking and older readership, limited space for visual demonstrations of the new fulfilment promise, and poor measurability compared with digital channels, given that 71% of HGE customers check online reviews before buying.

Social media advertising: Social campaigns let HGE target its exact 46% of surveyed shoppers who said free next-day delivery would decide where they buy, plus the 71% who research online. Spend is measurable click by click, creative can be adjusted quickly, and it keeps the cost far below television. Reach among younger appliance buyers is strong, though it demands consistent content production and some spend on paid promotion to stand out.

Recommendation: HGE should choose social media advertising. It is the cheapest of the three per relevant customer reached, it is measurable, and it targets precisely the online-review-checking segment identified in HGE's own research, reinforcing the 9,600-order online channel. National television is rejected as unaffordable and untargeted for a regional nine-superstore chain funding an $980,000 expansion from retained profit and a $600,000 loan; the regional newspaper is rejected as too narrow in reach and weak for younger buyers. Social media should be supported by in-store posters, but it should carry the launch.

    Question: HGE must retrain staff for the new fulfilment centre and in-house repair workshop. Consider on-the-job training in the superstores or off-the-job training at the Norwick regional college. Which should HGE choose? Justify your decision.

Decision: HGE should choose on-the-job training as the core route, reserving college places for a small number of lead technicians. It is cheaper, immediate, specific to the repair workshop's equipment, and avoids removing sales staff from the floor during a launch already straining service levels. Full off-the-job training for all 38 staff is rejected because $41,800 plus lost floor cover would strain the $500,000 fixed-cost base, and generic courses would still need in-store reinforcement; a blended approach captures the certificate benefit without the full cost.

    Question: Using Appendix 2, evaluate HGE's financial position by calculating the current ratio and the acid test ratio for 2024 and 2025. Has HGE's financial position improved? Justify your answer.
    Answer: Calculations:
Current Ratio 2024 = 1.44 : 1
Current Ratio 2025 = 1.60 : 1
Acid Test Ratio 2024 = 0.67 : 1
Acid Test Ratio 2025 = 0.80 : 1

Detailed workings: 2024 current assets = $480,000 inventories + $265,000 trade receivables + $150,000 cash = $895,000; 2025 current assets = $520,000 + $310,000 + $210,000 = $1,040,000. Ratio 2024 = $895,000 / $620,000 = 1.44; 2025 = $1,040,000 / $650,000 = 1.60. Excluding inventories: 2024 = ($895,000 - $480,000) / $620,000 = $415,000 / $620,000 = 0.67; 2025 = ($1,040,000 - $520,000) / $650,000 = $520,000 / $650,000 = 0.80.

Evaluation: Liquidity has strengthened. The coverage of current assets over current liabilities improved from 1.44 to 1.60, and the quick measure that excludes inventories improved from 0.67 to 0.80, helped by cash rising from $150,000 to $210,000 and current liabilities growing only from $620,000 to $650,000 while assets grew faster. Conclusion: HGE's financial position has improved. Both the current ratio (1.44 to 1.60) and the acid test ratio (0.67 to 0.80) show stronger short-term solvency, and the improvement is not an illusion created by warehouse stock. HGE should still tighten trade-customer credit control and monitor delivery performance before committing further capital, but the trend supports the $980,000 expansion.

  Q4(b) [12 marks]
    Question: Using Appendix 3, evaluate how the interest rate rise to 5.0%, the 7.1% minimum wage increase and the 3.6% fall in electronics prices will affect HGE. Which change will have the greatest impact? Justify your answer.
    Answer: Interest rate rise (4.25% to 5.0%): If HGE's $600,000 ten-year bank loan is variable-rate, the full 0.75% rise adds 0.0075 x $600,000 = $4,500 a year to repayments; on top of that, each 0.25% step is $1,500 a year. That is under 1% of HGE's $500,000 fixed-cost base and is manageable, though it raises the hurdle rate for any further borrowing for the $980,000 fulfilment centre. If the loan was fixed at the outset, the cash impact today is zero, but higher rates may also make consumers more cautious about big-ticket appliance purchases and would raise the cost of any future variable-rate borrowing.

Minimum wage increase (7.1%, to $12.64 per hour): HGE has a workforce of 132 and 38 shop-floor sales staff are hourly-paid, so this rise is unavoidable and applies to every hour they work. The insert gives no wage rates or hours, so no defensible annual total can be invented; the correct lens is productivity, 32,000 units / 132 employees = 242.4 units per employee. The wage rise is affordable only if this productivity holds or output grows; otherwise unit labour cost rises and the $30 variable cost per unit effectively increases, squeezing HGE's contribution per unit.

Fall in electronics prices (3.6% year-on-year): Lower prices reduce what HGE pays for stock, easing pressure on the $30 variable cost and margins. The same deflation, however, drags on the $55 selling price, so headline revenue per unit may fall even if volume grows; 2.2% growth in household spending on electrical goods against 3.4% inflation may mask weak real demand, and HGE cannot count on price increases to recover wage or delivery costs.

Conclusion: The minimum wage increase will have the greatest impact. It is certain, recurring and touches all 38 hourly-paid shop-floor staff directly, whereas the interest rise is at most $4,500 a year and could be zero if the loan is fixed, and falling electronics prices cut HGE's input costs as well as its selling prices, so they are partly self-offsetting. HGE should protect its contribution by lifting productivity through the rework fix rather than raising prices into a deflating market.
    Keywords: 5.0%, 7.1%, 3.6%, $12.64, $11.80, 2.2%
    Mark scheme: level_1_1_to_4: Identifies the external factors with limited application to HGE. | level_2_5_to_8: Analyses the impact of at least two external changes on HGE's costs, revenue or financing in context. | level_3_9_to_12: Detailed evaluation of all three external changes in the context of HGE with a well-justified judgement that the minimum wage increase has the greatest impact and why the other two are smaller.

--- MAIN STEM ---
Wren & Quill Booksellers (WQB) is a partnership in the independent book retail sector, employing a workforce of 34 across three bookshops in Elmsworth and an online store. It has fixed costs of $187,500 a year, a variable cost of $9 a unit and a selling price of $15, and currently produces 42,000 units a year. WQB faces a growing operational problem: warehouse absenteeism has reached 8%, delaying online orders and raising overtime costs.

Operations Log — Quarter 3 2026: The Elmsworth online hub dispatched 11,300 orders with a picking accuracy of 97.4%; 2.9% of parcels were reported damaged or incorrect. A survey of 450 loyalty members found 63% discover new titles through social media, 38% would pay $8 a month for a reading club, and average online basket value is $34. Average delivery time is 1.9 days. Off-the-job training at the Elmsworth logistics college costs $720 per employee, while on-the-job training is led by senior pickers.

Acid Test Ratio 2024 = 0.69 : 1
Acid Test Ratio 2025 = 0.89 : 1

Detailed workings: 2024 current assets = $150,000 inventories + $40,000 trade receivables + $85,000 cash = $275,000; 2025 current assets = $165,000 + $52,000 + $135,000 = $352,000. Ratio 2024 = $275,000 / $180,000 = 1.53; 2025 = $352,000 / $210,000 = 1.68. Excluding inventories: 2024 = ($275,000 - $150,000) / $180,000 = $125,000 / $180,000 = 0.69; 2025 = ($352,000 - $165,000) / $210,000 = $187,000 / $210,000 = 0.89.

Evaluation: Liquidity has strengthened. The coverage of current assets over current liabilities improved from 1.53 to 1.68, and the quick measure excluding inventories improved from 0.69 to 0.89, helped by cash and equivalents rising from $85,000 to $135,000 while current liabilities grew from $180,000 to $210,000. Trade receivables rose only from $40,000 to $52,000, which is safe for an online-and-shops retailer whose sales are mostly paid by card at the till or online before dispatch. Inventories edged up from $150,000 to $165,000 ahead of the $425,000 flagship opening and the click-and-collect hub, so the stock build should unwind as footfall arrives.

Conclusion: WQB's financial position has improved. Both the current ratio (1.53 to 1.68) and the acid test ratio (0.69 to 0.89) show stronger short-term solvency, and cash, rather than inventories, is driving the improvement. WQB should still watch the 2.9% damaged-or-incorrect rate and cafe food waste of 5.6% to keep cash conversion strong, but the trend comfortably supports the $425,000 second flagship.
    Keywords: 1.53, 1.68, 0.69, 0.89, $275,000, $352,000, $425,000
    Mark scheme: level_1_1_to_4: States financial figures or changes without accurate ratio calculations. | level_2_5_to_8: Accurately calculates the current ratio and acid test ratio for both 2024 and 2025 with contextual analysis of the trend. | level_3_9_to_12: Accurate ratio calculations for both years combined with detailed evaluation of inventories, receivables, cash and liabilities movements and a justified conclusion on whether WQB's financial position improved.

  Q4(a) [8 marks]
    Question: Explain one advantage and one disadvantage for WQB of installing a click-and-collect hub in the new flagship shop.
    Answer: Advantage: Click-and-collect converts the 450 loyalty members and online browsers who already buy an average basket of $34 into footfall for the new flagship, where the 63% who discover titles through social media can then browse the reading cafe, attend events and pick up reserved orders without paying delivery. It cuts last-mile delivery cost versus home drop-off, turns collections into impulse purchases, and strengthens WQB's local positioning against pure-play online rivals, supporting the whole $425,000 expansion case and the 1.9-day delivery promise that keeps members loyal to an independent shop.

Disadvantage: The hub adds shelving, staffing and handling costs on top of the cafe's 5.6% food waste problem and 1.6% stock shrinkage, and if parcels are not ready on time it damages the very 1.9-day promise that differentiates WQB online; that failure mode already sits behind the 2.9% damaged-or-incorrect rate. Poor stock control would also tie up cash in unsold, slow-moving titles on top of the $165,000 inventory balance, so WQB must pair click-and-collect with tight picking routines and clear collection logging before launch, or the new revenue channel could erode the $6 contribution per unit it is meant to protect.

  Q4(b) [12 marks]
    Question: Using Appendix 3, evaluate how the interest rate rise to 5.25%, the 6.2% minimum wage increase and the 9.8% rise in paper and printing costs will affect WQB. Which change will have the greatest impact? Justify your answer.
    Answer: Interest rate rise (4.5% to 5.25%): If WQB's $270,000 expansion loan is variable-rate, the additional annual cost is 0.75% x $270,000 = $2,025 a year (0.0075 x $270,000). That is modest against $187,500 of fixed costs and could be avoided entirely by fixing the rate; the bigger effect is psychological, raising the hurdle for any further borrowing beyond the flagship and squeezing consumer confidence on discretionary purchases such as hardback novels and the $8 reading club.

Minimum wage increase (6.2%, to $12.90 per hour): WQB's warehouse, cafe and shop teams include hourly-paid workers, so the rise flows straight into payroll and is unavoidable. No hours or pay rates are stated in the insert, so a firm total cannot be invented; judged against productivity, 42,000 units / 34 employees = 1,235.3 units per employee, the wage cost per unit stays manageable only if the 97.4% picking accuracy holds and absenteeism falls below 8%. Any slip raises unit labour cost and squeezes the $6 contribution per unit.

Paper and printing cost rise (9.8% year-on-year): Publisher input inflation is the change that scales across everything WQB sells. As an explicit upper bound built from insert figures, if the whole $9 variable cost reflected publisher paper inflation it would add 9.8% x $9 = $0.88 per unit; at 42,000 units a year that is about $37,000 a year (42,000 x $0.88 = $36,960), cutting contribution from $6 toward $5.12. Cover prices rarely move by 9.8%, so margins will likely absorb part of it; 3.9% inflation and 4.1% growth in book and leisure spending help demand, but WQB cannot fully recover the gap without pricing itself off competitors.

Conclusion: The 9.8% rise in paper and printing costs will have the greatest impact. It applies across every one of the 42,000 units sold, unlike the fixed $2,025 annual interest effect or the bounded wage rise, which depends on hours not stated; and unlike the wage rise, it directly attacks the $6 contribution that funds the flagship and reading cafe. WQB should widen its mix toward higher-margin sidelines such as the $8 reading club and gift lines to offset it.
    Keywords: 5.25%, 6.2%, 9.8%, $12.90, $12.15, 4.1%

--- MAIN STEM ---
Kettlewell Furniture (KWF) is a cooperative in the flat-pack and upholstered furniture retail sector, employing a workforce of 58 across its Brandleford workshop, showroom and delivery team. KWF faces a growing operational problem: material waste in the cutting workshop has risen to 9.4% and damaged-stock write-offs are increasing.

Showroom complaints about damaged deliveries fell from 27 to 15 per month. The assembly defect rate is 4.7%. A survey of 520 co-op members found 66% prefer locally made furniture and 41% would pay 8% more for it. Average delivery time is 6 days. Off-the-job training at the Brandleford college costs $850 per employee, while on-the-job training is supervised by workshop mentors.

KWF's control of its own cash becomes more precious now that the central bank has lifted the base rate to 5.0%: a variable-rate $400,000 loan already costs $2,000 a year for each 0.5% rise (0.005 x $400,000), so the 1.0% rise this year adds $4,000 a year, and borrowing any more would deepen that burden.

Point 2: Internal funding keeps the cooperative's member ownership undiluted and avoids lender covenants that could restrict showroom merchandising, pricing or member benefits. It also preserves KWF's standing with its 520 surveyed members, 66% of whom prefer locally made furniture: demonstrating that the $640,000 expansion is funded without overstretching debt reassures members, supports the membership drive behind the showroom, and protects the $34 price point while furniture spending grows only 1.3% and input costs inflate 14.6%.

For a single Brandleford showroom whose delivery range covers only the surrounding region, however, the wastage of national airtime is enormous, and the production and slot costs would dwarf KWF's $240,000 retained-profit contribution to the $640,000 budget at a time when input costs are rising 14.6%.

It is measurable, interactive and cheap, drives showroom footfall and click-and-collect pre-orders, and suits a flat-organisation founder brand like Margaret Ellison's; it does require consistent creative effort and at least a modest paid boost around launch week.

Recommendation: KWF should choose social media marketing. It aligns with KWF's member research, costs far less than television, reaches beyond radio's listener base with story-led owned media, and is measurable against showroom footfall and the 30,000-unit production plan. --- MAIN STEM ---
Foxglove Pet Supplies (FPS) is a private limited company in the online pet food and supplies retail sector, employing a workforce of 45. Founded in 2019 by Priya Nandakumar in Dunmarrow, the business sells pet food, toys and accessories online with two stores and operates a flat organisational structure with laissez-faire leadership. It has fixed costs of $96,000 a year, a variable cost of $14 a unit and a selling price of $20, and currently produces 24,500 units a year. --- APPENDIX 1 — MARKETING/OPS ---
Operations Log — September 2026: The subscription fulfilment kitchen packed 14,200 orders last quarter; 4.4% of shipments were short or incorrect, down from 6.8% a year ago. Customer complaints fell from 61 to 40 per month. Off-the-job training at the Dunmarrow logistics college costs $650 per employee, while on-the-job coaching is led by shift supervisors.

--- APPENDIX 2 — FINANCIAL DATA ---

(2) The national minimum wage will rise by 6.9% from $11.60 to $12.40 per hour from April 2026, raising wage bills for hourly-paid packing and delivery staff. (3) Pet food ingredient costs (poultry and cereals) rose 11.5% year-on-year, inflation is running at 3.8%, and online pet product spending grew 6.4% in the same period.

--- QUESTIONS ---
  Q1(a) [8 marks]
    Question: FPS plans to finance its $535,000 expansion partly with hire purchase. Explain two advantages for FPS of using hire purchase for the packing line rather than a bank loan.
    Answer: Point 1: Hire purchase spreads the $310,000 cost of the packing line across its working life, matching payments to the revenue the line will generate from the 14,200 orders it helps pack each quarter. FPS keeps its cash buffer intact, vital when 4.4% of shipments are still short or incorrect and complaints, though down from 61 to 40 per month, keep arriving; the $225,000 of retained profit can then stay available to stabilise operations rather than being swallowed by one asset purchase.

Point 2: Hire purchase agreements usually secure onto the equipment itself, so it can be simpler to arrange than a further bank loan when the base rate sits at 5.25%. Interest is fixed in the agreement, giving FPS certainty for budgeting the automated kitchen and second store, no surprises if rates rise again, and full ownership of the line at the end of the term, after which maintenance and staffing savings can be redirected into the subscription growth its members support, 57% of whom want a wider grain-free range and 49% of whom would bundle toys with food deliveries.
    Keywords: hire purchase, $310,000, $535,000, $225,000, 5.25%, 14,200

  Q1(b) [12 marks]
    Question: FPS is launching its subscription bundle. Consider paid social media advertising, influencer marketing with pet creators, or local radio sponsorship. Which should FPS choose to promote the subscription? Justify your recommendation.

It is measurable and fast to set up, but feeds are competitive, creative must be refreshed constantly, and subscription intent is hard to read from a cold ad alone.

Influencer marketing with pet creators: Partnering with pet creators reaches exactly the 57% of subscribers wanting a wider grain-free range and the 49% interested in toy bundles, with trusted, authentic content; unboxing videos of the fulfilment kitchen convert strongly in pet communities, and creators can demonstrate the actual box contents and next-day feel. Local radio sponsorship: Radio is cheap and local to Dunmarrow and reinforces brand familiarity for the two stores, and it can repeat a memorable subscription offer to commuters. But it cannot visualise the product, skews toward older listeners, and lacks a direct, trackable path to online subscription sign-up, which is FPS's growth engine and where 92% next-day coverage already applies.

Recommendation: FPS should choose influencer marketing with pet creators. It matches the research, fits the pet-community channel where subscription decisions are made, and scales cost with results rather than fixed airtime. Paid social is rejected as a follower rather than a leader; boosting creator posts should come second. Local radio is rejected as untargeted and unable to demonstrate the subscription offer or produce a measurable sign-up, so it cannot lead a digital-first launch.

    Mark scheme: level_1_1_to_4: Limited knowledge or outline of the promotional options with minimal application to FPS. | level_2_5_to_8: Detailed discussion of the advantages and disadvantages of at least two options in the context of FPS with some judgement. | level_3_9_to_12: Detailed discussion of all three options in the context of FPS with a well-justified recommendation explaining why paid social alone and radio are rejected.

  Q2(a) [8 marks]
    Question: FPS packing staff turnover has reached 18%. Explain two advantages for FPS of its laissez-faire leadership style for the packing team.
    Answer: Point 1: Laissez-faire leadership gives experienced packers the autonomy to organise their own pick-pack-seal routines around the 4.4% error problem, tapping operator knowledge rather than handed-down redesign. Skilled staff experimenting privately often build the fastest workflows, lifting both speed and accuracy without capital spend, and the calm, trusting environment suits a small 45-person team that cross-covers two stores and the fulfilment kitchen.

Point 2: Trust and autonomy raise morale and reduce friction for a group with 18% staff turnover, making FPS a more attractive employer than rigidly controlled warehouses. Autonomy also lets shift supervisors coach informally on the floor, which pairs naturally with the on-the-job route already in place, and it protects the 92% next-day coverage because motivated self-starters keep dispatch flowing during subscription peaks. The risk is drift into sloppy practice, so FPS must keep the short-or-incorrect shipment metric visible on the wall and step in decisively when standards slip, or the 4.4% error rate will creep back toward 6.8%.
    Keywords: laissez-faire leadership, staff turnover, 4.4%, workforce of 45, $46
    Mark scheme: knowledge_max_2: 1 mark for each valid advantage of laissez-faire leadership identified (max 2). | application_analysis_max_6: Up to 3 marks per point for detailed contextual development linked to FPS's turnover, error rate and packing environment.

  Q2(b) [12 marks]
    Question: FPS wants to cut short or incorrect shipments (4.4%) further. Consider on-the-job coaching by shift supervisors or off-the-job training at the Dunmarrow logistics college. Which should FPS choose? Justify your decision.
    Answer: On-the-job coaching: Supervisor-led coaching is embedded in the live pick-pack-seal flow, so the 4.4% error rate can be targeted at the exact failure points, wrong item, wrong quantity, missing treats or broken seals. It is immediate, specific to FPS's SOPs and equipment, and free in course fees, protecting the 92% next-day delivery promise across 14,200 orders a quarter. Weaknesses are that supervisors lose picking time and that quality and patience vary between coaches, so FPS should give them a simple checklist and short calibration sessions.

Off-the-job training: The college's $650 per employee course covers warehouse standards, scanning discipline and health-and-safety with certification, which would formalise FPS's processes and give a recognised credential for external recognition. Training all 45 employees would cost $29,250 (45 x $650) plus absence cover, a heavy sum at a moment when FPS is also absorbing hire-purchase repayments on $310,000 of equipment and cash fell from $55,000 to $40,000; cover for packers would be hard to find during the subscription peak. Content is generic and would still need adaptation to the Dunmarrow kitchen layout.

Decision: FPS should choose on-the-job coaching as the primary route, sending shift leads to the college to standardise their coaching. It is specific, immediate and fee-free, directly attacking the 4.4% error rate without stripping the packing line during peak subscription weeks. Full off-the-job training for the whole workforce is rejected because $29,250 plus cover costs strain cash precisely when liquidity has tightened, and generic modules would need customising to FPS's SOPs anyway; leads can then cascade the same checklist back to their crews.
    Keywords: on-the-job coaching, off-the-job training, $650, 4.4%, 92%, 14,200

    Question: Using Appendix 2, evaluate FPS's financial position by calculating the current ratio and the acid test ratio for 2024 and 2025. Has FPS's financial position improved? Justify your answer.
    Answer: Calculations:

Current Ratio 2025 = 1.13 : 1
Acid Test Ratio 2024 = 0.70 : 1
Acid Test Ratio 2025 = 0.59 : 1

Detailed workings: 2024 current assets = $120,000 inventories + $60,000 trade receivables + $55,000 cash = $235,000; 2025 current assets = $105,000 + $75,000 + $40,000 = $220,000. Ratio 2024 = $235,000 / $165,000 = 1.42; 2025 = $220,000 / $195,000 = 1.13. Both the current ratio (1.42 to 1.13) and the acid test ratio (0.70 to 0.59) show tighter short-term solvency, and even though the $535,000 expansion grew non-current assets from $720,000 to $980,000, it has been financed with debt and working-capital strain rather than matching internal cash generation.     Question: Explain one advantage and one disadvantage for FPS of promoting a grain-free subscription bundle to its subscribers.

Disadvantage: Grain-free ingredients cost more than standard poultry and cereal recipes, pushing up the $14 variable cost per unit and pressuring the already-thin contribution at precisely the moment ingredient costs are up 11.5% year-on-year. If the bundle fails quality checks or sells unevenly, the 4.4% short-or-incorrect rate worsens, margins are squeezed on every unit, and the stock risk rises; FPS may also find the 57% who want grain-free products are price-sensitive, so aggressive subscription discounting to win them could destroy the $46 basket economics before the second store even opens.

    Question: Using Appendix 3, evaluate how the interest rate rise to 5.25%, the 6.9% minimum wage increase and the 11.5% rise in pet food ingredient costs will affect FPS. Which change will have the greatest impact? Justify your answer.
    Answer: Interest rate rise (4.5% to 5.25%): If FPS's $310,000 hire purchase is variable-rate, each 0.25% adds 0.0025 x $310,000 = $775 a year, so the full 0.75% rise adds about $2,325 a year (0.0075 x $310,000). That is manageable in isolation, but combined with repayments it tightens a cash position that has already fallen to $40,000 in the 2025 extract and pushes up the cost of any future overdraft or second-store borrowing; fixing the rate or negotiating hire-purchase terms now is prudent.

Minimum wage increase (6.9%, to $12.40 per hour): FPS's packing and delivery teams include hourly-paid staff, so the rise is compulsory and recurring. No hours or pay rates are stated in the insert, so no defensible annual total can be invented; at productivity of 24,500 units / 45 employees = 544.4 units per employee, the cost is absorbable only if the 4.4% error rate keeps falling and throughput rises, otherwise unit labour cost rises and the $14 variable cost effectively increases, squeezing contribution per unit.

Ingredient cost inflation (11.5% poultry and cereals): As an explicit upper bound, if the full $14 variable cost rose with ingredient inflation it would add $1.61 per unit (0.115 x $14); across 24,500 units that is about $39,445 a year (24,500 x $1.61 = $39,445). Even partial pass-through erodes the $6 contribution toward roughly $4.39, and pet-owner price sensitivity limits how far subscriptions can be repriced, though 6.4% growth in online pet spending and the 57% grain-free demand give room on premium lines.

Conclusion: The 11.5% rise in pet food ingredient costs will have the greatest impact. It applies to every one of the 24,500 units sold, unlike the capped $2,325 annual interest effect or the productivity-contingent wage rise. FPS should re-price the grain-free premium range, lock in annual supplier contracts, keep the $225,000 retained-profit buffer intact, and monitor liquidity before committing to any further expansion.
    Keywords: 5.25%, 6.9%, 11.5%, $12.40, $11.60, 6.4%
    Mark scheme: level_1_1_to_4: Identifies the external factors with limited application to FPS. | level_2_5_to_8: Analyses the impact of at least two external changes on FPS's costs, revenue or financing in context. | level_3_9_to_12: Detailed evaluation of all three external changes in the context of FPS with a well-justified judgement that ingredient-cost inflation has the greatest impact and why the other two are smaller.
