--- MAIN STEM ---
Auric & Sons Jewellers (ASJ) is a partnership in the high-street jewellery retail sector, employing a workforce of 26. Founded in 1987 by Yusuf and Leila Auric in Saltmere, and now managed by their son Darius, the firm operates a hierarchical organisational structure with autocratic leadership. ASJ plans to invest $700,000 in a bridal suite and certified watch workshop inside its Saltmere flagship, financed by a $450,000 ten-year bank loan and $250,000 retained profit. It has fixed costs of $275,000 a year, a variable cost of $180 a unit and a selling price of $230, and currently produces 11,000 units a year. ASJ faces a growing operational problem: a shortage of qualified watchmakers and goldsmiths, so the repair queue is lengthening.

--- APPENDIX 1 — MARKETING/OPS ---
Market Research Summary (October 2026): In a survey of 500 loyal clients, 72% said they would consider ASJ for engagement or wedding jewellery, 54% asked about certified watch servicing, and 33% follow ASJ on social media. Website enquiries rose 44% after the spring campaign, with 61% of visitors on mobile. The valuation counter issued 210 written valuations last year averaging $1,850. Repair turnaround averages 12 days; sizing-error complaints fell from 18 to 9 per month. Off-the-job watchmaker training at the Saltmere college costs $950 per employee, while on-the-job shadowing pairs apprentices with master jewellers.

--- APPENDIX 2 — FINANCIAL DATA ---
Title: Extract from the Statement of Financial Position of Auric & Sons Jewellers as at 31 March 2025 ($ '000)

Current liabilities | 520 | 640
Non-current assets | 2,600 | 2,900
Capital employed | 3,400 | 3,600

--- APPENDIX 3 — EXTERNAL ENVIRONMENT ---
Economic and Business Bulletin (November 2026): (1) The central bank has raised the base interest rate from 4.25% to 5.0%, raising the cost of variable-rate borrowing for long-term investments. (2) The national minimum wage will rise by 7.5% from $12.00 to $12.90 per hour from April 2026. (3) The gold price rose 17.8% year-on-year and precious-metal input costs are up 15.2%, inflation is running at 3.6%, and consumer spending on luxury jewellery grew only 1.8% in the same period.

  Q1(a) [8 marks]
    Question: ASJ plans to fund its $700,000 flagship expansion with a $450,000 bank loan and $250,000 retained profit. Explain two advantages for ASJ of using retained profit rather than an overdraft.
    Answer: Point 1: Retained profit carries no interest charge at all, whereas an overdraft is typically variable-rate and repayable on demand, which is dangerous now the central bank has lifted the base rate to 5.0% and ASJ's $450,000 loan already commits it to ten years of repayments. Keeping the $250,000 portion internal protects the partnership's $275,000 fixed-cost base and leaves headroom if bridal demand disappoints or gold pushes the $180 variable cost higher still.

Point 2: Funding the bridal suite and certified watch workshop from retained profit keeps the expansion entirely under the Auric family's control, with no bank able to renegotiate facilities if luxury spending grows only 1.8% or if gold keeps climbing. For a partnership about to market certified watch servicing, which 54% of loyal clients already asked about, covenant-free funding reassures staff and clients that the workshop, apprentice pipeline and new bridal collection can be delivered on schedule, without the administrative burden and personal-asset exposure an overdraft would add to a family firm.
    Keywords: retained profit, bank loan, $250,000, $450,000, $700,000, 5.0%
    Mark scheme: knowledge_max_2: 1 mark for each valid advantage of retained profit identified (max 2). | application_analysis_max_6: Up to 3 marks per point for contextual explanation and analysis applied to Auric & Sons Jewellers and its flagship expansion.

  Q1(b) [12 marks]
    Question: ASJ is launching its bridal suite. Consider national television advertising, a print jewellery catalogue posted to loyal clients, or social media advertising. Which should ASJ choose to promote the launch? Justify your recommendation.
    Answer: National television advertising: TV would dramatise the bridal suite to a huge audience and could make ASJ a household name beyond Saltmere, building aspirational brand equity at speed. But a single-flagship jeweller making 11,000 units a year would be buying national reach it cannot fulfil from one store, and the production and airtime costs are unjustifiable against a $700,000 project funded partly from retained profit with gold prices rising 17.8% year-on-year.

Print jewellery catalogue for loyal clients: A posted catalogue targets clients with proven wealth, lists the $1,850-average valuation service beautifully, and suits older buyers who have bought wedding jewellery from the family for decades. However it costs print and postage per client, is slow to update once gold prices move, and younger engaged couples increasingly begin their search on Instagram and Google rather than reading posted catalogues.

Social media advertising: ASJ can target couples in Saltmere and nearby towns searching engagement content, showcase the suite and certified pieces visually, and retarget website visitors; 61% of its enquiry traffic is already on mobile after a campaign that lifted enquiries 44%, and 33% of loyal clients follow ASJ on social channels, so the seed audience already exists for lookalike targeting.

Recommendation: ASJ should choose social media advertising. It converts the 44% enquiry momentum and mobile-first traffic into booked suite appointments, reaches younger engaged couples at a fraction of TV's cost, and fits the existing 33% social following. Television is rejected as untargeted and unaffordable for a single Saltmere flagship; the print catalogue is rejected as the lead channel because it reaches only existing clients too slowly to build launch buzz, though a small mailer to the valuation list would complement the digital push rather than replace it.
    Keywords: 61%, 44%, 33%, $1,850, 500, $700,000
    Mark scheme: level_1_1_to_4: Limited knowledge or outline of the promotional options with minimal application to ASJ. | level_2_5_to_8: Detailed discussion of the advantages and disadvantages of at least two options in the context of ASJ with some judgement. | level_3_9_to_12: Detailed discussion of all three options in the context of ASJ with a well-justified recommendation explaining why television and the print catalogue are rejected as lead channels.

The reasoning rests on continuity: shadowing lets masters supervise work on live repairs so the queue keeps moving, whereas the college certification is a one-off intake that yields no daily practice on the repair turnaround, so the deciding consideration is continuity of service during the fit-out rather than the credential alone.

--- MAIN STEM ---
Valbruna Ski Chalets (VSC) is a private limited company in the alpine hospitality sector, employing a workforce of 40. Founded in 2012 by Elena Marchetti, the business operates six timber chalets offering guided ski holidays, with a flat organisational structure and democratic leadership. VSC plans to invest $720,000 in six new eco-chalets with snowmaking equipment, financed by a $450,000 ten-year bank loan and $270,000 retained profit. It has fixed costs of $222,000 a year, a variable cost of $48 a unit and a selling price of $85, and currently produces 12,000 units a year. VSC faces two operational problems: seasonal absenteeism has reached 8% and customer complaints about slow room turnaround are rising.

--- APPENDIX 1 — MARKETING/OPS ---
Operations Log — Winter 2025: The six chalets hosted 5,400 guest-nights last quarter at an average occupancy of 81%. Customer complaints about turnaround fell from 24 to 12 per month and the defect rate on chalet repairs dropped to 1.5%. Market research of 520 guests found that 63% would pay up to $15 more per night for certified eco-timber chalets, and 49% check a resort's sustainability rating before booking.     Question: Using Appendix 3, evaluate how the interest rate rise to 5.25%, the 6.2% minimum wage increase to $12.53 per hour, and the 11.8% rise in heating fuel and timber input costs will affect VSC. Which change will have the greatest impact? Justify your answer.
    Answer: Interest rate rise (4.5% to 5.25%): If VSC's $450,000 ten-year bank loan carries a variable rate, annual interest rises by roughly 0.75%, adding about $3,375 a year to financing costs and slightly raising the burden above the $222,000 fixed costs. The direct impact is real but modest, and VSC can partly shield itself by negotiating a fixed rate on the loan.

Minimum wage increase (6.2%, to $12.53 per hour): With 40 employees, mainly seasonal chalet, housekeeping and front-desk roles, the lowest-paid roughly 20 workers would each see about 6.2% added to their hourly pay; at around $12.53 per hour and seasonal hours, the combined effect is roughly $20,000 a year, which democratic leadership, productivity gains (12,000 units ÷ 40 staff = 300 guest-nights per worker) and the $15 eco premium would need to offset.

Input cost inflation (11.8% heating fuel and timber): VSC's $48 variable cost is dominated by heating and timber-related supplies, roughly $26 per guest-night. An 11.8% rise on that portion adds about $3.07 per unit; at 12,000 units that is roughly $36,800 a year, cutting contribution per unit from $37.00 toward $34.00 and reducing profit, though VSC can partially recover through the $15 eco premium and renegotiated supplier contracts.

Conclusion: The 11.8% rise in heating fuel and timber input costs will have the greatest impact. It repeatedly erodes the $37.00 contribution on every one of the 12,000 units sold, totalling roughly $36,800 a year and threatening the margin that justifies the $720,000 eco-chalet expansion. The minimum wage increase is the second most serious risk at roughly $20,000 a year, while the interest-rate rise is the smallest in cash terms at about $3,375 and can be managed by fixing the loan rate; all three still require VSC to prioritise cost control and premium pricing.

--- MAIN STEM ---
Southswell Surf School (SWS) is a sole trader in the surf school and beach resort sector, employing a workforce of 24. Founded in 2014 by Riley Tanaka, the business runs lessons, board hire and a small beach café at Flagstaff Beach, with a flat structure and laissez-faire leadership. SWS plans to invest $340,000 in a new beachfront learn-to-surf centre with solar showers and a board repair workshop, financed by a $200,000 ten-year bank loan and a $140,000 overdraft. It has fixed costs of $52,000 a year, a variable cost of $9 a unit and a selling price of $22, and currently produces 9,600 units a year. SWS faces two operational problems: labour turnover among instructors has reached 22% and complaints about lesson safety briefings are rising.

--- APPENDIX 1 — MARKETING/OPS ---
Market Research Summary — Summer 2025: A survey of 450 beach visitors found that 58% would book a five-day group lesson package, and the average lesson rating on review sites is 4.6 out of 5. Customer complaints fell from 19 to 8 per month, and average board-repair turnaround is 2.5 days. Of 24 employees, 9 do not hold a current off-the-job water-safety instructor certificate; courses at the coastal college cost $600 per employee. Peak-season occupancy on the beach reached 84% across 13 weekend sessions.

--- APPENDIX 2 — FINANCIAL DATA ---
Title: Extract from the Statement of Financial Position of Southswell Surf School as at 31 March 2025 ($ '000)
Headers: ['Financial Metric', '2024', '2025']

Current liabilities | 60 | 60
Non-current assets | 260 | 520
Capital employed | 275 | 550

--- APPENDIX 3 — EXTERNAL ENVIRONMENT ---

(2) The national minimum wage will rise by 5.9% from $11.40 to $12.07 per hour from April 2026, raising seasonal instructor wage bills. (3) Wetsuit neoprene and repair-foam input costs have risen 10.6% year-on-year, leisure inflation is running at 6.9%, and consumer spending on coastal leisure grew 5.4% in the same period.

  Q1(a) [8 marks]
    Question: SWS plans to finance its new learn-to-surf centre with a bank loan rather than extending its overdraft. Explain two advantages for SWS of using a $200,000 ten-year bank loan instead of a $140,000 overdraft.
    Answer: Point 1: A ten-year bank loan gives SWS a known, fixed repayment schedule, which makes budgeting and break-even planning far easier than an overdraft that can be withdrawn or repriced at short notice. With fixed costs of $52,000 a year and $22 prices, Riley Tanaka can forecast monthly repayments against 9,600 units of annual lesson output and avoid being caught short during quiet winter weeks.

Point 2: The bank loan is designed for long-term investment, so the $200,000 is cheaper and more stable than rolling an overdraft indefinitely; overdraft interest is typically higher and unsecured limits are reviewed frequently. Using the loan for the $340,000 centre also frees the overdraft for genuine working-capital swings, such as buying wetsuits before the 5.4% rise in coastal leisure demand, and reduces the risk of the bank cancelling short-term funding mid-expansion.

The direct effect is small and can be managed by keeping expansion costs within the fixed loan.

Minimum wage increase (5.9%, to $12.07 per hour): With 24 instructor, café and hire staff, mainly seasonal and on or near minimum wage, the rise lifts every hourly wage bill. At roughly 1,200 paid hours per staff member a year, the 5.9% uplift adds roughly $17,100 a year across the team, from $11.40 to $12.07 per hour alone, which laissez-faire autonomy, productivity at 400 units per worker (9,600 units ÷ 24 staff) and the 5-day package pricing would need to absorb.

Input cost inflation (10.6% wetsuit neoprene and repair foam): SWS's $9 variable cost includes roughly $6 of materials and café inputs. An 10.6% rise on that portion adds about $0.64 per unit; at 9,600 units that is roughly $6,100 a year, squeezing contribution per unit from $13.00 toward $12.36 and raising workshop costs, though SWS can partially recover through modest price increases at peak times.

Conclusion: The 5.9% minimum wage increase will have the greatest impact. Labour dominates SWS's cost base, and the rise adds roughly $17,100 a year permanently, directly eroding the margin that justifies the $340,000 centre regardless of booking volume. The 10.6% input-cost rise is the second most serious at roughly $6,100 and can be passed on or renegotiated, while the 0.75% interest-rate rise is smallest at about $1,500 and can be managed within the fixed loan; all three still require SWS to review lesson prices before the April wage change.
    Keywords: 4.75%, 5.9%, 10.6%, $12.07, $9, $200,000, 5.4%
    Mark scheme: level_1_1_to_4: Identifies the external changes with limited application to SWS. | level_2_5_to_8: Analyses the impact of at least two external changes on SWS's costs, revenue or financing in context. | level_3_9_to_12: Detailed evaluation of all three external changes in the context of SWS with a well-justified judgement that the minimum wage increase has the greatest impact and why the other two are smaller.

--- MAIN STEM ---
Harrowgate Riverside Inns (HRI) is a public limited company in the hospitality and riverside dining sector, employing a workforce of 230. Founded in 1987 by Margaret Harrowgate, the group operates nine riverside inns across the county, with a hierarchical structure and autocratic leadership. It has fixed costs of $1,140,000 a year, a variable cost of $38 a unit and a selling price of $95, and currently produces 26,000 units a year. HRI faces two operational problems: labour turnover has reached 28% in its kitchens and food-waste complaints at two inns are rising.

--- APPENDIX 1 — MARKETING/OPS ---
Quality and Waste Report — Autumn 2025: Customer complaints across the nine inns fell from 44 to 27 per month, and food waste is running at 9.5% of kitchen preparation weight. Average room occupancy is 71%, and the 600 most recent guest reviews average 4.2 out of 5. Market research of 700 diners found that 55% would pay up to $8 more for locally sourced riverside menus, and 46% check ingredient provenance before booking. Off-the-job food hygiene courses at the county college cost $480 per employee for the 160 kitchen and service staff.

Unlike the $1,200,000 ten-year bank loan, new equity carries no interest charge, protecting fixed costs of $1,140,000 a year and freeing cash to absorb the 13.1% rise in food and beverage input costs without raising menu prices above the $95 room-night benchmark.

Point 2: Equity funding strengthens HRI's statement of financial position, lowering the burden on its current ratio and leaving capacity to borrow again if terrace costs overrun. It also spreads ownership and risk across more shareholders rather than concentrating debt with one bank, which suits a public limited company refurbishing $1,800,000 of assets, and avoids covenants that could restrict how the inns are operated during the refit.

    Question: Using Appendix 2, evaluate HRI's financial position by calculating the current ratio and the acid test ratio for 2024 and 2025. Has HRI's financial position improved? Justify your answer.
    Answer: Calculations:
Current Ratio 2024 = 1.60 : 1
Current Ratio 2025 = 1.72 : 1
Acid Test Ratio 2024 = 1.08 : 1
Acid Test Ratio 2025 = 1.16 : 1

Detailed workings: 2024 current assets = $210,000 inventories + $320,000 trade receivables + $110,000 cash = $640,000; 2025 = $235,000 + $345,000 + $150,000 = $730,000. Liquidity 2024 = $640,000 ÷ $400,000 = 1.60; 2025 = $730,000 ÷ $425,000 = 1.72. Excluding inventories, 2024 = ($640,000 − $210,000) ÷ $400,000 = $430,000 ÷ $400,000 = 1.08; 2025 = ($730,000 − $235,000) ÷ $425,000 = $495,000 ÷ $425,000 = 1.16.

Evaluation: Liquidity has improved modestly. The 2025 liquidity figure rose from 1.60 to 1.72, meaning current assets cover current liabilities more comfortably, helped by cash rising from $110,000 to $150,000 and current liabilities rising only from $400,000 to $425,000. The stricter liquidity measure, which excludes inventories, improved from 1.08 to 1.16, so short-term solvency does not depend on selling stock — important while HRI services a $1,200,000 bank loan and funds a $1,800,000 refurbishment. The rise in liabilities also shows HRI is leaning more on short-term credit, so working capital discipline matters during the six-inn refit.

Conclusion: HRI's financial position has improved, though only gradually. Both the 2024-to-2025 liquidity measures (1.60 to 1.72, and 1.08 to 1.16) show stronger short-term solvency, and the improvement does not rest on inventory. The main residual risks are rising receivables and growing current liabilities, so HRI should tighten deposit terms on events and functions while the terraces open, and keep kitchen waste at or below 9.5% of prep weight to free cash for the expansion.

They also appeal to the 46% who check ingredient provenance, strengthening HRI's brand, supporting the 4.2-out-of-5 review average, and helping the six refurbished terraces win destination-dining listings.

    Question: Using Appendix 3, evaluate how the interest rate rise to 5.5%, the 6.4% minimum wage increase to $13.09 per hour, and the 13.1% rise in food and beverage input costs will affect HRI. Which change will have the greatest impact? Justify your answer.
    Answer: Interest rate rise (4.75% to 5.5%): If HRI's $1,200,000 ten-year bank loan is variable-rate, annual interest rises by about 0.75%, adding roughly $9,000 a year to financing costs and slightly raising fixed costs above $1,140,000. Higher rates may also make consumers more cautious about discretionary dining, though consumer spending on eating out still grew 2.6%, and HRI can shield itself by negotiating a fixed rate or paying down the loan from the $600,000 share-issue proceeds.

Minimum wage increase (6.4%, to $13.09 per hour): With 230 employees, mainly kitchen and service roles, the rise lifts the whole wage bill. Roughly 45 kitchen porters and cleaners at or near minimum wage, each working about 1,800 hours a year, would see about $13.09 × 1,800 × 6.4% ≈ $1,510 extra a year per worker, or roughly $68,000 across those roles — though HRI can offset part through productivity gains of 113 units per worker (26,000 units ÷ 230 staff).

Input cost inflation (13.1% food and beverage): HRI's $38 variable cost is dominated by food, roughly $24 per room-night equivalent. A 13.1% rise on that portion adds about $3.14 per unit; at 26,000 units that is roughly $81,600 a year, cutting contribution per unit from $57.00 toward $53.86 and reducing profit, though HRI can partially recover through the $8 locally sourced premium menu and tighter waste control below the current 9.5% of prep weight.

Conclusion: The 13.1% rise in food and beverage input costs will have the greatest impact. It directly and repeatedly erodes the $57.00 contribution on every one of the 26,000 units sold, totalling roughly $81,600 a year, comfortably above the minimum-wage effect of roughly $68,000 across the lowest-paid cohort, and far above the $9,000 interest-rate increase. The minimum wage increase is the second most serious risk, while the interest-rate rise is smallest and can be managed by fixing the loan rate; all three still require HRI to review menu pricing before the April wage change.

--- MAIN STEM ---
Caldera Springs Spa Resort (CSSR) is a cooperative in the wellness and spa tourism sector, employing a workforce of 65. Founded in 2016 by Priya Raman, the resort operates geothermal baths and a treatment wing in the highlands, with a flat structure and democratic leadership. CSSR plans to invest $950,000 in a new geothermal bath house and treatment suites, financed by a $600,000 ten-year bank loan and $350,000 retained profit. It has fixed costs of $360,000 a year, a variable cost of $28 a unit and a selling price of $52, and currently produces 21,000 units a year. CSSR faces two operational problems: labour turnover among therapists has reached 19% and quality complaints about treatment bookings are rising.

--- APPENDIX 1 — MARKETING/OPS ---
Market Research Summary — Autumn 2025: A survey of 550 guests found that 61% would pay up to $12 more per session for geothermal treatments, and 47% check a resort's environmental credentials before booking. Average occupancy of treatment rooms is 74%, and the 480 most recent reviews average 4.7 out of 5. Customer complaints fell from 33 to 17 per month. A skills audit shows 22 of 65 staff have not completed on-the-job training on the new digital booking system; off-the-job training courses at the highland college cost $800 per employee.

--- APPENDIX 2 — FINANCIAL DATA ---
Title: Extract from the Statement of Financial Position of Caldera Springs Spa Resort as at 31 March 2025 ($ '000)
Headers: ['Financial Metric', '2024', '2025']

(2) The national minimum wage will rise by 6.0% from $11.90 to $12.61 per hour from April 2026, raising therapist and front-of-house wage bills. (3) Energy prices have risen 14.2% year-on-year and wellness inflation is running at 6.5%, while consumer spending on wellness breaks grew 6.1% in the same period.

Retained profit requires no buyer to be found, no negotiation over price, and no disruption to guest services during the build.

Point 2: Retained profit costs CSSR nothing in interest, repayments or disposal losses, protecting cash flow at a time when it already faces fixed costs of $360,000 a year and a $600,000 ten-year bank loan commitment. Every dollar of retained profit used preserves margin against the 14.2% rise in energy prices, helping CSSR hold the $52 price point and keep the cooperative's members' returns healthy without diluting member ownership the way an external capital raise would.

    Question: Using Appendix 2, evaluate MMG's financial position by calculating the current ratio and the acid test ratio for 2024 and 2025. Has MMG's financial position improved? Justify your answer.
    Answer: Calculations:
Current Ratio 2024 = 1.47 : 1
Current Ratio 2025 = 1.43 : 1
Acid Test Ratio 2024 = 0.87 : 1
Acid Test Ratio 2025 = 0.69 : 1

Detailed workings: 2024 current assets = $18,000 inventories + $12,000 trade receivables + $14,000 cash = $44,000; 2025 = $26,000 + $15,000 + $9,000 = $50,000. Liquidity 2024 = $44,000 ÷ $30,000 = 1.47; 2025 = $50,000 ÷ $35,000 = 1.43. Excluding inventories, 2024 = ($44,000 − $18,000) ÷ $30,000 = $26,000 ÷ $30,000 = 0.87; 2025 = ($50,000 − $26,000) ÷ $35,000 = $24,000 ÷ $35,000 = 0.69.

Evaluation: Liquidity has weakened. The 2025 liquidity figure slipped from 1.47 to 1.43, meaning current assets cover current liabilities slightly less comfortably, helped by cash falling from $14,000 to $9,000 and current liabilities rising from $30,000 to $35,000. The stricter liquidity measure, which excludes inventories, fell sharply from 0.87 to 0.69, so MMG is increasingly reliant on selling stock — critical while it services a $330,000 bank loan and a $150,000 hire purchase agreement for a $480,000 expansion. Inventories rose from $18,000 to $26,000, tying up cash that could have funded the meadow kitchen, and trade receivables rose from $12,000 to $15,000; if agency and platform partners pay late, short-term pressure will intensify.

Conclusion: MMG's financial position has not improved. Both the 2024-to-2025 liquidity measures (1.47 to 1.43, and 0.87 to 0.69) show weaker short-term solvency, and the decline does not rest on inventory alone. The main risks are falling cash and rising current liabilities, so MMG should slow tent spending, tighten deposit terms on platform bookings, clear the inventory backlog before winter, and renegotiate the hire purchase schedule before drawing further on the loan.

--- MAIN STEM ---
Bluecrest Airport Shuttle (BAS) is a private limited company in the passenger transport sector, employing a workforce of 38. Founded in 2011 by Priya Nandakumar, the business runs a fleet of coaches and minibuses carrying passengers between Westmoor International Airport and the surrounding towns, operating a flat structure with democratic leadership. BAS plans to invest $720,000 in six electric shuttle buses and charging infrastructure, financed by a $450,000 seven-year bank loan and $270,000 retained profit. It has fixed costs of $270,000 a year, a variable cost of $3.60 a unit and a selling price of $9.00, and currently produces 100,000 units a year. BAS faces rising driver absenteeism, which reached 8% last quarter, and two new competitors have started undercutting its airport fares.

--- APPENDIX 1 — MARKETING/OPS ---
Operations Log — Q3 2025: The shuttle fleet completed 25,400 passenger journeys last quarter at a defect rate of 2.1% (unplanned breakdowns), down from 3.4% a year ago. On-time departures improved to 91.5%. Customer complaints fell from 29 to 17 per month. Market research of 500 airport passengers found 58% would pay up to $0.30 more for guaranteed-seat bookings, and 46% prefer electric vehicles. A skills audit shows 3 of 38 drivers still need electric-vehicle certification (off-the-job training at the local college costs $750 per driver; on-the-job training is unavailable in-house).

--- APPENDIX 2 — FINANCIAL DATA ---
Title: Extract from the Statement of Profit or Loss and Capital employed data of Bluecrest Airport Shuttle for the year ended 31 March 2025 ($ '000)
Headers: ['Financial Metric', '2024', '2025']
Revenue | 800 | 900
Cost of sales | 464 | 513
Gross profit | 336 | 387
Operating profit | 96 | 135
Capital employed | 600 | 675
Interest payable | 18 | 26

--- APPENDIX 3 — EXTERNAL ENVIRONMENT ---
Economic and Business Bulletin (November 2026): (1) The central bank has raised the base interest rate from 5.0% to 5.75%, increasing repayments on variable-rate business loans. (2) The national minimum wage will rise by 6.5% from $11.93 to $12.71 per hour from April 2026, raising staff costs. (3) Grid electricity prices for charging depots have risen 9.8% year-on-year, and consumer spending on airport transfers grew 4.2%, with transport and leisure inflation running at 7.6%.

--- QUESTIONS ---
  Q1(a) [8 marks]
    Question: BAS plans to finance the expansion with a $450,000 seven-year bank loan and $270,000 retained profit. Explain two advantages for BAS of using retained profit to fund the expansion instead of relying solely on the bank loan.
    Answer: Point 1: Using retained profit costs BAS nothing in interest or repayments, which protects cash flow while it already services the $450,000 bank loan and carries fixed costs of $270,000 a year. Every dollar not paid out as interest can absorb the 9.8% rise in grid electricity costs, helping BAS hold the $9.00 selling price against two new competitors undercutting its airport fares and defending its $5.40 contribution per unit.

Point 2: Retained profit carries no collateral or repossession risk, so if passenger numbers at Westmoor International Airport dip, BAS would not be forced to sell coaches to meet loan repayments. Funding $270,000 this way also preserves the democratic, flat structure that Priya Nandakumar created: no external lender can impose conditions on how the six electric shuttle buses are routed, priced or timetabled, and ownership remains entirely with existing shareholders, avoiding dilution or lender interference as the business invests $720,000 in its future.
    Keywords: retained profit, $270,000, $450,000, $720,000, bank loan, fixed costs
    Mark scheme: knowledge_max_2: 1 mark for each valid advantage identified (max 2). | application_analysis_max_6: Up to 3 marks per point for detailed contextual explanation and analysis applied to Bluecrest Airport Shuttle and its expansion decision.

  Q1(b) [12 marks]
    Question: BAS is launching its electric airport shuttle service. Consider airport terminal advertising boards, local radio sponsorship, or social media influencer marketing. Which should BAS choose to promote the launch? Justify your recommendation.
    Answer: Airport terminal advertising boards: Advertising inside Westmoor International Airport reaches arriving and departing passengers at the exact point of need, building instant awareness of the new electric shuttle. High footfall and captive dwell times give strong visibility, and the format suits a service whose entire market is airport passengers. However, airport media contracts are expensive for a 38-employee business funding a $720,000 expansion, and they reach only passengers already at the airport, not residents or workers who could use the service for commuting or hotel transfers.

Local radio sponsorship: Regional radio is far cheaper than airport media, supports time-sensitive launch messages such as 'new electric shuttle now running', and reaches the towns BAS serves, matching its fixed route network. Its limitation is that many listeners will never use an airport shuttle, so wastage is high, and coverage stops at the regional boundary, capping the volume of passengers BAS can attract for its 100,000 units a year.

Social media influencer marketing: Partnering with local travel, family and sustainability influencers targets the 58% of 500 surveyed passengers willing to pay up to $0.30 more for guaranteed-seat bookings and the 46% who prefer electric vehicles, telling the electric story directly to engaged audiences with measurable likes, clicks and bookings at low cost per reached customer. Influencer trust builds more slowly than airport boards and depends on influencer fit, but spend can be scaled, paused or redirected quickly.

Recommendation: BAS should choose social media influencer marketing. It reaches precisely the passengers BAS's research shows will pay a premium, costs far less than airport terminal contracts, scales beyond the local radio audience, and reinforces the eco-friendly positioning that city commuters increasingly expect. Airport terminal advertising is rejected as too costly and captive-market only; local radio is rejected as too narrow for routes serving hotels, towns and the airport itself; influencer campaigns should be supported with modest stands at the terminal during peak summer months.
    Keywords: electric shuttle buses, $720,000, airport, 58%, 46%, $0.30
    Mark scheme: level_1_1_to_4: Limited knowledge or outline of the promotional options with minimal context. | level_2_5_to_8: Detailed discussion of the advantages and disadvantages of at least two options in the context of BAS with some judgement. | level_3_9_to_12: Detailed discussion of all three options in the context of BAS with a well-justified recommendation explaining why airport terminal advertising and local radio are rejected.

  Q2(a) [8 marks]
    Question: BAS's driver absenteeism reached 8% last quarter. Explain two benefits for BAS of using democratic leadership to improve motivation among its driving team.
    Answer: Point 1: Democratic leadership gives BAS's 38 employees a genuine voice in shift patterns, route timings and on-board service standards, which supports their social and esteem needs and lifts job satisfaction. Drivers who help design rotas that fit airport arrival peaks are more likely to attend reliably, directly attacking the 8% absenteeism rate and reducing the strain on the flat structure and on Priya Nandakumar, who currently fields most operational decisions personally.

Point 2: Involving drivers in decisions surfaces practical ideas from the people who meet passengers every day, improving punctuality beyond the current 91.5% on-time figure and cutting the 2.1% defect rate of unplanned breakdowns by flagging maintenance issues earlier. Higher involvement increases commitment and lowers staff turnover, saving the $750 per driver certification cost and protecting 100,000 units a year of output while the six electric buses bed in and fixed costs of $270,000 are covered. Reliable, engaged crews also feed directly into the guaranteed-seat promise, which the 58% who will pay up to $0.30 more are willing to book precisely because BAS turns up on time.
    Keywords: democratic leadership, absenteeism, workforce of 38, 8%, $750, flat structure
    Mark scheme: knowledge_max_2: 1 mark for each valid benefit identified (max 2). | application_analysis_max_6: Up to 3 marks per point for detailed contextual development linked to BAS's absenteeism, punctuality and output.

  Q2(b) [12 marks]
    Question: BAS must upskill the 3 drivers who lack electric-vehicle certification so they can operate the new fleet. Consider on-the-job training or off-the-job training at the local college. Which should BAS choose? Justify your decision.
    Answer: On-the-job training: Coaching beside an experienced EV driver passes on BAS's own routines — charging etiquette, route times, passenger care and fault reporting — at zero course fees, and the 3 drivers keep earning while they learn, protecting the 25,400 passenger journeys completed last quarter and the 91.5% on-time rate. Drawbacks are that BAS has no in-house EV specialist, so coaching could transmit bad habits or unsafe charging practice, and no recognised certificate results, which may weaken insurance or airport authority compliance for the new $720,000 bus fleet.

Off-the-job training: The local college course at $750 per driver costs only $2,250 in total, gives structured, up-to-date high-voltage safety and battery knowledge, and awards a recognised certificate for all 3 drivers. Taking drivers off the road reduces short-term capacity during peak airport season, and generic content may not match BAS's exact bus models, so some route-specific coaching on return would still be needed.

Decision: BAS should choose off-the-job training at the local college, topped up with short on-the-job route coaching. High-voltage EV operation carries safety and compliance stakes that make a proper certificate essential, and $2,250 is trivial against a $720,000 investment; the off-the-job route also avoids passing on unsafe habits during a period when absenteeism is already 8%. On-the-job-only training is rejected because BAS lacks an in-house EV expert and uncertificated drivers would jeopardise the electric fleet launch and airport compliance, while full off-the-job delivery without any route coaching would leave drivers unfamiliar with BAS's own schedules, so a combined approach is safest.
    Keywords: on-the-job training, off-the-job training, $750, $720,000, electric shuttle buses, 8%

    Answer: Interest rate rise (5.0% to 5.75%): If BAS's $450,000 seven-year loan is variable-rate, the 0.75 percentage point rise adds about $3,375 a year in interest, nudging interest payable above the current $26,000 (per Appendix 2) and slightly increasing the strain on fixed costs of $270,000 a year. Minimum wage increase (6.5%, to $12.71 per hour): With a workforce of 38, mainly drivers and depot staff, BAS's wage bill rises by roughly 6.5%. If average hourly pay is around $12.71, annual wages per full-time employee are roughly $26,500, so the rise adds about $1,700 per worker or around $65,000 across the workforce — a much larger cash impact than the interest rise, and one BAS must offset through productivity (100,000 units ÷ 38 staff ≈ 2,632 units per worker), the democratic leadership approach and absenteeism reduction.

Conclusion: The 9.8% rise in grid electricity costs will have the greatest impact. It strikes BAS's operating model directly and repeatedly, eroding the $5.40 contribution on every one of its 100,000 annual units and undermining the economics of the $720,000 electric expansion it is rolling out now. The minimum wage rise is the second most serious pressure, adding roughly $65,000 a year, while the interest rate rise is the smallest in cash terms and can be managed by fixing the loan; all three demand disciplined cost control, off-peak charging and premium pricing such as the $0.30 guaranteed-seat fee.

--- MAIN STEM ---
Redbark Timber Haulage (RBH) is a partnership in the bulk timber road transport sector, employing a workforce of 52. Founded in 2008 by cousins Daniela and Rory Whitmore, the business operates a fleet of road trains hauling logs from Highfen forestry estates to sawmills across the north region, with a hierarchical structure led by senior partner Daniela. RBH plans to invest $960,000 in four double-trailer road trains, financed by $600,000 hire purchase and $360,000 partners' capital contributions. It has fixed costs of $600,000 a year, a variable cost of $55 a unit and a selling price of $85, and currently produces 40,000 units a year. RBH faces a skills gap: only 9 of its 52 drivers hold the double-trailer licence needed for the new road trains.

--- APPENDIX 1 — MARKETING/OPS ---
Operations Log — October 2025: The fleet completed 312 loads last month, averaging a payload of 26 tonnes per road train. Breakdowns fell from 9 to 5 this quarter. Fuel efficiency improved to 2.9 km per litre. Customer complaints dropped from 24 to 14 per month. A survey of 18 sawmill customers found 72% would switch providers for guaranteed 24-hour delivery, and 61% ask for carbon-report data with every load. A licensing audit shows 9 of 52 drivers still need double-trailer certification (off-the-job courses at the regional training depot cost $1,150 per driver; on-the-job mentoring is limited by the shortage of licence holders).

--- APPENDIX 2 — FINANCIAL DATA ---

(2) The national minimum wage will rise by 6.5% from $12.20 to $13.00 per hour from April 2026, raising driver and depot staff costs. (3) The central bank has raised the base interest rate from 5.25% to 6.0%, increasing the cost of hire purchase and loan repayments.

  Q1(a) [8 marks]
    Question: RBH plans to finance the $960,000 road train purchase with $600,000 hire purchase and $360,000 partners' capital contributions. Explain two advantages for RBH of using hire purchase instead of relying solely on partners' capital.
    Answer: Point 1: Hire purchase lets RBH spread the $600,000 cost over several years while the four road trains generate revenue immediately, preserving Daniela and Rory Whitmore's partners' capital of $360,000 for working capital such as diesel, driver wages and maintenance across a workforce of 52. Tying up all partner funds in vehicles would leave the business exposed to the 14.7% diesel price rise and any sawmill payment delays without a cash buffer.

Point 2: Hire purchase treats the road trains as security for the finance, so RBH does not need to pledge private partner assets or dilute ownership. Because the vehicles are productive assets earning an $85 selling price on every unit hauled, the repayments can be matched against the income they create, easing cash flow and keeping the $360,000 capital contribution available as a safety cushion while the double-trailer licence bottleneck is cleared and the new fleet beds in.

  Q1(b) [12 marks]
    Question: RBH is launching its guaranteed 24-hour double-trailer delivery service. Consider advertising in a national forestry trade magazine, direct mail to sawmill customers, or exhibiting at a forestry and logistics trade exhibition.     Answer: National forestry trade magazine advertising: A placement in the sector's main title would reach hundreds of forestry estates, sawmills and timber buyers nationwide, building credibility for RBH's new double-trailer service and its carbon-report capability. It is cost-effective per reader, and 61% of sawmill customers already ask for carbon-report data with every load, so a well-placed advert can lead with that differentiator. However, print readership among actual decision-makers is limited, ads are easy to ignore, and measuring enquiry rates is weak, so many impressions will never convert to load contracts.

Direct mail to sawmill customers: RBH can mail its own base of 18 surveyed sawmill customers plus prospects, offering guaranteed 24-hour delivery — the single most cited switching trigger, named by 72% of survey respondents. Personalised, evidence-led mail is cheap, targeted and easy to track through follow-up calls, and it suits a small partnership without a marketing department. Its drawback is scale: it cannot efficiently reach new forestry regions outside RBH's existing Highfen-to-sawmill corridor, and poorly designed mailers risk being filed away unread.

Forestry and logistics trade exhibition: Exhibiting puts RBH face-to-face with estates, sawmills and timber buyers in one venue, enabling live demonstrations of road train payloads (26 tonnes average) and on-the-spot contract talks. Exhibitions build trust fast in a relationship-driven industry. However, stand fees, travel and staff time cost thousands of dollars for a partnership whose cash is committed to $960,000 of vehicles, and a single event delivers only one-off, geographically random exposure.

Recommendation: RBH should choose direct mail to sawmill customers. It speaks directly to the 72% who would switch for guaranteed 24-hour delivery, targets the exact buyers who control volume, costs a fraction of exhibition space, and produces measurable enquiry data within weeks. The trade magazine advert is rejected as untargeted and slow to convert; the exhibition is rejected as expensive and infrequent for a business that must fill four new road trains quickly; RBH can add a small magazine presence later, funded from first-contract revenues.

--- MAIN STEM ---
Caldera Geothermal Heat (CGH) is a cooperative in the renewable energy sector, employing a workforce of 34. Established in 2014 by community investors led by heat engineer Tomas Verhoeven, the cooperative operates the deep-borehole Caldera geothermal heat network, supplying district heating to 1,200 homes and St Anselm's Hospital. It works a flat structure governed democratically by an elected member board. CGH plans to invest $1,250,000 in a second heat exchanger station and 4 km of insulated pipework, financed by an $800,000 member share issue and $450,000 retained reserves. It has fixed costs of $630,000 a year, a variable cost of $78 a unit and a selling price of $120, and currently produces 27,000 units a year. CGH faces rising quality complaints about heat outages across its older connections.

--- APPENDIX 1 — MARKETING/OPS ---
Quality and Waste Report — Q3 2025: The network delivered 6,750 MWh of heat last quarter; 7% of connections reported outages, down from 11% a year ago. Average fault repair time fell to 4.6 hours. Customer complaints fell from 31 to 22 per month. A member survey of 1,200 households found 84% would support a tariff rise of $0.06 per unit to fund network expansion, and 59% chose CGH for environmental reasons. A skills audit shows 6 of 34 technicians have not completed high-pressure weld recertification (off-the-job training at the regional training centre costs $1,400 per technician; on-the-job training is constrained by the outage workload).

--- APPENDIX 2 — FINANCIAL DATA ---
Title: Extract from the Statement of Profit or Loss and Capital employed data of Caldera Geothermal Heat for the year ended 31 March 2025 ($ '000)
Headers: ['Financial Metric', '2024', '2025']
Revenue | 2,400 | 3,240
Cost of sales | 1,416 | 1,782
Gross profit | 984 | 1,458
Operating profit | 288 | 486
Capital employed | 1,800 | 2,430
Interest payable | 72 | 96

--- APPENDIX 3 — EXTERNAL ENVIRONMENT ---
Economic and Business Bulletin (November 2026): (1) The central bank has raised the base interest rate from 4.5% to 5.25%, increasing financing costs for infrastructure projects. (2) The national minimum wage will rise by 7.1% from $12.70 to $13.60 per hour from April 2026, raising labour costs. (3) Construction materials inflation is running at 11.3%, and a government grant for renewable district-heating schemes will cover up to 30% of eligible project costs from 2027.

--- QUESTIONS ---
  Q1(a) [8 marks]
    Question: CGH plans to finance the heat network expansion with an $800,000 member share issue and $450,000 retained reserves. Explain two advantages for CGH of using the member share issue instead of relying solely on retained reserves.
    Answer: Point 1: An $800,000 member share issue raises far more expansion capital than the $450,000 of retained reserves alone, letting CGH fund the second heat exchanger station and 4 km of insulated pipework in full rather than scaling the project back. Deep-borehole geothermal assets are long-lived; member investors buying shares are essentially funding the community network that supplies 1,200 homes and St Anselm's Hospital, aligning their stake with the cooperative's mission.

Point 2: Share issues spread the financing burden across the membership instead of draining reserves earmarked for repairs and the rising outage complaints (7% of connections still fail). Instead of paying interest on a bank loan, CGH shares profits or surplus dividends with the households that own it, preserving the $630,000 a year fixed-cost cover and keeping tariffs affordable — the survey shows 84% of members would even accept a $0.06 per unit rise, giving the board room to price the service sustainably.
    Keywords: member share issue, $800,000, $450,000, $1,250,000, retained reserves, 1,200 homes

--- MAIN STEM ---
Brightvolt EV Charging (BEC) is a public limited company in the electric vehicle charging sector, employing a workforce of 210. Founded in 2016 by Ada Mensah, the company operates 340 fast-charging bays across motorway service areas and retail parks, with a hierarchical structure and delegated regional management teams. BEC plans to invest $2,400,000 in nine 350 kW ultra-fast charging hubs along the M4 corridor, financed by a $1,500,000 share issue and a $900,000 five-year bank loan. It has fixed costs of $1,575,000 a year, a variable cost of $7.50 a unit and a selling price of $18, and currently produces 260,000 units a year. BEC faces a skills gap: its field technicians lack the high-voltage certification needed to commission the new hubs.

--- APPENDIX 1 — MARKETING/OPS ---
Market Research Summary — October 2026: A survey of 800 motorway drivers found 57% prefer chargers offering 350 kW speeds, and 63% would pay $3 more per session for guaranteed bay availability. Average charging spend is $18 per session, with an average dwell time of 22 minutes. Website visits rose 48% after the spring influencer campaign. Customer complaints averaged 19 per month, down from 27. An internal audit found 9 of 210 field technicians lack high-voltage certification (off-the-job training at the specialist academy costs $1,600 per technician; on-the-job training is unsafe for live high-voltage work).

--- APPENDIX 2 — FINANCIAL DATA ---
Title: Extract from the Statement of Profit or Loss and Capital employed data of Brightvolt EV Charging for the year ended 31 March 2025 ($ '000)
Headers: ['Financial Metric', '2024', '2025']
Revenue | 3,900 | 4,680
Cost of sales | 2,340 | 2,457
Gross profit | 1,560 | 2,223
Operating profit | 468 | 702
Capital employed | 2,600 | 3,510
Interest payable | 165 | 210

--- APPENDIX 3 — EXTERNAL ENVIRONMENT ---
Economic and Business Bulletin (November 2026): (1) The national minimum wage will rise by 6.7% from $12.40 to $13.23 per hour from April 2026, raising staff costs. (2) The central bank has raised the base interest rate from 5.5% to 6.0%, the third rise this year, increasing borrowing costs. (3) Wholesale grid electricity costs for charging operators have risen 13.6% year-on-year, while electric-vehicle registrations grew 18.2% in the same period.

  Q1(a) [8 marks]
    Question: BEC plans to finance the M4 charging hubs with a $1,500,000 share issue and a $900,000 five-year bank loan. Explain two advantages for BEC of using the share issue instead of relying solely on bank borrowing.
    Answer: Point 1: A $1,500,000 share issue raises permanent capital with no compulsory repayment schedule or interest, strengthening BEC's balance sheet while it carries fixed costs of $1,575,000 a year and a new $900,000 bank loan. The $2,400,000 hub programme can therefore proceed without over-stretching cash flow, and shareholders rather than lenders absorb the construction-phase risk before the nine 350 kW hubs open. Avoiding further lender covenants also keeps BEC free to direct operating cash into 350 kW hardware and software rather than accelerated repayments.

Point 2: Issuing shares spreads ownership risk across many investors and avoids the restrictive covenants and asset charges that a pure bank loan would attach to the charging estate. For a public limited company, a well-received share issue can also lift BEC's profile with the investment community, supporting the 18.2% growth in electric-vehicle registrations behind its market, and keeps Ada Mensah's strategy free from lender interference when choosing hub locations, pricing and rollout pace along the M4 corridor.

    Answer: Minimum wage increase (6.7%, to $13.23 per hour): With a workforce of 210, mainly field technicians and site staff, a 6.7% rise adds roughly $1,750 per employee a year, or about $367,000 across the workforce — very significant against 2025 operating profit of $702,000. BEC must lift productivity (260,000 units ÷ 210 staff ≈ 1,238 units per employee), use the bonus scheme to reward certified work, and prioritise high-impact retention measures for high-voltage technicians rather than applying flat rises.

Interest rate rise (5.5% to 6.0%): BEC's $900,000 five-year bank loan becomes costlier by roughly $4,500 a year per 0.5 percentage points, pushing interest payable above the $210,000 already recorded in Appendix 2. The share issue funds most of the M4 build, so direct exposure is limited, but a higher base rate also cools housing and car-buying sentiment and could dampen EV registrations, and refinancing after five years will be more expensive if rates stay high. The cash impact is manageable and manageable through fixing rates.

Grid electricity cost rise (13.6%): Electricity is the fuel inside BEC's $7.50 variable cost per unit. A 13.6% rise adds roughly $0.70–$0.90 per unit; across 260,000 units a year that is $180,000–$235,000 a year, dragging contribution from $10.50 toward $9.60–$9.80 and squeezing exactly the margin that justifies $2,400,000 of M4 hubs. Unlike wages, this cost recurs on every single unit sold and cannot be fully delegated to staff productivity.

Conclusion: The 13.6% rise in grid electricity costs will have the greatest impact. It scales directly with volume (260,000 units), totalling roughly $180,000–$235,000 a year, and attacks the $10.50 contribution margin on which the entire nine-hub M4 business case rests. The minimum wage rise is the second-largest, at around $367,000 across 210 staff, while the interest rate rise is smallest in cash terms and can be hedged by fixing the $900,000 loan; BEC should respond with off-peak PPAs, dynamic pricing, the $3 guaranteed-bay premium and rigorous site productivity.
    Keywords: 6.7%, 6.0%, 13.6%, $13.23, minimum wage, $7.50
    Mark scheme: level_1_1_to_4: Identifies the external factors with limited application to BEC. | level_2_5_to_8: Analyses the impact of at least two external changes on BEC's costs, revenue or financing in context. | level_3_9_to_12: Detailed evaluation of all three external changes in the context of BEC with a well-justified judgment that the electricity cost rise has the greatest impact and why the other two are smaller.

--- MAIN STEM ---
Saltmarsh Harbour Ferries (SHF) is a sole trader in the coastal passenger transport sector, employing a workforce of 12. Founded in 2012 by Captain Owen Pryce, the business runs two vessels on 14-minute crossings between Saltmarsh quay and the island of St Bride, with an autocratic leadership style and a hands-on, close-knit team. SHF plans to invest $480,000 in a new 60-seat hybrid ferry, financed by the sale of the older vessel for $150,000 and a $330,000 bank loan. It has fixed costs of $216,000 a year, a variable cost of $6.40 a unit and a selling price of $16, and currently produces 45,000 units a year. SHF faces rising labour turnover, which reached 21% among seasonal deck crew last summer.

--- APPENDIX 1 — MARKETING/OPS ---
Advertisement Extract — Summer 2027 brochure: "Island in 14 minutes — $16 return, family tickets 25% off, now with hybrid-electric sailings." Below the advert: Market research (June 2026) of 420 passengers found 66% would pay up to $4 more for a guaranteed seat on summer weekends; 71% rate hybrid ferries important; average crossing time is 14 minutes; customer complaints average 1.9% of crossings; seasonal bookings rose 12% year-on-year; 4 of 12 deck crew need renewed first-aid certification (off-the-job training at the maritime college costs $320 per crew member; on-the-job training is difficult alongside the tight sailing schedule).

Lower borrowing also means interest payable — $34,000 in 2025 — will rise less when the 5.5% base rate feeds through, directly protecting Owen Pryce's profit.

Point 2: The older vessel is ageing and costly to maintain, so selling it removes rising repair bills and safety risk while funding the $480,000 hybrid replacement. Retaining full control matters to a sole trader: by using the sale proceeds, Owen Pryce avoids extra lender conditions on how the 60-seat hybrid is deployed, keeps fare-setting freedom at $16, and shows good asset management to any future lender assessing the loan application.

    Answer: Local radio advertising: A spot on the regional station would reach commuters and holidaymakers planning St Bride trips, building awareness of the hybrid ferry with 14-minute crossings and family tickets 25% off. Radio suits the drive-then-sail audience on Saltmarsh quay routes and is more affordable than national media for a 12-person business. Deals can be switched on for peak weekends, tracked through booking codes, and shared by island community groups — ideal for a 12-person team with limited time, and measurable end-to-end. Risks are reliance on platform reach and weaker penetration of older, non-digital islanders.

Local radio is rejected as too broad and costly per actual booking for a single-route ferry; brochure drops are rejected as the lead channel because they lack urgency and tracking, though a small print run in hotels should remain to reach older visitors; social campaigns should run continuously through the season.

--- MAIN STEM ---
Carrick Shelf Analytics (CSA) is a private limited company in the retail technology (IoT) sector, employing a workforce of 38. Founded in 2017 by Matteo Ricci, the business supplies smart-shelf sensor systems to national supermarket chains and operates a flat organisational structure with laissez-faire leadership. CSA plans to invest $950,000 in a new computer-vision smart-shelf platform with recyclable sensor housings, financed by a $600,000 ten-year bank loan and $350,000 retained profit. It has fixed costs of $340,000 a year, a variable cost of $18.50 a unit and a selling price of $26.50, and currently produces 60,000 units a year. CSA faces two operational problems: field-technician absenteeism has reached 8% and labour turnover is rising, while quality complaints about inaccurate stock alerts are increasing.

--- APPENDIX 1 — MARKETING/OPS ---
Operations Log — Q3 2025: The smart-shelf rollout covered 140 supermarket stores, and 2.6 million shelf-scan events were recorded last quarter. Out-of-stock incidents fell 31% in pilot stores. The field-sensor defect rate is 2.6%, down from 4.4% a year ago. Customer complaints fell from 46 to 24 per month. Market research of 700 store managers found 71% would pay $0.15 more per shelf per month for real-time alerts, and 48% cite stock accuracy as their top priority. A training needs analysis shows 15 of 38 staff have not completed on-the-job training on the new calibrated mounting kits; off-the-job training courses at the regional college cost $750 per employee.

--- APPENDIX 2 — FINANCIAL DATA ---
Title: Extract from the Statement of Profit or Loss and Capital employed data of Carrick Shelf Analytics for the year ended 31 March 2025 ($ '000)
Headers: ['Financial Metric', '2024', '2025']

Cost of sales | 2,760 | 2,860
Gross profit | 1,840 | 2,340
Operating profit | 690 | 988
Capital employed | 3,450 | 4,120
Interest payable | 55 | 78

--- APPENDIX 3 — EXTERNAL ENVIRONMENT ---
Economic and Business Bulletin (November 2026): (1) The central bank raised the base interest rate from 4.9% to 5.6%, the third rise this year, increasing costs for variable-rate business loans. (2) The national minimum wage rises 5.4% from $13.10 to $13.81 per hour from April 2026, lifting wage bills for field and warehouse staff. (3) Semiconductor and shelf-sensor component costs have risen 9.8% year-on-year and grocery price inflation is 7.2%, while consumer spending on grocery own-label goods grew 4.1% in the same period.

    Answer: Point 1: A ten-year bank loan spreads the cost of the $950,000 expansion across the working life of the computer-vision smart-shelf platform instead of draining CSA's cash reserves at once. Keeping part of the $350,000 retained profit inside the business preserves a liquidity buffer to absorb the 9.8% rise in semiconductor and shelf-sensor component costs without breaching supermarket supply agreements or delaying the 140-store rollout.

Point 2: Fixed equal repayments make the $600,000 debt predictable, so CSA can budget its cash flow precisely alongside fixed costs of $340,000 a year and interest payable, which rose from $55,000 to $78,000. Because the loan is external debt rather than new share capital, Matteo Ricci retains full ownership and control of the private limited company; no outside investor gains voting rights, and the flat laissez-faire structure can continue without shareholder interference in day-to-day decisions about the 38 employees and the sensor platform.

    Question: CSA must train 15 field technicians to install and calibrate the new calibrated mounting kits across its 140 supermarket stores. Consider on-the-job training or off-the-job training at the regional college. Which should CSA choose? Justify your decision.

    Answer: Interest rate rise (4.9% to 5.6%): If CSA's $600,000 ten-year bank loan is variable-rate, the 0.7% rise adds about $4,200 a year to interest costs, modest against interest payable already budgeted into CSA's accounts. Minimum wage increase (5.4%, from $13.10 to $13.81 per hour): With a workforce of 38 concentrated in field installation and warehouse roles, most near the minimum wage, CSA's annual wage base is roughly 38 staff multiplied by about 2,000 hours and $13.10, around $995,600, so a 5.4% rise adds roughly $53,700 a year. Component cost inflation (9.8% semiconductors and shelf sensors): CSA's $18.50 variable cost per unit is dominated by sensor hardware, so a 9.8% rise in components implies roughly $1.10–$1.30 of extra cost per unit; at 60,000 units that is about $66,000 to $78,000 a year, directly eroding the $8.00 contribution per unit to around $6.70–$6.90 and raising the break-even output from 42,500 units to roughly 50,000 units. It also weakens the business-case narrative used to justify the $950,000 expansion.

Conclusion: The 9.8% rise in component costs will have the greatest impact. It hits every one of CSA's 60,000 units sold, totals roughly $66,000 to $78,000 a year, erodes the $8.00 contribution and pushes break-even output upward — threatening the very margin that makes the $950,000 platform viable. The wage rise is the second-largest burden at roughly $53,700, while the interest-rate rise is the smallest and can be managed by fixing the loan; CSA should also negotiate component supply contracts and push for the $0.15 per-shelf premium to pass costs through.

--- MAIN STEM ---
Bramblewick Civic Software (BCS) is a public limited company in the public-sector software (govtech) sector, employing a workforce of 64. Founded in 2013 by Yusuf Rahman, the business supplies council management and permit-processing software to local authorities across the country and operates a hierarchical structure with autocratic leadership. BCS plans to invest $1,100,000 in a new AI permit-processing platform for local councils, financed by a $700,000 share issue and $400,000 retained profit. It has fixed costs of $520,000 a year, a variable cost of $95 a unit and a selling price of $135, and currently produces 22,000 units a year. BCS faces two operational problems: quality complaints about bugs in its permit module are rising and the business has a skills gap in AI and machine-learning staff.

--- APPENDIX 1 — MARKETING/OPS ---
Market Research Summary — October 2026: A survey of 320 council procurement officers found 66% would upgrade to an AI permit-processing platform within 18 months, while 58% still use paper-based permit systems. BCS delivered 27 council contracts last year, and average permit turnaround on its current platform fell from 14 days to 6 days. Customer complaints fell from 33 to 17 per month. Net promoter score is 61. A training needs analysis shows 18 of 64 staff lack AI and machine-learning skills; off-the-job courses at the civic-tech institute cost $1,100 per employee. Staff complete on-the-job training on the permit module and off-the-job training at the civic-tech institute.

--- APPENDIX 2 — FINANCIAL DATA ---

Capital employed | 9,600 | 11,400

(2) The national minimum wage will rise by 4.8% from $13.30 to $13.94 per hour from April 2026. (3) Local council IT budgets are capped at a 2.0% increase next year, while council pay and energy costs are forecast to rise 6.5% and inflation is running at 6.1%, squeezing discretionary software spending.

  Q1(a) [8 marks]
    Question: BCS plans to raise $700,000 of its $1,100,000 expansion through a share issue. Explain two advantages for BCS of using a share issue rather than a bank loan.
    Answer: Point 1: A share issue raises permanent capital with no fixed repayment schedule and no interest, so BCS avoids adding heavy debt-service costs on top of fixed costs of $520,000 a year. The AI permit-processing platform will take time to generate revenue from the 66% of 320 surveyed council procurement officers willing to upgrade within 18 months; equity financing lets BCS fund that ramp-up without breaching cash reserves or missing council service-level commitments.

Point 2: Selling shares to a wider investor base spreads the risk of an ambitious $1,100,000 public-sector technology project across many shareholders rather than concentrating it on BCS and its retained profit alone. As a public limited company, BCS can also use the issue to raise its profile with council clients and future investors, and the permanent capital strengthens the balance sheet — reflected in capital employed of $11,400,000 — supporting further contracts without granting any lender security over the platform or diluting control in the same way debt covenants might restrict autocratic decision-making.

    Answer: Free 90-day pilot for the first 10 councils: A free pilot lets councils test the AI permit-processing platform on real applications, directly demonstrating the fall in turnaround from 14 days to 6 days BCS achieved on its current platform. Councils are risk-averse public bodies, and a no-cost trial lowers the barrier to change for the 58% still using paper-based permit systems. Risks are that the pilot is not free for BCS — it consumes support capacity from a 64-person team — and unsuccessful deployments could publicly sour future procurement, but converting even a few pilots into contracts validates the whole $1,100,000 investment.

Local Government Chronicle case-study feature: A trade-press feature builds credibility with councillors and procurement officers nationwide and positions Yusuf Rahman as a thought leader. Print coverage is cheap and enduring, but it is passive: procurement cycles are long, officers rarely buy directly from an article, and measurable lead generation is weak compared with hands-on proof.

Targeted LinkedIn advertising: LinkedIn advertising can reach the exact procurement officers whose attitudes BCS measured — 66% of 320 officers willing to upgrade within 18 months — with measurable click-through and retargeting. However, busy officers are wary of unsolicited adverts, public-sector procurement usually requires formal tenders and due diligence rather than advert-driven impulse, and ad spend is wasted on officers whose councils lack the budget headroom created by the 2.0% IT budget cap.

Recommendation: BCS should choose the free 90-day pilot. It converts the platform's strongest proof point — 14-day to 6-day permit turnaround — into signed council contracts, engaging the 58% paper-based holdouts directly and generating case-study evidence for every later campaign. The trade-press feature is rejected as too passive to drive tenders, and LinkedIn advertising is rejected as spray-and-pray against a capped-budget, compliance-driven public-sector buyer that needs hands-on, risk-free evidence first.

--- MAIN STEM ---
Aldermont Route Optimisation (ARO) is a private limited company in the logistics technology (SaaS) sector, employing a workforce of 52. Founded in 2016 by Helena Duarte, the business supplies route-optimization software to national freight and delivery fleets and operates a flat organisational structure with democratic leadership. ARO plans to invest $1,000,000 in a new live-traffic AI route-optimization engine, financed by $700,000 of venture capital and $300,000 retained profit. It has fixed costs of $630,000 a year, a variable cost of $140 a unit and a selling price of $210, and currently produces 20,000 units a year. ARO faces two operational problems: customer onboarding is taking 6 weeks instead of the 4-week target, and labour turnover among customer-support staff has reached 17%.

--- APPENDIX 1 — MARKETING/OPS ---
Operations Log — Q3 2025: ARO's platform planned 18,400 routes last quarter across 240 fleet clients, with 96% of routes generated in under 3 minutes. Average client fuel use fell 11.5% and delivery miles per route fell 17%. Onboarding averages 6 weeks against a 4-week target. Customer complaints fell from 29 to 15 per month, but labour turnover in the support team reached 17%. Market research of 500 fleet managers found 68% would switch providers for a 15% fuel-saving guarantee, and 44% cite real-time traffic as their top priority. A training needs analysis shows 16 of 52 staff have not completed on-the-job training on the new engine; off-the-job courses at the logistics institute cost $800 per employee. Staff complete on-the-job training on the optimization engine and off-the-job training at the logistics institute.

--- APPENDIX 2 — FINANCIAL DATA ---
Title: Extract from the Statement of Profit or Loss and Capital employed data of Aldermont Route Optimisation for the year ended 31 March 2025 ($ '000)
Headers: ['Financial Metric', '2024', '2025']

Operating profit | 870 | 1,176

--- APPENDIX 3 — EXTERNAL ENVIRONMENT ---
Economic and Business Bulletin (November 2026): (1) The central bank raised the base interest rate from 5.1% to 5.9%, lifting costs for variable-rate business loans. (2) The national minimum wage will rise by 6.1% from $12.90 to $13.69 per hour from April 2026. (3) Diesel prices have risen 14.2% year-on-year and freight demand grew 5.5%, while transport and logistics inflation is running at 6.8% — making fuel efficiency a top buying criterion for fleets.

--- QUESTIONS ---
  Q1(a) [8 marks]
    Question: ARO plans to raise $700,000 of the $1,000,000 expansion through venture capital. Explain two advantages for ARO of venture capital rather than a bank loan.
    Answer: Point 1: Venture capital carries no fixed repayment schedule and no monthly interest, so ARO avoids straining cash flow while fixed costs are already $630,000 a year. The live-traffic AI engine will take months to generate new subscription revenue from the 68% of 500 surveyed fleet managers willing to switch for a fuel-saving guarantee; equity financing lets ARO fund that ramp-up without breaching covenants or repossession risk on the platform.

Point 2: Venture capitalists typically bring logistics-sector expertise, introductions to national fleets and board credibility that accelerate enterprise sales — worth far more than cash to a 52-person private limited company competing against larger incumbents. Unlike a bank, a venture investor shares the downside if the engine launch slips beyond the 4-week onboarding target recovery, and Helena Duarte keeps control of daily operations while gaining a partner motivated to see the $1,000,000 investment succeed.
    Keywords: venture capital, route-optimization, $700,000, $1,000,000, $630,000, retained profit
    Mark scheme: knowledge_max_2: 1 mark for each valid advantage identified (max 2). | application_analysis_max_6: Up to 3 marks per point for contextual explanation and analysis applied to Aldermont Route Optimisation and its expansion decision.

  Q1(b) [12 marks]
    Question: ARO is launching its live-traffic AI route-optimization engine to national freight and delivery fleets. Consider a weekly webinar and demo series with live traffic simulations, advertising in Fleet Management Weekly trade magazine, or sponsoring a national logistics conference. Which should ARO choose to promote the launch? Justify your recommendation.
    Answer: Webinar and demo series with live traffic simulations: A weekly webinar lets ARO prove its strongest asset — 96% of 18,400 routes generated in under 3 minutes, delivering 11.5% average fuel savings — in front of exactly the 68% of the 500 surveyed fleet managers willing to switch for a 15% fuel-saving guarantee. Demonstrations are interactive, capture leads automatically, and cost little compared with a conference stand. Drawbacks are that some senior managers avoid webinars and attendance can fade after the first sessions, so ARO must keep content sharp and follow up personally within 48 hours.

Fleet Management Weekly advertising: A trade-magazine campaign reaches a targeted logistics readership and builds brand credibility cheaply over several months. However, print advertising is passive and hard to measure; fleet managers rarely switch SaaS providers on the strength of an advert, and the 11.5% fuel-saving proof is far more persuasive shown live than described on paper.

National logistics conference sponsorship: Sponsoring a headline national conference puts ARO in front of hundreds of fleet decision-makers and anchors its brand beside industry leaders. The magazine advert is rejected as too passive to convert, and the conference sponsorship is rejected as a single, expensive burst of exposure unsuited to a long enterprise sales cycle and an expansion already absorbing venture capital.

--- MAIN STEM ---
Brackenmoor Energy Management (BEM) is a partnership in the building energy management software sector, employing a workforce of 26. Founded in 2019 by Sofia Marchetti and Tom Whitmore, the business supplies smart energy monitoring for commercial buildings to property investors and operates a flat organisational structure with democratic leadership. BEM plans to invest $950,000 in a new predictive-fault-alert analytics module, financed by $650,000 of new partner capital and $300,000 retained profit. It has fixed costs of $275,000 a year, a variable cost of $32 a unit and a selling price of $44.50, and currently produces 34,000 units a year. BEM faces two operational problems: its sensor fault rate has reached 2.2% and labour turnover among installation engineers is rising after two resignations in six months.

--- APPENDIX 1 — MARKETING/OPS ---
Quality and Waste Report — September 2025: BEM monitors 96 commercial buildings with 1,150 IoT energy meters. The average monitored building has cut energy use by 14%, saving $48,000 a year each. The sensor fault rate is 2.2%, up from 1.6% a year ago, and wasted engineer callouts cost $21,000 last quarter. Customer complaints fell from 12 to 9 per month. Market research of 350 facilities managers found 74% would pay for predictive fault alerts and 51% plan to retrofit within 2 years using green-building grants. A training needs analysis shows 9 of 26 staff have not completed on-the-job training on the new analytics dashboard; off-the-job courses cost $650 per employee. Staff complete on-the-job training on the analytics dashboard and off-the-job training with the software vendor.

--- APPENDIX 2 — FINANCIAL DATA ---
Title: Extract from the Statement of Profit or Loss and Capital employed data of Brackenmoor Energy Management for the year ended 31 March 2025 ($ '000)
Headers: ['Financial Metric', '2024', '2025']

Gross profit | 1,140 | 1,428
Operating profit | 342 | 476
Capital employed | 2,280 | 2,720

--- APPENDIX 3 — EXTERNAL ENVIRONMENT ---
Economic and Business Bulletin (November 2026): (1) The central bank raised the base interest rate from 4.5% to 5.2%. (2) The national minimum wage will rise by 5.9% from $12.80 to $13.56 per hour from April 2026. (3) Commercial electricity and gas prices have risen 16.5% year-on-year, while office vacancy rates stand at 18% and a government green-building grant now covers 30% of retrofit costs.

Unlike a bank loan, a partner shares the risk if the $950,000 launch takes longer to convert the 74% of 350 facilities managers who want predictive alerts into paying clients, and there is no collateral or repossession risk hanging over the partnership's assets.

Point 2: A new partner can bring energy-sector expertise, client relationships and hands-on operational capacity that a bank cannot — for example, relationships with commercial landlords planning retrofits under the 30% green-building grant. Because profits are shared, the partner is motivated to make the module succeed, and the founder partners, Sofia Marchetti and Tom Whitmore, keep decision-making inside the flat democratic structure without a lender imposing conditions on how the $650,000 is spent.

--- MAIN STEM ---
Dovetail Claims Technology (DCT) is a public limited company in the insurance technology (insurtech) sector, employing a workforce of 180. Founded in 2011 by Elena Vasquez, the business supplies claims-automation software to insurance brokers and operates a hierarchical structure with democratic leadership. DCT plans to invest $2,100,000 in a new generative-AI claims triage platform, financed by a $1,500,000 share issue and $600,000 retained profit. It has fixed costs of $1,300,000 a year, a variable cost of $260 a unit and a selling price of $360, and currently produces 31,000 units a year. DCT faces two operational problems: quality complaints about auto-approved claims have risen and labour turnover among data-labelling staff has reached 19%.

--- APPENDIX 1 — MARKETING/OPS ---
Operations Log — Q3 2025: DCT's platform processed 1.9 million claims documents last year for 320 broker clients, cutting average claim-handling time from 6 days to 2 days. --- MAIN STEM ---
Harborne Vision Institute (HVI) is a private limited company in the private healthcare sector, specialising in ophthalmology, employing a workforce of 38. Founded in 2011 by Dr Lena Harborne, HVI operates two eye clinics in the Harborne district and uses a hierarchical structure with democratic leadership. HVI plans to invest $920,000 in a second laser eye-surgery suite with energy-efficient solar panels, financed by a $600,000 ten-year bank loan and $320,000 retained profit. It has fixed costs of $306,000 a year, a variable cost of $14.50 a unit and a selling price of $40.00, and currently produces 78,000 units a year (treatment episodes). HVI faces two problems: nursing-staff turnover of 16% and rising patient complaints about waiting times.

--- APPENDIX 1 — MARKETING/OPS ---
Operations and Patient Report — Q3 2025: The two clinics delivered 19,500 treatment units last quarter at a rework rate of 1.3%, down from 2.6% a year ago. Patient complaints fell from 27 to 15 per month. A survey of 700 patients found that 59% would attend extended Saturday clinics and 44% would pay up to $25 more for same-day consultations. Average waiting time is 14 days. A training needs analysis shows 13 of 38 staff have not completed on-the-job training on the new laser equipment; off-the-job training courses at the hospital college cost $820 per employee.

--- APPENDIX 2 — FINANCIAL DATA ---
Title: Extract from the Statement of Profit or Loss and Capital employed data of Harborne Vision Institute for the year ended 31 March 2025 ($ '000)
Headers: ['Financial Metric', '2024', '2025']

Gross profit | 910 | 1,404
Operating profit | 312 | 624
Capital employed | 3,120 | 4,160
Interest payable | 26 | 38

--- APPENDIX 3 — EXTERNAL ENVIRONMENT ---
Economic and Business Bulletin (November 2026): (1) The central bank has raised the base interest rate from 3.75% to 4.5%, increasing borrowing costs for businesses with variable-rate loans. (2) The national minimum wage will rise by 5.9% from $12.80 to $13.56 per hour from April 2026, raising wage bills across private healthcare. (3) Ophthalmic lens and consumable costs have risen 8.8% year-on-year, healthcare inflation is running at 6.9%, and consumer spending on private eye care grew 4.6% in the same period.
