  Q1(a) [8 marks]
    Question: HVI plans to finance part of its laser expansion with a ten-year bank loan. Explain two advantages for HVI of using retained profit to fund the expansion instead of the bank loan.
    Answer: Point 1: Using retained profit costs HVI nothing in interest or repayments, protecting cash flow at a time when it already carries fixed costs of $306,000 a year and a $600,000 bank loan commitment. Every dollar not paid to a lender can absorb the 8.8% rise in ophthalmic lens and consumable costs, helping HVI hold its $40.00 selling price and protect the $25.50 contribution per treatment unit without squeezing patients or margins.

Point 2: Retained profit avoids the collateral and repayment risk attached to a bank loan, so the $320,000 is available without putting the new $920,000 laser eye-surgery suite at risk of repossession if demand disappoints. It also preserves Dr Lena Harborne's ownership and control, since no external lender can impose conditions on how the second suite is staffed or run. Retained profit is also flexible — it carries no fixed monthly repayment schedule, unlike the loan, which matters while the 16% nursing-staff turnover is being addressed and waiting times stabilise.

However, HVI is a 38-employee ophthalmology clinic funding a $920,000 expansion; national production and airtime costs are extremely high, and most of the audience would live outside HVI's referral catchment or not be suitable laser candidates, so a large share of spend would be wasted. Social media influencer marketing: Working with trusted local health and lifestyle influencers targets exactly the 59% of surveyed patients who would attend extended Saturday clinics and the 44% who would pay up to $25 more for same-day consultations. Cost per reached patient is low, engagement is measurable, and the eco-conscious, health-focused positioning of the new suite with solar panels can be shown directly. Results build more slowly than TV and depend on influencer credibility, so content must be medically accurate.

Recommendation: HVI should choose social media influencer marketing. It reaches the precise segment already identified in its research (59% and 44%), costs far less than television for a 38-person business, scales better than local radio, and reinforces the clinic's modern, patient-centred image. Television is rejected as unaffordable and untargeted for a two-site clinic; local radio is rejected as the lead channel because its reach is too narrow for county-wide laser referrals, though short local bursts could support the launch. Influencers alone lack mass reach, so HVI should pair them with its own patient-referral programme and in-clinic leaflets.

    Question: Explain one advantage and one disadvantage for HVI of installing energy-efficient solar panels at its clinics.

They also strengthen HVI's image with health-conscious patients — the same audience behind the 59% Saturday-clinic and 44% same-day-consultation demand — signalling that modern private care can be delivered responsibly, which supports retention of private patients and differentiation from NHS alternatives.

Disadvantage: The panels add an upfront cost on top of an already stretched $920,000 project funded partly by a $600,000 bank loan, increasing immediate cash strain and the amount HVI must borrow or repay. Installation can also disrupt clinical sessions and the 14-day waiting-time target: roof works above surgery theatres raise safety and continuity-of-care risks, and any fault or maintenance visit takes rooms offline, which HVI cannot afford while nursing-staff turnover is 16% and full laser capacity is not yet proven.
    Keywords: solar panels, $920,000, $306,000, $600,000, 59%, 14 days
    Mark scheme: knowledge_max_2: 1 mark for a valid advantage and 1 mark for a valid disadvantage. | application_analysis_max_6: Up to 3 marks per point for detailed contextual development linked to HVI's costs, demand data and expansion.

  Q4(b) [12 marks]
    Question: Using Appendix 3, evaluate how the interest rate rise to 4.5%, the 5.9% minimum wage increase and the 8.8% rise in input costs will affect HVI. Which change will have the greatest impact? Justify your answer.
    Answer: Interest rate rise (3.75% to 4.5%): If HVI's $600,000 ten-year bank loan is variable-rate, the 0.75 percentage point rise adds about $4,500 a year to financing costs — real but modest next to $306,000 of fixed costs. Higher rates also make further borrowing for clinic number three more expensive, could raise renewal quotes on the hire-purchase-style equipment leases, and may make patients more cautious about elective procedures, softening the 4.6% growth in private eye-care spending. HVI can partly shield itself by fixing the loan rate.

Minimum wage increase (5.9%, to $13.56 per hour): HVI employs 38 staff, mostly nurses, technicians and reception alongside clinical leadership; clinical pay sits well above minimum wage, but support, cleaning and administrative roles are affected. If even 15 of the 38 staff sit near the minimum wage on roughly 40-hour weeks, the 5.9% rise adds roughly $1,250 per affected worker per year — around $19,000 a year — on top of the 16% turnover already inflating recruitment and the $820-per-head retraining bill. The impact is material but concentrated on the support-staff budget.

Input cost inflation (8.8% ophthalmic lens and consumables): HVI's variable cost of $14.50 a unit is dominated by lenses, viscoelastics and sterile consumables. An 8.8% rise on the consumable share (say 60% of the variable cost, $8.70) adds roughly $0.77 per treatment unit; at 78,000 units a year that is about $60,000 a year, cutting contribution per unit from $25.50 toward $24.73 and eroding roughly 3% of margin. The private eye-care market grew 4.6%, so passing on only part of the increase risks a competitive backlash while absorbing it all bites directly into ROCE.

Conclusion: The 8.8% rise in input costs will have the greatest impact. It strikes every one of the 78,000 units sold, totalling roughly $60,000 a year and steadily eroding the $25.50 contribution margin that justifies the $920,000 laser suite. The minimum wage rise is the second most serious risk, concentrated in support roles and amplified by 16% turnover, while the interest-rate increase is the smallest in cash terms (about $4,500 a year on the drawn loan) and can be managed by fixing the rate. Even so, HVI must address all three — negotiate consumable contracts, redesign support-role rosters productively, and review the loan structure — or the improved cost-of-sales performance shown in Appendix 2 will unwind.
    Keywords: 4.5%, 5.9%, 8.8%, $13.56, $14.50, $600,000
    Mark scheme: level_1_1_to_4: Identifies the external factors with limited application to HVI. | level_2_5_to_8: Analyses the impact of at least two external changes on HVI's costs, revenue or financing in context. | level_3_9_to_12: Detailed evaluation of all three external changes in the context of HVI with a well-justified judgement that input-cost inflation has the greatest impact and why the other two are smaller.

--- MAIN STEM ---
Hexfield Code Academy (HCA) is a private limited company in the education sector, specialising in digital-skills training, employing a workforce of 26. Founded in 2018 by Rhea Calloway, HCA runs coding bootcamps for career-changers and uses a flat organisational structure with laissez-faire leadership. HCA plans to invest $650,000 in a second campus in Leeds with expanded data-analytics labs and solar panels, financed by a $400,000 five-year bank loan and a $250,000 share issue. It has fixed costs of $715,000 a year, a variable cost of $450 a unit and a selling price of $1,000, and currently produces 6,800 units a year (course enrolments). HCA faces two problems: an instructor skills gap in cloud computing and rising learner complaints about outdated course materials.

--- APPENDIX 1 — MARKETING/OPS ---
Market Research Summary — Q3 2025: Market research of 800 prospective learners found that 57% would enrol on a data-analytics bootcamp and 46% would pay up to $150 more per month for evening and weekend classes. Completion rates last term reached 87%, up from 79% a year ago. Learner complaints fell from 44 to 26 per intake across the 1,675 enrolments delivered in Q3. An on-the-job training needs analysis shows 9 of 26 staff have not completed platform upskilling; off-the-job training courses at the city college cost $700 per employee.

--- APPENDIX 2 — FINANCIAL DATA ---

(2) The national minimum wage will rise by 6.2% from $12.20 to $12.96 per hour from April 2026, raising wage bills across the education sector. (3) Cloud licensing and laptop costs have risen 10.8% year-on-year, education inflation is running at 7.2%, and consumer spending on private digital-skills training grew 5.4% in the same period.

    Question: HCA plans to finance part of its Leeds expansion with a bank loan and a share issue. Explain two advantages for HCA of using a share issue instead of a larger bank loan.

Every dollar not paid to a lender can absorb the 10.8% rise in cloud licensing and laptop costs, helping HCA hold its $1,000 course price and protect the $550 contribution per enrolment rather than passing costs straight on to learners.

Point 2: Issuing shares spreads the ownership of HCA across more shareholders, so the expansion risk is shared rather than borne by Rhea Calloway alone, and no extra collateral is required over the Leeds campus assets. It also avoids the repayment-pressure and covenant risk of a larger loan at a time when the base interest rate has just risen from 4.25% to 5.0% — interest payable already rose from $30,000 to $41,000, and a bigger loan would compound that burden just as the Leeds site ramps up enrolments.

    Question: HCA is launching its data-analytics bootcamp and new Leeds campus. Consider a national television campaign, local radio sponsorship, or social media influencer marketing. Which should HCA choose to promote the launch? Justify your recommendation.
    Answer: Television campaign: A national television campaign would reach millions of viewers very quickly and build instant name recognition for the new Leeds campus. However, HCA is a 26-person academy funding a $650,000 expansion; national production and airtime costs are extremely high, and most viewers neither want to change careers into data analytics nor live near Leeds, so most spend would be wasted on the wrong audience. Television is also hard to measure beyond broad reach, which a private training business needs to justify its marketing budget.

Local radio sponsorship: Local radio is cheap, reaches Leeds and surrounding commuter belt repeatedly, and suits time-boxed messages such as enrolment deadlines for the new intake. Social media influencer marketing: Partnering with data-career YouTubers and LinkedIn creators targets exactly the 57% of surveyed learners who would enrol on a data-analytics bootcamp and the 46% who would pay up to $150 more per month for evening and weekend classes. Content can demonstrate real student outcomes, cost per reached learner is low, engagement is measurable, and the solar-powered Leeds campus and completion-rate story (87%, up from 79%) give influencers credible material. Results take time to compound and depend on influencer credibility, but the audience match is far better than TV or radio.

Recommendation: HCA should choose social media influencer marketing. It reaches the precise segment already identified in its research (57% and 46%), costs far less than television for a 26-person business, scales nationally where local radio cannot, and lets prospects see the campus and graduate outcomes directly. Television is rejected as unaffordable and untargeted; local radio is rejected as the lead channel because its reach is too narrow for a national online bootcamp, though short Leeds radio bursts could support the launch affordably. --- MAIN STEM ---
Vital Roots Meal Prep (VRM) is a private limited company in the consumer services sector, specialising in plant-based meal-prep delivery, employing a workforce of 52. Founded in 2020 by Sofia Marin, VRM prepares and delivers weekly plant-based meal boxes across the Bristol region and uses a hierarchical structure with autocratic leadership. VRM plans to invest $780,000 in a second kitchen with a refrigerated delivery fleet, financed by a $450,000 hire purchase agreement on the vans and $330,000 retained profit. It has fixed costs of $247,500 a year, a variable cost of $7.25 a unit and a selling price of $12.75, and currently produces 96,000 units a year (meal boxes). VRM faces two problems: food waste of 7.4% in the kitchen and labour turnover of 19% among delivery drivers.

--- APPENDIX 1 — MARKETING/OPS ---
Quality and Waste Report — Q3 2025: The Bristol kitchen packed 24,000 meal boxes last quarter at a mislabel and wrong-item defect rate of 2.2%, down from 3.6% a year ago. Food waste fell from 9.1% to 7.4% but remains above the 5% target. Customer complaints fell from 41 to 23 per month. A market research survey of 650 subscribers found 63% would pay up to $1.50 more per box for fully compostable packaging, and 49% of new customers cite plant-based health benefits. Average delivery time is 1.8 days. On-the-job training in food-safety is incomplete for 16 of 52 staff; off-the-job training courses at the culinary college cost $750 per employee.

--- APPENDIX 2 — FINANCIAL DATA ---
Title: Extract from the Statement of Profit or Loss and Capital employed data of Vital Roots Meal Prep for the year ended 31 March 2025 ($ '000)

Interest payable | 15 | 24

--- APPENDIX 3 — EXTERNAL ENVIRONMENT ---
Economic and Business Bulletin (November 2026): (1) The central bank has raised the base interest rate from 3.75% to 4.5%, increasing borrowing costs for businesses with variable-rate loans and hire purchase. (2) The national minimum wage will rise by 6.4% from $12.50 to $13.30 per hour from April 2026, raising wage bills across food delivery and kitchens. (3) Plant-protein and compostable packaging input costs have risen 11.2% year-on-year, food inflation is running at 7.8%, and consumer spending on plant-based products grew 6.1% in the same period.

  Q1(a) [8 marks]

Every dollar not paid as hire-purchase interest can absorb the plant-protein and compostable-packaging inflation or fund the new kitchen's launch marketing, helping VRM keep its $12.75 price competitive against other meal-prep firms.

Point 2: Retained profit carries no repossession risk on the refrigerated vans if weekly payments are missed or demand dips over winter, so VRM keeps full ownership and control of the delivery fleet from day one. It also avoids adding to the hire-purchase burden at a time when the base interest rate has risen from 3.75% to 4.5% — interest payable already rose from $15,000 to $24,000 — and unlike external finance it imposes no usage mileage or maintenance conditions on how the second kitchen and its vans are operated.

  Q1(b) [12 marks]
    Question: VRM is launching its second kitchen and expanded delivery zone. Consider a national television campaign, local radio sponsorship, or social media influencer marketing. Which should VRM choose to promote the launch? Justify your recommendation.
    Answer: Television campaign: A national television campaign would put the Vital Roots brand in front of millions of viewers quickly and could build strong awareness of the plant-based subscription offer. However, VRM is a 52-employee regional business funding a $780,000 expansion; national production and airtime costs are extremely high, and most viewers live far outside the Bristol delivery zone, where delivery time averages 1.8 days — distant customers cannot receive fresh boxes, so spend would be largely wasted.     Mark scheme: level_1_1_to_4: Limited knowledge or outline of the promotional options with minimal context. | level_2_5_to_8: Detailed discussion of the advantages and disadvantages of at least two options in the context of VRM with some judgement. | level_3_9_to_12: Detailed discussion of all three options in the context of VRM with a well-justified recommendation explaining why television and radio are rejected.

    Question: VRM's labour turnover is 19% among delivery drivers and food waste of 7.4% persists in the kitchen. Explain two benefits for VRM of autocratic leadership in this context.

A single decisive manager can re-plan deliveries mid-week without committee delay, directly protecting delivery reliability and the fall in complaints from 41 to 23 per month.

In a 52-person operation with 16 of 52 staff still untrained in food-safety, clear instruction reduces errors quickly, contains the 2.2% mislabel defect rate and tightens portion control, while turnover of 19% is addressed through induction and pay review rather than diluted decision-making.

    Question: VRM must train 16 kitchen staff on food-safety procedures. Consider on-the-job training or off-the-job training at the culinary college. Which should VRM choose? Justify your decision.
    Answer: On-the-job training: Training in the kitchen itself is directly relevant to VRM's own recipes, labelling and fridge-temperature routines, costs nothing in course fees, and keeps the 16 staff productive, protecting output of 24,000 meal boxes last quarter and the 1.8-day delivery promise. Drawbacks are that senior kitchen staff lose preparation time while training others, bad habits can spread between pickers, and no external certificate is awarded — a problem if a retail partner audits food-safety compliance or if VRM wants to prove standards to insurers after any contamination incident.

Off-the-job training: The culinary college course at $750 per employee gives structured, current food-safety certification for all 16 staff, costing $12,000 in total — affordable against a $780,000 second-kitchen investment. It removes kitchen staff from production, however, reducing short-term capacity during peak subscription weeks, and the generic content may not match VRM's exact labelling and allergen workflows, so follow-up on-site coaching would still be needed.

Decision: VRM should choose on-the-job training for the bulk of the 16 staff, supported by off-the-job culinary college places for two supervisors who can then deliver refresher food-safety sessions in-house. On-the-job training is cheapest, kitchen-specific and avoids cutting into delivery capacity while turnover is 19% and waste is above target. Full off-the-job training is rejected because withdrawing 16 staff and spending $12,000 up front would strain the launch of the second kitchen; college certification can be phased in once the 2.2% defect rate and 7.4% waste figure move decisively downward and the second kitchen reaches stable output.
    Keywords: on-the-job training, off-the-job training, $750, 16 of 52 staff, food-safety, $780,000
    Mark scheme: level_1_1_to_4: Basic description of the two training methods with limited application to VRM. | level_2_5_to_8: Detailed analysis of the benefits and drawbacks of one or both training methods in the context of VRM. | level_3_9_to_12: Comprehensive evaluation of both training methods in the context of VRM with a well-justified decision covering cost, capacity, certification and compliance.

Evaluation: Performance improved, though from a low base. Gross profit grew $135,000 (41.7%) as revenue rose $144,000 and the cost of sales share of revenue fell from 70.0% to 62.5%, helped by the defect rate falling from 3.6% to 2.2%, food waste dropping from 9.1% to 7.4% and complaints from 41 to 23 a month. Disadvantage: Compostable materials cost more than conventional plastic, increasing the $7.25 variable cost per box and squeezing margins unless the $1.50 premium is accepted by enough subscribers or backed by the new second-kitchen scale. Any failure in the new packaging — weaker seals, shorter chill life or leaks in transit — would also raise the 2.2% mislabel/defect rate, increase food waste above the 7.4% level and destroy the 1.8-day delivery promise that underpins VRM's reputation with retail and corporate customers.

    Question: Using Appendix 3, evaluate how the interest rate rise to 4.5%, the 6.4% minimum wage increase and the 11.2% rise in input costs will affect VRM. Which change will have the greatest impact? Justify your answer.
    Answer: Interest rate rise (3.75% to 4.5%): If the $450,000 hire purchase agreement on the vans is variable-rate, the 0.75 percentage point rise adds about $3,400 a year to finance costs — real but modest next to $247,500 of fixed costs. Higher rates also make further borrowing for a third kitchen more expensive, could raise the cost of renewing the fleet, and may temper consumer appetite for subscription meal services, slowing the 6.1% growth in plant-based spending. VRM can fix the hire-purchase rate or accelerate retained-profit repayments to limit exposure.

Minimum wage increase (6.4%, to $13.30 per hour): VRM employs 52 staff, many drivers, pickers and kitchen operatives near or below middle-band wages. If roughly 30 of the 52 staff sit close to the minimum wage on 40-hour weeks, the 6.4% rise adds roughly $1,660 per affected worker a year — around $50,000 a year — on top of 19% driver turnover already inflating recruitment and onboarding costs. This is materially larger than the rate impact and lands directly on VRM's largest cost line, wages, though many Bristol drivers are paid above minimum.

Input cost inflation (11.2% plant-protein and compostable packaging): VRM's variable cost of $7.25 a unit is dominated by plant proteins, grains, fresh produce and packaging. An 11.2% rise on, say, 70% of the variable cost ($5.08) adds roughly $0.57 per box; at 96,000 boxes a year that is about $55,000 a year, cutting contribution per unit from $5.50 toward $4.93 and eroding roughly 10% of margin. With 6.1% growth in plant-based spending intact, VRM can pass through part of the increase via the $1.50 compostable premium, but full pass-through would surrender its price edge against own-label supermarket ready meals.

Conclusion: The 11.2% rise in input costs will have the greatest impact. It strikes every one of the 96,000 boxes, totalling roughly $55,000 a year and steadily eroding the $5.50 contribution margin that justifies the $780,000 second-kitchen expansion. The minimum wage rise is the second most serious risk, around $50,000 a year on support and delivery roles and amplified by 19% turnover, while the interest-rate increase is the smallest in cash terms (roughly $3,400 a year) and can be managed by fixing the hire-purchase rate. VRM should therefore renegotiate protein supply contracts, push the compostable premium and optimise routes — or the gross-margin gains in Appendix 2 will be reversed within a year.
    Keywords: 4.5%, 6.4%, 11.2%, $13.30, $7.25, $450,000
    Mark scheme: level_1_1_to_4: Identifies the external factors with limited application to VRM. | level_2_5_to_8: Analyses the impact of at least two external changes on VRM's costs, revenue or financing in context. | level_3_9_to_12: Detailed evaluation of all three external changes in the context of VRM with a well-justified judgement that input-cost inflation has the greatest impact and why the other two are smaller.

--- MAIN STEM ---
Rowan Physio & Sports Clinic (RPS) is a private limited company in the healthcare sector, specialising in physiotherapy and sports rehabilitation, employing a workforce of 31. Founded in 2015 by Dr Natalie Rowan, RPS uses a flat organisational structure with democratic leadership from its Guildford clinic. RPS plans to invest $540,000 in a second clinic in Woking with a hydrotherapy pool and water-recycling technology, financed by a $300,000 five-year bank loan and $240,000 retained profit. It has fixed costs of $342,000 a year, a variable cost of $22.00 a unit and a selling price of $60.00, and currently produces 42,000 units a year (treatment sessions). RPS faces two problems: a skills gap in qualified sports physiotherapists and rising patient complaints about waiting times.

--- APPENDIX 1 — MARKETING/OPS ---
Clinic Operations Report — Q3 2025: The Guildford clinic delivered 10,500 treatment sessions last quarter at a rework error rate of 1.1%, down from 2.4% a year ago. Patient complaints fell from 25 to 14 per month. A survey of 620 patients found 61% would use the new Woking clinic and 47% would pay up to $20 more per session for early-morning appointments. Average waiting time is 12 days. On-the-job training on the new hydrotherapy equipment is incomplete for 11 of 31 staff; off-the-job training courses at the hospital college cost $950 per employee.

--- APPENDIX 2 — FINANCIAL DATA ---
Title: Extract from the Statement of Profit or Loss and Capital employed data of Rowan Physio & Sports Clinic for the year ended 31 March 2025 ($ '000)

(2) The national minimum wage will rise by 6.0% from $12.90 to $13.67 per hour from April 2026, raising wage bills across private healthcare. (3) Medical equipment and consumable costs have risen 9.2% year-on-year, healthcare inflation is running at 6.7%, and consumer spending on private physiotherapy grew 4.2% in the same period.

  Q1(a) [8 marks]
    Question: RPS plans to finance part of its Woking expansion with a five-year bank loan. Explain two advantages for RPS of using retained profit to fund the expansion instead of the bank loan.
    Answer: Point 1: Using $240,000 of retained profit instead of borrowing more costs RPS nothing in interest or repayment charges, protecting cash flow at a time when it already carries fixed costs of $342,000 a year and a $300,000 five-year bank loan. Every dollar not paid to a lender can absorb the 9.2% rise in medical equipment and consumable costs, helping RPS hold its $60.00 session price and protect the $38.00 contribution per session without squeezing patients or referring clinicians.

Point 2: Retained profit avoids the collateral and repayment risk attached to a bank loan, so the $240,000 is available without putting the new $540,000 Woking clinic or its hydrotherapy pool at risk of repossession if demand disappoints. It also preserves Dr Natalie Rowan's ownership and control, since no external lender can impose conditions on how Woking is staffed, marketed or equipped. At a time when the base interest rate has risen from 4.0% to 4.75%, keeping borrowings low also shields RPS's variable-rate loan from further cost increases and keeps the 12-day waiting list affordable to run down.
    Keywords: retained profit, bank loan, $240,000, $300,000, $540,000, $342,000
    Mark scheme: knowledge_max_2: 1 mark for each valid advantage identified (max 2). | application_analysis_max_6: Up to 3 marks per point for contextual explanation and analysis applied to Rowan Physio & Sports Clinic and its expansion decision.

  Q1(b) [12 marks]
    Question: RPS is launching its second clinic in Woking with a hydrotherapy pool. Consider a national television campaign, local radio sponsorship, or social media influencer marketing. Which should RPS choose to promote the launch? Justify your recommendation.
    Answer: Television campaign: A national television campaign would put the Rowan Physio & Sports Clinic brand in front of millions of viewers quickly and could build awareness of the hydrotherapy offer. However, RPS is a 31-employee clinic funding a $540,000 expansion; national production and airtime costs are extremely high, and most viewers live far outside the Guildford–Woking catchment or have no need for private physiotherapy, so most spend would be wasted. Television also suits mass consumer brands rather than appointment-led healthcare, where local trust and clinician reputation drive bookings.

Local radio sponsorship: Local radio is far cheaper, reaches Guildford and Woking commuters repeatedly, and suits appointment-led messages such as early-morning sessions and waiting-time reductions. Its limitation is reach beyond the catchment — patients travel from across Surrey and Hampshire for specialist sports rehabilitation, so a purely local station cannot fill the Woking hydrotherapy pool or build county-wide referral relationships with clubs and gyms.

Social media influencer marketing: Working with local sports clubs, fitness creators and post-injury recovery bloggers targets exactly the 61% of surveyed patients who would use the Woking clinic and the 47% willing to pay up to $20 more per session for early-morning appointments. Content can show real recoveries, cost per reached patient is low, engagement is measurable through booking codes, and the water-recycling and sustainability story of the hydrotherapy pool gives influencers distinctive material. Results build more slowly than TV and depend on influencer credibility, but the audience match is far better.

Recommendation: RPS should choose social media influencer marketing. It reaches the precise segment identified in its research (61% Woking interest, 47% early-morning premium), costs far less than television for a 31-person clinic, scales across the county where local radio cannot, and showcases the hydrotherapy pool effectively. Television is rejected as unaffordable and untargeted; local radio is rejected as the lead channel because its reach is too narrow for county-wide sports-referral growth, though short Woking drive-time bursts could support the launch. Influencers alone lack broadcast reach, so RPS should pair them with club partnerships and GP referral letters.

--- MAIN STEM ---
Halcyon Montessori Preschool (HMP) is a private limited company in the education and childcare sector, specialising in early-years education, employing a workforce of 22. An on-the-job training needs analysis shows 7 of 22 staff have not completed early-years safeguarding training; off-the-job training courses at the early-years college cost $650 per employee.

--- APPENDIX 3 — EXTERNAL ENVIRONMENT ---

Recommendation: HMP should choose parenting influencer marketing on social media.   Q4(b) [12 marks]
    Question: Using Appendix 3, evaluate how the interest rate rise to 5.75%, the 6.8% minimum wage increase and the 8.4% rise in input costs will affect HMP. Which change will have the greatest impact? Justify your answer.
    Answer: Interest rate rise (5.00% to 5.75%): If HMP's $250,000 ten-year bank loan is variable-rate, the 0.75 percentage point rise adds about $1,875 a year to financing costs — real but small next to $155,000 of fixed costs. Higher rates also make further borrowing for the second site more expensive, may dampen consumer confidence in discretionary early-years spending, and raise the cost of servicing the loan ahead of the new preschool's opening. HMP can partly shield itself by fixing the rate or issuing more shares.

Minimum wage increase (6.8%, to $13.14 per hour): Early-years education is labour-intensive — wages dominate HMP's cost structure, and many nursery practitioners sit near the minimum wage. If roughly 18 of the 22 staff are near it on 40-hour weeks, the 6.8% rise adds roughly $1,840 per affected worker a year — around $33,000 a year — on top of 21% practitioner turnover already inflating recruitment and induction costs, and the 7 of 22 staff still awaiting safeguarding certification. This lands directly on HMP's largest cost line and is compounded by the April 2026 timing, mid-expansion.

Input cost inflation (8.4% toys, learning materials and food): HMP's variable cost of $2.30 a unit includes play materials, food for extended hours and garden supplies. An 8.4% rise on the materials-and-food share (say 60% of variable cost, $1.38) adds roughly $0.12 per session; at 96,000 sessions a year that is about $11,000 a year, cutting contribution per unit from $6.20 toward $6.08 — under 2% of margin. With 4.9% growth in private early-years spending, HMP can absorb or modestly pass this on through the $1.20 extended-hours premium (the 45% willing to pay more), but parents remain price-sensitive given waiting-list-driven scarcity pricing power is limited.

Conclusion: The 6.8% minimum wage increase will have the greatest impact. Early-years preschools are people-heavy businesses, and roughly $33,000 a year on near-minimum wages lands on top of a 21% turnover crisis HMP is already managing badly — it threatens the 96% satisfaction rating and the second-site launch directly. The input-cost rise is the next risk, about $11,000 a year and manageable through pricing; the interest-rate increase is the smallest in cash terms (roughly $1,875 a year) and can be managed by fixing the loan rate. HMP should therefore restructure rosters, seek efficiency in extended-hours delivery, consider a modest fee review justified by nature-garden quality, and complete safeguarding training promptly — or the Appendix 2 profit gains will be unwound by the April 2026 wage bill.
    Keywords: 5.75%, 6.8%, 8.4%, $13.14, $2.30, $250,000
    Mark scheme: level_1_1_to_4: Identifies the external factors with limited application to HMP. | level_2_5_to_8: Analyses the impact of at least two external changes on HMP's costs, revenue or financing in context. | level_3_9_to_12: Detailed evaluation of all three external changes in the context of HMP with a well-justified judgement that the minimum wage increase has the greatest impact and why the other two are smaller.

--- MAIN STEM ---
Wexley Plasterboard (WPB) is a private limited company in the building materials sector, employing a workforce of 85. Founded in 2011 by Priya Wexley, the business manufactures gypsum plasterboard with recycled-paper facings for the construction industry and operates a hierarchical organisational structure with autocratic leadership. WPB plans to invest $1,400,000 in a new automated drying and cutting line, financed by a $900,000 ten-year bank loan and $500,000 retained profit. It has fixed costs of $600,000 a year, a variable cost of $7.50 a unit and a selling price of $12.50, and currently produces 170,000 units a year. WPB faces two operational problems: a board defect rate of 2.6% with rising cutting-line waste, and labour turnover among machine operators has reached 14%.

--- APPENDIX 1 — MARKETING/OPS ---
Operations and Quality Report — Q3 2025: The drying line produced 44,000 boards in the quarter at a defect rate of 2.6%, down from 4.0% a year ago. Customer complaints fell from 30 to 16 per month. Market research of 480 builders' merchants found that 71% would stock certified low-carbon plasterboard and 58% would pay up to $0.60 more per sheet. Average delivery time is 4 days and cutting waste is running at 6.5% of output. A training needs analysis shows 18 of 85 staff have not completed on-the-job training on the new saws; off-the-job training courses at the technical college cost $750 per employee.

--- APPENDIX 2 — FINANCIAL DATA ---
Title: Extract from the Statement of Profit or Loss and Capital employed data of Wexley Plasterboard for the year ended 31 March 2025 ($ '000)
Headers: ['Financial Metric', '2024', '2025']

Cost of sales | 5,040 | 5,280
Gross profit | 3,360 | 4,320
Operating profit | 1,050 | 1,440
Capital employed | 6,000 | 7,200
Interest payable | 120 | 150

--- APPENDIX 3 — EXTERNAL ENVIRONMENT ---
Economic and Business Bulletin (November 2026): (1) The central bank has raised the base interest rate from 4.25% to 4.75%, the third rise this year, lifting borrowing costs on variable-rate loans. (2) The national minimum wage will rise by 5.9% from $11.40 to $12.07 per hour from April 2026, raising total wage bills. (3) Gypsum and recycled paper input costs have risen 9.8% year-on-year, and construction-materials inflation is running at 7.3%, while housing starts grew 3.2% in the same period.

  Q1(a) [8 marks]
    Question: WPB plans to finance part of its automated drying and cutting line expansion with a ten-year bank loan. Explain two advantages for WPB of using retained profit to fund the expansion instead of the bank loan.
    Answer: Point 1: Using retained profit costs WPB nothing in interest or repayment charges, which protects cash flow at a time when the company already carries fixed costs of $600,000 a year and has committed to a $900,000 ten-year bank loan for the $1,400,000 automated drying and cutting line. Avoiding interest on the retained $500,000 leaves more operating cash to absorb the 9.8% rise in gypsum and recycled paper input costs, so WPB can defend its $12.50 selling price against cheaper imports and keep the 2.6% defect-reduction programme funded without straining merchant order books.

Point 2: Retained profit avoids the collateral and repayment risk attached to a bank loan, so the $500,000 is available without putting the new $1,400,000 line at risk of repossession if construction demand disappoints. It also preserves Priya Wexley's ownership and control of the private limited company, since no lender can impose covenants or conditions on how the automated line is operated, priced or expanded in later phases — particularly valuable while housing starts are only growing 3.2% a year.

    Answer: National trade-press advertising: Full-page adverts in construction and builders' merchant journals would reach procurement officers and merchant owners nationally with a credible technical message about certified low-carbon board. However, colour space is expensive, the readership is broad — much of it is architects or DIY readers outside WPB's merchant coverage — and a single insertion gives no measurable response data, making it hard to judge against a tight launch budget on top of an $900,000 loan commitment.

Radio also struggles to convey technical performance such as facing strength and defect rates.

Social media influencer marketing: Working with builders, joiners and sustainable-construction influencers targets exactly the 58% of 480 surveyed merchants willing to pay $0.60 more per sheet and the 71% planning to stock low-carbon board. Cost per reached buyer is low, engagement and click-throughs are measurable, and influencers can demonstrate the recycled-paper facing story on real sites — ideal for a technical B2B product. Credibility depends on honest, experienced voices rather than celebrities.

Recommendation: WPB should choose social media influencer marketing. National trade-press advertising is rejected as too expensive and insufficiently targeted for launch; regional radio is rejected as too narrow for national merchant listings.   Q4(a) [8 marks]
    Question: Explain one advantage and one disadvantage for WPB of producing its plasterboard with recycled-paper facings instead of virgin-paper facings.
    Answer: Advantage: Recycled-paper facings match the 58% of 480 surveyed builders' merchants willing to pay up to $0.60 more per sheet for certified low-carbon board, letting WPB charge a premium that protects its $5.00 contribution per unit even as gypsum and recycled paper input costs rise 9.8%. It also satisfies the 71% of merchants planning to stock certified low-carbon plasterboard, strengthening WPB's brand with housebuilders chasing their own sustainability targets and supporting the case for the $1,400,000 expansion.

Disadvantage: Recycled facing supply can be inconsistent in moisture content and strength, raising the risk of delamination and pushing the 2.6% defect rate and 6.5% cutting waste back up before the new automated drying line stabilises. If merchants will not pay the $0.60 premium nationally, WPB could be left with a higher variable cost than $7.50 and no compensating revenue — squeezing margins and weakening the returns needed to service the $900,000 bank loan.

  Q4(b) [12 marks]
    Question: Using Appendix 3, evaluate how the interest rate rise to 4.75%, the 5.9% minimum wage increase and the 9.8% rise in gypsum and recycled paper input costs will affect WPB. Which change will have the greatest impact? Justify your answer.
    Answer: Interest rate rise (4.25% to 4.75%): If WPB's $900,000 ten-year bank loan is variable-rate, the annual interest cost rises by about 0.5%, adding roughly $4,500 a year — small beside fixed costs of $600,000. Higher rates also raise the hurdle for any future phase of the $1,400,000 expansion and may cool housing starts (already only growing 3.2%), but the direct cash impact is modest and WPB could negotiate a fixed rate at renewal.

Minimum wage increase (5.9%, to $12.07 per hour): Only a minority of WPB's 85 staff sit at or near the minimum wage, mostly production operatives on the drying line. For around 40 production staff, the increase adds about $0.67 an hour, or roughly $1,400 per worker a year — about $56,000 across the affected group. Manageable, but it will press on margins if WPB cannot raise prices above $12.50, and democratic input (or at least better appraisal feedback) would help contain the 14% turnover it worsens.

Input cost inflation (9.8% gypsum and recycled paper): Ingredients dominate the $7.50 variable cost; assume roughly 70% ($5.25) is materials. A 9.8% rise adds about $0.51 per unit; at 170,000 units that is roughly $87,000 a year, cutting contribution from $5.00 to about $4.49 and reducing annual profit by around 14% if not passed on. WPB can recover part through the $0.60 eco-premium and merchant price reviews, but not all, since 71% of merchants will resist across-the-board rises.

Conclusion: The 9.8% input cost rise will have the greatest impact. It recurs on every one of the 170,000 units sold, eroding the $5.00 contribution directly and totalling roughly $85,000–$90,000 a year — well above the wage rise (~$56,000) and the loan interest increase (~$4,500). The wage rise is the second most serious threat, while the rate rise is the least damaging and easiest to hedge; all three nevertheless demand supplier contracts, premium pricing and tighter cost control to protect the expansion's returns.
    Keywords: 4.75%, 5.9%, 9.8%, interest rate, $12.07, $7.50

--- MAIN STEM ---
Wrenford Limestone Walling (WLW) is a partnership in the stone quarrying and building materials sector, employing a workforce of 32. Founded in 2004 by Tom Wrenford, the business extracts and dresses limestone walling stone for landscapers and builders and operates a flat organisational structure with democratic leadership. WLW plans to invest $750,000 in a new diamond-wire cutting and dressing shed, financed by a $450,000 ten-year bank loan and $300,000 retained profit. It has fixed costs of $375,000 a year, a variable cost of $10.50 a unit and a selling price of $18.00, and currently produces 72,000 units a year. WLW faces two operational problems: labour turnover among quarry operatives has reached 16% and a skills gap in diamond-wire sawing, alongside rising cutting waste.

--- APPENDIX 1 — MARKETING/OPS ---
Operations and Sales Report — Q3 2025: The dressing shed processed 18,500 units of walling stone at a breakage rate of 3.4%, down from 5.2% a year ago. Customer complaints fell from 17 to 9 per month. Market research of 300 architects and landscapers found that 68% specify natural limestone and 54% would pay up to $1.20 more per unit for certified low-carbon stone. Average delivery time is 5 days. Cutting waste is 9.0% of output, and on-the-job wire-saw certification for 12 of the 32 operatives would cost $600 per employee at the technical college.

A takeover of a rival quarry would fuse two workforces overnight, create clashes over pay and rostering, and risk losing the very operatives WLW needs to close its diamond-wire sawing skills gap — with turnover already at 16%, cultural disruption could prove expensive and slow.

Point 2: Organic growth avoids the premium price, lawyers' fees and hidden liabilities a takeover would carry, keeping the $750,000 investment within reach of a $450,000 bank loan and $300,000 retained profit. --- MAIN STEM ---
Ferndale Green Steel (FGS) is a public limited company in the steel recycling sector, employing a workforce of 120. Founded in 2016 by Raya Ferndale, the business melts scrap steel in electric arc furnaces to produce certified low-carbon steel for construction and manufacturing and operates a hierarchical organisational structure with democratic leadership. FGS plans to invest $2,400,000 in a new automated scrap-sorting line and baghouse filter, financed by a $1,300,000 share issue and $1,100,000 retained profit. It has fixed costs of $3,600,000 a year, a variable cost of $440 a unit and a selling price of $620, and currently produces 34,000 units a year. FGS faces two operational problems: absenteeism has reached 10% and scrap contamination is driving rework in the melt shop.

--- APPENDIX 1 — MARKETING/OPS ---
Operations Report — Q3 2025: The melt shop processed 8,600 tonnes of scrap steel at a rework rate of 2.2%, down from 3.4% a year ago. Customer complaints fell from 12 to 7 per month. Market research of 250 industrial buyers found that 74% would pay up to 8% more for certified low-carbon steel. Average delivery lead time is 6 days, and scrap-sorting trials have lifted metal recovery to 92%. A training needs analysis shows 22 of 120 staff have not completed on-the-job training on the new shredder; off-the-job training courses at the technical college cost $1,100 per employee.

--- APPENDIX 2 — FINANCIAL DATA ---
Title: Extract from the Statement of Profit or Loss and Capital employed data of Ferndale Green Steel for the year ended 31 March 2025 ($ '000)
Headers: ['Financial Metric', '2024', '2025']
Revenue | 15,800 | 18,400
Cost of sales | 10,270 | 11,500
Gross profit | 5,530 | 6,900
Operating profit | 1,580 | 2,208
Capital employed | 7,900 | 9,600
Interest payable | 240 | 310

--- APPENDIX 3 — EXTERNAL ENVIRONMENT ---
Economic and Business Bulletin (November 2026): (1) The central bank has raised the base interest rate from 4.50% to 5.25%, a 0.75 percentage point rise, lifting borrowing costs on the variable portion of long-term loans. (2) The national living wage will rise by 6.6% from $12.30 to $13.11 per hour from April 2026, raising wage costs across the melt shop. (3) Steel scrap costs have risen 11.2% year-on-year and industrial electricity costs 9.5%, while producer price inflation is running at 4.6% and construction steel demand grew 3.8% in the same period.

--- QUESTIONS ---
  Q1(a) [8 marks]
    Question: FGS plans to finance part of its $2,400,000 expansion with a share issue. Explain two advantages for FGS of using a share issue instead of a bank loan.
    Answer: Point 1: A share issue raises finance without creating interest or repayment obligations, protecting FGS's cash flow at a time when the company already carries fixed costs of $3,600,000 a year and services $240,000–$310,000 of annual interest. Avoiding extra debt repayments on the $2,400,000 automated scrap-sorting line leaves more operating cash to absorb the 11.2% rise in scrap costs and the 9.5% rise in industrial electricity prices — critical for a furnaces business whose variable cost is already $440 a unit.

Point 2: New equity strengthens FGS's balance sheet and credit rating, making later borrowing cheaper if the line outperforms. There is also no collateral at risk: if low-carbon steel demand disappoints, shareholders bear the loss rather than the melt shop being repossessed. The trade-off is dilution of existing shareholders' control and future dividends, but Raya Ferndale judged this worthwhile to fund the certified low-carbon programme that 74% of 250 surveyed industrial buyers would pay 8% more for.
    Keywords: share issue, retained profit, $1,300,000, $1,100,000, $2,400,000, $3,600,000
    Mark scheme: knowledge_max_2: 1 mark for each valid advantage identified (max 2). | application_analysis_max_6: Up to 3 marks per point for contextual explanation and analysis applied to Ferndale Green Steel and its expansion decision.

  Q1(b) [12 marks]
    Question: FGS is launching its certified low-carbon steel for construction buyers. Consider advertising in national business newspapers, a targeted LinkedIn campaign aimed at procurement managers, or sponsorship of the Green Manufacturing Expo. Which should FGS choose to promote the launch? Justify your recommendation.
    Answer: National business newspaper advertising: Full-page adverts in national papers would reach a broad business audience and raise FGS's profile among institutional investors as well as buyers, signalling the permanence of a public limited company. However, national print is very expensive, much of the readership is irrelevant to steel specification, response is hard to measure, and a single issue barely dents the procurement habits of the 74% of buyers willing to pay 8% more for certified low-carbon steel.

Sponsorship of the Green Manufacturing Expo: Exhibiting and speaking at a green-manufacturing expo would put FGS face-to-face with sustainability officers, specifiers and major contractors, with strong credibility from the 92% scrap recovery and certified low-carbon positioning. The weaknesses are high one-off fees, attendance limited to event days, and poor reach for the hundreds of regional fabricators and distributors who also buy steel; it builds depth, not breadth.

A targeted LinkedIn campaign aimed at procurement managers: Precise targeting by industry, role and company size lets FGS deliver technical carbon-footprint content directly to the people who specify steel — at low cost per reached decision-maker, with measurable enquiries, and sustained all year. It suits a B2B technical product perfectly, though it requires continuous quality content and may under-reach less digitally active small buyers.

Recommendation: FGS should choose the targeted LinkedIn campaign. It reaches the precise procurement audience identified in research, costs least per qualified lead, runs year-round beyond one expo, and produces the measurable enquiry data a public limited company needs to justify the $2,400,000 investment to shareholders. Business-newspaper advertising is rejected as too expensive and too broad; the expo is rejected as too narrow and event-limited, though FGS could add a small stand later once the certified range wins its first major framing contract.
    Keywords: low-carbon steel, 74%, 8%, 250, 92%, $2,400,000
    Mark scheme: level_1_1_to_4: Limited knowledge or outline of the promotional options with minimal context. | level_2_5_to_8: Detailed discussion of the advantages and disadvantages of at least two options in the context of FGS with some judgement. | level_3_9_to_12: Detailed discussion of all three options in the context of FGS with a well-justified recommendation explaining why business newspapers and the expo are rejected.

  Q2(a) [8 marks]
    Question: Explain two benefits for FGS of using team working in the melt shop to tackle its 10% absenteeism and scrap contamination.
    Answer: Point 1: Team working pools the furnace crew's practical knowledge of why scrap contamination happens, generating joint fixes such as better pre-sort checks and clearer signals between cranes and furnace operators. Teams also cover for each other during absences, keeping the melt shop running at 8,600 tonnes a quarter instead of losing output when one of the 120 staff is off — directly relieving the 10% absenteeism and the rework driven by contaminated charges.

Point 2: Teams build peer accountability and social support, satisfying Maslow's social needs and reversing the isolation behind high absence. Operators who help each other also learn faster on the new shredder, support the 22 staff awaiting training, and sustain the improvement from a 3.4% to 2.2% rework rate. Lower absenteeism and rework cut overtime, scrap-disposal and quality-failure costs, protecting the $620 selling price and the margins FGS needs to justify the $2,400,000 expansion.
    Keywords: melt shop, workforce of 120, absenteeism, 10%, 8,600, $2,400,000
    Mark scheme: knowledge_max_2: 1 mark for each valid benefit identified (max 2). | application_analysis_max_6: Up to 3 marks per point for detailed contextual development linked to FGS's absenteeism, rework and expansion.

  Q2(b) [12 marks]
    Question: FGS must upskill 22 scrap-sorting operators for the new automated line. Consider on-the-job training or off-the-job training at the technical college at $1,100 per employee. Which should FGS choose? Justify your decision.
    Answer: On-the-job training: Training beside the shredder and furnace is directly relevant to FGS's own scrap grades, recovery targets and safety regime, costs nothing in course fees, and keeps the 22 operators productive — protecting throughput of 8,600 tonnes a quarter and the drop in rework from 3.4% to 2.2%. Weaknesses: trainers are production staff whose own duties suffer, informal bad habits spread, and no external certificate is issued to demonstrate competence to clients auditing FGS's certified low-carbon claims.

Off-the-job training: The technical college course at $1,100 per employee would cost $24,200 for all 22 — easily affordable against a $2,400,000 investment. It provides structured, up-to-date theory (metallurgy, sorting standards, safety regulation) and recognised certification, strengthening FGS's certified credentials with buyers willing to pay 8% more. However, it removes over 18% of the workforce from the melt shop for course days, risks delivery delays, and the generic syllabus may not match FGS's exact shredder settings, so site coaching would still be required.

Decision: FGS should choose on-the-job training for the initial rollout, reserving college certification for two lead operators and the quality supervisor. This is the cheapest and most machine-specific route, keeps the furnaces fed, and avoids withdrawing 22 of 120 staff while absenteeism is already 10%. Full off-the-job training is rejected as too disruptive to the delivery schedule and poor value for operators who need hands-on sorting practice; the $24,200 would be better spent on a follow-up QA audit once the line is stable and rework falls toward 1.5%.
    Keywords: on-the-job training, off-the-job training, $1,100, 8,600, 10%, workforce of 120

    Question: Using Appendix 2, evaluate FGS's profitability by calculating the gross profit margin, profit margin and ROCE for 2024 and 2025. Has FGS's profitability improved? Justify your answer.

    Question: Explain one advantage and one disadvantage for FGS of producing certified low-carbon steel from recycled scrap instead of from virgin ore.
    Answer: Advantage: Certified low-carbon steel from recycled scrap matches the 74% of 250 surveyed industrial buyers willing to pay up to 8% more, letting FGS charge a premium that protects its $180 contribution per unit even as scrap costs rise 11.2%. It also uses roughly a quarter of the energy of primary steelmaking, supports FGS's environmental brand with construction specifiers, and — reinforced by the 92% scrap recovery rate — builds the certified credentials that differentiate FGS from conventional mills competing for the $620-a-unit market.

Disadvantage: Recycled scrap quality is inconsistent — copper and tin contamination force costly sorting and rework (the very problem the $2,400,000 automated line must fix) and can cap the grades FGS can certify. Scrap price volatility (up 11.2% year-on-year) also destabilises the $440 variable cost; if FGS cannot pass rises on, contribution shrinks and the returns needed to justify the share issue and retained-profit mix are at risk, while contamination-driven rework at 2.2% still erodes margins.

    Question: Using Appendix 3, evaluate how the interest rate rise to 5.25%, the 6.6% living wage increase and the 11.2% rise in steel scrap costs will affect FGS. Which change will have the greatest impact? Justify your answer.
    Answer: Interest rate rise (4.50% to 5.25%): On the variable portion of FGS's borrowings, a 0.75 percentage point rise on around $310,000 of annual interest adds roughly $44,000 a year — noticeable but absorbable, and largely avoidable once loans are refinanced or fixed. Higher rates may also lift shareholders' required returns, but the direct cash impact is the smallest of the three for FGS.

Living wage increase (6.6%, to $13.11 per hour): FGS employs 120 staff, mostly in the melt shop on hourly rates near or above the living wage. The rise adds about $0.81 an hour, or roughly $1,685 per worker a year — around $200,000 across the whole workforce if applied broadly. That is over 9% of 2025 operating profit and will press on the democratic leaders recently to hold pay settlements without productivity gains through team working and lower rework.

Scrap cost inflation (11.2% year-on-year, plus 9.5% electricity): Scrap likely represents 60–70% of the $440 variable cost (about $270–$300). An 11.2% rise adds roughly $30–$34 per unit; at 34,000 units that is $1,020,000–$1,156,000 a year — potentially wiping out half of operating profit before price recovery. Electricity adds hundreds of thousands more. Recovery depends on passing costs into contract steel prices, where FGS has the 8% certified premium as partial cover.

Conclusion: The 11.2% scrap cost rise will have the greatest impact. It recurs on every one of the 34,000 units sold and is an order of magnitude larger than the wage bill increase or the interest rise, directly compressing the $180 contribution and the certified premium FGS relies on. FGS must lock in multi-year scrap contracts, accelerate sorting-line throughput and push through indexed pricing; the wage rise is the second-largest threat and the rate rise the least damaging, though all three demand margin discipline through 2027.

--- MAIN STEM ---
Aldervan Engineered Timber (AET) is a cooperative in the engineered timber sector, employing a workforce of 64. Founded in 2013 by Jonas and Petra Aldervan, the business presses cross-laminated timber panels and glulam beams from certified Scandinavian spruce for sustainable construction and operates a flat organisational structure with democratic leadership. AET plans to invest $1,850,000 in a new CLT press and finger-jointing line, financed by a $700,000 ten-year bank loan and $1,150,000 retained profit. It has fixed costs of $1,640,000 a year, a variable cost of $128 a unit and a selling price of $210, and currently produces 26,500 units a year. AET faces two operational problems: offcut waste is running at 8% of input timber and labour turnover among press operators has reached 13%.

--- APPENDIX 1 — MARKETING/OPS ---
Production and Market Report — Q3 2025: The press line laminated 6,800 CLT panels at a reject rate of 2.9%, down from 4.1% a year ago. Customer complaints fell from 15 to 7 per month. Market research of 380 architects and contractors found that 62% specify mass timber for low-carbon builds and 55% would pay up to 6% more for certified CLT. Average delivery time is 7 days, and offcut waste is 8% of input timber. A training needs analysis shows 15 of 64 staff have not completed CNC press training; off-the-job courses at the technical college cost $850 per employee.

--- APPENDIX 2 — FINANCIAL DATA ---

Cost of sales | 4,140 | 4,290
Gross profit | 2,760 | 3,510
Operating profit | 828 | 1,170
Capital employed | 4,600 | 5,200
Interest payable | 85 | 105

--- APPENDIX 3 — EXTERNAL ENVIRONMENT ---
Economic and Business Bulletin (November 2026): (1) The central bank has raised the base interest rate from 5.50% to 6.00%, the fifth rise this year, increasing variable-rate borrowing costs. (2) The national minimum wage will rise by 6.4% from $11.95 to $12.71 per hour from April 2026, raising wage bills. (3) Structural spruce and pine input costs have risen 8.8% year-on-year, while green-building material demand grew 9.3% and overall construction output grew 2.1% in the same period.

  Q1(a) [8 marks]
    Question: AET plans to finance part of its CLT press expansion with a ten-year bank loan. Explain two advantages for AET of using retained profit to fund the expansion instead of the bank loan.
    Answer: Point 1: Using retained profit costs AET nothing in interest or repayment charges, protecting cash flow while the cooperative already carries fixed costs of $1,640,000 a year and has committed to a $700,000 ten-year bank loan for the $1,850,000 press. Avoiding interest on the $1,150,000 retained portion leaves more operating cash to absorb the 8.8% rise in spruce and pine input costs, so AET can defend its $210 selling price and keep the certified CLT programme funded without raising member prices or compromising the 2.9% reject-rate drive.

Point 2: Retained profit avoids collateral and repayment risk, so the $1,150,000 is available without putting the new press at risk of repossession if mass-timber demand disappoints. It also preserves the cooperative's member ownership and democratic control — no external lender can impose covenants over how the press is scheduled, priced or staffed, which matters while green-building demand is growing 9.3% but overall construction output only 2.1%, and while members vote on reinvestment.
    Keywords: retained profit, bank loan, $1,150,000, $700,000, $1,850,000, $1,640,000

    Question: AET is launching its certified CLT panel range. Consider print advertising in construction trade magazines, social media marketing with sustainability influencers, or sponsoring a televised eco-home series. Which should AET choose to promote the launch? Justify your recommendation.
    Answer: Print advertising in construction trade magazines: Specialist magazines would reach the 62% of surveyed architects and contractors specifying mass timber with technical credibility — spans, fire ratings, carbon savings — in a durable format specifiers keep on their desks. However, full-colour space is expensive, monthly circulation slows response, and much of the readership is not decision-ready on a new CLT supplier, making it hard to tie spend to orders against an $1,850,000 investment funded partly by a loan.

Sponsoring a televised eco-home series: A sponsorship slot would give AET the widest possible reach and powerful emotional association with sustainable homes — ideal for the public-facing story of timber replacing concrete and steel. Social media marketing with sustainability influencers: Working with green-architecture and self-build influencers reaches exactly the 62% specifying mass timber and the 55% paying 6% more for certified CLT, with measurable engagement, low cost per reached specifier and year-round momentum. It demonstrates carbon credentials and real building case studies directly to the 380 architects and contractors in AET's research, though it depends on influencer credibility and consistent quality content.

Recommendation: AET should choose social media marketing with sustainability influencers. It reaches the precise dual-audience of professional specifiers and engaged self-builders identified in research, costs least per qualified lead, runs continuously rather than around one series or monthly issue, and reinforces the certified low-carbon positioning behind the 6% premium. Trade print is rejected as slow and hard to measure; the TV sponsorship is rejected as unaffordable and untargeted; influencers plus modest trade-press advertorials later would reinforce professional credibility once first contracts land.

Decision: AET should choose job enrichment. --- MAIN STEM ---
Ashcombe Eco Bricks (AEB) is a private limited company in the building materials sector, employing a workforce of 140. Founded in 1998 by Marta Ashcombe, the business manufactures recycled-content eco blocks and facing blocks for the housebuilding market and operates a flat organisational structure with autocratic leadership. AEB plans to invest $980,000 in a new recycled-aggregate batching plant and vibro-compaction press, financed by hire purchase, a $550,000 bank loan and $430,000 retained profit. It has fixed costs of $888,000 a year, a variable cost of $4.80 a unit and a selling price of $8.50, and currently produces 305,000 units a year. AEB faces two operational problems: absenteeism has reached 11% and recycled-aggregate inconsistency is causing occasional sub-standard batches.

--- APPENDIX 1 — MARKETING/OPS ---
Quality and Sales Report — Q3 2025: The batching plant produced 84,000 blocks in the quarter at a sub-standard batch rate of 1.6%, down from 2.7% a year ago. Customer complaints fell from 25 to 11 per month. Market research of 420 housebuilders found that 69% specify recycled-content blocks and 61% would pay up to $0.80 more per block. Average delivery time is 3 days, and dust-control upgrades costing $35,000 are scheduled for winter. Average strength of blocks is 7.3 N/mm².

--- APPENDIX 2 — FINANCIAL DATA ---
Title: Extract from the Statement of Profit or Loss and Capital employed data of Ashcombe Eco Bricks for the year ended 31 March 2025 ($ '000)
Headers: ['Financial Metric', '2024', '2025']
Revenue | 5,200 | 6,000
Cost of sales | 2,860 | 3,180
Gross profit | 2,340 | 2,820
Operating profit | 650 | 840
Capital employed | 3,250 | 3,500
Interest payable | 110 | 135

--- APPENDIX 3 — EXTERNAL ENVIRONMENT ---
Economic and Business Bulletin (November 2026): (1) The central bank has raised the base interest rate from 4.75% to 5.25%, the third rise this year, raising variable-rate borrowing costs. (2) The national minimum wage will rise by 6.7% from $12.60 to $13.44 per hour from April 2026, materially raising wage bills. (3) Cement and recycled aggregate input costs have risen 7.6% year-on-year, while housing construction output grew 2.4% and building-materials inflation is running at 6.1% in the same period.

--- QUESTIONS ---
  Q1(a) [8 marks]
    Question: AEB plans to acquire its new vibro-compaction press by hire purchase. Explain two advantages for AEB of using hire purchase for the press instead of a bank loan.
    Answer: Point 1: Hire purchase spreads the $980,000 cost of the batching plant and vibro-compaction press into fixed instalments without an immediate capital outlay, easing cash flow while AEB already carries fixed costs of $888,000 a year and services a $550,000 bank loan. Crucially, ownership passes to AEB once the final payment is made, so the press becomes a long-term asset producing 305,000 units a year without the flat structure straining to raise or secure a larger unsecured facility.

Point 2: Hire purchase keeps the specific press asset as security for the finance provider rather than general charges over AEB's premises or other equipment, protecting Marta Ashcombe's flexibility to mortgage land later if the eco-block range expands. It also matches payments to output: as the recycled-content blocks generate revenue at $8.50 a unit, instalments track productive use, and AEB keeps $430,000 of retained profit in reserve for the $35,000 dust-control upgrades and for materials during aggregate-price spikes.
    Keywords: hire purchase, bank loan, $550,000, $430,000, $980,000, $888,000
    Mark scheme: knowledge_max_2: 1 mark for each valid advantage identified (max 2). | application_analysis_max_6: Up to 3 marks per point for contextual explanation and analysis applied to Ashcombe Eco Bricks and its expansion decision.

  Q1(b) [12 marks]
    Question: AEB is launching its recycled-content eco blocks. Consider local radio sponsorship, builders' merchant in-store promotion, or a social media campaign targeting self-build homeowners. Which should AEB choose to promote the launch? Justify your recommendation.
    Answer: Local radio sponsorship: Sponsoring a local home-and-garden show would reach self-build homeowners across AEB's distribution radius cheaply and with high frequency, reinforcing the family-firm brand founded by Marta Ashcombe in 1998. Its weaknesses are narrow reach beyond the region, difficulty communicating technical benefits such as 7.3 N/mm² strength, and no targeting of the 69% of professional housebuilders who specify recycled-content blocks — most radio listeners are private individuals, not AEB's core trade customers.

Builders' merchant in-store promotion: Stands, leaflets, staff briefings and demonstration samples inside merchants put the product in front of trade buyers at the exact point of specification and purchase — reaching the 61% willing to pay $0.80 more per block. It is tactile and persuasive, but depends on merchant goodwill and staff effort, competes with rival brands for counter space, and cannot build mass awareness outside the merchant network.

Social media campaign targeting self-build homeowners: Content on recycled aggregate, carbon savings and strength tests reaches a fast-growing DIY audience directly, at low cost, with measurable engagement — ideal for driving them into merchants asking for AEB blocks. However, self-builders are a minority of volume demand; housebuilders still drive most of the 305,000-unit output, and social content requires ongoing budget and creative to stay fresh.

Recommendation: AEB should choose builders' merchant in-store promotion supported by light social media. The merchant channel reaches the professional buyers who specify blocks on every housing estate — the 69% specifying recycled content — at the moment of purchase, and reinforces AEB's 3-day delivery promise. Local radio is rejected as too narrow and untargeted for trade demand; a pure social campaign is rejected as consumer-facing reach that does not guarantee specification; in-store plus digital proof (QR codes linking to test certificates) should convert interest at the counter.

  Q2(a) [8 marks]
    Question: AEB's absenteeism has reached 11%. Explain two advantages for AEB of introducing a bonus scheme linked to block output for its machine operators.
    Answer: Point 1: An output-linked bonus gives each of AEB's 140 machine operators a direct financial stake in hitting the 84,000 blocks produced last quarter and the 305,000-unit annual target, satisfying a basic financial motivator (Herzberg) on top of the flat autocratic supervision.   Q2(b) [12 marks]
    Question: AEB must choose its production method for the new eco blocks. Consider flow production or batch production. Which should AEB choose? Justify your decision.
    Answer: Flow production: A continuous line through batching, vibro-compaction, curing and packing would slash unit costs, spread the $980,000 fixed investment over maximum volume, minimise handling damage — helping hold strength at 7.3 N/mm² — and deliver the 3-day delivery promise consistently. It suits the standardised eco block that the 69% of specifying housebuilders want in repeat, identical quantities, and maximises the 305,000-unit annual output. Its weaknesses are inflexibility: any change to block size, facing mix or aggregate specification stops the whole line, and a breakdown idles the entire plant.

Batch production: Producing in batches lets AEB switch between eco blocks, facing blocks and specialist shapes (retaining units, lintel packs), using the same batching plant flexibly — valuable while aggregate consistency causes 1.6% sub-standard batches, as suspect batches can be isolated and rejected without scrapping a whole continuous run. Unit costs are higher and changeover times add waste, but it suits AEB's variable order pattern from housebuilders and reduces risk during commissioning of the new press.

Decision: AEB should choose flow production for its core eco block, with a small batch-production cell retained for specialist products. The core range is standardised, demand from housebuilders is repeatable, and flow production gives the lowest unit cost and best route to dilute the $980,000 investment — rejected batch production as the main method because it would raise handling, changeover and unit costs precisely when input inflation is 7.6%. Batch flexibility stays as insurance for specification variety and for quarantining sub-standard aggregate without losing a shift's output.
    Keywords: batching, 305,000, 1.6%, absenteeism, $4.80, $980,000

    Question: Using Appendix 3, evaluate how the interest rate rise to 5.25%, the 6.7% minimum wage increase and the 7.6% rise in cement and recycled aggregate input costs will affect AEB. Which change will have the greatest impact? Justify your answer.
    Answer: Interest rate rise (4.75% to 5.25%): On AEB's $550,000 bank loan, a 0.50 percentage point rise adds roughly $2,750 a year — trivial beside fixed costs of $888,000. Higher rates may cool housebuilding finance and slow the 2.4% growth in construction output, trimming orders, and raise the cost of future borrowing; AEB could fix rates at renewal to neutralise this.

Minimum wage increase (6.7%, to $13.44 per hour): AEB employs 140 staff, mostly machine operators and yard crew on or near the minimum wage. The rise adds about $0.84 an hour, roughly $1,750 per worker a year — around $245,000 across the workforce if applied to all 140. That is nearly 29% of 2025 operating profit of $840,000 and would land on top of 11% absenteeism, making attendance management and the planned output-linked bonus essential to protect margins; it is a severe, recurring cash drain regardless of volume.

Input cost inflation (7.6% cement and recycled aggregate): Materials make up roughly 65% of the $4.80 variable cost (about $3.12). A 7.6% rise adds about $0.24 per unit; at 305,000 units that is roughly $73,000 a year. AEB can recover much of this through the $0.80 certified premium and housebuilder price reviews, and has aggregate contracts to renegotiate — but partial recovery is the realistic ceiling this year.

Conclusion: The 6.7% minimum wage increase will have the greatest impact. It applies to all 140 employees whatever happens to sales volume, adding roughly $245,000 a year — more than three times the input-cost rise and nearly ninety times the loan interest increase — and it strikes the labour-heavy part of the process hardest. Input costs (~$73,000) are the second-greatest threat and are partly recoverable through price reviews; the rate rise is the smallest and most easily hedged, though all three demand AEB prioritise attendance, productivity and premium pricing to defend its margins through 2027.

--- MAIN STEM ---
Mistral Coffee Roasters (MCR) is a private limited company in the beverage sector, specialising in specialty coffee roasting, employing a workforce of 36. Founded in 2011 by Sofia Mistral, the business supplies independent cafes across the region and operates a flat organisational structure with democratic leadership. MCR plans to invest $540,000 in a new automated roasting and packing line, financed by a $320,000 ten-year bank loan and $220,000 retained profit. It has fixed costs of $189,000 a year, a variable cost of $4.20 a unit and a selling price of $10.50, and produces 80,000 units a year. MCR faces two problems: quality complaints about inconsistent roast colour have risen sharply and absenteeism has reached 7% among packing staff.

--- APPENDIX 1 — MARKETING/OPS ---
Operations and Quality Report - Q3 2025: MCR roasted 19,500 units of coffee last quarter at a defect rate of 2.4%, down from 3.6% a year ago. Customer complaints fell from 44 to 26 a month. Average delivery lead time is 2.8 days. A survey of 500 cafe buyers found 68% would pay up to $0.50 more for certified sustainable beans, and 47% check origin labelling. A skills audit shows 14 of 36 staff have not completed on-the-job training on the new roasting controls; off-the-job training courses at the local college cost $750 per employee.

--- APPENDIX 2 — FINANCIAL DATA ---
Title: Extract from the Statement of Financial Position of Mistral Coffee Roasters as at 31 March 2025 ($ '000)

Current liabilities | 210 | 198
Non-current assets | 1,240 | 1,610
Capital employed | 1,700 | 2,010

--- APPENDIX 3 — EXTERNAL ENVIRONMENT ---

(2) The national minimum wage will rise by 5.8% from $12.80 to $13.54 an hour from April 2026. (3) Green coffee bean import prices have risen 9.6% year-on-year, while cafe-sector input inflation is 6.3% and consumer spending on specialty coffee grew 4.1%.
