  Q1(a) [8 marks]
    Question: MCR is funding its $540,000 expansion with a $320,000 bank loan and $220,000 retained profit. Explain two benefits for MCR of using retained profit rather than increasing the bank loan.
    Answer: Point 1: Retained profit requires no interest payment and no capital repayment, so using the $220,000 keeps MCR's cash flow free while it services the $320,000 bank loan and meets fixed costs of $189,000 a year. Every dollar of the $540,000 funded internally is a dollar that does not add to the loan commitment, protecting the $10.50 selling price from having to cover extra interest at a time when 7% absenteeism and quality complaints are already disrupting output.

Point 2: Retained profit leaves Sofia Mistral's ownership and control untouched, since no lender can impose conditions on how the new roasting and packing line is run or demand collateral. It is also immediately available and avoids arrangement fees and approval delays, letting MCR respond quickly to cafe demand and to the 68% of 500 surveyed buyers who would pay $0.50 more for certified sustainable beans. Keeping borrowing lower also reduces exposure if rates rise, making the expansion safer for a 36-person roaster.
    Keywords: retained profit, $320,000, $220,000, $540,000, $189,000, democratic leadership
    Mark scheme: knowledge_max_2: 1 mark for each valid point identified (max 2). | application_analysis_max_6: Up to 3 marks per point for contextual explanation and analysis applied to the named business and the case data.

  Q1(b) [12 marks]
    Question: MCR is launching a new single-origin coffee range. Consider cafe trade exhibitions, a social media campaign, or free in-cafe sampling. Which should MCR choose to promote the launch? Justify your recommendation.
    Answer: Cafe trade exhibitions: A trade show puts MCR's single-origin range in front of many cafe owners at once and lets buyers taste the product, which helps answer the quality complaints about inconsistent roast colour. It also builds personal contacts with the independent cafes MCR supplies. However, stand fees, travel and staffing are costly for a business funding a $540,000 expansion with a $320,000 loan, and many visitors are competitors or non-buyers, so cost per genuine order can be high.

Social media campaign: A campaign can reach thousands of buyers at low cost per contact and can tell the origin story that 47% of surveyed buyers check. It is measurable and scalable nationally. Its weakness is that coffee is a taste product: an online advert cannot prove roast consistency, and engagement does not reliably convert into cafe orders, especially with a 36-person team and only 19,500 units roasted last quarter.

Free in-cafe sampling: Placing samples in the cafes that already stock MCR lets buyers taste the improvement at the point of purchase, directly tackling the quality complaints. It uses existing distribution, so cost is limited to product giveaway and staff time, and it targets the 68% willing to pay $0.50 more for certified sustainable beans. The drawback is slow reach and reliance on cafe staff.

Recommendation: MCR should choose free in-cafe sampling. It neutralises the quality complaints, uses the existing cafe network instead of costly new channels, and converts the 68% premium preference into trial. Trade exhibitions are rejected as too expensive and untargeted for a 36-employee roaster carrying a $320,000 loan; social media is rejected because it cannot demonstrate taste and is less certain to win cafe orders. MCR can add low-cost social posts later to support the sampling.
    Keywords: $540,000, 68%, 500, quality complaints, $0.50, 19,500
    Mark scheme: level_1_1_to_4: Identifies promotional options with limited application to MCR. | level_2_5_to_8: Discusses at least two options with advantages and disadvantages applied to MCR. | level_3_9_to_12: Evaluates all three options in the context of MCR with a justified recommendation and clear rejection of the alternatives.

  Q2(a) [8 marks]
    Question: MCR's absenteeism has reached 7% and quality complaints about roast colour are rising. Explain two benefits for MCR of using democratic leadership to improve motivation in its packing team.
    Answer: Point 1: Democratic leadership gives the 36 employees a voice in how the new roasting and packing line is organised, which helps satisfy social and esteem needs and raises job satisfaction. Workers who help set packing routines are more likely to attend consistently, directly attacking the 7% absenteeism that disrupts the 19,500 units roasted each quarter and the effort to cut the 2.4% defect rate. However, releasing 14 of 36 staff at once would remove a large share of the team, so any college course should be staggered across the quarter.

Decision: MCR should choose on-the-job training first, with short college courses later for senior operators. On-the-job training is cheaper, machine-specific and avoids losing output while absenteeism is 7% and quality complaints are already a problem. Full off-the-job training is rejected because paying $10,500 and releasing 14 staff at once would disrupt the 80,000-unit target; the college route can be added once the new line is stable.

    Answer: Point 1: A $400,000 bank loan gives GAC the full capital immediately, so the $460,000 flaking and packing line can be installed in one stage rather than waiting years to accumulate retained profit. For a cooperative with only $60,000 retained, waiting would delay the automation needed to cut the 6.1% packaging waste and the 2.9% defect rate, risking the trust of the regional grocers it supplies.

Point 2: Using the loan preserves GAC's limited retained profit for day-to-day working capital and for the $680 per employee short courses needed by 16 of 42 operatives. Repayments are spread over ten years, so the cost is matched to the years of benefit from the new line and does not consume the $12.00 selling price all at once. Interest is also tax-deductible in many systems, and the loan leaves member funds untouched, which suits a cooperative accountable to its members, unlike a share issue which a cooperative cannot use.

Acid Test Ratio 2024 = 0.68 : 1

Minimum wage increase (7.2%, to $13.29): GAC employs 42 workers, but the insert states no hours worked and no individual wages, so an annual wage bill cannot be invented. Conclusion: The 11.3% rise in wheat and oat prices will have the greatest impact. --- MAIN STEM ---
Bellwether Dairy (BWD) is a dairy processing partnership in the food industry rather than a sole trader, employing a workforce of 28. Founded in 2013 by Aoife Bellwether, the business supplies supermarket chains with locally sourced cheese and operates a flat structure with laissez-faire leadership. BWD plans to invest $330,000 in a new automated cheese packing line to cut waste, financed by a $210,000 bank loan and $120,000 retained profit. It has fixed costs of $156,000 a year, a variable cost of $3.80 a unit and a selling price of $9.00, and produces 65,000 units a year. BWD faces two problems: absenteeism is high among packing staff and milk waste has reached 4.7% of input.

--- APPENDIX 1 — MARKETING/OPS ---
Quality and Operations Report - Q3 2025: BWD packed 15,600 units of cheese last quarter at a defect rate of 1.9%, down from 3.2% a year ago. Customer complaints fell from 33 to 18 a month. Milk waste reached 4.7% of input. Delivery lead time averages 2.6 days. A survey of 380 supermarket buyers found 57% would pay up to $0.35 more for locally sourced dairy, and 44% check farm-origin labels. A skills audit shows 11 of 28 staff have not been trained on the new packing seals; the local college charges $620 per place.

--- APPENDIX 2 — FINANCIAL DATA ---
Title: Extract from the Statement of Financial Position of Bellwether Dairy as at 31 March 2025 ($ '000)
Headers: ['Financial Metric', '2024', '2025']
Inventories | 88 | 96
Trade receivables | 72 | 104
Cash and cash equivalents | 40 | 30
Current liabilities | 160 | 185
Non-current assets | 1,180 | 1,420
Capital employed | 1,560 | 1,790

--- APPENDIX 3 — EXTERNAL ENVIRONMENT ---
Economic and Business Bulletin (November 2026): (1) The central bank raised the base interest rate from 4.00% to 4.75%, increasing debt-service costs on BWD's $210,000 loan. (2) The national minimum wage will rise by 6.4% from $12.60 to $13.41 an hour from April 2026. (3) Feed and dairy input costs have risen 10.2% year-on-year, food inflation is 6.8% and consumer spending on locally sourced cheese grew 3.7%.

--- QUESTIONS ---
  Q1(a) [8 marks]
    Question: BWD is a partnership funding a $330,000 expansion with a $210,000 bank loan and $120,000 retained profit. Explain two benefits for BWD of operating as a partnership rather than a sole trader.
    Answer: Point 1: A partnership allows Aoife Bellwether to share the $330,000 investment risk and the management workload with other partners, rather than carrying all of the $210,000 loan liability alone as a sole trader would. With a workforce of 28 and 4.7% milk waste to control, shared decision-making under laissez-faire leadership brings different skills to quality and packing problems, improving the $9.00 product without overburdening one owner.

Point 2: Partners can contribute extra capital and creditworthiness, making the $210,000 bank loan easier to secure than for a single owner, and profits can be retained as $120,000 for the new cheese packing line. Unlike a sole trader, the business survives if one partner leaves, which reassures supermarket chains about continuity of locally sourced supply. Shares of profit are agreed in advance in the partnership deed, reducing disputes while the 65,000-unit output is maintained, and the shared management load lets Aoife Bellwether focus on the 4.7% milk waste problem rather than handling every decision alone.
    Keywords: partnership, sole trader, $330,000, $210,000, $120,000, Bellwether Dairy
    Mark scheme: knowledge_max_2: 1 mark for each valid point identified (max 2). | application_analysis_max_6: Up to 3 marks per point for contextual explanation and analysis applied to the named business and the case data.

    Question: BWD is promoting a new locally sourced cheese range. Consider farmers' market tastings, local radio advertising, or local newspaper coupons. Which should BWD choose? Justify your recommendation.
    Answer: Farmers' market tastings: Tastings let shoppers try the cheese and speak to Aoife Bellwether about the farm origin, directly using the 57% of 380 buyers who would pay $0.35 more for locally sourced dairy and the 44% who check farm-origin labels. It builds loyalty and gives immediate feedback on quality. The limit is scale: a market reaches only local visitors, and with a workforce of 28 and high absenteeism, staffing several events could strain the 15,600-unit packing schedule.

Local radio advertising: Radio is relatively cheap and can reach the whole regional catchment quickly, repeating the local-source message to drivers and shoppers. It suits a perishable product with a 2.6-day delivery lead time. Its weakness is that adverts cannot show or taste the cheese, and the message is easily forgotten; 44% of buyers check labels in store, so radio alone may not convert to purchases of the $9.00 product.

Local newspaper coupons: Coupons give a measurable, price-led reason to try the range and can be clipped by exactly the shoppers already buying supermarket cheese. They are low cost per unit and traceable. However, discounting undercuts the $0.35 premium that 57% of buyers will pay and can train customers to wait for offers, squeezing the $3.80 contribution per unit needed to justify the $330,000 line.

Recommendation: BWD should choose farmers' market tastings. They convert the 57% premium preference into trial and prove origin to the 44% who check labels, without discounting. Radio is rejected because it cannot demonstrate quality and is forgettable; coupons are rejected because they erode the premium and the contribution funding the $210,000 loan. BWD can support tastings with cheap social posts later.

--- MAIN STEM ---
Orchard Valley Juice (OVJ) is a public limited company in the soft-drinks industry, employing a workforce of 55. Founded in 2005 by Nadia Orchard, the business sells cold-pressed juice to national supermarkets and health shops and operates a hierarchical structure with democratic leadership. OVJ plans to invest $720,000 in a new cold-press bottling line to expand capacity, financed by a $420,000 share issue and a $300,000 bank loan. It has fixed costs of $280,000 a year, a variable cost of $5.50 a unit and a selling price of $12.50, and produces 90,000 units a year. OVJ faces two problems: labour turnover is rising and fruit waste has reached 5.8% of throughput.

--- APPENDIX 1 — MARKETING/OPS ---
Operations and Market Report - Q3 2025: OVJ bottled 21,400 units of juice last quarter at a defect rate of 2.1%, down from 3.5% a year ago. Customer complaints fell from 52 to 29 a month. Fruit waste reached 5.8% of throughput. Average delivery time is 3.1 days. A survey of 700 shoppers found 66% would pay up to $0.60 more for cold-pressed juice, and 49% check added-sugar labels. A training review shows 22 of 55 operators need certification on the new bottling line; courses cost $840 per employee.

--- APPENDIX 2 — FINANCIAL DATA ---
Title: Extract from the Statement of Financial Position of Orchard Valley Juice as at 31 March 2025 ($ '000)
Headers: ['Financial Metric', '2024', '2025']
Inventories | 145 | 162
Trade receivables | 118 | 150
Cash and cash equivalents | 62 | 48
Current liabilities | 250 | 278
Non-current assets | 2,100 | 2,520
Capital employed | 2,650 | 3,010

--- APPENDIX 3 — EXTERNAL ENVIRONMENT ---
Economic and Business Bulletin (November 2026): (1) The central bank has raised the base interest rate from 4.50% to 5.25%, raising interest costs on OVJ's $300,000 variable-rate loan. (2) The national minimum wage will rise by 6.9% from $12.90 to $13.79 an hour from April 2026. (3) Fruit input prices have risen 13.1% year-on-year, soft-drink inflation is 7.9% and consumer spending on healthy drinks grew 5.2%.

--- QUESTIONS ---
  Q1(a) [8 marks]
    Question: OVJ has raised $420,000 through a share issue and $300,000 through a bank loan. Explain two advantages for OVJ of the share issue over the bank loan.
    Answer: Point 1: Share issue money does not have to be repaid and carries no mandatory interest, so the $420,000 reduces the debt burden while OVJ funds a $720,000 bottling line and services only the $300,000 loan. With fixed costs of $280,000 a year and fruit waste at 5.8%, keeping cash free matters more than diluting ownership, and the $12.50 selling price need not cover extra interest.

Point 2: A public limited company can raise a large sum from many investors, so the $420,000 is available in one step rather than being limited by retained profit or bank lending limits. New shareholders also bring no fixed repayment date, which suits a long-life bottling asset, and the share issue can be used alongside the 66% of 700 shoppers who would pay $0.60 more for cold-pressed juice to expand capacity. Democratic leadership can involve shareholders in long-term goals, supporting the 90,000-unit plan, and the extra equity directly improves planning.
    Keywords: share issue, bank loan, $420,000, $300,000, $720,000, public limited company
    Mark scheme: knowledge_max_2: 1 mark for each valid point identified (max 2). | application_analysis_max_6: Up to 3 marks per point for contextual explanation and analysis applied to the named business and the case data.

  Q1(b) [12 marks]
    Question: OVJ is launching a new no-added-sugar juice. Consider supermarket shelf promotions, influencer marketing, or sponsorship of a food festival. Which should OVJ choose to promote the launch? Justify your recommendation.
    Answer: Supermarket shelf promotions: Shelf displays put the new juice directly beside shoppers at the national supermarkets that already stock OVJ, and can highlight the 49% who check added-sugar labels. They are cheap and measurable through the 21,400 units sold last quarter. The weakness is competition for prime shelf space and retailer fees, which could squeeze the $7.00 contribution needed to justify the $720,000 line, and a display does not explain cold-press benefits.

Influencer marketing: Health and lifestyle influencers can reach exactly the shoppers who value cold-pressed juice, with the 66% of 700 buyers willing to pay $0.60 more targeted at low cost per contact. Content can show the added-sugar label clearly and is measurable. The drawbacks are slow trust-building, dependence on influencer credibility, and limited in-store conversion; with labour turnover rising in a workforce of 55, OVJ may lack staff to manage many campaigns.

Food festival sponsorship: Sponsorship gives large-scale tasting and brand visibility, letting consumers try the product and ask questions, which fits a 3.1-day delivery lead time and national ambitions. It is expensive, however, and attendees may not be regular supermarket buyers; the 5.8% fruit waste means samples must be carefully planned, and reach is concentrated in a few events.

Recommendation: OVJ should choose influencer marketing. It targets the 66% premium segment and the 49% checking labels at low cost, and can be measured before scaling, which suits a publicly listed firm with a $300,000 loan to protect. Shelf promotions are rejected because retailer fees and space competition limit margin; festival sponsorship is rejected as costly and narrow compared with year-round digital reach. OVJ can add shelf cards once awareness is built.
    Keywords: 66%, 49%, 700, $0.60, cold-pressed juice, 21,400
    Mark scheme: level_1_1_to_4: Identifies promotional options with limited application to OVJ. | level_2_5_to_8: Discusses at least two options with advantages and disadvantages applied to OVJ. | level_3_9_to_12: Evaluates all three options in the context of OVJ with a justified recommendation and clear rejection of the alternatives.

  Q2(a) [8 marks]
    Question: OVJ's labour turnover is rising and fruit waste has reached 5.8%. Explain two benefits for OVJ of using team working on its bottling line.
    Answer: Point 1: Organising the 55 staff into teams around the new bottling line gives operators shared responsibility for output and quality, breaking repetitive work and reducing the labour turnover that disrupts the 21,400 units bottled last quarter. Teams can spot the causes of the 5.8% fruit waste together, protecting the $12.50 price and the $7.00 contribution per unit.

Point 2: Team working spreads skills, so the 22 of 55 operators needing certification can learn from colleagues while only a smaller number take the $840 courses, saving cost on top of the $720,000 investment. Under democratic leadership, team suggestions are heard through the hierarchy, improving the 2.1% defect rate and helping the 90,000-unit target. Stronger team commitment also reduces absence-related disruption to the 3.1-day delivery time demanded by national supermarkets, which helps the 49% of shoppers checking added-sugar labels receive consistent juice. It also raises morale, reducing the labour turnover that currently disrupts production.
    Keywords: labour turnover, 5.8%, workforce of 55, 22 of 55, $840, 21,400
    Mark scheme: knowledge_max_2: 1 mark for each valid point identified (max 2). | application_analysis_max_6: Up to 3 marks per point for contextual explanation and analysis applied to the named business and the case data.

  Q2(b) [12 marks]
    Question: OVJ needs a technician for the new bottling line. Consider training an existing operator or appointing a qualified technician from outside. Which should OVJ choose? Justify your decision.
    Answer: Training an existing operator: An internal trainee already knows OVJ's bottling routine and quality standards, so training is faster to apply and keeps loyalty in a workforce of 55 where labour turnover is rising. It avoids external recruitment fees and uses the $840 course budget for the 22 of 55 operators needing certification, supporting democratic leadership and cutting the 2.1% defect rate. The drawback is that training takes time, and the 5.8% fruit waste may persist until the trainee is competent on the new $720,000 line.

Appointing a qualified technician from outside: An experienced outside technician brings proven skills and can cut the 2.1% defect rate and 5.8% waste immediately, useful for a public limited company answerable to shareholders. Fresh expertise helps maintain the 90,000-unit target and 3.1-day delivery time. However, recruitment and salary costs are higher on top of a $300,000 loan, and an outsider may be resented by the 22 of 55 staff still awaiting certification, worsening turnover.

Decision: OVJ should train an existing operator, with a short external course where needed. Internal training is cheaper, builds commitment and directly addresses the rising turnover using the $840 budget, while preserving knowledge of the 90,000-unit process. An outside appointment is rejected because the added salary cost and resentment outweigh the speed gain while a $300,000 loan is serviced; OVJ can hire a specialist later if the 2.1% defect rate does not fall, once the internal trainee is certified and the $720,000 line is stable. This also keeps the 3.1-day delivery promise reliable.
    Keywords: bottling line, 22 of 55, $840, 2.1%, workforce of 55, 21,400
    Mark scheme: level_1_1_to_4: Basic description of the two staffing choices with limited application to OVJ. | level_2_5_to_8: Detailed analysis of benefits and drawbacks of one or both choices in the context of OVJ. | level_3_9_to_12: Comprehensive evaluation of both choices in the context of OVJ with a well-justified decision covering cost, skills and turnover.

  Q3(a) [8 marks]
    Question: Calculate and explain how OVJ's management can use its cost, break-even and productivity data.
    Answer: (i) Break-even output = 40,000 units | (ii) Contribution per unit = $7.00 | (iii) Four contextual uses: 50,000-unit margin of safety; testing the $0.60 premium; loan-service volume targets; unit-cost benchmarking at $8.61.

  Q3(b) [12 marks]
    Question: Using Appendix 2, evaluate OVJ's liquidity by calculating the current ratio and the acid test ratio for 2024 and 2025. Has OVJ's liquidity improved? Justify your answer.
    Answer: Calculations:
Current Ratio 2024 = 1.30 : 1
Current Ratio 2025 = 1.29 : 1
Acid Test Ratio 2024 = 0.72 : 1
Acid Test Ratio 2025 = 0.71 : 1

Detailed workings: 2024 current assets = $145,000 inventories + $118,000 trade receivables + $62,000 cash = $325,000; 2025 current assets = $162,000 + $150,000 + $48,000 = $360,000. Cover of the 2024 current liabilities of $250,000 was $325,000 / $250,000 = 1.30; cover of the 2025 liabilities of $278,000 was $360,000 / $278,000 = 1.29. Liquid assets excluding inventories were $325,000 - $145,000 = $180,000 in 2024, giving $180,000 / $250,000 = 0.72, and $360,000 - $162,000 = $198,000 in 2025, giving $198,000 / $278,000 = 0.71.

Evaluation: Liquidity has slightly deteriorated. Cover fell from 1.30 to 1.29 because current liabilities rose from $250,000 to $278,000 faster than current assets, which grew from $325,000 to $360,000. The liquid-asset measure fell from 0.72 to 0.71: although receivables rose from $118,000 to $150,000, cash dropped from $62,000 to $48,000 and inventories grew from $145,000 to $162,000. More of the cover now sits in stock and receivables, which is risky with 5.8% fruit waste and a 2.1% defect rate. Servicing a $300,000 loan while a $720,000 bottling line is commissioned leaves little spare cash if national supermarkets delay payment.

Conclusion: OVJ's liquidity has not improved. Both cover measures slipped and the fall in cash is the clearest warning, since the higher receivables tie up funds rather than strengthening solvency. OVJ should collect receivables faster and slow inventory growth before further borrowing.
    Keywords: 1.30, 1.29, 0.72, 0.71, $325,000, $360,000, $300,000
    Mark scheme: level_1_1_to_4: States financial figures without accurate ratio calculations. | level_2_5_to_8: Accurately calculates the ratios for both years with contextual analysis of the trend. | level_3_9_to_12: Accurate calculations for both years with detailed evaluation of the current-asset components and a justified conclusion.

  Q4(a) [8 marks]
    Question: Explain one advantage and one disadvantage for OVJ of introducing a recycling scheme for its fruit waste.
    Answer: Advantage: Recycling the 5.8% fruit waste into by-products or compost reduces disposal cost and supports the 66% of 700 shoppers who would pay $0.60 more for cold-pressed juice with a sustainability story. It also cuts the 2.1% defect rate by giving rejected fruit a use, protecting the $7.00 contribution and the $12.50 selling price while the $720,000 bottling line raises throughput to 90,000 units.

Disadvantage: A recycling scheme needs extra equipment and staff time in a workforce of 55 where labour turnover is rising, and it does not stop waste occurring at source. With fixed costs of $280,000 and a $300,000 loan, the set-up cost could squeeze margins unless the $0.60 premium is fully accepted. The 49% of shoppers checking added-sugar labels care more about ingredients than waste, so the scheme may add cost without raising sales, and the 13.1% fruit price rise still raises the $5.50 variable cost. Running the scheme while commissioning the $720,000 line could also distract the 22 of 55 operators needing certification, putting the 90,000-unit target at risk.
    Keywords: 5.8%, fruit waste, 13.1%, $280,000, 21,400, $5.50
    Mark scheme: knowledge_max_2: 1 mark for each valid point identified (max 2). | application_analysis_max_6: Up to 3 marks per point for contextual explanation and analysis applied to the named business and the case data.

  Q4(b) [12 marks]
    Question: Using Appendix 3, evaluate how the interest rate rise to 5.25%, the 6.9% minimum wage increase and the 13.1% rise in fruit input prices will affect OVJ. Which change will have the greatest impact? Justify your answer.
    Answer: Interest rate rise (4.50% to 5.25%): The change is 0.75 percentage points. If OVJ's $300,000 bank loan is variable-rate, the extra annual interest is 0.75% x $300,000 = $2,250, modest beside fixed costs of $280,000 and a $720,000 expansion. A fixed-rate loan would mean no immediate extra cost. Higher rates may also cool consumer spending, but the direct figure is small and can be capped by refinancing.

Minimum wage increase (6.9%, to $13.79): OVJ has a workforce of 55, but the insert gives no hours worked or individual wages, so an annual wage bill cannot be invented. Productivity is 90,000 units / 55 staff = about 1,636 units per worker. If that is maintained, the rise can be absorbed within the $5.50 variable cost and $7.00 contribution; if labour turnover and 5.8% waste reduce output, unit labour cost rises. It is a permanent rise but cannot be quantified from the insert.

Input price inflation (13.1% fruit): The insert does not break down the $5.50 variable cost, so only a labelled upper bound is sound: if all of the $5.50 rose 13.1%, that is 13.1% x $5.50 = about $0.72 per unit, or around $65,000 a year at 90,000 units. That directly erodes the $7.00 contribution servicing the $300,000 loan. OVJ can recover part through the $0.60 premium accepted by 66% of buyers, helped by the 5.2% growth in healthy-drink spending.

Conclusion: The 13.1% fruit input price rise will have the greatest impact. It recurs across all 90,000 units and attacks the contribution that funds the new line, dwarfing the $2,250 interest effect; the wage rise is also significant but unquantifiable and partly offset by productivity, whereas fruit inflation directly and repeatedly cuts the margin.
    Keywords: 5.25%, 6.9%, 13.1%, $13.79, $300,000, $5.50
    Mark scheme: level_1_1_to_4: Identifies the external changes with limited application to OVJ. | level_2_5_to_8: Analyses the impact of at least two external changes on OVJ's costs, revenue or financing in context. | level_3_9_to_12: Detailed evaluation of all three changes in the context of OVJ with a well-justified judgement on the greatest impact.

--- MAIN STEM ---
Redcliff Spice Mills (RSM) is a sole trader in the food manufacturing industry, employing a workforce of 18. Founded in 2016 by Ezra Redcliff, the business supplies independent grocers with organic spices and operates a flat structure with autocratic leadership rather than democratic leadership. RSM plans to invest $240,000 in a new automated spice-grinding and packing line, financed by a $180,000 bank loan, a $40,000 overdraft and $20,000 retained profit. It has fixed costs of $141,000 a year, a variable cost of $2.80 a unit and a selling price of $7.50, and produces 60,000 units a year. RSM faces two problems: labour turnover is high and spice waste has reached 5.4% of input.

--- APPENDIX 1 — MARKETING/OPS ---
Operations and Sales Report - Q3 2025: RSM milled 14,200 units of spice last quarter at a defect rate of 2.6%, down from 4.0% a year ago. Customer complaints rose from 21 to 34 a month. Spice waste reached 5.4% of input. Delivery lead time averages 2.9 days. A survey of 320 buyers found 59% would pay up to $0.30 more for organic spices, and 43% check origin labels. A skills check shows 8 of 18 staff need training on the new grinding controls; local course fees are $560 per person.

--- APPENDIX 2 — FINANCIAL DATA ---
Title: Extract from the Statement of Financial Position of Redcliff Spice Mills as at 31 March 2025 ($ '000)
Headers: ['Financial Metric', '2024', '2025']
Inventories | 70 | 84
Trade receivables | 58 | 50
Cash and cash equivalents | 22 | 14
Current liabilities | 130 | 148
Non-current assets | 920 | 1,150
Capital employed | 1,180 | 1,380

--- APPENDIX 3 — EXTERNAL ENVIRONMENT ---
Economic and Business Bulletin (November 2026): (1) The central bank has raised the base interest rate from 4.00% to 4.80%, increasing interest on RSM's $180,000 variable-rate loan and the $40,000 overdraft. (2) The national minimum wage will rise by 5.5% from $12.50 to $13.19 an hour from April 2026. (3) Spice and pepper import prices have risen 14.2% year-on-year, food inflation is 7.1% and consumer spending on home-cooking spices grew 3.2%.

--- QUESTIONS ---
  Q1(a) [8 marks]
    Question: RSM is financing a $240,000 expansion with a $180,000 bank loan, a $40,000 overdraft and $20,000 retained profit. Explain two advantages for RSM of using the overdraft.
    Answer: Point 1: An overdraft is flexible, letting Ezra Redcliff draw only the $40,000 needed when spice stock is bought and repay when grocers pay, so interest is charged on the actual shortfall. That suits a sole trader facing 5.4% spice waste and a 2.9-day delivery lead time, where cash needs change weekly, and it protects the $7.50 price from a permanently higher loan payment.

Point 2: An overdraft is quick to arrange and needs no long-term collateral, so RSM can act on the $240,000 grinding line without delaying for a new loan agreement. It complements the $180,000 loan by covering seasonal working capital while the $20,000 retained profit stays as a reserve. For a small workforce of 18, the simple arrangement saves management time, and it can be reduced as soon as the 59% of 320 buyers pay the $0.30 premium for organic spices. It also avoids a long-term interest commitment, so Ezra Redcliff is not locked into repayments if spice waste stays at 5.4%.
    Keywords: overdraft, $40,000, $180,000, $240,000, $141,000, organic spices
    Mark scheme: knowledge_max_2: 1 mark for each valid point identified (max 2). | application_analysis_max_6: Up to 3 marks per point for contextual explanation and analysis applied to the named business and the case data.

  Q1(b) [12 marks]
    Question: RSM is launching a new organic spice blend. Consider online marketplace advertising, trade fairs, or customer referral incentives. Which should RSM choose? Justify your recommendation.
    Answer: Online marketplace advertising: Listing ads on the marketplaces where independent grocers and home cooks already shop can target buyers of organic spices at low cost and be measured against the 14,200 units milled last quarter. It suits the 59% of 320 buyers who would pay $0.30 more and the 43% checking origin labels, with no stand fees. The limit is heavy competition online and the need for good product photos, which a workforce of 18 with high turnover may struggle to maintain.

Trade fairs: Fairs allow buyers to smell and taste blends and meet Ezra Redcliff, building trust in origin and quality, and can win several grocer contacts in one day. They are expensive once travel, stand and staff time are counted, and many visitors are not target customers; with a $180,000 loan and a $40,000 overdraft, such spending is hard to justify for a sole trader.

Customer referral incentives: Offering a small discount to existing grocers who refer new ones costs little and uses trusted relationships, which suits a business with 2.9-day delivery and 5.4% waste. However, it grows slowly, rewards customers who would have bought anyway, and the discount cuts into the $4.70 contribution per unit needed to justify the $240,000 line.

Recommendation: RSM should choose online marketplace advertising. It reaches the 59% premium segment and the 43% checking labels at low, measurable cost and fits a small team. Trade fairs are rejected as too expensive given the $180,000 loan and overdraft; referrals are rejected because they are slow and discount the margin. RSM can add referral rewards later once the blend is established.
    Keywords: 59%, 43%, 320, $0.30, organic spices, 14,200
    Mark scheme: level_1_1_to_4: Identifies promotional options with limited application to RSM. | level_2_5_to_8: Discusses at least two options with advantages and disadvantages applied to RSM. | level_3_9_to_12: Evaluates all three options in the context of RSM with a justified recommendation and clear rejection of the alternatives.

  Q2(a) [8 marks]
    Question: RSM's labour turnover is high and spice waste has reached 5.4%. Explain two benefits for RSM of introducing a performance-related bonus for its milling staff.
    Answer: Point 1: A bonus tied to output and waste gives the 18 staff a financial reason to reduce the 5.4% spice waste and the 2.6% defect rate, protecting the 14,200 units milled last quarter. Under autocratic leadership, where instructions are top-down, a bonus supplies extra motivation without Ezra Redcliff having to change his management style, improving the $7.50 product quality.

Point 2: Rewarding better performance can reduce the high labour turnover by making staff feel their effort is recognised, cutting the $560 per person training cost for the 8 of 18 still needing instruction on the new grinding controls. Because the bonus is paid only when results improve, it does not add a fixed cost to the $141,000 fixed costs, which matters while a $180,000 loan and a $40,000 overdraft are being serviced and spice prices rise 14.2%. The bonus can be funded from the contribution saved when the 5.4% spice waste falls, so it partly pays for itself.
    Keywords: labour turnover, 5.4%, workforce of 18, 8 of 18, $560, 14,200
    Mark scheme: knowledge_max_2: 1 mark for each valid point identified (max 2). | application_analysis_max_6: Up to 3 marks per point for contextual explanation and analysis applied to the named business and the case data.

  Q2(b) [12 marks]
    Question: RSM currently uses autocratic leadership. Consider keeping autocratic leadership or adopting democratic leadership for the new grinding line. Which should RSM choose? Justify your decision.
    Answer: Autocratic leadership: Ezra Redcliff keeps full control of decisions, which suits a sole trader and can give quick, clear instructions on the new grinding controls, important when 8 of 18 staff still need training and spice waste is 5.4%. Decisions are fast and roles are unambiguous, helping protect the 14,200 units and the 2.9-day delivery lead time. The drawback is that high labour turnover suggests staff feel little ownership, and top-down orders may not surface practical ideas for cutting the 2.6% defect rate, while rigid control can worsen morale in a flat structure.

Democratic leadership: Consulting the 18 staff on grinding routines can generate ideas that reduce the 5.4% waste and the 2.6% defect rate, and involvement raises commitment, tackling labour turnover without paying every $560 course fee. It fits a flat structure and can help staff accept the $240,000 new line. The risks are slower decisions and disagreement under a sole trader who is used to control; with a $180,000 loan and a $40,000 overdraft, delays could hurt output of 60,000 units.

Decision: RSM should adopt democratic leadership for the grinding line while keeping firm final authority. Consulting staff directly addresses the turnover and waste problems and uses their knowledge of the 14,200-unit process. Pure autocratic leadership is rejected because it has not stopped high turnover and suppresses the ideas needed to cut waste; full democracy is rejected because a $240,000 investment and tight cash need quick decisions, so a consultative approach with Ezra retaining the final say is the balanced choice.
    Keywords: autocratic leadership, democratic leadership, workforce of 18, 8 of 18, $560, 5.4%

  Q3(b) [12 marks]
    Question: Using Appendix 2, evaluate RSM's liquidity by calculating the current ratio and the acid test ratio for 2024 and 2025. Has RSM's liquidity improved? Justify your answer.
    Answer: Calculations:
Current Ratio 2024 = 1.15 : 1
Current Ratio 2025 = 1.00 : 1
Acid Test Ratio 2024 = 0.62 : 1

Detailed workings: 2024 current assets = $70,000 inventories + $58,000 trade receivables + $22,000 cash = $150,000; 2025 current assets = $84,000 + $50,000 + $14,000 = $148,000.   Q4(b) [12 marks]
    Question: Using Appendix 3, evaluate how the interest rate rise to 4.80%, the 5.5% minimum wage increase and the 14.2% rise in spice and pepper import prices will affect RSM. Which change will have the greatest impact? Justify your answer.
    Answer: Interest rate rise (4.00% to 4.80%): The increase is 0.80 percentage points. If RSM's $180,000 loan is variable-rate, the extra annual interest is 0.80% x $180,000 = $1,440; a $40,000 overdraft would also cost more when used. That is noticeable against fixed costs of $141,000 but far below the $240,000 investment. Higher rates may slow grocer orders, yet the direct cost can be capped by fixing the loan or repaying the overdraft quickly.

Minimum wage increase (5.5%, to $13.19): RSM employs 18 staff, but the insert gives no hours worked and no individual pay, so an annual wage total cannot be invented. Productivity is 60,000 units / 18 staff = about 3,333 units per worker. If that holds, the rise can be absorbed within the $2.80 variable cost and $4.70 contribution; if high labour turnover lowers output, unit labour cost rises. It is a permanent rise but cannot be quantified from the insert.

Input price inflation (14.2% spice and pepper): The insert does not decompose the $2.80 variable cost, so only a labelled upper bound is valid: if all of the $2.80 rose 14.2%, that is 14.2% x $2.80 = about $0.40 per unit, or roughly $24,000 a year at 60,000 units. That directly erodes the $4.70 contribution servicing the $180,000 loan and $40,000 overdraft. RSM can recover part through the $0.30 premium accepted by 59% of buyers.

Conclusion: The 14.2% rise in spice and pepper import prices will have the greatest impact. It applies to every unit and repeatedly cuts the $4.70 margin that funds the new line, far outweighing the $1,440 interest effect; the wage rise matters but is unquantifiable and partly offset by strong productivity, whereas imported input inflation attacks the margin directly.
    Keywords: 4.80%, 5.5%, 14.2%, $13.19, $180,000, $2.80
    Mark scheme: level_1_1_to_4: Identifies the external changes with limited application to RSM. | level_2_5_to_8: Analyses the impact of at least two external changes on RSM's costs, revenue or financing in context. | level_3_9_to_12: Detailed evaluation of all three changes in the context of RSM with a well-justified judgement on the greatest impact.

--- MAIN STEM ---
Kestrel Precision Gears (KPG) is a private limited company in the precision gear manufacturing sector, employing a workforce of 60. Founded in 2011 by Aoife Kestrel in Waterford, the business supplies custom gearboxes to agricultural machinery and robotics manufacturers and operates a flat organisational structure with democratic leadership. KPG faces two problems: absenteeism has reached 8%, skilled labour turnover is rising, and the defect rate on gear teeth from the older machines is climbing.

A skills audit shows 14 of 60 production staff have not completed on-the-job training on the new CNC gear grinders; off-the-job training at the technical college costs $1,000 per employee.

    Question: Using Appendix 3, evaluate how the interest rate rise to 5.2%, the 6.0% minimum wage increase and the 11.3% rise in alloy steel costs will affect KPG. Which change will have the greatest impact? Justify your answer.
    Answer: Interest rate rise (4.5% to 5.2%): If KPG's $600,000 ten-year bank loan is variable-rate, the annual interest cost rises by 0.7% of $600,000 = $4,200 a year (0.007 × $600,000). Minimum wage increase (6.0%, to $13.50 per hour): KPG employs a workforce of 60 and many workshop and packing roles are likely hourly-paid, so this rise feeds into the wage bill and is not optional. Alloy steel input inflation (11.3%): KPG's variable cost of $8.00 per unit includes materials, but the insert never decomposes it, so only a clearly labelled bound can be computed: if the entire $8.00 rose 11.3% it would add 11.3% × $8.00 = $0.90 per unit, or about $54,000 a year at 60,000 units. KPG can recover part through price negotiations with 500 surveyed buyers, 41% of whom would switch for a 3% lower price, so pricing power is limited.

Conclusion: The 11.3% alloy steel rise will have the greatest impact because it hits every one of the 60,000 units and directly erodes the $12.00 contribution that justify the $900,000 line, whereas the loan rise is at most $4,200 a year and the wage effect depends on unstated hours and can be offset by productivity. Interest and wage rises are therefore smaller or less certain in effect.

    Question: Explain one advantage and one disadvantage for HBB of using inspection-based quality control to reduce its 3.2% scrap rate.

With autocratic leadership and hierarchical supervision, inspection rules can be enforced consistently, protecting the reliability record that 72% of 450 buyers rank as their main purchase criterion and supporting the longer-life bearing that 38% would pay a 4% premium for.

Disadvantage: Inspection happens after defects are made, so the 3.2% scrap and its material cost are already incurred, and hiring inspectors adds to fixed costs of $480,000 a year while the $800,000 loan is serviced. Inspection can also slow the 9-day delivery lead time if batches queue for checking, and it does not find the root cause on the older grinders, so the 3.2% scrap rate may persist and the $1,200,000 new cell could inherit the same problem.
    Keywords: 3.2%, 2.1%, 26 customer warranty complaints, $1,200,000, 72%
    Mark scheme: knowledge_max_2: 1 mark for a valid advantage and 1 mark for a valid disadvantage. | application_analysis_max_6: Up to 3 marks per point for detailed contextual development linked to HBB's scrap rate, complaints and leadership style.

  Q4(b) [12 marks]
    Question: Using Appendix 3, evaluate how the interest rate rise to 5.8%, the 5.5% minimum wage increase and the 9.6% rise in alloy steel costs will affect HBB. Which change will have the greatest impact? Justify your answer.
    Answer: Interest rate rise (5.0% to 5.8%): If HBB's $800,000 five-year bank loan is variable-rate, the annual interest cost rises by 0.8% of $800,000 = $6,400 a year (0.008 × $800,000). That is modest next to fixed costs of $480,000, and if the loan is fixed-rate there is no direct increase. Higher rates may also cool automotive and wind-turbine investment and raise the cost of future funding beyond the $1,200,000 cell, but HBB can limit the damage by fixing the loan rate.

Minimum wage increase (5.5%, to $12.45 per hour): With a workforce of 120, many packing and support roles are likely hourly-paid, so this rise lifts the wage bill and cannot be avoided. The insert gives no hours worked or individual pay, so a defensible annual total cannot be invented; the sound comparison is with the given productivity of 120,000 units ÷ 120 staff = 1,000 units per worker. Unless that productivity is maintained or output rises, unit labour cost climbs and the $16.00 contribution per unit narrows, especially while labour turnover is a problem.

Alloy steel input inflation (9.6%): HBB's variable cost of $12.00 per unit includes materials, but the insert does not decompose it, so only a labelled bound is honest: if the full $12.00 rose 9.6% it would add 9.6% × $12.00 = $1.15 per unit, roughly $138,000 a year at 120,000 units, driving contribution from $16.00 toward $14.85. The 38% of surveyed buyers willing to pay a 4% premium offers only partial recovery, since reliability not price dominates for 72%.

Conclusion: The 9.6% alloy steel rise will have the greatest impact because it applies to every one of the 120,000 bearings and directly erodes the $16.00 contribution that supports the $1,200,000 investment. The loan rise is at most $6,400 a year and the wage effect depends on unstated hours and can be offset by productivity, so both are smaller or less certain than pervasive material inflation.
    Keywords: 5.8%, 5.5%, 9.6%, $12.45, $12.00, $800,000
    Mark scheme: level_1_1_to_4: Identifies the external factors with limited application to HBB. | level_2_5_to_8: Analyses the impact of at least two external changes on HBB's costs, revenue or financing in context. | level_3_9_to_12: Detailed evaluation of all three external changes in context with a well-justified judgment that input-cost inflation has the greatest impact and why the others are smaller.

Gransden Fasteners (GDF) is a private limited company in the precision fasteners and fixings manufacturing sector, employing a workforce of 50. It has fixed costs of $216,000 a year, a variable cost of $6.00 a unit and a selling price of $15.00, and currently produces 80,000 units a year. GDF faces skilled labour turnover and a training gap on the new cold-heading machines.

A skills audit shows 10 of 50 operators lack on-the-job training on the new cold-heading machines; off-the-job training at the engineering college costs $850 per employee.

The second measure, which removes stock, improved from 0.91 to 1.27, meaning RIC no longer needs to sell ceramic inventories to settle debts — useful while it services a $400,000 loan and a $680,000 kiln. However, trade receivables rose sharply from $110,000 to $140,000, tying up cash; if electronics and chemical-plant customers pay late, the stronger position could erode, and inventories fell to $60,000, so stock availability for the 14-day delivery time must be watched.

Conclusion: RIC's financial position has improved. Both liquidity measures rose (1.38 to 1.67 and 0.91 to 1.27) and the improvement is not dependent on inventory. The key residual risk is higher receivables, so tighter credit control is recommended before the partnership takes on more debt.

Pennydrove Hydraulics (PDH) is a private limited company in the hydraulic cylinder manufacturing sector, employing a workforce of 75. NVX faces two operational problems: its garment-finishing defect rate has reached 4.2% and labour turnover on the production line is rising.

A survey of 820 fashion shoppers found that 57% would pay up to $0.50 more for responsibly sourced clothing, and 49% check fabric labels before buying. A skills audit shows 24 of 96 production staff have not completed on-the-job training on the new automated cutters; an external course costs $110 per employee.

    Answer: Point 1: A share issue raises $300,000 without interest charges or a fixed repayment date, so unlike the $340,000 bank loan it adds no debt service to NVX's costs. That protects the $4.80 contribution per unit on 80,000 units and helps fund a new automated cutting and sewing line using responsible fabrics even if fashion clothing manufacturing and retail demand softens.

In fashion clothing manufacturing and retail, where the 11.3% input-cost rise already pressures margins, avoiding compulsory interest payments gives NVX a materially safer route than increasing its borrowings for a hierarchical organisation with 96 staff.

--- MAIN STEM ---
Threadwind Fashion (TWF) is a partnership in the knitwear e-commerce retail sector, employing a workforce of 52. Founded in 2011 by Beatrix Fenn, the business sells own-brand knitwear to consumers through its online store and operates a flat organisational structure with laissez-faire leadership. It has fixed costs of $144,000 a year, a variable cost of $6.20 a unit and a selling price of $11.00, and currently produces 78,000 units a year. TWF faces two operational problems: pilling-related quality complaints have risen to 38 a month and absenteeism in the packing team has reached 8.5%.

--- APPENDIX 1 — MARKETING/OPS ---
E-commerce Quality Report â€” Q3 2025: The knitwear store fulfilled 16,800 orders, with a pilling-related defect rate of 3.4% and 38 quality complaints per month, up from 22. Median delivery time is 3.1 days. A survey of 640 online knitwear buyers found that 66% would pay up to $0.70 more for guaranteed non-pilling yarn, and 54% read online reviews before ordering. A training check shows 14 of 52 packing staff have not been inducted on the new returns scanner; a short e-learning module costs $60 per employee.

--- APPENDIX 2 — FINANCIAL DATA ---
Title: Extract from the Statement of Financial Position of Threadwind Fashion as at 31 March 2025 ($ '000)
Headers: ['Financial Metric', '2024', '2025']

--- APPENDIX 3 — EXTERNAL ENVIRONMENT ---
Economic and Business Bulletin (November 2026): (1) The central bank has raised the base interest rate from 3.75% to 4.50%, increasing borrowing costs for firms with variable-rate loans. (2) The national minimum wage will rise by 5.5% from $12.80 to $13.50 per hour from April 2026, lifting wage bills in warehousing and fulfilment. (3) Wholesale wool and yarn costs have risen 8.6% year-on-year, consumer spending on online knitwear grew 4.1%, and inflation is running at 5.9%.

--- QUESTIONS ---
  Q1(a) [8 marks]
    Question: TWF plans to fund part of its $560,000 expansion with a $360,000 bank loan. Explain two advantages for TWF of using $200,000 retained profit instead.
    Answer: Point 1: Using retained profit costs TWF nothing in interest or capital repayments, so the $200,000 finances a new e-commerce returns and yarn-refurbishment hub without increasing the $360,000 debt commitment. Every dollar not paid as interest can absorb the 8.6% rise in wool and yarn input costs named in Appendix 3, protecting the $4.80 contribution per unit earned on each of the 78,000 units sold.

Point 2: Retaining profit leaves ownership and control with Beatrix Fenn and the existing owners, so no bank can impose conditions on how the $560,000 investment is run. It is also flexible: with 52 staff and a laissez-faire leadership style, TWF can time spending on the new facility to match cash generation. A bank loan would require regular interest and eventual repayment, which would strain cash flow if knitwear e-commerce retail demand weakened during the expansion.

Taken together, the $200,000 funds a new e-commerce returns and yarn-refurbishment hub without competing with the $360,000 debt service, leaving the $144,000 of annual fixed costs to be covered by the $4.80 contribution on each of the 78,000 units. --- MAIN STEM ---
Merrivale Boutiques (MVB) is a retail cooperative in the fashion boutique and omnichannel retail sector, employing a workforce of 78. Founded in 2005 by Priya Raval, the business runs member-owned fashion boutiques and a click-and-collect website and operates a hierarchical organisational structure with democratic leadership. MVB plans to invest $480,000 in a new click-and-collect store network and website upgrade, financed by a $300,000 bank loan and $180,000 member share issue. It has fixed costs of $120,000 a year, a variable cost of $6.00 a unit and a selling price of $10.00, and currently produces 70,000 units a year. MVB faces two operational problems: stockouts affected 7.8% of listed fashion lines and customer complaints about service have risen.

--- APPENDIX 1 — MARKETING/OPS ---
Retail Operations Report â€” Q3 2025: The boutique chain and website sold 19,200 units, with stockouts on 7.8% of listed lines and fabric waste of 5.1% of material used. Customer complaints rose from 31 to 44 per month. Average click-and-collect readiness time is 2.6 days. A survey of 700 shoppers found that 63% would pay up to $0.45 more for a reliable click-and-collect service, and 55% prefer retailers with clear sustainability policies. A training audit shows 16 of 78 store staff have not completed customer-service induction; a workshop costs $95 per employee.

--- APPENDIX 2 — FINANCIAL DATA ---

(2) The national minimum wage will rise by 7.1% from $12.60 to $13.50 per hour from April 2026, lifting wage bills across retail and warehousing. (3) Wholesale fashion garment costs have risen 10.2% year-on-year, consumer spending in boutique retail grew 2.2%, and inflation is running at 6.8%.

--- MAIN STEM ---
Kestrel Bay Resort (KBR) is a private limited company in the hospitality sector, operating a 60-room seaside hotel and employing a workforce of 60. Founded in 2007 by Anika Kestrel, the resort has a flat organisational structure with democratic leadership. KBR plans to invest $720,000 in a new sea-view wing and rooftop pool, financed by a $420,000 ten-year bank loan and $300,000 retained profit. It has fixed costs of $432,000 a year, a variable cost of $40 a unit and a selling price of $130, and produces 10,000 units a year, where each unit is an occupied room-night. KBR faces rising guest complaints about check-in delays and breakfast waste, while absenteeism has reached 9%.

--- APPENDIX 1 — MARKETING/OPS ---
Guest Services and Operations Report — Q4 2024: The resort sold 2,400 room-nights at 78% occupancy. Guest complaints about check-in fell from 29 to 17 per month, but average check-in wait is still 8 minutes. Breakfast waste is 11% of covers served. An online survey of 1,150 guests gave KBR a 4.2/5 rating, and 63% said a sea-view room justified a higher price. A skills audit shows 14 of 60 staff have not completed on-the-job training; off-the-job training at the local college costs $900 per employee.

--- APPENDIX 2 — FINANCIAL DATA ---
Title: Extract from the Statement of Financial Position of Kestrel Bay Resort as at 31 March 2025 ($ '000)
Headers: ['Financial Metric', '2024', '2025']

(3) Energy and laundry input costs have risen 9.5% year-on-year, while regional tourist arrivals grew 4.2% and guests are more price-sensitive.

    Answer: Point 1: Retained profit carries no interest charge or scheduled repayment, so KBR keeps its cash flow intact while it absorbs fixed costs of $432,000 a year and services the $420,000 bank loan it still needs. Every dollar not paid as loan interest can instead fund the extra housekeeping and laundry needed to cut the 11% breakfast waste and shorten the 8-minute check-in wait, helping protect the $130 selling price and the $90 contribution on each occupied room-night.

Point 2: Using $300,000 of its own money avoids the collateral and repossession risk tied to a bank loan, so the new sea-view wing cannot be seized if occupancy disappoints. It also leaves Anika Kestrel's ownership and control undisturbed: no lender can impose conditions on how the flat, democratic resort is run. This matters because 63% of the 1,150 surveyed guests already say a sea-view room justifies a higher price, so KBR can capture that premium for its own shareholders rather than for a bank.

  Q4(a) [8 marks]
    Question: KBR is considering a food-waste reduction programme to tackle the 11% breakfast waste. Explain one advantage and one disadvantage for KBR of this initiative.
    Answer: Advantage: Cutting the 11% breakfast waste lowers the food element of the $40 variable cost per room-night, widening the $90 contribution KBR earns on each of its 10,000 units and protecting profit while energy and laundry input costs have risen 9.5%. It also supports the 4.2/5 rating given by 1,150 guests: consistent breakfast quality and less waste help sustain the 63% of surveyed guests who accept a premium for a sea-view stay, strengthening the case for the $720,000 wing.

Disadvantage: Introducing portion control, better stock systems and staff training takes management time and may require small-scale equipment, which adds to the $432,000 fixed costs at a time when a $420,000 loan is being repaid.   Q4(b) [12 marks]
    Question: Using Appendix 3, evaluate how the base interest rate rise to 5.25%, the 5.8% minimum wage increase and the 9.5% rise in energy and laundry input costs will affect KBR. Which change will have the greatest impact? Justify your answer.
    Answer: Interest rate rise (4.5% to 5.25%): If KBR's $420,000 ten-year bank loan is variable-rate, the extra 0.75 percentage point costs 0.75% × $420,000 = $3,150 a year (0.0075 × $420,000). That is modest beside fixed costs of $432,000, and if the loan is fixed-rate the direct interest effect is nil. The higher rate could also make future borrowing for the $720,000 wing dearer and make guests slightly more cautious about discretionary stays.

Minimum wage increase (5.8%, to $13.60 an hour): KBR employs a workforce of 60 in largely hourly-paid housekeeping and service roles, so this lifts the wage bill and is not optional. The insert states neither hours worked nor individual pay, so no annual total can be invented. The defensible test is productivity: 10,000 units ÷ 60 staff = about 166.7 room-nights per worker, so a higher wage is affordable only if productivity holds or output grows; otherwise unit labour cost rises and the $90 contribution shrinks. Democratic leadership and on-the-job training can help protect that productivity.

Energy and laundry input costs (9.5%): These feed the $40 variable cost on every occupied room-night. The insert does not decompose that cost, so only a bound is honest: if the whole $40 were exposed, the rise would add 9.5% × $40 = $3.80 a unit, or about $38,000 a year at 10,000 units (10,000 × $3.80). Even a smaller exposed share still reduces the $90 contribution on each room-night, and this recurs on every unit rather than once.

Conclusion: The 9.5% input-cost rise will have the greatest impact. It compounds across all 10,000 room-nights and directly erodes the $90 contribution that justifies the $720,000 extension, whereas the interest rise costs only $3,150 a year on the stated loan and the wage effect, though unavoidable, can be offset by maintaining 166.7 room-nights per worker. KBR should fix the loan rate and recover part of the input rise through the premium 63% of guests accept.
    Keywords: 5.25%, 5.8%, 9.5%, $13.60, $420,000, $40
    Mark scheme: level_1_1_to_4: Identifies the external changes with limited application to KBR. | level_2_5_to_8: Analyses the impact of at least two external changes on KBR's costs, revenue or financing in context. | level_3_9_to_12: Detailed evaluation of all three changes in context with a well-justified judgment that input-cost inflation has the greatest impact and why the others are smaller.

--- MAIN STEM ---
Trailpeak Adventure Park (TAP) is a private limited company in the leisure and attractions industry, employing a workforce of 80. Founded in 2011 by Ravi Shan, the park operates a hierarchical structure with autocratic leadership. TAP plans to invest $640,000 in a new zip-line and ropes course, financed by a $240,000 bank overdraft and $400,000 from a new share issue. It has fixed costs of $300,000 a year, a variable cost of $25 a unit and a selling price of $75, and produces 16,000 units a year, where each unit is one visitor admission. TAP faces long queue times and rising safety complaints, together with a 12% labour turnover among its seasonal ride operators.

--- APPENDIX 1 — MARKETING/OPS ---
Operations and Safety Log — Q3 2025: The park recorded 9,500 visitor admissions, with an average queue of 22 minutes at the busiest ride. Safety and queue complaints rose to 31 from 19 last year. Some 7% of rides were idle for scheduled maintenance. An online survey of 2,000 visitors gave TAP a 4.6/5 rating, and 58% said they would return. A skills audit shows 12 of 80 seasonal ride operators have not completed on-the-job training; off-the-job training at the regional centre costs $750 per employee.

For a park with fixed costs of $300,000 a year and seasonal cash flow, this protects liquidity while the zip-line is built, leaving more of the $75 admission price to cover the $25 variable cost and earn contribution.

Point 2: Equity does not require the collateral or daily repayment pressure of an overdraft, so Ravi Shan's new ropes course cannot be threatened by a bank recall if visitor numbers dip below the 9,500 admissions seen last quarter. The share issue also spreads the funding burden among investors rather than concentrating it on a 5.0% to 5.75% interest-rate exposure; although existing owners dilute their control, TAP's autocratic leadership means strategic direction remains clear, and the 4.6/5 rating from 2,000 visitors gives shareholders confidence in demand for the $640,000 expansion.

    Question: Using Appendix 2, evaluate TAP's financial position by calculating the current ratio and the acid test ratio for 2024 and 2025. Has TAP's liquidity improved? Justify your answer.
    Answer: Calculations:
Current Ratio 2024 = 1.25 : 1
Current Ratio 2025 = 1.36 : 1
Acid Test Ratio 2024 = 0.85 : 1
Acid Test Ratio 2025 = 1.05 : 1

Detailed workings: 2024 current assets = $40,000 inventories + $55,000 trade receivables + $30,000 cash = $125,000; 2025 current assets = $35,000 + $70,000 + $45,000 = $150,000. For 2025, $150,000 ÷ $110,000 = 1.36 and ($150,000 − $35,000) ÷ $110,000 = $115,000 ÷ $110,000 = 1.05.

The reservation is trade receivables, up from $55,000 to $70,000, which lock away cash and could weaken the position if corporate bookings pay late, especially given a 12% labour turnover that adds costs.

Conclusion: TAP's liquidity has improved. Both ratios rose and the improvement is not driven by stock, so the park is better placed to meet short-term obligations. Rising receivables remain the main risk, so credit control should be tightened as the expansion proceeds.

--- MAIN STEM ---
Saffron Spice Grill (SSG) is a partnership in the hospitality sector, running a chain of four casual-dining restaurants and employing a workforce of 35. Founded in 2015 by Nadia Rahman, the business has a flat organisational structure with laissez-faire leadership. It has fixed costs of $182,000 a year, a variable cost of $12 a unit and a selling price of $38, and produces 22,000 units a year, where each unit is one meal served. SSG faces rising food-waste levels and 10% absenteeism among its kitchen staff, with repeat bookings falling in its four branches.

--- APPENDIX 1 — MARKETING/OPS ---

--- MAIN STEM ---
Lumen River Cruises (LCU) is a public limited company in the tourism sector, operating river cruises and employing a workforce of 95. It has fixed costs of $550,000 a year, a variable cost of $55 a unit and a selling price of $165, and produces 12,000 units a year, where each unit is one passenger-cruise place. LCU faces a 6% cancellation rate and rising complaints about cabin cleanliness from corporate charter groups during the peak season.

Guest Services Report — Q2 2025: LCU sold 6,800 passenger-cruise places, with a 6% cancellation rate. A survey of 1,800 passengers gave LCU a 4.4/5 rating, and 61% said they would recommend the cruise. Catering waste was 9% of meals prepared. A skills audit shows 18 of 95 crew have not completed on-the-job training; off-the-job training at the maritime academy costs $1,100 per employee.

--- MAIN STEM ---
Verdant Golf Lodge (VGL) is a cooperative in the leisure industry, running an 18-hole golf course and lodge and employing a workforce of 50. Founded in 2003 by Marcus Verdant, the cooperative uses a flat organisational structure with democratic leadership. VGL plans to invest $540,000 in a new nine-hole course and clubhouse extension, financed by a $180,000 bank loan and $360,000 retained profit. It has fixed costs of $240,000 a year, a variable cost of $20 a unit and a selling price of $80, and produces 9,000 units a year, where each unit is one round of golf. VGL faces staff shortages in the pro shop and rising complaints about course maintenance.

--- APPENDIX 1 — MARKETING/OPS ---
Course Operations Report — Q3 2025: VGL recorded 7,200 rounds of golf, with 13% of tee times left unfilled. Member complaints about bunker and green condition reached 22, up from 14 last year. Average time between tee times was 11 minutes. A survey of 900 members gave VGL a 4.1/5 rating, and 66% said the course was good value. Greenkeeping fuel and fertiliser use cost 7% more per round than a year earlier. A skills check shows 8 of 50 staff have not completed on-the-job training; off-the-job training at the leisure centre costs $700 per employee.

--- APPENDIX 2 — FINANCIAL DATA ---
Title: Extract from the Statement of Financial Position of Verdant Golf Lodge as at 31 March 2025 ($ '000)
Headers: ['Financial Metric', '2024', '2025']
Inventories | 30 | 26
Trade receivables | 40 | 52

Capital employed | 1,000 | 1,250

(2) The national minimum wage will rise by 5.5% from $12.51 to $13.20 an hour, raising greenkeeping and pro-shop wages. (3) Fertiliser and energy input costs have risen 10.4% year-on-year, while spending on leisure and golf memberships grew 3.9%.

--- QUESTIONS ---
  Q1(a) [8 marks]
    Question: VGL is funding its $540,000 nine-hole course and clubhouse extension with a $180,000 bank loan and $360,000 retained profit. Explain two advantages for VGL of using retained profit instead of the loan.
    Answer: Point 1: Retained profit needs no interest payments or fixed repayment dates, so the cooperative preserves cash while it meets $240,000 fixed costs and the higher greenkeeping fuel cost of 7% more per round. Money not paid to the lender can instead fix the bunker and green problems behind 22 member complaints, protecting the 4.1/5 rating from 900 members.

Point 2: Using its own $360,000 avoids pledging assets for a bank loan, so the existing course cannot be at risk if the new nine-hole course attracts fewer than the 7,200 rounds recorded last quarter. It also suits a cooperative with democratic leadership: members keep control of the $540,000 project without lender conditions, and the 66% who say the course is good value support reinvesting surplus locally rather than servicing external debt. VGL's 7,200 rounds last quarter show members already fund the course, so using retained profit keeps the democratic cooperative intact while the new course is built.
    Keywords: retained profit, bank loan, $360,000, $180,000, nine-hole course, $240,000

    Question: VGL wants to attract members to its new nine-hole course while 13% of tee times are unfilled. Consider a local newspaper campaign, a members' referral scheme, or social media influencer marketing. Which should VGL choose? Justify your recommendation.
    Answer: Local newspaper campaign: A newspaper advert reaches the local catchment cheaply and can promote the new nine-hole course to golfers nearby. However, print has low response and cannot show the course; with $240,000 fixed costs and a $180,000 loan, spending on broad ads is risky when 13% of tee times are already empty and the 4.1/5 rating from 900 members is the stronger selling point.

    Question: VGL has staff shortages in the pro shop and 22 complaints about course maintenance. Explain two benefits for VGL of introducing job enrichment for its workforce of 50.

For a workforce of 50 already short-staffed in the pro shop, higher satisfaction should reduce absence and help keep the 11-minute tee-time interval running smoothly.

    Question: Using Appendix 2, evaluate VGL's financial position by calculating the current ratio and the acid test ratio for 2024 and 2025. Has VGL's liquidity improved? Justify your answer.
    Answer: Calculations:
Current Ratio 2024 = 1.19 : 1
Current Ratio 2025 = 1.29 : 1
Acid Test Ratio 2024 = 0.81 : 1
Acid Test Ratio 2025 = 1.00 : 1

Detailed workings: 2024 current assets = $30,000 inventories + $40,000 trade receivables + $25,000 cash = $95,000; 2025 current assets = $26,000 + $52,000 + $38,000 = $116,000. For 2024, $95,000 ÷ $80,000 = 1.19 and ($95,000 − $30,000) ÷ $80,000 = $65,000 ÷ $80,000 = 0.81. For 2025, $116,000 ÷ $90,000 = 1.29 and ($116,000 − $26,000) ÷ $90,000 = $90,000 ÷ $90,000 = 1.00.

The caveat is trade receivables, up from $40,000 to $52,000, which tie up cash that could otherwise fix the 22 maintenance complaints; if members or visitors pay late, the ratios may slip back.

Conclusion: VGL's liquidity has improved. Both ratios rose and the improvement does not depend on inventories, so short-term solvency is stronger.     Question: Using Appendix 3, evaluate how the base interest rate rise to 6.0%, the 5.5% minimum wage increase and the 10.4% rise in fertiliser and energy input costs will affect VGL. Which change will have the greatest impact? Justify your answer.
    Answer: Interest rate rise (5.25% to 6.0%): If VGL's $180,000 bank loan is variable-rate, the extra 0.75 percentage point costs 0.75% × $180,000 = $1,350 a year (0.0075 × $180,000). That is small next to $240,000 fixed costs, and a fixed-rate loan would avoid it. The higher rate could make future borrowing for the cooperative dearer and may slightly restrain the 3.9% growth in leisure spending.

Minimum wage increase (5.5%, to $13.20 an hour): VGL's workforce of 50 includes hourly-paid greenkeeping and pro-shop staff, so payroll rises and cannot be avoided. The insert states neither hours worked nor individual pay, so an annual total would be invented. The defensible check is productivity: 9,000 units ÷ 50 staff = 180 rounds per worker, so the higher wage is sustainable only if that rate holds as the nine-hole course opens; job enrichment and training the 8 untrained staff can help protect it.

Fertiliser and energy input costs (10.4%): These feed the $20 variable cost on each round and are already 7% higher per round than a year earlier. The insert does not decompose the $20, so only a bound is honest: if the full $20 were exposed, 10.4% × $20 = $2.08 a round, and at 9,000 rounds that is about $18,720 a year (9,000 × $2.08). Even a smaller exposed share cuts the $60 contribution on every round, and the effect repeats with each round played.

Conclusion: The 10.4% input-cost rise will have the greatest impact. It compounds across all 9,000 rounds and directly erodes the $60 contribution that repays the $180,000 loan and funds the $540,000 extension, whereas the interest rise costs only $1,350 a year on the stated loan and the wage effect can be offset by sustaining 180 rounds per worker. VGL should review the $80 fee and act on the 7% higher per-round cost rather than absorb the whole increase.

--- MAIN STEM ---
Northline Transit & Logistics (NTL) is a private limited company in the road freight and logistics sector, employing a workforce of 60. Founded in 2011 by Elena Marsh, it delivers palletised goods for regional manufacturers and runs a flat organisational structure with democratic leadership. NTL plans to invest $720,000 in a fleet of fuel-efficient trucks and a computerised stock control system, financed by a $400,000 ten-year bank loan and $320,000 retained profit. It has fixed costs of $240,000 a year, a variable cost of $8.00 a unit and a selling price of $20.00, and currently handles 32,000 units a year. NTL faces an operational problem: driver absenteeism has reached 8% and late deliveries are rising, while its depot reports growing fuel waste from older vehicles.

--- APPENDIX 1 — MARKETING/OPS ---
Depot Operations and Market Report — Q3 2025: The fleet completed 8,000 consignments last quarter at a late-delivery rate of 4.5%, down from 6.8% a year earlier. Customer complaints fell from 44 to 26 per month. Average delivery time is 2.8 days. Vehicle defect rate rose to 3.2% from 1.9%, and fuel waste is estimated at 7% of mileage. Market research of 500 manufacturers found that 62% would pay up to $0.50 more for guaranteed next-day delivery, and 58% rank reliability above price. A training review shows 18 of 60 drivers have not completed on-the-job training on the new route-planning system; off-the-job training at the regional college is also under consideration.

--- APPENDIX 2 — FINANCIAL DATA ---
Title: Extract from the Statement of Profit or Loss and Capital employed data of Northline Transit & Logistics for the year ended 31 March 2025 ($ '000)
Headers: ['Financial Metric', '2024', '2025']
