Cost of sales | 1,200 | 1,375
Gross profit | 800 | 1,125
Operating profit | 250 | 375
Capital employed | 1,250 | 1,500
Interest payable | 30 | 25

--- APPENDIX 3 — EXTERNAL ENVIRONMENT ---
Economic and Business Bulletin (November 2026): (1) The central bank has raised the base interest rate from 4.25% to 5.0%, increasing borrowing costs for firms with variable-rate loans. (2) The national minimum wage will rise by 5.8% from $12.60 to $13.33 an hour from April 2026, raising wage bills across the transport sector. (3) Diesel and vehicle input costs have risen 9.5% year-on-year and road-fuel inflation is 7.2%, while demand for next-day freight grew 4.1%.

--- QUESTIONS ---
  Q1(a) [8 marks]
    Question: NTL plans to fund part of its $720,000 fleet expansion with $320,000 retained profit. Explain two advantages for NTL of using retained profit instead of the $400,000 bank loan.
    Answer: Point 1: Using retained profit costs NTL no interest or capital repayments, which protects cash flow while the business already carries fixed costs of $240,000 a year and is servicing a $400,000 bank loan. Every dollar saved on interest can be spent on tackling the 8% driver absenteeism and the rising late deliveries, for example by supporting the $0.50 next-day delivery promise without raising the $20.00 selling price. With the base rate due to rise to 5.0% (Appendix 3), a variable-rate loan would become more expensive, so retained profit avoids that exposure entirely.

Point 2: Retained profit leaves ownership and control with NTL's existing shareholders and imposes no lender covenants or collateral risk on the $720,000 fleet investment. There is no danger of trucks being repossessed if demand for next-day freight disappoints, which matters because the late-delivery rate is still 4.5% and the depot must first prove the reliability that 62% of surveyed manufacturers want. It also gives NTL quicker, more flexible access to funds than negotiating further debt, letting the automated stock control system be installed before the next peak period.
    Keywords: retained profit, bank loan, $320,000, $400,000, $720,000, $240,000
    Mark scheme: knowledge_max_2: 1 mark for each valid point identified (max 2). | application_analysis_max_6: Up to 3 marks per point for contextual explanation and analysis applied to NTL and the case data.

  Q1(b) [12 marks]
    Question: NTL is launching a guaranteed next-day delivery service. Consider national television advertising, local radio sponsorship, or social media influencer marketing. Which should NTL choose to promote the service? Justify your recommendation.
    Answer: National television advertising: A TV campaign would build awareness of next-day delivery very quickly across the whole country and could help NTL win new manufacturing accounts. However, airtime and production are extremely expensive for a 60-employee haulier already funding a $720,000 fleet, and most viewers are outside NTL's regional delivery network, so much of the spend would be wasted.

Local radio sponsorship: Local radio is much cheaper and reaches the regional manufacturers NTL already serves, so it fits the 8,000 consignments a year handled from the depot. Its weakness is limited reach: it cannot build the wider reputation needed when 58% of surveyed customers rank reliability above price and the late-delivery rate is only just down to 4.5%.

Social media influencer marketing: Logistics and business influencers can demonstrate reliable next-day delivery with real tracking data to a targeted audience of e-commerce and manufacturing buyers at low cost per contact. Results build more slowly than television, and credibility depends on the influencer, but the message can directly address the 62% of 500 surveyed manufacturers who would pay $0.50 more for guaranteed next-day delivery.

Recommendation: NTL should choose social media influencer marketing. It reaches the exact segment identified in the research, costs far less than television, and scales beyond local radio's narrow catchment. Television is rejected as unaffordable and untargeted, and radio is rejected as too limited to support a $400,000 loan-funded expansion; NTL should reinforce the campaign with direct mail to the manufacturers it already supplies.

The campaign can also be measured against the 26 monthly complaints now received, giving NTL a clear baseline for judging whether the new service is genuinely improving reliability rather than simply shifting demand.
    Keywords: next-day delivery, 62%, 58%, $0.50, 500, 8,000
    Mark scheme: level_1_1_to_4: Identifies promotional options with limited reference to NTL's next-day launch. | level_2_5_to_8: Discusses advantages and disadvantages of at least two options with some NTL context and emerging judgement. | level_3_9_to_12: Evaluates all three options in the context of NTL's survey data, costs and delivery performance, with a justified recommendation that explains why television and radio are rejected.

  Q2(a) [8 marks]
    Question: NTL's driver absenteeism has reached 8% and late deliveries are rising. Explain two benefits for NTL of its flat organisational structure and democratic leadership in addressing these problems.
    Answer: Point 1: Democratic leadership gives the 60 drivers a real voice in how routes and shifts are organised, which helps meet their social and esteem needs and raises job satisfaction. Drivers who help set their own schedules are more likely to attend consistently, so NTL can attack the 8% absenteeism rate directly rather than simply replacing drivers, protecting the 8,000 consignments handled each quarter.

Point 2: A flat organisational structure shortens the chain of command, so a late-delivery problem or a 3.2% vehicle defect can be reported and fixed quickly without passing through several management layers. Combined with democratic leadership, this encourages drivers to share practical ideas on route planning and fuel-efficient driving, which can reduce the 7% fuel waste and push the 4.5% late-delivery rate down further, strengthening the reliability that 58% of surveyed manufacturers value most.

Staff involvement also makes the 18 drivers still to complete on-the-job training more receptive to the new route-planning routines, so the $720,000 investment delivers its intended fuel savings instead of being resisted on the depot floor.

  Q2(b) [12 marks]
    Question: NTL needs drivers who can use the new route-planning system. Consider on-the-job training or off-the-job training at the regional college. Which should NTL choose? Justify your decision.
    Answer: On-the-job training: Training at the depot uses NTL's own vehicles and route-planning system, so it is directly relevant and keeps all 18 affected drivers productive while they learn. --- MAIN STEM ---
PeakWest Renewables (PWR) is a private limited company in the renewable energy equipment sector, employing a workforce of 80. Founded in 2013 by Tomas Reid, it manufactures solar photovoltaic panels for commercial installers and operates a hierarchical structure with autocratic leadership. PWR plans to invest $960,000 in an automated solar-cell assembly line with offcut recycling, financed by a $560,000 ten-year bank loan and $400,000 retained profit. It has fixed costs of $300,000 a year, a variable cost of $30 a unit and a selling price of $45, and currently produces 48,000 units a year. PWR faces a quality problem: the panel defect rate has reached 3.4% and labour turnover is rising, while its plant reports growing material waste from older cutting machines.

--- APPENDIX 1 — MARKETING/OPS ---
Quality and Operations Report — Q3 2025: The plant produced 12,000 panels last quarter at a defect rate of 3.4%, up from 1.7% a year ago. Customer complaints rose from 19 to 37 per month. Average order lead time is 4.6 days. Material waste is 6.2% of inputs and energy use is 2.1 kWh per panel. A skills audit shows 22 of 80 production staff have not completed on-the-job training on the new assembly machines; off-the-job training at the technical college is also being considered. A staff survey found 22 of 80 workers felt their views were ignored under the current autocratic leadership, with democratic leadership and laissez-faire leadership suggested as alternatives. HR is also considering a bonus scheme linked to quality.

--- APPENDIX 2 — FINANCIAL DATA ---
Title: Extract from the Statement of Profit or Loss and Capital employed data of PeakWest Renewables for the year ended 31 March 2025 ($ '000)
Headers: ['Financial Metric', '2024', '2025']
Revenue | 3,200 | 3,600
Cost of sales | 2,240 | 2,340
Gross profit | 960 | 1,260
Operating profit | 384 | 540
Capital employed | 2,400 | 2,700
Interest payable | 40 | 35

--- APPENDIX 3 — EXTERNAL ENVIRONMENT ---
Economic and Business Bulletin (November 2026): (1) The central bank has raised the base interest rate from 4.5% to 5.25%, increasing borrowing costs for firms with variable-rate loans. (2) The national minimum wage will rise by 6.2% from $12.60 to $13.60 an hour from April 2026, raising wage bills across manufacturing. (3) Polysilicon and silver input costs have risen 11.3% year-on-year, renewable-equipment inflation is 8.4%, and demand for commercial solar installations grew 6.0%.

--- QUESTIONS ---
  Q1(a) [8 marks]
    Question: PWR plans to fund part of its $960,000 assembly line with $400,000 retained profit. Explain two advantages for PWR of using retained profit instead of the $560,000 bank loan.
    Answer: Point 1: Retained profit carries no interest or repayment schedule, so it protects PWR's cash flow while the firm already bears fixed costs of $300,000 a year and is taking on a $560,000 bank loan. The money saved can be spent on reducing the 3.4% defect rate and the 6.2% material waste without raising the $45 selling price to commercial installers. With the base rate rising to 5.25% (Appendix 3), debt will get dearer, so funding part of the line internally reduces exposure to that increase.

Point 2: Using $400,000 retained profit preserves the ownership and control of founder Tomas Reid and the existing shareholders, with no lender conditions attached to the $960,000 investment. There is also no collateral risk: if the new assembly line fails to cut the 3.4% defect rate, the automated machines cannot be repossessed. Retained profit can be released immediately, allowing the offcut-recycling equipment to be installed before the next order cycle rather than waiting for loan approval.

    Question: Using Appendix 3, evaluate how the rise in the base interest rate to 5.25%, the 6.2% minimum wage increase and the 11.3% rise in polysilicon and silver input costs will affect PWR. Which change will have the greatest impact? Justify your answer.
    Answer: Base interest rate (4.5% to 5.25%): If PWR's $560,000 ten-year bank loan is variable-rate, the annual interest cost rises by 0.75% of $560,000 = $4,200 a year (0.0075 × $560,000). That is small relative to fixed costs of $300,000 a year and would be zero on a fixed-rate loan. Higher rates could also make commercial installers delay projects and raise the cost of future borrowing for the $960,000 line, but the direct effect is bounded.

Minimum wage increase (6.2%, to $13.60 an hour): With a workforce of 80 in production roles, this raises the wage bill and cannot be avoided. The insert states no hours worked or individual pay, so an annual total cannot be invented; the proper test is productivity, 48,000 panels ÷ 80 staff = 600 panels per worker. If output per worker holds and the 3.4% defect rate falls, the rise is affordable; otherwise unit labour cost climbs and the $15 contribution narrows.

Input-cost inflation (11.3% polysilicon and silver): The $30 variable cost is not broken down in the insert, so only a bound is honest: if the whole $30 rose 11.3%, that adds 11.3% × $30 = $3.39 a panel; across 48,000 panels a year that is about $162,720 (48,000 × $3.39). That would cut contribution from $15.00 towards $11.61 on every panel, far exceeding the interest effect, and it comes on top of 6.2% material waste. Only part can be recovered through price negotiations with installers.

Conclusion: The 11.3% rise in polysilicon and silver input costs will have the greatest impact. It hits all 48,000 panels and directly erodes the $15 contribution that underpins the $960,000 investment, whereas the interest rise is a bounded $4,200 a year and the wage rise can be absorbed if productivity holds at 600 panels per worker. PWR should cut the 6.2% waste first.

--- MAIN STEM ---
Redwood Trail Express (RTE) is a partnership in the parcel delivery and logistics sector, employing a workforce of 55. Founded in 2015 by Priya Raman and Dan Okoro, it delivers e-commerce parcels for online retailers and operates a flat structure with laissez-faire leadership. RTE plans to invest $450,000 in an automated parcel-sorting hub and electric delivery vans, financed by a $290,000 bank loan and $160,000 retained profit. It has fixed costs of $140,000 a year, a variable cost of $2.50 a unit and a selling price of $6.00, and currently handles 95,000 units a year. RTE faces an operational problem: parcel damage has reached 3.1% and absenteeism is rising, while its depot reports growing sorting errors during peak periods.

--- APPENDIX 1 — MARKETING/OPS ---
Depot Sorting and Market Report — Q3 2025: The hub sorted 24,000 parcels last quarter with a damage rate of 3.1%, down from 4.7% a year ago. Customer complaints fell from 61 to 34 per month. Average delivery time is 2.4 days and sorting errors affected 2.6% of parcels. Van downtime is 5.3% of scheduled hours. Market research of 700 online shoppers found 66% would pay $0.40 more for a same-day parcel service, and 57% choose couriers on reliability. A review shows 16 of 55 staff have not completed on-the-job training on the new sorters; off-the-job training at the local college is also an option. Managers are considering a bonus scheme and job rotation to cut sorting errors.

--- APPENDIX 2 — FINANCIAL DATA ---
Title: Extract from the Statement of Profit or Loss and Capital employed data of Redwood Trail Express for the year ended 31 March 2025 ($ '000)
Headers: ['Financial Metric', '2024', '2025']
Revenue | 1,800 | 2,100
Cost of sales | 1,260 | 1,365
Gross profit | 540 | 735
Operating profit | 270 | 378
Capital employed | 1,500 | 1,800
Interest payable | 18 | 15

--- APPENDIX 3 — EXTERNAL ENVIRONMENT ---
Economic and Business Bulletin (November 2026): (1) The central bank has raised the base interest rate from 4.0% to 4.75%, increasing borrowing costs on variable-rate loans. (2) The national minimum wage will rise by 5.5% from $12.40 to $13.20 an hour from April 2026, raising wage bills across courier firms. (3) Fuel and packaging input costs have risen 8.8% year-on-year, transport inflation is 6.5%, and e-commerce parcel volumes grew 5.4%.

    Answer: Point 1: Retained profit requires no interest or instalments, which protects the cash flow of a 55-employee partnership already carrying fixed costs of $140,000 a year and a $290,000 bank loan. The savings can be spent on reducing the 3.1% parcel damage rate and the 2.6% sorting errors without raising the $6.00 selling price to online retailers. With the base rate rising to 4.75% (Appendix 3), internal funds avoid the dearer debt.

Point 2: Retained profit keeps control with founders Priya Raman and Dan Okoro, with no bank conditions attached to the $450,000 investment and no asset at risk of repossession if the new hub fails to cut the 5.3% van downtime. It is also faster to deploy than negotiating more debt, so the electric vans and sorters can be installed before the next peak period when sorting errors currently rise, protecting the 57% of shoppers who choose couriers on reliability.

--- MAIN STEM ---
Eastline Power (ELP) is a public limited company in the electricity generation and supply sector, employing a workforce of 120. Founded in 2008 by Amina Yusuf, it supplies electricity to households and small businesses and operates a hierarchical structure with democratic leadership. ELP plans to invest $1,200,000 in a smart-meter rollout and battery storage units, financed by a $700,000 share issue and a $500,000 bank loan. It has fixed costs of $1,500,000 a year, a variable cost of $60 a unit and a selling price of $85, and currently supplies 150,000 units a year. ELP faces a service problem: billing complaints have reached 6.1% of customers and skilled-engineer turnover is rising, while its network reports increasing outage hours.

--- APPENDIX 1 — MARKETING/OPS ---
Customer Service and Network Report — Q3 2025: ELP served 38,000 accounts last quarter with a billing-complaint rate of 6.1%, up from 3.8% a year ago. Complaints rose from 92 to 168 per month. Average outage duration is 3.4 hours per customer and the network fault rate is 2.9%. Meter-reading accuracy is 96.5%. A skills review shows 30 of 120 engineers have not completed on-the-job training on the new smart meters; off-the-job training at the technical institute is also under consideration. HR is considering formal appraisals and a performance-related bonus to cut engineer turnover.

  Q1(a) [8 marks]

    Answer: Point 1: A $700,000 share issue raises equity that needs no interest or repayment, protecting cash flow while ELP already carries fixed costs of $1,500,000 a year and a $500,000 bank loan. With the base rate rising to 5.5% (Appendix 3), debt would cost more, so equity keeps the smart-meter rollout affordable and leaves more cash to cut the 6.1% billing-complaint rate and the 3.4-hour outages.

Point 2: Equity improves ELP's financial resilience because there is no risk of the $1,200,000 programme being jeopardised by loan covenants or repossession if demand grows only 2.7%. As a public limited company, ELP can access a wide pool of investors, spreading the funding risk among many shareholders rather than one lender, and the new capital supports the battery storage units without forcing Amina Yusuf to rely solely on retained profits or further borrowing.

Equity also avoids adding to the interest burden on the $500,000 bank loan at a time when the base rate has risen from 4.75% to 5.5%, protecting the $1,200,000 programme from debt-service pressure.

    Answer: National television advertising: TV could quickly inform millions of households about smart meters and help justify the $1,200,000 programme, but airtime is costly for a utility whose fixed costs are already $1,500,000 a year, and it cannot answer individual questions about the 6.1% billing complaints or 3.4-hour outages. Social media campaigns: Low-cost, targeted ads can reach households and small businesses with installation dates and energy-saving advice, and are easy to update. However, they lack the personal reassurance many customers need after 3.4-hour outages and depend on customers actively engaging with the message.

Recommendation: ELP should choose door-to-door sales teams. Given that 6.1% of customers already complain and the network fault rate is 2.9%, direct contact restores confidence and supports the $700,000 share-issue-funded rollout far better than mass media. Television is rejected as expensive and untargeted, and social media is rejected as too impersonal for a service with 168 monthly complaints; ELP can use social media only as a supporting channel.

Face-to-face teams can also demonstrate the 96.5% meter-reading accuracy and explain how the new meters cut estimated bills, directly addressing the rise in complaints from 3.8% to 6.1% of customers.

  Q4(b) [12 marks]
    Question: Using Appendix 3, evaluate how the rise in the base interest rate to 5.5%, the 6.0% minimum wage increase and the 14.2% rise in wholesale gas and carbon-permit input costs will affect ELP. Which change will have the greatest impact? Justify your answer.
    Answer: Base interest rate (4.75% to 5.5%): If ELP's $500,000 bank loan is variable-rate, the annual interest cost rises by 0.75% of $500,000 = $3,750 a year (0.0075 × $500,000). That is small beside fixed costs of $1,500,000 a year and zero on a fixed-rate loan. Because ELP is capital-intensive and also raised $700,000 by share issue, higher rates mainly affect future borrowing and customer demand rather than this year's profit.

Minimum wage increase (6.0%, to $13.50 an hour): With a workforce of 120 in engineering and customer service, this raises the wage bill and cannot be avoided. The insert gives no hours worked or individual pay, so no annual total can be invented; the relevant comparison is productivity, 150,000 units ÷ 120 staff = 1,250 units per employee. If that holds and the 6.1% complaint rate falls, the rise is bearable; if outages and turnover cut productivity, unit labour cost rises and the $25 contribution falls.

Input-cost inflation (14.2% gas and carbon permits): The $60 variable cost is not decomposed in the insert, so only a bound is defensible: if the whole $60 rose 14.2%, that adds 14.2% × $60 = $8.52 a unit; over 150,000 units a year that is about $1,278,000 (150,000 × $8.52). That would cut contribution from $25.00 to about $16.48 on every unit, dwarfing the interest effect, though battery storage and the $85 price give ELP some ability to respond.

Conclusion: The 14.2% rise in wholesale gas and carbon input costs will have the greatest impact. It applies to all 150,000 units and directly erodes the $25 contribution that supports the $1,200,000 programme, whereas the interest rise is a bounded $3,750 a year and the wage rise can be absorbed if productivity stays at 1,250 units per employee. ELP should accelerate battery storage to cut exposure.

--- MAIN STEM ---
Transgreen Logistics (TGL) is a cooperative in the recycling and green freight sector, employing a workforce of 70. Founded in 2012 by Nia Okafor, it collects and processes recyclable materials for local authorities and runs a flat structure with democratic leadership. TGL plans to invest $540,000 in an electric collection-truck fleet and a computerised stock control system, financed by a $340,000 bank loan and $200,000 retained profit. It has fixed costs of $200,000 a year, a variable cost of $4.00 a unit and a selling price of $9.00, and currently handles 100,000 units a year. TGL faces an operational problem: load contamination has reached 5.6% and vehicle defect rates are rising, while its depot reports growing fuel waste from older diesel vehicles.

--- APPENDIX 1 — MARKETING/OPS ---
Operations and Quality Report — Q3 2025: The fleet completed 26,000 collections last quarter with a contamination rate of 5.6%, down from 7.2% a year ago. Customer complaints fell from 41 to 23 per month. Average collection time is 3.7 days and the vehicle defect rate is 4.1%. Fuel waste is 8% of mileage. Market research of 450 local authority officers found 63% would pay $0.30 more for guaranteed contamination-free collections, and 59% rank reliability above price. A review shows 19 of 70 drivers have not completed on-the-job training on the electric trucks; off-the-job training at the regional college is also being considered. Managers are considering job rotation and team working to cut contamination and vehicle defects.

--- APPENDIX 2 — FINANCIAL DATA ---
Title: Extract from the Statement of Profit or Loss and Capital employed data of Transgreen Logistics for the year ended 31 March 2025 ($ '000)

Gross profit | 600 | 840

Capital employed | 2,000 | 2,450
Interest payable | 22 | 18

--- APPENDIX 3 — EXTERNAL ENVIRONMENT ---

(2) The national minimum wage will rise by 5.9% from $12.50 to $13.35 an hour from April 2026, raising wage bills across the recycling sector. (3) Diesel and recycling input costs have risen 10.1% year-on-year, waste-services inflation is 7.6%, and demand for recycled materials grew 3.9%.

    Question: TGL plans to fund part of its $540,000 electric-fleet investment with $200,000 retained profit. Explain two advantages for TGL of using retained profit instead of the $340,000 bank loan.
    Answer: Point 1: Retained profit costs no interest or repayments, protecting the cash flow of a cooperative with fixed costs of $200,000 a year and a $340,000 bank loan. The saving can be used to cut the 5.6% contamination rate and the 8% fuel waste without raising the $9.00 selling price to local authorities. With the base rate rising to 5.0% (Appendix 3), internal funds avoid the cost of dearer debt.

Point 2: Retained profit keeps control with the cooperative's members and founder Nia Okafor, with no lender conditions on the $540,000 investment and no asset at risk if the electric trucks fail to reduce the 4.1% vehicle defect rate. It is available immediately, so the computerised stock control system can be installed before the next collection cycle, helping deliver the contamination-free service that 63% of surveyed officers will pay $0.30 more for.

The $340,000 loan is also exposed to a base rate that has risen from 4.25% to 5.0%, so using more internal funds reduces the cooperative's exposure to debt-service costs during the electric-fleet programme.
    Keywords: retained profit, bank loan, $200,000, $340,000, $540,000, cooperative

    Question: TGL is promoting a guaranteed contamination-free collection service to local authorities. Consider national television advertising, local radio sponsorship, or social media influencer marketing. Which should TGL choose to promote the service? Justify your recommendation.
    Answer: National television advertising: TV could raise awareness of recycling services quickly, but airtime is very expensive for a cooperative funding a $540,000 fleet and most viewers are not the local authority officers who award collection contracts.     Question: Using Appendix 3, evaluate how the rise in the base interest rate to 5.0%, the 5.9% minimum wage increase and the 10.1% rise in diesel and recycling input costs will affect TGL. Which change will have the greatest impact? Justify your answer.
    Answer: Base interest rate (4.25% to 5.0%): If TGL's $340,000 bank loan is variable-rate, the annual interest cost rises by 0.75% of $340,000 = $2,550 a year (0.0075 × $340,000). That is modest beside fixed costs of $200,000 a year and zero on a fixed-rate loan. Higher rates could make local authorities delay contracts and raise future borrowing costs, but the direct interest effect is bounded.

Minimum wage increase (5.9%, to $13.35 an hour): With a workforce of 70 in driving and processing, this raises the wage bill and cannot be avoided. The insert gives no hours worked or individual pay, so no annual total can be invented; the fair comparison is productivity, 100,000 collections ÷ 70 staff = about 1,429 collections per worker. If that holds, the rise is manageable; if rising defects and contamination reduce efficiency, unit labour cost rises and the $5.00 contribution falls.

Input-cost inflation (10.1% diesel and recycling inputs): The $4.00 variable cost is not decomposed in the insert, so only a bound is honest: if the whole $4.00 rose 10.1%, that adds 10.1% × $4.00 = $0.404 a collection; across 100,000 collections a year that is about $40,400 (100,000 × $0.404). That would cut contribution from $5.00 to about $4.60 on every collection and compounds on the existing 8% fuel waste. Part can be recovered through the $0.30 contamination-free premium.

Conclusion: The 10.1% rise in diesel and recycling input costs will have the greatest impact. It applies to all 100,000 collections and erodes the $5.00 contribution that supports the $540,000 fleet, whereas the interest rise is a bounded $2,550 a year and the wage rise can be absorbed if productivity stays around 1,429 collections per worker. --- MAIN STEM ---
Northstar Cloud Systems (NCS) is a private limited company in the cloud computing and software services sector, employing a workforce of 60. On-the-job training on NCS's own servers is available at no course fee, while off-the-job cloud-security courses at the local college cost $1,100 per employee.

--- MAIN STEM ---
Kite Digital Studio (KDS) is a private limited company in the mobile app development and digital services sector, employing a workforce of 35. --- MAIN STEM ---
VoltLine Mobility (VLM) is a private limited company in the electric mobility and digital platform sector, employing a workforce of 42. Founded in 2017 by Sofia Marchetti, who also chairs the board, the business operates a hierarchical structure with democratic leadership. VLM plans to invest $720,000 in an automated e-bike battery-swapping network with contactless payment kiosks, financed by a $450,000 eight-year bank loan and $270,000 retained profit. It has fixed costs of $330,000 a year, a variable cost of $9 a unit and a selling price of $33, and currently produces 40,000 units a year. VLM faces an operational problem: complaints about scooter condition are rising and the defect rate on returned scooters has reached 2.7%.

--- APPENDIX 1 — MARKETING/OPS ---
Operations and Quality Report — Q3 2025: VLM recorded 9,600 rides with a 97.4% on-time battery-swap rate, down from 98.9% a year earlier. Complaints about scooter condition rose from 31 to 58 per month, and average swap time is 3.4 minutes. A survey of 700 riders found 63% prefer contactless payment and 49% would pay $1.50 more for guaranteed battery availability. Manual inspection of a returned scooter takes 12 minutes per unit.

--- APPENDIX 2 — FINANCIAL DATA ---

(3) Lithium battery input costs have risen 14.2% year-on-year, and consumer spending on mobility services grew 4.8% in the same period.

That cash can be spent on the $720,000 automated swapping network and on fixing the 2.7% defect rate on returned scooters without increasing the $330,000 annual fixed costs or the $33 selling price.

Point 2: Funding with $270,000 retained profit leaves Sofia Marchetti and the board free of lender conditions on how the contactless payment kiosks are rolled out, which matters when 58 riders a month already complain about scooter condition. It also avoids risking company assets if the 97.4% on-time swap rate cannot be restored, giving VLM time to improve service before adding debt. Given that 49% of riders would pay $1.50 more for guaranteed battery availability, internally funded investment can improve the service that generates that revenue, while interest on the $450,000 loan would absorb cash needed to answer the 58 monthly complaints.

The monitoring system should be introduced at the busiest kiosks first, where 9,600 rides create the most pressure, and its effect measured against the 2.7% defect rate and 58 complaints. --- MAIN STEM ---
Quanta Data Solutions (QDS) is a public limited company in the business analytics and software services sector, employing a workforce of 75. It has fixed costs of $504,000 a year, a variable cost of $16 a unit and a selling price of $44, and currently produces 45,000 units a year. QDS faces a skills and quality problem: reporting errors have risen to 2.8% and 12 analysts have not completed data-security training.

(3) Cloud-computing and data-centre input costs have risen 10.6% year-on-year, and business analytics spending grew 7.3% in the same period.

    Question: QDS needs analysts with data-security skills. Consider internal recruitment or external recruitment of security specialists. Which should QDS choose? Justify your decision.
    Answer: Internal recruitment: Promoting or retraining existing analysts is cheaper and faster, and the 75 staff already know QDS's reporting systems and clients. Training the 12 untrained analysts at $1,250 per course would build loyalty. The drawback is that the insert states a current data-security skills gap and a 2.8% error rate, so internal candidates may simply reproduce the same weaknesses unless training is thorough, and no new expertise enters the business.

External recruitment: Hiring experienced security specialists brings up-to-date skills and fresh practice, which directly addresses the 2.8% error rate and the 12 analysts without training. It widens the pool beyond the 75 current employees and supports the $1,050,000 data-warehouse launch. The costs are higher and induction takes time, with the risk that a new hire does not fit the hierarchical structure.

Decision: QDS should choose external recruitment for the security specialists, while offering the $1,250 course to existing analysts. External hiring is justified because the skills gap is explicit and cannot be solved from within quickly; internal recruitment alone is rejected as too slow and likely to perpetuate the 5.2-day turnaround and 39 complaints, though it remains suitable for non-security roles. A sensible compromise is to recruit externally for the missing security skills and enrol the 12 existing analysts on the $1,250 course, but the primary decision must be external hiring because the skills gap is explicit. Success should be measured against the 2.8% error rate, the 5.2-day turnaround and the 39 complaints. The insert gives no salary figures, so no cost comparison is invented; the judgement rests on the need for skills not currently present among the 75 staff.
    Keywords: data-security training, $1,250, 12, 2.8%, 75, $1,050,000, 39, QDS
    Mark scheme: level_1_1_to_4: Basic description of internal and external recruitment with limited application to QDS. | level_2_5_to_8: Detailed analysis of the benefits and drawbacks of both methods in the context of QDS. | level_3_9_to_12: Comprehensive evaluation of both methods with a well-justified decision covering skills gap, cost, speed and quality.

--- MAIN STEM ---
Axiom Security Software (AXS) is a private limited company in the cybersecurity software and digital services sector, employing a workforce of 50. Founded in 2013 by Noah Bergman, the business operates a flat structure with laissez-faire leadership. AXS plans to invest $880,000 in an automated penetration-testing platform with a self-service client portal, financed by a $580,000 five-year bank loan and $300,000 retained profit. It has fixed costs of $400,000 a year, a variable cost of $14 a unit and a selling price of $46, and currently produces 35,000 units a year. AXS faces a people and quality problem: staff turnover has reached 14% and the defect rate in software patches has risen, causing complaints about missed deadlines.

--- APPENDIX 1 — MARKETING/OPS ---
Quality and HR Report — Q3 2025: AXS released 2,100 software patches, with a defect rate of 4.1%, up from 2.2% a year ago. Complaints about missed deadlines rose from 22 to 41 per month, and average patch turnaround is 3.8 days. Staff turnover reached 14%. A survey of 380 clients found 66% value automated security testing and 53% would pay $5 more per month for faster patching.

--- APPENDIX 2 — FINANCIAL DATA ---

(3) Specialist developer software licences and cloud testing costs have risen 8.9% year-on-year, and cybersecurity spending grew 9.4% in the same period.

That cash can cover fixed costs of $400,000 a year and the work on the $880,000 penetration-testing platform while turnover is 14%, without adding to the pressure that has already produced 41 monthly complaints.

Point 2: Using $300,000 retained profit keeps control with Noah Bergman's team rather than a lender, so no external conditions dictate how the self-service client portal is developed. It also avoids pledging assets when the 4.1% defect rate and 14% staff turnover still need attention, giving the 50-strong firm room to stabilise quality before taking on more debt. The 53% who would pay $5 more for faster patching shows where internally saved cash can be reinvested, rather than paying interest that would compete with the $400,000 fixed costs and the 14% turnover problem.

Summit Trail Guides (STG) is a private limited company in the outdoor recreation and guided tourism sector, employing a workforce of 28.   Q1(a) [8 marks]

Point 2: Financing the $520,000 trail-mapping centre with retained profit means there is no external lender condition on how the centre is run or expanded, so STG keeps full control of the capital and equity.
    Keywords: bank loan, retained profit, $300,000, $520,000, STG, $360,000, guided trips

  Q2(a) [8 marks]
    Question: STG's customers report cancelled trips due to weather delays, and staff have become careless in packing guide bags. Explain two benefits for STG of using flat structure with democratic leadership to improve motivation in its guide team.

--- MAIN STEM ---
Havenwell Physio Group (HPG) is a private limited company in the healthcare equipment sector, employing a workforce of 40. Founded in 2013 by Priya Raval, the business supplies adjustable treatment tables to private clinics and operates with democratic leadership in a hierarchical structure. HPG plans to invest $640,000 in a new automated treatment-table assembly line with recycled aluminium frames, financed by a $400,000 seven-year bank loan and $240,000 retained profit. It has fixed costs of $240,000 a year, a variable cost of $85 a unit and a selling price of $145, and currently produces 10,000 units a year. HPG faces two problems: absenteeism has reached 8% and the assembly line has reported a rising defect rate in welded frames.

--- APPENDIX 1 — MARKETING/OPS ---
Operations and Quality Report — Q3 2025: HPG assembled 2,400 treatment tables last quarter at a defect rate of 2.2%, down from 3.6% a year ago. Customer complaints about uneven welds fell from 17 to 6 per month. Average order fulfilment time is 4.1 days. Market research of 300 clinic buyers found that 68% would pay up to $6 more for tables with recycled aluminium frames, and 55% check environmental credentials before ordering.

--- APPENDIX 2 — FINANCIAL DATA ---
Title: Extract from the Statement of Profit or Loss and Capital employed data of Havenwell Physio Group for the year ended 31 March 2025 ($ '000)
Headers: ['Financial Metric', '2024', '2025']

Cost of sales | 540 | 588
Gross profit | 360 | 462
Operating profit | 135 | 189
Capital employed | 750 | 900
Interest payable | 20 | 24

--- APPENDIX 3 — EXTERNAL ENVIRONMENT ---
Economic and Business Bulletin (November 2026): (1) The central bank has raised the base interest rate from 4.2% to 5.1%. (2) The national minimum wage will rise by 5.8% from $13.50 to $14.28 per hour from April 2027. (3) Aluminium and steel input costs have risen 9.6% year-on-year, healthcare equipment inflation is 6.3%, and consumer spending on medical equipment grew 2.8% in the same period.

--- QUESTIONS ---
  Q1(a) [8 marks]
    Question: HPG is funding part of its $640,000 assembly line with a $400,000 seven-year bank loan. Explain two advantages for HPG of using retained profit to fund the expansion instead of the bank loan.
    Answer: Point 1: Retained profit carries no interest charges or capital repayments, so the $240,000 contributed from internal funds costs HPG nothing to service. Every dollar not paid as interest on the $400,000 seven-year loan remains inside the business to absorb the $240,000 a year fixed costs, which is valuable while 8% absenteeism and a rising defect rate in welded frames are already disrupting output of 10,000 units. This protects cash flow and the $145 selling price from short-term pressure.

Point 2: Using retained profit keeps control with Priya Raval and the existing shareholders because no outside lender can attach conditions to how the new recycled-aluminium line is run. There is no collateral at risk of repossession if clinic demand for treatment tables disappoints, and no new lender to satisfy, so HPG can rebuild the 1,050 revenue line and tackle the weld complaints on its own timetable while preserving the full benefit of the expansion.
    Keywords: retained profit, bank loan, $400,000, $240,000, $640,000, HPG, 8%
    Mark scheme: knowledge_max_2: 1 mark for each valid advantage identified (max 2). | application_analysis_max_6: Up to 3 marks per point for detailed contextual explanation applied to HPG, its costs and its expansion decision.

  Q1(b) [12 marks]
    Question: HPG is launching its new recycled-aluminium treatment tables. Consider a national television campaign, local radio sponsorship, or social media influencer marketing. Which should HPG choose to promote the launch? Justify your recommendation.
    Answer: Television campaign: A national TV advert would build awareness of the recycled-aluminium tables among private clinics nationwide very quickly, giving the $640,000 assembly line a strong launch. However, airtime and production are extremely costly for a 40-employee firm already servicing a $400,000 loan, and most viewers are not clinical buyers, so much of the spend would be wasted.

Local radio sponsorship: Local radio is much cheaper and suits a time-limited launch message, and it can reach clinics in HPG's home region where deliveries already average 4.1 days. Its weakness is narrow geographic reach: the business supplies private clinics more widely, so radio alone cannot generate the 10,000-unit volume needed to cover $240,000 fixed costs.

Social media influencer marketing: Physiotherapy and clinic-management influencers can demonstrate the adjustable frames directly to the buying audience. This is measurable and low cost per contact, and it lets HPG tell the story that 68% of 300 surveyed clinic buyers would pay $6 more for recycled frames and 55% check environmental credentials — turning the research in Appendix 1 into a precise message.

Recommendation: HPG should choose social media influencer marketing. It targets the exact clinic buyers identified in the survey, is far cheaper than television and reaches further than local radio, while reinforcing the recycled-aluminium premium. Television is rejected as unaffordable and untargeted for a $400,000-loan-funded launch, and radio is rejected as too geographically narrow for a supplier aiming at 10,000 units a year.

It also avoids the heavy wastage of spend that a broad television campaign would create for a specialist clinical product bought by a relatively small group of clinic managers.
    Keywords: $640,000, $400,000, 68%, 300 clinic buyers, 55%, 2,400, HPG
    Mark scheme: level_1_1_to_4: Limited outline of the promotional options with minimal application to HPG. | level_2_5_to_8: Discussion of advantages and disadvantages of at least two options in the context of HPG with some judgement. | level_3_9_to_12: Detailed analysis of all three options in the context of HPG with a justified recommendation explaining why television and radio are rejected.

  Q2(a) [8 marks]
    Question: HPG's absenteeism has reached 8% and welded-frame defects are rising. Explain two benefits for HPG of using democratic leadership to improve motivation in its assembly team.
    Answer: Point 1: Democratic leadership gives the 40 employees a real voice in how the new assembly line is organised, so they feel valued and are more willing to attend regularly. Since absenteeism has reached 8%, involving welders in setting shift patterns and frame-handling routines addresses the cause of lost time directly, protecting the 10,000-unit output target and the 2,400 tables assembled last quarter.

Point 2: Consulting the people who actually weld the frames generates practical ideas for reducing the 2.2% defect rate, for example better jigs or ordering of recycled aluminium stock. Higher involvement raises commitment and reduces the complaints that fell from 17 to 6 per month, so quality improves at source instead of relying on inspection, and the hierarchical structure benefits from front-line knowledge that senior managers do not have.

The resulting fall in rework also frees capacity to meet the 4.1-day order fulfilment promise to private clinics.

  Q2(b) [12 marks]
    Question: HPG wants to cut its 2.2% defect rate on welded frames and reduce 8% absenteeism. Consider introducing quality circles or paying a performance-related bonus for weld quality. Which should HPG choose? Justify your decision.
    Answer: Quality circles: Small groups of welders meeting regularly to identify and solve frame-weld problems fit HPG's democratic style and the 2.2% defect rate. They use the workers' own knowledge, are inexpensive, and can also improve attendance because staff feel heard. They take time to produce results and need trained facilitators, and they do not by themselves reward the individual effort needed on the new line.

Performance-related bonus: Paying extra for defect-free welds gives a direct financial incentive and could quickly lower the 17-to-6 monthly complaint count and the 3.6% defect rate of a year ago. The weakness is cost and measurement: HPG would have to judge each welder's output fairly, and a bonus focused only on welds may ignore the 8% absenteeism problem or encourage rushing elsewhere.

Decision: HPG should introduce quality circles first. They attack the weld problem at source, are affordable for a 40-employee firm funding a $640,000 expansion, and support the democratic leadership already in the stem; the bonus can be added later once reliable quality data exist. The bonus is rejected as costly to administer and narrow, because it rewards weld quality without tackling the absenteeism that disrupts the 2,400 tables assembled each quarter.

A further consideration is cost control: HPG is already committing $240,000 of retained profit and servicing a $400,000 loan, so a bonus paid every quarter would be harder to sustain than time spent in short team meetings. Quality circles also build problem-solving habits that remain useful after the new assembly line is installed, whereas a bonus stops influencing behaviour as soon as payment stops. For these reasons the circles are the more durable answer to the welded-frame complaints, provided managers act on the suggestions made.

    Mark scheme: level_1_1_to_4: Basic description of the two approaches with limited application to HPG. | level_2_5_to_8: Analysis of benefits and drawbacks of both approaches in the context of HPG. | level_3_9_to_12: Evaluation of both approaches with a justified decision covering cost, quality data and motivation, explaining why the alternative is rejected.

--- MAIN STEM ---
Northbridge Learning Resources (NLR) is a private limited company in the education publishing sector, employing a workforce of 32. Founded in 2010 by Daniel Okafor, the business produces printed assessment packs for private schools and operates a flat structure with laissez-faire leadership. It has fixed costs of $180,000 a year, a variable cost of $9 a unit and a selling price of $24, and currently produces 20,000 units a year. NLR faces two problems: labour turnover is rising and a growing number of schools report binding defects in delivered packs.

--- APPENDIX 2 — FINANCIAL DATA ---

(2) The national minimum wage will rise by 6.1% from $12.80 to $13.58 per hour from January 2027. (3) Paper and print-input costs have risen 8.4% year-on-year, education supply inflation is 5.5%, and school procurement spending grew 3.1% in the same period.

  Q1(a) [8 marks]
    Question: NLR is funding part of its $480,000 printing and binding centre with a $280,000 five-year bank loan. Explain two advantages for NLR of using retained profit to fund the expansion instead of the bank loan.
    Answer: Point 1: Retained profit requires no interest payments or instalments, so the $200,000 contributed internally is cheaper than the $280,000 five-year bank loan. The cash saved can cover the $180,000 a year fixed costs while labour turnover and binding defects in 5,200 packs disrupt production, protecting the $24 selling price from short-term pressure and leaving more of the 720 revenue line as operating profit.

Point 2: Internal funding leaves control with Daniel Okafor and the existing owners, since no lender can impose conditions on the recycled-paper centre or demand security over NLR's assets. With a flat structure and laissez-faire leadership, managers value that autonomy; if school demand falls below the 20,000-unit target there is no loan to reschedule and no risk of repossession, so the business can respond quickly to late-delivery complaints.

Internal funding is especially helpful while binding defects require rework on the 5,200 packs made each quarter, and it avoids the monthly cash outflow that could strain the 2.6-day fulfilment operation.

    Question: NLR is launching its new recycled-paper assessment packs. Consider a national television campaign, local radio sponsorship, or social media influencer marketing. Which should NLR choose to promote the launch? Justify your recommendation.
    Answer: Television campaign: A national TV advert could build awareness of recycled-paper packs among schools everywhere, supporting the $480,000 centre. The cost of airtime and production is very high for a 32-employee publisher already committing to a $280,000 loan, and most viewers are not school buyers, so a large share of the budget would be wasted.

  Q2(a) [8 marks]
    Question: NLR has rising labour turnover and schools report binding defects. Explain two benefits for NLR of using laissez-faire leadership to improve motivation in its production team.
    Answer: Point 1: Laissez-faire leadership gives experienced packers freedom to decide how to set up the digital presses and binding machines, which can raise intrinsic motivation and job satisfaction. For a 32-employee publisher with a flat structure, that autonomy makes staff feel trusted, and it can reduce the labour turnover that is currently disrupting the 5,200 packs made each quarter.

Point 2: Because workers closest to the machines choose their own methods, they can experiment with ways to cut the 1.9% binding-defect rate and the complaints that fell from 22 to 9 per month. Solving quality problems themselves gives a sense of achievement, and the approach suits a skilled team more than close supervision, helping NLR keep the 2.6-day fulfilment time while the new centre is installed.

Because decisions need not pass through several management levels, a packer can adjust a machine setting as soon as a defect is spotted, keeping the 2.6-day fulfilment promise.
    Keywords: laissez-faire leadership, labour turnover, binding, 1.9%, 5,200, NLR, 22 to 9
    Mark scheme: knowledge_max_2: 1 mark for each valid benefit identified (max 2). | application_analysis_max_6: Up to 3 marks per point for contextual development linked to NLR's turnover, defect rate and delivery performance.

  Q2(b) [12 marks]
    Question: NLR wants to reduce labour turnover and the 1.9% binding-defect rate. Consider introducing job rotation or offering team-based bonuses. Which should NLR choose? Justify your decision.
    Answer: Job rotation: Moving staff between printing, binding and packing broadens skills and reduces boredom, which can lower labour turnover and build cover for absent colleagues. It also spreads understanding of where the 1.9% binding-defect rate arises, so workers spot errors earlier. The drawbacks are initial training time and a short dip in output of the 20,000-unit target while people learn each station.

Team-based bonuses: A shared payment linked to fewer defects and on-time dispatch gives a clear collective incentive and could cut the 22-to-9 monthly complaint count further. It is easy to link to the flat structure and laissez-faire culture, but the reward depends on reliable measurement of each pack's quality, and a group payment may let individual carelessness pass unnoticed while still costing NLR cash.

Decision: NLR should introduce job rotation first. It tackles turnover by making work more varied, improves quality understanding across the 32 staff and needs no new cash outlay beyond training, which matters while funding a $480,000 centre. The team bonus is rejected because it requires measurement systems NLR does not yet have and does not address the root cause of repetitive, high-turnover work; it can be introduced later once quality data are consistent.

Cost is also relevant: NLR is already funding a $480,000 centre from a $280,000 loan and retained profit, so a recurring bonus payment would reduce the cash available for new presses. Job rotation uses existing staff and builds a more flexible 32-person team, which is valuable when labour turnover is high. The bonus is therefore rejected on both cost and cultural grounds, since it pays for a result without developing the skills that prevent defects in the first place.

--- MAIN STEM ---
Swiftclean Laundry Services (SLS) is a private limited company in the commercial laundry and dry-cleaning sector, employing a workforce of 55. Founded in 2008 by Grace Mensah, the business cleans hotel uniform bundles and operates a hierarchical structure with autocratic leadership. SLS plans to invest $720,000 in a new automated washing line with a water-recycling system, financed by a $450,000 eight-year bank loan and $270,000 retained profit. It has fixed costs of $300,000 a year, a variable cost of $12 a unit and a selling price of $27, and currently produces 30,000 units a year. SLS faces two problems: absenteeism has reached 7% and a growing number of hotels report stained uniforms needing rewash.

--- APPENDIX 1 — MARKETING/OPS ---
Operations and Quality Report — Q3 2025: SLS processed 7,500 uniform bundles last quarter with a rewash rate of 2.8%, down from 4.1% a year ago. Complaints about stained uniforms fell from 31 to 12 per month. Average turnaround is 3.4 days. A survey of 350 hotel managers found that 66% would pay up to $0.90 more per bundle for water-recycled cleaning, and 58% check environmental practices when choosing a laundry supplier.

--- APPENDIX 2 — FINANCIAL DATA ---

Capital employed | 640 | 800

Economic and Business Bulletin (November 2026): (1) The central bank has raised the base interest rate from 4.4% to 5.3%. (2) The national minimum wage will rise by 6.4% from $12.60 to $13.41 per hour from April 2027. (3) Energy and detergent input costs have risen 10.4% year-on-year, laundry services inflation is 5.9%, and hotel outsourcing spending grew 2.6% in the same period.

--- QUESTIONS ---
  Q1(a) [8 marks]
    Question: SLS is funding part of its $720,000 washing line with a $450,000 eight-year bank loan. Explain two advantages for SLS of using retained profit to fund the expansion instead of the bank loan.
    Answer: Point 1: Retained profit has no interest or repayment burden, so the $270,000 provided internally is cheaper than the $450,000 eight-year bank loan. The money saved can be spent on tackling the 2.8% rewash rate and on covering the $300,000 a year fixed costs, protecting the $27 selling price and the cash needed to pay 55 staff while 7% absenteeism reduces capacity.

Point 2: Using internal funds keeps ownership and control with Grace Mensah rather than a lender, so no bank can impose conditions on how the water-recycling line is operated or on which hotels are served. With a hierarchical structure, this avoids another external approval layer and there is no asset at risk if hotel contracts slip; SLS can use the full benefit of the $720,000 investment to answer the 31-to-12 fall in stained-uniform complaints.

This is valuable while stained bundles require rewash and use extra capacity, and it avoids regular repayments that would compete with the cost of detergents and machine maintenance.
    Keywords: retained profit, bank loan, $270,000, $450,000, $720,000, SLS, rewash rate

However, production and airtime are very expensive for a 55-employee laundry already servicing a $450,000 loan, and most viewers are not hotel procurement managers, so a large part of the spend would not reach buyers.

It lets SLS use the survey result that 66% of 350 hotel managers would pay $0.90 more for water-recycled cleaning and 58% check environmental practices, converting Appendix 1 into a precise selling message.

Recommendation: SLS should choose social media influencer marketing. It reaches hotel buyers directly, costs much less than television and travels further than local radio, and reinforces the $0.90 premium needed after the 10.4% input-cost rise. Television is rejected as unaffordable for a $450,000-loan-funded launch, and radio is rejected as too narrow for a business aiming at 30,000 units a year.

Influencer content can also be changed quickly if hotel feedback on the 3.4-day turnaround changes, which a fixed television booking cannot accommodate.

A bonus can still be introduced later if stain-free results fail to improve, but at present the measurement burden and recurring cost make it the weaker choice for a 55-employee laundry with hierarchical control.

    Question: WHC wants to reduce labour turnover and the 2.4% packing-error rate. Consider introducing job enrichment or offering a performance-related bonus for error-free kits. Which should WHC choose? Justify your decision.

Performance-related bonus: Paying extra for kits that pass the final check creates an immediate financial incentive and could build on the fall in complaints from 26 to 8 per month. Decision: WHC should introduce job enrichment. The bonus is rejected because it rewards the outcome without changing the boring work, needs reliable measurement and adds expense; it can be considered later if error rates remain high.

Cost matters too: WHC is funding $240,000 of the $560,000 centre from retained profit, and a recurring bonus would compete with that commitment and with the $270,000 fixed costs. Job enrichment uses the existing democratic style and builds multi-skilled staff who can cover for absent colleagues, which is more valuable than a payment that stops rewarding behaviour once it ends. The bonus is rejected for that reason and because it does not change the routine that drives turnover.

--- MAIN STEM ---
Kirkstone Quarry Products (KQP) is a private limited company in the construction aggregates sector, employing a workforce of 60. Founded in 1998 by Duncan Kirkstone, it supplies crushed rock to regional road builders and operates a hierarchical structure with autocratic leadership on its quarry site. KQP plans to invest $960,000 in a mobile crushing and screening plant that produces recycled aggregate from demolition waste, financed by a $600,000 ten-year bank loan and $360,000 retained profit. It has fixed costs of $420,000 a year, a variable cost of $9.00 a unit and a selling price of $16.00, and currently produces 84,000 units a year. KQP faces two problems: the reject rate on crushed stone is 2.4% after rework, and dust complaints from nearby residents are rising.

--- APPENDIX 1 — MARKETING/OPS ---
Quarterly Operations Log, Q4 2025: the mobile crusher processed 21,000 tonnes at a reject rate of 2.4%, down from 4.0% a year earlier. Dust-suppression complaints from nearby residents fell from 17 to 9 per month. Average lorry turnaround is 38 minutes. Market research of 400 local builders found that 58% would pay up to $0.50 more per tonne for recycled aggregate, and 46% check for eco-certification when ordering. A skills audit shows 14 of 60 site staff are not certified on the new screening plant; external accreditation courses cost $750 per operative.

Every dollar not paid to the lender can be kept to absorb the 9.5% rise in diesel and tyre costs, helping KQP hold its $16.00 selling price while it brings the new screening plant into use and tries to cut the 2.4% reject rate.

Point 2: Retained profit avoids the collateral and repossession risk that come with a bank loan, so the $360,000 is available without putting KQP's $960,000 crushing plant at risk if road-building demand falls. It also leaves Duncan Kirkstone's ownership untouched, since no outside lender can impose covenants on how the recycled aggregate operation is run or how quickly the remaining expansion is financed.

For KQP this matters because the plant must first turn demolition feedstock into saleable recycled aggregate before any of the $0.50 premium is earned; retained profit gives it time to reach 84,000 units without adding interest to the $420,000 fixed costs.

--- MAIN STEM ---
Nestwood Eco Boards (NEB) is a private limited company in the eco-friendly building board sector, employing a workforce of 48. Founded in 2015 by Priya Nestor, it makes straw-fibre boards for green construction projects and operates a flat structure with democratic leadership. NEB plans to invest $720,000 in a new board-pressing line using low-formaldehyde eco-resin, financed by a $300,000 bank loan, a $250,000 share issue and $170,000 retained profit. It has fixed costs of $286,000 a year, a variable cost of $7.50 a unit and a selling price of $14.00, and currently produces 72,000 units a year. NEB faces two problems: waste on the old board line is 3.8%, and 12 of its operators are not yet certified on the new press.

--- APPENDIX 1 — MARKETING/OPS ---
Market Research Summary, 2025: a survey of 350 architects and builders' merchants found that 62% prefer low-formaldehyde eco boards and 54% would pay up to $0.60 more per board. Defect complaints on standard board fell from 26 to 14 per 1,000 boards. Delivery lead time averages 6 days. A quality log records waste of 3.8% on the old line against 1.9% on the new pilot line. Training records show 12 of 48 operators trained on the new press; certification courses cost $680 per person.

--- APPENDIX 2 — FINANCIAL DATA ---
Title: Extract from the Statement of Profit or Loss and Capital employed data of Nestwood Eco Boards for the year ended 31 March 2025 ($ '000)
Headers: ['Financial Metric', '2024', '2025']

Gross profit | 360 | 462
Operating profit | 108 | 189

Interest payable | 9 | 14

--- APPENDIX 3 — EXTERNAL ENVIRONMENT ---
Economic and Business Bulletin (November 2026): (1) The base interest rate rose from 4.0% to 4.75%, increasing loan and overdraft costs for borrowers. (2) The national minimum wage increased 6.2% from $12.90 to $13.70 an hour from April 2026. (3) Straw and resin input prices rose 8.4% year-on-year while construction inflation reached 5.5% and green-building sales grew 4.1%.

--- QUESTIONS ---
  Q1(a) [8 marks]
    Question: NEB financed $170,000 of its $720,000 expansion with retained profit. Explain two advantages for NEB of using retained profit rather than a bank loan.
    Answer: Point 1: Retained profit carries no interest or repayment schedule, which eases NEB's cash flow while it carries fixed costs of $286,000 a year and a $300,000 bank loan. The $170,000 can be deployed immediately to install the low-formaldehyde eco-resin press without lender approval, helping NEB cut waste from 3.8% toward the 1.9% achieved on the pilot line.

Point 2: Using internal funds keeps Priya Nestor's control intact and avoids pledging assets as collateral, so the $720,000 board-pressing line is not at risk of repossession if green-building demand disappoints. It also preserves the $250,000 share issue and existing cash for working capital, giving NEB room to wait the average 6-day delivery cycle and to meet its share of the 8.4% rise in resin costs without returning to the bank.

Keeping the $170,000 internal also preserves headroom under the $286,000 fixed-cost base while the 12 uncertified operators are trained and waste moves from 3.8% toward the 1.9% pilot rate.
    Keywords: retained profit, bank loan, $170,000, $720,000, $300,000, $286,000
    Mark scheme: knowledge_max_2: 1 mark for each valid advantage identified (max 2). | application_analysis_max_6: Up to 3 marks per point for contextual explanation applied to NEB's retained profit, loan and waste data.

  Q1(b) [12 marks]
    Question: NEB is launching its low-formaldehyde eco boards. Consider trade journals and builders' merchant exhibitions, social media campaigns, or sponsorship of a green-building award. Which should NEB choose to promote the launch? Justify your recommendation.
    Answer: Trade journals and merchants' exhibitions: These reach the 350 architects and builders' merchants in NEB's own survey directly, where 62% prefer low-formaldehyde eco boards and 54% would pay $0.60 more. Technical stands let NEB show the 1.9% pilot waste figure and certification evidence, and generate specification decisions and orders quickly. The drawbacks are stand costs and a narrow audience, but for a 48-employee firm funding a $720,000 line the targeting is efficient.

Social media campaigns: Social platforms can build broad awareness of green construction cheaply and can be measured, with creative content showing the straw-fibre production story. However, most users are householders rather than the architects and merchants who specify boards, so engagement may not convert into the volume needed to fill 72,000 units of capacity, and the 6-day delivery cycle limits any direct-sales benefit.

Green-building award sponsorship: Sponsorship would raise NEB's profile among sustainability-minded developers and could support a premium brand, fitting the 54% premium signal. It is, however, the most expensive and least controllable of the three, with no guaranteed orders, and its impact is slow compared with the immediate specification conversations available at trade events.

--- MAIN STEM ---
Quillstone Low-Carbon Concrete (QLC) is a public limited company in the low-carbon construction materials sector, employing a workforce of 75. Founded in 2007 by Elena Quill, it supplies ready-mixed concrete to contractors and operates a hierarchical structure with democratic leadership. QLC plans to invest $1,050,000 in a new batching plant using recycled aggregate and a geopolymer binder, financed by a $400,000 bank loan and a $650,000 share issue. It has fixed costs of $450,000 a year, a variable cost of $12.00 a unit and a selling price of $21.00, and currently produces 90,000 units a year. QLC faces two problems: failed batches run at 2.2% and offcut waste from the conventional line is 4.5%.

--- APPENDIX 1 — MARKETING/OPS ---
Operations and Quality Log, Q2 2025: the pilot batching line produced 18,000 cubic metres with a failed-batch rate of 2.2%, down from 3.6% a year earlier. Customer complaints about strength variation fell from 31 to 16 per month. Average delivery is 4 days. A survey of 500 contractors found that 57% would specify low-carbon concrete and 49% accept a price premium of $0.80 per cubic metre. Offcut waste is 4.5% on the conventional line against 2.1% on the pilot. Records show 18 of 75 plant staff are certified on the geopolymer mixer; courses cost $820 each.

--- APPENDIX 2 — FINANCIAL DATA ---

Interest payable | 20 | 26

(3) Recycled aggregate and cement input costs increased 10.2% year-on-year while construction inflation is 5.8% and infrastructure output grew 3.2%.

    Question: QLC raised $650,000 through a share issue to fund its $1,050,000 batching plant. Explain two advantages for QLC of a share issue over a bank loan.
    Answer: Point 1: A share issue brings $650,000 with no interest or capital repayment, so QLC can commit the money to the geopolymer batching plant while already bearing fixed costs of $450,000 a year and a $400,000 bank loan. Unlike debt, dividends are payable only if profits allow, which suits a business whose 2.2% failed-batch rate may take time to fall.

Point 2: Equity does not require collateral or place the $1,050,000 plant at risk of repossession if infrastructure demand slips, and it strengthens the balance sheet for future borrowing. As a public limited company QLC can also use the issue to widen its shareholder base, giving access to further capital for the 4-day delivery operation and helping absorb the 10.2% rise in recycled aggregate and cement costs without increasing its loan burden.

The $650,000 also reduces reliance on the $400,000 bank loan, leaving more of the $450,000 fixed-cost budget available to bring the 2.2% failed-batch rate down as the new plant beds in.
    Keywords: share issue, $650,000, $1,050,000, $400,000, $450,000, bank loan

  Q1(b) [12 marks]
    Question: QLC is launching its low-carbon concrete. Consider national television advertising, trade press and contractor seminars, or influencer social media marketing. Which should QLC choose to promote the launch? Justify your recommendation.
    Answer: National television: TV would create rapid, wide awareness of low-carbon concrete among millions of viewers, which could help a public limited company build its brand. The trouble is that the buyers are the 500 contractors in QLC's research, not the general public, so most of the airtime is wasted. With $1,050,000 already committed to the plant, a national campaign is expensive and cannot convey the technical strength data contractors need before specifying.

Trade press and contractor seminars: These reach the 500 surveyed contractors directly, of whom 57% would specify low-carbon concrete and 49% accept a $0.80 premium. Seminars let QLC demonstrate the 2.1% pilot waste and 2.2% failed-batch performance, answer engineering questions and capture specifications. Costs are modest and measurable, though the audience is narrow and results depend on getting specifiers into the room.

Influencer social media: Influencers can generate cheap, engaging content and raise awareness of green construction quickly, which may support the 49% premium signal. But influencer audiences are largely consumer-oriented rather than the contractors who buy ready-mixed concrete, and the 4-day delivery cycle means awareness without specification does not create orders, so conversion would be weak.

Recommendation: QLC should choose trade press and contractor seminars. They target the exact 500 buyers, prove the technical and environmental case, and cost far less than television, rejected as costly and untargeted. Influencer marketing is rejected as consumer-focused and unlikely to convert into specifications for the $1,050,000 plant; QLC can use it as low-cost supporting content later.

Because QLC supplies ready-mixed concrete within a 4-day window, close contact with contractors also supports delivery reliability, not just the launch message, which helps defend the 57% specification interest.

--- APPENDIX 1 — MARKETING/OPS ---

--- APPENDIX 2 — FINANCIAL DATA ---

  Q1(a) [8 marks]

Retaining $250,000 also avoids new loan covenants while ZSR works to bring the 3.1% breakage down to the 1.4% pilot level, so the $640,000 line can approach its 36,000-unit target before further debt is taken on. That leaves the loan available for later working-capital needs.

--- MAIN STEM ---
Yarrow Hempcrete Works (YHC) is a cooperative in the eco-insulation building materials sector, employing a workforce of 54. Founded in 2012 by Aisha Yarrow, it makes carbon-negative hempcrete blocks for green builders and operates a democratic leadership structure. YHC plans to invest $880,000 in a hemp-processing and block-pressing line using a carbon-negative lime binder, financed by a $350,000 bank loan, a $280,000 share issue and $250,000 retained profit. It has fixed costs of $330,000 a year, a variable cost of $8.00 a unit and a selling price of $15.50, and currently produces 75,000 units a year. YHC faces two problems: crack defects average 4.2% and hemp shiv waste is 5.2%.

--- APPENDIX 1 — MARKETING/OPS ---
Quality and Waste Report, 2025: the new hempcrete block line produced 19,000 blocks with a crack-defect rate of 2.6%, down from 4.2% on the old line. Customer complaints about insulation performance fell from 28 to 13 per month. Delivery lead time averages 5 days. A survey of 380 green builders found that 59% would specify hempcrete and 52% would pay up to $0.70 more per block for carbon-negative certification. Hemp shiv waste is 5.2% on the old process against 2.4% on the new. Logs show 13 of 54 members trained on the new press; external courses cost $700 each.

--- APPENDIX 2 — FINANCIAL DATA ---
Title: Extract from the Statement of Profit or Loss and Capital employed data of Yarrow Hempcrete Works for the year ended 31 March 2025 ($ '000)
Headers: ['Financial Metric', '2024', '2025']

Cost of sales | 620 | 696
Gross profit | 380 | 504
Operating profit | 100 | 168
Capital employed | 800 | 960
Interest payable | 12 | 16

--- APPENDIX 3 — EXTERNAL ENVIRONMENT ---
Economic and Business Bulletin (November 2026): (1) The base rate rose from 4.0% to 4.9%, increasing borrowing costs. (2) The minimum wage increased 6.4% from $12.80 to $13.62 an hour from April 2026. (3) Hemp shiv and lime input costs rose 9.8% year-on-year; construction inflation is 6.0% and green-material sales grew 3.9%.

Dividends need only be paid if profits allow, which suits a cooperative still trying to cut crack defects from 4.2% toward 2.6%.

Point 2: Equity does not require collateral, so the $880,000 pressing line is not exposed to repossession if green-material sales slow to 3.9%, and the balance sheet is strengthened for future borrowing. The share issue also lets YHC keep its $250,000 retained profit for the 5-day delivery cycle and to absorb the 9.8% rise in hemp shiv and lime costs, rather than committing every source of cash to debt service.

Equity also suits a cooperative, since members share in the upside of the $880,000 line, and keeping the $350,000 loan as the only debt limits interest exposure while the 4.2% crack-defect rate is reduced.

--- MAIN STEM ---
Goldenfield Grain Mills (GGM) is a private limited company in the grain milling and food processing sector, employing a workforce of 50. Founded in 2011 by Priya Goldenfield, it supplies fortified flour to regional bakeries and operates a hierarchical structure with autocratic leadership. GGM plans to invest $720,000 in a new automated flour-milling line with recyclable packaging, financed by a $420,000 ten-year bank loan and $300,000 retained profit. It has fixed costs of $240,000 a year, a variable cost of $5.00 a unit and a selling price of $11.00, and currently produces 100,000 units a year. GGM faces two problems: grain-dust waste has risen sharply and a recent quality audit found a 2.4% defect rate on the new line.

--- APPENDIX 1 — MARKETING/OPS ---
Quality and Operations Report — Q4 2025: The new milling line produced 24,000 units last quarter at a defect rate of 2.4%, down from 3.6% a year earlier. Customer complaints fell from 44 to 26 per month. Average order fulfilment time is 4.1 days. Grain-dust waste reached 3.2% of output. A survey of 400 regional bakery buyers found that 68% would pay up to $0.50 more for recyclable packaging, and 55% check packaging sustainability before ordering. Staff training records show 18 of 50 employees have not completed on-the-job training on the new milling machinery; off-the-job training courses at the technical college cost $800 per employee.

--- APPENDIX 2 — FINANCIAL DATA ---

  Q1(a) [8 marks]
    Question: GGM plans to finance part of its milling expansion with a ten-year bank loan. Explain two advantages for GGM of using retained profit to fund the expansion instead of the bank loan.
    Answer: Point 1: Using retained profit costs GGM nothing in interest or capital repayments, which protects cash flow at a time when the firm already carries fixed costs of $240,000 a year and a $420,000 bank loan. Every dollar not paid as interest can be used to absorb the 9.5% rise in wheat and grain input costs, helping GGM hold its $11.00 selling price for regional bakeries rather than passing costs on.

Point 2: Retained profit avoids the collateral and default risk of a bank loan, so the $300,000 available from internal funds leaves the new $720,000 milling line free from any lender repossession if demand from bakeries disappoints. It also preserves Priya Goldenfield's ownership and control of the business, since no external lender can impose conditions on how the automated flour-milling operation is run. Retaining profit also signals confidence to stakeholders and avoids the variable-rate exposure created when the base interest rate rose from 4.50% to 5.25%, which would have raised the cost of borrowing. Overall, internal finance keeps both the cost and the risk of the expansion lower than taking on more debt.
    Keywords: retained profit, bank loan, $300,000, $420,000, $240,000, $720,000, $5.00

  Q1(b) [12 marks]
    Question: GGM is launching its new fortified flour range. Consider a national television campaign, trade press advertising, or social media influencer marketing. Which should GGM choose to promote the launch? Justify your recommendation.
    Answer: National television campaign: A TV campaign would build rapid, wide brand awareness for the new fortified flour range across many regions at once. However, airtime and production costs are very high for a 50-employee private limited company already funding a $720,000 expansion with a $420,000 loan, and much of the mass audience would not be commercial bakeries, so a large share of the spend would be wasted.

Trade press advertising: Advertising in milling and bakery trade journals is cheap, reaches exactly the regional bakeries GGM supplies, and carries technical credibility for a fortified flour product. Its weakness is narrow reach: it cannot build consumer pull or support a premium, and with only 68% of surveyed buyers willing to pay $0.50 more, trade press alone may not shift enough volume to fill the new line.

Social media influencer marketing: Food and baking influencers can demonstrate fortified flour recipes to exactly the 55% of the 400 surveyed buyers who check packaging sustainability, with measurable engagement and low cost per reached buyer. Results take time to build and depend on influencer credibility, but the message can highlight the recyclable packaging that underpins the premium.

Recommendation: GGM should choose trade press advertising as the primary channel, supported by modest social media activity. Trade press reaches the actual decision-makers — regional bakeries — at a cost proportionate to a firm with $240,000 fixed costs, and it suits a technical fortified product. Television is rejected as unaffordable and untargeted, wasting spend on non-buyers; influencer marketing is rejected as the lead channel because it builds awareness slowly and GGM sells to bakeries rather than households, so the 68% premium signal is best triggered through the trade channel that already buys the flour.

Current Ratio 2025 = 1.60 : 1
Acid Test Ratio 2024 = 0.85 : 1

    Question: Explain one advantage and one disadvantage for GGM of introducing recyclable packaging for its fortified flour range.

It also strengthens the brand with the 55% who check packaging sustainability, helping GGM keep or win listings with regional bakeries for the $720,000 line.
