  Q4(b) [12 marks]
    Question: Using Appendix 3, evaluate how the interest rate rise to 5.25%, the 5.8% minimum wage increase and the 9.5% rise in input costs will affect GGM. Which change will have the greatest impact? Justify your answer.
    Answer: Interest rate rise (4.50% to 5.25%): If GGM's $420,000 bank loan is variable-rate, the annual interest cost rises by 0.75 percentage points × $420,000 = $3,150 a year (0.0075 × $420,000). That is modest against $240,000 fixed costs, and if the loan is fixed-rate the effect is zero. Higher rates may also make customers cautious and raise the cost of any future borrowing for the $720,000 expansion, but GGM can limit this by fixing the rate.

Minimum wage increase (5.8%, to $13.75 an hour): GGM employs a workforce of 50, and production and packing roles are largely hourly-paid, so this rise feeds into the wage bill and cannot be avoided. No hours worked or individual pay figures are given, so a defensible annual total cannot be invented; the honest test is productivity: 100,000 units ÷ 50 staff = 2,000 units per worker, so the rise is affordable only if productivity holds or output grows, otherwise unit labour cost climbs and the $6.00 contribution per unit shrinks.

Input cost inflation (9.5% grain and wheat): GGM's $5.00 variable cost per unit contains ingredients, but the insert never decomposes it, so only a bound is honest: if the whole variable cost rose 9.5% that adds about 9.5% × $5.00 = $0.48 per unit, and at 100,000 units that is roughly $47,500 a year. Even a smaller increase erodes contribution, but the $0.50 recyclable-packaging premium and bakery price talks can recover part of it.

Conclusion: The 9.5% input-cost rise will have the greatest impact because it compounds on every one of the 100,000 units and directly erodes the $6.00 contribution that justifies the $720,000 expansion, and unlike the loan it cannot be neutralised by fixing a rate. The wage rise is real but manageable if productivity holds, and the interest rise adds only about $3,150, so both are smaller.
    Keywords: 5.25%, 5.8%, 9.5%, interest rate, $13.75, $5.00
    Mark scheme: level_1_1_to_4: Identifies the external factors with limited application to GGM. | level_2_5_to_8: Analyses the impact of at least two external changes on GGM's costs, revenue or financing in context. | level_3_9_to_12: Detailed evaluation of all three external changes in the context of GGM with a well-justified judgment that input-cost inflation has the greatest impact and why the other two are smaller.

--- MAIN STEM ---
Harvestvale Dairy Co-operative (HDC) is a cooperative in the dairy farming and milk processing sector, employing a workforce of 64. Founded in 2004 by farmer Elena Harvestvale, it supplies yoghurt and cheese to independent grocers and operates a flat structure with democratic leadership. HDC plans to invest $960,000 in a new automated yoghurt and cheese processing plant, financed by a $560,000 ten-year bank loan and $400,000 of member share capital. It has fixed costs of $320,000 a year, a variable cost of $8.00 a unit and a selling price of $16.00, and currently produces 110,000 units a year. HDC faces two problems: milk spoilage waste has reached 4.1% and staff absenteeism is rising across the processing floor.

--- APPENDIX 1 — MARKETING/OPS ---
Market Research Summary — Q4 2025: A survey of 750 shoppers at independent grocers found 72% would pay up to $0.80 more for locally sourced yoghurt and 61% read dairy-origin labels. In-store trials sold 31,000 pots with a complaint rate of 1.6%, down from 2.9% in the previous trial. Milk spoilage waste measured 4.1% of intake. Average delivery time to grocers is 2.7 days. Training logs show 22 of 64 staff have not finished on-the-job training on the new pasteurisers; off-the-job training at the agricultural college costs $950 per employee.

--- APPENDIX 2 — FINANCIAL DATA ---
Title: Extract from the Statement of Financial Position of Harvestvale Dairy Co-operative as at 31 March 2025 ($ '000)
Headers: ['Financial Metric', '2024', '2025']
Inventories | 150 | 130
Trade receivables | 110 | 140
Cash and cash equivalents | 40 | 80
Current liabilities | 200 | 200
Non-current assets | 1,600 | 2,100
Capital employed | 2,000 | 2,400

--- APPENDIX 3 — EXTERNAL ENVIRONMENT ---
Economic and Business Bulletin (November 2026): (1) The central bank has raised the base interest rate from 4.00% to 4.75%, increasing borrowing costs for businesses with variable-rate loans. (2) The national minimum wage will rise by 7.2% from $13.20 to $14.15 per hour from April 2026, raising total wage bills. (3) Animal-feed and dairy input costs have risen 11.3% year-on-year, and food-price inflation is 7.1%, while consumer spending on branded yoghurt grew 4.0% in the same period.

  Q1(a) [8 marks]
    Question: HDC plans to fund part of its processing plant expansion with a ten-year bank loan. Explain two advantages for HDC of using member share capital instead of the bank loan.
    Answer: Point 1: Member share capital does not require the regular interest payments or capital repayments that a $560,000 bank loan demands, which protects the cooperative's cash flow while it already carries fixed costs of $320,000 a year. The $400,000 raised from members can therefore be spent on the $960,000 processing plant rather than on servicing debt, and it helps absorb the 11.3% rise in animal-feed and dairy input costs without raising the $16.00 selling price for independent grocers.

Point 2: Share capital from members carries no collateral or repossession risk, so the new yoghurt and cheese plant cannot be seized if sales to grocers disappoint. It also preserves the cooperative's member ownership and democratic control, since no outside lender can impose conditions on how Elena Harvestvale and the members run the business. Because member shares are a permanent source of funds, HDC avoids the variable-rate exposure created when the base rate rose from 4.00% to 4.75%. Overall, member share capital lowers both the financing cost and the risk of the expansion compared with borrowing more from a bank.
    Keywords: member share capital, bank loan, $400,000, $560,000, $320,000, $960,000, $8.00
    Mark scheme: knowledge_max_2: 1 mark for each valid advantage identified (max 2). | application_analysis_max_6: Up to 3 marks per point for contextual explanation and analysis applied to HDC and its expansion decision.

However, airtime and production costs are very high for a 64-member cooperative already funding a $960,000 plant with a $560,000 loan, and much of the audience will not shop at the independent grocers that stock HDC's cheese and yoghurt, so a significant part of the budget would be wasted.

Results build slowly and depend on influencer credibility, and the audience is less certain to visit an independent grocer.

    Answer: Interest rate rise (4.00% to 4.75%): If HDC's $560,000 bank loan is variable-rate, the annual interest cost rises by 0.75 percentage points × $560,000 = $4,200 a year (0.0075 × $560,000). That is modest against $320,000 fixed costs, and if the loan is fixed-rate the effect is zero. Higher rates may also make consumers cautious and raise the cost of future borrowing for the $960,000 plant, but HDC can limit this by fixing the rate.

Minimum wage increase (7.2%, to $14.15 an hour): HDC employs a workforce of 64 in processing and packing, so this rise feeds into the wage bill and cannot be avoided. No hours worked or individual pay figures are given, so a defensible annual total cannot be invented; the honest test is productivity: 110,000 units ÷ 64 staff = 1,718.75 units per worker, so the rise is affordable only if productivity holds or output grows, otherwise unit labour cost climbs and the $8.00 contribution per unit shrinks.

Input cost inflation (11.3% animal feed and dairy): HDC's $8.00 variable cost per unit contains milk and feed inputs, but the insert never decomposes it, so only a bound is honest: if the whole variable cost rose 11.3% that adds about 11.3% × $8.00 = $0.90 per unit, and at 110,000 units that is roughly $99,000 a year. Even a smaller rise erodes contribution, but the $0.80 local-sourcing premium and grocer price talks can recover part of it.

Conclusion: The 11.3% input-cost rise will have the greatest impact because it compounds on every one of the 110,000 units and directly erodes the $8.00 contribution that justifies the $960,000 plant, and unlike the loan it cannot be neutralised by fixing a rate. The wage rise is real but manageable if productivity holds, and the interest rise adds only about $4,200, so both are smaller.
    Keywords: 4.75%, 7.2%, 11.3%, interest rate, $14.15, $8.00

--- MAIN STEM ---
Orchardale Beverages (OAB) is a public limited company in the soft drinks and fruit juice manufacturing sector, employing a workforce of 72. Founded in 1998 by Marcus Orchardale, it supplies cold-pressed juice to national retailers and operates a hierarchical structure with laissez-faire leadership. It has fixed costs of $360,000 a year, a variable cost of $4.00 a unit and a selling price of $10.00, and currently produces 120,000 units a year. OAB faces two problems: packaging waste has reached 3.4% and customer quality complaints are rising across the bottling floor.

--- APPENDIX 1 — MARKETING/OPS ---
Operations Log — Q4 2025: The cold-pressed line filled 28,000 bottles last quarter with a defect rate of 2.6%, down from 3.8% a year ago. Customer quality complaints fell from 51 to 33 per month. Average delivery time to retailers is 3.4 days. Packaging waste measured 3.4% of output. A pilot team working scheme cut line stoppages by 18%. A survey of 800 shoppers found 66% would pay up to $0.60 more for cold-pressed juice and 58% choose drinks by brand reputation. The new equity can fund the $1,200,000 bottling line directly and help absorb the 10.2% rise in fruit and packaging costs without pushing the $10.00 selling price above what national retailers will accept.

Point 2: Share issue finance does not require collateral, so OAB's other assets are not at risk of repossession if sales of cold-pressed juice disappoint. It also spreads ownership among new shareholders rather than leaving Marcus Orchardale dependent on a lender that could impose conditions on how the business is run. As a public limited company, OAB can access a wide pool of investors, making a share issue a practical way to raise the $500,000 needed. --- MAIN STEM ---
Stonebrook Fine Foods (SFF) is a partnership in the specialty preserves and condiments sector, employing a workforce of 38. Founded in 2015 by chef Daniel Stonebrook, it supplies artisan jams and chutneys to independent delicatessens and operates a hierarchical structure with democratic leadership. SFF plans to invest $640,000 in a new automated preserves bottling and labelling line, financed by a $340,000 ten-year bank loan and $300,000 retained profit. It has fixed costs of $200,000 a year, a variable cost of $3.00 a unit and a selling price of $8.00, and currently produces 90,000 units a year. SFF faces two problems: labour turnover has risen to 11% and defect rates on the labelling line are high.

--- APPENDIX 1 — MARKETING/OPS ---
Quality and Waste Report — Q4 2025: The labelling line filled 19,000 jars last quarter with a defect rate of 2.8%, up from 1.9% a year ago. Customer complaints rose from 22 to 37 per month. Average delivery time to delicatessens is 3.9 days. Ingredient waste measured 4.6% of output. Labour turnover reached 11% over the year. A survey of 500 delicatessen customers found 63% would pay up to $0.45 more for artisan preserves and 57% value distinctive labelling. Training records show 12 of 38 staff have not completed on-the-job training on the new labeller; off-the-job training at the food technology centre costs $750 per employee.

  Q4(a) [8 marks]
    Question: Explain one advantage and one disadvantage for SFF of using distinctive labelling on its artisan preserves.
    Answer: Advantage: Distinctive labelling appeals to the 57% of surveyed delicatessen customers who value it and supports the premium that 63% of 500 customers would pay $0.45 more for, protecting the $5.00 contribution per unit even as sugar, fruit and glass-jar costs rise 8.7%.     Question: Using Appendix 3, evaluate how the interest rate rise to 4.50%, the 6.4% minimum wage increase and the 8.7% rise in input costs will affect SFF. Which change will have the greatest impact? Justify your answer.
    Answer: Interest rate rise (3.75% to 4.50%): If SFF's $340,000 bank loan is variable-rate, the annual interest cost rises by 0.75 percentage points × $340,000 = $2,550 a year (0.0075 × $340,000). Higher rates may also make consumers cautious and raise the cost of future borrowing for the $640,000 line, but SFF can limit this by fixing the rate.

Minimum wage increase (6.4%, to $13.94 an hour): SFF employs a workforce of 38 in bottling and labelling, so this rise feeds into the wage bill and cannot be avoided. Input cost inflation (8.7% sugar, fruit and glass jars): SFF's $3.00 variable cost per unit contains these inputs, but the insert never decomposes it, so only a bound is honest: if the whole variable cost rose 8.7% that adds about 8.7% × $3.00 = $0.26 per unit, and at 90,000 units that is roughly $23,500 a year. Even a smaller rise erodes contribution, but the $0.45 premium and delicatessen price talks can recover part of it.

Conclusion: The 8.7% input-cost rise will have the greatest impact because it compounds on every one of the 90,000 jars and directly erodes the $5.00 contribution that justifies the $640,000 line, and unlike the loan it cannot be neutralised by fixing a rate. The wage rise is real but manageable if productivity holds, and the interest rise adds only about $2,550, so both are smaller.

--- MAIN STEM ---
Meadowlands Poultry (MPP) is a sole trader business in the poultry farming and meat processing sector, employing a workforce of 30. Founded in 2007 by farmer Aisha Meadowlands, it supplies packaged chicken to regional supermarkets and operates a flat structure with autocratic leadership. MPP plans to invest $880,000 in a new automated poultry processing and packaging line, financed by a $480,000 ten-year bank loan and $400,000 from the sale of unused farmland. It has fixed costs of $280,000 a year, a variable cost of $6.00 a unit and a selling price of $13.00, and currently produces 95,000 units a year. MPP faces two problems: a 3.1% defect rate on the packaging line and rising labour turnover.

--- APPENDIX 1 — MARKETING/OPS ---
Operations Log — Q4 2025: The packaging line processed 21,000 birds last quarter at a defect rate of 3.1%, down from 4.2% a year earlier. Customer complaints fell from 46 to 29 per month. Average delivery time to regional supermarkets is 2.9 days. Carcass waste measured 3.7% of output. Labour turnover reached 12% over the year, but a pilot bonus scheme reduced absence on the packaging shift. A survey of 650 supermarket shoppers found 69% would pay up to $0.70 more for free-range packaged chicken and 60% check animal-welfare labels. Training logs show 14 of 30 staff need on-the-job training on the new packer; off-the-job training at the agriculture college costs $850 per employee.

(2) The national minimum wage will rise by 6.9% from $13.05 to $13.95 per hour from April 2026, raising total wage bills. (3) Feed grain and packaging input costs have risen 9.8% year-on-year, and food-price inflation is 6.6%, while consumer spending on free-range chicken grew 4.4% in the same period.

    Question: MPP plans to fund part of its packaging line expansion with a ten-year bank loan. Explain two advantages for MPP of using the sale of unused farmland instead of the bank loan.
    Answer: Point 1: Selling unused farmland raises $400,000 in cash without any interest payments or capital repayments, unlike the $480,000 bank loan, so MPP's cash flow is protected while it already carries fixed costs of $280,000 a year. The proceeds can go directly into the $880,000 packaging line and help absorb the 9.8% rise in feed grain and packaging costs without raising the $13.00 selling price charged to regional supermarkets.

Point 2: Asset sale finance needs no collateral on the trading business and carries no repossession risk, so the new processing line cannot be seized if demand for packaged chicken falls. It also keeps control firmly with Aisha Meadowlands as sole trader, since no lender can impose conditions on how the farm is run. Because the land was unused, the sale releases idle value rather than taking on new debt, and it avoids the variable-rate exposure created when the base rate rose from 4.10% to 4.85%. Overall, the sale is cheaper and less risky than borrowing more.
    Keywords: sale of unused farmland, bank loan, $400,000, $480,000, $280,000, $880,000, $6.00

    Answer: Television advertising campaign: Television would give the free-range chicken range wide reach quickly across many regions. However, airtime and production costs are high for a 30-employee sole trader already funding an $880,000 line with a $480,000 loan, and much of the mass audience will not shop at the regional supermarkets that stock MPP, so a large part of the spend would be wasted.

Its reach is narrow and the link to free-range chicken is indirect, so it may do little to shift product off supermarket shelves in the short term.

Social media influencer marketing: Food and family influencers can explain free-range and welfare benefits to a targeted audience at low cost per reached shopper and speak directly to the 69% of 650 surveyed shoppers who would pay $0.70 more. Results build slowly and depend on influencer credibility, but the message supports the premium positioning.

Recommendation: MPP should choose social media influencer marketing as the lead channel, with a small local sponsorship to build community goodwill. Influencers reach the exact welfare-conscious segment in the research, cost far less than television, and can justify the $0.70 premium. Television is rejected as unaffordable and untargeted for a sole trader servicing a $480,000 loan, and sponsorship is rejected as the lead channel because its reach is narrow and its connection to packaged chicken is weaker than a targeted welfare message.
    Keywords: free-range packaged chicken, $880,000, 69%, 60%, $0.70, 650

    Question: Using Appendix 2, evaluate MPP's financial position by calculating the current ratio and the acid test ratio for 2024 and 2025. Has MPP's financial position improved? Justify your answer.
    Answer: Calculations:
Current Ratio 2024 = 1.40 : 1
Current Ratio 2025 = 1.61 : 1
Acid Test Ratio 2024 = 0.77 : 1
Acid Test Ratio 2025 = 1.08 : 1

Detailed workings: 2024 current assets = $110,000 inventories + $90,000 trade receivables + $45,000 cash = $245,000; 2025 current assets = $95,000 + $120,000 + $75,000 = $290,000. However, trade receivables rose from $90,000 to $120,000, tying up cash; if regional supermarkets pay late the position could weaken, and the fall in inventories to $95,000 should be watched to avoid shortages.

Conclusion: MPP's financial position has improved. Both liquidity measures moved favourably (1.40 to 1.61 and 0.77 to 1.08), and the improvement does not rely on stock. --- MAIN STEM ---
Kestrel Precision Components (KPC) is a private limited company in the precision engineering sector, employing a workforce of 60. Founded in 2011 by Freya Kestrel, it machines aerospace engine components for civil aircraft manufacturers and operates a flat organisational structure with democratic leadership. KPC plans to invest $720,000 in a new CNC machining cell with automated inspection, financed by a $450,000 ten-year bank loan and $270,000 retained profit. It has fixed costs of $300,000 a year, a variable cost of $14.00 a unit and a selling price of $24.00, and currently produces 40,000 units a year. KPC faces two problems: its defect rate has reached 4.2% with rising quality complaints, and labour turnover is increasing among CNC programmers.

--- APPENDIX 1 — MARKETING/OPS ---
Operations and Quality Report — Q4 2025: The new machining cell inspected 8,400 components last month at a defect rate of 4.2%, down from 6.5% a year ago, and each defective unit costs $28 to rework. Customer quality complaints have risen from 19 to 34 per month. Average order delivery lead time is 12 days. A survey of 250 aerospace buyers found that 68% rank on-time delivery as their top supplier criterion, and 57% would switch supplier after two late deliveries. A skills audit shows 18 of 60 production staff lack CNC programming certification; on-the-job training is available internally, while off-the-job courses at the technical college cost $1,100 per employee.

--- APPENDIX 2 — FINANCIAL DATA ---
Title: Extract from the Statement of Financial Position of Kestrel Precision Components as at 31 March 2025 ($ '000)
Headers: ['Financial Metric', '2024', '2025']
Inventories | 140 | 165
Trade receivables | 210 | 195
Cash and cash equivalents | 55 | 70
Current liabilities | 250 | 230
Non-current assets | 1,600 | 2,150
Capital employed | 2,100 | 2,540

--- APPENDIX 3 — EXTERNAL ENVIRONMENT ---
Economic and Business Bulletin (November 2026): (1) The central bank has raised the base interest rate from 4.25% to 5.00%, increasing borrowing costs for firms with variable-rate loans. (2) The national minimum wage will rise by 5.8% from $13.80 to $14.60 per hour from April 2026, raising wage bills across engineering. (3) Steel and aluminium input prices have risen 9.6% year-on-year, industrial producer inflation is 6.3%, and demand from aerospace manufacturers grew 4.1%.

--- QUESTIONS ---
  Q1(a) [8 marks]
    Question: KPC plans to fund part of its $720,000 CNC expansion with a $450,000 ten-year bank loan. Explain two advantages for KPC of using retained profit to fund the expansion instead of the bank loan.
    Answer: Point 1: Using the $270,000 of retained profit costs KPC no interest or capital repayments, which protects cash flow while the company already carries fixed costs of $300,000 a year and is servicing a $450,000 bank loan. Every dollar saved in interest can be spent on tackling the 4.2% defect rate, for example by cutting the $28-per-unit rework burden or funding the $1,100 CNC courses, helping KPC hold its $24.00 selling price for aerospace buyers who rank on-time delivery first.

Point 2: Retained profit avoids the collateral and repossession risk of a bank loan, so the $720,000 machining cell is not endangered if the 68% of surveyed buyers who demand on-time delivery are disappointed and orders slip. It also preserves the ownership and control of founder Freya Kestrel: no lender can impose conditions on how the flat, democratically led team runs the new CNC cell, letting KPC react quickly to the 57% of buyers who say they would switch supplier after two late deliveries. Retained profit therefore speeds the decision and keeps control local.
    Keywords: retained profit, $270,000, $450,000, $720,000, bank loan, $300,000
    Mark scheme: knowledge_max_2: 1 mark for each valid advantage identified, max 2. | application_analysis_max_6: Up to 3 marks per point for contextual explanation applied to KPC's costs, defect rate, finance and ownership.

  Q1(b) [12 marks]
    Question: KPC is promoting its new precision-machined aerospace components. Consider a national trade-press advertising campaign, sponsorship of an aerospace industry exhibition, or targeted email marketing to known OEM buyers. Which should KPC choose to promote the launch? Justify your recommendation.
    Answer: National trade-press campaign: Advertisements in aerospace magazines would build wide awareness of KPC's new CNC-machined components across the whole industry, reinforcing the 8,400 components inspected monthly and the fall from 6.5% to 4.2% in defects. However, print is costly, has a long lead time and reaches many firms outside KPC's civil-aircraft niche; with a $720,000 expansion and fixed costs of $300,000 a year, much of the spend would be wasted on readers who never buy engine components.

Exhibition sponsorship: Sponsoring an aerospace trade exhibition gives face-to-face credibility and direct access to procurement teams, valuable because 68% of 250 surveyed buyers rank on-time delivery first and 57% would switch after two late deliveries, so trust must be built personally. The drawbacks are high stand fees, staff time away from the 40,000-unit production target and results that depend on a single event; for a 60-employee firm with a $450,000 loan this is a large, lumpy risk.

Targeted email marketing: Sending focused technical messages to KPC's known OEM buyer list is cheap, immediate and measurable, and can carry the 12-day delivery lead time and quality data straight to the engineers who decide. It lacks the brand reach of print and the personal trust of an exhibition, and works only where contact data is accurate, but its cost per qualified enquiry is far lower than either alternative.

Recommendation: KPC should choose targeted email marketing, supported later by a small exhibition presence. It reaches exactly the civil-aircraft buyers who matter, can be justified against $300,000 fixed costs and a $450,000 loan, and directly communicates the reliability message the survey identifies. National trade-press advertising is rejected as expensive and untargeted, and full exhibition sponsorship is rejected as too costly and disruptive for a 60-staff firm; email can be scaled up once the machining cell proves its 4.2% defect improvement.
    Keywords: CNC, $720,000, 40,000, 68%, 250, 12 days
    Mark scheme: level_1_1_to_4: Limited description of the three promotional options with minimal application to KPC. | level_2_5_to_8: Discussion of at least two options with advantages and disadvantages in the context of KPC and some judgement. | level_3_9_to_12: Detailed evaluation of all three options applied to KPC with a justified recommendation explaining why trade-press advertising and exhibition sponsorship are rejected.

  Q2(a) [8 marks]
    Question: KPC's labour turnover is rising among CNC programmers and its defect rate has reached 4.2%. Explain two benefits for KPC of using democratic leadership to improve motivation in its production team.
    Answer: Point 1: Democratic leadership gives KPC's 60 employees a real voice in how the new CNC machining cell is organised, which helps satisfy higher social and esteem needs and lifts job satisfaction. Programmers who help set inspection routines and shift patterns are more likely to stay, directly reducing the labour turnover that is losing scarce CNC skills and forcing repeated $1,100 off-the-job training spending.

Point 2: Consulting the people who operate the machines generates practical ideas for reducing the 4.2% defect rate and the $28-per-unit rework cost, because operators see faults before managers do. Higher involvement also strengthens commitment to the 12-day delivery promise, which matters because 68% of 250 surveyed buyers rank on-time delivery first and 57% would switch after two late deliveries.     Mark scheme: knowledge_max_2: 1 mark for each valid benefit identified, max 2. | application_analysis_max_6: Up to 3 marks per point for contextual explanation linked to KPC's turnover, defect rate, delivery promise and costs.

  Q2(b) [12 marks]
    Question: KPC must upskill 18 production staff to operate the new CNC machines. Consider on-the-job training or off-the-job training at the technical college. Which should KPC choose? Justify your decision.
    Answer: On-the-job training: Coaching at the machining cell is directly relevant to KPC's own CNC machines and inspection standards, costs no course fees and keeps the 18 staff productive while they learn, protecting the 8,400 components inspected each month and the improvement from 6.5% to 4.2% defects. It also suits the 12-day delivery lead time because nobody leaves the line. The weaknesses are that trainers are themselves production staff whose output suffers, bad habits can be passed on, and there is no external certificate, a concern when 68% of surveyed aerospace buyers demand reliable delivery and may audit supplier competence.

Decision: KPC should choose on-the-job training for the initial rollout, with short college top-ups for the most senior programmers. On-the-job training is machine-specific, avoids the $19,800 fee and protects output while the defect rate is being brought under control.     Keywords: on-the-job training, off-the-job courses, $1,100, 18, CNC, 4.2%

    Question: Using Appendix 3, evaluate how the rise in the base interest rate to 5.00%, the 5.8% minimum wage increase and the 9.6% rise in steel and aluminium input costs will affect KPC. Which change will have the greatest impact? Justify your answer.
    Answer: Interest rate rise (4.25% to 5.00%): If KPC's $450,000 bank loan is variable-rate, the annual interest cost rises by 0.75% of $450,000 = $3,375 a year (0.0075 × $450,000). --- MAIN STEM ---
Dunsmore Forged Metals (DFM) is a public limited company in the metal-forging sector, employing a workforce of 120. Founded in 1998 by Gordon Dunsmore, it supplies forged steel components to construction-equipment makers and operates a hierarchical structure with autocratic leadership. DFM plans to invest $1,100,000 in a new forging press with heat-recovery equipment, financed by a $600,000 bank loan and a $500,000 share issue. It has fixed costs of $540,000 a year, a variable cost of $22.00 a unit and a selling price of $38.00, and currently produces 60,000 units a year. DFM faces two problems: its scrap rate has reached 7.4% and client quality complaints have been rising steadily in recent months.

--- APPENDIX 1 — MARKETING/OPS ---
Waste and Quality Report — Q3 2025: The forge produced 15,000 castings last quarter with a scrap rate of 7.4%, down from 9.1% a year earlier, and scrap metal rework costs $41 per tonne. Client quality complaints have risen from 22 to 31 per month. Average delivery lead time to construction sites is 18 days. A survey of 180 plant managers found that 62% would pay 3% more for lower-carbon forged parts, and 55% require formal quality records. A maintenance audit shows 26 of 120 workers lack press-operation certification; on-the-job training is available internally and off-the-job accreditation costs $950 per employee.

--- APPENDIX 2 — FINANCIAL DATA ---

Trade receivables | 300 | 275
Cash and cash equivalents | 80 | 95
Current liabilities | 400 | 380
Non-current assets | 2,800 | 3,450
Capital employed | 3,200 | 3,750

--- APPENDIX 3 — EXTERNAL ENVIRONMENT ---
Economic and Business Bulletin (November 2026): (1) The central bank has raised the base interest rate from 4.00% to 4.75%, increasing debt-service costs for leveraged firms. (2) The national minimum wage rises 6.2% from $14.00 to $14.87 per hour from April 2026. (3) Steel scrap and electricity input costs have risen 11.3% year-on-year, industrial inflation is 7.2%, and construction output grew 2.8%.

    Question: DFM is financing its $1,100,000 forging press with a $600,000 bank loan and a $500,000 share issue. Explain two advantages for DFM of using the share issue rather than further bank borrowing.
    Answer: Point 1: A $500,000 share issue commits DFM to no interest payments and no capital repayment, unlike the $600,000 bank loan, so cash flow is protected while the company already bears fixed costs of $540,000 a year and a 7.4% scrap rate that creates $41-per-tonne rework spending. Money that would have serviced debt can instead fund the quality improvements needed to answer the 31 client complaints a month, protecting the $38.00 selling price without raising borrowing.

Point 2: Equity does not require collateral, so the $1,100,000 press and the firm's other assets are not exposed to repossession if construction demand, which grew only 2.8%, falls short of the 60,000-unit plan. As a public limited company DFM can raise capital from a wide shareholder base rather than depending on one lender, keeping the $600,000 loan facility available as a reserve for working capital or for the 18-day delivery lead time. Issuing shares therefore strengthens the balance sheet and spreads financial risk without adding fixed repayment obligations.
    Keywords: share issue, $500,000, $600,000, $1,100,000, bank loan, $540,000

    Answer: Construction trade exhibition: A major exhibition lets DFM demonstrate forgings directly to the plant managers who buy them, supporting the 62% of 180 surveyed managers who would pay 3% more for lower-carbon parts and allowing engineers to answer questions about the new press and the 18-day delivery lead time. Targeted LinkedIn campaigns: Social-media ads aimed by job title at plant managers are relatively cheap, quick and measurable, and can carry the 3% lower-carbon message and formal quality records straight to the decision-makers, including the 55% who require such records. They lack the physical proof of an exhibition and may miss older buyers, but cost per qualified contact is low.

Recommendation: DFM should choose the construction trade exhibition as the lead activity, with LinkedIn used for follow-up. High-value forged contracts are won on trust and visible quality, which a stand demonstrates better than print or online ads, and the 62% premium signal justifies the cost against $540,000 fixed costs. Magazine advertising is rejected as slow and untargeted, and LinkedIn alone is rejected as too passive to prove quality for a $1,100,000 investment; the smaller digital spend can support the exhibition rather than replace it.

PAPER 2 — P2_SET_268

--- MAIN STEM ---
Tarrant Rubber Mouldings (TRM) is a partnership in the rubber-products sector, employing a workforce of 38. Founded in 2013 by Dev Tarrant, it makes moulded rubber seals and gaskets for car manufacturers and operates a flat structure with laissez-faire leadership. TRM plans to invest $480,000 in a new injection-moulding machine with a recycled-rubber feed system, financed by a $180,000 bank loan and $300,000 retained profit. It has fixed costs of $175,000 a year, a variable cost of $9.00 a unit and a selling price of $16.00, and currently produces 45,000 units a year. TRM faces two problems: labour turnover has reached 14% and waste from rubber off-cuts on the line is rising steadily.

--- APPENDIX 1 — MARKETING/OPS ---
Quality and Waste Report — Q2 2025: The moulding line produced 11,250 gaskets last quarter at a defect rate of 3.6%, up from 2.4% a year ago, with off-cut waste costing $16 per kilogram. Customer complaints rose from 14 to 27 per month. Average delivery lead time is 7 days. A survey of 200 automotive buyers found that 71% prefer suppliers using recycled rubber, and 48% check environmental credentials before ordering. A skills audit shows 12 of 38 staff lack injection-moulding certification; on-the-job training is available internally, while off-the-job courses at the local college cost $780 per employee.

--- APPENDIX 2 — FINANCIAL DATA ---
Title: Extract from the Statement of Financial Position of Tarrant Rubber Mouldings as at 31 March 2025 ($ '000)
Headers: ['Financial Metric', '2024', '2025']
Inventories | 95 | 110
Trade receivables | 130 | 118
Cash and cash equivalents | 38 | 52
Current liabilities | 165 | 155
Non-current assets | 980 | 1,240
Capital employed | 1,150 | 1,380

--- APPENDIX 3 — EXTERNAL ENVIRONMENT ---
Economic and Business Bulletin (November 2026): (1) The central bank raised the base interest rate from 3.75% to 4.50%, raising borrowing costs for smaller firms. (2) The national minimum wage will rise by 7.1% from $13.50 to $14.46 per hour from April 2026. (3) Synthetic and natural rubber input costs have risen 8.7% year-on-year, inflation is 5.9%, and car production grew 3.2%.

--- QUESTIONS ---
  Q1(a) [8 marks]
    Question: TRM is financing its $480,000 moulding machine with a $180,000 bank loan and $300,000 retained profit. Explain two advantages for TRM of using the bank loan rather than relying only on retained profit.
    Answer: Point 1: The $180,000 bank loan lets TRM keep the $300,000 of retained profit as a cash buffer against the problems in the case, namely off-cut waste costing $16 per kilogram and a defect rate that has risen to 3.6%. With fixed costs of $175,000 a year and car production growing only 3.2%, holding that reserve protects the 7-day delivery lead time and avoids a cash crisis if a batch of gaskets has to be remade.

Point 2: Borrowing the $180,000 spreads the cost of the $480,000 machine over time instead of draining the partnership's own funds at once, preserving working capital for raw rubber and wages. It also leaves the partners' personal capital untouched, so the business can fund the 12 staff requiring injection-moulding certification from revenue rather than asking the partners for more money. Used alongside the $300,000 retained profit, the loan keeps the 45,000-unit operation liquid while it adjusts to the new machine.
    Keywords: bank loan, $180,000, $300,000, $480,000, $175,000, retained profit
    Mark scheme: knowledge_max_2: 1 mark for each valid advantage identified, max 2. | application_analysis_max_6: Up to 3 marks per point for contextual explanation applied to TRM's waste, costs, liquidity and ownership.

  Q1(b) [12 marks]
    Question: TRM is promoting its new recycled-rubber seals. Consider sponsorship of a motorsport team, advertising in automotive supplier magazines, or listings on industrial e-commerce marketplaces. Which should TRM choose to promote the launch? Justify your recommendation.
    Answer: Motorsport sponsorship: Associating TRM with a racing team would raise brand recognition quickly among car enthusiasts and could suggest high-performance rubber, but it is extremely expensive for a 38-staff partnership and reaches the general public rather than the procurement engineers who buy 45,000 gaskets. With fixed costs of $175,000 and a $180,000 loan, such spend would be hard to justify against the 3.6% defect problem.

Automotive supplier magazines: Print advertisements would reach a specialist readership and could explain the recycled-rubber feed message, which 71% of 200 surveyed buyers prefer. However, magazines have long lead times, high costs and no immediate response mechanism, and only 48% of buyers check environmental credentials, so much of the spend would not convert into orders for a small firm with a 7-day lead time.

Industrial e-commerce listings: Listing the seals on established B2B marketplaces puts TRM in front of buyers actively searching for gaskets, is relatively low-cost and gives measurable enquiries and orders. The recycled-rubber story can be shown in the product description, appealing directly to the 71% who prefer such suppliers. Listings alone do not build deep brand loyalty and depend on good product data and prompt fulfilment, but they suit a small partnership.

Recommendation: TRM should choose industrial e-commerce listings, supported by modest magazine advertising later. Marketplaces reach active buyers cheaply and measurably, which matters against $175,000 fixed costs and a $180,000 loan. Motorsport sponsorship is rejected as unaffordable and aimed at the wrong audience, and magazine advertising alone is rejected as slow and hard to measure; online listings can generate the volume that makes later print worthwhile.
    Keywords: $480,000, 45,000, 71%, 200, 7 days

  Q2(a) [8 marks]

In a small partnership there are few layers, so skilled staff are trusted rather than closely supervised; that freedom can reduce the 14% labour turnover by making operators want to stay, avoiding repeated recruitment and the $780-per-employee cost of replacing certified staff.

    Question: TRM must upskill 12 staff to operate the new injection-moulding machine. Consider on-the-job training or off-the-job courses at the local college. Which should TRM choose? Justify your decision.

However, it takes 12 of a workforce of 38 away from production, risking the 45,000-unit target and the 7-day lead time, and the generic content may need site-specific follow-up. With labour turnover at 14%, newly qualified staff could also leave.

Decision: TRM should choose on-the-job training, with short college modules for the most senior operators. It is cheap, machine-specific and protects output and delivery while the partnership absorbs a $180,000 loan. Full off-the-job training is rejected because removing 12 of 38 staff would disrupt the 7-day lead time and the 45,000-unit target, and the $9,360 fee can be spent later once the machine is stable and the 3.6% defect rate is understood.

    Answer: Advantage: A recycled-rubber feed system would let TRM reuse off-cuts that currently cost $16 per kilogram in waste, cutting the $9.00 variable cost per unit and helping counter the 8.7% rise in rubber input costs. It also matches the 71% of 200 surveyed automotive buyers who prefer suppliers using recycled rubber and the 48% who check environmental credentials, supporting sales of the 45,000 units and the 7-day delivery promise at the $16.00 selling price.

  Q4(b) [12 marks]
    Question: Using Appendix 3, evaluate how the rise in the base interest rate to 4.50%, the 7.1% minimum wage increase and the 8.7% rise in rubber input costs will affect TRM. Which change will have the greatest impact? Justify your answer.
    Answer: Interest rate rise (3.75% to 4.50%): If TRM's $180,000 bank loan is variable-rate, the extra interest is 0.75% of $180,000 = $1,350 a year (0.0075 × $180,000), small against fixed costs of $175,000, and nil if the loan is fixed. The more meaningful effect is that dearer credit discourages car buyers, whose production is forecast to grow only 3.2%, so TRM may struggle to sell all 45,000 units. Fixing the rate would remove most of this risk.

Minimum wage increase (7.1%, to $14.46 per hour): With a workforce of 38, many moulding and packing jobs are hourly paid, so the wage bill rises and cannot be avoided. The insert states no hours worked or individual pay, so an annual total would be invented; the defensible comparison is productivity of 45,000 units ÷ 38 staff = 1,184 units per worker. If productivity holds, the $7.00 contribution can absorb the rise; if labour turnover of 14% persists, retraining costs and lower output will squeeze the $12.89 average total cost.

Input cost inflation (8.7% rubber): The $9.00 variable cost includes rubber, but the insert does not decompose it, so only a bound is honest: if the whole variable cost rose 8.7% that adds 8.7% × $9.00 = $0.78 per unit, about $35,000 a year at 45,000 units (45,000 × $0.78). The recycled-rubber feed system can offset some of this, but not all of a broad input-price rise.

Conclusion: The 8.7% rise in rubber input costs will have the greatest impact. It applies to every one of the 45,000 units and directly reduces the $7.00 contribution that must cover $175,000 fixed costs and the $180,000 loan. The interest rise is tiny and fixable, and the wage rise can be managed through productivity and retention; input inflation is the threat TRM can least control.
    Keywords: 4.50%, 7.1%, 8.7%, $14.46, $9.00, 3.2%
    Mark scheme: level_1_1_to_4: Identifies the external changes with limited application to TRM. | level_2_5_to_8: Analyses the impact of at least two external changes on TRM's costs, revenue or financing in context. | level_3_9_to_12: Detailed evaluation of all three external changes applied to TRM with a well-justified judgement that input-cost inflation has the greatest impact and why the other two are smaller.

PAPER 2 — P2_SET_269

--- MAIN STEM ---
Westmore Kiln & Ceramics (WKM) is a cooperative in the industrial ceramics sector, employing a workforce of 70. Founded in 1987 by Elaine Westmore, it makes refractory bricks and kiln furniture for foundries and operates a hierarchical structure with democratic leadership. WKM plans to invest $640,000 in an energy-efficient kiln with waste-heat recovery, financed by a $340,000 bank loan and $300,000 retained profit. It has fixed costs of $260,000 a year, a variable cost of $12.50 a unit and a selling price of $22.50, and currently produces 50,000 units a year. WKM faces two problems: energy waste at the kiln is persistently high and its defect rate has reached 5.3%, worrying foundry customers.

--- APPENDIX 1 — MARKETING/OPS ---
Operations and Sustainability Report — Q1 2025: The kiln fired 9,600 refractory units last quarter with a defect rate of 5.3%, down from 7.0% last year, and broken units cost $23 each to remake. Energy waste accounts for 14% of kiln costs. Customer complaints rose from 17 to 29 per month. Average delivery time is 15 days. A survey of 220 construction and foundry buyers found that 66% would pay 2% more for low-energy ceramic products, and 54% check sustainability credentials. A skills audit shows 15 of 70 workers lack kiln-control certification; on-the-job training is available internally and off-the-job courses cost $860 per employee.

--- APPENDIX 2 — FINANCIAL DATA ---
Title: Extract from the Statement of Financial Position of Westmore Kiln & Ceramics as at 31 March 2025 ($ '000)
Headers: ['Financial Metric', '2024', '2025']
Inventories | 175 | 160
Trade receivables | 145 | 170
Cash and cash equivalents | 60 | 72
Current liabilities | 230 | 245
Non-current assets | 2,100 | 2,480
Capital employed | 2,500 | 2,850

--- APPENDIX 3 — EXTERNAL ENVIRONMENT ---
Economic and Business Bulletin (November 2026): (1) The central bank raised the base interest rate from 4.50% to 5.25%, increasing loan costs for borrower-funded firms. (2) The national minimum wage rises 6.4% from $13.90 to $14.79 per hour from April 2026. (3) Natural gas and clay input costs have risen 10.8% year-on-year, inflation is 6.6%, and foundry output grew 2.4%.

--- QUESTIONS ---
  Q1(a) [8 marks]
    Question: WKM plans to fund part of its $640,000 kiln project with a $340,000 bank loan. Explain two advantages for WKM of using retained profit rather than the bank loan for this part of the investment.
    Answer: Point 1: The $300,000 of retained profit carries no interest or repayment, protecting cash flow while WKM already has fixed costs of $260,000 a year and energy waste equal to 14% of kiln costs. Money not paid to the bank can be spent on reducing the 5.3% defect rate and the $23-per-unit remake cost, or on the $860 kiln-control courses, helping the cooperative hold its $22.50 selling price and answer the 29 monthly complaints.

Point 2: Retained profit needs no collateral, so the $640,000 kiln is not at risk of repossession if foundry output, which grew only 2.4%, disappoints and the 50,000-unit plan is missed. It also suits WKM's cooperative structure: member-control is preserved because no lender can impose conditions on how the democratic leadership runs the business or reinvests surplus. Using internal funds therefore speeds the decision and keeps control with the members while the $340,000 loan remains available for other needs.
    Keywords: retained profit, $300,000, $340,000, $640,000, bank loan, $260,000
    Mark scheme: knowledge_max_2: 1 mark for each valid advantage identified, max 2. | application_analysis_max_6: Up to 3 marks per point for contextual explanation applied to WKM's energy waste, defects, finance and ownership.

  Q1(b) [12 marks]
    Question: WKM is promoting its new low-energy refractory products. Consider a foundry trade exhibition, direct mail to industrial buyers, or search-engine advertising. Which should WKM choose to promote the launch? Justify your recommendation.
    Answer: Foundry trade exhibition: A specialist exhibition would let WKM show the new kiln's output to foundry buyers face to face, supporting the 66% of 220 surveyed buyers who would pay 2% more for low-energy ceramics and allowing technicians to explain the 15-day delivery time. Yet exhibitions are costly in stands and staff time, and with fixed costs of $260,000 and a $340,000 loan, a poor event would be an expensive risk for a 70-member cooperative.

Direct mail: Sending technical brochures to a targeted list of construction and foundry buyers is relatively cheap and reaches the right firms, and can highlight the 54% of buyers who check sustainability credentials. Response rates are usually low and hard to track, however, and printed material can be ignored; it also does not demonstrate the product or the reduced energy waste, which is the central selling point of the $640,000 kiln.

Search-engine advertising: Paid search puts WKM in front of buyers actively looking for refractory bricks and kiln furniture, is measurable, can be budgeted to a 70-staff cooperative and can carry the 2% low-energy premium message and the 15-day lead time. It lacks the physical reassurance of an exhibition and depends on accurate keywords, but it delivers enquiries at a controllable cost and can be adjusted quickly if foundry output grows only 2.4%.

Recommendation: WKM should choose search-engine advertising as the main launch channel, with a small exhibition presence later. Search reaches active buyers cheaply and measurably, which matters against $260,000 fixed costs and a $340,000 loan. A full exhibition is rejected as too costly and risky, and direct mail alone is rejected as slow and low-response; successful online enquiries can fund a modest stand once the 5.3% defect rate is reduced.
    Keywords: $640,000, 50,000, 66%, 220, 15 days
    Mark scheme: level_1_1_to_4: Limited description of the three promotional options with minimal application to WKM. | level_2_5_to_8: Discussion of at least two options with advantages and disadvantages in the context of WKM and some judgement. | level_3_9_to_12: Detailed evaluation of all three options applied to WKM with a justified recommendation explaining why exhibitions and direct mail alone are rejected.

--- MAIN STEM ---
Pinnion Gear Manufacturing (PGM) is a private limited company in the engineering sector, employing a workforce of 65. It has fixed costs of $240,000 a year, a variable cost of $11.00 a unit and a selling price of $19.00, and currently produces 52,000 units a year. PGM faces two problems: a skills gap in gear grinding and a defect rate of 4.8%.

--- APPENDIX 1 — MARKETING/OPS ---
Quality and Training Report — Q4 2025: The grinding line produced 13,000 gears last quarter at a defect rate of 4.8%, down from 6.2% a year ago, with rework costing $32 per gear. Customer quality complaints rose from 20 to 26 per month. Average delivery lead time is 10 days. A survey of 240 agricultural-equipment buyers found that 69% rate precision as their top purchasing criterion, and 61% would switch supplier after repeated quality failures. A skills audit shows 16 of 65 staff lack gear-grinding certification; on-the-job training is available internally, while off-the-job courses at the technical centre cost $1,050 per employee.

--- APPENDIX 2 — FINANCIAL DATA ---
Title: Extract from the Statement of Financial Position of Pinnion Gear Manufacturing as at 31 March 2025 ($ '000)
Headers: ['Financial Metric', '2024', '2025']

Non-current assets | 1,750 | 2,100
Capital employed | 2,150 | 2,470

--- APPENDIX 3 — EXTERNAL ENVIRONMENT ---

    Question: Using Appendix 3, evaluate how the rise in the base interest rate to 4.80%, the 6.9% minimum wage increase and the 9.9% rise in alloy steel and energy input costs will affect PGM. Which change will have the greatest impact? Justify your answer.
    Answer: Interest rate rise (4.00% to 4.80%): If PGM's $260,000 bank loan is variable-rate, the extra interest is 0.80% of $260,000 = $2,080 a year (0.008 × $260,000), modest against fixed costs of $240,000. The $100,000 overdraft is more exposed because it is usually variable-rate and repayable on demand, so the full 0.80% rise would add about $800 a year at that drawn amount (0.008 × $100,000). PGM can cut this risk by replacing the overdraft with a fixed-term facility.

Minimum wage increase (6.9%, to $14.65 per hour): With a workforce of 65, many grinding and packing roles are hourly paid, so wage costs rise and cannot be avoided. The insert states no hours worked or individual pay, so an annual total would be invented; the defensible check is productivity of 52,000 units ÷ 65 staff = 800 units per worker. If that holds, the $8.00 contribution can absorb the rise; if the 4.8% defect rate lowers effective output, unit labour cost pushes up the $15.62 average total cost.

Input cost inflation (9.9% alloy steel and energy): The $11.00 variable cost includes these inputs, but the insert does not decompose it, so only a bound is honest: if the whole variable cost rose 9.9% that adds 9.9% × $11.00 = $1.09 per unit, roughly $56,700 a year at 52,000 units (52,000 × $1.09). Oil recycling and price discussions with buyers can recover only part of this; the 3.6% growth in machinery sales limits the ability to pass costs on.

Conclusion: The 9.9% rise in alloy steel and energy costs will have the greatest impact. It applies to every one of the 52,000 units and directly erodes the $8.00 contribution that must cover $240,000 fixed costs and service both the $260,000 loan and the $100,000 overdraft. The interest rise is small and fixable, and the wage rise can be managed through productivity; input inflation is the least controllable and therefore the most damaging.
    Keywords: 4.80%, 6.9%, 9.9%, $14.65, $11.00, 3.6%
    Mark scheme: level_1_1_to_4: Identifies the external changes with limited application to PGM. | level_2_5_to_8: Analyses the impact of at least two external changes on PGM's costs, revenue or financing in context. | level_3_9_to_12: Detailed evaluation of all three external changes applied to PGM with a well-justified judgement that input-cost inflation has the greatest impact and why the other two are smaller.

--- MAIN STEM ---
Quill & Reed Fashion (QRF) is a private limited company in the online fashion retail sector, employing a workforce of 50. Founded in 2013 by Priya Quill, the business sells womenswear through its own website and operates a flat organisational structure with democratic leadership. QRF plans to invest $620,000 in a new e-commerce fulfilment centre with automated garment sorting, financed by a $400,000 ten-year bank loan and $220,000 retained profit. It has fixed costs of $180,000 a year, a variable cost of $14.00 a unit and a selling price of $38.00, and currently produces 20,000 units a year. QRF faces two problems: its online return rate has reached 14% and parcel-picking errors are rising as order volumes grow.

--- APPENDIX 1 — MARKETING/OPS ---
Market Research Summary — Q3 2025: An online survey of 800 shoppers found 58% prefer free returns and 47% would pay more for sustainably sourced womenswear. The website recorded 4,600 orders last quarter at a 14% return rate, down from 18% a year earlier. Average delivery time is 2.8 days. Customer complaints fell from 64 to 39 per month. The email launch campaign reached a 26% open rate and the mobile app conversion rate was 3.4%. A training needs review shows 18 of 50 staff have not completed on-the-job training on the new sorting machines; off-the-job training courses at the local college cost $850 per employee.

--- APPENDIX 2 — FINANCIAL DATA ---
Title: Extract from the Statement of Financial Position of Quill & Reed Fashion as at 31 March 2025 ($ '000)
Headers: ['Financial Metric', '2024', '2025']
Inventories | 95 | 120
Trade receivables | 60 | 75
Cash and cash equivalents | 30 | 45
Current liabilities | 120 | 130
Non-current assets | 700 | 980
Capital employed | 900 | 1,150

--- APPENDIX 3 — EXTERNAL ENVIRONMENT ---

(2) The national minimum wage will rise by 5.5% to $14.20 per hour from April 2026, lifting wage bills across QRF's workforce of 50. (3) Packaging and courier input costs have risen 9.8% year-on-year, while consumer spending on online fashion grew just 1.2% and the sector's average return rate is 16%.

Point 2: Using internal funds avoids the collateral and default risk of the $400,000 bank loan, so the new $620,000 fulfilment centre cannot be repossessed if the launch disappoints or the return rate stays at 14%. It also preserves Priya Quill's ownership and control: no lender can impose conditions on how the automated sorting operation is run, which suits QRF's flat structure and democratic leadership and leaves the founder free to redirect the $220,000 if customer demand shifts.

Input cost inflation (9.8% packaging and courier): The insert does not decompose the $14.00 variable cost, so only a bound can be computed: if the whole variable cost rose 9.8% that adds 9.8% × $14.00 = $1.37 per unit; at 20,000 units that is about $27,400 a year. Even a smaller effect on packaging alone would cut the $24.00 contribution, and QRF has only a limited ability to recover it because consumer spending on fashion grew just 1.2% and the sector return rate is 16%.

Conclusion: The 9.8% rise in input costs will have the greatest impact. It applies to every one of the 20,000 units and directly erodes the $24.00 contribution that justifies the $620,000 expansion, whereas the interest rise costs only about $2,000 and the wage rise can be offset if 400-unit productivity holds. Input inflation is rejected as smaller only if packaging is a tiny share of cost, which the insert does not state, so it must be treated as the largest risk.
    Keywords: 3.75%, 4.25%, 5.5%, $14.20, 9.8%, $400,000
    Mark scheme: level_1_1_to_4: Identifies the external changes with limited application to QRF. | level_2_5_to_8: Analyses the impact of at least two external changes on QRF's costs, revenue or financing in context. | level_3_9_to_12: Detailed evaluation of all three external changes in the context of QRF with a well-justified judgment on which has the greatest impact and why the others are smaller.

Tidewater Surfwear (TSW) is a private limited company in the coastal apparel retail sector, employing a workforce of 40.     Question: Using Appendix 3, evaluate how the interest rate rise from 4.0% to 4.75%, the 6.0% minimum wage increase and the 11.3% rise in fabric input costs will affect TSW. Which change will have the greatest impact? Justify your answer.
    Answer: Interest rate rise (4.0% to 4.75%): If TSW's $300,000 loan is variable-rate, the annual interest cost rises by 0.75% of $300,000 = $2,250 a year (0.0075 × $300,000). Even a smaller increase in cotton and synthetics would erode contribution, and with apparel spending up only 2.1% and the sector return rate at 18%, TSW may struggle to pass the cost on through its $39.00 price.

Conclusion: The 11.3% rise in fabric input costs will have the greatest impact. It hits every unit produced, directly threatening the $27.00 contribution that supports the $540,000 expansion, and it compounds with the existing 11% fabric waste. The interest rise costs only about $2,250 and the wage rise can be offset if 375-unit productivity holds, so fabric inflation is the larger threat.

--- MAIN STEM ---
Nova Vale Leather (NVL) is a private limited company in the leather goods retail and e-commerce sector, employing a workforce of 35. Founded in 2011 by Sofia Vale, the business sells handmade bags and wallets through its flagship website, and operates a flat structure with laissez-faire leadership. NVL plans to invest $780,000 in a new eco-tannery and online fulfilment hub, financed by a $450,000 bank loan and $330,000 retained profit. It has fixed costs of $210,000 a year, a variable cost of $20.00 a unit and a selling price of $62.00, and currently produces 14,000 units a year. NVL faces two problems: labour turnover has reached 18% and finishing defects are rising as orders grow.

--- APPENDIX 1 — MARKETING/OPS ---
Quality and Waste Report — Q3 2025: The workshop finished 3,400 leather goods last quarter at a defect rate of 3.3%, down from 5.0% a year ago. Leather offcut waste fell to 8% of material use from 12%. Staff turnover reached 18%, with 6 of 35 workers leaving in the quarter. Customer returns were 4.5% of orders. A survey of 400 online customers found 55% value handcrafted quality most, and 38% would pay a $15 premium for traceable leather. With 6 finishing vacancies, HR is comparing internal recruitment and external recruitment, and job rotation is being piloted to cut the 18% turnover.

--- APPENDIX 2 — FINANCIAL DATA ---
Title: Extract from the Statement of Financial Position of Nova Vale Leather as at 31 March 2025 ($ '000)
Headers: ['Financial Metric', '2024', '2025']
Inventories | 210 | 185

Capital employed | 1,150 | 1,400

(2) The national minimum wage rises 7.2% to $13.90 per hour from April 2026, affecting NVL's workforce of 35. (3) Raw hide and freight input costs rose 13.6% year-on-year, while consumer spending on luxury accessories fell 0.8% and online return rates in fashion average 17%.

  Q1(a) [8 marks]
    Question: NVL is funding its $780,000 eco-tannery with a $450,000 bank loan and $330,000 retained profit. Explain two advantages for NVL of using the bank loan rather than relying only on retained profit.
    Answer: Point 1: A $450,000 bank loan lets NVL keep its $330,000 retained profit as a cash buffer against fixed costs of $210,000 a year and an 18% labour turnover that forces repeated hiring and retraining. Preserving that internal reserve is valuable when the eco-tannery may overrun and when customer returns already run at 4.5% of orders, so the business can meet short-term commitments without running out of cash.

Point 2: Borrowing the $450,000 allows the full $780,000 project to go ahead immediately, capturing the 38% of surveyed customers who would pay a $15 premium for traceable leather, rather than delaying until enough profit is accumulated. Faster completion lets NVL start earning from the new capacity sooner, and a predictable bank loan repayment plan is easier to budget for than an uncertain stream of future retained profit in a market where accessory spending fell 0.8%, rather than waiting for profits that may not appear if demand stays weak.

    Answer: Social media influencers: Craft and fashion influencers can demonstrate the handmade quality that 55% of 400 surveyed customers value most, and can show the traceable leather story behind the $15 premium. Engagement is measurable and cost can be controlled. It also reinforces the handcrafted quality that 55% value most and helps justify the $780,000 investment, appealing to increasingly sustainability-conscious online shoppers.

Disadvantage: Building the eco-tannery needs $780,000 of capital and adds fixed costs beyond the $210,000 already incurred, raising the break-even output above 5,000 units and increasing risk if accessory spending fell 0.8%. Traceable leather may also cost more than standard hides, lifting the $20.00 variable cost, and the insert gives no figure for that premium, so the benefit of the $15 charge cannot be confirmed; if customers reject it, margins will suffer while 18% turnover and 3.3% defects persist. With accessory spending already down 0.8%, NVL cannot assume buyers will accept a higher price.

  Q4(b) [12 marks]
    Question: Using Appendix 3, evaluate how the interest rate rise from 3.5% to 4.25%, the 7.2% minimum wage increase and the 13.6% rise in raw hide and freight costs will affect NVL. Which change will have the greatest impact? Justify your answer.
    Answer: Interest rate rise (3.5% to 4.25%): If NVL's $450,000 loan is variable-rate, the annual interest cost rises by 0.75% of $450,000 = $3,375 a year (0.0075 × $450,000). That is significant next to fixed costs of $210,000 a year, and it would also raise the cost of financing the remaining $780,000 eco-tannery. If the loan is fixed, the immediate effect is zero, so NVL can reduce this risk by fixing the rate, and the fall in accessory spending of 0.8% is a separate demand concern.

Minimum wage increase (7.2%, to $13.90 per hour): With a workforce of 35 and 18% labour turnover, this rise feeds directly into wage costs for cutting, finishing and fulfilment and cannot be avoided. The insert states no hours worked or individual pay, so no defensible annual total can be invented. The correct benchmark is the given productivity figure: 14,000 units ÷ 35 staff = 400 units per worker. If productivity holds at 400 units and turnover falls, the rise is absorbable; otherwise unit labour cost climbs and the $42.00 contribution per unit is squeezed.

Raw hide and freight inflation (13.6%): The insert does not decompose the $20.00 variable cost, so only a bound can be shown: if the whole variable cost rose 13.6%, that adds 13.6% × $20.00 = $2.72 per unit, or about $38,080 a year at 14,000 units. Even a partial increase would erode the contribution that funds the $780,000 project, and with spending on luxury accessories down 0.8% and fashion returns averaging 17%, NVL has limited scope to raise the $62.00 price.

Conclusion: The 13.6% rise in hide and freight costs will have the greatest impact. It applies to every unit, is larger than the $3,375 interest increment and the absorbable wage rise, and directly attacks the $42.00 contribution on which the $780,000 expansion depends. The interest rise is smaller and manageable by fixing the rate; the wage rise can be offset by 400-unit productivity, so input inflation is the dominant threat.
    Keywords: 3.5%, 4.25%, 7.2%, $13.90, 13.6%, $450,000
    Mark scheme: level_1_1_to_4: Identifies the external changes with limited application to NVL. | level_2_5_to_8: Analyses the impact of at least two external changes on NVL's costs, revenue or financing in context. | level_3_9_to_12: Detailed evaluation of all three external changes in the context of NVL with a well-justified judgment on which has the greatest impact and why the others are smaller.

--- MAIN STEM ---
Zaara Eyewear (ZAE) is a public limited company in the eyewear e-commerce sector, employing a workforce of 50. Founded in 2008 by Zaara Nasser, the business sells prescription frames and sunglasses online, and operates a hierarchical structure with democratic leadership. It has fixed costs of $222,000 a year, a variable cost of $18.00 a unit and a selling price of $55.00, and currently produces 18,500 units a year. ZAE faces two problems: the lens-fitting defect rate has reached 4.2% and online returns are rising as sales grow.

The web store shipped 4,600 orders last quarter with a 4.2% defect-related return rate, down from 6.8% a year earlier. Average delivery time is 3.1 days. Social-media campaign reach was 220,000 impressions with a 2.9% click-through rate, and customer satisfaction averaged 4.3 out of 5. A team working pilot in the fitting bay is under review, and HR is comparing an individual accuracy bonus with a profit sharing scheme to reduce the 4.2% defect rate.

--- MAIN STEM ---
Kirsi Home Stores (KHS) is a private limited company in the home furnishings e-commerce sector, employing a workforce of 40. Founded in 2014 by Kirsi Salo, the business sells flat-pack furniture and decor through its website, and operates a hierarchical structure with laissez-faire leadership. KHS plans to invest $700,000 in an automated furniture warehouse and a new dropshipping platform, financed by a $350,000 bank loan and $350,000 retained profit. It has fixed costs of $192,000 a year, a variable cost of $16.00 a unit and a selling price of $48.00, and currently produces 16,000 units a year. KHS faces two problems: delivery damage complaints have reached 7% of orders and stock-outs are rising as demand grows.

--- APPENDIX 1 — MARKETING/OPS ---
Operations Log — Q3 2025: The warehouse dispatched 4,000 furniture orders last quarter, with a 7% damage-related complaint rate, down from 11% a year earlier. Stock-outs affected 5.4% of listed lines. Average delivery time is 5.6 days. A survey of 650 customers found 57% choose free delivery over speed, and 42% would pay $25 more for flat-pack sustainable furniture. The repeat-purchase rate is 29%, and the online conversion rate is 2.7%. HR is comparing a formal induction programme with mentoring by experienced warehouse staff to cut the 7% damage rate.

--- APPENDIX 2 — FINANCIAL DATA ---
Title: Extract from the Statement of Financial Position of Kirsi Home Stores as at 31 March 2025 ($ '000)
Headers: ['Financial Metric', '2024', '2025']

(2) The national minimum wage rises 5.8% to $13.40 an hour from April 2026, affecting KHS's workforce of 40. (3) Flat-pack timber and courier input costs rose 8.9% year-on-year, while consumer spending on home furnishings grew 1.6% and fuel surcharges add 3.2% to delivery costs.

  Q1(a) [8 marks]

Keeping that reserve is prudent while stock-outs are rising and inventories stand at $205,000, giving Kirsi Salo flexibility to buy stock or handle a delayed launch without exhausting internal cash.

Point 2: Borrowing lets the whole $700,000 automated warehouse and dropshipping platform proceed at once rather than waiting to accumulate profit, so KHS can capture the 42% of surveyed customers who would pay $25 more for flat-pack sustainable furniture. With the base rate cut from 5.0% to 4.5%, loan interest is cheaper than it was, making debt an attractive way to fund the project while the 1.6% growth in home-furnishing spending offers a chance to win new demand. A lower interest burden also supports the $28.00 average total cost and leaves more cash for the 5.6-day delivery operation.
    Keywords: bank loan, $350,000, $700,000, retained profit, $192,000, $48.00

    Question: KHS wants to cut the 7% delivery damage rate as it grows. Consider running its own delivery fleet, using a third-party courier, or switching to dropshipping. Which should KHS choose for delivery? Justify your recommendation.
    Answer: Own delivery fleet: Controlling delivery in-house lets KHS set careful handling standards, directly attacking the 7% damage-related complaint rate and protecting the $48.00 selling price from refunds. It also supports the 57% of 650 surveyed customers who choose free delivery over speed. However, buying vehicles and employing drivers adds fixed costs on top of $192,000 a year and the $700,000 warehouse plan, and a fleet may be underused, so it is expensive for a 40-employee retailer.

Dropshipping: Suppliers dispatch directly to customers, removing warehouse handling and much of KHS's stock risk, which eases the stock-out problem and cuts the need for the $700,000 facility. In practice KHS loses control of packing and timing, and a 5.6-day average delivery plus 7% damage suggests fragile items need close oversight; margins are also thinner, squeezing the $32.00 contribution per unit.

Recommendation: KHS should use a third-party courier with strict handling agreements and its own quality checks. It gives national scale without the fixed cost of a fleet and more control than dropshipping, which is rejected because it removes control of packing when damage is already 7%. An in-house fleet is rejected as too capital-intensive alongside a $700,000 investment and 5.6-day delivery targets.

    Question: KHS's delivery damage complaints have reached 7% of orders and stock-outs are rising. Explain two benefits for KHS of clear downward communication in its hierarchical structure when tackling these problems.

    Question: Using Appendix 2, evaluate KHS's financial position by calculating the current ratio and the acid test ratio for 2024 and 2025. Has KHS's financial position improved? Justify your answer.
    Answer: Calculations:
Current Ratio 2024 = 1.80 : 1
Current Ratio 2025 = 1.88 : 1
Acid Test Ratio 2024 = 0.60 : 1
Acid Test Ratio 2025 = 0.64 : 1

Detailed workings: 2024 current assets = $180,000 inventories + $50,000 trade receivables + $40,000 cash = $270,000; 2025 current assets = $205,000 + $45,000 + $60,000 = $310,000. The 2024 figure is $270,000 ÷ $150,000 = 1.80; the 2025 figure is $310,000 ÷ $165,000 = 1.88. Excluding stock, 2024 liquid assets are $50,000 + $40,000 = $90,000, giving $90,000 ÷ $150,000 = 0.60; 2025 liquid assets are $45,000 + $60,000 = $105,000, giving $105,000 ÷ $165,000 = 0.64.

Evaluation: Liquidity has improved on both measures. The 1.80 to 1.88 rise shows current assets cover short-term debts more comfortably, helped by cash rising from $40,000 to $60,000. The 0.60 to 0.64 improvement shows KHS is a little less dependent on selling inventory to meet debts, useful while it repays a $350,000 loan and funds a $700,000 warehouse. However, both stock-excluding measures remain well below 1, so liquid assets still fall short of liabilities, and inventories rose from $180,000 to $205,000 partly to guard against the 5.4% stock-out rate; with a 7% damage rate, some of that stock may be hard to sell, so the quality of the asset base is questionable.

Conclusion: KHS's financial position has improved, but only modestly. Both measures rose and the rise is not purely a stock build-up, since receivables actually fell from $50,000 to $45,000. The main weakness is low liquid cover, so KHS should keep tight cash control while investing the $350,000 retained profit and $350,000 loan in the new warehouse.

  Q4(a) [8 marks]
    Question: Explain one advantage and one disadvantage for KHS of selling flat-pack sustainable furniture as promoted in its market research.
    Answer: Advantage: Flat-pack sustainable furniture matches the 42% of 650 surveyed customers who would pay $25 more, letting KHS lift its $48.00 selling price and add to the $32.00 contribution per unit while appealing to the 57% who value free delivery and low prices. It also supports the $700,000 automated warehouse, because flat packs are compact to store and dispatch, helping reduce the 5.4% stock-out rate and the 7% damage rate.

Disadvantage: Sustainable materials and eco-packaging often cost more than standard inputs, raising the $16.00 variable cost per unit and eroding contribution unless the $25 premium is fully accepted; the insert gives no figure for this extra cost, so the benefit cannot be quantified. Flat packs can also arrive damaged or incomplete, and with a 7% damage-related complaint rate and 2.7% conversion, any quality slip would raise refunds and weaken the 29% repeat-purchase rate, so the 4.5% base rate is welcome as cheaper credit to fund the transition.

  Q4(b) [12 marks]
    Question: Using Appendix 3, evaluate how the interest rate cut from 5.0% to 4.5%, the 5.8% minimum wage increase and the 8.9% rise in timber and courier input costs will affect KHS. Which change will have the greatest impact? Justify your answer.
    Answer: Interest rate cut (5.0% to 4.5%): This is a favourable change. If KHS's $350,000 loan is variable-rate, the annual interest cost falls by 0.5% of $350,000 = $1,750 a year (0.005 × $350,000), easing the burden of fixed costs of $192,000 a year and freeing cash for the $700,000 warehouse. If the loan is fixed, the saving is delayed until refinancing. Lower rates may also support the 1.6% growth in home-furnishing spending, though the benefit is a modest, one-off gain rather than a change to unit costs.

Minimum wage increase (5.8%, to $13.40 per hour): With a workforce of 40, this rise pushes up wage costs in warehousing and packing and is unavoidable. The insert states no hours worked or individual pay, so no defensible annual total can be invented. The correct benchmark is the given productivity figure: 16,000 units ÷ 40 staff = 400 units per worker. If productivity holds at 400 units, the rise is absorbable; otherwise unit labour cost climbs and the $32.00 contribution per unit is squeezed at a time when the 7% damage rate already adds cost.

Timber and courier input inflation (8.9%): The insert does not decompose the $16.00 variable cost, so only a bound can be shown: if the whole variable cost rose 8.9%, that adds 8.9% × $16.00 = about $1.42 per unit, or roughly $22,784 a year at 16,000 units. Courier inflation also makes the 7% damage problem more expensive to fix through returns, and with home-furnishing spending up only 1.6% and fuel surcharges adding 3.2% to delivery, KHS has limited power to pass costs on through its $48.00 price.

Conclusion: The 8.9% rise in timber and courier costs will have the greatest impact. It applies to every unit, is far larger than the $1,750 interest saving, and directly threatens the $32.00 contribution that funds the $700,000 expansion. The wage rise can be offset if 400-unit productivity holds, and the rate cut is a benefit rather than a threat, so input inflation is clearly the dominant external change.
    Keywords: 5.0%, 4.5%, 5.8%, $13.40, 8.9%, $350,000
    Mark scheme: level_1_1_to_4: Identifies the external changes with limited application to KHS. | level_2_5_to_8: Analyses the impact of at least two external changes on KHS's costs, revenue or financing in context. | level_3_9_to_12: Detailed evaluation of all three external changes in the context of KHS with a well-justified judgment on which has the greatest impact and why the others are smaller.

--- MAIN STEM ---
Harbour Bay Poultry (HBP) is a private limited company in the food processing sector, converting fresh chicken into frozen ready-to-cook meals sold through national supermarket chains. Founded in 2012 by Jernej Munoz, the business employs a workforce of 42. It operates a flat structure with autocratic leadership. It has fixed costs of $620,000 a year, a variable cost of $12.50 a unit and a selling price of $16.50, and currently produces 180,000 units a year. HBP faces a worsening defect rate record on sealing and rising quality complaint levels from retail buyers.

--- APPENDIX 1 — MARKETING/OPS ---
Operations and Quality Report — Q3 2026: The frozen meal line has grown to 180,000 units produced a year, up from 155,000 a year ago. Defect rate on sealing is now 3.9%, down from 5.2% a year ago. Customer complaints fell from 41 to 27 per month. Average delivery time to processors is 1.9 days. A survey of 320 processors found that 62% would pay a $2.10 premium per meal for eco-packaging, and 48% check shelf life before buying. Off-the-job training at the regional college costs $800 per employee; 12 of the 42 staff need recertification of the new freezing equipment.

(2) Agricultural nitrogen and fuel input costs have risen 14.2% year-on-year, while food-price inflation is running at 6.9%. (3) Consumer spending on ready-to-cook frozen meals fell 2.1% while spending on fresh chilled meals grew 4.7% in the same period.

It also avoids the collateral and default risk attached to the ten-year bank loan, so the whole frozen-line grading and packaging plant is not at risk of repossession.

Point 2: Retained profit keeps ownership with the management team, so no lender can impose conditions on how HBP runs the freezing automation or sets prices; HBP keeps full flexibility to reinvest surplus into further capacity or quality improvements once the plant stabilises.
