    Question: Using Appendix 3, evaluate how the rise in the base interest rate to 5.25%, the 6.5% minimum wage increase and the 11.6% rise in input costs will affect ACR. Which change will have the greatest impact? Justify your answer.
    Answer: Base interest rate rise from 4.5% to 5.25%: If ACR's $600,000 ten-year bank loan is variable-rate, the increase adds 0.75% × $600,000 = $4,500 a year (0.0075 × $600,000). That is small beside $480,000 of fixed costs, and if the loan is fixed-rate the extra interest is zero. Higher rates may still deter guests financing short breaks and raise the cost of any future borrowing, but ACR can reduce this risk by fixing the loan rate.

Minimum wage rise of 6.5% from $13.80 to $14.70 per hour: With a workforce of 160, this feeds into the wage bill and cannot be avoided. The insert gives no hours worked or individual pay, so no annual total can be calculated honestly. The defensible comparison is with productivity: 24,000 units ÷ 160 staff = 150 units per employee, so the rise is absorbable only if productivity holds at that level or room-nights grow; otherwise unit labour cost climbs and the $120 contribution shrinks.

Input-cost inflation of 11.6%: The insert does not decompose the $55 variable cost, so only a bound can be shown: if the whole $55 were exposed, 11.6% × $55 = $6.38 a unit, and at 24,000 units that is $153,120 a year. A smaller exposed share would cost proportionally less. ACR can recover part through the $20 eco-villa premium identified by 68% of 500 surveyed guests.

Conclusion: The 11.6% input-cost inflation has the greatest impact. It applies to every one of the 24,000 room-nights and directly erodes the $120 contribution that supports the $900,000 villa wing, whereas the $4,500 interest effect is small and the wage effect depends on unknown hours. ACR should negotiate supply contracts and push the $20 premium.

--- MAIN STEM ---
Treetop Canopy Lodges (TCL) is a private limited company in the leisure and tourism sector, operating forest eco-pods and canopy walkways in a northern rainforest reserve. Founded in 2015 by Nathan Oyelaran, it employs a workforce of 90 and uses a flat structure with laissez-faire leadership. TCL plans to invest $750,000 in twelve new treehouse pods with automated eco-sensors, financed by a $400,000 ten-year bank loan and a $350,000 share issue. It has fixed costs of $360,000 a year, a variable cost of $40 a unit and a selling price of $140, and currently produces 15,000 units a year. TCL faces rising labour turnover among its guides and a worsening guest complaint rate about pod maintenance.

--- APPENDIX 1 — MARKETING/OPS ---
Operations and Quality Report — Q4 2026: TCL sold 15,000 guest-nights (units) last year, up from 13,200 a year ago. Pod maintenance rework affected 5.8% of stays, down from 8.1% previously. Guest complaints fell from 36 to 19 per month, and average check-in time is 3.1 minutes. A survey of 420 guests found that 71% would pay a $25 premium for canopy-view pods and 58% prefer to book through the mobile app. Team working is used across the guide and maintenance teams. On-the-job training covers routine checks, while off-the-job training at the regional centre costs $620 per employee; 14 of the 90 staff need recertification on the new monitoring systems.

--- APPENDIX 2 — FINANCIAL DATA ---

Trade receivables | 85 | 96
Cash and cash equivalents | 38 | 44
Current liabilities | 150 | 165
Non-current assets | 1,200 | 1,480
Capital employed | 1,450 | 1,760

--- APPENDIX 3 — EXTERNAL ENVIRONMENT ---
Economic and Business Bulletin (November 2026): (1) The central bank has raised the base interest rate from 4.25% to 5.0%, raising the cost of variable-rate borrowing. (2) The national minimum wage rises by 5.8% from $14.00 to $14.81 per hour from May 2026, increasing wage bills for leisure operators. (3) Fuel and timber input costs have risen 9.4% year-on-year, while domestic tourism spending grew 5.6% over the same period.

With $360,000 of annual fixed costs already committed, TCL avoids the 0.75% rise in borrowing cost and preserves cash to absorb the 9.4% increase in fuel and timber inputs, protecting the $100 contribution per unit ($140 − $40) on its 15,000 guest-nights.

Point 2: The new shareholders share the risk of the twelve pods with automated eco-sensors, so Nathan Oyelaran's business is not solely exposed if the 5.8% minimum wage rise pushes costs up or the worsening guest complaints delay bookings. Equity also strengthens the statement of financial position shown in appendix 2, giving TCL more headroom than piling another loan onto existing debt before the $750,000 programme is complete.

    Answer: National eco-travel magazine advertising: A full-page campaign in national magazines would build prestige for TCL's forest reserve and reach educated travellers who might pay the $25 premium for canopy-view pods. The downside is high production and media cost against $360,000 of fixed costs, long lead times, and waste: most readers will never visit a northern rainforest reserve, and a static photograph cannot show the automated eco-sensors.

Recommendation: TCL should choose partnerships with specialist outdoor tourism websites. They reach the precise segment willing to pay the premium, support the app booking channel and cost less than print. National magazine advertising is rejected as costly and geographically wasteful, and local radio is rejected as too narrow to sustain 15,000 guest-nights; TCL can add small in-resort signage as a support.

--- MAIN STEM ---
Summit Ridge Tours (SRT) is a public limited company in the tourism sector, organising guided mountain treks and alpine base-camp stays. Founded in 2008 by Priya Raghunathan, it employs a workforce of 120 and operates a hierarchical structure with autocratic leadership for safety. SRT plans to invest $1,100,000 in a new alpine base camp with automated safety-monitoring equipment, financed by a $700,000 share issue and a $400,000 bank loan. It has fixed costs of $540,000 a year, a variable cost of $85 a unit and a selling price of $205, and currently produces 22,000 units a year. SRT faces rising labour turnover among guides and a worsening equipment defect rate found during safety inspection.

--- APPENDIX 1 — MARKETING/OPS ---
Operations and Quality Report — Q1 2027: SRT sold 22,000 trek places (units) last year, up from 19,400 a year ago. Equipment inspection found a 4.3% defect rate, down from 7.0% previously. Client complaints fell from 33 to 18 per month, and average group departure delay is 12 minutes. A survey of 380 clients found that 66% would pay a $30 premium for small-group guided treks and 54% check safety certification before booking. Job rotation across three trail routes is used; on-the-job training covers routine checks while off-the-job training at the training centre costs $950 per employee, and 16 of the 120 guides need safety-equipment certification.

--- APPENDIX 2 — FINANCIAL DATA ---

Headers: ['Financial Metric', '2024', '2025']

--- APPENDIX 3 — EXTERNAL ENVIRONMENT ---

(2) The national minimum wage rises by 7.2% from $14.20 to $15.22 per hour from May 2026, lifting wage bills. (3) Transport fuel and climbing-equipment input costs have risen 10.8% year-on-year, while bookings for adventure tourism grew 6.3% in the same period.

  Q1(a) [8 marks]
    Question: Explain two advantages for SRT of financing the $1,100,000 base camp with a share issue rather than a larger bank loan.

With $540,000 of fixed costs already committed, SRT avoids extra debt service as the base rate climbs from 5.0% to 5.75%, leaving cash to absorb the 10.8% rise in fuel and climbing-equipment costs and protecting the $120 contribution per unit ($205 − $85) on 22,000 trek places.

Point 2: Equity shares the risk of the new alpine base camp and automated safety-monitoring equipment with shareholders, so Priya Raghunathan's company is not solely exposed if the 7.2% minimum wage rise pushes costs up or the worsening equipment defect rate delays departures.     Keywords: share issue, $700,000, $400,000, $1,100,000, $205, $85, 10.8%

    Question: SRT must certify 16 of its 120 guides on the new automated safety-monitoring equipment. Consider on-the-job training or off-the-job training at the training centre. Which should SRT choose? Justify your decision.

--- MAIN STEM ---
Meridian Leisure Group (MLG) is a partnership in the leisure sector, running an indoor theme park and family attractions in a large city. Founded in 2003 by Elena Vasquez, it employs a workforce of 200 and operates a hierarchical structure with democratic leadership. MLG plans to invest $750,000 in a new indoor leisure dome with automated ride-monitoring and contactless ticketing, financed by a $500,000 ten-year bank loan and $250,000 retained profit. It has fixed costs of $720,000 a year, a variable cost of $28 a unit and a selling price of $88, and currently produces 40,000 units a year. MLG faces rising labour turnover among ride operators and increasing visitor complaints about queue times.

--- APPENDIX 1 — MARKETING/OPS ---
Operations and Quality Report — Q4 2026: MLG sold 40,000 admissions (units) last year, up from 36,500 a year ago. Ride inspection found a 3.4% defect rate, down from 5.9% previously. Visitor complaints fell from 58 to 31 per month, and average queue time is 24 minutes. A survey of 700 visitors found that 63% would pay a $12 premium for fast-track entry and 49% book online. A bonus scheme for ride operators is being piloted; on-the-job training covers routine rides while off-the-job training on automated ride-monitoring at the technical college costs $540 per employee, and 22 of the 200 staff need it.

--- APPENDIX 2 — FINANCIAL DATA ---

With $720,000 of fixed costs a year, predictable instalments make budgeting far easier, especially as the base rate has risen from 4.75% to 5.5%.

Point 2: The loan provides a large, committed $500,000 alongside $250,000 retained profit, so MLG can complete the automated ride-monitoring project without draining the cash needed to run 40,000 admissions and ease the 24-minute queue time. An overdraft would leave the partnership exposed to sudden calls on its cash and could undermine the 3.4% defect-rate improvements just as the new dome opens.

--- MAIN STEM ---
Trailpine Freight (TPF) is a private limited company in the road freight and logistics sector, employing a workforce of 40. Founded in 2011 by Nelia Brooks, it operates a hierarchical structure with democratic leadership. TPF plans to invest $480,000 in an electric delivery truck fleet and depot charging hub, financed by a $300,000 five-year bank loan and $180,000 retained profit. It has fixed costs of $180,000 a year, a variable cost of $8.00 a unit and a selling price of $14.00, and produces 45,000 units a year. TPF faces a rising consignment damage rate of 3.2% and driver absenteeism of 7%, which are slowing depot turnaround and worrying retail clients. The founder still chairs the board and sets delivery targets personally.

--- APPENDIX 1 — MARKETING/OPS ---
Operations Log — Q3 2025: TPF handled 45,000 consignments last year, up 6% on the previous year, with a consignment damage rate of 3.2% and 24 written customer complaints last month. On-time delivery stands at 91%, against a 97% target, and average depot turnaround is 38 minutes. A survey of 250 business clients found 68% would pay $0.60 more for guaranteed next-day delivery, and 54% choose carriers on environmental performance. Eleven of the 40 drivers still need electric-vehicle training, and the accredited course costs $700 per driver.

--- APPENDIX 2 — FINANCIAL DATA ---
Title: Extract from the Statement of Profit or Loss and Capital employed data of Trailpine Freight (TPF) for the year ended 31 March 2025 ($ '000)
Headers: ['Financial Metric', '2024', '2025']

Cost of sales | 324,000 | 352,800
Gross profit | 216,000 | 277,200
Operating profit | 54,000 | 75,600
Capital employed | 360,000 | 420,000
Interest payable | 9,000 | 8,000

--- APPENDIX 3 — EXTERNAL ENVIRONMENT ---
Economic and Business Bulletin (November 2026): (1) The central bank has raised the base interest rate from 4.5% to 5.25%, lifting borrowing costs on variable-rate business loans. (2) Diesel and depot electricity prices have risen 11.3% year-on-year, pushing up per-consignment operating costs. (3) The national minimum wage will rise 5.8% from $12.40 to $13.11 per hour from April 2026, increasing wage bills across the logistics sector.

--- QUESTIONS ---
  Q1(a) [8 marks]
    Question: Explain two advantages for TPF of funding the $480,000 electric fleet from retained profit rather than the $300,000 bank loan.
    Answer: Point 1: Retained profit carries no interest or repayment obligation, so TPF keeps the cash needed to run 45,000 consignments a year. The base rate has moved from 4.5% to 5.25%, making the $300,000 five-year bank loan more expensive, whereas the $180,000 retained profit is free. With a $14.00 selling price and an $8.00 variable cost, every consignment earns $6.00 contribution, or $270,000 a year at current volume, and that cash can absorb the 11.3% rise in diesel and depot electricity without pushing the $14.00 price up to business clients.

Point 2: Using retained profit avoids collateral and repossession risk on the $480,000 truck fleet and charging hub. If the 3.2% damage rate and 7% driver absenteeism delay the return from the new vehicles, no lender can seize the trucks or impose conditions on Nelia Brooks's delivery targets. Ownership and control stay with the founder, which suits a private limited company that wants to reinvest surplus in further depot capacity once the electric fleet is working.
    Keywords: retained profit, $300,000, $480,000, $180,000, $14.00, $8.00, 45,000
    Mark scheme: knowledge_max_2: 1 mark for each valid advantage identified (max 2). | application_analysis_max_6: Up to 3 marks per point for detailed contextual explanation linked to Trailpine Freight (TPF), its fleet investment and its cost structure.

However, airtime and production are very expensive for a 40-employee private limited company funding a $480,000 electric fleet, and most viewers are not business buyers of road freight, so much of the spend would be wasted.

It is measurable, far cheaper than television, and can demonstrate the 91% on-time delivery record and the guaranteed next-day service bought by the 68% who would pay $0.60 more. Its weakness is slower mass-brand recognition than television.

    Question: Consider quality circles in which drivers solve the 3.2% damage problem, or a cash bonus for damage-free deliveries. Which should TPF choose? Justify your decision.
    Answer: Quality circles: Regular driver groups would examine why 3.2% of consignments are damaged and propose loading or routing improvements. This uses the knowledge of the 40 drivers, suits democratic leadership, and can lift on-time delivery from 91% toward the 97% target without adding a new payment. It is slow to produce results and needs management time, and some suggestions may conflict with the $480,000 fleet schedule.

Cash bonus: A payment for damage-free deliveries gives an immediate individual incentive and could quickly reduce the 24 written complaints. It rewards the right outcome and is easy to understand, but the insert gives no bonus rate or number of eligible drivers, so its total cost cannot be calculated. It may also encourage drivers to record damage inaccurately and does not fix underlying depot causes.

Decision: TPF should choose quality circles first, adding a bonus only if progress stalls. Quality circles address the cause of the 3.2% damage rate, fit the existing leadership style and cost nothing quantified in the insert, protecting the $6.00 contribution on 45,000 consignments. The cash bonus is rejected because its cost is unquantified and it treats symptoms rather than causes; TPF can introduce it later alongside the $700 training programme if the damage rate does not fall.
    Keywords: 3.2%, 24, 91%, $700, 45,000, $8.00, 7%

    Answer: Base interest rate rise (4.5% to 5.25%): The increase is 0.75 percentage points. Diesel and depot electricity prices (up 11.3%): This is a cost on every one of the 45,000 consignments. That would cut contribution from $6.00 toward $5.10 and threaten the $0.60 premium plan.

Minimum wage rise (5.8%, $12.40 to $13.11 an hour): The insert gives no hours worked or driver pay, so no annual wage total can be invented. The honest benchmark is productivity: 45,000 consignments ÷ 40 drivers = 1,125 consignments per driver, so the rise is affordable only if productivity holds or volume grows.

Conclusion: The 11.3% energy-price rise will have the greatest impact. It compounds across all 45,000 consignments and directly erodes the $6.00 contribution that funds the fleet, unlike the conditional $2,250 interest effect and the wage rise, which cannot be quantified from the insert. --- MAIN STEM ---
Solstice Solar Systems (SSS) is a private limited company in the renewable energy sector, installing rooftop solar panels and battery storage, with a workforce of 28. Founded in 2016 by Rohan Mehta, it operates a flat organisational structure with laissez-faire leadership. SSS plans to invest $600,000 in a solar-panel assembly and battery-storage line, financed by a $300,000 five-year bank loan and a $300,000 share issue. It has fixed costs of $144,000 a year, a variable cost of $9.00 a unit and a selling price of $16.50, and produces 36,000 units a year. SSS faces a panel rework rate of 4.1% and rising installation-quality complaints from households. Experienced installation teams set their own schedules.

--- APPENDIX 1 — MARKETING/OPS ---
Quality and Waste Report — Q3 2025: SSS assembled 36,000 solar units last year, a 9% rise on the previous year, but 4.1% needed rework and 18 warranty claims were logged last month. Only 86% of installations were completed on the booked date. A survey of 300 households found 71% would pay $0.80 more for a battery-ready system, and 47% compare installers by warranty length. Nine of the 28 technicians lack battery-storage certification; the accredited course costs $1,100 each. Panel material waste is 6.5% of purchases.

--- APPENDIX 2 — FINANCIAL DATA ---

(2) Lithium and solar-grade silicon input prices have risen 13.6% year-on-year, pushing up component costs. (3) The national minimum wage will rise 6.1% from $12.40 to $13.16 per hour from April 2026, raising installation wage bills.

    Question: Explain two advantages for SSS of funding the $600,000 assembly line through a share issue rather than the $300,000 bank loan.
    Answer: Point 1: Share capital does not require interest or capital repayments, so SSS keeps cash to cover $144,000 of fixed costs while the assembly line is commissioned. The base rate has risen from 4.25% to 5.0%, making the $300,000 five-year bank loan more expensive; equity avoids that interest entirely. With a $16.50 selling price and a $9.00 variable cost, each system contributes $7.50, or $270,000 at 36,000 units, and keeping that cash helps absorb the 13.6% rise in lithium and silicon prices.

Point 2: Equity is permanent capital suited to a long-lived solar and battery facility, so no lender can repossess the line if the 4.1% rework rate delays output. A share issue also spreads risk among investors instead of leaving Rohan Mehta's firm solely exposed to debt. The trade-off is some dilution of ownership, but SSS retains the $300,000 bank loan for flexibility and can use the extra headroom to improve the 86% on-time installation record.

--- MAIN STEM ---
Northgate Logistics (NGL) is a private limited company in the distribution and courier sector, employing a workforce of 55. Founded in 2005 by Priya Raman, it operates a hierarchical structure with autocratic leadership. NGL plans to invest $840,000 in an automated warehouse sorting system and an electric van fleet, financed by a $480,000 five-year bank loan and $360,000 retained profit. It has fixed costs of $300,000 a year, a variable cost of $10.00 a unit and a selling price of $17.50, and produces 75,000 units a year. NGL faces a parcel mis-sorting rate of 2.8% and rising damage complaints from online retailers. Priya Raman personally approves all capital spending, and the depot runs two shifts a day.

--- APPENDIX 1 — MARKETING/OPS ---
Operations Log — Q3 2025: NGL handled 75,000 consignments last year, up 12% on the previous year, but 2.8% were mis-sorted and 33 written complaints were received last month. On-time delivery is 93.5% against a 96% target, and average dispatch time is 4.6 hours from order to van. A survey of 350 e-commerce retailers found 66% would pay $0.55 more for guaranteed same-day delivery, and 58% rank damage-free handling first. Fourteen of the 55 warehouse staff need scanner training at $650 each. The warehouse return rate is 5.2%.

--- APPENDIX 2 — FINANCIAL DATA ---
Title: Extract from the Statement of Profit or Loss and Capital employed data of Northgate Logistics (NGL) for the year ended 31 March 2025 ($ '000)
Headers: ['Financial Metric', '2024', '2025']

Cost of sales | 648,000 | 693,000
Gross profit | 432,000 | 567,000
Operating profit | 108,000 | 151,200
Capital employed | 720,000 | 840,000
Interest payable | 18,000 | 15,000

--- APPENDIX 3 — EXTERNAL ENVIRONMENT ---
Economic and Business Bulletin (November 2026): (1) The base interest rate has risen from 4.6% to 5.35%, raising the cost of variable-rate business loans. (2) Fuel and warehouse electricity prices have risen 2.4% year-on-year, only slightly above recent levels. (3) Consumer spending on online retail fell 7.8% in the latest quarter, while spending on in-store shopping rose 1.9%.

--- QUESTIONS ---
  Q1(a) [8 marks]
    Question: Explain two advantages for NGL of funding the $840,000 sorting system from retained profit rather than the $480,000 bank loan.
    Answer: Point 1: Retained profit has no interest charge or instalments, preserving cash while the automated sorter is installed. The base rate has moved from 4.6% to 5.35%, so the $480,000 five-year bank loan is becoming dearer; the $360,000 retained profit is free. Each consignment earns $7.50 ($17.50 − $10.00), giving $562,500 of contribution at 75,000 consignments, which NGL can use to absorb the 2.8% mis-sorting cost without raising the $17.50 price.

Point 2: Equity funding avoids collateral and the risk of repossession if the new sorter fails to cut the 33 monthly complaints. No lender can impose conditions on Priya Raman's capital decisions, which suits her centralised, autocratic control of spending. Using retained profit also keeps the bank's credit headroom intact for a later van-fleet purchase, giving NGL flexibility if the 7.8% fall in online retail spending reduces the volume passing through the warehouse. The 12% growth in consignment volume recorded in Appendix 1 makes that internal cash especially valuable if the sorter needs further adjustment.
    Keywords: retained profit, bank loan, $480,000, $360,000, $840,000, $17.50, $10.00, 75,000
    Mark scheme: knowledge_max_2: 1 mark for each valid advantage identified (max 2). | application_analysis_max_6: Up to 3 marks per point for detailed contextual explanation linked to Northgate Logistics (NGL), its sorting investment and its cost structure.

  Q1(b) [12 marks]
    Question: Consider national television advertising, local radio sponsorship, or trade-magazine advertising. Which should NGL choose to promote same-day delivery to e-commerce retailers? Justify your recommendation.
    Answer: National television advertising: Television would create wide awareness of NGL's same-day service and could impress the public, but the airtime cost is high for a 55-employee firm already funding an $840,000 sorter. Most viewers do not buy courier contracts, so the campaign would reach few of the 350 retailers in the survey.

Local radio sponsorship: Radio is cheaper and quick to book, and it could cover NGL's depot catchment. However, e-commerce retailers buy nationally, and local listeners are largely consumers rather than business decision-makers; the reach is too narrow to fill the 75,000-consignment plan needed against $300,000 of fixed costs.

Trade-magazine advertising: Advertising in logistics and e-commerce publications reaches the purchasing managers who decide on carriers, matching the 350 retailers surveyed. It is far cheaper than television, can show the 93.5% on-time delivery record and the $0.55 same-day premium, and can be repeated in issues timed to peak seasons. Its weakness is long lead time and limited reach outside the trade.

Recommendation: NGL should choose trade-magazine advertising. It targets exactly the retailers who rank damage-free handling first, is affordable alongside the $480,000 loan, and supports the $0.55 premium. National television is rejected as costly and untargeted; local radio is rejected as too narrow and consumer-focused. NGL should follow up magazine leads with direct sales visits, since the 7.8% fall in online spending means contracts must be won actively. --- MAIN STEM ---
Voltway Charging (VWC) is a private limited company in the electric-vehicle charging and energy retail sector, employing a workforce of 32. Founded in 2018 by Sofia Alvarez, it operates a flat structure with democratic leadership. VWC plans to invest $720,000 in a rapid-charging hub network with solar canopies, financed by a $450,000 five-year bank loan and a $270,000 share issue. It has fixed costs of $252,000 a year, a variable cost of $7.20 a unit and a selling price of $15.60, and produces 60,000 units a year. VWC faces a charger fault rate of 6.4% and rising billing complaints from fleet drivers. Sofia Alvarez consults her technicians before changing prices.

--- APPENDIX 1 — MARKETING/OPS ---
Operations Log — Q3 2025: VWC delivered 60,000 charging sessions last year, up 14% on the previous year, but 6.4% of sessions ended in a charger fault and 29 billing complaints were logged last month. Charger availability was 94.2%, against a 98% target, and the average session lasted 27 minutes. A survey of 280 fleet managers found 73% would pay $0.45 more per session for guaranteed charger availability, and 61% choose networks by reliability. Ten of the 32 technicians need high-voltage certification at $1,250 each.

--- APPENDIX 2 — FINANCIAL DATA ---

Each session earns $8.40 ($15.60 − $7.20), or $504,000 at current volume, and that cash can absorb the 15.2% wholesale electricity rise without raising the $15.60 price to fleet drivers.

Point 2: Equity is permanent funding for long-life charging hardware and solar canopies, so no lender can repossess the hubs if the 6.4% charger fault rate delays the expected usage. Investors share the risk of the $720,000 network with the founder, and Sofia Alvarez keeps the bank's credit line free for later hub sites. The cost is some dilution of control, but it is preferable to tying the whole programme to a variable-rate loan in a rising-rate environment.

--- MAIN STEM ---
Harbourline Ferries (HLF) is a private limited company in the coastal ferry and tourism transport sector, employing a workforce of 48. Founded in 1998 by Eamon Doyle, it operates a flat structure with autocratic leadership. HLF plans to invest $560,000 in a hybrid-electric ferry and online booking system, financed by a $320,000 five-year bank loan and $240,000 retained profit. It has fixed costs of $220,000 a year, a variable cost of $8.00 a unit and a selling price of $13.50, and produces 60,000 units a year. HLF faces a 4.6% passenger complaint rate and rising crew absenteeism. Eamon Doyle approves every timetable change himself, and all sailings still use the old port terminal.

--- APPENDIX 1 — MARKETING/OPS ---
Operations Log — Q3 2025: HLF sold 60,000 passenger trips last year, up 5% on the previous year, but 4.6% of passengers complained and 26 written complaints were logged last month. Only 89% of sailings left on time, against a 95% target, and average berth turnaround was 42 minutes. A survey of 420 tourists found 70% would pay $1.20 more for a guaranteed-seat premium service, and 55% book by price. Thirteen of the 48 crew need hybrid-engine training at $950 each. The ticket refund rate is 3.4%.

--- APPENDIX 2 — FINANCIAL DATA ---
Title: Extract from the Statement of Profit or Loss and Capital employed data of Harbourline Ferries (HLF) for the year ended 31 March 2025 ($ '000)
Headers: ['Financial Metric', '2024', '2025']

Cost of sales | 486,000 | 495,000
Gross profit | 324,000 | 405,000
Operating profit | 81,000 | 108,000
Capital employed | 540,000 | 600,000
Interest payable | 13,500 | 12,000

--- APPENDIX 3 — EXTERNAL ENVIRONMENT ---
Economic and Business Bulletin (November 2026): (1) The base interest rate has risen from 4.4% to 5.1%, increasing the cost of variable-rate business borrowing. (2) Marine fuel and electricity input prices have risen 2.1% year-on-year. (3) Consumer spending on coastal day trips fell 8.5% in the latest quarter, while spending on city breaks rose 2.7%.

--- QUESTIONS ---
  Q1(a) [8 marks]
    Question: Explain two advantages for HLF of funding the $560,000 hybrid ferry from retained profit rather than the $320,000 bank loan.
    Answer: Point 1: Retained profit carries no interest or repayment, so HLF keeps cash to run 60,000 passenger trips a year. The base rate has risen from 4.4% to 5.1%, making the $320,000 five-year bank loan more costly, while the $240,000 retained profit is free. Each trip earns $5.50 ($13.50 − $8.00), or $330,000 at current volume, and that cash can absorb the 8.5% fall in coastal day-trip spending without raising the $13.50 fare.

Point 2: Funding from internal reserves avoids collateral and repossession risk on the $560,000 ferry if the 4.6% complaint rate delays the return from the new vessel. No lender can impose terms on Eamon Doyle's timetable decisions, which suits his direct control, and HLF keeps bank headroom for later booking-system upgrades. The retained profit also signals that the existing service generates enough surplus to support expansion without diluting ownership. The 5% growth in trips recorded in Appendix 1 makes that reserve useful if the new ferry needs early adjustment.

--- MAIN STEM ---
Pinecrest Analytics (PCA) is a private limited company in the software and cloud-computing sector, employing a workforce of 60. Founded in 2011 by Asha Nair, the firm supplies cloud inventory software to independent retailers across the country and operates a flat organisational structure with democratic leadership. Pinecrest plans to invest $720,000 in a new cloud analytics platform, financed by a $400,000 ten-year bank loan and $320,000 retained profit. It has fixed costs of $280,000 a year, a variable cost of $9.00 a unit and a selling price of $16.00, and currently produces 60,000 units a year. The firm faces two problems: client quality complaints have risen and developer absenteeism has reached 8%.

--- APPENDIX 1 — MARKETING/OPS ---
Operations and Quality Report — Q3 2025: The cloud platform rolled out 15,000 software licence units last quarter at a defect rate of 2.2%, down from 3.6% a year ago. Client support tickets fell from 54 to 29 per month. Average resolution time is 2.4 days. A survey of 450 business clients found that 68% would pay up to $0.50 more for priority support and 57% rank data security as their top buying criterion. A skills audit shows 18 of 60 staff lack training on the new analytics tools; external certification courses cost $1,100 per employee.

    Answer: Point 1: Retained profit carries no interest or repayment obligation, so PCA keeps the cash it would otherwise pay on the $400,000 ten-year bank loan. With fixed costs of $280,000 a year and a $720,000 platform to fund, preserving cash strengthens liquidity and lets Asha Nair absorb the 9.6% rise in cloud hosting input costs without raising the $16.00 selling price. Every dollar of interest avoided directly protects the $7.00 contribution per unit and gives the 60-employee firm more room to respond to client quality complaints.

Point 2: Using the $320,000 retained profit avoids the collateral and default risk attached to a bank loan, so the new cloud analytics platform cannot be repossessed if sales of the 60,000 units disappoint. It also keeps control with the existing owners, since no lender can impose conditions on how the platform is run, and it avoids the 4.5% base-rate environment that makes further borrowing more expensive for a software business.

--- MAIN STEM ---
Redshield Cyber (RSC) is a private limited company in the cybersecurity and managed-IT sector, employing a workforce of 75. Founded in 2008 by Mei Lin, the firm provides managed security monitoring to corporate clients across the region and operates a hierarchical structure with autocratic leadership. Redshield plans to invest $1,200,000 in a new security operations centre, financed by a $700,000 bank loan and a $500,000 share issue. It has fixed costs of $450,000 a year, a variable cost of $12.00 a unit and a selling price of $21.00, and currently produces 80,000 units a year. The firm faces two problems: a shortage of certified analysts and rising client complaints about false alerts.

--- APPENDIX 1 — MARKETING/OPS ---
Security Operations Report — Q2 2025: The team monitored 12,000 client endpoints and closed 9,600 alert cases last quarter, with a false-positive rate of 5.5%, down from 8.2% a year earlier. Client complaints about alert quality fell from 36 to 19 a month. Mean response time is 1.8 hours. A survey of 520 corporate clients found 66% would pay up to $0.60 more for round-the-clock monitoring, and 59% rate certification as essential. A skills audit shows 22 of 75 analysts lack advanced certification; training places cost $1,250 each.

--- APPENDIX 2 — FINANCIAL DATA ---

(3) Specialist cybersecurity software licences and hardware input costs have risen 10.5% year-on-year, while business IT spending grew 6.8% and general inflation is 3.4%.

--- MAIN STEM ---
Vertex Apps (VAP) is a private limited company in the mobile-app and fintech sector, employing a workforce of 55. --- MAIN STEM ---
Helio Cloud Cooperative (HCC) is a cooperative in the cloud-hosting and data-centre sector, employing a workforce of 90. Founded in 2010 by Sofia Almeida, it provides green web-hosting and cloud storage to business clients across the region and operates a flat structure with democratic leadership. Helio plans to invest $1,500,000 in a new energy-efficient data centre, financed by a $900,000 bank loan and $600,000 retained profit. It has fixed costs of $540,000 a year, a variable cost of $10.00 a unit and a selling price of $19.00, and currently produces 100,000 units a year. The cooperative faces two problems: rising energy waste in its server halls and a shortage of qualified technicians.

--- APPENDIX 1 — MARKETING/OPS ---

Client downtime complaints fell from 48 to 26 a month. Average server uptime reached 99.7%. A survey of 380 business clients found 64% would pay up to $0.45 more for green hosting, and 56% check energy credentials. A skills audit shows 25 of 90 technicians need renewable-energy training; accredited courses cost $1,300 per employee.

    Answer: Point 1: Retained profit carries no interest or repayment, so the cooperative avoids adding to the interest payable of 24 ($'000) and keeps the $900,000 loan manageable. With fixed costs of $540,000 a year and 100,000 units to deliver, preserving cash lets Sofia Almeida absorb the 14.2% rise in electricity and hardware costs without raising the $19.00 price.

It also leaves borrowing capacity for future renewable-energy investment, though heavy use of reserves reduces the cushion available if energy waste pushes costs above plan. For a 90-person cooperative with democratic leadership, keeping $600,000 of reserves under member control also avoids the covenants a larger lender might impose on the green data centre, and leaves room to fund the $1,300 renewable-energy courses for the 25 technicians who need them.

--- MAIN STEM ---
Kestrel Medical Supplies (KMS) is a private limited company in the healthcare sector, employing a workforce of 50. KMS faces two problems: absenteeism has reached 8% and complaints about torn sterile packaging are rising.

Customer complaints about torn packaging fell from 44 to 19 per month. Average order fulfilment is 4.1 days. A survey of 500 hospital procurement staff found 68% would pay up to $0.30 more for tamper-evident packs and 57% check sterility certification before ordering. Records show 18 of 50 staff have not completed on-the-job training on the new sealing machines; external certification courses cost $780 per employee.

Every dollar not paid as interest can absorb the 9.6% rise in fabric and packaging input costs without pushing the $10.50 selling price above what hospital groups will accept, preserving the $5.00 contribution per unit on 110,000 units.

Point 2: Using retained profit avoids the security and default risk of the $420,000 loan, so the new automated line cannot be repossessed if hospital orders fall short. It also leaves Priya Kestrel's ownership and control intact, since no lender can attach conditions to how the sterile-dressing line is run. Retained profit is immediately available with no application delay, letting KMS respond quickly to the torn-packaging complaints and begin the 48-hour delivery improvements its hospital contracts demand. Together these advantages let KMS direct scarce cash toward the 8% absenteeism problem and the torn-packaging complaints rather than toward a lender.

    Question: Using Appendix 3, evaluate how the interest rate rise to 5.0%, the 5.8% minimum wage increase and the 9.6% rise in input costs will affect KMS. Which change will have the greatest impact? Justify your answer.
    Answer: Interest rate rise (4.25% to 5.0%): If KMS's $420,000 ten-year bank loan is variable-rate, the 0.75 percentage-point increase adds 0.75% x $420,000 = $3,150 a year (0.0075 x $420,000). That is small beside fixed costs of $240,000, and if the loan is fixed-rate the extra cost is zero. Higher rates might also make hospital groups slower to pay and raise the cost of future borrowing. Minimum wage increase (5.8%, to $13.75 an hour): With a workforce of 50 and output of 110,000 units, labour productivity is 110,000 ÷ 50 = 2,200 units per worker. The insert gives no hours worked or individual pay rates, so an annual wage total cannot be invented; the honest test is whether each worker keeps producing around 2,200 units. If productivity slips while absenteeism is 8%, unit labour costs rise and the $5.00 contribution per unit shrinks.

Input-cost inflation (9.6% in fabric and packaging): The insert states a variable cost of $5.50 per unit but does not decompose it, so only an illustrative upper bound can be calculated. If the whole $5.50 rose by 9.6%, that is 9.6% x $5.50 = $0.528, about $0.53 per unit; across 110,000 units that is roughly $58,000 a year (110,000 x $0.53). Even a smaller $0.40-per-unit rise would cost $44,000 a year (110,000 x $0.40), pulling contribution from $5.00 toward about $4.60.

Conclusion: The 9.6% rise in input costs will have the greatest impact. It applies to every one of the 110,000 units and directly erodes the $5.00 contribution that justifies the $720,000 line, and at up to about $58,000 a year it dwarfs the conditional $3,150 interest effect. The wage rise is serious but its size cannot be quantified from the insert and depends on the 2,200-unit productivity holding, while interest costs can be fixed and are small. KMS should seek supplier deals and pass part of the cost on through the $0.30 tamper-evident premium.

Gross Profit Margin 2024 = 40.0%
Gross Profit Margin 2025 = 45.0%
Profit Margin 2024 = 13.0%
Profit Margin 2025 = 15.0%
ROCE 2024 = 19.5%
ROCE 2025 = 21.5%

Detailed workings: Gross profit of $720,000 on revenue of $1,800,000 in 2024 gives 720 ÷ 1,800 = 40.0%; in 2025 gross profit of $967,000 on $2,150,000 gives 967 ÷ 2,150 = 45.0%. Operating profit of $234,000 ÷ $1,800,000 = 13.0% in 2024 and $322,000 ÷ $2,150,000 = 15.0% in 2025. The return on capital employed divides operating profit by capital employed: $234,000 ÷ $1,200,000 = 19.5% and $322,000 ÷ $1,500,000 = 21.5%. Cost of sales of $1,080,000 and $1,183,000 reconciles exactly to gross profit in both years.

Operating profitability rose from 13.0% to 15.0%, suggesting the flat structure kept overheads controlled as enrolment grew. The return on capital increased from 19.5% to 21.5%, so the $1,500,000 of capital employed is being used more productively, which supports the $540,000 studio. Interest payable fell from $28,000 to $24,000, reducing the drag on profit.

Conclusion: LMA's financial performance has improved. Every margin rose, the return on capital strengthened and interest payable fell, leaving the business better able to service the $300,000 loan. Management should still address the 7% tutor absenteeism and 3.2% material-error rate, which could undermine these gains.

  Q4(b) [12 marks]
    Question: Using Appendix 3, evaluate how the interest rate rise to 4.5%, the 4.9% minimum wage increase and the 11.3% rise in input costs will affect LMA. Which change will have the greatest impact? Justify your answer.
    Answer: Interest rate rise (3.75% to 4.5%): If LMA's $300,000 five-year bank loan is variable-rate, the 0.75 percentage-point rise adds 0.75% x $300,000 = $2,250 a year (0.0075 x $300,000), small against fixed costs of $180,000. If the loan is fixed-rate the extra cost is zero. Parents may also cut discretionary tuition spending when borrowing is dearer, but LMA can largely remove this risk by fixing the rate.

Minimum wage increase (4.9%, to $13.22 an hour): With a workforce of 40 and output of 80,000 units, labour productivity is 80,000 ÷ 40 = 2,000 units per worker. The insert gives no hours worked or individual pay rates, so an annual wage bill cannot be invented; the defensible test is whether each tutor maintains around 2,000 units. With absenteeism at 7%, any fall in productivity would raise unit labour costs and shrink the $5.00 contribution.

Input-cost inflation (11.3% in paper, broadband and energy): The insert states a variable cost of $4.00 per unit without decomposing it, so only an illustrative bound is possible. If the entire $4.00 rose 11.3%, that is 11.3% x $4.00 = $0.452, about $0.45 per unit; over 80,000 units that is roughly $36,000 a year (80,000 x $0.45). Even a $0.35 rise would cost $28,000 a year (80,000 x $0.35), pulling contribution from $5.00 to about $4.65.

Conclusion: The 11.3% rise in input costs will have the greatest impact. It hits all 80,000 units and directly erodes the $5.00 contribution that underpins the $540,000 studio, and at up to about $36,000 a year it far exceeds the conditional $2,250 interest cost. The wage rise is real but cannot be quantified from the insert and depends on the 2,000-unit productivity holding, while interest risk can be fixed. LMA should renegotiate supplier contracts and recover part of the increase through the $0.50 premium.

--- MAIN STEM ---
Pinecrest Health Centre (PHC) is a partnership in the healthcare sector, employing a workforce of 60. Founded in 2008 by Dr Sofia Pinecrest, it provides private outpatient consultations and diagnostic scans and operates a hierarchical structure with autocratic leadership. PHC plans to invest $680,000 in a new minor-operations suite and scanner, financed by a $400,000 ten-year bank loan and $280,000 retained profit. It has fixed costs of $300,000 a year, a variable cost of $8.00 a unit and a selling price of $14.00, and currently produces 90,000 units a year, each a patient visit. Demand from local employers has grown steadily. PHC faces two problems: patient waiting times have risen and nursing absenteeism has reached 10%.

--- APPENDIX 1 — MARKETING/OPS ---
Operations and Quality Report, Q4 2025: The diagnostics pilot handled 21,000 patient visits last quarter with a re-scan rate of 2.7%, down from 4.4% a year ago. Patient complaints about appointment delays fell from 61 to 28 per month. Average waiting time is 38 minutes. A survey of 700 patients found 66% would pay up to $0.80 more for same-day scans and 59% check waiting-time ratings before choosing a clinic. Records show 22 of 60 staff have not completed on-the-job training on the new scanner; external accreditation courses cost $950 per employee.

--- APPENDIX 2 — FINANCIAL DATA ---

Gross profit | 1,200 | 1,566
Operating profit | 480 | 612
Capital employed | 2,400 | 2,800
Interest payable | 60 | 52

--- APPENDIX 3 — EXTERNAL ENVIRONMENT ---

(2) The national minimum wage will rise by 7.2% from $13.10 to $14.04 per hour, pushing up wage costs in healthcare. (3) Medical consumables and energy input costs have risen 10.5% year-on-year, private-healthcare inflation is 6.8%, and consumer spending on private clinics grew 4.1% over the same period.

  Q1(a) [8 marks]
    Question: PHC plans to fund part of its $680,000 minor-operations suite with a $400,000 ten-year bank loan. Explain two advantages for PHC of using retained profit rather than the bank loan.
    Answer: Point 1: Retained profit brings no interest bill or fixed repayment schedule, so the $280,000 drawn from past profits protects the partnership's cash flow while it meets fixed costs of $300,000 a year. Cash saved can absorb the 10.5% rise in medical consumables and energy costs without raising the $14.00 price, preserving the $6.00 contribution on 90,000 patient visits.

Point 2: Retained profit avoids the collateral and default risk of the $400,000 loan, so the new scanner suite cannot be threatened if patient numbers disappoint. It also keeps decision-making with Dr Sofia Pinecrest and the partners, since no lender can impose conditions. Because it is already in the business, it can be released at once to cut the 38-minute waiting time and address the 10% nursing absenteeism. Its hierarchical structure can then direct the cash saved specifically to cutting the 38-minute waiting time that patients complain about while the new scanner suite beds in.
    Keywords: retained profit, $280,000, $400,000, $680,000, $300,000, $14.00
    Mark scheme: knowledge_max_2: 1 mark for each valid advantage of retained profit over a bank loan (max 2). | application_analysis_max_6: Up to 3 marks per point for contextual explanation applied to PHC, its suite, costs and services.

  Q1(b) [12 marks]
    Question: PHC is promoting its new minor-operations suite. Consider advertising in local newspapers, sponsoring a regional healthcare conference, or targeted social media and email marketing to existing patients. Which should PHC choose? Justify your recommendation.
    Answer: Local newspaper advertising: Newspaper adverts would reach the local community and build awareness of the new suite. Costs are moderate but readership is ageing and falling, and a general audience includes many who will never need private scans, so much of the spend is wasted for a 60-staff partnership committing $680,000. The message is also static and hard to measure.

Regional healthcare conference sponsorship: This would put PHC in front of GPs and employers who refer patients, and allows demonstration of the scanner, supporting the 59% of surveyed patients who check waiting-time ratings. It is prestigious but a costly one-off event with limited reach; with 700 patients surveyed and 21,000 visits last quarter, one conference alone cannot fill 90,000 visits a year.

Targeted social media and email marketing: Digital messages to existing patients can promote same-day scans directly to the 66% who would pay $0.80 more, show current waiting times and be tracked cheaply. Content can be updated as the 38-minute waiting time falls. The weakness is that some patients ignore email and word-of-mouth still drives clinic choice, so personal reminders from reception staff would help.

Recommendation: PHC should choose targeted social media and email marketing, supported by a small conference presence. It reaches the 66% willing to pay $0.80 more at low cost and can run continuously to sustain 90,000 visits, unlike a single event. Newspapers are rejected as wasteful and declining; major conference sponsorship is rejected as too expensive and one-off for a partnership already servicing a $400,000 loan.

    Question: PHC's nursing absenteeism has reached 10% and waiting times have risen. Explain two benefits for PHC of introducing a performance-related bonus for its nursing staff.
    Answer: Point 1: A performance-related bonus links part of pay to measurable targets such as reducing the 38-minute waiting time and keeping the 2.7% re-scan rate low, giving the 60 staff a clear financial incentive (Herzberg's motivator) to improve service quality. Faster appointments would strengthen the appeal of same-day scans to the 66% of surveyed patients willing to pay $0.80 more.

Decision: PHC should choose on-the-job training initially, with accreditation for senior radiographers later. It is cheaper, equipment-specific and avoids lengthening waiting lists while absenteeism is 10%; full external training is rejected because the $20,900 and the loss of 22 staff would disrupt the 90,000-visit target and patient satisfaction, and accreditation can be added once the scanner is running smoothly, beginning with senior radiographers who demonstrate it to patients; the rest can follow once the suite is profitable, keeping the 90,000-visit plan on track.

--- MAIN STEM ---
Eastbrook Training (EBT) is a workers' cooperative in the education sector, employing a workforce of 35. Founded in 2015 by Amina Eastbrook, it delivers vocational training units to local employers and operates a flat structure with democratic leadership. EBT plans to invest $480,000 in a virtual-reality simulation workshop, financed by a $260,000 five-year bank loan and $220,000 retained profit. It has fixed costs of $210,000 a year, a variable cost of $5.00 a unit and a selling price of $11.00, and currently produces 70,000 units a year. Its courses have won two regional awards for employability. EBT faces two problems: equipment downtime has reached 9% and labour turnover among trainers is rising.

--- APPENDIX 1 — MARKETING/OPS ---
Training Quality Report, Q1 2026: The simulation workshop delivered 16,500 trainee units last quarter with an assessment re-sit rate of 3.6%, down from 5.8% a year ago. Employer complaints about trainer availability fell from 37 to 18 per month. Average equipment downtime is 9% of scheduled hours. A survey of 380 employers found 69% would pay up to $0.60 more for VR-enhanced courses and 55% check accreditation before commissioning training. Records show 12 of 35 trainers have not completed on-the-job training on the VR rigs; certificated courses cost $840 per trainer.

--- APPENDIX 2 — FINANCIAL DATA ---
Title: Extract from the Statement of Profit or Loss and Capital employed data of Eastbrook Training for the year ended 31 March 2025 ($ '000)
Headers: ['Financial Metric', '2024', '2025']

Gross profit | 600 | 774
Operating profit | 210 | 270
Capital employed | 1,000 | 1,200
Interest payable | 24 | 20

--- APPENDIX 3 — EXTERNAL ENVIRONMENT ---
Economic and Business Bulletin (November 2026): (1) The central bank has raised the base interest rate from 4.5% to 5.25%, increasing variable-rate borrowing costs. (2) The national minimum wage will rise by 6.1% from $12.90 to $13.69 per hour, adding to wage bills. (3) VR hardware and broadband input costs have risen 13.2% year-on-year, training-services inflation is 5.9%, and employer spending on staff development grew 3.3% over the same period.

--- QUESTIONS ---
  Q1(a) [8 marks]
    Question: EBT plans to fund part of its $480,000 VR workshop with a $260,000 five-year bank loan. Explain two advantages for EBT of using retained profit rather than the bank loan.
    Answer: Point 1: Retained profit has no interest charges or fixed repayments, so the $220,000 from earlier surpluses protects the cooperative's cash flow while it meets fixed costs of $210,000 a year. Cash preserved can absorb the 13.2% rise in VR hardware and broadband costs without lifting the $11.00 price, keeping the $6.00 contribution on 70,000 units.

Point 2: Retained profit needs no security, so the $480,000 workshop is not exposed to repossession if employer orders fall. It also preserves member control, since no lender can set conditions on how the cooperative is run. Because funds are already internal, EBT can act at once to replace the equipment behind 9% downtime and tackle rising trainer turnover. Fixed costs of $210,000 a year are already a heavy commitment for 35 trainers, and the cooperative's two regional awards depend on reliable delivery that debt service could jeopardise, whereas internal funds can be released without lender approval.
    Keywords: retained profit, $220,000, $260,000, $480,000, $210,000, $11.00
    Mark scheme: knowledge_max_2: 1 mark for each valid advantage of retained profit over a bank loan (max 2). | application_analysis_max_6: Up to 3 marks per point for contextual explanation applied to EBT, its workshop, costs and cooperative structure.

  Q1(b) [12 marks]
    Question: EBT is promoting its new VR-enhanced courses. Consider advertising in regional business newspapers, sponsoring a large employer skills fair, or targeted social media and email marketing to local employers. Which should EBT choose? Justify your recommendation.
    Answer: Regional business newspapers: Newspaper adverts would reach local managers and build awareness cheaply, but readership is declining and a general audience includes many firms that do not buy vocational training. For a 35-staff cooperative investing $480,000, much of the spend is wasteful and the static message cannot demonstrate the VR equipment.

Employer skills fair sponsorship: A major skills fair would put EBT in front of the exact HR managers who commission training and allow live VR demonstrations, supporting the 55% of surveyed employers who check accreditation.   Q2(a) [8 marks]
    Question: EBT has a flat structure with democratic leadership and rising labour turnover among trainers. Explain two benefits for EBT of introducing job rotation for its trainers.
    Answer: Point 1: Job rotation lets the 35 trainers switch between VR simulation delivery, assessment and course design, breaking the monotony that contributes to rising labour turnover. Varied work satisfies esteem needs in Maslow's hierarchy and builds a wider skill base, helping reduce the 12 of 35 trainers still without VR rig training and the 3.6% re-sit rate.

  Q2(b) [12 marks]
    Question: EBT must train 12 of its 35 trainers on the new VR rigs. Consider on-the-job training or certificated external courses costing $840 per trainer. Which should EBT choose? Justify your decision.
    Answer: On-the-job training: Learning on the VR rigs is tailored to EBT's own workshop and costs no fees, keeping the 12 trainers productive while they learn. That protects the 16,500 units delivered last quarter and the improvement in re-sit rate from 5.8% to 3.6%. Drawbacks are that mentor trainers deliver fewer sessions, local habits may spread, and there is no certificate to satisfy the 55% of employers who check accreditation.

Certificated external courses: At $840 per trainer, certificating all 12 costs $10,080 ($840 x 12), affordable against the $480,000 investment, and gives recognised qualifications that appeal to accreditation-conscious employers. However, it removes 12 of 35 trainers from delivery temporarily, worsening the 9% downtime pressure, and generic content may not match EBT's exact VR rigs, so follow-up coaching would still be required. The $10,080 must be weighed against 9% equipment downtime, which already cuts into the 16,500 units delivered last quarter. Certificates would help with the 55% of employers who check accreditation, but only a few trainers need them immediately.

Decision: EBT should choose on-the-job training first, adding certificates for senior trainers later. It is cheaper, rig-specific and avoids losing capacity while downtime is 9% and turnover is rising; full external training is rejected because the $10,080 and the loss of 12 trainers would disrupt the 70,000-unit target, and accreditation can be added once the workshop is established, spreading the cost across financial years after one term's review, while senior trainers coach the rest on site; a short external course for two senior trainers would still secure the accreditation signal valued by 55% of employers.
    Keywords: on-the-job training, $840, 12 of 35, VR rigs, 9%, $480,000
    Mark scheme: level_1_1_to_4: Describes the two training methods with little application to EBT. | level_2_5_to_8: Analyses the benefits and drawbacks of each method in the context of EBT's costs, capacity and staffing. | level_3_9_to_12: Comprehensive evaluation of both methods with a justified decision that rejects the alternative and refers to cost, disruption and equipment relevance.

  Q3(a) [8 marks]
    Question: Calculate and explain how EBT's management can use its cost, break-even and productivity data.
    Answer: (i) Break-even output = 35,000 units | (ii) Contribution per unit = $6.00 | (iii) Four contextual uses: a margin of safety of 35,000 units against 70,000 output; a $0.60 premium adding $42,000; covering $210,000 fixed costs and $260,000 loan interest; and unit-cost benchmarking at $8.00 to track 13.2% input inflation.

  Q3(b) [12 marks]
    Question: Using Appendix 2, evaluate EBT's financial performance by calculating the gross profit margin, profit margin and ROCE for 2024 and 2025. Has EBT's financial performance improved? Justify your answer.
    Answer: Calculations:

Gross Profit Margin 2025 = 43.0%
Profit Margin 2024 = 14.0%
Profit Margin 2025 = 15.0%
ROCE 2024 = 21.0%
ROCE 2025 = 22.5%

Operating profit of $210,000 ÷ $1,500,000 = 14.0% in 2024 and $270,000 ÷ $1,800,000 = 15.0% in 2025. The return on capital employed divides operating profit by capital employed: $210,000 ÷ $1,000,000 = 21.0% and $270,000 ÷ $1,200,000 = 22.5%. Cost of sales of $900,000 and $1,026,000 reconciles exactly with gross profit in both years.

Operating profitability rose from 14.0% to 15.0%, suggesting the cooperative controlled overheads as units grew. The return on capital improved from 21.0% to 22.5%, so the $1,200,000 capital employed is being used more efficiently, which supports the $480,000 workshop. Interest payable fell from $24,000 to $20,000, reducing the drag on surpluses.

Conclusion: EBT's financial performance has improved.     Question: Using Appendix 3, evaluate how the interest rate rise to 5.25%, the 6.1% minimum wage increase and the 13.2% rise in input costs will affect EBT. Which change will have the greatest impact? Justify your answer.
    Answer: Interest rate rise (4.5% to 5.25%): If EBT's $260,000 five-year bank loan is variable-rate, the 0.75 percentage-point rise adds 0.75% x $260,000 = $1,950 a year (0.0075 x $260,000), small alongside fixed costs of $210,000, and zero if the loan is fixed. Input-cost inflation (13.2% in VR hardware and broadband): The insert states a $5.00 variable cost per unit without decomposing it, so only an illustrative bound is defensible. Conclusion: The 13.2% rise in input costs will have the greatest impact. --- MAIN STEM ---
SwiftShine Cleaning (SSC) is a private limited company in the consumer services sector, employing a workforce of 80. Founded in 2017 by Noah Swift, it provides eco-friendly domestic and office cleaning and operates a hierarchical structure with democratic leadership. It has fixed costs of $264,000 a year, a variable cost of $6.00 a unit and a selling price of $12.00, and currently produces 100,000 units a year, each a cleaning job. Household demand has grown as more families outsource cleaning. SSC faces two problems: staff absenteeism has reached 11% and complaints about missed appointments are rising.

--- APPENDIX 1 — MARKETING/OPS ---
Operations and Quality Report, Q4 2025: The eco-cleaning pilot completed 24,000 jobs last quarter with a re-clean rate of 2.9%, down from 4.7% a year ago. Customer complaints about missed appointments fell from 73 to 31 per month. Average job completion time is 96 minutes. A survey of 550 household customers found 74% would pay up to $0.70 more for eco-friendly cleaning and 61% check environmental credentials before booking. Records show 26 of 80 staff have not completed on-the-job training on the new low-moisture machines; external courses cost $560 per employee.

Cash kept can absorb the 12.7% rise in eco-product and vehicle-energy costs without raising the $12.00 price, preserving the $6.00 contribution on 100,000 jobs.

Internal funds are available at once, letting SSC replace the machines behind the 2.9% re-clean rate and reduce the 11% absenteeism disrupting appointments. Fixed costs of $264,000 a year are a real burden for a company founded only in 2017, so avoiding interest on the $320,000 loan protects its early growth; the electric vans also need capital, and preserving cash protects the 100,000-job target.

--- MAIN STEM ---
Norwood Valley Preserves (NVP) is a private limited company in the food processing sector, employing a workforce of 60. Founded in 2011 by Ines Norwood, the business makes fruit preserves and chutneys for regional grocery chains and independent supermarkets, and operates a hierarchical structure with autocratic leadership. NVP plans to invest $720,000 in an automated glass-jar filling line with recyclable eco-packaging, financed by a $450,000 ten-year bank loan and $270,000 retained profit. It has fixed costs of $240,000 a year, a variable cost of $5.80 a unit and a selling price of $10.80, and currently produces 96,000 units a year. NVP faces rising warehouse waste and an increase in customer quality complaints about jar seals.

--- APPENDIX 1 — MARKETING/OPS ---
Operations and Quality Report — Q4 2025: The preserves line filled 24,000 jars last quarter at a defect rate of 2.4%, down from 3.6% a year earlier. Customer complaints about seals fell from 44 to 19 per month. Average order fulfilment is 4.1 days. A survey of 500 shoppers found that 62% would pay up to $0.50 more for recyclable eco-packaging, and 48% check jar recycling labels before buying. A skills audit shows 18 of 60 staff have not been trained on the new filling machines; off-the-job courses at the college cost $850 per employee.

--- APPENDIX 2 — FINANCIAL DATA ---
Title: Extract from the Statement of Profit or Loss and Capital employed data of Norwood Valley Preserves for the year ended 31 March 2025 ($ '000)
Headers: ['Financial Metric', '2024', '2025']

Cost of sales | 2,730 | 3,024
Gross profit | 1,470 | 2,016
Operating profit | 630 | 1,008
Capital employed | 3,500 | 4,200
Interest payable | 90 | 120

--- APPENDIX 3 — EXTERNAL ENVIRONMENT ---
Economic and Business Bulletin (November 2026): (1) The central bank has raised the base interest rate from 5.0% to 5.75%, increasing borrowing costs for firms with variable-rate loans. (2) The national minimum wage will rise by 5.5% from $13.40 to $14.14 per hour from April 2026, lifting total wage bills. (3) Glass and packaging input costs have risen 9.5% year-on-year, while consumer spending on preserves grew 2.8% over the same period.

--- QUESTIONS ---
  Q1(a) [8 marks]
    Question: Explain two advantages for NVP of using retained profit to fund the glass-jar filling line instead of the bank loan.
    Answer: Point 1: Using $270,000 of retained profit costs NVP nothing in interest or capital repayments, which protects cash flow at a time when it already carries $240,000 of fixed costs a year. With the base interest rate at 5.75%, servicing a $450,000 bank loan would add a substantial interest burden, whereas internally funded money lets every dollar of the $5.00 contribution on each jar stay in the business to absorb the 9.5% rise in glass and packaging costs. This matters for a preserves maker selling at $10.80 to regional grocery chains that resist price increases.

Point 2: Retained profit avoids the collateral and repossession risk attached to a bank loan, so Ines Norwood's $720,000 automated filling line is not jeopardised if demand for chutneys disappoints. It also keeps ownership and control inside the founder's private limited company: no lender can impose conditions on how the recyclable eco-packaging line is run, and no outside party gains a claim on future profits, which suits NVP's hierarchical, autocratic style where the founder retains tight control of strategy and of the warehouse waste problem.
    Keywords: retained profit, $270,000, $450,000, $720,000, bank loan, $240,000
    Mark scheme: knowledge_max_2: 1 mark for each valid point identified (max 2). | application_analysis_max_6: Up to 3 marks per point for detailed contextual explanation applied to the named business.

  Q1(b) [12 marks]
    Question: Consider national television advertising, local radio sponsorship, or social media influencer marketing. Which should NVP choose to promote its new jar range? Justify your recommendation.
    Answer: National television advertising: A TV campaign would build awareness of NVP's recyclable glass-jar preserves across all the regional grocery chains and independent supermarkets at once. However, airtime and production costs are very high relative to a 60-staff business funding a $720,000 line, and much of a national audience would never see the product on a local shelf, so a large share of the spend would be wasted.

Local radio sponsorship: Radio is much cheaper and reaches the regional catchment where NVP's preserves are actually stocked, and it suits short messages about the $0.50 eco-packaging premium. Its weakness is narrow reach: with output of 96,000 jars a year aimed at several chains, local listeners alone cannot shift enough volume, and audio cannot show the recyclable jar and recycling label that 48% of shoppers check.

Social media influencer marketing: Food and family influencers can demonstrate the jar, the seal quality and the recyclable eco-packaging directly to the 62% of 500 surveyed shoppers who would pay $0.50 more, and engagement is measurable at low cost per reached shopper. Results build more slowly than television and depend on influencer credibility, but the message travels nationally without TV-scale budgets.

Recommendation: NVP should choose social media influencer marketing. It targets exactly the segment identified in the research, shows the packaging that 48% of buyers inspect, and costs far less than television while reaching beyond radio's local audience. Television is rejected as unaffordable and untargeted for a 60-employee company servicing a $450,000 loan; radio is rejected as too narrow for 96,000 units of national-chain supply. NVP should support influencers with modest in-store shelf promotions.

    Question: Using Appendix 3, evaluate how the base interest rate rise to 5.75%, the 5.5% minimum wage increase and the 9.5% rise in glass and packaging input costs will affect NVP. Which change will have the greatest impact? Justify your answer.
    Answer: Base interest rate (5.0% to 5.75%): If NVP's $450,000 bank loan is variable-rate, the 0.75 percentage point rise adds 0.0075 × $450,000 = $3,375 a year. That is modest against $240,000 of fixed costs, and if the loan is fixed-rate the extra cost is zero. Higher base rates could also make future borrowing for the $720,000 line dearer and make consumers more cautious about premium preserves, but NVP can cap this risk by fixing the rate.

Minimum wage (5.5%, to $14.14 from $13.40 per hour): With a workforce of 60 in packing and warehouse roles, this feeds into wage bills and cannot be avoided. The insert gives no hours worked or individual pay rates, so no honest annual total can be invented; the defensible test is productivity of 96,000 units ÷ 60 staff = 1,600 units per worker. If output per worker holds, the rise is absorbable; if it slips, unit labour cost rises and the $5.00 contribution shrinks.

Input cost inflation (9.5% glass and packaging): The insert does not decompose the $5.80 variable cost, so only a bound can be computed: if all of it rose 9.5%, that adds 9.5% × $5.80 = $0.55 per unit; across 96,000 units that is about $52,800 a year (96,000 × $0.55). Only part can be recovered through the $0.50 eco-packaging premium, while spending on preserves grew just 2.8%.

Conclusion: The 9.5% input-cost rise has the greatest impact because it compounds on every one of the 96,000 jars and directly erodes the $5.00 contribution that underpins the $720,000 investment. The interest effect is small and fixable, and the wage rise can be offset if productivity holds, whereas input inflation strikes the core unit economics with little pricing room.
    Keywords: 5.75%, 5.5%, 9.5%, 5.0%, $14.14, $450,000, $5.80, 2.8%
    Mark scheme: level_1_1_to_4: Identifies the three external changes with limited application to NVP. | level_2_5_to_8: Analyses the impact of at least two changes on NVP's costs, revenue or financing in context. | level_3_9_to_12: Detailed evaluation of all three changes in the context of NVP with a well-justified judgment that input-cost inflation has the greatest impact.

--- MAIN STEM ---
Kestrel Ridge Footwear (KRF) is a public limited company in the footwear manufacturing sector, employing a workforce of 80. Founded in 2008 by Ravi Kestrel, the business supplies durable work boots to national retailers and operates a flat organisational structure with democratic leadership. KRF plans to invest $960,000 in an automated stitching line using recycled leather alternatives, financed by a $560,000 share issue and a $400,000 five-year bank loan. It has fixed costs of $360,000 a year, a variable cost of $12.00 a unit and a selling price of $20.00, and currently produces 120,000 units a year. KRF faces a rising defect rate on stitching and growing labour turnover in its cutting room.

--- APPENDIX 1 — MARKETING/OPS ---
Quality and Operations Report — Q3 2025: The stitching line produced 30,000 boots last quarter with a defect rate of 2.2%, down from 3.8% a year ago. Customer returns fell from 55 to 26 per month. Average delivery lead time is 5.3 days. Market research with 700 trade buyers found that 58% would pay up to $1.20 more for boots made with recycled materials, and 46% check sustainability claims before ordering. A skills review shows 22 of 80 operatives lack training on the new stitching machines; college courses cost $1,100 per employee.

--- APPENDIX 2 — FINANCIAL DATA ---
Title: Extract from the Statement of Profit or Loss and Capital employed data of Kestrel Ridge Footwear for the year ended 31 March 2025 ($ '000)
Headers: ['Financial Metric', '2024', '2025']

Cost of sales | 4,200 | 4,680
Gross profit | 1,800 | 2,520
Operating profit | 720 | 1,080
Capital employed | 4,000 | 4,800
Interest payable | 120 | 150

--- APPENDIX 3 — EXTERNAL ENVIRONMENT ---
Economic and Business Bulletin (November 2026): (1) The central bank has lifted the base interest rate from 4.25% to 5.0%, raising debt-servicing costs for variable-rate borrowers. (2) The national minimum wage will increase by 6.2% from $13.00 to $13.81 per hour from April 2026, pushing up wage costs. (3) Leather and synthetic upper input costs have risen 8.4% year-on-year, while consumer spending on footwear grew 2.1% in the same period.

  Q1(a) [8 marks]
    Question: Explain two advantages for KRF of financing the stitching line with a share issue rather than the bank loan.
    Answer: Point 1: A $560,000 share issue brings in equity that carries no interest or compulsory repayment, protecting KRF's cash flow while it carries $360,000 of fixed costs a year. With the base interest rate at 5.0%, a $400,000 bank loan would create an annual interest commitment; share capital instead lets the full $8.00 contribution on each boot remain available to absorb the 8.4% rise in upper-material costs without squeezing the $20.00 selling price to national retailers.

Point 2: Equity does not have to be secured against KRF's assets, so the automated stitching line cannot be repossessed if demand for work boots falls, which matters given the current 2.2% defect rate and labour turnover. As a public limited company, KRF can access a wide pool of investors for the $960,000 project without depending on one lender's conditions or covenants. The trade-off is dilution of existing shareholders, but for a large capital scheme this spreads risk more widely than concentrating it in a single bank loan.
    Keywords: share issue, $560,000, $400,000, $960,000, bank loan, $360,000

Costs are moderate and the message lasts, but print has no demonstration of boot durability and a long lead time, so it may not shift the 120,000-unit target quickly, and readership is shrinking.

--- MAIN STEM ---
Thornbury Mill Bakery (TMB) is a partnership in the commercial baking sector, employing a workforce of 50. Founded in 2013 by Amara Okafor, the business supplies bread and pastries to local cafes and schools and operates a hierarchical structure with democratic leadership. TMB plans to invest $540,000 in energy-efficient ovens and recyclable packaging, financed by a $300,000 bank loan and $240,000 retained profit. It has fixed costs of $180,000 a year, a variable cost of $4.20 a unit and a selling price of $9.20, and currently produces 72,000 units a year. TMB faces high ingredient waste and a rising rate of customer complaints about stale deliveries, which are damaging its reputation with schools.

--- APPENDIX 1 — MARKETING/OPS ---
Quality and Waste Report — Q4 2025: The bakery produced 18,000 units last month with a waste rate of 4.6%, down from 6.1% a year earlier. Customer complaints about freshness fell from 33 to 14 per week. Average delivery time is 2.8 days. A survey of 400 customers found that 66% would pay up to $0.30 more for recyclable packaging, and 51% check packaging before buying.     Question: Using Appendix 3, evaluate how the base interest rate rise to 4.5%, the 7.1% minimum wage increase and the 11.2% rise in flour and dairy input costs will affect TMB. Which change will have the greatest impact? Justify your answer.
    Answer: Base interest rate (3.75% to 4.5%): If TMB's $300,000 bank loan is variable-rate, the 0.75 percentage point rise adds 0.0075 × $300,000 = $2,250 a year. That is small beside $180,000 of fixed costs, and zero if the loan is fixed-rate. Higher rates may make future borrowing dearer, but the direct annual cost is modest and TMB can reduce it by fixing the rate.

Minimum wage (7.1%, to $13.49 from $12.60 per hour): With a workforce of 50 in baking and delivery, this feeds into wage bills and cannot be avoided. The insert gives no hours worked or individual pay rates, so an annual total cannot be honestly invented; the defensible test is productivity of 72,000 units ÷ 50 staff = 1,440 units per worker. If productivity holds, the rise is absorbable; if it slips, unit labour costs rise and the $5.00 contribution narrows.

Input cost inflation (11.2% flour and dairy): The insert does not decompose the $4.20 variable cost, so only a bound can be stated: if all of it rose 11.2%, that adds 11.2% × $4.20 = $0.47 per unit; across 72,000 units that is about $33,800 a year (72,000 × $0.47). The $0.30 recyclable-packaging premium recovers only part of this, while bakery spending grew just 1.9%.

Conclusion: The 11.2% input-cost rise has the greatest impact because it applies to every one of the 72,000 units and directly erodes the $5.00 contribution that supports the $540,000 investment. The interest effect is minor and fixable, and the wage rise can be offset if productivity holds, whereas input inflation hits unit economics with almost no pricing room.
    Keywords: 4.5%, 7.1%, 11.2%, 3.75%, $13.49, $300,000, $4.20, 1.9%

--- MAIN STEM ---
Eastmere Eco-Laminates (ELC) is a cooperative in the sustainable building materials sector, employing a workforce of 45. Founded in 2015 by Noor Eastmere, the business makes recycled-fibre insulation panels for house builders and operates a flat structure with laissez-faire leadership. ELC plans to invest $1,200,000 in a recycled-fibre panel plant using eco-packaging, financed by a $700,000 share issue and a $500,000 bank overdraft. It has fixed costs of $450,000 a year, a variable cost of $14.00 a unit and a selling price of $23.00, and currently produces 90,000 units a year. ELC faces a rising defect rate in panel bonding and complaints about delivery damage to panels arriving at busy building sites.

--- APPENDIX 1 — MARKETING/OPS ---
Operations and Quality Report — Q2 2025: The panel line produced 22,500 panels last quarter at a defect rate of 3.1%, down from 4.7% a year ago. Delivery-damage complaints fell from 28 to 11 per month. Average lead time is 6.2 days. A survey of 350 builders found that 71% would pay up to $1.50 more for recycled-fibre panels, and 57% check environmental claims before specifying materials. A skills audit shows 16 of 45 members have not been trained on the new bonding presses; college courses cost $1,250 per employee.

--- APPENDIX 2 — FINANCIAL DATA ---
Title: Extract from the Statement of Profit or Loss and Capital employed data of Eastmere Eco-Laminates for the year ended 31 March 2025 ($ '000)
Headers: ['Financial Metric', '2024', '2025']

Cost of sales | 5,250 | 6,030
Gross profit | 2,250 | 2,970
Operating profit | 1,125 | 1,620
Capital employed | 6,250 | 7,500
Interest payable | 150 | 180

--- APPENDIX 3 — EXTERNAL ENVIRONMENT ---
Economic and Business Bulletin (November 2026): (1) The central bank has raised the base interest rate from 4.0% to 4.75%, raising the cost of overdraft borrowing. (2) The national minimum wage will increase by 6.9% from $13.10 to $14.00 per hour from April 2026, lifting wage costs. (3) Recycled-fibre and resin input costs have risen 10.3% year-on-year, while construction output grew 2.4% over the same period.

    Question: Explain two advantages for ELC of funding the panel plant with a share issue rather than a bank overdraft.
    Answer: Point 1: A $700,000 share issue provides permanent capital with no interest or repayment schedule, protecting ELC's cash flow while it meets $450,000 of fixed costs a year. A $500,000 bank overdraft would charge interest at a rate linked to the 4.75% base rate and could be withdrawn on demand; share funds instead let the full $9.00 contribution on each panel stay in the cooperative to absorb the 10.3% rise in recycled-fibre and resin costs without increasing the $23.00 price to builders.

Point 2: Share capital does not require security over the cooperative's assets, so the $1,200,000 panel plant is safe from seizure if construction demand falls, which matters while the 3.1% bonding defect rate persists. An overdraft is a short-term source ill-suited to a long-lived plant and could leave ELC exposed if the bank cuts its facility. Equity from members also aligns ownership with the cooperative's sustainable aims, keeping control of the eco-packaging strategy inside the business rather than with an external lender.
