Input cost inflation (10.3% recycled fibre and resin): The insert does not decompose the $14.00 variable cost, so only a bound can be calculated: if all of it rose 10.3%, that adds 10.3% × $14.00 = $1.44 per unit; across 90,000 panels that is about $129,600 a year (90,000 × $1.44). The $1.50 environmental premium can recover only part of this, while construction output grew just 2.4%.

Conclusion: The 10.3% input-cost rise has the greatest impact because it applies to every one of the 90,000 panels and directly attacks the $9.00 contribution funding the $1,200,000 plant. The overdraft interest effect is smaller and can be refinanced, and the wage rise can be offset if productivity holds, whereas input inflation hits unit economics with limited pricing power.
    Keywords: 4.75%, 6.9%, 10.3%, 4.0%, $14.00, $500,000, 2.4%, $23.00
    Mark scheme: level_1_1_to_4: Identifies the three external changes with limited application to ELC. | level_2_5_to_8: Analyses the impact of at least two changes on ELC's costs, revenue or financing in context. | level_3_9_to_12: Detailed evaluation of all three changes in the context of ELC with a well-justified judgment that input-cost inflation has the greatest impact.

It has fixed costs of $360,000 a year, a variable cost of $8 a unit and a selling price of $16, and produces 120,000 units a year.     Answer: Advantage: Recyclable tubs match the 61% of 750 surveyed shoppers who would pay $0.30 more and the 48% who check the origin label, letting GFD charge a premium that protects the $8.00 contribution per unit even as feed and packaging costs rise 9.8%. The switch also strengthens the brand with national supermarkets and supports the $960,000 filling-line investment.

Disadvantage: Recyclable materials usually cost more than standard plastic, which would raise the $8.00 variable cost per unit unless the $0.30 premium is accepted on every tub. The insert gives no figure for the extra material cost, so the net effect cannot be quantified. Any sealing failure would also lift the current 2.2% defect rate and worsen the 6% spillage waste before the new line stabilises, squeezing returns on the launch.
    Keywords: recyclable tub, 61%, $0.30, 48%, 6%, $960,000
    Mark scheme: knowledge_max_2: 1 mark for a valid advantage and 1 mark for a valid disadvantage. | application_analysis_max_6: Up to 3 marks per point for detailed contextual development linked to GFD's research, costs and defect data.

  Q4(b) [12 marks]
    Question: Using Appendix 3, evaluate how the base interest rate rise to 5.25%, the 6.5% minimum wage increase and the 9.8% rise in feed and packaging input costs will affect GFD. Which change will have the greatest impact? Justify your answer.
    Answer: Interest rate rise (4.50% to 5.25%): If GFD's $600,000 ten-year loan is variable-rate, the extra 0.75 percentage point costs 0.75% × $600,000 = $4,500 a year (0.0075 × $600,000). That is modest beside fixed costs of $360,000, and a fixed-rate loan would avoid it entirely. Higher rates may also make future borrowing for the $960,000 expansion dearer and slightly dampen the 4.2% growth in branded yoghurt spending.

Minimum wage increase (6.5%, to $14.27 an hour): GFD's workforce of 60 includes hourly-paid production and packing staff, so payroll rises and cannot be avoided. The insert does not state hours worked or individual pay, so an annual total would be invented. The defensible test is productivity: 120,000 units ÷ 60 staff = 2,000 tubs per worker, so the higher wage is affordable only if that rate holds or improves; cutting 8% absenteeism and training the 15 untrained staff can help sustain it.

Input cost inflation (9.8%): Feed and packaging feed the $8.00 variable cost on every tub. The insert does not decompose that cost, so only a bound is honest: if the entire $8.00 were exposed, 9.8% × $8.00 = $0.784, about $0.78 a tub, and at 120,000 units that is roughly $94,080 a year (120,000 × $0.784). A smaller exposed share would still erode the $8.00 contribution each time GFD sells a tub, and the effect repeats with every unit.

Conclusion: The 9.8% input-cost rise will have the greatest impact. It recurs across 120,000 tubs and directly attacks the contribution that funds the $600,000 loan and $960,000 line, whereas the interest rise costs $4,500 a year and the wage effect can be offset by sustaining 2,000 tubs per worker. GFD should cut the 6% waste and seek the $0.30 recyclable-tub premium rather than absorb the whole increase.
    Keywords: 5.25%, 6.5%, 9.8%, $14.27, $600,000, $8
    Mark scheme: level_1_1_to_4: Identifies the external changes with limited application to GFD. | level_2_5_to_8: Analyses the impact of at least two external changes on GFD's costs, revenue or financing in context. | level_3_9_to_12: Detailed evaluation of all three changes in context with a well-justified judgment that input-cost inflation has the greatest impact and why the others are smaller.

--- MAIN STEM ---
Harbourview Seafoods (HVS) is a public limited company in the seafood-processing industry, based on the Atlantic coast and employing a workforce of 50. Founded in 2008 by Derek Osei, it supplies frozen fillets to supermarket chains and operates a hierarchical structure with autocratic leadership. HVS plans to invest $720,000 in a new cold-storage and filleting facility, financed by a $260,000 bank overdraft and $460,000 from a share issue. It has fixed costs of $240,000 a year, a variable cost of $14 a unit and a selling price of $26, and produces 84,000 units a year. HVS faces fish-spoilage losses of 7% of catch and labour turnover of 11% among its processing staff.

--- APPENDIX 1 — MARKETING/OPS ---
Operations and Quality Log — Q3 2025: The filleting line processed 19,800 cartons last quarter at a defect rate of 2.6%, down from 4.0% a year earlier. Customer complaints fell from 39 to 22 a month. Average delivery time to retailers was 3.1 days. A survey of 540 customers found 57% would pay $0.45 more for sustainably sourced fillets, and 51% check the origin label. Spoilage was 7% of catch. A skills audit shows 11 of 50 staff have not completed on-the-job training on the new filleting machines; off-the-job training at the technical college costs $680 per employee.

--- APPENDIX 2 — FINANCIAL DATA ---

Capital employed | 1,560 | 1,960

(3) Diesel and ice input costs have risen 10.5% year-on-year, while consumer spending on frozen seafood grew 3.3%.

  Q1(a) [8 marks]
    Question: HVS is funding its $720,000 cold-storage and filleting facility with a $260,000 bank overdraft and a $460,000 share issue. Explain two advantages for HVS of the share issue compared with the overdraft.
    Answer: Point 1: A share issue brings in $460,000 that does not have to be repaid and carries no interest charge, unlike the $260,000 bank overdraft whose cost rises whenever the base rate moves. For a company with fixed costs of $240,000 a year and seasonal fish supplies, this protects liquidity while the facility is built, leaving more of the $26 selling price to cover the $14 variable cost.

Point 2: Equity does not carry the daily repayment pressure of an overdraft, so Derek Osei's new filleting facility cannot be threatened by a bank recall if catches fall below the 19,800 cartons processed last quarter. The share issue also spreads funding among investors instead of concentrating it on a 5.00% to 5.75% rate exposure; although existing shareholders dilute their control, the 57% of 540 surveyed customers willing to pay $0.45 more supports demand for the $720,000 expansion.
    Keywords: share issue, bank overdraft, $460,000, $260,000, filleting, $720,000

Television is rejected as unaffordable and untargeted for a $720,000 facility funded partly by overdraft; newspapers alone are rejected as too passive to showcase a premium frozen product.

    Question: Using Appendix 2, evaluate HVS's financial position by calculating the current ratio and the acid test ratio for 2024 and 2025. Has HVS's liquidity improved? Justify your answer.
    Answer: Calculations:

Current Ratio 2025 = 1.75 : 1
Acid Test Ratio 2024 = 0.94 : 1
Acid Test Ratio 2025 = 1.21 : 1

Detailed workings: 2024 current assets = $90,000 inventories + $75,000 trade receivables + $38,000 cash = $203,000; 2025 current assets = $70,000 + $95,000 + $62,000 = $227,000. For 2025, $227,000 ÷ $130,000 = 1.75 and ($227,000 − $70,000) ÷ $130,000 = $157,000 ÷ $130,000 = 1.21.

Evaluation: Liquidity has improved on both measures. The first ratio rose from 1.69 to 1.75 even though current liabilities increased from $120,000 to $130,000, because current assets grew faster, helped by cash rising from $38,000 to $62,000. The second measure climbed from 0.94 to 1.21 and is the more useful signal for a seasonal processor: it shows HVS could meet bills without relying on selling $70,000 of frozen stock, valuable while a $260,000 overdraft and a $720,000 facility are outstanding. The reservation is trade receivables, up from $75,000 to $95,000, which lock away cash if supermarket customers pay late, especially with 11% labour turnover adding costs.

Conclusion: HVS's liquidity has improved. Both ratios rose and the gain is not driven by inventory, so short-term solvency is stronger. Rising receivables remain the main risk, so credit control should be tightened as the new facility starts up.

    Question: Using Appendix 3, evaluate how the base interest rate rise to 5.75%, the 5.8% minimum wage increase and the 10.5% rise in diesel and ice input costs will affect HVS. Which change will have the greatest impact? Justify your answer.
    Answer: Interest rate rise (5.00% to 5.75%): An overdraft is variable-rate, so if the $260,000 overdraft is fully drawn the extra 0.75 percentage point costs 0.75% × $260,000 = $1,950 a year (0.0075 × $260,000). The caution is trade receivables, up from $160,000 to $195,000, which tie up cash if cafe customers pay late, and inventories have fallen to $180,000, so stock cover for the new juice launch should be monitored.

Conclusion: OBV's liquidity has improved. Both ratios rose and the improvement is not dependent on stock, so short-term solvency is stronger. Rising receivables are the main residual risk, so OBV should tighten credit control as the cold-press line ramps up.

    Question: Using Appendix 3, evaluate how the base interest rate rise to 5.00%, the 7.0% minimum wage increase and the 11.5% rise in fruit and glass-bottle input costs will affect OBV. Which change will have the greatest impact? Justify your answer.
    Answer: Interest rate rise (4.25% to 5.00%): Higher rates make borrowing and venture-capital-backed expansion more expensive for OBV. Even a smaller exposed share reduces the $8.00 contribution on every litre and recurs with each unit sold.

Conclusion: The 11.5% input-cost rise will have the greatest impact. It repeats across 150,000 litres and directly erodes the contribution that funds the $1,150,000 bottling line, whereas the interest effect on existing operations is limited and the wage rise can be offset by sustaining 1,363.6 litres per worker. OBV should cut the 5% waste and use the $0.35 premium accepted by 66% of shoppers rather than absorb the whole increase.

--- MAIN STEM ---
Millbrook Grain Cooperative (MBG) is a cooperative in the grain-milling industry, based on the Canadian prairies and employing a workforce of 72 worker-members. Founded in 1998 by Amina Yusuf, it sells flour to regional bakeries and operates a hierarchical structure with democratic leadership. MBG plans to invest $840,000 in a new flour mill and grain-silo upgrade, financed by a $500,000 member share issue and $340,000 retained profit. It has fixed costs of $300,000 a year, a variable cost of $9 a unit and a selling price of $21, and produces 100,000 units a year. MBG faces grain losses in storage of 6% of intake and absenteeism of 9% among its mill workers.

--- APPENDIX 1 — MARKETING/OPS ---
Quality and Storage Log — Q4 2025: The mill processed 24,600 sacks of flour last quarter at a defect rate of 2.1%, down from 3.8% a year earlier. Customer complaints fell from 34 to 18 a month. Average delivery to bakeries was 3.4 days. A survey of 640 bakery buyers found 63% would pay $0.25 more for locally milled flour, and 54% check the origin label. Grain loss in storage was 6% of intake. A skills audit shows 14 of 72 worker-members have not completed on-the-job training on the new mill; off-the-job training at the agricultural college costs $640 per member.

--- APPENDIX 2 — FINANCIAL DATA ---

(2) The national minimum wage will rise by 6.2% from $13.80 to $14.66 an hour, lifting mill-floor payroll costs. (3) Fertiliser and transport input costs have risen 9.4% year-on-year, while consumer spending on artisan bread grew 3.8%.

    Answer: Point 1: A member share issue raises $500,000 without draining the cooperative's cash reserve, so MBG keeps $340,000 retained profit to absorb the 9.4% rise in fertiliser and transport costs. For a business with fixed costs of $300,000 a year, that liquidity protects the 3.4-day delivery service to regional bakeries while the new mill is built.

Point 2: Raising funds from members spreads the $840,000 cost across the cooperative rather than waiting for profits to accumulate, so Amina Yusuf can upgrade the mill and silos at once. Members who buy shares also have a stake in the business, which fits democratic ownership and can support the 63% of 640 bakery buyers willing to pay $0.25 more for locally milled flour, whereas relying only on retained profit could delay the project.

--- MAIN STEM ---
Tropicfruit Exports (TFE) is a partnership in the fresh-fruit export sector, based near Accra and employing a workforce of 48. It has fixed costs of $180,000 a year, a variable cost of $11 a unit and a selling price of $23, and produces 60,000 units a year. TFE faces post-harvest spoilage of 8% of the crop and labour turnover of 12% among its packhouse staff.

--- APPENDIX 1 — MARKETING/OPS ---

Post-harvest loss was 8% of the crop. A skills audit shows 10 of 48 staff have not completed on-the-job training on the new graders; off-the-job training at the agricultural institute costs $700 per employee.

    Answer: Calculations:
Current Ratio 2024 = 1.64 : 1
Current Ratio 2025 = 1.74 : 1
Acid Test Ratio 2024 = 0.92 : 1
Acid Test Ratio 2025 = 1.22 : 1

Detailed workings: 2024 current assets = $75,000 inventories + $65,000 trade receivables + $32,000 cash = $172,000; 2025 current assets = $58,000 + $82,000 + $55,000 = $195,000. For 2024, $172,000 ÷ $105,000 = 1.64 and ($172,000 − $75,000) ÷ $105,000 = $97,000 ÷ $105,000 = 0.92. For 2025, $195,000 ÷ $112,000 = 1.74 and ($195,000 − $58,000) ÷ $112,000 = $137,000 ÷ $112,000 = 1.22.

Evaluation: Liquidity has improved. The first ratio rose from 1.64 to 1.74 because current assets grew from $172,000 to $195,000 faster than current liabilities, which increased from $105,000 to $112,000. The second measure climbed from 0.92 to 1.22, so TFE can now meet short-term obligations without relying on selling $58,000 of perishable mango stock, valuable while a $360,000 loan and a $560,000 packhouse are outstanding. The caution is trade receivables, up from $65,000 to $82,000, which lock away cash if European importers pay late, and 12% labour turnover could disrupt the 2.6-day dispatch promise.

Conclusion: TFE's liquidity has improved. Both ratios rose and the improvement does not depend on inventory, so short-term solvency is stronger. Rising receivables are the main risk, so the partners should tighten credit control as the cold chain starts up.

  Q4(a) [8 marks]
    Question: TFE is considering a certified premium grade for its mangoes. Explain one advantage and one disadvantage for TFE of this decision.
    Answer: Advantage: A certified premium grade matches the 62% of 480 importers who would pay $0.40 more and the 49% who check phytosanitary certification, protecting the $12.00 contribution per carton against 10.2% packaging and freight inflation.   Q4(b) [12 marks]
    Question: Using Appendix 3, evaluate how the base interest rate rise to 5.25%, the 6.9% minimum wage increase and the 10.2% rise in packaging and refrigerated-freight input costs will affect TFE. Which change will have the greatest impact? Justify your answer.
    Answer: Interest rate rise (4.50% to 5.25%): If TFE's $360,000 bank loan is variable-rate, the extra 0.75 percentage point costs 0.75% × $360,000 = $2,700 a year (0.0075 × $360,000). That is modest beside fixed costs of $180,000, and a fixed-rate loan would avoid it entirely. Higher rates may also make the 4.7% growth in export demand harder to finance and raise the cost of any future borrowing for the $560,000 project.

Minimum wage increase (6.9%, to $14.22 an hour): TFE's workforce of 48 includes hourly-paid packhouse staff, so payroll rises and cannot be avoided. The insert gives no hours worked or individual pay, so an annual wage total would be invented. The defensible check is productivity: 60,000 units ÷ 48 staff = 1,250 cartons per worker, so the higher wage is affordable only if that rate holds; cutting 12% labour turnover and training the 10 untrained staff can help sustain it.

Input cost inflation (10.2%): Packaging and refrigerated freight feed the $11.00 variable cost on every carton. The insert does not decompose that cost, so only a bound is honest: if the full $11.00 were exposed, 10.2% × $11.00 = $1.122, about $1.12 a carton, and at 60,000 units that is roughly $67,320 a year (60,000 × $1.122). Even a smaller exposed share reduces the $12.00 contribution on every carton and recurs with each export order.

Conclusion: The 10.2% input-cost rise will have the greatest impact. It repeats across 60,000 cartons and directly attacks the $12.00 contribution that services the $360,000 loan and the $560,000 packhouse, whereas the interest rise costs $2,700 a year and the wage effect can be offset by sustaining 1,250 cartons per worker. TFE should cut the 8% post-harvest loss and seek the $0.40 premium from 62% of importers rather than absorb the whole rise.

--- MAIN STEM ---
Marson Industrial Precision (MIP) is a private limited company in the precision engineering sector, employing a workforce of 60. Founded in 2011 by Elias Marson, it machines steel shafts and gear housings for industrial equipment and operates a hierarchical structure with democratic leadership. MIP plans to invest $720,000 in a new CNC machining cell, financed by a $450,000 ten-year bank loan and $270,000 retained profit. It has fixed costs of $300,000 a year, a variable cost of $14 a unit and a selling price of $22, and currently produces 50,000 units a year. MIP faces two operational problems: a defect rate of 4.2% on machined shafts and rising metal-waste levels in the workshop.

--- APPENDIX 1 — MARKETING/OPS ---
Operations and Quality Report — Q3 2025: The machining cell produced 12,500 precision shafts last quarter at a defect rate of 4.2%, down from 6.1% a year earlier. Customer complaints fell from 44 to 26 a month and average delivery lead time is 5.5 days. A survey of 400 industrial buyers found that 58% would pay up to $0.60 more for certified precision shafts, while 47% check supplier quality accreditation before placing orders. A training needs analysis shows 18 of the 60 operators have not completed on-the-job training in CAM on the new CNC cell; an off-the-job training course in CNC programming at the local college costs $1,100 per employee.

--- APPENDIX 2 — FINANCIAL DATA ---
Title: Extract from the Statement of Financial Position of Marson Industrial Precision as at 31 March 2025 ($ '000)
Headers: ['Financial Metric', '2024', '2025']

Trade receivables | 110 | 130
Cash and cash equivalents | 50 | 70
Current liabilities | 200 | 200
Non-current assets | 1,200 | 1,500
Capital employed | 1,250 | 1,600

--- APPENDIX 3 — EXTERNAL ENVIRONMENT ---
Economic and Business Bulletin (November 2026): (1) The central bank has raised the base interest rate from 4.50% to 5.25%, increasing borrowing costs for firms with variable-rate loans. (2) The national minimum wage will rise by 5.8% from $13.00 to $13.75 an hour from April 2026, lifting total wage bills. (3) Steel and alloy input costs have risen 8.5% year-on-year, producer price inflation is 6.2%, and demand for industrial equipment components grew 2.8% over the same period.

--- QUESTIONS ---
  Q1(a) [8 marks]
    Question: MIP plans to fund part of its $720,000 CNC machining cell with a $450,000 bank loan. Explain two advantages for MIP of using retained profit instead of the bank loan.
    Answer: Point 1: Retained profit costs MIP no interest payments or capital repayments, which protects cash flow at a time when the business already carries fixed costs of $300,000 a year and a $450,000 bank loan commitment. Using the $270,000 of retained profit means every dollar of the $8 contribution per shaft stays in the business to absorb the 8.5% steel and alloy input-cost inflation reported in Appendix 3, rather than being paid to a lender, so the new cell can reach its 50,000-unit target without extra finance charges.

Point 2: Retained profit carries no collateral or repossession risk, so the $720,000 CNC cell cannot be seized if industrial buyers delay orders and the defect rate stays at 4.2%. It also keeps control in Elias Marson's hands: no bank can impose conditions on how the hierarchical firm is run, which matters because democratic leadership depends on management being able to keep promises to the 60 staff while the workshop absorbs the new technology.
    Keywords: retained profit, bank loan, $270,000, $450,000, $720,000, $300,000
    Mark scheme: knowledge_max_2: 1 mark for each valid advantage identified (max 2). | application_analysis_max_6: Up to 3 marks per point for contextual explanation and analysis applied to MIP's expansion, costs and financing.

  Q1(b) [12 marks]
    Question: MIP is launching certified precision shafts to industrial buyers. Consider a trade-exhibition stand, print advertising in engineering magazines, or e-commerce listings on an industrial marketplace. Which should MIP choose to reach these buyers? Justify your recommendation.
    Answer: Trade-exhibition stand: A trade exhibition puts MIP's certified shafts directly in front of engineers from industrial equipment manufacturers and allows live demonstration of machining tolerances, which is valuable when 47% of surveyed buyers check quality accreditation. However, stand space, travel and sample costs are high for a 60-employee firm already funding a $720,000 expansion through a $450,000 loan, and attendance is limited to a few events a year, so the reach cannot be sustained.

Print advertising in engineering magazines: Print ads build credibility with a specialist readership and stay visible for months, suiting technical components with a 5.5-day lead time. The drawback is that circulation is narrow and ageing, response is hard to measure, and an advert cannot show the 4.2% defect reduction as vividly as a demonstration; spend may be wasted on readers who do not buy shafts.

E-commerce listings on an industrial marketplace: A marketplace listing reaches industrial buyers nationally and internationally at low fixed cost, displays certification to the 58% who would pay $0.60 more, and generates measurable enquiries and repeat orders. It suits standard machined shafts produced at 12,500 a quarter and can be scaled up as the CNC cell beds in. Its weakness is price comparison with rivals and the need for good product photographs and descriptions.

Recommendation: MIP should choose e-commerce listings on an industrial marketplace as the primary channel. They reach the exact industrial buyers in the survey at the lowest cost, avoid the heavy fixed spend of exhibitions and the poor measurability of print, and can highlight certification to the 58% willing to pay a premium. Exhibitions are rejected as too expensive and infrequent, and print is rejected as narrow and unmeasurable; MIP can add a small exhibition presence later once online enquiries justify it.
    Keywords: $720,000, 58%, 47%, industrial buyers, certified, 5.5 days

  Q2(a) [8 marks]
    Question: MIP's defect rate is 4.2% and metal waste is rising. Explain two benefits for MIP of using democratic leadership to improve motivation among its production team.
    Answer: Point 1: Democratic leadership gives the 60 operators a real voice in how the new CNC machining cell is organised, so they feel valued and are more likely to take care over each shaft. Consulting the people who actually set up the machines can surface practical fixes for the 4.2% defect rate and the metal-waste problem faster than instructions from a distant manager, and it fits the flat decision-making that a hierarchical structure with democratic leadership is meant to encourage.

Point 2: Involvement builds commitment and reduces resistance to the $720,000 expansion, which is important when 18 operators still lack on-the-job training. Staff who help design quality checks and shift routines are more likely to attend and to apply the $1,100 off-the-job programming course, so output of 12,500 shafts a quarter is protected, scrap falls, and the $450,000 loan can be serviced without costly rework.   Q2(b) [12 marks]
    Question: MIP must upskill 18 operators to run the new CNC cell. Consider on-the-job training on the cell or off-the-job training at the local college at $1,100 per employee. Which should MIP choose? Justify your decision.
    Answer: On-the-job training: Training at the CNC cell uses MIP's own machines, fixtures and quality standards, so the 18 operators learn exactly the routines that caused the 4.2% defect rate and the metal waste. Decision: MIP should choose on-the-job training first, with short college modules for the most senior operators. It is cheaper, machine-specific and avoids losing output while absenteeism and scrap are already problems; full off-the-job training is rejected because $19,800 of fees and 18 people away from the cell would disrupt the delivery schedule just as the $450,000 loan begins to be repaid. Accredited college modules can be added later once the cell is stable. With 18 staff needing the skill and 60 employees in total, that staged approach spreads cost while keeping the 4.2% defect rate under review and the 12,500-unit quarter intact before further investment.

    Question: Using Appendix 3, evaluate how the interest rate rise to 5.25%, the 5.8% minimum wage increase and the 8.5% rise in steel and alloy input costs will affect MIP. Which change will have the greatest impact? Justify your answer.
    Answer: Interest rate rise (4.50% to 5.25%): If the $450,000 ten-year bank loan is variable-rate, the rise is 5.25% − 4.50% = 0.75 percentage points, so extra annual interest = 0.75% × $450,000 = 0.0075 × $450,000 = $3,375 a year. That is small against fixed costs of $300,000, and if the loan is fixed-rate the direct cost is zero. Higher rates could still make future borrowing dearer, but the effect on MIP is modest and can be capped by fixing the rate.

Minimum wage increase (5.8%, $13.00 to $13.75 an hour): The insert gives a workforce of 60 and output of 50,000 units, but it states neither hours worked nor individual pay, so no annual wage total can be calculated honestly. What can be derived is labour productivity = 50,000 units ÷ 60 staff = 833.3 units per worker. A wage rise is affordable only if that productivity is maintained or improved; otherwise unit labour cost climbs and the $8 contribution per shaft narrows. The impact is real but depends on factors the insert does not give.

Input-cost inflation (8.5% on steel and alloy): The insert does not decompose the $14 variable cost, so only a clearly labelled upper bound can be shown: if the whole $14 rose by 8.5%, the increase = 8.5% × $14 = 0.085 × $14 = $1.19 a unit; at 50,000 units a year that is 50,000 × $1.19 = $59,500 a year. Even a smaller pass-through would erode contribution on every shaft, and the figure is compounded by the 6.2% producer price inflation.

Conclusion: The 8.5% rise in steel and alloy input costs will have the greatest impact. It applies to every one of the 50,000 units and directly attacks the $8 contribution that justifies the $720,000 CNC cell, with a computable upper bound of $59,500 a year. By contrast the interest rise adds a known $3,375 a year at most, and the wage effect cannot be quantified from the insert and can be offset by productivity. Input inflation is therefore the change management must address first, through supplier renegotiation and the $0.60 certified-shaft premium.

--- MAIN STEM ---
Quentin Metal Fasteners (QMF) is a private limited company in the industrial fasteners sector, employing a workforce of 48. Founded in 2003 by Sofia Quentin, it produces high-strength threaded bolts and nuts for construction equipment and railway suppliers and operates a hierarchical structure with autocratic leadership, exporting to nearby markets. QMF plans to invest $640,000 in an automated bolt-threading line, financed by a $400,000 bank loan and $240,000 retained profit, with an overdraft facility for working capital. It has fixed costs of $270,000 a year, a variable cost of $10 a unit and a selling price of $19, and currently produces 60,000 units a year. QMF faces two problems: labour turnover of 14% and a defect rate of 3.6% on threaded bolts.

--- APPENDIX 1 — MARKETING/OPS ---
Quality and Operations Log — Q3 2025: The line threaded 15,000 high-strength bolts last quarter at a defect rate of 3.6%, down from 5.2% a year earlier. Customer complaints fell from 34 to 19 a month and average delivery time is 4.1 days. A survey of 350 industrial distributors found 62% value certified thread tolerance and 55% prefer a local supplier. A new quality control inspection regime is being introduced on the line; labour turnover reached 14%, and an external quality-audit training course costs $750 per employee.

--- APPENDIX 2 — FINANCIAL DATA ---
Title: Extract from the Statement of Financial Position of Quentin Metal Fasteners as at 31 March 2025 ($ '000)
Headers: ['Financial Metric', '2024', '2025']

Trade receivables | 95 | 110

Economic and Business Bulletin (November 2026): (1) The central bank has raised the base interest rate from 4.25% to 5.00%, increasing borrowing costs on variable-rate business loans. (2) The national minimum wage will rise by 6.2% from $12.90 to $13.70 an hour from April 2026, lifting total wage bills. (3) Steel wire rod input costs have risen 9.4% year-on-year, producer price inflation is 5.5%, and demand from industrial distributors grew 3.1% over the same period.

--- QUESTIONS ---
  Q1(a) [8 marks]
    Question: QMF plans to fund its $640,000 bolt-threading line with a $400,000 bank loan. Explain two advantages for QMF of using the bank loan instead of its overdraft facility.
    Answer: Point 1: A bank loan gives QMF a fixed repayment schedule spread over the life of the $640,000 threading line, so the cost of the asset is matched by steady outflows that can be planned alongside fixed costs of $270,000 a year. An overdraft is repayable on demand and is meant for short-term working capital; using it for a long-lived asset would leave Sofia Quentin unsure when the money might be called back, just as the line needs to produce 60,000 units.

Point 2: Bank loan interest is normally lower than overdraft interest, so choosing the $400,000 loan keeps finance charges down and protects the $9 contribution on each bolt. That matters when labour turnover is 14% and the defect rate is 3.6%, both of which already cost money. The $240,000 of retained profit also lowers the amount borrowed, so the firm keeps headroom on its overdraft for the 4.1-day delivery gap instead of exhausting it on capital equipment.
    Keywords: bank loan, overdraft, $640,000, $400,000, $240,000, retained profit
    Mark scheme: knowledge_max_2: 1 mark for each valid advantage identified (max 2). | application_analysis_max_6: Up to 3 marks per point for contextual explanation applied to QMF's investment, costs and working-capital position.

  Q1(b) [12 marks]
    Question: QMF is expanding sales of certified bolts. Consider a direct sales force, regional industrial distributors, or an online industrial marketplace. Which should QMF choose to reach industrial distributors? Justify your recommendation.

This suits a technical product and the 62% of surveyed distributors who value certification. However, salaries, travel and commissions are a heavy fixed cost for a 48-employee firm funding a $640,000 line with a $400,000 loan, and covering the whole region would take years.

  Q2(a) [8 marks]
    Question: QMF has a defect rate of 3.6% and labour turnover of 14%. Explain two benefits for QMF of using inspection-based quality control on its threading line.
    Answer: Point 1: Inspection catches faulty threads before bolts leave the line, so QMF can protect the improvement from 5.2% to 3.6% defects and avoid sending bad batches to the 350 industrial distributors surveyed.   Q2(b) [12 marks]
    Question: QMF needs a manager to run quality on the new threading line. Consider promoting an existing worker or recruiting a qualified specialist from outside. Which should QMF choose? Justify your decision.
    Answer: Promoting an existing worker: An internal candidate already knows QMF's machines, the 3.6% defect problem and the expectations of the 350 distributors, so induction is short and morale may rise because staff see a career path — useful when turnover is 14%. Promotion is also cheap, avoiding recruitment fees. The risk is that the worker lacks formal audit skills, and the $750 quality-audit course may not be enough to manage certification claims or to challenge long-standing habits under autocratic leadership.

Recruiting a qualified specialist from outside: An external quality manager brings current audit methods and an unbiased eye, which suits the 62% of distributors who value certified thread tolerance and supports the $640,000 investment. Drawbacks are higher salary, a longer settling-in period, and possible resentment among the 48 staff, especially when a promotion route would have helped retention.

Decision: QMF should promote an existing worker and send that person on the $750 external quality-audit course, with a short mentoring spell from a consultant. This keeps cost low, rewards loyalty at a time when turnover is 14%, and preserves knowledge of the line that cut defects from 5.2% to 3.6%. External recruitment is rejected because the added salary and disruption are hard to justify on a $400,000-loan-funded expansion when training can close the specific skills gap; the specialist can be hired later if certification demands grow. That keeps the $750 course budget focused on the 14% turnover problem and avoids a second salary while the $640,000 line is still settling in.
    Keywords: $750, 14%, 62%, 15,000, 3.6%, $640,000
    Mark scheme: level_1_1_to_4: Basic description of the two recruitment choices with limited application to QMF. | level_2_5_to_8: Detailed analysis of benefits and drawbacks of both choices in the context of QMF. | level_3_9_to_12: Comprehensive evaluation of both choices in the context of QMF with a justified decision covering cost, skills and staff retention.

  Q3(a) [8 marks]

  Q3(b) [12 marks]
    Question: Using Appendix 2, evaluate QMF's financial position by calculating the current ratio and the acid test ratio for 2024 and 2025. Has QMF's financial position improved? Justify your answer.
    Answer: Calculations:

Current Ratio 2025 = 1.50 : 1
Acid Test Ratio 2024 = 0.78 : 1
Acid Test Ratio 2025 = 1.00 : 1

Detailed workings: 2024 current assets = $75,000 inventories + $95,000 trade receivables + $30,000 cash = $200,000; 2025 current assets = $80,000 + $110,000 + $50,000 = $240,000. Excluding inventories: ($200,000 − $75,000) ÷ $160,000 = $125,000 ÷ $160,000 = 0.78 in 2024, and ($240,000 − $80,000) ÷ $160,000 = $160,000 ÷ $160,000 = 1.00 in 2025.

Cash also rose from $30,000 to $50,000, strengthening the immediate buffer for the overdraft. There is a caveat: trade receivables rose from $95,000 to $110,000, so cash is tied up with distributors, and the overdraft facility could be drawn if those distributors pay late. Inventories also edged up to $80,000, so slow-moving stock should be monitored.

Conclusion: QMF's financial position has improved. Both measures are higher, and the rise does not depend on stock, which is the more demanding test. The residual risk is slower collections from distributors, so credit control should be tightened before the next expansion.

    Question: Explain one advantage and one disadvantage for QMF of switching to recycled steel and eco-packaging for its bolts.

It strengthens the certified fastener brand and supports the 15,000 bolts a quarter produced on the new $640,000 line without cutting the $19 selling price.

Disadvantage: Recycled steel may vary in quality and raise the 3.6% defect rate if inclusions cause thread failures, while eco-packaging usually costs more than standard cartons, pushing up the $10 variable cost per unit.   Q4(b) [12 marks]
    Question: Using Appendix 3, evaluate how the interest rate rise to 5.00%, the 6.2% minimum wage increase and the 9.4% rise in steel input costs will affect QMF. Which change will have the greatest impact? Justify your answer.
    Answer: Interest rate rise (4.25% to 5.00%): The increase is 5.00% − 4.25% = 0.75 percentage points. If the $400,000 bank loan is variable-rate, the extra annual interest = 0.75% × $400,000 = 0.0075 × $400,000 = $3,000 a year. That is modest beside fixed costs of $270,000, and if the loan is fixed-rate there is no direct extra charge. Higher rates could make the overdraft more expensive, but a shown figure for that is not possible because the insert gives no overdraft balance or rate.

Minimum wage increase (6.2%, $12.90 to $13.70 an hour): QMF employs a workforce of 48 and produces 60,000 units, so labour productivity = 60,000 ÷ 48 = 1,250 units per worker. The insert gives neither hours worked nor individual pay, so an honest annual wage cost cannot be invented. The wage rise is compulsory and will lift unit labour cost unless the 3.6% defect rate is reduced and output per worker holds at 1,250; otherwise the $9 contribution per bolt is squeezed.

Steel input-cost inflation (9.4%): The insert does not split the $10 variable cost, so only a clearly labelled upper bound can be calculated: if the entire $10 rose by 9.4%, the increase = 9.4% × $10 = 0.094 × $10 = $0.94 a bolt; at 60,000 units that is 60,000 × $0.94 = $56,400 a year. Even a partial pass-through would cut contribution on every bolt, and the $19 price may be hard to raise when 55% of distributors prefer local suppliers.

Conclusion: The 9.4% rise in steel input costs will have the greatest impact. It is the only change with a computable annual exposure on every unit of $56,400 at the upper bound, directly eroding the $9 contribution that supports the $640,000 investment. The interest rise adds at most $3,000, and the wage effect cannot be quantified from the insert and can be offset by productivity gains. Management should therefore renegotiate steel supply and seek a certified-quality premium before considering price rises.

    Mark scheme: level_1_1_to_4: Identifies the external changes with limited application to QMF. | level_2_5_to_8: Analyses the impact of at least two changes on QMF's costs, revenue or financing with figures derived from the insert. | level_3_9_to_12: Detailed evaluation of all three changes in context with shown derivations and a well-justified judgement that input-cost inflation has the greatest impact.

--- MAIN STEM ---
Zephyr Precision Foundry (ZPF) is a private limited company in the aluminium casting sector, employing a workforce of 72. Founded in 2007 by Priya Zend, it die-casts aluminium housings for industrial machinery from its riverside plant and operates a flat organisational structure with laissez-faire leadership. ZPF plans to invest $900,000 in a robotic die-casting cell, financed by a $600,000 bank loan and a $300,000 share issue. It has fixed costs of $360,000 a year, a variable cost of $16 a unit and a selling price of $28, and currently produces 45,000 units a year. ZPF faces two operational problems: a scrap rate of 5.4% and high energy waste in the melting furnace.

--- APPENDIX 1 — MARKETING/OPS ---
Operations and Waste Report — Q3 2025: The foundry cast 11,250 housings last quarter at a scrap rate of 5.4%, down from 7.1% a year earlier. Energy cost $48,000 a quarter and customer complaints fell from 41 to 24 a month. Delivery lead time is 6.3 days. A survey of 500 manufacturers found 66% would pay $0.75 more for low-carbon castings and 54% check environmental certification. Some 22 of the 72 operatives lack robotics training; a certification course costs $1,250 per operative.

--- APPENDIX 2 — FINANCIAL DATA ---

Capital employed | 1,700 | 2,170

(2) The national minimum wage will rise by 5.5% from $13.40 to $14.14 an hour from April 2026, increasing total wage bills. (3) Aluminium input costs have risen 7.8% year-on-year, energy price inflation is 9.1%, and industrial output grew 2.4% over the same period.

    Question: ZPF plans to raise $300,000 through a share issue for its $900,000 robotic cell. Explain two advantages for ZPF of the share issue instead of a larger bank loan.

With fixed costs of $360,000 a year and a scrap rate of 5.4%, ZPF can put every dollar of the $12 contribution per casting into covering costs and the 9.1% energy inflation rather than servicing more debt, improving the $900,000 project's chance of reaching its 45,000-unit target.

Point 2: New equity strengthens the balance sheet and leaves more of the borrowing capacity unused for the $600,000 loan already taken, which helps liquidity ratios and gives Priya Zend room to seek further finance if the robotic cell needs modifications. The 72-strong workforce and the 22 operatives needing robotics training can therefore be supported without raising loan interest; the cost is dilution of ownership and possible dividend pressure, but no fixed repayment is created. The $300,000 also spreads the risk of the $900,000 project among investors instead of leaving the downside with Priya Zend.
    Keywords: share issue, bank loan, $300,000, $600,000, $900,000, workforce of 72

    Answer: Sponsoring an engineering podcast: A podcast sponsorship reaches a loyal, technically qualified audience and can explain the low-carbon story in the sponsor's own words. It is relatively cheap against the $900,000 investment and suits a 72-employee foundry. However, reach is narrow and slow to build, there is no immediate enquiry data, and listeners may not be among the 500 manufacturers surveyed, so the message may miss buyers needing 6.3-day delivery.

Leads are immediate and relationships can start there. Costs for stands and staff time are high, and results depend on which buyers attend, but the audience is far better matched than a general podcast or influencer campaign.

Recommendation: ZPF should choose an industrial trade fair stand as its main promotion. It delivers the face-to-face technical credibility that certification-focused buyers need and generates leads for a $900,000 robotic cell, which podcast reach and influencer clicks cannot match. Podcasts are rejected as too narrow and slow, and influencers are rejected as lacking the authority for audited low-carbon claims; a short podcast series can be used later to reinforce the message.

Decision: ZPF should choose job enrichment supported by short rotation between casting and inspection. Enrichment gives the authority to reject faulty castings that a 5.4% scrap problem needs, and it fits the flat, delegated culture better than routine rotation. Rotation alone is rejected because it spreads staff thinly without ownership and can increase changeover errors; the $1,250 course should still be completed before operators take on settings responsibility. --- MAIN STEM ---
Kestrel Motor Components (KMC) is a public limited company in the automotive components sector, employing a workforce of 95. Founded in 1998 by Nadia Kestrel, it grinds precision gears for vehicle assemblers from two plants and operates a hierarchical structure with democratic leadership. KMC plans to invest $1,200,000 in an automated gear-grinding line, financed by a $700,000 bank loan and a five-year lease on the grinding machines. It has fixed costs of $420,000 a year, a variable cost of $21 a unit and a selling price of $35, and currently produces 70,000 units a year. KMC faces two problems: a defect rate of 2.8% on gears and labour turnover of 11%.

--- APPENDIX 1 — MARKETING/OPS ---
Quality Report — Q3 2025: The plants ground 17,500 gears last quarter at a defect rate of 2.8%, down from 3.9% a year earlier. Warranty claims fell from 52 to 31 a month and average delivery time is 3.8 days. A survey of 650 vehicle assemblers found 61% would switch supplier for a two-day shorter lead time and 49% audit quality systems before placing orders. Some 30 of the 95 technicians need gear-grinding training; a certified course costs $1,400 per technician.

--- APPENDIX 2 — FINANCIAL DATA ---
Title: Extract from the Statement of Financial Position of Kestrel Motor Components as at 31 March 2025 ($ '000)
Headers: ['Financial Metric', '2024', '2025']
Inventories | 180 | 200
Trade receivables | 220 | 250
Cash and cash equivalents | 70 | 90
Current liabilities | 300 | 300
Non-current assets | 2,200 | 2,600
Capital employed | 2,370 | 2,840

--- APPENDIX 3 — EXTERNAL ENVIRONMENT ---
Economic and Business Bulletin (November 2026): (1) The central bank has raised the base interest rate from 4.00% to 4.75%, increasing costs for firms with variable-rate borrowing. (2) The national minimum wage will rise by 7.1% from $12.60 to $13.49 an hour from April 2026, raising total wage bills. (3) Alloy-steel input costs have risen 6.6% year-on-year, producer price inflation is 4.8%, and demand for vehicle components grew 4.2% over the same period.

--- QUESTIONS ---
  Q1(a) [8 marks]
    Question: KMC plans to finance its $1,200,000 grinding line with a $700,000 bank loan and a five-year lease. Explain two advantages for KMC of the lease instead of borrowing to buy the machines.
    Answer: Point 1: A lease spreads the cost of the grinding machines over five years, so KMC does not pay $1,200,000 up front and the $700,000 bank loan can remain available for other working capital. With fixed costs of $420,000 a year and a 2.8% defect rate, preserving cash helps the firm cover the $1,400 per technician training for the 30 staff who need it while the line reaches 70,000 units.

Point 2: Under a lease the lessor usually maintains and replaces the machines, reducing the risk that a breakdown stops precision gear grinding and cuts the $14 contribution per unit. That suits a public limited company answerable to shareholders, because the $1,200,000 investment need not appear as a large immediate debt; the trade-off is that total lease payments can exceed a purchase price and the asset is never owned, but cash flow is protected during the 11% turnover problem. It also avoids tying up security against the two plants.
    Keywords: lease, bank loan, $1,200,000, $700,000, $420,000, workforce of 95
    Mark scheme: knowledge_max_2: 1 mark for each valid advantage identified (max 2). | application_analysis_max_6: Up to 3 marks per point for contextual explanation applied to KMC's investment, costs and cash flow.

  Q1(b) [12 marks]
    Question: KMC is promoting faster delivery of precision gears. Consider sponsoring a motorsport team, hosting technical webinars, or direct mail to vehicle assemblers. Which should KMC choose to win assemblers? Justify your recommendation.
    Answer: Sponsoring a motorsport team: Motor racing gives KMC high brand visibility and links its gears to performance engineering, which can impress the 650 assemblers surveyed. It is glamorous and memorable. However, sponsorship fees are large for a firm funding a $1,200,000 line with a $700,000 loan, and the link to a 3.8-day delivery promise is weak; most viewers are not purchasing engineers, so the spend is largely untargeted.

Technical webinars: Online webinars let KMC demonstrate grinding accuracy, explain the fall in defects from 3.9% to 2.8% and answer engineers' questions live, directly addressing the 49% who audit quality systems. They are low-cost, measurable and can be replayed, and delivery improvements can be explained to many assemblers at once. The weakness is that attendance must be earned and webinars do not by themselves prove the two-day lead time the 61% want.

Direct mail to vehicle assemblers: Printed technical brochures mailed to named purchasing managers are highly targeted and can include certification data and delivery guarantees. They suit a small, identifiable customer set. Drawbacks are printing and postage costs, low response rates, and no immediate feedback, so a $1,200,000 investment cannot be justified on mail alone.

Recommendation: KMC should choose technical webinars as the lead channel, followed up by targeted direct mail to assemblers who attend. Webinars prove technical quality to the 49% who audit quality systems at low cost, and technical proof matters more than brand glamour. Motorsport sponsorship is rejected as expensive and untargeted, and direct mail alone is rejected as a weak one-way medium; combining it with webinars uses it where interest is already shown.
    Keywords: $1,200,000, 61%, 49%, 650, 3.8 days, quality systems

  Q2(a) [8 marks]
    Question: KMC has a 2.8% defect rate and 11% labour turnover. Explain two benefits for KMC of using democratic leadership with its technicians.
    Answer: Point 1: Democratic leadership invites the 95 technicians to suggest improvements, and those closest to the grinders are best placed to explain the 2.8% defect rate.   Q2(b) [12 marks]
    Question: KMC wants to reduce 11% labour turnover among its technicians. Consider an individual production bonus or company-wide profit sharing. Which should KMC choose? Justify your decision.
    Answer: Individual production bonus: Paying a bonus tied to output and the 2.8% defect rate rewards each technician directly and can raise effort and precision on the $1,200,000 grinding line. It is easy to link to the 17,500 gears made last quarter and can be varied with results, so cost rises only when output rises. The drawback is that individual bonuses can discourage teamwork and encourage speed over quality, and with 30 staff needing training, poorly set targets could raise defects and warranty claims.

Company-wide profit sharing: Sharing profit across the workforce of 95 encourages cooperation, which suits democratic leadership and the two-plant operation, and gives everyone a stake in the firm's performance. It can reduce turnover because staff feel rewarded when KMC succeeds. However, the link between an individual's work and the reward is weak, so free-riding is possible, and profits may be thin while the $700,000 loan and the lease are being serviced, meaning the payment could be small.

Decision: KMC should choose an individual production bonus with a quality condition attached, paying extra only when gears meet the 2.8% defect standard. It targets the effort that reduces defects and turnover directly and is affordable because it varies with output. Profit sharing is rejected because its reward is too remote from each technician's work and profits may be absorbed by financing costs; profit sharing can be introduced later once the line is profitable. The bonus can be tied to the 2.8% defect rate as well as output, so speed does not undermine the quality the 49% of assemblers audit.
    Keywords: $1,400, 2.8%, 11%, 17,500, $1,200,000, 95

    Question: Using Appendix 3, evaluate how the interest rate rise to 4.75%, the 7.1% minimum wage increase and the 6.6% rise in alloy-steel input costs will affect KMC. Which change will have the greatest impact? Justify your answer.
    Answer: Interest rate rise (4.00% to 4.75%): The rise is 4.75% − 4.00% = 0.75 percentage points. On the $700,000 variable-rate bank loan, extra interest = 0.75% × $700,000 = 0.0075 × $700,000 = $5,250 a year. This is modest against fixed costs of $420,000, and it is zero if the loan is fixed. The five-year lease is unaffected, so only a part of the $1,200,000 financing is exposed; the rate rise can largely be managed.

Minimum wage increase (7.1%, $12.60 to $13.49 an hour): KMC employs a workforce of 95 and makes 70,000 gears, so labour productivity = 70,000 ÷ 95 = 736.8 gears per worker. The insert gives no hours worked or individual pay, so no annual wage total can be calculated honestly. The increase is compulsory and will lift unit labour costs unless productivity holds at that level; otherwise the $14 contribution per gear narrows, but the size cannot be stated from the data supplied.

Alloy-steel input-cost inflation (6.6%): The insert does not decompose the $21 variable cost, so only a labelled upper bound is shown: if the entire $21 rose 6.6%, the increase = 6.6% × $21 = 0.066 × $21 = $1.386 a gear; at 70,000 units a year that is 70,000 × $1.386 = $97,020. Even a fraction of that pass-through reduces contribution on every gear, and price increases may be hard to win when 61% of assemblers already threaten to switch for better delivery.

Conclusion: The 6.6% rise in alloy-steel input costs will have the greatest impact. It directly attacks the $14 contribution on 70,000 gears, with a computable upper-bound exposure of $97,020 a year, far larger than the $5,250 interest figure, and it cannot be offset by fixing a loan rate. The wage effect is real but unquantifiable from the insert. KMC should renegotiate steel contracts and use the $1,200,000 line's quality gains to justify prices before worrying about the smaller rate rise.

--- MAIN STEM ---
Lorne River Fabrications (LRF) is a private limited company in the fabricated steel components sector, employing a workforce of 36. Founded in 2015 by Tomas Lorne, it welds steel frames for industrial machinery makers from its estuary workshop and operates a flat structure with autocratic leadership. LRF plans to invest $540,000 in a robotic welding cell, financed by a $340,000 bank loan and $200,000 retained profit. It has fixed costs of $210,000 a year, a variable cost of $12 a unit and a selling price of $20, and currently produces 40,000 units a year. LRF faces two problems: a weld defect rate of 3.3% on frames and rising absenteeism of 8%.

--- APPENDIX 1 — MARKETING/OPS ---
Welding Quality Log — Q3 2025: The cell welded 10,000 frames last quarter at a weld defect rate of 3.3%, down from 4.9% a year earlier. Rework costs $18 per defective frame and complaints fell from 27 to 15 a month. Delivery time is 5.2 days. A survey of 300 machinery buyers found 59% would pay $0.50 more for certified welds and 44% check supplier certification. Nine of the 36 welders lack robotic-welding training; a course costs $950 per welder, and a team working pilot has started on the cell.

--- APPENDIX 2 — FINANCIAL DATA ---

Headers: ['Financial Metric', '2024', '2025']
Inventories | 60 | 70
Trade receivables | 85 | 95
Cash and cash equivalents | 25 | 40
Current liabilities | 125 | 125
Non-current assets | 760 | 940
Capital employed | 805 | 1,020

--- APPENDIX 3 — EXTERNAL ENVIRONMENT ---
Economic and Business Bulletin (November 2026): (1) The central bank has raised the base interest rate from 4.50% to 5.25%, increasing borrowing costs for firms with variable-rate loans. (2) The national minimum wage will rise by 6.4% from $13.10 to $13.94 an hour from April 2026, lifting total wage bills. (3) Steel input costs have risen 8.1% year-on-year, energy price inflation is 7.3%, and orders for industrial machinery grew 3.6% over the same period.

  Q1(a) [8 marks]
    Question: LRF is funding its $540,000 welding cell with a $340,000 bank loan and retained profit. Explain two advantages for LRF of using the $200,000 retained profit instead of more bank borrowing.
    Answer: Point 1: Retained profit carries no interest or repayment, so LRF avoids adding to the $340,000 bank loan while it already has fixed costs of $210,000 a year and an 8% absence problem. The $200,000 can fund the robotic cell directly, leaving the $8 contribution on each frame to cover rework at $18 per defective frame and the 7.3% energy inflation rather than finance charges.

Point 2: Using internal funds keeps control with Tomas Lorne and avoids further collateral, so the flat, autocratic firm is not answerable to another lender as it retools the workshop. It also preserves borrowing headroom for the $18-per-frame rework problem and for the $950 welder course: if the 3.3% defect rate delays the 40,000-unit target, LRF can draw on unused credit rather than default on an enlarged loan. Since the insert gives no loan interest rate, no exact saving can be quantified; the clear advantage is that no fixed charge attaches to the $200,000.
    Keywords: retained profit, bank loan, $200,000, $340,000, $540,000, $210,000
    Mark scheme: knowledge_max_2: 1 mark for each valid advantage identified (max 2). | application_analysis_max_6: Up to 3 marks per point for contextual explanation applied to LRF's investment, costs and financing.

  Q1(b) [12 marks]
    Question: LRF wants to learn why machinery buyers value certified welds. Consider a posted survey, focus groups, or observation at trade counters. Which should LRF use to research these buyers? Justify your recommendation.
    Answer: Posted survey: A questionnaire sent to the 300 machinery buyers in the insert can reach many respondents cheaply and produce figures such as the 59% who would pay $0.50 more for certified welds. It is easy to tabulate. However, response rates are often low, closed questions cannot explain why 44% check supplier certification, and the 5.2-day delivery context is hard to capture in a form.

Focus groups: Bringing together a small number of buyers lets LRF probe attitudes to certification and rework quality in depth, generating ideas for the $540,000 welding cell. The discussion is rich and can explain the reasons behind the 59% premium. The drawbacks are high organising cost and a small, unrepresentative sample, so findings cannot be treated as a reliable measure of the whole market, and a 36-employee firm has limited research staff.

Observation at trade counters: Watching buyers choose frames shows real behaviour rather than stated opinions and can reveal whether certification badges are noticed during the 5.2-day ordering process. It is cheap and natural. The weakness is that it reveals what buyers do, not why, and is slow, so it cannot explain the 44% who say they check certification or quantify demand for the $0.50 premium.

Recommendation: LRF should use a posted survey as the primary method, backed by one focus group. The survey quantifies the 59% premium and 44% certification check across a large sample at low cost, while the focus group explains the reasons behind those answers. Focus groups alone are rejected as unrepresentative and expensive, and observation is rejected because it cannot explain motivations; together the two methods make the $540,000 investment better targeted.
    Keywords: $540,000, 59%, 44%, 300, 5.2 days, certified

Coaching also fits the team working pilot and the 36-strong workshop, where nine people learning together can be supported by existing welders during the 5.2-day delivery cycle. The $950 course can follow once basic welding is safe.

--- MAIN STEM ---
Thistledown Knitwear (TDK) is a private limited company in the fashion retail sector, selling knitwear online to UK customers and employing a workforce of 32. Founded in 2016 by Priya Thistlewaite, the business operates a flat organisational structure with democratic leadership and ships its garments from a small Bristol warehouse. TDK plans to invest $420,000 in an automated knitting machine and a new e-commerce fulfilment warehouse, financed by a $250,000 ten-year bank loan and $170,000 retained profit. It has fixed costs of $180,000 a year, a variable cost of $14 a unit and a selling price of $38, and produces 15,000 units a year. TDK faces a rising defect rate of 4.2% on finished garments and growing customer complaints about late online deliveries.

--- APPENDIX 1 — MARKETING/OPS ---
E-commerce Operations Report — Q4 2025: TDK fulfilled 4,200 online orders last quarter, with a defect rate of 4.2% on finished garments, up from 2.6% a year ago. Customer complaints about late deliveries rose to 47 from 29 per month, and average dispatch time reached 3.4 days. A survey of 750 online shoppers found that 61% value free returns and 54% would pay more for locally made knitwear. A skills audit shows 9 of 32 staff have not completed on-the-job training on the new knitting machines; off-the-job training at the local college costs $700 per employee.

--- APPENDIX 2 — FINANCIAL DATA ---
Title: Extract from the Statement of Financial Position of Thistledown Knitwear as at 31 March 2025 ($ '000)
Headers: ['Financial Metric', '2024', '2025']
Inventories | 90 | 70
Trade receivables | 60 | 80
Cash and cash equivalents | 30 | 50
Current liabilities | 120 | 100
Non-current assets | 900 | 1,200
Capital employed | 1,050 | 1,320

--- APPENDIX 3 — EXTERNAL ENVIRONMENT ---
Economic and Retail Bulletin (November 2026): (1) The central bank raised the base interest rate from 4.0% to 4.75%, increasing the cost of TDK's $250,000 variable-rate bank loan. (2) The national minimum wage will rise by 5.8% from $13.50 to $14.28 an hour from April 2026, raising payroll costs in the fulfilment warehouse. (3) Wool and synthetic fibre input costs have risen 9.6% year-on-year, while online spending on fashion grew 4.3%.

--- QUESTIONS ---
  Q1(a) [8 marks]
    Question: TDK is funding part of its $420,000 expansion with $170,000 retained profit rather than an additional bank loan. Explain two advantages for TDK of using retained profit.

With a $250,000 bank loan already committed and fixed costs of $180,000 a year, avoiding extra debt interest leaves more of the $38 selling price available to cover the $14 variable cost and absorb the 9.6% rise in fibre input costs.

Point 2: Using $170,000 of its own funds avoids the collateral and covenant conditions of a bank loan, so Priya Thistlewaite and the other shareholders keep full control of the e-commerce expansion and cannot face lender restrictions on how the warehouse is run. It is also quicker than arranging new borrowing, letting TDK respond to the 4.2% defect rate by fitting the new knitting machines immediately rather than waiting for lender approval. That speed helps protect the 61% of 750 surveyed shoppers who value free returns and keeps the growing base of online customers satisfied while the new fulfilment warehouse becomes operational.

  Q1(b) [12 marks]
    Question: TDK wants to grow online knitwear sales. Consider paid social media advertising, fashion influencer marketing, or a search-engine advertising campaign. Which should TDK choose to promote the launch? Justify your recommendation.
    Answer: Paid social media advertising: Platforms such as Instagram and TikTok let TDK target UK knitwear shoppers by interest and age, and short videos can show garment quality to the 54% of 750 surveyed shoppers who would pay more for locally made knitwear. Search-engine advertising: Shopping adverts appear exactly when a customer searches for a wool cardigan, capturing high-intent buyers and driving immediate traffic to the e-commerce warehouse. They are measurable and scale with budget, but cost-per-click in fashion is high, they do little to build long-term brand loyalty, and they cannot show texture or quality as well as video; the 4.2% defect problem would also show up as returns.

Recommendation: TDK should choose paid social media advertising, reinforced later by a small influencer pilot.   Q3(b) [12 marks]
    Question: Using Appendix 2, evaluate TDK's financial position by calculating the current ratio and the acid test ratio for 2024 and 2025. Has TDK's financial position improved? Justify your answer.
    Answer: Calculations:
Current Ratio 2024 = 1.50 : 1
Current Ratio 2025 = 2.00 : 1
Acid Test Ratio 2024 = 0.75 : 1
Acid Test Ratio 2025 = 1.30 : 1

Detailed workings: 2024 current assets = $90,000 inventories + $60,000 trade receivables + $30,000 cash = $180,000; 2025 current assets = $70,000 + $80,000 + $50,000 = $200,000. Dividing by current liabilities gives 2024 $180,000 ÷ $120,000 = 1.50 and ($180,000 − $90,000) ÷ $120,000 = $90,000 ÷ $120,000 = 0.75. For 2025, $200,000 ÷ $100,000 = 2.00 and ($200,000 − $70,000) ÷ $100,000 = $130,000 ÷ $100,000 = 1.30.

Evaluation: Short-term solvency has strengthened on both measures. The first measure rose from 1.50 to 2.00 even though trade receivables increased from $60,000 to $80,000, because cash doubled from $30,000 to $50,000 and current liabilities fell from $120,000 to $100,000. The second measure, which strips out stock, climbed from 0.75 to 1.30 and is the more important signal here: TDK can now meet its short-term bills without relying on selling the $70,000 of knitwear inventory, which is valuable while it services a $250,000 loan and spends $420,000 on the new fulfilment warehouse. The reservation is that trade receivables have risen by $20,000, tying up cash that could otherwise fund the 9.6% fibre-input increase; if online customers or wholesale accounts pay late, the stronger position could weaken quickly.

Conclusion: TDK's financial position has improved. Both measures rose and the improvement does not depend on inventory, so the business is better placed to meet its obligations. Rising receivables are the main residual risk, so tighter credit control should accompany the expansion.
    Keywords: 1.50, 2.00, 0.75, 1.30, $180,000, $200,000, $420,000
    Mark scheme: level_1_1_to_4: States financial figures or changes without accurate ratio calculations. | level_2_5_to_8: Accurately calculates both ratios for 2024 and 2025 with contextual analysis of the trend. | level_3_9_to_12: Accurate calculations for both years with detailed evaluation of inventories, receivables and liabilities and a justified conclusion on the financial position.

  Q4(a) [8 marks]
    Question: TDK is considering a free-returns policy for its online knitwear. Explain one advantage and one disadvantage for TDK of this approach.
    Answer: Advantage: A free-returns policy directly answers the 61% of 750 surveyed shoppers who value free returns, reducing a barrier to buying knitwear online and supporting the $38 selling price and $24 contribution on each garment. Higher conversion on the 4,200-order baseline would spread the $180,000 fixed costs over more units and help justify the $420,000 fulfilment investment.

Disadvantage: Free returns create reverse-logistics costs and can be abused, which would raise the $14 variable cost per unit and squeeze margins, especially as the defect rate is already 4.2% and may generate avoidable returns. The insert gives no figure for the cost of handling a return or for how much sales would rise, so the net effect cannot be quantified; the decision must be judged qualitatively. TDK should trial the policy on a single product line and compare return rates and the 47 monthly complaints before extending it nationally, keeping the $250,000 loan commitment in mind.

  Q4(b) [12 marks]
    Question: Using Appendix 3, evaluate how the base interest rate rise to 4.75%, the 5.8% minimum wage increase and the 9.6% rise in fibre input costs will affect TDK. Which change will have the greatest impact? Justify your answer.
    Answer: Interest rate rise (4.0% to 4.75%): If TDK's $250,000 bank loan is variable-rate, the extra 0.75 percentage point adds 0.75% × $250,000 = $1,875 a year (0.0075 × $250,000). That is small beside fixed costs of $180,000, and a fixed-rate loan would avoid it altogether. The higher rate could still make future borrowing for the $420,000 expansion dearer and slightly dampen the 4.3% growth in online fashion spending.

Minimum wage increase (5.8%, to $14.28 an hour): The workforce of 32 includes hourly-paid packing and warehouse staff, so the wage bill rises and cannot be avoided. The insert does not state hours worked or individual pay, so an annual total would be invented. The defensible check is productivity: 15,000 units ÷ 32 staff = 468.75 garments per worker, so the higher wage is affordable only if that rate holds or improves; reducing the 4.2% defect rate and training the 9 untrained staff would help sustain it.

Fibre input costs (9.6%): These feed the $14 variable cost on every garment. The insert does not decompose that cost, so only a bound is honest: if the full $14 were exposed, 9.6% × $14 = $1.344, about $1.34 a unit, and at 15,000 units that is roughly $20,160 a year (15,000 × $1.344). Even a smaller exposed share erodes the $24 contribution, and it recurs on every unit.

Conclusion: The 9.6% rise in fibre input costs will have the greatest impact. It compounds across all 15,000 garments and directly attacks the $24 contribution that services the $250,000 loan and funds the $420,000 expansion, whereas the interest rise costs only $1,875 a year and the wage effect can be offset by sustaining 468.75 garments per worker. TDK should cut the 4.2% defect rate and review the $38 price rather than absorb the whole increase.
    Keywords: 4.75%, 5.8%, 9.6%, $14.28, $250,000, $14
    Mark scheme: level_1_1_to_4: Identifies the external changes with limited application to TDK. | level_2_5_to_8: Analyses the impact of at least two external changes on TDK's costs, revenue or financing in context. | level_3_9_to_12: Detailed evaluation of all three changes in context with a well-justified judgment that fibre input-cost inflation has the greatest impact and why the others are smaller.

--- MAIN STEM ---
Velvet Vale Boutiques (VVB) is a private limited company in the fashion retail sector, operating a chain of six women's clothing boutiques and employing a workforce of 40. Founded in 2013 by Elena Vale, the business has a hierarchical organisational structure with autocratic leadership. VVB plans to invest $560,000 in refurbishing three boutiques and launching an online store, financed by a $200,000 bank loan and a $360,000 share issue. It has fixed costs of $240,000 a year, a variable cost of $18 a unit and a selling price of $48, and produces 20,000 units a year. VVB faces labour turnover of 14% among sales assistants and a rising number of complaints about out-of-stock sizes in its boutiques.

--- APPENDIX 1 — MARKETING/OPS ---
Boutique Operations Report — Q4 2025: VVB sold 5,400 garments across its six boutiques last quarter, with labour turnover of 14% among sales assistants and 38 customer complaints about unavailable sizes, up from 22 a year earlier. Average queueing time at tills was 6 minutes, and 91% of planned deliveries arrived on time. A survey of 900 shoppers found 58% preferred shops with knowledgeable staff and 49% would use an online store. A skills audit shows 11 of 40 staff have not completed on-the-job training; off-the-job training at the regional college costs $620 per employee.

--- APPENDIX 2 — FINANCIAL DATA ---
Title: Extract from the Statement of Financial Position of Velvet Vale Boutiques as at 31 March 2025 ($ '000)
Headers: ['Financial Metric', '2024', '2025']
Inventories | 130 | 160
Trade receivables | 25 | 20
Cash and cash equivalents | 40 | 30
Current liabilities | 100 | 100
Non-current assets | 700 | 980
Capital employed | 850 | 1,100

--- APPENDIX 3 — EXTERNAL ENVIRONMENT ---
Economic and Retail Bulletin (November 2026): (1) The central bank raised the base interest rate from 4.25% to 5.0%, increasing the cost of VVB's $200,000 bank loan. (2) The national minimum wage will rise by 6.4% from $13.10 to $13.94 an hour from April 2026, raising the wages of sales assistants. (3) Wholesale clothing input costs have risen 10.8% year-on-year, while consumer spending on fashion rose 2.6%.

  Q1(a) [8 marks]
    Question: VVB is funding its $560,000 expansion with a $200,000 bank loan and a $360,000 share issue. Explain two advantages for VVB of the share issue compared with the bank loan.
    Answer: Point 1: A share issue brings in $360,000 that never has to be repaid and carries no regular interest charge, unlike the $200,000 bank loan whose cost rises whenever the base rate moves. For a firm with fixed costs of $240,000 a year and stock problems, this protects cash flow while three boutiques are refurbished, leaving more of the $48 selling price to cover the $18 variable cost and absorb the 10.8% rise in wholesale clothing costs.

Point 2: Equity does not require the collateral or monthly repayment pressure of a bank loan, so Elena Vale's expansion cannot be threatened by a bank recall if sales disappoint during the launch of the new online store. Although a share issue dilutes existing ownership, it spreads the funding burden among investors rather than concentrating risk on one lender, and it supports the $560,000 project without committing the boutiques' limited cash reserves. That matters when labour turnover of 14% and 38 complaints about unavailable sizes already strain the workforce of 40 and require spending on staff and stock before the refurbished boutiques generate extra revenue.

--- MAIN STEM ---
Riverlyn Retail Group (RRG) is a private limited company in the retail sector, running a chain of nine home-and-lifestyle stores and employing a workforce of 55. Founded in 2011 by Daniel Rivera, the business operates a flat organisational structure with laissez-faire leadership. RRG plans to invest $720,000 in two new stores and a distribution centre, financed by a $300,000 bank loan and $420,000 retained profit. It has fixed costs of $320,000 a year, a variable cost of $9 a unit and a selling price of $25, and produces 40,000 units a year. RRG faces stock shrinkage of 5.1% of inventory and absenteeism of 8% among its store staff, which has slowed deliveries and left shelves empty at peak times in several branches.

--- APPENDIX 1 — MARKETING/OPS ---
Store Operations Report — Q3 2025: RRG sold 11,200 units across its nine stores last quarter, with stock shrinkage of 5.1% of inventory, up from 3.4% a year ago. Absenteeism reached 8% and customer complaints about empty shelves rose to 52 from 31 per month. Average checkout time was 4.1 minutes. A survey of 1,100 shoppers found 63% valued competitive prices and 46% said store layout affected their purchases. A skills audit shows 14 of 55 staff have not completed on-the-job training; off-the-job training at the local college costs $540 per employee.

With a $300,000 bank loan already committed and fixed costs of $320,000 a year, using the $420,000 of internal funds avoids extra debt service and leaves more of the $25 selling price to cover the $9 variable cost and absorb the 8.7% rise in wholesale input costs.

Point 2: Internal finance carries no lender covenants or collateral risk, so Daniel Rivera keeps full strategic freedom over where the two new stores open and how the distribution centre is run. It is also faster than negotiating additional borrowing, letting RRG respond to 5.1% stock shrinkage and 52 complaints about empty shelves by investing in control systems immediately rather than waiting for a bank decision.     Question: Using Appendix 2, evaluate RRG's financial position by calculating the current ratio and the acid test ratio for 2024 and 2025. Has RRG's financial position improved? Justify your answer.
    Answer: Calculations:
Current Ratio 2024 = 2.00 : 1
Current Ratio 2025 = 2.04 : 1
Acid Test Ratio 2024 = 0.75 : 1
Acid Test Ratio 2025 = 0.56 : 1

Detailed workings: 2024 current assets = $150,000 inventories + $35,000 trade receivables + $55,000 cash = $240,000; 2025 current assets = $185,000 + $30,000 + $40,000 = $255,000. Trade receivables improved from $35,000 to $30,000, freeing some cash, but not enough to offset the $35,000 inventory build-up and $15,000 cash fall.

Conclusion: RRG's financial position has not improved in quality.     Question: Using Appendix 3, evaluate how the base interest rate rise to 5.25%, the 6.9% minimum wage increase and the 8.7% rise in home-goods input costs will affect RRG. Which change will have the greatest impact? Justify your answer.
    Answer: Interest rate rise (4.5% to 5.25%): If RRG's $300,000 bank loan is variable-rate, the extra 0.75 percentage point adds 0.75% × $300,000 = $2,250 a year (0.0075 × $300,000). That is modest against fixed costs of $320,000, and a fixed-rate loan would remove it. The rise may still make future borrowing for the $720,000 expansion more expensive and could slightly dampen the 3.9% growth in homeware spending.

Minimum wage increase (6.9%, to $14.06 an hour): The workforce of 55 includes many hourly-paid store staff, so payroll rises and cannot be avoided, especially with 8% absenteeism forcing cover. The insert does not state hours worked or individual pay, so an annual total would be invented. The defensible check is productivity: 40,000 units ÷ 55 staff = 727.27 units per worker, so the higher wage is sustainable only if that rate holds or improves; cutting 5.1% shrinkage and training the 14 untrained staff would help protect it.

Home-goods input costs (8.7%): These feed the $9 variable cost on every unit sold. The insert does not decompose that cost, so only a bound is honest: if the full $9 were exposed, 8.7% × $9 = $0.783, about $0.78 a unit, and at 40,000 units that is roughly $31,320 a year (40,000 × $0.783). Even a smaller exposed share reduces the $16 contribution on each unit, and it recurs with every sale.

Conclusion: The 8.7% rise in home-goods input costs will have the greatest impact. It compounds across all 40,000 units and directly erodes the $16 contribution that services the $300,000 loan and funds the $720,000 expansion, whereas the interest rise costs only $2,250 a year and the wage effect can be offset by sustaining 727.27 units per worker. RRG should cut the 5.1% shrinkage and review the $25 price rather than absorb the whole increase.
