--- MAIN STEM ---
BrightPath Learning (BPL) is a private limited company in the education sector, employing a workforce of 48. Founded in 2013 by Samuel Okafor, it delivers short courses and tutoring to school pupils and adult learners, and operates a hierarchical structure with autocratic leadership. BPL plans to invest $540,000 in a new digital learning studio and e-learning platform, financed by a $300,000 ten-year bank loan and a $240,000 share issue. It has fixed costs of $200,000 a year, a variable cost of $22 a unit and a selling price of $72 for a course unit, and currently delivers 10,000 units a year. BPL faces two problems: labour turnover has reached 14%, and complaints about the quality of online course materials are rising.

--- APPENDIX 1 — MARKETING/OPS ---
Market Research Summary — October 2025: A survey of 800 parents and adult learners found 67% would pay up to $8 more for live small-group tutoring, and 58% preferred evening classes. Enrolments last quarter were 2,450 units against a target of 2,800. The complaint rate rose to 3.6% of course units, and 31 formal complaints were logged in September. Average course-material download time is 4.1 minutes. 12 of 48 tutors have not completed on-the-job training on the new e-learning platform; an external trainer charges $550 per tutor for a certified course.

--- APPENDIX 2 — FINANCIAL DATA ---

--- MAIN STEM ---
VitalCore Fitness (VCF) is a private limited company in the leisure and fitness sector, employing a workforce of 35. Founded in 2015 by Nadia Rahman, it runs two city gyms and operates a flat structure with laissez-faire leadership. It has fixed costs of $240,000 a year, a variable cost of $12 a unit and a selling price of $42 for a membership unit, and currently delivers 15,000 units a year. --- APPENDIX 1 — MARKETING/OPS ---

    Question: Using Appendix 3, evaluate how the base interest rate rise to 4.5%, the 6.4% minimum wage increase and the 11.3% rise in imported equipment prices will affect VCF. Which change will have the greatest impact? Justify your answer.
    Answer: Interest rate rise (4.0% to 4.5%): If VCF's $380,000 ten-year loan is variable-rate, the annual interest cost rises by 0.5% of $380,000 = $1,900 a year (0.005 × $380,000). Higher rates could still cool consumer spending on leisure memberships and make future finance for the $620,000 expansion dearer, but VCF can limit this by fixing the rate.

Minimum wage increase (6.4%, to $13.62 an hour): With a workforce of 35 across two gyms, this raises wage bills for gym and reception staff and cannot be avoided. The insert gives no hours worked or individual pay, so no annual total can be invented. The proper comparison is productivity: 15,000 units ÷ 35 staff = 428.6 units per worker, so the rise is affordable only if output per worker holds or grows; otherwise unit labour cost rises and the $30 contribution per unit is squeezed, made worse by 8% absenteeism.

Imported equipment prices (11.3%): This raises the cost of replacing the 6% of equipment out of service and of fitting out two new gyms. If the entire $620,000 investment were imported equipment, 11.3% × $620,000 = $70,060; this is an illustrative upper bound because the insert does not state the equipment share. The $12 variable cost is not decomposed, so no per-unit addition can be claimed. Growth of 4.2% in leisure spending offers some pricing room.

Conclusion: The 11.3% rise in imported equipment prices has the greatest impact. It inflates the $620,000 expansion and the replacement of faulty machines at the same time, with a possible $70,060 upper-bound effect, whereas the interest rise costs only $1,900 and the wage effect cannot be quantified from the insert and can be offset by productivity and membership growth.

--- MAIN STEM ---
ClearScan Diagnostics (CSD) is a private limited company in the healthcare diagnostics sector, employing a workforce of 52. Founded in 2008 by Dr Priya Nair, it runs three imaging centres and operates a hierarchical structure with democratic leadership. CSD plans to invest $890,000 in a new MRI scanner and telemedicine reporting hub, financed by a $500,000 ten-year bank loan and a $390,000 share issue. It has fixed costs of $450,000 a year, a variable cost of $48 a unit and a selling price of $138 for a diagnostic scan, and currently performs 12,000 units a year. CSD faces two problems: a 3.2% scan retake rate and rising patient complaints about report delays.

--- APPENDIX 1 — MARKETING/OPS ---
Quality and Operations Report — Q4 2025: The scanning centres performed 2,900 scans in December with a 3.2% retake rate, down from 5.1% a year earlier. Patient complaints about report delays rose from 22 to 41 per month. Average report turnaround is 3.7 days. A survey of 450 patients found that 73% would pay $20 more for same-day digital reports, and 56% choose a provider on the speed of results. 14 of 52 radiographers have not completed on-the-job training on the new MRI scanner; a vendor certification course costs $760 per employee.

--- APPENDIX 2 — FINANCIAL DATA ---
Title: Extract from the Statement of Profit or Loss and Capital employed data of ClearScan Diagnostics for the year ended 31 March 2025 ($ '000)
Headers: ['Financial Metric', '2024', '2025']

Cost of sales | 1,650 | 1,800
Gross profit | 1,350 | 1,800
Operating profit | 450 | 720
Capital employed | 2,500 | 3,200
Interest payable | 60 | 50

--- APPENDIX 3 — EXTERNAL ENVIRONMENT ---
Economic and Business Bulletin (November 2026): (1) The central bank has raised the base interest rate from 4.5% to 5.25%, increasing borrowing costs for businesses with variable-rate loans such as CSD's $500,000 scanner loan. (2) The national minimum wage will rise by 5.4% from $13.00 to $13.70 per hour from April 2026, raising wage bills for radiography and administrative staff. (3) Medical consumables and imaging contrast import costs have risen 10.8% year-on-year, while private healthcare spending grew 3.9% over the same period.

    Question: CSD plans to fund part of its $890,000 scanner investment with a $500,000 ten-year bank loan. Explain two advantages for CSD of raising the $390,000 through a share issue instead of borrowing more.
    Answer: Point 1: A $390,000 share issue provides equity that requires no interest or capital repayment, so CSD avoids extra debt service on top of the $500,000 loan while meeting fixed costs of $450,000 a year. The money can be spent on the telemedicine reporting hub and on reducing the 3.7-day report turnaround, rather than being paid to a lender as finance charges on the $890,000 investment.

Point 2: Equity improves resilience if the 3.2% retake rate delays scans and depresses revenue below the current 12,000 units, because there is no fixed repayment that could trigger a liquidity crisis. It also spreads the risk of the new MRI scanner among investors rather than leaving Dr Priya Nair's original centres wholly exposed to the bank. A larger loan would demand repayments whether or not the telemedicine hub reduces the 41 monthly complaints, whereas equity gives CSD time to establish the service. New shareholders may also bring healthcare contacts that help CSD win referrals to the three imaging centres.

    Answer: Recruiting extra radiographers: More staff would directly reduce the backlog behind the 3.7-day turnaround and the 41 monthly complaints. However, recruitment and salaries add to fixed costs of $450,000 a year, and with 14 of 52 radiographers still needing scanner training, new hires would also require costly induction before becoming productive.

Telemedicine reporting partnership: Sending scans to specialist radiologists abroad could give same-day digital reports, matching the 73% of 450 surveyed patients who would pay $20 more and the 56% who choose on speed. It converts a fixed staffing cost into a variable one and can flex with the 12,000-scan volume, but it depends on reliable data links and may reduce control over quality and the 3.2% retake rate.

Automated reporting software: Software could triage normal scans and issue routine reports instantly, cutting turnaround without the ongoing salary cost of new hires. It fits the $890,000 technology investment and supports the 73% premium for same-day reports, but it requires validation, may not handle complex cases, and does not by itself fix radiographer shortages.

A partnership also avoids the 14 radiographer training gap becoming a bottleneck, because reporting capacity can be bought in while local staff are upskilled.

Recommendation: CSD should choose the telemedicine reporting partnership, supported by automated software for routine scans. Together they deliver the same-day reports the survey values and cut the 3.7-day wait without permanently raising fixed costs. Recruitment is rejected because it adds long-term salary costs on top of $450,000 fixed costs and training needs; software alone is rejected because it cannot cover complex scans or the full backlog.

The insert states no hours worked or individual pay, so no annual wage total can be invented. Medical consumables inflation (10.8%): The $48 variable cost is not decomposed in the insert, so only a bound can be calculated: if the whole variable cost rose 10.8% it would add 0.108 × $48 = $5.18 per scan; at 12,000 scans that is $62,208 a year. This cuts the $90 contribution on every scan, and the 3.2% retake rate multiplies usage, though the $20 same-day premium and 3.9% growth in private healthcare spending provide some recovery.

Conclusion: The 10.8% rise in medical consumables has the greatest impact. It compounds across all 12,000 scans and directly erodes the $90 contribution that justifies the $890,000 investment, and retakes amplify it; the interest rise is only $3,750 a year and the wage effect, though real, cannot be quantified from the insert and can be offset by productivity and the premium.
    Keywords: 5.25%, 5.4%, 10.8%, $13.70, $500,000, $48
    Mark scheme: level_1_1_to_4: Identifies the three external changes with limited application to CSD. | level_2_5_to_8: Analyses the impact of at least two changes on CSD's costs, revenue or financing in context. | level_3_9_to_12: Detailed evaluation of all three changes with a well-justified judgement that consumables inflation has the greatest impact and why the others are smaller.

--- MAIN STEM ---
Harbourview Pharmacy (HVP) is a public limited company in the retail pharmacy and consumer health sector, employing a workforce of 120. Founded in 1998 by Margaret Chen, it runs 18 high-street branches and operates an autocratic leadership style within a flat structure. HVP plans to invest $950,000 in automated dispensing robots and a click-and-collect e-commerce platform, financed by a $550,000 ten-year bank loan, $250,000 retained profit and a $150,000 share issue. It has fixed costs of $600,000 a year, a variable cost of $18 a unit and a selling price of $58 for a prescription or OTC item, and currently dispenses 25,000 units a year. HVP faces two problems: a 2.7% dispensing error rate and rising complaints about a 9.6-minute counter wait.

--- APPENDIX 1 — MARKETING/OPS ---
Quality and Service Report — Q3 2025: HVP dispensed 6,200 prescription and OTC units last month with a 2.7% dispensing error rate, up from 1.6% a year earlier. Customer complaints about queue times rose from 48 to 77 per month. Average wait at the counter is 9.6 minutes. A survey of 1,000 shoppers found that 66% would use click-and-collect if it cut waiting time, and 54% buy more when staff offer health advice. 18 of 120 pharmacy staff have not completed on-the-job training on the automated dispensing robots; a vendor course costs $640 per employee.

The $150,000 can be spent on the click-and-collect e-commerce platform and on cutting the 9.6-minute counter wait, rather than being paid to a lender as finance charges on the $950,000 programme.

Point 2: Equity improves resilience if the 2.7% dispensing error rate forces costly rework and revenue falls below the current 25,000 units, because there is no fixed repayment that could strain liquidity. It also spreads the risk of the 18-branch automation across new shareholders rather than leaving the company wholly exposed to the bank. A larger loan would require repayments whether or not click-and-collect reduces the 77 monthly complaints, whereas equity gives HVP time to embed the robots. New shareholders may also bring retail property experience useful when rolling click-and-collect out to all 18 branches.

    Answer: Click-and-collect e-commerce platform: Allowing customers to order online and skip the queue directly addresses the 9.6-minute wait, and the survey of 1,000 shoppers found 66% would use it. PAPER 2 — P2_SET_336
UNIT: Paper 2 Case Study

--- MAIN STEM ---
Kestrel Ridge Aggregates (KRA) is a private limited company in the quarrying and construction aggregates sector, employing a workforce of 52. Founded in 2007 by Bryn Kestrel, the business supplies crushed stone to regional building contractors and operates a hierarchical structure with autocratic leadership. KRA plans to invest $720,000 in a recycled-aggregate crushing plant with stormwater recycling, financed by a $450,000 ten-year bank loan and $270,000 retained profit. It has fixed costs of $240,000 a year, a variable cost of $8.00 a unit and a selling price of $14.00, and produces 96,000 units of crushed aggregate a year. KRA faces two operational problems: stone-dust complaints from nearby residents are rising, and labour turnover is increasing among crusher operators.

--- APPENDIX 1 — MARKETING/OPS ---
Quarry Operations and Quality Log — Q3 2025: The new screening line processed 24,000 units last quarter at a defect rate of 2.4%, down from 4.1% a year earlier. Customer complaints about stone dust fell from 34 to 19 per month. Average delivery time to building sites is 4.5 days. A survey of 500 local builders found that 61% would pay up to $0.50 more per unit for recycled aggregate, and 47% check a supplier's environmental credentials before ordering. A skills audit shows 14 of 52 operators have not completed on-the-job training on the new crusher; off-the-job courses at the technical college cost $850 per employee.

--- APPENDIX 2 — FINANCIAL DATA ---
Title: Extract from the Statement of Profit or Loss and Capital employed data of Kestrel Ridge Aggregates for the year ended 31 March 2025 ($ '000)
Headers: ['Financial Metric', '2024', '2025']
Revenue | 1,320 | 1,440
Cost of sales | 792 | 792
Gross profit | 528 | 648
Operating profit | 165 | 216
Capital employed | 1,100 | 1,200
Interest payable | 18 | 22

--- APPENDIX 3 — EXTERNAL ENVIRONMENT ---
Economic and Business Bulletin (November 2026): (1) The central bank has raised the base interest rate from 4.25% to 5.00%, increasing borrowing costs for businesses with variable-rate loans. (2) The national minimum wage will rise by 5.8% from $12.60 to $13.33 per hour from April 2026, raising total wage bills. (3) Diesel and tyre input costs for haulage have risen 9.5% year-on-year, while construction output grew 2.8% over the same period.

--- QUESTIONS ---
  Q1(a) [8 marks]
    Question: KRA plans to fund part of its recycled-aggregate crushing plant with retained profit rather than the $450,000 bank loan. Explain two advantages for KRA of using the $270,000 retained profit instead of the loan.
    Answer: Point 1: Using $270,000 of retained profit costs KRA no interest charges or capital repayments, which protects cash flow at a time when the business already carries fixed costs of $240,000 a year and a $450,000 ten-year bank loan. Every dollar not paid as interest can instead absorb the 9.5% rise in diesel and tyre costs, helping KRA hold its $14.00 selling price for crushed stone and stay competitive against other quarries supplying regional building contractors. Retained profit also has no fixed repayment timetable, so the $720,000 recycling plant can be commissioned at the quarry's own pace.

Point 2: Retained profit carries no collateral or repossession risk. If demand for recycled aggregate disappoints, the bank cannot seize the new crusher or the quarry site, so Bryn Kestrel's owner-managed company keeps control of its core asset. The bank loan, by contrast, would require security and regular servicing whatever the level of stone-dust complaints or output. Using internal funds also preserves the company's borrowing headroom for later investment in stormwater recycling, and it avoids the lender conditions that could restrict how the 96,000-unit operation is run or expanded.
    Keywords: retained profit, bank loan, $450,000, $270,000, $720,000, $240,000
    Mark scheme: knowledge_max_2: 1 mark for each valid advantage identified (max 2). | application_analysis_max_6: Up to 3 marks per point for contextual explanation and analysis applied to KRA's cash flow, costs and ownership.

  Q1(b) [12 marks]
    Question: KRA is promoting its new recycled aggregate to building contractors. Consider advertising in trade magazines, sponsoring a local building show, or a targeted social media campaign. Which should KRA choose? Justify your recommendation.
    Answer: Trade magazine advertising: A trade magazine reaches building contractors directly and gives KRA space to explain the recycled content and stormwater recycling of the new plant, which matters to the 47% of surveyed builders who check environmental credentials. It is a credible, permanent medium for technical claims. However, a full-page campaign is expensive for a 52-employee quarry already servicing a $450,000 loan, the audience is narrower than the regional contractor base KRA supplies, and print cannot demonstrate the product or respond to the 61% of builders who would pay $0.50 more until long after the $720,000 plant is running.

Local building show sponsorship: A stand at a local show lets KRA meet contractors face to face, hand over samples of recycled aggregate and answer questions about quality, directly tackling the stone-dust complaints by showing the stormwater system. It is cheaper than national print and builds relationships in KRA's own region. Its weakness is reach: a three-day event touches only the contractors who attend, so it cannot by itself sell enough of the 96,000 units the quarry produces, and the cost per order can be high.

Targeted social media campaign: Paid social ads can be aimed at regional contractors and sustainability-focused builders, showing short videos of the crushing line and linking the 61% premium finding to a clear $0.50 message. It is measurable, scalable and cheap per contact, and can be adjusted quickly if the 2.4% defect rate or delivery times of 4.5 days need explaining. It depends on builders actually using the platforms and on sustained spend to keep visibility.

Recommendation: KRA should choose the targeted social media campaign. It reaches the exact segment identified in the 500-builder survey, costs far less than trade print, and scales regionally in a way a single local show cannot. The building show is rejected as too limited in reach; trade magazines are rejected as costly and slow. KRA should use the show only as a low-cost supporting opportunity.
    Keywords: 61%, 47%, 500, $0.50, recycled aggregate, 24,000
    Mark scheme: level_1_1_to_4: Limited outline of the promotional options with minimal application to KRA. | level_2_5_to_8: Detailed discussion of the advantages and disadvantages of at least two options in the context of KRA with some judgement. | level_3_9_to_12: Detailed discussion of all three options in the context of KRA with a well-justified recommendation explaining why trade magazines and the building show are rejected.

    Question: Using Appendix 2, evaluate KRA's financial performance by calculating the gross profit margin, profit margin and ROCE for 2024 and 2025. Has performance improved? Justify your answer.

The 12.5% to 15.0% rise in operating profitability shows fixed costs of $240,000 were absorbed more effectively as output rose, and the 15.0% to 18.0% return on capital shows the asset base is being used more productively. The 47% of builders checking credentials also means some of the revenue gain may depend on maintaining the eco positioning.

Conclusion: KRA's performance has improved. Higher revenue, unchanged cost of sales and rising operating profit lift both margins and the return on capital, so the business is more profitable and uses its assets better. The main risk is rising interest and input costs, which management should watch, but on the 2024–2025 evidence the improvement is genuine and broad-based.

    Mark scheme: level_1_1_to_4: States financial figures or changes without accurate ratio calculations. | level_2_5_to_8: Accurately calculates the three profitability measures for both 2024 and 2025 with contextual analysis of the trend. | level_3_9_to_12: Accurate calculations for both years combined with detailed evaluation of revenue, cost of sales, capital employed and interest movements and a justified conclusion on whether performance improved.

  Q4(a) [8 marks]
    Question: Explain one advantage and one disadvantage for KRA of producing recycled aggregate at its new crushing plant.
    Answer: Advantage: Recycled aggregate matches the survey evidence that 61% of the 500 builders questioned would pay up to $0.50 more per unit, allowing KRA to protect the $6.00 contribution per unit on its $8.00 variable cost even as diesel and tyre costs rise 9.5%. Disadvantage: Producing recycled aggregate can require extra sorting and screening, which would push up the $8.00 variable cost per unit and squeeze margins unless the full $0.50 premium is accepted.   Q4(b) [12 marks]
    Question: Using Appendix 3, evaluate how the base interest rate rise to 5.00%, the 5.8% minimum wage increase and the 9.5% rise in diesel and tyre costs will affect KRA. Which change will have the greatest impact? Justify your answer.
    Answer: Interest rate rise (4.25% to 5.00%): If the $450,000 ten-year bank loan is variable-rate, the annual interest cost rises by 0.75% of $450,000 = $3,375 a year (0.0075 × $450,000). That is small beside fixed costs of $240,000 and can be removed by fixing the rate; if the loan is already fixed, the direct effect is zero. Higher rates could still make future borrowing for the $720,000 plant dearer.

Minimum wage increase (5.8%, to $13.33 an hour): KRA employs a workforce of 52, many of them crusher operators, so wage costs will rise and cannot be avoided. The insert gives neither hours worked nor individual pay, so no defensible annual wage total can be calculated. The honest comparison is with productivity: 96,000 units ÷ 52 workers ≈ 1,846 units per worker a year, so the rise is affordable only if output per worker holds or improves; otherwise unit labour cost climbs and the $6.00 contribution shrinks.

Diesel and tyre costs (9.5%): Haulage is central to delivering crushed stone to builders. The $8.00 variable cost is not broken down in the insert, so only a labelled upper bound can be shown: if the whole variable cost rose 9.5%, that adds 0.095 × $8.00 = $0.76 per unit; across 96,000 units that is $72,960 a year (96,000 × $0.76). Even a smaller pass-through would cut contribution from $6.00 toward roughly $5.24 and threaten the returns needed to justify the new plant.

Conclusion: The 9.5% rise in diesel and tyre costs will have the greatest impact. It applies to every one of the 96,000 units sold, directly erodes the contribution that funds the $450,000 loan and the $720,000 investment, and cannot be neutralised by a one-off action. The interest rise is quantifiably small at $3,375 and can be fixed, while the wage effect depends on hours that are not given and can be offset by productivity, so both are smaller threats.

--- MAIN STEM ---
Thornbury Timber & Board (TTB) is a cooperative in the sustainable forestry and recycled board sector, employing a workforce of 38. Founded in 2011 by Fiona Thorn, the business supplies low-energy fibreboard to furniture makers and operates a flat organisational structure with democratic leadership. TTB plans to invest $640,000 in a low-energy board-pressing line using recycled wood fibre, financed by a $300,000 bank overdraft and $340,000 of new member share capital. It has fixed costs of $198,000 a year, a variable cost of $5.50 a unit and a selling price of $11.00, and produces 84,000 units of board a year. TTB faces two operational problems: wood-fibre waste is above target, and defects on the new press are frequent.

--- APPENDIX 1 — MARKETING/OPS ---
Quality and Waste Report — Q3 2025: The pressing line produced 21,000 boards last quarter with a defect rate of 3.4%, down from 5.2% a year ago. Wood-fibre waste ran at 8.6% of input, above the 6% target. Customer complaints fell from 41 to 26 per month. Delivery to furniture makers averaged 5.5 days. A survey of 450 furniture manufacturers found that 58% would pay up to $0.45 more for low-energy recycled board, and 44% require environmental certification before placing orders. A training audit shows 11 of 38 members have not completed on-the-job training on the new press; off-the-job courses at the college cost $780 per member.

--- APPENDIX 2 — FINANCIAL DATA ---

For a cooperative running fixed costs of $198,000 a year, that saving protects the $5.50 contribution on each board and helps absorb the 11.3% rise in fibre and resin costs without increasing the $11.00 selling price to furniture makers.

Point 2: Share capital does not require the security or daily repayment pressure of an overdraft, so the $640,000 pressing line cannot be withdrawn by a bank at short notice if member withdrawals or a dip in orders occur. It also keeps decision-making in the hands of the cooperative's members, including founder Fiona Thorn, rather than giving a lender influence over how the recycled wood fibre is sourced. With the right to share in future profits, members have a direct incentive to reduce the 8.6% wood-fibre waste and improve the 3.4% defect rate, aligning financing with the 84,000-unit output target.

However, 9 of 26 staff are away from the workshop, slowing the 6.2-day lead time, and the course may not cover MHF's exact spraying equipment, so on-site follow-up would still be needed.

Decision: MHF should choose on-the-job training as the main method, with a short college module for certification. It is cheaper, specific to the low-VOC line and avoids output loss while the shortage of skilled joiners is acute; full off-the-job training alone is rejected because removing 9 staff and spending $6,480 would disrupt the 60,000-unit plan and still leave machine-specific habits to be learned on site.

--- MAIN STEM ---
Grange Lane Bricks (GLB) is a public limited company in the construction materials and recycled bricks sector, employing a workforce of 74. Founded in 1998 by Aoife Grange, the business supplies bricks to housebuilders and operates a hierarchical structure with autocratic leadership. GLB plans to invest $880,000 in a recycled-content brick kiln with waste-heat recovery, financed by a $500,000 ten-year bank loan and a $380,000 share issue. It has fixed costs of $300,000 a year, a variable cost of $4.00 a unit and a selling price of $10.00, and produces 110,000 units of brick a year. GLB faces two operational problems: kiln temperature variation is raising the defect rate, and off-spec rejection is wasting output.

--- APPENDIX 1 — MARKETING/OPS ---
Quality and Waste Report — Q3 2025: The recycled-content kiln produced 27,500 bricks last quarter with a defect rate of 4.2%, down from 6.8% a year ago. Off-spec rejection wasted 7.4% of output, against a 5% target. Customer complaints from housebuilders fell from 52 to 31 per month. Average delivery is 3.8 days. A survey of 700 housebuilders found that 63% would pay up to $0.35 more per brick for recycled-content products, and 49% check environmental credentials when tendering. A maintenance audit shows 18 of 74 workers have not completed on-the-job training on the new kiln controls; off-the-job courses at the technical centre cost $910 per worker.

--- APPENDIX 2 — FINANCIAL DATA ---
Title: Extract from the Statement of Profit or Loss and Capital employed data of Grange Lane Bricks for the year ended 31 March 2025 ($ '000)

Gross profit | 420 | 540
Operating profit | 126 | 180
Capital employed | 1,050 | 1,200
Interest payable | 24 | 30

(2) The national minimum wage will rise by 7.1% from $13.10 to $14.03 per hour from April 2026, raising total wage bills. (3) Clay, recycled aggregate and natural-gas energy costs rose 13.2% year-on-year, while new housing starts fell 2.3% over the same period.

The saving helps cover fixed costs of $300,000 a year and protects the $6.00 contribution on each brick as clay and energy costs rise 13.2%, allowing the $10.00 price to hold for housebuilders.

Point 2: Equity has no fixed maturity and no security over the kiln, so the $880,000 waste-heat recovery plant cannot be at risk of repossession if the 4.2% defect rate persists or housing starts fall 2.3%. As a public limited company, GLB can also reach a wide pool of investors without surrendering control to a single lender, keeping founder Aoife Grange's strategy intact. The new shareholders share the risk of the recycled-content venture, and the capital strengthens the balance sheet for future borrowing while the 110,000-unit output is established.

--- MAIN STEM ---
Westmoor Eco Panels (WEP) is a private limited company in the construction materials and recycled panel sector, employing a workforce of 31. Founded in 2015 by Rhys Westmoor, the business supplies composite wall panels to builders and operates a flat organisational structure with laissez-faire leadership. WEP plans to invest $690,000 in a recycled-composite panel line using agricultural waste fibre, financed by a $260,000 lease and $430,000 retained profit. It has fixed costs of $186,000 a year, a variable cost of $7.50 a unit and a selling price of $13.50, and produces 72,000 units of panel a year. WEP faces two problems: a shortage of trained machine operators and rising panel waste.

--- APPENDIX 1 — MARKETING/OPS ---
Operations and Waste Log — Q3 2025: The panel line produced 18,000 units last quarter at a defect rate of 2.2%, up from 1.4% a year ago. Waste fibre ran at 9.1% of input against a 6% target. Customer complaints rose from 22 to 35 per month. Average delivery to builders is 4.1 days. A survey of 520 building contractors found that 59% would pay up to $0.55 more for recycled-composite panels, and 51% check the environmental credentials of panel suppliers. A training audit shows 12 of 31 staff lack on-the-job training on the new pressing line; off-the-job courses at the college cost $820 per employee.

--- APPENDIX 2 — FINANCIAL DATA ---
Title: Extract from the Statement of Profit or Loss and Capital employed data of Westmoor Eco Panels for the year ended 31 March 2025 ($ '000)
Headers: ['Financial Metric', '2024', '2025']
Revenue | 800 | 960
Cost of sales | 480 | 528
Gross profit | 320 | 432
Operating profit | 96 | 144
Capital employed | 800 | 960
Interest payable | 15 | 20

--- APPENDIX 3 — EXTERNAL ENVIRONMENT ---
Economic and Business Bulletin (November 2026): (1) The central bank has raised the base interest rate from 4.25% to 5.00%, raising the cost of the $260,000 lease. (2) The national minimum wage will rise by 6.5% from $12.70 to $13.53 per hour from April 2026, raising total wage bills. (3) Recycled fibre, resin and transport input costs rose 12.1% year-on-year, while commercial building activity grew 2.2% over the same period.

--- QUESTIONS ---
  Q1(a) [8 marks]
    Question: WEP plans to fund its recycled-composite panel line with retained profit rather than the $260,000 lease. Explain two advantages for WEP of using the $430,000 retained profit instead of the lease.
    Answer: Point 1: Using $430,000 of retained profit avoids the regular rental payments and finance charges attached to the $260,000 lease, protecting cash flow while WEP already carries fixed costs of $186,000 a year. The saving can be used to reduce the 2.2% defect rate and the 9.1% waste fibre level, or absorbed if recycled fibre, resin and transport costs keep rising 12.1%, allowing the $13.50 selling price to hold for builders.

Point 2: Retained profit leaves ownership of the new panel line with Rhys Westmoor and the company, so there is no risk of the leased equipment being repossessed if the shortage of trained machine operators delays commissioning or panel waste stays high. The lease would lock WEP into fixed payments irrespective of the 35 monthly complaints. Internal funds also keep the $690,000 investment free of lender conditions and preserve borrowing capacity for later expansion of the recycled-composite range.
    Keywords: retained profit, lease, $430,000, $260,000, $690,000, $186,000
    Mark scheme: knowledge_max_2: 1 mark for each valid advantage identified (max 2). | application_analysis_max_6: Up to 3 marks per point for contextual explanation and analysis applied to WEP's cash flow, waste and ownership.

  Q1(b) [12 marks]
    Question: WEP is promoting its recycled-composite panels to building contractors. Consider advertising in a building trade magazine, sponsoring a construction exhibition, or a targeted social media campaign. Which should WEP choose? Justify your recommendation.
    Answer: Building trade magazine advertising: A trade magazine reaches contractors and can explain the agricultural waste fibre content and panel specifications, relevant to the 51% who check suppliers' environmental credentials. It is a credible medium that supports a $13.50 price. However, it is costly for a 31-employee company with a $260,000 lease, the readership is wider than WEP's builder base, and print cannot demonstrate the panels or react quickly to the 2.2% defect rate.

Construction exhibition sponsorship: A stand lets contractors see and handle the recycled-composite panels, ask about waste fibre and verify credentials face to face, directly addressing the 51% who check suppliers. It also supports the 59% who would pay $0.55 more by making quality visible. The drawbacks are the cost of a good stand, reach limited to attendees, and the fact that one exhibition cannot win orders for 72,000 units a year on its own.

Targeted social media campaign: Paid social ads can be aimed at regional builders and contractors, showing short videos of the pressing line and linking the $0.55 premium message to the environmental story. It applies to every panel, directly reduces the contribution that covers the $260,000 lease and supports the $690,000 investment, and cannot be removed by a refinancing decision. PAPER 2 — P2_SET_341
UNIT: Paper 2 Case Study

--- MAIN STEM ---
Marrowvale Organic Farms (MOF) is a private limited company in the agribusiness sector, growing and packing organic vegetables for regional supermarkets and veg-box subscribers. The business has a workforce of 42 and operates a flat structure with democratic leadership, with founder Priya Nandra consulting growers at weekly planning meetings. MOF plans to invest $720,000 in a new wash-and-grade packhouse with cold storage, financed by a $450,000 five-year bank loan and $270,000 retained profit. It has fixed costs of $252,000 a year, a variable cost of $5.20 a unit and a selling price of $12.20, and currently produces 82,000 units a year, where each unit is a packed carton. MOF faces two problems: 9.5% of harvested crates are rejected at grading for blemishing, and absenteeism among packing staff has reached 8%.

--- APPENDIX 1 — MARKETING/OPS ---
Operations and Quality Report - Q3 2025: MOF packed 19,600 cartons last quarter, of which 9.5% were rejected at grading for blemishing, up from 6.8% a year earlier. Organic veg-box complaints rose to 33 from 20 a month. Average delivery to the depot is 2.8 days. A survey of 500 subscribers found that 68% would pay up to $0.50 more for certified organic boxes and 57% choose farms with published waste-reduction plans. A trial of the new wash line on one bay cut rejected crates to 4.2% and reduced water use by 15%. A separate packaging trial showed recyclable cardboard boxes reduced transit bruising by 11% but added $0.12 to each box. A skills audit found 11 of 42 staff had not completed on-the-job training on the new grader; off-the-job training at the county college costs $780 per employee.

--- APPENDIX 2 — FINANCIAL DATA ---
Title: Extract from the Statement of Financial Position of Marrowvale Organic Farms as at 31 March 2025 ($ '000)
Headers: ['Financial Metric', '2024', '2025']
Inventories | 96 | 88
Trade receivables | 132 | 158
Cash and cash equivalents | 44 | 70
Current liabilities | 200 | 190
Non-current assets | 1,120 | 1,480
Capital employed | 1,400 | 1,720

--- APPENDIX 3 — EXTERNAL ENVIRONMENT ---
Economic and Agribusiness Bulletin (November 2026): (1) The central bank has raised the base interest rate from 4.5% to 5.25%, increasing the cost of variable-rate borrowing for capital investment. (2) The national minimum wage rises by 6.5% from $12.60 to $13.42 an hour from April 2026, raising the cost of packing crews. (3) Organic compost and feed input costs have risen 9.8% year-on-year, while average retail prices for organic vegetables rose only 3.1% and consumer spending on organic veg boxes grew 2.4%.

  Q1(a) [8 marks]
    Question: MOF plans to fund part of its $720,000 packhouse with a five-year bank loan. Explain two advantages for MOF of using retained profit instead of the bank loan to finance the investment.
    Answer: Point 1: Retained profit carries no interest charge and no fixed repayment schedule, which matters because MOF must cover fixed costs of $252,000 a year from a contribution of only $7.00 a carton ($12.20 − $5.20). Interest on a $450,000 loan would be a commitment in every month, including months when a poor harvest pushes the 9.5% rejection rate higher; keeping that cash inside the business protects the seasonal wage bill and the spending needed to cut rejected crates.

Point 2: Using MOF's own $270,000 removes the lender's security and conditions, so no bank can claim rights over the new wash-and-grade packhouse or veto the cropping plans that Priya Nandra agrees with growers at weekly meetings. Control stays with the existing owners, which suits the flat, democratic structure. The cost is that $270,000 of reserves can no longer act as a buffer if 8% absenteeism disrupts packing or if organic input costs keep rising.
    Keywords: retained profit, bank loan, $270,000, $450,000, $720,000, $252,000

    Answer: Organic trade magazines: A technical advert reaches supermarket produce buyers and wholesale decision-makers, and it can carry the evidence buyers now demand, such as the wash-line trial that cut rejected crates from 9.5% to 4.2%. Readership is small, and the message does not reach the 500 subscribers among whom 68% would pay $0.50 more.

Farmers' market tastings: Sampling at markets lets shoppers taste the vegetables and builds local loyalty, which supports the 57% who choose farms with waste-reduction plans. It is cheap and gives instant feedback, but each event reaches only a few hundred people, lasts a day, and is slow to grow the 19,600 cartons packed each quarter, so the link to the $720,000 packhouse is weak.

Social media campaign: A subscriber-facing campaign can show harvests, the wash line and recyclable cardboard boxes at low cost per view, with results measured click by click. It converts the 68% willing to pay $0.50 more into actual premium sales and reinforces the 2.8-day delivery story. It demands constant content and cannot present detailed quality evidence to supermarket buyers.

Recommendation: MOF should choose the social media campaign, supported by occasional market tastings. It targets the subscribers already identified in the survey, scales beyond a single market and costs far less than magazine advertising while the $450,000 loan is being serviced. Trade magazines are rejected because they miss the subscribers who will pay the premium, and market tastings are rejected as too small and short-lived to fill a packhouse built for 82,000 cartons a year.

    Question: Using Appendix 2, evaluate MOF's liquidity by calculating the current ratio and the acid test ratio for 2024 and 2025. Has MOF's financial position improved? Justify your answer.

--- MAIN STEM ---
Kestrel Creek Creamery (KCC) is a public limited company in the dairy processing sector, making milk, butter and soft cheese for supermarkets and food-service wholesalers. --- APPENDIX 1 — MARKETING/OPS ---

Customer complaints rose to 28 from 19 a month. Average delivery to supermarkets is 3.1 days. A trial of the new bottling line on one shift cut failed cartons to 3.2%. A skills audit found 9 of 37 staff had not completed on-the-job training on the filler; off-the-job training at the regional college costs $720 per employee.

--- APPENDIX 2 — FINANCIAL DATA ---

Headers: ['Financial Metric', '2024', '2025']

    Answer: Interest rate rise (4.75% to 5.5%): If the $360,000 bank loan is variable-rate, the 0.75 percentage-point rise adds 0.75% × $360,000 = $2,700 a year to interest. --- MAIN STEM ---
Harbourleaf Tea Company (HTC) is a partnership in the hot-beverage sector, blending and packing loose-leaf and bagged teas for cafes and supermarkets. The partnership has a workforce of 26 and operates a flat structure with laissez-faire leadership under founder Mei Treasury. HTC plans to invest $430,000 in a new blending and automated packing line, financed by a $250,000 bank loan and $180,000 retained profit. It has fixed costs of $154,000 a year, a variable cost of $3.10 a unit and a selling price of $8.10, and produces 58,000 units a year, where each unit is a tea caddy. HTC faces two problems: 12% labour turnover among packing staff and rising complaints about inconsistent blends.

--- APPENDIX 1 — MARKETING/OPS ---
Quality and Operations Extract - Q4 2025: HTC packed 14,200 caddies last quarter, with 6.3% of batches rejected for inconsistent blends, down from 9.1% a year earlier. Customer complaints rose to 24 from 15 a month. Average order fulfilment is 4.1 days. A survey of 420 cafe buyers found 66% would pay $0.40 more for single-origin certified tea and 53% check ethical sourcing before ordering. A trial of the new blender on one shift cut rejected batches to 2.7%. A skills audit found 8 of 26 staff had not completed on-the-job training on the new packing line; off-the-job training at the regional college costs $640 per employee.

--- APPENDIX 2 — FINANCIAL DATA ---

(3) Tea leaf and packaging input costs have risen 8.6% year-on-year, while retail tea prices rose only 1.8% and consumer spending on speciality tea grew 4.2%.

The insert gives no hours worked and no individual pay, so an annual total cannot be calculated honestly; the sound judgement is that 12% labour turnover forces repeated hiring at the higher rate, and unless productivity holds near 58,000 caddies from a workforce of 26, unit labour cost rises and the $5.00 contribution falls.

Tea leaf and packaging costs (up 8.6%): These feed the $3.10 variable cost on every caddy. The insert does not decompose that cost, so only a labelled upper bound is defensible: if the entire $3.10 were exposed, 8.6% × $3.10 = $0.27 a caddy, and at 58,000 caddies that is roughly $15,500 a year (58,000 × $0.2666). Even a smaller share cuts the $5.00 contribution on every unit, and retail tea prices rose only 1.8%, so little of the rise can be passed on.

Conclusion: The 8.6% rise in tea leaf and packaging costs will have the greatest impact. It recurs across all 58,000 caddies and directly erodes the $5.00 contribution that must repay the $250,000 loan and justify the $430,000 line, whereas the interest rise costs only $1,875 a year and can be capped by fixing the rate. The wage rise is second because it recurs with each new hire, but team working can offset part of it. HTC should cut the 6.3% rejection rate and seek the $0.40 premium instead of absorbing every increase.
    Keywords: 4.75%, 5.9%, 8.6%, $13.24, $250,000, $3.10
    Mark scheme: level_1_1_to_4: Identifies the external changes with limited application to HTC. | level_2_5_to_8: Analyses the impact of at least two changes on HTC's costs, prices or finance in context. | level_3_9_to_12: Detailed evaluation of all three changes with a justified judgement that input-cost inflation has the greatest impact and why the others are smaller.

PAPER 2 — P2_SET_344
UNIT: Paper 2 Case Study

--- MAIN STEM ---
Sunhill Citrus Packers (SCP) is a private limited company in the agribusiness sector, grading, waxing and exporting citrus fruit for overseas supermarket chains. The company has a workforce of 54 and operates a hierarchical structure with democratic leadership, with founder Rafael Sunhill consulting shift leaders each week. SCP plans to invest $880,000 in an automated grading and waxing line with a cold store, financed by a $520,000 five-year bank loan and $360,000 retained profit. It has fixed costs of $286,000 a year, a variable cost of $6.20 a unit and a selling price of $14.20, and produces 96,000 units a year, where each unit is a graded crate. SCP faces two problems: 8.6% of fruit is rejected for blemishing and absenteeism among graders has reached 11%.

--- APPENDIX 1 — MARKETING/OPS ---
Packing and Export Log - Q3 2025: SCP graded 24,600 crates last quarter, of which 8.6% were rejected for blemishing, up from 5.9% a year earlier. Export rejection notices rose to 36 from 22 a month. Average dispatch to the port is 3.4 days. A survey of 700 supermarket produce buyers found 61% would pay up to $0.60 more for waxed grade-A fruit and 49% require a residue-testing certificate before placing orders. A trial of the new optical grader cut rejections to 3.8%. A skills audit found 15 of 54 staff had not completed on-the-job training on the grader; off-the-job training at the provincial college costs $810 per employee.

--- APPENDIX 2 — FINANCIAL DATA ---
Title: Extract from the Statement of Financial Position of Sunhill Citrus Packers as at 31 March 2025 ($ '000)
Headers: ['Financial Metric', '2024', '2025']
Inventories | 210 | 190
Trade receivables | 260 | 298
Cash and cash equivalents | 70 | 96
Current liabilities | 360 | 340
Non-current assets | 1,860 | 2,240
Capital employed | 2,100 | 2,480

--- APPENDIX 3 — EXTERNAL ENVIRONMENT ---
Economic and Export Bulletin (November 2026): (1) The central bank has raised the base interest rate from 5.0% to 5.75%, increasing the cost of variable-rate borrowing for capital investment. (2) The national minimum wage rises by 7.0% from $13.00 to $13.91 an hour from April 2026, raising packing wages. (3) Fertiliser, wooden crating and freight input costs have risen 11.3% year-on-year, while export citrus prices rose only 2.6% and overseas demand for citrus grew 3.8%.

  Q1(a) [8 marks]
    Question: SCP plans to fund part of its $880,000 grading line and cold store with a five-year bank loan. Explain two advantages for SCP of using retained profit instead of the loan.
    Answer: Point 1: Retained profit carries no interest charge and no fixed repayment date, which matters because SCP must cover fixed costs of $286,000 a year from $8.00 contribution per crate ($14.20 − $6.20). Interest on a $520,000 loan would be payable even when the 8.6% rejection rate rises; using the $360,000 already earned keeps cash available to pay the 11%-absence-hit grading team and to fund quality improvements.

Point 2: Internal funds avoid the security and covenants a bank would require, so Rafael Sunhill and the shift leaders can run the new line without lender conditions attached to the cold store. Control stays with the company rather than a creditor. The cost is that $360,000 of reserves is no longer a buffer if export rejection notices keep climbing from 36 a month or freight costs keep rising, leaving SCP reliant on its 96,000-crate output to absorb shocks. Rafael Sunhill could phase the $880,000 project so retained profit funds the grader first and the $520,000 loan is drawn only when the 3.8% export demand growth justifies the cold store.
    Keywords: retained profit, bank loan, $360,000, $520,000, $880,000, $286,000

  Q1(b) [12 marks]
    Question: SCP wants to win more overseas listings for its graded citrus. Consider hosting buyer visits to the packing house, advertising in an export trade journal, or a social media campaign for consumers. Which should SCP choose? Justify your recommendation.
    Answer: Buyer visits to the packing house: Inviting supermarket buyers to see the optical grader lets them witness the fall in rejections from 8.6% to 3.8% and inspect the residue-testing process that 49% of buyers require. This builds trust and can secure listings directly, but it is time-consuming, only reaches a few buyers at a time, and diverts managers while the $880,000 line is being commissioned.

Export trade journal advertising: An advert in a specialist journal reaches many produce buyers at once and can carry the 3.8% trial result and the 3.4-day dispatch promise. It is cheaper than hosting visits, but print cannot demonstrate the fruit's quality, and readership may include buyers outside SCP's export markets, so part of the spend is wasted while a $520,000 loan is outstanding.

Social media campaign: A campaign can show the groves, grading and waxing to consumers in importing countries, supporting the 61% who would pay $0.60 more for waxed grade-A fruit and building pull-through for supermarket buyers. Engagement is measurable against the 24,600 crates graded last quarter, but results build slowly and consumer interest does not itself sign an export contract.

Recommendation: SCP should choose buyer visits to the packing house, supported by a small trade journal advert. Visits directly convert the 3.8% trial evidence and residue-testing proof into listings, which is what sells 96,000 crates a year. Journal advertising alone is rejected because print cannot demonstrate quality, and social media is rejected as an indirect consumer channel that cannot close an overseas order while the $520,000 loan must be serviced.

    Question: SCP must train 15 of 54 staff to use the new optical grader. Consider on-the-job training at the packing house or off-the-job training at the provincial college. Which should SCP choose? Justify your decision.

Decision: SCP should choose on-the-job training at the packing house, with a short certified college module for supervisors. It is cheaper, specific to the installed grader and avoids losing sorting capacity while 11% absenteeism is already disrupting shifts. Full off-the-job training is rejected because the $12,150 fee and lost shifts would slow the 24,600-crate operation and cannot directly reduce the 8.6% rejection rate.     Question: Using Appendix 2, evaluate SCP's liquidity by calculating the current ratio and the acid test ratio for 2024 and 2025. Has SCP's financial position improved? Justify your answer.
    Answer: Calculations:

Current Ratio 2025 = 1.72 : 1
Acid Test Ratio 2024 = 0.92 : 1

--- MAIN STEM ---
Quarryfield Ale Brewers (QAB) is a cooperative in the beverage sector, brewing craft ale for independent retailers and taprooms. The cooperative has a workforce of 33 and operates a flat structure with democratic leadership, with founder Elin Quarryfield putting major decisions to member votes. QAB plans to invest $680,000 in new fermentation tanks and a canning line, financed by a $420,000 bank overdraft and $260,000 retained surplus. It has fixed costs of $245,000 a year, a variable cost of $5.10 a unit and a selling price of $12.10, and produces 80,000 units a year, where each unit is a can of ale. QAB faces two problems: 6.8% of cans are rejected for leaking seals and absenteeism among brewing staff has reached 9.5%.

--- APPENDIX 1 — MARKETING/OPS ---
Brewery Quality Log - Q4 2025: QAB filled 17,800 cans last quarter, of which 6.8% were rejected for leaking seals, down from 10.2% a year earlier. Taproom complaints rose to 29 from 18 a month. Average delivery to distributors is 2.9 days. A survey of 560 ale drinkers found 63% would pay $0.45 more for locally brewed craft ale in recyclable cans and 55% check brewery provenance before buying. A trial of the new canning line cut rejected cans to 2.9%. A skills audit found 10 of 33 workers had not completed on-the-job training on the canning line; off-the-job training at the technical college costs $700 per employee.

--- APPENDIX 2 — FINANCIAL DATA ---

(3) Barley, hops and aluminium input costs have risen 14.2% year-on-year, while craft ale retail prices rose 3.4% and consumer spending on local ale grew 5.2%.

Acid Test Ratio 2025 = 1.16 : 1

Dividing by current liabilities gives $224,000 ÷ $170,000 = 1.32 and $264,000 ÷ $162,000 = 1.63. Excluding inventories: ($224,000 − $84,000) ÷ $170,000 = $140,000 ÷ $170,000 = 0.82, and ($264,000 − $76,000) ÷ $162,000 = $188,000 ÷ $162,000 = 1.16.

Evaluation: Short-term liquidity improved on both measures. Current liabilities fell from $170,000 to $162,000 while current assets rose from $224,000 to $264,000, helped by cash rising from $38,000 to $62,000. The stricter test, which removes ale stock that may be rejected for leaking seals, moved from 0.82 to 1.16, so QAB can now meet short-term debts from cash and receivables alone instead of relying on the $76,000 of inventory. That matters while the cooperative uses $260,000 of surplus and carries a $420,000 overdraft for the $680,000 project. The caution is that receivables rose from $102,000 to $126,000, so retailers and distributors are holding more of QAB's cash, and 9.5% absence plus 6.8% seal failures could add costs faster than the ratios suggest.

Conclusion: QAB's financial position has improved. Both measures rose and the 1.16 figure shows the gain does not depend on unsold stock, giving the cooperative more headroom to meet bills. Rising receivables are the main risk, so Elin Quarryfield should tighten credit control with distributors before drawing more on the $420,000 overdraft.
    Keywords: 1.32, 1.63, 0.82, 1.16, $224,000, $264,000, $680,000
    Mark scheme: level_1_1_to_4: States figures or changes without accurate ratio calculations. | level_2_5_to_8: Accurately calculates the current ratio and acid test ratio for both years with contextual analysis of the trend. | level_3_9_to_12: Accurate calculations for both years with detailed evaluation of inventory, receivables and liability movements and a justified conclusion on whether liquidity improved.

    Question: Using Appendix 3, evaluate how the interest rate rise to 5.25%, the 6.4% minimum wage increase and the 14.2% rise in barley, hops and aluminium costs will affect QAB. Which change will have the greatest impact? Justify your answer.
    Answer: Interest rate rise (4.5% to 5.25%): If the $420,000 overdraft remains drawn, the 0.75 percentage-point rise adds 0.75% × $420,000 = $3,150 a year to interest, and unlike a term loan an overdraft is variable-rate, so the cost arrives quickly. --- MAIN STEM ---
Marden Industrial Pumpworks (MIPW) is a private limited company in the industrial machinery sector, manufacturing precision pumps for water-treatment plants and supplying municipal contracts across two regions, with a workforce of 60. Founded in 2007 by Anja Marden, it operates a hierarchical structure with autocratic leadership. MIPW plans to invest $720,000 in a CNC machining cell for pump impellers, financed by a $450,000 ten-year bank loan and $270,000 retained profit. It has fixed costs of $360,000 a year, a variable cost of $18.00 a unit and a selling price of $30.00, and produces 40,000 units a year. MIPW faces a 5.5% defect rate on impeller castings and rising scrap levels that threaten distributor deliveries under tight customer windows.

--- APPENDIX 1 — MARKETING/OPS ---
Operations and Quality Log — Q4 2025: The impeller line inspected 9,800 units last quarter at a defect rate of 5.5%, down from 7.2% a year earlier. Customer complaints fell from 41 to 26 per month. Average supplier lead time is 21 days. Market research of 500 water-treatment buyers found that 68% would pay up to $0.90 more for certified precision impellers, and 57% check supplier quality records before ordering. Rework on defective castings cost $6,800 last quarter.

--- APPENDIX 2 — FINANCIAL DATA ---

Capital employed | 1,500 | 1,850

(2) The national minimum wage rose 5.8% to $14.60 per hour from April 2026. (3) Steel and cast-iron input prices rose 9.6% year-on-year while industrial machinery price inflation ran at 6.3% and business confidence fell 2.1 points.

  Q1(a) [8 marks]
    Question: MIPW plans to fund part of its CNC machining cell with a ten-year bank loan. Explain two advantages for MIPW of using retained profit to fund the expansion instead of the bank loan.
    Answer: Point 1: Using the $270,000 retained profit costs MIPW no interest or scheduled repayments, protecting cash flow while the business already carries fixed costs of $360,000 a year and a $450,000 bank loan. Every dollar saved can absorb the 9.6% rise in steel and cast-iron input costs, helping Anja Marden keep the $30.00 selling price competitive on municipal water-treatment contracts without borrowing more.

Point 2: Retained profit does not require collateral or give a lender power to repossess the new CNC cell if demand slips, so the $720,000 investment is safer. It also preserves the existing owners' control: no bank can impose conditions on how the 60-worker site is run, which matters when a 5.5% defect rate is already straining output and management needs freedom to re organise production quickly.

For a firm of 60 employees producing 40,000 units, the choice also affects risk: retained profit is internal and already earned, so it cannot be withdrawn by a lender if the 5.5% defect rate pushes rework above the $6,800 spent last quarter. Founder Anja Marden keeps control of the $720,000 cell and can redirect the $270,000 if municipal orders slip. By contrast, servicing the $450,000 loan on top of $360,000 fixed costs would consume contribution from the 30,000 units needed to break even, so internal funding protects the 10,000-unit margin of safety.

    Answer: Trade journal advertising: Print and online trade journals reach precisely the municipal and water-treatment engineers who buy precision impellers, and they are relatively cheap for a 60-employee firm. The drawback is that a static advert cannot demonstrate machining accuracy, and readership is narrow, so it may not generate the volume needed to justify the $720,000 CNC cell.

Reach is slow and travel costs mount, but each visit targets a genuine prospective contract.

Technical visits give engineers the certification evidence behind the 68% premium acceptance, and results from the 9,800 inspected units can be shown directly. A campaign that merely builds awareness would not fix the 5.5% defect rate that caused 26 monthly complaints, so spending on broad reach before quality is consistent would waste cash needed for the $450,000 loan.

Recommendation: MIPW should choose direct technical sales visits, supported by short trade-journal adverts. They convert the 68% acceptance of a premium into orders and demonstrate quality personally. Exhibition sponsorship is rejected as too expensive and risky while the defect rate is unresolved; journals alone are rejected as too passive to sell a precision component.

  Q2(b) [12 marks]
    Question: MIPW wants to cut its 5.5% defect rate. Consider final inspection (quality control) or prevention through quality assurance and operator training. Which should MIPW choose? Justify your decision.
    Answer: Final inspection (quality control): Checking finished impellers would catch defective castings before dispatch, protecting the 26-per-month complaint figure and the $30.00 price. It costs time and requires a culture change from autocratic leadership, and results appear more slowly than inspection.

Implementation should be measured: MIPW can drive the 5.5% rate lower (it has already fallen from 7.2%) and require the $6,800 rework bill to fall, with weekly review under the democratic style. Training must cover all 60 workers because the CNC cell changes every impeller setting; excluding one shift would leave a skills gap. The insert gives no course fees or training hours, so no exact cost or payback is asserted; the recommendation rests on attacking the source of the defect and protecting the 10,000-unit margin of safety at 40,000 units.

Decision: MIPW should choose prevention through quality assurance and operator training, retaining only light final sampling. It removes the $6,800 rework bill at source and protects the margin of safety. Pure inspection is rejected because it finds faults after the cost is incurred, and training alone without process checks would not give the consistent tolerances water-treatment buyers demand.

--- MAIN STEM ---
Norhaven Technical Fasteners (NTF) is a public limited company in the metal components sector, producing threaded fasteners for construction equipment and exporting to three continents, with a workforce of 85. Founded in 1998 by Soren Norhaven, it uses a flat organisational structure and laissez-faire leadership. NTF will invest $1,080,000 in an automated thread-rolling line, financed by a $600,000 share issue, a $300,000 bank loan and $180,000 retained profit. It has fixed costs of $420,000 a year, a variable cost of $14.00 a unit and a selling price of $26.00, and produces 60,000 units a year. NTF suffers labour turnover of 14% and a 3.4% defect rate on threaded components, delaying shipments to distributors.

--- APPENDIX 1 — MARKETING/OPS ---
Quality and Operations Log — Q2 2025: 15,200 fasteners were sampled; the defect rate was 3.4%, down from 5.1%. There were 47 customer complaints about thread stripping, against 61 a year before. Average delivery lead time is 18 days and 91% of orders arrive on time. Rework cost $7,200 last quarter. A survey of 350 purchasing managers found 63% value certified thread quality and 49% would switch supplier for a 2% price cut.

--- APPENDIX 2 — FINANCIAL DATA ---
Title: Extract from the Statement of Financial Position of Norhaven Technical Fasteners as at 31 March 2025 ($ '000)
Headers: ['Financial Metric', '2024', '2025']
Inventories | 210 | 195
Trade receivables | 165 | 185
Cash and cash equivalents | 55 | 80
Current liabilities | 250 | 230
Non-current assets | 1,540 | 2,320
Capital employed | 1,900 | 2,280

--- APPENDIX 3 — EXTERNAL ENVIRONMENT ---
Economic and Business Bulletin (November 2026): (1) The base interest rate rose from 4.50% to 5.25%, raising the cost of bank borrowing. (2) The minimum wage increased 4.9% to $13.80 per hour. (3) Alloy steel and nickel input costs rose 11.2% year-on-year, while engineering wage inflation reached 5.6% and export demand grew 2.4%.

--- QUESTIONS ---
  Q1(a) [8 marks]
    Question: NTF plans to finance part of its thread-rolling line with a bank loan. Explain two advantages for NTF of using a share issue rather than the bank loan.
    Answer: Point 1: A $600,000 share issue brings equity that needs no interest and no fixed repayment dates, leaving the $300,000 bank loan as the only debt commitment. With fixed costs of $420,000 a year and output of 60,000 units, that protects cash flow and lets Soren Norhaven direct funds to reducing the 3.4% defect rate rather than servicing debt.

Point 2: Equity widens NTF's shareholder base and spreads the risk of the $1,080,000 investment across investors instead of pledging company assets. As a public limited company it can access many shareholders, so the automated line can be funded without pushing the 85-worker business further into borrowing, though existing shareholders would be diluted.

For a public limited company with 85 workers and $420,000 fixed costs, equity also avoids the risk that a 5.25% base rate raises the $300,000 loan cost further. Shareholders share the risk of the $1,080,000 line in return for dividends, whereas a lender must be paid whether or not the 3.4% defect rate is fixed, so the $600,000 issue protects the 25,000-unit margin of safety.
    Keywords: share issue, bank loan, $600,000, $300,000, $1,080,000, $420,000
    Mark scheme: knowledge_max_2: 1 mark for each valid point identified (max 2). | application_analysis_max_6: Up to 3 marks per point for detailed contextual explanation and analysis applied to the named business.

  Q1(b) [12 marks]
    Question: NTF is launching a certified thread-quality range. Consider trade-journal advertising, an industry exhibition, or technical webinars for purchasing managers. Which should NTF choose to promote the launch? Justify your recommendation.
    Answer: Trade-journal advertising: Specialist engineering journals reach the 63% of surveyed managers who value certified thread quality at low cost per reader, but static pages cannot prove the 3.4% defect rate improvement and the message is easily ignored.

Industry exhibition: An exhibition allows live demonstration of the thread-rolling line and face-to-face discussion of the 18-day lead time and 91% on-time record. It suits a component sold on trust. Yet stand costs are high and with 14% labour turnover the staff showing the product may lack product knowledge, and only a small number of buyers attend.

Technical webinars: Live online sessions can show tolerance data to purchasing managers across three continents, record the session for later viewing and directly address the 49% who would switch for a 2% price cut. Webinars collect qualified leads across three continents and address the 49% who would switch for a 2% price cut, whereas a broad exhibition audience would not justify the $1,080,000 commitment.

Certification evidence from the 15,200 sampled fasteners should be shown in each session, since 63% of managers value it.

Recommendation: NTF should choose technical webinars, backed by short journal adverts. They reach the exact surveyed audience cheaply and demonstrate certification across export markets. Exhibitions are rejected as costly and exposed by labour turnover; journals alone are rejected because they cannot demonstrate quality.
    Keywords: $1,080,000, 60,000, workforce of 85, 3.4%, 15,200, 63%
    Mark scheme: level_1_1_to_4: Identifies relevant factors with limited application to the named business. | level_2_5_to_8: Discussion of at least two promotional options applied to NTF with emerging judgement. | level_3_9_to_12: Discussion of all three options in context with a justified recommendation that rejects exhibitions and journals.

  Q2(a) [8 marks]
    Question: NTF has labour turnover of 14% and uses laissez-faire leadership. Explain two benefits for NTF of introducing regular appraisal and team working for its workforce of 85.
    Answer: Point 1: Regular appraisal gives each of the 85 workers feedback and agreed targets, replacing the drift that laissez-faire leadership can allow on the thread-rolling line. Clear expectations and recognition address the causes of 14% labour turnover, keeping skilled operators who are needed to sustain the fall in defect rate from 5.1% to 3.4% and protect the $1,080,000 investment.

Under Maslow's social and esteem needs, belonging to a team raises commitment, so delivery lead time of 18 days and the 91% on-time rate are more likely to hold while production reaches 60,000 units.

--- MAIN STEM ---
Preston Gearbox Assemblies (PGB) is a worker cooperative in the automotive components sector, assembling gearboxes for commercial vehicles and supplying two domestic fleet operators, with a workforce of 42. PGB faces absenteeism of 8% and a 2.7% defect rate in final gear assembly, which is straining its delivery schedule.

--- APPENDIX 1 — MARKETING/OPS ---

There were 19 formal quality complaints from commercial-vehicle customers. Average assembly time is 42 minutes per unit. A survey of 240 drivers and fleet buyers found 72% rate gear reliability as the top purchase factor and 55% would pay $0.70 more for a two-year warranty.

--- MAIN STEM ---
Ridgeway Quality Castings (RQC) is a private limited company in the foundry sector, making iron castings for agricultural machinery and serving four regional equipment makers, with a workforce of 110. Founded in 2003 by Tomas Ridgeway, it operates a hierarchical structure with democratic leadership. RQC plans to invest $960,000 in a sand-casting moulding line using recycled metal feedstock, financed by a $560,000 bank loan and $400,000 retained profit. It has fixed costs of $480,000 a year, a variable cost of $16.00 a unit and a selling price of $28.00, and produces 50,000 units a year. RQC reports waste of 6.8% and labour turnover of 12%, raising unit costs across the foundry.

--- APPENDIX 1 — MARKETING/OPS ---
Foundry Operations Report — Q1 2025: 12,400 castings were poured; the scrap rate was 6.8%, down from 9.3%. There were 54 quality complaints from agricultural-machinery customers. Energy use is 3.4 kWh per casting, and 78% of melt is recycled. Average order lead time is 23 days. A survey of 410 buyers found 66% prefer castings with recycled content and 58% would pay $0.80 more for certified low-waste production.

--- APPENDIX 2 — FINANCIAL DATA ---
Title: Extract from the Statement of Financial Position of Ridgeway Quality Castings as at 31 March 2025 ($ '000)
Headers: ['Financial Metric', '2024', '2025']

(2) The minimum wage went up 6.2% to $13.90 per hour. (3) Scrap-metal and energy input costs rose 10.5% year-on-year, while foundry equipment inflation was 7.4% and agricultural machinery demand fell 1.6%.

--- QUESTIONS ---
  Q1(a) [8 marks]
    Question: RQC plans to fund its sand-casting line with a bank loan. Explain two advantages for RQC of using retained profit instead of the bank loan.
    Answer: Point 1: Using $400,000 retained profit avoids interest on that part of the $960,000 scheme, easing cash flow while RQC already carries fixed costs of $480,000 a year and a $560,000 loan. The saving can be spent on reducing the 6.8% waste rate and the $13.90 wage pressure, protecting the $12.00 contribution on 50,000 castings.

Point 2: Retained profit needs no security and leaves control with Tomas Ridgeway, so the hierarchical structure can act quickly on the 12% labour turnover problem without lender conditions. It also avoids piling more debt onto a foundry already exposed to the 4.75% base rate.

For a foundry with 110 workers and $480,000 fixed costs, retained profit also avoids the 4.75% rate environment on $400,000 of the scheme. The $560,000 loan must still be served, but keeping the $400,000 internal protects the $12.00 contribution on 50,000 castings and the 10,000-unit margin of safety while 12% turnover is tackled.

--- MAIN STEM ---
Thistle & Loom Retail (TLR) is a private limited company in the online fashion retail sector, employing a workforce of 60. Founded in 2016 by Fiona Thistlewaite, the business sells knitwear and lifestyle clothing through its own e-commerce website and operates a flat organisational structure with democratic leadership. TLR plans to invest $420,000 in a new automated e-commerce fulfilment centre with computer stock control, financed by a $300,000 ten-year bank loan and $120,000 retained profit. It has fixed costs of $180,000 a year, a variable cost of $18.00 a unit and a selling price of $30.00, and currently produces 24,000 units a year. TLR faces two problems: labour turnover has reached 16% and its online return rate is 14%, with picking errors rising.

--- APPENDIX 1 — MARKETING/OPS ---
Operations and E-commerce Report — Q3 2025: The online store fulfilled 6,200 orders last quarter with a picking error rate of 2.1%, down from 3.6% a year earlier. Product returns ran at 14% of orders, costing an average $22 per parcel. Customer complaints fell from 44 to 19 per month. Average delivery time is 4.1 days. A survey of 500 online fashion shoppers found that 71% value fast delivery and 58% would switch brand after a returns problem. A training needs analysis shows 18 of 60 staff have not been trained on the new computer stock-control system; off-the-job courses at the local college cost $750 per employee.

--- APPENDIX 2 — FINANCIAL DATA ---
Title: Extract from the Statement of Financial Position of Thistle & Loom Retail as at 31 March 2025 ($ '000)
Headers: ['Financial Metric', '2024', '2025']
Inventories | 90 | 75
Trade receivables | 60 | 80
Cash and cash equivalents | 30 | 45
Current liabilities | 120 | 100
Non-current assets | 600 | 850
Capital employed | 660 | 950

--- APPENDIX 3 — EXTERNAL ENVIRONMENT ---
Economic and Business Bulletin (November 2026): (1) The central bank has raised the base interest rate from 3.75% to 4.25%, increasing borrowing costs for businesses with variable-rate loans. (2) The national minimum wage will rise by 5.0% from $13.00 to $13.65 per hour from April 2026, raising total wage bills. (3) Wholesale cotton and synthetic fabric input costs have risen 9.5% year-on-year, while online fashion consumer spending grew 4.2% in the same period.

--- QUESTIONS ---
  Q1(a) [8 marks]
    Question: TLR plans to finance part of its $420,000 expansion with a ten-year bank loan. Explain two advantages for TLR of using retained profit to fund the expansion instead of the bank loan.
    Answer: Point 1: Using the $120,000 of retained profit costs TLR no interest or capital repayments, which protects cash flow at a time when the firm already carries fixed costs of $180,000 a year and a $300,000 bank loan. Every dollar not paid to the lender can absorb the 9.5% rise in cotton and fabric input costs, letting TLR hold its $30.00 selling price and protect the $12.00 contribution per unit on each of its 24,000 units. This matters when the online return rate is already 14% and each returned parcel costs an average $22.

Point 2: Retained profit avoids the security and repayment risk of the bank loan, so the automated fulfilment centre is not exposed to repossession if demand for the new range disappoints. It also preserves Fiona Thistlewaite's ownership and control: no lender can impose covenants on how the e-commerce operation is run, which fits the flat, democratic structure and lets TLR react quickly to the 16% labour turnover problem without seeking external approval.

  Q1(b) [12 marks]
    Question: TLR is launching a new knitwear range through its e-commerce website. Consider a national television campaign, local radio sponsorship, or social-media influencer marketing. Which should TLR choose to promote the launch? Justify your recommendation.

  Q3(b) [12 marks]
    Question: Using Appendix 2, evaluate TLR's liquidity position by calculating the current ratio and the acid test ratio for 2024 and 2025. Has TLR's liquidity improved? Justify your answer.
    Answer: Calculations:
Current Ratio 2024 = 1.50 : 1
Current Ratio 2025 = 2.00 : 1
Acid Test Ratio 2024 = 0.75 : 1
Acid Test Ratio 2025 = 1.25 : 1

Detailed workings: 2024 current assets = $90,000 inventories + $60,000 trade receivables + $30,000 cash = $180,000; 2025 current assets = $75,000 + $80,000 + $45,000 = $200,000. The 2024 liquidity comparison is $180,000 ÷ $120,000 = 1.50; for 2025 it is $200,000 ÷ $100,000 = 2.00. The stricter 2024 measure is ($180,000 − $90,000) ÷ $120,000 = $90,000 ÷ $120,000 = 0.75; for 2025 it is ($200,000 − $75,000) ÷ $100,000 = $125,000 ÷ $100,000 = 1.25.

Evaluation: Short-term solvency has clearly strengthened. The broader measure rose from 1.50 to 2.00 as current liabilities fell from $120,000 to $100,000 while current assets rose from $180,000 to $200,000. The stricter measure, which strips out inventories, improved from 0.75 to 1.25, so TLR no longer depends on selling stock to meet short-term debts — important while it services a $300,000 bank loan and funds a $420,000 fulfilment centre. The stronger of the two signals is the stricter measure, because it still exceeds 1.0 without relying on inventory that may be slow to sell given the 14% return rate. The main residual risk is trade receivables rising from $60,000 to $80,000, tying up cash; if online shoppers or wholesale customers pay late, the improvement could unravel, and inventories fell from $90,000 to $75,000, which may limit stock available for peak fashion demand.

Conclusion: TLR's liquidity has improved. Both the broader measure (1.50 to 2.00) and the stricter measure (0.75 to 1.25) show stronger short-term solvency, and the gain does not rest on inventory. The outstanding concern is rising trade receivables, so TLR should tighten credit control while proceeding with the expansion.

    Question: Explain one advantage and one disadvantage for TLR of introducing an automated computer stock-control system in its new fulfilment centre.
    Answer: Advantage: Computer stock control gives real-time inventory counts, which directly attacks the 2.1% picking error rate and the 14% return rate by ensuring the correct item and size is dispatched.   Q4(b) [12 marks]
    Question: Using Appendix 3, evaluate how the base interest rate rise to 4.25%, the 5.0% minimum wage increase and the 9.5% rise in fabric input costs will affect TLR. Which change will have the greatest impact? Justify your answer.
    Answer: Interest rate rise (3.75% to 4.25%): If TLR's $300,000 ten-year bank loan is variable-rate, the annual interest cost rises by 0.5% of $300,000 = $1,500 a year (0.005 × $300,000). That is modest next to $180,000 fixed costs, and if the loan is fixed-rate the direct effect is zero. Higher base rates may still make consumers more cautious about discretionary fashion spending and raise the cost of any future borrowing for the $420,000 centre, but TLR can largely neutralise this by fixing the loan rate.

Minimum wage increase (5.0%, to $13.65 per hour): With a workforce of 60 in packing and fulfilment, this feeds into the wage bill and is not optional. The insert gives no hours worked or individual pay, so no defensible annual total can be invented; the honest test is productivity — 24,000 units ÷ 60 staff = 400 units per worker. A wage rise is affordable only if productivity holds at that level or output grows, otherwise unit labour cost rises and the $12.00 contribution per unit is squeezed.

Fabric input-cost inflation (9.5%): The insert never decomposes the $18.00 variable cost, so only an explicitly labelled bound can be computed: if the whole variable cost rose 9.5%, that adds 9.5% × $18.00 = $1.71 a unit; at 24,000 units a year this is about $41,040 a year (24,000 × $1.71). Even a partial pass-through would cut contribution per unit materially, and the 14% return rate means some of this cost is wasted. TLR can recover part through price negotiations and better stock control, but the pressure is continuous.

Conclusion: The 9.5% rise in fabric input costs will have the greatest impact. It applies to every one of the 24,000 units and directly erodes the $12.00 contribution that justifies the $420,000 expansion, whereas the interest rise is around $1,500 a year on a fixed-sum loan and can be hedged, and the wage effect depends on 400-unit productivity that management can influence through training.

    Mark scheme: level_1_1_to_4: Identifies the external changes with limited application to TLR. | level_2_5_to_8: Analyses the impact of at least two external changes on TLR's costs, revenue or financing in context. | level_3_9_to_12: Detailed evaluation of all three external changes applied to TLR with a well-justified judgement that fabric input-cost inflation has the greatest impact and why the other two are smaller.
