It has fixed costs of $252,000 a year, a variable cost of $5.00 a unit and a selling price of $17.00, and currently produces 63,000 units a year. QBD faces two problems: its app crash rate has risen to 3.1% and its product-return rate is 6.4%, damaging its reputation with retail clients.

A survey of 420 smartphone users found that 75% discovered new apps through social media, 63% trusted influencer recommendations and 41% used QR codes in-store. In-house code-review training costs $340 per developer; external certification courses cost $1,250 each.

Keeping the $240,000 in the business means every dollar not paid to a lender can be spent on code-review training at $340 per developer to cut crashes, or on fixing the 6.4% product-return rate. --- MAIN STEM ---
Brighthaven Private Clinic (BPC) is a private limited company in the healthcare sector, operating private outpatient screening clinics and employing a workforce of 60. Founded in 2011 by Dr Elena Brightwell, it runs a hierarchical structure with democratic leadership. BPC plans to invest $720,000 in a new diagnostic imaging suite, financed by a $450,000 ten-year bank loan and $270,000 retained profit. It has fixed costs of $360,000 a year, a variable cost of $40 a unit and a selling price of $100, and currently produces 12,000 units a year, each a standard screening package. BPC faces two problems: staff absenteeism has reached 11% and patient complaints about waiting times are rising. Its Q3 quality report shows a 2.4% re-scan rate.

--- APPENDIX 1 — MARKETING/OPS ---
Quality and Operations Report — Q3 2025: The screening unit delivered 3,100 screening packages last quarter at a re-scan rate of 2.4%, down from 4.0% a year ago. Patient complaints about waiting times fell from 46 to 19 per month. Average appointment turnaround is 28 minutes. A survey of 500 patients found that 68% would pay up to $8 more for same-day results, and 55% rank short waiting times as the top factor when choosing a clinic. Staff records show 14 of 60 employees have not completed on-the-job training on the new imaging software; external certification courses cost $750 per employee.

--- APPENDIX 2 — FINANCIAL DATA ---
Title: Extract from the Statement of Profit or Loss and Capital employed data of Brighthaven Private Clinic for the year ended 31 March 2025 ($ '000)
Headers: ['Financial Metric', '2024', '2025']
Revenue | 1,800 | 2,000
Cost of sales | 1,080 | 1,100
Gross profit | 720 | 900
Operating profit | 180 | 250
Capital employed | 1,000 | 1,250
Interest payable | 40 | 50

--- APPENDIX 3 — EXTERNAL ENVIRONMENT ---
Economic and Business Bulletin (November 2026): (1) The central bank has raised the base interest rate from 4.0% to 4.8%, increasing borrowing costs for businesses with variable-rate loans. (2) The national minimum wage will rise by 5.5% from $13.00 to $13.72 per hour from April 2026, raising wage bills for clinical and reception staff. (3) Medical supply input costs have risen 9.4% year-on-year and private screening prices are under pressure, while consumer spending on private health screening grew 2.8%.

--- QUESTIONS ---
  Q1(a) [8 marks]
    Question: BPC plans to fund part of its $720,000 imaging suite with a $450,000 ten-year bank loan. Explain two advantages for BPC of using retained profit to fund the expansion instead of the bank loan.
    Answer: Point 1: Using retained profit of $270,000 costs BPC no interest charges or capital repayments, which protects cash flow while the clinic already carries fixed costs of $360,000 a year and a $450,000 loan commitment. With contribution of $60 on each $100 screening package, every dollar of interest saved can help absorb the 9.4% rise in medical supply costs reported in the bulletin, allowing BPC to hold its selling price at $100 rather than passing costs on to patients.

Point 2: Retained profit avoids the collateral and default risk attached to a bank loan, so the new imaging suite cannot be repossessed if demand for screening disappoints. It also preserves Dr Elena Brightwell's ownership and control: no external lender can impose conditions on how the diagnostic service is run or on the 12,000 units a year target, and BPC avoids adding to the interest payable of $40,000 shown in Appendix 2.
    Keywords: retained profit, $270,000, $450,000, $720,000, $360,000, $100
    Mark scheme: knowledge_max_2: 1 mark for each valid advantage identified (max 2). | application_analysis_max_6: Up to 3 marks per point for contextual explanation and analysis applied to BPC, its financing mix and its screening operation.

  Q1(b) [12 marks]
    Question: BPC is promoting its new diagnostic imaging suite. Consider a national television campaign, local newspaper advertising, or social media marketing. Which should BPC choose to attract private patients? Justify your recommendation.
    Answer: National television campaign: Television delivers mass awareness quickly and could build the BPC brand across the whole country. However, airtime and production are extremely costly for a business funding a $720,000 imaging suite with a $450,000 loan, and most viewers would be outside BPC's clinic catchment or unlikely to self-fund a $100 screening, so much of the spend would be wasted.

Local newspaper advertising: Print is far cheaper than television and reaches patients in BPC's immediate area, and it suits a message about same-day results at a local clinic. Its weakness is narrow, ageing readership: it cannot build the brand beyond one catchment, which is a problem when the new suite must help reach the 12,000-unit annual target, and it gives no way to demonstrate the 28-minute turnaround.

Social media marketing: Targeted social advertising can reach exactly the patients in BPC's research — the 68% of 500 surveyed who would pay $8 more for same-day results and the 55% who rank short waiting times first. It allows BPC to show the faster turnaround and new scanner visually, measures engagement cheaply, and scales nationally without television's waste. It builds trust more slowly for a clinical service and depends on credible health content, but cost per relevant patient is low.

Recommendation: BPC should choose social media marketing. It targets the segment already identified in the survey, is far cheaper than television, and reaches beyond the local newspaper's catchment while supporting the same-day-results message. Television is rejected as unaffordable and untargeted for a 60-employee clinic, and local newspaper advertising is rejected as too narrow; BPC can add a small print notice for older patients later.
    Keywords: 68%, 500, $8, 55%, $720,000, 60
    Mark scheme: level_1_1_to_4: Limited identification of the promotional options with minimal reference to BPC. | level_2_5_to_8: Discussion of advantages and disadvantages of at least two options with some application to BPC and partial judgement. | level_3_9_to_12: Detailed evaluation of all three options in the context of BPC with a well-justified recommendation that explains why television and local newspaper advertising are rejected.

  Q2(a) [8 marks]
    Question: BPC's staff absenteeism has reached 11% and patient complaints about waiting times are rising. Explain two benefits for BPC of introducing team working to improve attendance and reduce complaints.
    Answer: Point 1: Team working allows BPC's 60 staff to cover one another's shifts when absenteeism reaches 11%, so the screening list keeps moving and appointment turnaround stays near the 28 minutes reported in Appendix 1. When colleagues share patient preparation and scanning tasks, no single absence closes the imaging suite, which protects the 12,000 units a year needed to justify the $720,000 investment and reduces the waiting-time complaints patients are making.

Point 2: Working in teams spreads practical knowledge about the new imaging software, so the 14 of 60 employees still untrained can learn from colleagues during normal shifts rather than waiting for a course. Shared problem-solving cuts the 2.4% re-scan rate and improves service quality, while group loyalty raises commitment and helps bring absenteeism down, easing pressure on Dr Elena Brightwell's hierarchical structure.
    Keywords: 11%, 60, 28 minutes, 14, 2.4%, $720,000
    Mark scheme: knowledge_max_2: 1 mark for each valid benefit identified (max 2). | application_analysis_max_6: Up to 3 marks per point for detailed contextual explanation linked to BPC's absenteeism, turnaround time and quality data.

  Q2(b) [12 marks]
    Question: BPC must upskill 14 clinical staff on the new imaging software. Consider on-the-job training or external certification courses costing $750 per employee. Which should BPC choose? Justify your decision.
    Answer: On-the-job training: Training at the scanner teaches BPC's own routines and quality standards, costs no course fees, and keeps the 14 staff productive while they learn, protecting the 3,100 screening packages delivered last quarter. It also lets senior operators mentor colleagues and directly tackles the fact that 14 of 60 employees are untrained. The drawbacks are that trainers are working staff whose own output falls, bad habits can spread, and there is no external certificate, which may matter if private insurers ask for formal records.

External certification courses: At $750 per employee, training all 14 costs $10,500 (14 × $750), which is small beside the $720,000 suite but still a real cash outflow. Courses give structured, up-to-date skills and a recognised certificate, and remove staff from the distracting clinic floor. The weaknesses are that 14 of a 60-strong workforce would be off the rota, worsening the 11% absenteeism problem, and generic course content may not match BPC's exact scanner settings, so follow-up coaching would still be needed.

Decision: BPC should choose on-the-job training for the rollout, with short external certification for a few lead operators. On-the-job training is cheaper, machine-specific and avoids losing capacity while absence is already 11%; full external training is rejected because $10,500 plus 14 staff off the rota would disrupt the screening service for little extra relevance.
    Keywords: on-the-job training, $750, 14, 60, 3,100, 11%

    Question: Using Appendix 3, evaluate how the base interest rate rise to 4.8%, the 5.5% minimum wage increase and the 9.4% rise in medical supply costs will affect BPC. Which change will have the greatest impact? Justify your answer.
    Answer: Base interest rate rise (4.0% to 4.8%): If BPC's $450,000 ten-year loan is variable-rate, the rate is 0.8 percentage points higher, so the added annual interest is 0.8% × $450,000 = $3,600. That is modest beside fixed costs of $360,000, and if the loan is fixed-rate the extra cost is zero. Higher rates may also make patients more cautious about self-funded screening, and future borrowing for expansion dearer, but BPC can largely neutralise this by fixing the loan rate.

Minimum wage increase (5.5%, to $13.72 an hour): BPC employs a workforce of 60, and clinical and reception roles include hourly-paid staff, so this raises the wage bill and cannot be avoided. The insert gives no hours worked or individual pay rates, so no honest annual total can be calculated; the defensible test is productivity. Output of 12,000 units across 60 staff is 200 screening packages per employee, so a wage rise is absorbable only if that productivity holds or output grows, otherwise unit labour cost pushes the $70 unit cost up and narrows the $60 contribution.

Medical supply cost inflation (9.4%): The $40 variable cost per package is not broken down in the insert, so only an explicitly labelled illustrative upper bound can be computed. If the whole $40 were exposed, 9.4% × $40 = $3.76 extra per unit, and across 12,000 units that is $45,120 a year (12,000 × $3.76), cutting contribution from $60 toward $56.24. BPC can recover part of this through the $8 same-day premium that 68% of surveyed patients accept.

Conclusion: The 9.4% rise in medical supply costs will have the greatest impact. It compounds on every one of the 12,000 packages sold and directly erodes the $60 contribution that justifies the $720,000 suite, and it cannot be removed simply by fixing a loan rate. The minimum-wage rise is second but cannot be quantified from the insert, while the interest-rate rise adds only $3,600 a year at most and is the smallest of the three.

--- MAIN STEM ---
Crestview Learning Group (CLG) is a private limited company in the education sector, running after-school numeracy centres and employing a workforce of 48. Founded in 2013 by Marcus Crest, it operates a hierarchical structure with autocratic leadership. CLG plans to invest $540,000 in six new numeracy learning centres, financed by a $300,000 bank loan and a $240,000 share issue. It has fixed costs of $270,000 a year, a variable cost of $15 a unit and a selling price of $60, and currently produces 12,000 units a year, each a funded course place. CLG faces two problems: tutor absenteeism has reached 8% and parent complaints about lesson quality at its centres are rising.

--- APPENDIX 1 — MARKETING/OPS ---
Operations and Quality Extract — Q3 2025: CLG delivered 2,800 funded course places last quarter with a re-assessment pass rate of 86%, up from 79% a year ago. Parent complaints rose from 24 to 41 per month. Average lesson waitlist is 9 days. A survey of 450 parents found that 72% would pay $12 more per course for small-group tuition, and 61% choose providers by pass rates. Records show 12 of 48 tutors have not completed on-the-job training on the new numeracy software; accredited courses cost $650 per tutor.

--- APPENDIX 2 — FINANCIAL DATA ---

(3) School funding per pupil was reduced by 4.5% and education technology input costs rose 8.3%, while household spending on tutoring grew 3.1%.

    Question: CLG plans to fund part of its $540,000 expansion with a $300,000 bank loan. Explain two advantages for CLG of using a share issue rather than the bank loan.
    Answer: Point 1: A $240,000 share issue brings in equity that never has to be repaid and carries no compulsory interest, unlike the $300,000 bank loan. With contribution of $45 on each $60 course place, cash that would have serviced debt can instead cover the $270,000 fixed costs and the 8.3% rise in education technology input costs, protecting CLG's 12 places per tutor target without raising the price to parents.

Point 2: Share issue finance does not require collateral, so the six new learning centres cannot be repossessed if enrolment falls short, and it spreads financial risk among shareholders rather than leaving Marcus Crest's firm solely exposed. It also increases capital employed to $1,200,000, giving CLG a stronger equity base from which to borrow later, even though existing owners dilute their control.

The 61% who choose by pass rates can be given that evidence directly. Results take time to build and require careful, truthful content, but cost per enrolled parent is low and campaigns can be scaled centre by centre.

Recommendation: CLG should choose social media marketing. It targets parents precisely, supports the pass-rate message parents value and scales across six centres far better than radio or newsletters. Local radio is rejected as geographically limited and wasteful, and printed newsletters are rejected as too narrow and dependent on third parties; CLG can keep a small newsletter insert as a backup channel.

--- MAIN STEM ---
Pinecrest Home Services (PHS) is a private limited company in the consumer services sector, providing domestic cleaning and maintenance visits and employing a workforce of 32. Founded in 2015 by Aisha Pine, it operates a flat structure with laissez-faire leadership. PHS plans to invest $480,000 in electric service vans and a mobile booking app, financed by $280,000 hire purchase and $200,000 retained profit. It has fixed costs of $240,000 a year, a variable cost of $20 a unit and a selling price of $70, and currently produces 10,000 units a year, each a standard home visit. PHS faces two problems: labour turnover has reached 14% and customer complaints about missed bookings are rising.

--- APPENDIX 1 — MARKETING/OPS ---
Marketing and Operations Extract — Q3 2025: PHS completed 2,400 home visits last quarter with a first-time-fix rate of 91%, down from 95% a year ago. Customer complaints rose from 33 to 52 per month. Average booking-to-visit time is 4.6 days. A survey of 380 households found that 66% would pay $9 more for eco-friendly cleaning, and 58% rebook based on punctuality. Records show 10 of 32 cleaners have not finished on-the-job training on the new booking app; certification courses cost $500 per cleaner.

--- APPENDIX 2 — FINANCIAL DATA ---

(2) The national minimum wage rose by 7.0% from $12.80 to $13.70 per hour from April 2026. (3) Fuel and cleaning-product input costs rose 10.5% and consumer spending on home services grew 2.2%, while household income fell 1.4%.

--- QUESTIONS ---
  Q1(a) [8 marks]
    Question: PHS plans to fund part of its $480,000 expansion with $280,000 hire purchase. Explain two advantages for PHS of using retained profit instead of hire purchase.
    Answer: Point 1: Retained profit of $200,000 needs no deposit, interest or monthly instalments, unlike the $280,000 hire-purchase agreement on the electric vans. With contribution of $50 on each $70 home visit, money not paid in hire-purchase charges can cover the $240,000 fixed costs and absorb the 10.5% rise in fuel and cleaning-product costs, protecting PHS's flat-structure cash flow.

Point 2: Retained profit keeps ownership of the vans and app with Aisha Pine from day one, whereas under hire purchase the lender owns the assets until the final payment and can repossess them if instalments are missed. Using internal funds avoids that risk on the vehicles central to 10,000 visits a year, and adds no interest payable beyond the $30,000 shown in Appendix 2, keeping the service competitive on the $70 price.
    Keywords: retained profit, hire purchase, $200,000, $280,000, $480,000, $240,000
    Mark scheme: knowledge_max_2: 1 mark for each valid advantage identified (max 2). | application_analysis_max_6: Up to 3 marks per point for contextual explanation applied to PHS's financing choice and home-visit economics.

  Q1(b) [12 marks]
    Question: PHS is promoting its electric-van service and booking app. Consider local newspaper advertisements, customer referral incentives, or social media marketing. Which should PHS choose to win household customers? Justify your recommendation.
    Answer: Local newspaper advertisements: Print reaches households in PHS's immediate service area and can carry a coupon for a first $70 visit. It is cheap per insertion but has a short reading life and cannot show the booking app or the eco-friendly message; much of the readership will not need cleaning, so it wastes part of the promotion budget needed alongside the $480,000 expansion.

Customer referral incentives: Offering existing clients a discount for introducing neighbours uses trusted word of mouth and suits a service where 58% of customers rebook on punctuality. Social media marketing: Targeted local ads can reach exactly the households in PHS's service area and speak to the 66% of 380 surveyed who would pay $9 more for eco-friendly cleaning. It takes time to build trust and needs honest, consistent content, but cost per booked visit is low and campaigns can be scaled as new vans arrive.

Recommendation: PHS should choose social media marketing. It targets households precisely, carries the eco-friendly message the survey supports and scales with the new vans. Newspaper advertisements are rejected as untargeted and forgettable, and referral incentives are rejected as too slow and risky while complaints are high; PHS can add a modest referral bonus later once punctuality recovers.
    Keywords: 66%, 380, $9, 58%, $480,000, 32

    Question: PHS's labour turnover has reached 14% and complaints about missed bookings are rising. Explain two benefits for PHS of using team working to reduce turnover and improve reliability.

    Question: PHS must train 10 cleaners on the new booking app. Consider on-the-job training or certification courses at $500 per cleaner. Which should PHS choose? Justify your decision.

--- MAIN STEM ---
Meridian Dental Care (MDC) is a partnership in the healthcare sector, running private dental practices and employing a workforce of 26. Founded in 2008 by Dr Ravi Meridian, it operates a flat structure with democratic leadership. MDC plans to invest $600,000 in two dental surgery suites with 3D scanning, financed by a $350,000 bank loan and $250,000 retained profit. It has fixed costs of $350,000 a year, a variable cost of $30 a unit and a selling price of $100, and currently produces 11,000 units a year, each a standard dental treatment. MDC faces two problems: dental nurse absenteeism has reached 12% and patient complaints about appointment delays are rising.

--- APPENDIX 1 — MARKETING/OPS ---
Quality and Operations Extract — Q3 2025: MDC completed 2,700 treatments last quarter with a complication rate of 1.5%, down from 2.8% a year ago. Patient complaints fell from 37 to 22 per month. Average appointment lead time is 6.1 days. A survey of 420 patients found that 70% would pay $14 more for same-day 3D scanning, and 59% choose a dentist by waiting time. Records show 9 of 26 staff have not completed on-the-job training on the new scanner; external courses cost $800 per employee.

--- APPENDIX 2 — FINANCIAL DATA ---

(3) Dental material input costs rose 11.2% and private dental insurance reimbursement fell 5.8%, while consumer spending on cosmetic dentistry grew 4.0%.

    Question: MDC plans to fund part of its $600,000 expansion with a $350,000 bank loan. Explain two advantages for MDC of using retained profit rather than the bank loan.

With contribution of $70 on each $100 treatment, cash saved from debt service can absorb the $350,000 fixed costs and the 11.2% rise in dental material costs, letting the partnership hold its price at $100 while it equips the two new surgery suites.

Point 2: Using retained profit avoids the collateral and repossession risk of a bank loan, so the new 3D scanners cannot be seized if treatment volumes disappoint. It also leaves Dr Ravi Meridian and the partners in full control of clinical decisions, with no lender conditions on how the 11,000 treatments a year are delivered, and avoids adding to the interest payable of $55,000 shown in Appendix 2.

It measures enquiries cheaply and can be scaled as the two suites open. It builds trust more slowly for a clinical service and needs careful, accurate health content, but cost per booked patient is low.

Recommendation: MDC should choose social media marketing. It reaches the patients the survey identifies, communicates same-day scanning at lower cost than radio and spreads faster than referrals. Radio is rejected as costly and untargeted, and referral partnerships are rejected as too slow; MDC can add dentist referrals as a supporting channel once the suites are busy.

--- MAIN STEM ---
Northbrook Nursery Group (NNG) is a cooperative in the education sector, providing early-years childcare and employing a workforce of 38. It has fixed costs of $180,000 a year, a variable cost of $12 a unit and a selling price of $48, and currently produces 14,000 units a year, each a funded childcare place. NNG faces two problems: nursery assistant absenteeism has reached 10% and parent complaints about waiting lists in the new rooms are rising.

--- APPENDIX 1 — MARKETING/OPS ---

(3) Nursery equipment and food input costs rose 9.8% and government childcare funding fell 3.6%, while parental spending on childcare grew 3.9%.

  Q1(a) [8 marks]

The cash saved can cover the $180,000 fixed costs and the 9.8% rise in food and equipment costs, helping the cooperative hold the price parents pay while two new rooms open.

Point 2: Retained profit leaves ownership of the new rooms and outdoor areas with the cooperative, whereas under leasing the lessor owns the assets until the term ends and may repossess them if payments lapse. Since NNG is a cooperative with 38 staff and 14,000 funded places to protect, avoiding that commitment preserves member control and adds no further interest payable beyond the $26,000 shown in Appendix 2.
    Keywords: retained profit, leasing, $200,000, $220,000, $420,000, $180,000

The limitations are that trainers have less time for their own duties, habits may be copied, and there is no certificate that parents choosing by inspection rating can see.

Certification courses: At $550 per employee, certifying 11 staff costs $6,050 (11 × $550), affordable beside the $420,000 expansion. However, 11 of 38 staff would be away from rooms, worsening 10% absenteeism and lengthening the waiting list, and generic content may not match NNG's exact app, so on-site follow-up would still be needed.

Decision: NNG should choose on-the-job training for all 11 assistants and fund one certification course for a lead practitioner. On-the-job training is cheaper, specific to NNG's procedures and avoids losing room capacity while absence is 10%; full certification is rejected because $6,050 and 11 staff off the rota would lengthen the 11-day waiting list for limited extra relevance.

--- MAIN STEM ---
Ridgeway Aggregates (RGA) is a private limited company in the quarrying and crushed-rock aggregates sector, employing a workforce of 62. Founded in 2005 by Duncan Ridgeway, it supplies graded aggregate to regional construction firms and operates a hierarchical structure with autocratic leadership on safety-critical sites. RGA plans to invest $720,000 in a new mobile crushing and screening plant with dust-suppression and water-recycling technology, financed by a $450,000 ten-year bank loan and $270,000 retained profit. It has fixed costs of $360,000 a year, a variable cost of $12.00 a unit and a selling price of $20.00, and currently produces 60,000 units a year. RGA faces two problems: quality complaints about off-spec grading have risen to 4.2% of loads, and site absenteeism has reached 8%. Duncan wants growth without risking its extraction licence.

--- APPENDIX 1 — MARKETING/OPS ---
Operations and Quality Report — Q3 2025: The quarry dispatched 15,000 tonnes last quarter at an off-spec rejection rate of 4.2%, up from 2.6% a year earlier. Customer quality complaints rose from 12 to 27 per month, and average delivery turnaround is 4.1 days. Diesel use per tonne fell 3.0% after a trial of the dust-suppression system, while dust complaints from nearby residents numbered 9. A survey of 300 regional contractors found that 58% would switch supplier for reliably graded, lower-dust aggregate and 47% check a quarry's environmental record before tendering. A skills audit shows 18 of 62 staff lack certification on the new screening plant; accredited external courses cost $780 per operator.

--- APPENDIX 2 — FINANCIAL DATA ---
Title: Extract from the Statement of Profit or Loss and Capital employed data of Ridgeway Aggregates for the year ended 31 March 2025 ($ '000)
Headers: ['Financial Metric', '2024', '2025']

Cost of sales | 2,400 | 2,750
Gross profit | 1,600 | 2,250
Operating profit | 500 | 750
Capital employed | 2,500 | 3,000
Interest payable | 40 | 55

--- APPENDIX 3 — EXTERNAL ENVIRONMENT ---
Economic and Business Bulletin (November 2026): (1) The central bank has raised the base interest rate from 4.50% to 5.25%, increasing borrowing costs for firms with variable-rate loans such as RGA's $450,000 expansion loan. (2) The national minimum wage will rise by 5.9% from $12.80 to $13.55 per hour from April 2026, lifting wage bills across quarrying and haulage. (3) Diesel and tyre input costs have risen 9.6% year-on-year, while construction output grew 2.8% and regional demand for graded aggregate increased 3.1%.

--- QUESTIONS ---
  Q1(a) [8 marks]
    Question: RGA plans to fund part of its $720,000 crushing-plant expansion with a ten-year bank loan. Explain two advantages for RGA of using $270,000 retained profit to fund the expansion instead of taking a larger bank loan.
    Answer: Point 1: Retained profit is internally generated, so using the $270,000 avoids interest and capital repayments on a larger loan and leaves RGA's cash flow intact at a time when it already services a $450,000 ten-year bank loan and carries fixed costs of $360,000 a year. Every dollar of interest saved can be spent on the dust-suppression and water-recycling plant without raising the $20.00 selling price for construction clients, which matters when 58% of surveyed contractors say they would switch supplier for more reliable, lower-dust aggregate.

Point 2: Funding from retained profit keeps decision-making with Duncan Ridgeway and the existing owners, since no lender can attach covenants to how the $720,000 mobile crushing plant is operated. It also avoids the repossession risk that a bigger loan would create if the 4.2% off-spec rejection rate persisted and cash generation disappointed. Retained profit is therefore the lower-risk source for a quarrying business whose hierarchical, safety-critical sites already work within tight margins.
    Keywords: retained profit, bank loan, $270,000, $450,000, $720,000, $360,000
    Mark scheme: knowledge_max_2: 1 mark for each valid advantage of retained profit over a larger loan (max 2). | application_analysis_max_6: Up to 3 marks per point for contextual explanation applied to RGA, its $720,000 expansion, existing $450,000 loan and contractor survey evidence.

  Q1(b) [12 marks]
    Question: RGA is launching its new dust-suppressed, lower-dust graded aggregate to regional contractors. Consider national trade-press advertising, local radio sponsorship, or direct sales visits to construction firms. Which should RGA choose to promote the launch? Justify your recommendation.
    Answer: National trade-press advertising: A campaign in construction and quarrying journals would build awareness of RGA's new dust-suppressed aggregate among the 300 contractors surveyed, many of whom specify materials on regional projects. It reaches a professional audience and supports a premium positioning. However, print advertising is costly for a 62-employee firm already funding a $720,000 plant, and much of the readership lies outside RGA's regional delivery radius, so spend would be wasted where the quarry cannot physically supply.

Local radio sponsorship: Sponsoring regional radio is cheaper and repeats the message to local contract managers and hauliers who actually buy RGA's output. It suits a time-sensitive launch and reinforces the lower-dust story. Its weakness is reach and detail: radio cannot demonstrate graded consistency or the 3.0% diesel reduction, and it will not persuade the 47% of contractors who check environmental records before tendering.

Direct sales visits: RGA's technical team can call on the largest regional contractors, present test certificates and a credible plan to bring the 4.2% off-spec rate back towards the 2.6% level of a year ago, and quote for tailored grading. This uses the existing sales force, gives immediate feedback and targets the 58% who would switch for reliability. It is slower to scale and depends on staff time where absenteeism is 8%.

Recommendation: RGA should choose direct sales visits, supported by short trade-press notices. Direct visits target exactly the regional contractors who buy and specify aggregate, let RGA prove the lower-dust, better-graded product and win the 58% willing to switch, at a cost far below national press. National advertising is rejected as unaffordable and geographically wasteful; radio is rejected because it cannot carry the technical evidence that 47% of environmentally-checking buyers demand.

Point 2: The same clarity helps tackle 8% site absenteeism. With defined roles and autocratic decisions, supervisors can reallocate shifts immediately when crushers are short-staffed, keeping the $720,000 crushing plant running and limiting disruption to customers. Formal downward communication also makes safety and quality expectations explicit, reducing the chance that rushed work raises defects further. In a quarrying firm with 62 staff and fixed costs of $360,000 a year, this top-down control protects both output and the extraction licence that the business depends on.

--- MAIN STEM ---
Tarnfield Blockworks (TBK) is a private limited company in the construction materials sector, employing a workforce of 48. Founded in 2011 by Priya Tarnfield, it makes precast concrete blocks for housebuilders and operates a flat organisational structure with democratic leadership. TBK plans to invest $560,000 in an automated block-moulding line using recycled aggregate, financed by a $200,000 ten-year bank loan and $360,000 from a new share issue. It has fixed costs of $280,000 a year, a variable cost of $8.00 a unit and a selling price of $15.00, and currently produces 55,000 units a year. TBK faces a defect rate of 3.4% in finished blocks and rising labour turnover among mould operators, which Priya wants solved before the new line starts.

--- APPENDIX 1 — MARKETING/OPS ---
Quality and Operations Report — Q3 2025: The moulding line produced 13,750 blocks last quarter with a defect rate of 3.4%, down from 4.9% a year earlier but still above the 1.5% target. Customer complaints about chipped blocks rose from 16 to 31 per month. Average order turnaround is 3.6 days. Trial use of recycled aggregate cut raw-material waste by 2.8% but raised mixing time by 1.2 minutes per batch. A survey of 250 housebuilders found that 61% would pay up to $0.30 more for lower-carbon blocks and 44% check a supplier's recycled content when tendering. A skills audit shows 14 of 48 operators lack training on the automated moulds; certified courses at the local college cost $640 per person.

--- APPENDIX 2 — FINANCIAL DATA ---
Title: Extract from the Statement of Profit or Loss and Capital employed data of Tarnfield Blockworks for the year ended 31 March 2025 ($ '000)
Headers: ['Financial Metric', '2024', '2025']

Cost of sales | 3,250 | 3,600
Gross profit | 1,750 | 2,400
Operating profit | 500 | 720
Capital employed | 3,125 | 3,600
Interest payable | 35 | 45

--- APPENDIX 3 — EXTERNAL ENVIRONMENT ---
Economic and Business Bulletin (November 2026): (1) The central bank has raised the base interest rate from 4.25% to 5.00%, raising borrowing costs for firms with variable-rate debt including TBK's $200,000 expansion loan. (2) The national minimum wage will rise by 6.2% from $12.20 to $12.96 per hour from April 2026, lifting wage bills in manufacturing. (3) Cement, steel and recycled-aggregate input costs have risen 11.3% year-on-year, while housing starts grew 4.0% and regional construction output expanded 3.6%.

--- QUESTIONS ---
  Q1(a) [8 marks]
    Question: TBK plans to fund part of its $560,000 moulding-line expansion with a $200,000 bank loan. Explain two advantages for TBK of financing the expansion with $360,000 from a new share issue instead of a larger bank loan.
    Answer: Point 1: A $360,000 share issue brings in equity that carries no interest and no fixed repayment dates, so TBK avoids loading a larger bank loan onto the $200,000 it already plans to borrow. With fixed costs of $280,000 a year and a 3.4% defect rate to fix, preserving cash flow matters: money not spent on loan interest can fund quality checks on the new automated moulds without raising the $15.00 selling price for housebuilders.

Point 2: New equity strengthens TBK's balance sheet and gives a larger capital base to absorb the risk of the $560,000 moulding line, which is why the board chose it over extra debt. Unlike a bigger loan, shares cannot be called in if the 3.4% defect rate persists and cash generation slips, so the business is less exposed to repossession. The trade-off is that Priya's existing ownership is diluted, but for a young 48-employee firm the reduced financial risk supports the lower-carbon positioning that 61% of surveyed builders value.
    Keywords: share issue, bank loan, $360,000, $200,000, $560,000, $280,000
    Mark scheme: knowledge_max_2: 1 mark for each valid advantage of a share issue over a larger loan (max 2). | application_analysis_max_6: Up to 3 marks per point for contextual explanation applied to TBK's expansion, existing loan and housebuilder survey.

  Q1(b) [12 marks]
    Question: TBK is launching lower-carbon recycled blocks. Consider trade-journal advertising, sponsorship of a local builders' association, or direct meetings with housebuilders. Which should TBK choose to promote the launch? Justify your recommendation.
    Answer: Trade-journal advertising: Placing adverts in housebuilding and construction journals would reach the 250 surveyed builders and many specifiers nationwide, supporting a premium lower-carbon image. It is credible and long-lived. Yet national print is expensive for a 48-employee company funding a $560,000 line, and much of the circulation lies beyond TBK's regional delivery area, so a large share of the spend cannot be converted into sales of 55,000 blocks.

Local builders' association sponsorship: Sponsoring a regional association is relatively cheap, builds goodwill and repeatedly exposes TBK to local small builders who make frequent repeat purchases. It suits a regional manufacturer. However, it cannot explain technical details such as the 2.8% waste reduction or the 1.5% defect target, and it will not reach the 44% of builders who check recycled content only when formally tendering.

Direct meetings with housebuilders: Priya's team can meet the largest regional housebuilders, present test data showing progress from 4.9% to a 3.4% defect rate and quote for lower-carbon blocks. This uses existing staff, gives immediate objections and answers, and directly targets the 61% who would pay up to $0.30 more. It is slower to scale and consumes scarce management time while labour turnover is rising.

Recommendation: TBK should choose direct meetings with housebuilders, supported by a small trade-journal notice. Direct meetings convert the 61% willing to pay a premium and let TBK prove its recycled content to the 44% who check it. National advertising is rejected as costly and geographically wasteful; association sponsorship is rejected because it lacks the technical detail that tender decisions require.

--- MAIN STEM ---
Verdemoor Eco-Materials (VEM) is a worker cooperative in the eco-materials sector, employing a workforce of 54. Founded in 2013 by Nadia Verdemoor, it makes recycled-fibre biodegradable packaging and operates a flat structure with laissez-faire leadership. VEM plans to invest $880,000 in a recycled-fibre moulding line with solar-powered drying, financed by $300,000 of hire purchase and $580,000 retained profit. It has fixed costs of $440,000 a year, a variable cost of $5.50 a unit and a selling price of $11.00, and currently produces 95,000 units a year. VEM faces a production waste rate of 5.6% and absenteeism of 7.4%, which Nadia wants reduced before the new line opens next year, protecting the cooperative's reputation.

--- APPENDIX 1 — MARKETING/OPS ---
Operations and Waste Report — Q3 2025: The moulding hall packed 23,750 units last quarter at a waste rate of 5.6%, down from 7.1% a year ago but still costly. Customer complaints about brittle packaging fell from 34 to 19 per month, and average despatch time is 2.9 days. Solar-assisted drying cut energy use per batch by 4.3%, while rejected batches numbered 22. A survey of 400 eco-conscious retailers found that 67% would pay up to $0.35 more for certified biodegradable packaging and 55% check sustainability credentials before ordering. A skills audit shows 16 of 54 members have not been trained on the new moulds; external eco-material training costs $720 per member.

--- APPENDIX 2 — FINANCIAL DATA ---
Title: Extract from the Statement of Profit or Loss and Capital employed data of Verdemoor Eco-Materials for the year ended 31 March 2025 ($ '000)
Headers: ['Financial Metric', '2024', '2025']

Cost of sales | 6,000 | 6,300
Gross profit | 2,000 | 2,700
Operating profit | 600 | 900
Capital employed | 5,000 | 6,000
Interest payable | 70 | 85

--- APPENDIX 3 — EXTERNAL ENVIRONMENT ---
Economic and Business Bulletin (November 2026): (1) The central bank has raised the base interest rate from 4.75% to 5.50%, increasing the cost of hire-purchase agreements such as VEM's $300,000 equipment deal. (2) The national minimum wage will rise by 7.1% from $13.00 to $13.92 per hour from April 2026, lifting the cooperative's wage bill. (3) Recycled-fibre and additive input costs have risen 14.2% year-on-year, while the eco-packaging market grew 6.5% and consumer spending on sustainable goods rose 4.8%.

    Question: VEM plans to fund its $880,000 moulding line with $300,000 of hire purchase. Explain two advantages for VEM of using $580,000 retained profit instead of increasing hire purchase.
    Answer: Point 1: Retained profit spreads the cost of the $880,000 line without adding to the $300,000 of hire-purchase commitments, so VEM avoids further interest and the risk that a financing house repossesses equipment if cash flow weakens. With fixed costs of $440,000 a year and a 5.6% waste rate to tackle, keeping the $5.50 variable cost and $11.00 selling price competitive matters more when no extra interest is loaded onto each unit.

Point 2: Using $580,000 of retained profit keeps control with the cooperative's 54 members and Nadia Verdemoor rather than a lender imposing terms on the new solar-dried line. It also matches the cooperative's aim of building long-term assets from its own surpluses. Because retained profit has no fixed repayment schedule, VEM can absorb the 7.4% absenteeism and the training bill of $720 per member without the pressure of another hire-purchase instalment, supporting steady expansion.

A further practical point is that the cooperative's retained profit is tied up in the current line, so using $580,000 for the new moulding plant could leave little reserve for 7.4% absenteeism cover and the $720-per-member training, whereas spreading payments through hire purchase would preserve working capital. Nadia should weigh this before committing the full amount.

--- MAIN STEM ---
Kalder Timber Products (KTP) is a public limited company in the sustainable forestry and timber-board sector, employing a workforce of 73. Founded in 1998 by Elowen Kalder, it supplies graded board to furniture makers and operates a hierarchical structure with formal downward communication. KTP plans to invest $640,000 in a biomass-powered kiln-drying line, financed by a $250,000 bank loan and $390,000 from the sale of surplus land. It has fixed costs of $330,000 a year, a variable cost of $14.00 a unit and a selling price of $25.00, and currently produces 45,000 units a year. KTP faces a board-grading defect rate of 3.8% and rising labour turnover among kiln operators, which Elowen wants addressed.

--- APPENDIX 1 — MARKETING/OPS ---
Quality and Production Report — Q3 2025: The plant graded 11,250 boards last quarter with a defect rate of 3.8%, up from 2.4% a year ago. Customer quality complaints rose from 21 to 38 per month, and average order lead time is 5.2 days. Biomass drying trials cut kiln fuel use by 3.6% but raised drying time by 0.8 days per batch. A survey of 320 furniture manufacturers found that 59% would pay up to $0.45 more for sustainably sourced, accurately graded board and 51% check forest certification before ordering. A skills audit shows 20 of 73 staff lack certification on the new kilns; accredited external courses cost $810 per operator.

    Answer: Point 1: Selling surplus land raises $390,000 without interest or repayment obligations, so KTP avoids enlarging the $250,000 bank loan and protects cash flow while carrying $330,000 fixed costs and a 3.8% defect rate. Interest saved can be spent on grading checks, protecting the $25.00 selling price and the 45,000-unit output needed to justify the $640,000 biomass kiln.

Point 2: Using asset sales reduces the company's debt and the risk that lenders impose conditions or call in loans if cash generation slips, which is valuable for a public limited company accountable to shareholders. It also converts an idle asset into a productive one without dilution. Given rising labour turnover among kiln operators, the lower fixed-commitment burden gives Elowen Kalder more flexibility to invest in training and stability rather than meeting larger loan instalments.

A further point is that the $390,000 asset sale is a one-off: once the land is sold it cannot fund a second phase, whereas a loan could be drawn as needed. Elowen should ensure the proceeds cover the $640,000 project alongside the $250,000 loan, leaving reserves for the 20 kiln certifications at $810 each and the 3.8% defect clean-up, rather than tying up all cash in one project.

    Question: Using Appendix 3, evaluate how the interest rate rise to 4.75%, the 6.4% minimum wage increase and the 10.8% rise in resin, transport and fuel input costs will affect KTP. Which change will have the greatest impact? Justify your answer.
    Answer: Interest rate rise (4.00% to 4.75%): The increase is 0.75 percentage points. If KTP's $250,000 expansion loan is variable-rate, the extra annual interest is 0.75% x $250,000 = $1,875, small relative to $330,000 fixed costs. A fixed-rate loan removes the immediate cash effect, though future borrowing may cost more and higher rates could slow housing completions, a source of demand for furniture and board.

Minimum wage rise (6.4%, to $13.41 per hour): KTP employs a workforce of 73 in grading and kiln roles largely paid hourly, so wage costs rise and cannot be avoided. The insert gives no hours worked or pay rates, so an annual wage total cannot be invented; the defensible comparison is productivity of 45,000 units / 73 staff, about 616 boards per worker. If that holds, the rise is manageable; if rising labour turnover reduces it, unit labour cost climbs and the $11.00 contribution narrows.

Input cost inflation (10.8% on resin, transport and fuel): The insert does not decompose the $14.00 variable cost, so only a bounded calculation is shown: if the whole variable cost rose 10.8%, that adds 10.8% x $14.00 = $1.512, about $1.51 a unit; across 45,000 units that is about $68,040 a year. Contribution would fall from $11.00 toward $9.49.

Conclusion: The 10.8% input-cost rise has the greatest impact. It applies to every board graded, directly erodes the $11.00 contribution that funds the $640,000 kiln and cannot be removed by fixing a loan. The interest rise is at most $1,875 and the wage rise can be offset by productivity; neither affects every unit.

--- MAIN STEM ---
Solstice Insulation Systems (SIS) is a private limited company in the sustainable building-materials sector, employing a workforce of 66. Founded in 2016 by Tomas Solstice, it makes recycled-cellulose insulation and operates a hierarchical structure with autocratic leadership on its production floor. SIS plans to invest $960,000 in a recycled-cellulose insulation line with low-energy manufacturing, financed by a $400,000 bank loan and $560,000 from a new share issue. It has fixed costs of $504,000 a year, a variable cost of $9.00 a unit and a selling price of $16.00, and currently produces 90,000 units a year. SIS faces a production waste rate of 6.1% and rising quality complaints about inconsistent density, which Tomas wants cut before the new line starts.

--- APPENDIX 1 — MARKETING/OPS ---
Operations and Quality Report — Q3 2025: The line produced 22,500 insulation batches last quarter with a waste rate of 6.1%, down from 8.0% a year earlier. Customer complaints about inconsistent density rose from 25 to 42 per month, and average delivery time is 4.4 days. Low-energy manufacturing trials cut power use per batch by 5.2%, while rejected batches numbered 31. A survey of 350 green builders found that 63% would pay up to $0.40 more for certified recycled insulation and 49% check environmental product declarations before specifying. A skills audit shows 19 of 66 staff lack training on the new line; accredited courses cost $690 per employee.

--- APPENDIX 2 — FINANCIAL DATA ---
Title: Extract from the Statement of Profit or Loss and Capital employed data of Solstice Insulation Systems for the year ended 31 March 2025 ($ '000)
Headers: ['Financial Metric', '2024', '2025']
Revenue | 6,000 | 7,500
Cost of sales | 4,800 | 5,625
Gross profit | 1,200 | 1,875
Operating profit | 300 | 600
Capital employed | 3,000 | 3,750
Interest payable | 30 | 40

--- APPENDIX 3 — EXTERNAL ENVIRONMENT ---
Economic and Business Bulletin (November 2026): (1) The central bank has raised the base interest rate from 4.50% to 5.25%, increasing borrowing costs for firms with variable-rate loans such as SIS's $400,000 expansion loan. (2) The national minimum wage will rise by 6.0% from $12.50 to $13.25 per hour from April 2026, lifting wage bills in manufacturing. (3) Recycled-paper and fire-retardant additive input costs have risen 13.5% year-on-year, while green-building investment grew 7.2% and retrofit spending rose 3.9%.

    Answer: Point 1: A $560,000 share issue provides equity with no interest or fixed repayment dates, so SIS avoids enlarging the $400,000 bank loan and protects cash flow while carrying $504,000 fixed costs and a 6.1% waste rate. Money not spent on loan interest can fund density checks on the new line, protecting the $16.00 selling price and 90,000-unit output and letting SIS act on the 63% of builders who will pay a premium.

Point 2: New equity strengthens the balance sheet and gives a wider capital base to absorb the risk of the $960,000 recycled-cellulose line, which is why a share issue was chosen over more debt. Unlike a larger loan, shares cannot be called in if the rising density complaints persist and cash generation slips. Although Tomas Solstice's ownership is diluted, the lower financial risk helps a young 66-employee manufacturer invest in training and quality while the line beds in.

    Question: Using Appendix 3, evaluate how the interest rate rise to 5.25%, the 6.0% minimum wage increase and the 13.5% rise in recycled-paper and additive input costs will affect SIS. Which change will have the greatest impact? Justify your answer.
    Answer: Interest rate rise (4.50% to 5.25%): The increase is 0.75 percentage points. If SIS's $400,000 expansion loan is variable-rate, the extra annual interest is 0.75% x $400,000 = $3,000, modest beside $504,000 fixed costs. If the loan is fixed-rate, the immediate cash effect is nil. Higher rates could still raise the cost of future borrowing and may slow the 7.2% growth in green-building investment.

Minimum wage rise (6.0%, to $13.25 per hour): SIS employs a workforce of 66 in production and packing roles largely paid hourly, so wage costs rise and cannot be avoided. If that holds, the rise is absorbable; if it falls, unit labour cost rises and the $7.00 contribution narrows.

Input cost inflation (13.5% on recycled paper and additives): The insert does not decompose the $9.00 variable cost, so only a bounded figure is shown: if the whole variable cost rose 13.5%, that adds 13.5% x $9.00 = $1.215, about $1.22 a unit; across 90,000 units that is about $109,350 a year. Contribution would fall from $7.00 toward $5.78.

Conclusion: The 13.5% input-cost rise has the greatest impact. It applies to every unit, directly erodes the $7.00 contribution that funds the $960,000 line and cannot be removed by fixing a loan rate. The interest rise is at most $3,000 and the wage rise can be offset by productivity; neither touches every unit.

Saffron Crest Spices (SCS) is a private limited company in the spice-processing sector, based in the Southern Highlands and employing a workforce of 40.     Question: Using Appendix 2, evaluate SCS's financial position by calculating the current ratio and the acid test ratio for 2024 and 2025. Has SCS's financial position improved? Justify your answer.

Current Ratio 2025 = 1.66 : 1
Acid Test Ratio 2024 = 0.91 : 1

Conclusion: SCS's financial position has improved. Both measures show stronger short-term solvency and the improvement does not rely on inventory. The residual risk is rising receivables, so credit control should be tightened while the expansion proceeds.

    Answer: Interest rate rise (4.25% to 5.0%): The base rate rises by 0.75 percentage points. The defensible comparison is with productivity derived from the insert: 80,000 units ÷ 40 staff = 2,000 units per worker. Conclusion: The 9.6% input-cost inflation will have the greatest impact because it compounds on every unit sold and directly attacks the $5.00 contribution that justifies the $840,000 expansion. --- MAIN STEM ---
Cocoa Bloom Chocolate (CBC) is a public limited company in the confectionery sector, based near the Pacific coast and employing a workforce of 60. It has fixed costs of $420,000 a year, a variable cost of $7.50 a unit and a selling price of $13.50, and currently produces 120,000 units a year. CBC faces rising quality complaints about inconsistent tempering and absenteeism has reached 7%.

--- APPENDIX 1 — MARKETING/OPS ---
Operations and Quality Report — Q3 2025: The moulding line produced 31,200 bars last quarter with a waste rate of 5.4%, up from 3.9% a year ago. Quality complaints rose from 26 to 41 per month. Average delivery lead time is 5.6 days. A survey of 750 consumers found that 61% would pay up to $0.60 more for single-origin cocoa bars, and 55% read sustainability labels. Skills records show 18 of 60 production staff have not completed on-the-job training on the tempering machines; off-the-job courses at the coastal technical institute cost $1,250 per employee. The inventory-excluding measure improved from 0.92 to 1.08, so CBC is less dependent on selling chocolate stock to meet short-term debts while it services a $500,000 bank loan and a $1,200,000 expansion. There are caveats: inventories rose from $210,000 to $245,000, which may reflect slow-moving stock given the 5.4% waste rate, and receivables, although lower at $230,000, still tie up cash that could fund the 18 staff still needing training.

Conclusion: CBC's financial position has improved. Both measures show stronger short-term solvency and the improvement does not rest on inventory alone. The remaining risk is higher stock, so waste control should be tightened as the new tempering line starts up.
    Keywords: 1.50, 1.90, 0.92, 1.08, $540,000, $570,000, $1,200,000
    Mark scheme: level_1_1_to_4: States financial figures or changes without accurate ratio calculations. | level_2_5_to_8: Accurately calculates the current ratio and acid test ratio for both 2024 and 2025 with contextual analysis of the trend. | level_3_9_to_12: Accurate ratio calculations for both years combined with detailed evaluation of inventory, receivables and liabilities movements and a justified conclusion on whether CBC's financial position improved.

  Q4(a) [8 marks]
    Question: Explain one advantage and one disadvantage for CBC of introducing single-origin cocoa sourcing for its premium bars.
    Answer: Advantage: Single-origin sourcing supports the premium positioning that 61% of 750 surveyed consumers are willing to pay $0.60 more for, protecting the $6.00 contribution per unit even while cocoa bean prices rise 14.3%. It also gives CBC a clearer sustainability story for the 55% who read labels, strengthening its appeal to export distributors and the $1,200,000 tempering investment.

Disadvantage: Single-origin beans are usually scarcer and more expensive than blended beans, which would push up the $7.50 variable cost per unit unless the $0.60 premium is fully accepted by consumers and retailers.     Keywords: 61%, 55%, $0.60, 14.3%, 5.4%, $7.50
    Mark scheme: knowledge_max_2: 1 mark for a valid advantage and 1 mark for a valid disadvantage. | application_analysis_max_6: Up to 3 marks per point for detailed contextual development linked to CBC's research data, costs and expansion.

  Q4(b) [12 marks]
    Question: Using Appendix 3, evaluate how the interest rate rise to 4.5%, the 7.2% minimum wage increase and the 14.3% rise in cocoa bean prices will affect CBC. Which change will have the greatest impact? Justify your answer.
    Answer: Interest rate rise (3.75% to 4.5%): The base rate increases by 0.75 percentage points. If the $500,000 bank loan is variable-rate, the extra annual interest is 0.0075 × $500,000 = $3,750 a year, which is small next to fixed costs of $420,000 a year; if the loan is fixed-rate it is zero. Higher rates might dampen consumer spending on premium chocolate, but CBC can largely remove the direct risk by fixing the loan rate, and the $700,000 share issue reduces reliance on debt.

Minimum wage increase (7.2%, from $11.80 to $12.65 per hour): This raises CBC's wage bill for a workforce of 60 and cannot be avoided. The insert states no hours worked and no individual pay rates, so an annual wage total cannot be invented. The honest comparison uses productivity derived from the insert: 120,000 units ÷ 60 staff = 2,000 units per worker. If that productivity is maintained the rise is absorbable; if output falls because 18 staff remain untrained, unit labour cost climbs and the $6.00 contribution per unit narrows.

Cocoa bean price rise (14.3%): The insert does not decompose the $7.50 variable cost, so only a labelled bound can be calculated: if the whole variable cost rose 14.3%, the increase is 0.143 × $7.50 = $1.07 per unit, and at 120,000 units a year that is about $128,700. That is an upper bound rather than a forecast; the real figure depends on how much of the $7.50 is cocoa, which is not given. CBC can pass part on through the $0.60 premium that 61% of surveyed consumers accept.

Conclusion: The 14.3% cocoa price rise will have the greatest impact. It applies to every bar and threatens the $6.00 contribution underlying the $1,200,000 expansion, whereas the interest cost of $3,750 is small and fixable and the wage rise can be offset if 2,000-units-per-worker productivity holds. Input-cost inflation therefore demands the strongest response.
    Keywords: 4.5%, 7.2%, 14.3%, $12.65, $500,000, $7.50
    Mark scheme: level_1_1_to_4: Identifies the external factors with limited application to CBC. | level_2_5_to_8: Analyses the impact of at least two external changes on CBC's costs, revenue or financing in context. | level_3_9_to_12: Detailed evaluation of all three external changes in the context of CBC with a well-justified judgment that input-cost inflation has the greatest impact and why the other two are smaller.

--- MAIN STEM ---
Almond Grove Nut Company (AGN) is a cooperative in the tree-nut farming and processing sector, based in a dry inland valley and employing a workforce of 50. Founded in 1998 by a group of growers led by Tomas Bergström, it supplies shelled almonds to health-food wholesalers and operates a flat structure with democratic leadership. AGN plans to invest $690,000 in a new shelling and packing facility, financed by a $390,000 bank loan and $300,000 retained profit. It has fixed costs of $225,000 a year, a variable cost of $4.80 a unit and a selling price of $9.30, and currently produces 100,000 units a year. AGN faces rising quality rejects: 3.6% of packs fail inspection and labour turnover is increasing.

--- APPENDIX 1 — MARKETING/OPS ---
Operations and Quality Report — Q3 2025: The shelling line processed 26,400 units last quarter with a reject rate of 3.6%, down from 5.1% a year ago. Customer returns fell from 33 to 19 per month. Average dispatch time is 3.8 days. A survey of 420 buyers found that 72% would pay up to $0.45 more for residue-free almonds, and 58% check country-of-origin labels. Records show 14 of 50 members have not completed on-the-job training on the new optical sorters; off-the-job training courses at the agricultural college cost $950 per member.

--- APPENDIX 2 — FINANCIAL DATA ---
Title: Extract from the Statement of Financial Position of Almond Grove Nut Company as at 31 March 2025 ($ '000)
Headers: ['Financial Metric', '2024', '2025']
Inventories | 88 | 70
Trade receivables | 112 | 125
Cash and cash equivalents | 52 | 75
Current liabilities | 180 | 180
Non-current assets | 1,100 | 1,520
Capital employed | 1,400 | 1,750

--- APPENDIX 3 — EXTERNAL ENVIRONMENT ---
Economic and Business Bulletin (November 2026): (1) The central bank has raised the base interest rate from 4.0% to 4.75%, increasing borrowing costs on variable-rate loans. (2) The national minimum wage will rise by 6.1% from $12.30 to $13.05 per hour from April 2026. (3) Wholesale nut and packaging input costs have risen 8.7% year-on-year, food inflation is 5.2%, and consumer spending on health-food snacks grew 3.3%.

--- QUESTIONS ---
  Q1(a) [8 marks]
    Question: AGN plans to fund part of its shelling-facility expansion with a ten-year bank loan. Explain two advantages for AGN of using retained profit to fund the expansion instead of the bank loan.
    Answer: Point 1: Retained profit costs AGN no interest or capital repayments, protecting the cash flow of a cooperative that already carries fixed costs of $225,000 a year and a variable cost of $4.80 a unit. The $300,000 of retained profit is generated by the grower members themselves, so money that would have gone to the $390,000 bank loan can instead be used to cut the 3.6% reject rate on the new optical sorters or to absorb the 8.7% rise in nut and packaging costs.

Point 2: Using retained profit keeps control with the grower members led by Tomas Bergström, since no lender can impose conditions on how the $690,000 shelling and packing facility is run. This matters for a cooperative with democratic leadership where members expect a say in decisions. It also avoids the collateral and default risk of the bank loan: if health-food wholesalers cut orders, the facility cannot be repossessed, and the project can start at once without waiting for loan approval while the 26,400-unit quarterly throughput is maintained.
    Keywords: retained profit, $300,000, $390,000, $690,000, $225,000, cooperative
    Mark scheme: knowledge_max_2: 1 mark for each valid advantage identified (max 2). | application_analysis_max_6: Up to 3 marks per point for contextual explanation and analysis applied to AGN and its expansion decision.

  Q1(b) [12 marks]
    Question: AGN is launching a new residue-free almond range. Consider trade fair exhibitions, local radio advertising, or social media influencer marketing. Which should AGN choose to promote the launch? Justify your recommendation.
    Answer: Trade fair exhibitions: Food fairs let AGN demonstrate residue-free almonds to health-food wholesalers face to face, answer questions about country of origin and win listings directly — valuable when 58% of 420 surveyed buyers check origin labels. However, stand fees, travel and staff time are costly for a cooperative funding a $690,000 facility, and each fair reaches only a limited number of buyers.

Local radio advertising: Radio is relatively cheap and can repeatedly reach listeners in the dry inland valley and nearby towns, building awareness of the new range. Its weakness is that AGN sells to health-food wholesalers well beyond one local area, and radio cannot show the residue-free certification or the product itself, so it is a poor fit for a 72% premium segment that wants proof.

Social media influencer marketing: Health-food and cooking influencers can show the almonds and explain residue-free certification visually, reaching the exact buyers identified in the survey at modest cost with measurable engagement. Credibility must be protected and results take time to build, but the message can be shared nationally and adapted quickly.

Recommendation: AGN should choose social media influencer marketing, backed by selected trade fairs for wholesale buyers. It reaches the researched 72% premium segment and demonstrates origin credentials that radio cannot show. Radio is rejected as too narrow and unable to prove certification; trade fairs alone are rejected as too expensive and limited in reach for a 50-member cooperative with a $390,000 loan to service.
    Keywords: 72%, 58%, $0.45, 420, health-food wholesalers, 26,400
    Mark scheme: level_1_1_to_4: Limited knowledge or outline of the promotional options with minimal context. | level_2_5_to_8: Detailed discussion of the advantages and disadvantages of at least two options in the context of AGN with some judgement. | level_3_9_to_12: Detailed discussion of all three options in the context of AGN with a well-justified recommendation explaining why radio and trade fairs are rejected.

  Q2(a) [8 marks]
    Question: AGN's reject rate is 3.6% and labour turnover is rising. Explain two benefits for AGN of using democratic leadership to improve motivation among its grower-members.
    Answer: Point 1: Democratic leadership lets the 50 grower-members share decisions about how the new shelling and packing facility is organised, which suits a cooperative and raises commitment. Members who help set inspection routines are more likely to take the 3.6% reject problem seriously, offering practical ideas that can build on the fall from 5.1% to 3.6% and protect the $9.30 selling price to health-food wholesalers.

Because 14 of 50 members still need on-the-job training on the optical sorters, consulting those who operate the equipment helps target that training properly while the $690,000 facility beds in and the $390,000 loan is serviced.

It is cheaper, machine-specific and protects output while the reject rate is only just improving; full off-the-job training is rejected because withdrawing $13,300 and 14 of 50 members from the line would disrupt supply to health-food wholesalers when a $390,000 loan must be serviced.

    Question: Using Appendix 2, evaluate AGN's financial position by calculating the current ratio and the acid test ratio for 2024 and 2025. Has AGN's financial position improved? Justify your answer.
    Answer: Calculations:
Current Ratio 2024 = 1.40 : 1
Current Ratio 2025 = 1.50 : 1
Acid Test Ratio 2024 = 0.91 : 1
Acid Test Ratio 2025 = 1.11 : 1

Detailed workings: 2024 current assets = $88,000 inventories + $112,000 trade receivables + $52,000 cash = $252,000; 2025 current assets = $70,000 + $125,000 + $75,000 = $270,000. Excluding inventories gives 2024 = ($252,000 − $88,000) ÷ $180,000 = $164,000 ÷ $180,000 = 0.91 and 2025 = ($270,000 − $70,000) ÷ $180,000 = $200,000 ÷ $180,000 = 1.11.

Receivables did rise from $112,000 to $125,000, tying up cash, so credit control with health-food wholesalers matters; inventories fell to $70,000, which supports the 26,400-unit quarterly throughput but leaves little buffer if the 3.6% reject rate worsens.

Conclusion: AGN's financial position has improved. Both measures are higher and the gain does not depend on inventory. The residual risk is slower-paying wholesalers, so members should tighten collection while the new facility operates.

    Question: Using Appendix 3, evaluate how the interest rate rise to 4.75%, the 6.1% minimum wage increase and the 8.7% rise in nut and packaging input costs will affect AGN. Which change will have the greatest impact? Justify your answer.
    Answer: Interest rate rise (4.0% to 4.75%): The base rate rises by 0.75 percentage points. If the $390,000 bank loan is variable-rate, the additional annual interest is 0.0075 × $390,000 = $2,925 a year, which is modest against fixed costs of $225,000 a year; if the loan is fixed-rate the increase is zero. Conclusion: The 8.7% input-cost rise will have the greatest impact because it applies to every unit and directly erodes the $4.50 contribution that supports the $690,000 facility. The interest effect of $2,925 is small and fixable, and the wage effect can be softened if 2,000-units-per-member productivity holds, so input-cost inflation requires the strongest management response.

--- MAIN STEM ---
Kelpwave Seaweed Farms (KSF) is a private limited company in the seaweed aquaculture sector, based off the northern Atlantic coast and employing a workforce of 55. KSF plans to invest $780,000 in a new drying and packaging plant, financed by a $480,000 bank loan and $300,000 retained profit. It has fixed costs of $330,000 a year, a variable cost of $6.10 a unit and a selling price of $11.60, and currently produces 110,000 units a year.     Question: Using Appendix 2, evaluate KSF's financial position by calculating the current ratio and the acid test ratio for 2024 and 2025. Has KSF's financial position improved? Justify your answer.
    Answer: Calculations:

Current Ratio 2025 = 1.50 : 1
Acid Test Ratio 2024 = 0.87 : 1

    Question: Using Appendix 3, evaluate how the interest rate rise to 5.25%, the 6.4% minimum wage increase and the 10.2% rise in packaging and energy costs will affect KSF. Which change will have the greatest impact? Justify your answer.
    Answer: Interest rate rise (4.5% to 5.25%): The base rate goes up by 0.75 percentage points. If the $480,000 bank loan is variable-rate, the extra annual interest is 0.0075 × $480,000 = $3,600 a year, modest beside fixed costs of $330,000 a year and zero if the loan is fixed-rate. Higher rates could make consumers cautious about seaweed snacks, but KSF can largely remove the direct cost by fixing the loan rate.

Minimum wage increase (6.4%, from $12.00 to $12.77 per hour): This raises the wage bill for a 55-person workforce and cannot be avoided. The insert gives no hours worked and no individual pay rates, so an annual wage total cannot be invented. The comparison that can be derived is productivity: 110,000 units ÷ 55 staff = 2,000 units per worker. Input cost inflation (10.2% on packaging and energy): The insert does not decompose the $6.10 variable cost, so only a labelled bound is honest: if the entire variable cost rose 10.2%, the addition is 0.102 × $6.10 = $0.62 per unit, and at 110,000 units a year that is about $68,420. This is an upper bound, not a forecast; the real addition depends on the packaging-and-energy share, which is not stated. KSF can recover part through the $0.55 organic premium accepted by 66% of surveyed buyers.

Conclusion: The 10.2% rise in packaging and energy costs will have the greatest impact. It applies to every unit and attacks the $5.50 contribution that supports the $780,000 plant, whereas the interest effect of $3,600 is small and fixable and the wage effect can be offset if 2,000-units-per-worker productivity holds. PAPER 2 — P2_SET_386
UNIT: Paper 2 Case Study
