--- MAIN STEM ---
Mendip Gasket & Fasteners (MGF) is a private limited company in the industrial components sector, employing a workforce of 60. Founded in 2011 by Priya Mendip, it supplies precision gaskets and fasteners to commercial vehicle assemblers and operates a hierarchical structure with autocratic leadership. MGF plans to invest $720,000 in a new CNC machining cell, financed by a $450,000 ten-year bank loan and $270,000 retained profit. It has fixed costs of $300,000 a year, a variable cost of $8.00 a unit and a selling price of $14.00, and produces 75,000 units a year. MGF faces two operational problems: the defect rate on machined seals has reached 2.4% and labour turnover is rising among skilled machinists.

--- APPENDIX 1 — MARKETING/OPS ---
Operations and Quality Report — Q4 2025: The gasket line machined 18,750 units last quarter at a defect rate of 2.4%, up from 1.6% a year earlier. Customer returns rose from 14 to 31 per month. Average delivery lead time is 6.5 days, against a promised 5 days. A survey of 400 commercial vehicle buyers found that 58% rank dimensional accuracy as the main purchase criterion and 47% would switch supplier after two late deliveries. Time-and-attendance records show 11 of 60 skilled machinists took more than 10 days of unplanned leave last quarter; replacement agency cover costs $280 a day.

--- APPENDIX 2 — FINANCIAL DATA ---
Title: Extract from the Statement of Financial Position of Mendip Gasket & Fasteners as at 31 March 2025 ($ '000)
Headers: ['Financial Metric', '2024', '2025']
Inventories | 140 | 165
Trade receivables | 190 | 210
Cash and cash equivalents | 55 | 70
Current liabilities | 250 | 240
Non-current assets | 1,900 | 2,350
Capital employed | 2,300 | 2,700

--- APPENDIX 3 — EXTERNAL ENVIRONMENT ---
Economic and Business Bulletin (January 2026): (1) The central bank has raised the base interest rate from 4.50% to 5.25%, increasing borrowing costs for firms with variable-rate loans. (2) The national minimum wage will rise by 7.2% from $12.50 to $13.40 per hour from April 2026, raising wage bills across engineering firms. (3) Wholesale steel and alloy prices have risen 9.0% year-on-year, while industrial input-cost inflation stands at 6.3% and demand from commercial vehicle assemblers is forecast to grow 2.8%.

--- QUESTIONS ---
  Q1(a) [8 marks]
    Question: MGF plans to fund part of its $720,000 CNC machining cell from retained profit. Explain two advantages for MGF of using retained profit rather than increasing its $450,000 bank loan.
    Answer: Point 1: Retained profit carries no interest charge and no compulsory repayment. MGF must already meet fixed costs of $300,000 a year and service a $450,000 ten-year bank loan, so funding $270,000 of the $720,000 CNC cell internally avoids adding another fixed interest commitment. With the base rate raised to 5.25%, any further variable-rate borrowing would increase costs again, whereas retained profit leaves cash flow free to absorb the rework caused by the 2.4% defect rate on machined seals.

Point 2: Using $270,000 of retained profit keeps control with founder Priya Mendip and avoids the collateral and lender conditions attached to more debt. Because MGF is already committed to a $450,000 loan, a smaller debt burden reduces the risk that a fall in orders from commercial vehicle assemblers leaves the firm unable to meet repayments. Internal funding also shows that the business can support part of its own expansion, which strengthens its position if it seeks finance later.
    Keywords: retained profit, $270,000, $720,000, $450,000, bank loan, $300,000
    Mark scheme: knowledge_max_2: 1 mark for each valid point identified (max 2). | application_analysis_max_6: Up to 3 marks per point for detailed contextual explanation and analysis applied to MGF.

  Q1(b) [12 marks]
    Question: MGF is launching a new alloy fastener range. Consider trade press advertising, an industry exhibition, or direct sales visits to assemblers. Which should MGF choose to win new contracts? Justify your recommendation.
    Answer: Trade press advertising: A campaign in a commercial-vehicle engineering magazine would reach assemblers' technical managers nationally at a low cost per reader. However, print cannot demonstrate the dimensional accuracy that 58% of the 400 surveyed buyers rank as the main purchase criterion, and it does nothing to answer concerns about the 6.5-day delivery lead time against a 5-day promise. For a business carrying $300,000 of fixed costs, spending that does not prove tolerances is difficult to justify.

Industry exhibition: A stand would let MGF show machined samples and meet several assemblers in one place, giving technical credibility. Yet stand fees, travel and staff time are expensive, and results depend on who visits. With a workforce of 60, the machinists manning the stand would be away from the CNC cell while the defect rate is already 2.4%, so output of 75,000 units could suffer.

Direct sales visits: An engineer can visit procurement teams with test certificates, answer questions on accuracy and negotiate delivery personally. This directly addresses the 47% of surveyed buyers who would switch supplier after two late deliveries, because MGF can explain how it will shorten the 6.5-day lead time. The cost per contract is higher in travel time, but each buyer approached is already qualified, so conversion is more likely than with print.

Recommendation: MGF should choose direct sales visits. They convert the 58% who buy on accuracy and reassure the 47% at risk from late delivery, which neither print advertising nor a passive exhibition stand achieves as reliably. Trade press is rejected as too indirect and unable to prove tolerances; the exhibition is rejected because its high fixed cost and staffing demands pull scarce machinists away from the $720,000 CNC cell. MGF should follow up visits with brief emails containing dimensional data.
    Keywords: $720,000, workforce of 60, 58%, 47%, 6.5 days, $300,000
    Mark scheme: level_1_1_to_4: Limited description of the three promotional routes with little reference to MGF's buyers. | level_2_5_to_8: Discussion of at least two routes with applied reference to MGF's survey, lead time and costs and some judgement. | level_3_9_to_12: Detailed evaluation of all three routes applied to MGF, with a clear recommendation explaining why trade press and the exhibition are rejected.

  Q2(a) [8 marks]
    Question: MGF's defect rate on machined seals has reached 2.4% and labour turnover is rising. Explain two benefits for MGF of using democratic leadership instead of its current autocratic style.
    Answer: Point 1: Democratic leadership gives MGF's 60 employees a voice in how the new CNC machining cell is organised, tackling the rising labour turnover among skilled machinists. Under the current autocratic style, decisions come from Priya Mendip alone, so the machinists who handle the seals daily have no route to flag problems. Involving them in setting tolerances raises ownership and job satisfaction, which should reduce the 11 of 60 workers who took more than ten days of unplanned leave.

Point 2: Consultation produces practical suggestions that an autocratic manager may miss. Machinists closest to the 2.4% defect rate can propose fixture or cutting-speed changes, improving quality without further capital beyond the $720,000 cell. Fewer defects mean less rework and less demand for agency cover at $280 a day, protecting the $300,000 fixed-cost base. Democratic leadership also helps retain the skilled staff needed to operate the cell once the $450,000 loan repayments begin.
    Keywords: autocratic leadership, hierarchical structure, 2.4%, labour turnover, 11 of 60, $280
    Mark scheme: knowledge_max_2: 1 mark for each valid point identified (max 2). | application_analysis_max_6: Up to 3 marks per point for detailed contextual explanation and analysis applied to MGF.

  Q2(b) [12 marks]
    Question: MGF wants to reduce the 2.4% defect rate and the absence among 11 of 60 machinists. Consider a productivity bonus or team working. Which should MGF choose? Justify your decision.
    Answer: Productivity bonus: Paying machinists for output above a target would raise effort and could spread the $300,000 fixed costs over more of the 75,000 units. It is easy to understand and links pay to results. However, a volume-based bonus rewards speed at precisely the wrong time: the defect rate on machined seals is already 2.4%, and 58% of surveyed buyers rank dimensional accuracy first, so faster working could create more rejected parts and more returns, undoing the benefit of extra output.

Team working: Organising machinists into small teams responsible for a whole batch means members check one another's work, so defects are caught before parts leave the cell. Teams can rotate tasks, reducing the boredom behind 11 of 60 workers taking more than ten days of unplanned leave, and peer support eases the pressure that drives labour turnover. This uses the skilled staff MGF already employs, avoiding further agency cover at $280 a day while the $720,000 cell beds in. The weaknesses are that group norms can shield slow members and that targets must be explicit.

Decision: MGF should choose team working. It attacks both problems at source — the 2.4% defect rate and the absence among 11 of 60 machinists — while a productivity bonus risks trading quality for volume when 58% of customers buy on accuracy and 47% would change supplier after late deliveries. A bonus could be added only after the defect rate falls; it should not be introduced now. Across 75,000 units a year, fewer rejected parts protect the $14.00 selling price and the cash available to meet the $300,000 fixed costs.
    Keywords: 2.4%, 11 of 60, $280, 58%, workforce of 60, $300,000
    Mark scheme: level_1_1_to_4: Basic description of a bonus and team working with little application to MGF. | level_2_5_to_8: Analysis of the benefits and drawbacks of one or both methods using MGF's defect, absence and agency-cover data. | level_3_9_to_12: Full evaluation of both methods applied to MGF with a justified decision and clear rejection of the productivity bonus.

  Q3(a) [8 marks]
    Question: Calculate and explain how MGF's management can use its cost, break-even and productivity data.

  Q3(b) [12 marks]
    Question: Using Appendix 2, evaluate MGF's liquidity by calculating the current ratio and the acid test ratio for 2024 and 2025. Has MGF's liquidity improved? Justify your answer.
    Answer: Calculations:

Current Ratio 2025 = 1.85 : 1
Acid Test Ratio 2024 = 0.98 : 1

Detailed workings: 2024 current assets = $140,000 inventories + $190,000 trade receivables + $55,000 cash = $385,000; 2025 current assets = $165,000 + $210,000 + $70,000 = $445,000. Excluding inventories, the stricter measure is ($385,000 − $140,000) ÷ $250,000 = $245,000 ÷ $250,000 = 0.98 in 2024 and ($445,000 − $165,000) ÷ $240,000 = $280,000 ÷ $240,000 = 1.17 in 2025.

Inventories also rose to $165,000, and with a 2.4% defect rate some of that stock may be slow-moving.

Conclusion: MGF's liquidity has improved. Both measures are higher and the stricter one now exceeds 1.0, so the gain is not dependent on stock. The residual risk is rising receivables, so MGF should tighten credit control before drawing further on its loan.

    Answer: Advantage: Recycling offcuts reduces the volume of waste sent to landfill and can lower material spending at a time when wholesale steel and alloy prices have risen 9.0%. Disadvantage: Segregating and storing different alloy grades needs bins, labour and a collection contract, adding to the $300,000 fixed-cost base before savings are certain. CNC swarf contaminated by cutting fluid may be worth little, so the scheme might not cover its own cost. With the defect rate already at 2.4% and $450,000 of loan interest to meet, management time spent on recycling could be better used reducing rework first.     Question: Using Appendix 3, evaluate how the base interest rate rise to 5.25%, the 7.2% minimum wage increase and the 9.0% rise in wholesale steel prices will affect MGF. Which change will have the greatest impact? Justify your answer.
    Answer: Interest rate rise (4.50% to 5.25%): The increase is 0.75 percentage points. If the $450,000 ten-year loan carries a variable rate, the extra annual cost is 0.75% × $450,000 = $3,375 a year (0.0075 × $450,000). That is modest beside fixed costs of $300,000, and if the loan is fixed the direct effect is zero. Higher rates could still make future borrowing for the $720,000 cell more expensive.

Minimum wage increase (7.2%, from $12.50 to $13.40): Each paid hour rises by $13.40 − $12.50 = $0.90. MGF has a workforce of 60 and the insert gives no hours worked, so no annual wage total can be claimed honestly. The useful comparison is productivity: 75,000 units ÷ 60 workers = 1,250 units per worker. If that holds, the higher wage is absorbed by the $14.00 selling price; if absence among 11 of 60 machinists cuts output, unit labour cost rises. Agency cover at $280 a day makes absence expensive already.

Wholesale steel and alloy inflation (9.0%): The insert does not split the $8.00 variable cost into materials, so only an explicit bound is defensible. If the whole $8.00 were steel-linked, 9.0% × $8.00 = $0.72 a unit; across 75,000 units that is $72,000 a year (75,000 × $0.72). Even a quarter of that, $18,000, would cut into the $6.00 contribution on every part and compound the rework from the 2.4% defect rate.

Conclusion: The 9.0% rise in steel prices will have the greatest impact. It applies to every unit sold, cannot be avoided by fixing a loan rate, and directly erodes the contribution that justifies the $720,000 investment. The interest rise is small and conditional, while the wage rise can be offset if productivity stays at 1,250 units per worker.

--- MAIN STEM ---
Kelvin Valve and Pump (KVP) is a public limited company in the industrial equipment sector, employing a workforce of 120. Founded in 1998 by Danica Kelvin, it supplies control valves to water utilities and operates a flat structure with democratic leadership. KVP plans to invest $1,200,000 in an automated valve-testing line, financed by a $700,000 five-year bank loan and a $500,000 share issue. It has fixed costs of $450,000 a year, a variable cost of $11.00 a unit and a selling price of $20.00, and produces 100,000 units a year. KVP faces two problems: absenteeism has reached 8% and the defect rate on cast valve bodies is rising at its Stoke foundry, delaying deliveries.

--- APPENDIX 1 — MARKETING/OPS ---
Quality and Waste Report — March 2025: The valve-testing line completed 25,000 units last month, with a defect rate of 3.1% on cast bodies, down from 4.0% in December. Customer complaints fell from 52 to 29 a month. Average delivery time is 8.2 days. A survey of 350 water-utility purchasing officers found 61% require a pressure-test certificate and 44% had delayed an order because of late delivery; 12 of 120 workers took unplanned leave exceeding nine days last month, and agency cover costs $230 a day.

--- APPENDIX 2 — FINANCIAL DATA ---

Trade receivables | 260 | 300

Current liabilities | 340 | 300

Capital employed | 3,000 | 3,500

  Q1(a) [8 marks]
    Question: KVP is funding its $1,200,000 valve-testing line with a $700,000 bank loan and a $500,000 share issue. Explain two advantages for KVP of using a share issue rather than the bank loan.
    Answer: Point 1: Share capital does not have to be repaid and dividends can be paid only when profits allow, unlike the fixed interest and instalments on a $700,000 five-year bank loan. As a public limited company KVP can issue shares to investors, so the $500,000 raised strengthens the balance sheet without adding to the $450,000 annual fixed costs. This matters while the defect rate on cast bodies is still 3.1% and output of 100,000 units has to be maintained.

Point 2: Equity finance avoids the collateral and covenants a lender would demand, leaving KVP's existing assets free and its flat structure of democratic leadership unencumbered by lender conditions. With a workforce of 120 and absenteeism at 8%, the firm needs flexibility to spend on agency cover at $230 a day rather than commit cash to debt service. A share issue also spreads the risk of the $1,200,000 testing line across shareholders instead of leaving Danica Kelvin's management exposed to a single bank.
    Keywords: share issue, $500,000, $700,000, $1,200,000, $450,000, absenteeism

    Answer: Trade-directory advertising: Listing in a water-industry directory gives KVP a permanent, low-cost presence where purchasing officers search for suppliers. It reaches many potential buyers, but a small entry cannot demonstrate that 61% of the 350 surveyed officers require a pressure-test certificate, and it does not tackle the 8.2-day delivery time that has already caused 44% to delay orders. For a firm with $450,000 fixed costs, such passive exposure converts slowly.

It is cheap per contact, measurable through replies, and can address the 44% who have delayed orders by offering a firm delivery promise. Response rates are usually low, so KVP would need a large, accurate list, and a mailing alone cannot answer technical questions as well as a meeting.

Recommendation: KVP should choose direct mail. It targets the exact procurement officers who require certificates, lets KVP answer the 44% delivery concern in writing, and costs far less than an exhibition stand while the $700,000 loan is being repaid. Trade-directory advertising is rejected as too passive to prove certification; the exhibition is rejected because it is expensive and pulls staff from the testing line at a time when 12 of 120 workers are already absent. KVP should follow up replies with technical calls.

  Q2(b) [12 marks]

This prevents faults at source, which is valuable when the defect rate is 3.1% and 61% of utility buyers require a pressure-test certificate. With $450,000 fixed costs and a $1,200,000 testing line, inspecting rather than preventing wastes capacity, and 12 of 120 workers are already absent, so extra inspectors would add cost or slow the 8.2-day delivery further.

Decision: KVP should choose quality circles. They remove the cause of the 3.1% defect rate instead of merely sorting bad valves, which matters when 61% of buyers demand certification and 44% have delayed orders. End-of-line inspection is rejected because it detects waste after it has been created and would worsen delivery performance and staffing pressure. KVP can keep a light final check, but prevention must come first. With 25,000 units tested each month and complaints already falling from 52 to 29, stopping faults at source protects that improvement rather than merely sorting bad valves after the metal and labour have been spent.

--- MAIN STEM ---
Redwood Gear Works (RGW) is a partnership in the precision engineering sector, employing a workforce of 35. Founded in 2005 by Callum Redwood and Imani Redwood, it makes custom gearboxes for renewable-energy converters and operates a hierarchical structure with laissez-faire leadership. RGW plans to invest $640,000 in a gear-grinding cell, financed by $240,000 partners' capital, a $250,000 bank loan and $150,000 of hire purchase. It has fixed costs of $210,000 a year, a variable cost of $9.00 a unit and a selling price of $16.00, and produces 60,000 units a year. RGW faces a rising scrap rate of 3.6% on gear blanks and a shortage of skilled grinders in its Bristol workshop.

--- APPENDIX 1 — MARKETING/OPS ---
Operations Log — Week 18 2025: The grinding cell completed 1,450 gear blanks with a scrap rate of 3.6%, compared with 2.1% in Week 10. Rework hours rose from 26 to 58 a week. Delivery promises were missed on 17 of 94 orders. A customer survey of 220 renewable-energy firms found 66% rate delivery reliability as critical and 39% had changed supplier after a missed order. A skills audit shows 7 of 35 workers are certified on the new grinding cell; a certification course costs $780 per person.

--- APPENDIX 2 — FINANCIAL DATA ---
Title: Extract from the Statement of Financial Position of Redwood Gear Works as at 31 March 2025 ($ '000)
Headers: ['Financial Metric', '2024', '2025']
Inventories | 95 | 120
Trade receivables | 130 | 145
Cash and cash equivalents | 30 | 50
Current liabilities | 175 | 160
Non-current assets | 1,150 | 1,400
Capital employed | 1,320 | 1,580

--- APPENDIX 3 — EXTERNAL ENVIRONMENT ---
Economic and Business Bulletin (March 2026): (1) The central bank raised the base interest rate from 4.00% to 4.75%, raising costs on variable-rate borrowing. (2) The national minimum wage will rise by 6.4% from $12.60 to $13.41 per hour from April 2026. (3) Wholesale alloy-steel prices have risen 10.5% year-on-year, while engineering input inflation is 7.1% and orders from renewable-energy converters are forecast to grow 4.0%.

--- QUESTIONS ---
  Q1(a) [8 marks]
    Question: RGW is financing its $640,000 grinding cell with $240,000 partners' capital, a $250,000 bank loan and $150,000 of hire purchase. Explain two advantages for RGW of using hire purchase rather than the bank loan for the equipment.
    Answer: Point 1: Hire purchase spreads the $150,000 cost of the grinding equipment into regular payments, so RGW keeps its $250,000 bank loan available as working capital. That matters when 17 of 94 delivery promises were missed and 39% of surveyed firms had changed supplier after a late order; the partnership needs cash to improve deliveries rather than tying it all up in machinery.

Point 2: With hire purchase RGW can use the asset immediately while paying for it, and the gear-grinding cell starts reducing the 3.6% scrap rate and 58 weekly rework hours right away. The $210,000 fixed-cost base is not increased by a second full loan, so the partners, Callum and Imani Redwood, retain more control and the $640,000 expansion can proceed even with only 7 of 35 workers certified. Hire purchase also matches payment to the life of the asset, so the partnership is not still paying for the cell once it is obsolete; with 17 of 94 orders late and 39% of surveyed firms having changed supplier, keeping the $250,000 loan free for delivery improvements is more valuable than extra equipment debt.
    Keywords: hire purchase, $150,000, $250,000, $640,000, $210,000
    Mark scheme: knowledge_max_2: 1 mark for each valid point identified (max 2). | application_analysis_max_6: Up to 3 marks per point for detailed contextual explanation and analysis applied to RGW.

  Q1(b) [12 marks]
    Question: RGW is promoting its custom gearboxes. Consider a website catalogue with e-commerce, a trade journal advertisement, or a technical sales agent. Which should RGW choose to win renewable-energy orders? Justify your recommendation.
    Answer: Website catalogue with e-commerce: A site lets converters browse specifications, request quotes and place orders at any time, giving a small partnership of 35 a national reach without a sales team. It suits technical buyers who want data before speaking to anyone. The drawback is that the 66% of surveyed firms who rate delivery reliability critically cannot be reassured by a web page alone, and RGW currently misses 17 of 94 delivery promises, so a slick catalogue could attract orders it cannot fulfil.

Trade journal advertisement: An advert in a renewable-energy engineering magazine reaches the right technical readers and builds credibility cheaply. However, an advert is passive, cannot show custom tolerances in detail, and provides no mechanism for a buyer to check the 66% delivery concern. With $210,000 fixed costs and $150,000 of hire purchase payments, RGW cannot afford spend that generates enquiries rather than contracts.

Technical sales agent: An agent with engineering knowledge can visit converter manufacturers, discuss custom designs and confirm delivery schedules face to face. The cost is commission and loss of direct control, and one agent can cover only a limited region.

The trade journal is rejected as too passive for bespoke engineering, and the website alone is rejected because it cannot overcome the 17 of 94 missed deliveries. RGW should pair the agent with a simple catalogue.

--- MAIN STEM ---
Tarn Polymer Works (TPW) is a private limited company in the polymer components sector, employing a workforce of 80. Founded in 2014 by Sofia Tarn, it moulds technical plastic parts for domestic appliance makers and operates a flat structure with autocratic leadership. TPW plans to invest $880,000 in a new injection-moulding press, financed by a $600,000 bank loan and $280,000 retained profit. It has fixed costs of $350,000 a year, a variable cost of $5.50 a unit and a selling price of $12.50, and produces 120,000 units a year. TPW faces a waste rate of 4.2% in moulding and a rising number of quality complaints from appliance assemblers in its Newton plant.

--- APPENDIX 1 — MARKETING/OPS ---
Quality and Waste Report — Q2 2025: The press produced 30,000 parts in the quarter with a waste rate of 4.2%, up from 2.8% in Q2 2024. Customer complaints rose from 23 to 41 a month, and the batch rejection rate reached 2.6%. Delivery lead time averaged 4.4 days against a 3-day target. A survey of 500 appliance buyers found 57% would pay more for consistent quality and 35% had rejected a batch for visible defects. Retraining on the new press costs $650 per operator; 14 of 80 operators have completed it.

--- APPENDIX 2 — FINANCIAL DATA ---
Title: Extract from the Statement of Financial Position of Tarn Polymer Works as at 31 March 2025 ($ '000)
Headers: ['Financial Metric', '2024', '2025']
Inventories | 110 | 140
Trade receivables | 150 | 175
Cash and cash equivalents | 35 | 45
Current liabilities | 230 | 250
Non-current assets | 1,500 | 1,850
Capital employed | 1,750 | 2,100

--- APPENDIX 3 — EXTERNAL ENVIRONMENT ---
Economic and Business Bulletin (April 2026): (1) The central bank cut the base interest rate from 5.25% to 4.50%, reducing variable-rate loan costs. (2) The national minimum wage will rise by 6.9% from $12.90 to $13.79 per hour from April 2026. (3) Wholesale polymer resin prices have risen 8.7% year-on-year, while manufacturing inflation is 5.9% and domestic appliance sales are forecast to fall 1.5%.

--- QUESTIONS ---
  Q1(a) [8 marks]
    Question: TPW is funding its $880,000 press with a $600,000 bank loan and $280,000 retained profit. Explain two advantages for TPW of using retained profit instead of the bank loan.
    Answer: Point 1: Retained profit requires no interest or repayment, so TPW avoids increasing the fixed commitment on its $600,000 loan while it already carries $350,000 of fixed costs. The $280,000 saved in interest can be spent on retraining at $650 per operator, addressing the 4.2% waste rate and 41 monthly complaints, or on absorbing the 8.7% resin price rise without raising the $12.50 selling price.

Point 2: Internal finance keeps Sofia Tarn's control intact and avoids the security a lender would demand over the new press. A smaller loan also leaves TPW better placed if appliance sales fall by the forecast 1.5% and output drops below the 120,000 units needed to cover costs. Using $280,000 of profit demonstrates that the business generates enough cash to support part of the $880,000 investment, which could help if further finance is needed. Avoiding extra loan interest also leaves more of the $12.50 selling price available to meet the $650 retraining cost for the remaining 66 operators (80 − 14) who have not completed it.
    Keywords: retained profit, $280,000, $600,000, $880,000, $350,000
    Mark scheme: knowledge_max_2: 1 mark for each valid point identified (max 2). | application_analysis_max_6: Up to 3 marks per point for detailed contextual explanation and analysis applied to TPW.

  Q1(b) [12 marks]
    Question: TPW is trying to cut its 4.2% waste rate and 41 monthly complaints. Consider end-of-line inspection, quality circles, or a total quality management programme. Which should TPW choose? Justify your recommendation.
    Answer: End-of-line inspection: Checking finished parts before dispatch is straightforward and would stop the 35% of buyers who rejected batches for visible defects from receiving faulty goods. It gives immediate feedback to the 80-strong workforce. However, inspection catches waste only after resin, machine time and labour have been used, so the 4.2% waste rate and the rise from 2.8% remain. With $350,000 fixed costs and a $600,000 loan, paying inspectors to sort scrap is less useful than preventing it, and the 4.4-day lead time against a 3-day target would lengthen.

Quality circles: Small groups of operators meet to find and fix the causes of moulding defects. This tackles waste at source, uses the knowledge of the operators, and suits a firm where only 14 of 80 have completed retraining. Circles can target the 41 complaints and 2.6% rejection rate directly, and they cost little beyond meeting time. Results depend on management acting on suggestions, and improvements may take weeks.

Total quality management: TQM embeds quality in every process and could transform the 4.2% waste rate and lift the 57% of buyers who would pay more for consistency. It is powerful but demands culture change, training across all 80 workers and sustained leadership — expensive and slow for a company servicing $600,000 of debt and a $880,000 press.

Recommendation: TPW should choose quality circles. They attack the causes of the 4.2% waste and 41 complaints at a cost the firm can afford while only 14 of 80 operators are trained. Inspection is rejected because it detects defects after the material is wasted, and TQM is rejected as too broad and slow given the loan burden. TPW can move toward TQM once circles have delivered results.
    Keywords: 4.2%, 41, 35%, 14 of 80, $650
    Mark scheme: level_1_1_to_4: Names the three quality approaches with little reference to TPW. | level_2_5_to_8: Discusses at least two approaches with applied reference to TPW's waste, complaints and training data. | level_3_9_to_12: Evaluates all three approaches in TPW's context, recommends quality circles and explains why inspection and TQM are rejected.

Decision: TPW should move to a hierarchical structure with democratic leadership. The flat autocratic option is rejected because speed alone has not stopped waste rising from 2.8% to 4.2% and complaints reaching 41. TPW should keep decision rights clear so democracy does not delay urgent line stops. With 30,000 parts made each quarter, a fault spotted by an operator can be escalated immediately through the hierarchy, whereas the present autocratic style relies on one manager noticing; that difference matters when 35% of buyers have already rejected batches.

--- APPENDIX 1 — MARKETING/OPS ---

Rejected batches rose from 9 to 16 a month, and delivery time averaged 5.8 days. A survey of 300 marine-engine builders found 63% rank corrosion resistance first and 49% would pay a premium for certified stainless couplings. --- APPENDIX 2 — FINANCIAL DATA ---

Capital employed | 1,500 | 1,750

--- APPENDIX 3 — EXTERNAL ENVIRONMENT ---
Economic and Business Bulletin (May 2026): (1) The central bank raised the base interest rate from 3.75% to 4.50%, increasing borrowing costs on variable-rate loans. (2) The national minimum wage will rise by 7.5% from $12.70 to $13.65 per hour from April 2026. (3) Wholesale stainless-steel prices have risen 9.4% year-on-year, while engineering input inflation is 6.0% and marine-engine orders are forecast to grow 2.2%.

  Q1(a) [8 marks]

    Question: Using Appendix 2, evaluate ZNC's liquidity by calculating the current ratio and the acid test ratio for 2024 and 2025. Has ZNC's liquidity improved? Justify your answer.
    Answer: Calculations:
Current Ratio 2024 = 1.38 : 1
Current Ratio 2025 = 1.50 : 1
Acid Test Ratio 2024 = 0.88 : 1
Acid Test Ratio 2025 = 0.89 : 1

Detailed workings: 2024 current assets = $100,000 inventories + $125,000 trade receivables + $50,000 cash = $275,000; 2025 current assets = $115,000 + $140,000 + $30,000 = $285,000. The broader liquidity measure is $275,000 ÷ $200,000 = 1.375, about 1.38, in 2024 and $285,000 ÷ $190,000 = 1.50 in 2025. Excluding inventories, the stricter measure is ($275,000 − $100,000) ÷ $200,000 = $175,000 ÷ $200,000 = 0.875, about 0.88, in 2024 and ($285,000 − $115,000) ÷ $190,000 = $170,000 ÷ $190,000 = 0.89 in 2025.

Evaluation: The headline picture looks better but the improvement is weak. The broader measure rose from 1.38 to 1.50 mainly because current liabilities fell from $200,000 to $190,000, while current assets grew only $10,000. The stricter measure barely moved, from 0.88 to 0.89, and remains below 1.0, so ZNC still depends on selling inventories to meet short-term obligations. Cash actually fell from $50,000 to $30,000, which is concerning while the cooperative services a $400,000 loan and commits $800,000 to a new machine. Inventories rose to $115,000 despite a 2.9% defect rate and 16 rejected batches a month, so some stock may be slow to sell, and receivables climbed to $140,000.

Conclusion: ZNC's liquidity has not meaningfully improved. The broader measure is higher, but the stricter measure at 0.89 and the fall in cash show the gain relies on inventory rather than liquid funds. Management should rebuild cash and tighten credit control before expanding further.

    Question: Using Appendix 3, evaluate how the base interest rate rise to 4.50%, the 7.5% minimum wage increase and the 9.4% rise in stainless-steel prices will affect ZNC. Which change will have the greatest impact? Justify your answer.
    Answer: Interest rate rise (3.75% to 4.50%): The rise is 0.75 percentage points. If the $400,000 bank loan is variable-rate, extra interest is 0.75% × $400,000 = $3,000 a year (0.0075 × $400,000), manageable against $270,000 fixed costs but a drain on funds for the $800,000 machine. If the loan is fixed, the direct effect is deferred.

Minimum wage increase (7.5%, from $12.70 to $13.65): Each hour rises by $13.65 − $12.70 = $0.95. ZNC has a workforce of 50 but the insert gives no hours worked, so no annual total may be assumed. Productivity is 90,000 units ÷ 50 = 1,800 units per worker; if that is maintained, the $13.20 price can absorb the rise. With 8 of 50 machinists having left and $720 certification costs, any fall in productivity would quickly raise unit labour cost.

Stainless-steel inflation (9.4%): The insert does not split the $7.20 variable cost, so an explicit bound is the honest method: if all of it were steel-linked, 9.4% × $7.20 = $0.6768, about $0.68 a unit; over 90,000 units that is roughly $60,912 a year. Even one sixth of that, about $10,000, exceeds the loan interest increase and would cut the $6.00 contribution while the 2.9% defect rate already wastes material.

Conclusion: The 9.4% rise in stainless-steel prices will have the greatest impact. It touches every coupling, cannot be removed by fixing a loan rate and directly erodes the contribution needed for the $800,000 investment. The interest rise is small and conditional; the wage rise is absorbable while productivity holds near 1,800 units per worker.
    Keywords: 4.50%, 7.5%, 9.4%, $13.65, $400,000, $7.20

--- MAIN STEM ---
Tanner & Rowe Boutique (TNR) is a private limited company in the online fashion retail sector, employing a workforce of 38. Founded in 2013 by Imogen Tanner in Manchester, the business sells women's clothing through its own website and operates a flat organisational structure with democratic leadership. TNR plans to invest $620,000 in a new e-commerce fulfilment warehouse and click-and-collect hub, financed by a $400,000 ten-year bank loan and $220,000 retained profit. It has fixed costs of $180,000 a year, a variable cost of $14.00 a unit and a selling price of $26.00, and sells 30,000 units a year. TNR faces two operational problems: the online return rate has risen to 8.5% and customers have complained about sizing errors.

--- APPENDIX 1 — MARKETING/OPS ---
E-commerce Operations Log — Q4 2026: The online store fulfilled 7,200 orders last month at an average delivery time of 4.1 days. The product return rate rose to 8.5% from 5.2%, and complaints about garment sizing reached 64 while the fulfilment error rate was 2.3%. A survey of 450 online shoppers found 71% want free returns and 58% check delivery speed before ordering. A training needs analysis shows 12 of the 38 staff have not completed on-the-job training on the new returns system; off-the-job training at the local college costs $700 per employee. Reworking a returned garment costs $9 per unit.

--- APPENDIX 2 — FINANCIAL DATA ---
Title: Extract from the Statement of Financial Position of Tanner & Rowe Boutique as at 31 March 2025 ($ '000)
Headers: ['Financial Metric', '2024', '2025']
Inventories | 90 | 70
Trade receivables | 65 | 80
Cash and cash equivalents | 25 | 30
Current liabilities | 120 | 100
Non-current assets | 900 | 1,150
Capital employed | 1,100 | 1,300

--- APPENDIX 3 — EXTERNAL ENVIRONMENT ---
Economic and Business Bulletin (January 2027): (1) The central bank raised the base interest rate from 5.0% to 5.75%, increasing debt-servicing costs for firms with variable-rate borrowing. (2) The national minimum wage will rise by 5.2% from $13.41 to $14.10 an hour from April 2027, lifting wage bills across retail and fulfilment. (3) Parcel-delivery and packaging input costs have increased 9.3% year-on-year, while consumer spending on online fashion fell 2.1% over the same period.

  Q1(a) [8 marks]
    Question: TNR plans to fund part of its $620,000 e-commerce fulfilment warehouse with a $400,000 bank loan. Explain two advantages for TNR of using $220,000 retained profit instead of the bank loan.
    Answer: Point 1: Using $220,000 of retained profit avoids interest payments and capital repayments on that portion of the $620,000 warehouse, protecting TNR's cash flow while it already services a $400,000 ten-year bank loan. With fixed costs of $180,000 a year and an 8.5% return rate that creates reworking costs, every dollar saved in interest can be spent on reducing sizing errors rather than paid to lenders, and the $26.00 selling price does not have to be raised to cover finance charges.

Point 2: Retained profit carries no collateral or repossession risk, so the new click-and-collect hub is not endangered if online demand falls short of the 30,000-unit target. It also preserves Imogen Tanner's control of the private limited company: no lender can impose conditions on how the fulfilment operation is run, allowing the democratic leadership team to redirect spending quickly towards the 71% of shoppers who want free returns. Retaining the $220,000 also signals financial strength to suppliers when TNR negotiates delivery terms amid 9.3% parcel-cost inflation.

--- MAIN STEM ---
Rowan & Jade Cooperative (RJC) is a fashion retail cooperative in the ethical clothing sector, employing a workforce of 52. Founded in 2011 by Aoife Rowan in Galway, the business sells recycled-fabric garments online and through two outlets, and operates a flat structure with democratic leadership. RJC plans to invest $480,000 in a recycled-fabric clothing range and an e-commerce returns hub, financed by a $300,000 bank loan and $180,000 retained profit. It has fixed costs of $210,000 a year, a variable cost of $11.00 a unit and a selling price of $25.00, and sells 28,000 units a year. RJC faces two operational problems: fabric offcut waste has reached 7.4% and supplier deliveries are arriving late.

--- APPENDIX 1 — MARKETING/OPS ---
Quality and Waste Report — Q4 2026: The Galway cutting room generated 7.4% fabric offcut waste by value, down from 9.1%, and 18 garments failed final inspection out of a batch of 1,200. Customer returns were 640 units and the complaint rate was 4.6% of orders. Average supplier delivery lead time lengthened to 12 days from 8 days. A survey of 500 members found 67% value recycled fabric and 62% would pay $2.00 more for it. Retraining one cutter in quality control costs $450, while a supplier quality assurance programme would cost $6,000 a year.

(3) Organic cotton and recycled-fabric input costs have risen 11.2% year-on-year, while consumer spending on ethical clothing grew 1.8% over the same period.

  Q1(a) [8 marks]
    Question: RJC plans to finance its $480,000 recycled-fabric range with a $300,000 bank loan. Explain two advantages for RJC of using $180,000 retained profit instead of the bank loan.
    Answer: Point 1: Applying $180,000 of retained profit to the $480,000 range means RJC borrows less and avoids interest and capital repayments on that portion, protecting cash flow alongside fixed costs of $210,000 a year. The money saved can be spent on tackling the 7.4% offcut waste or on the $6,000 quality assurance programme, rather than being paid to a lender, and the $25.00 selling price need not be raised to cover finance costs.

Point 2: Retained profit carries no security or repossession risk, so the new e-commerce returns hub is safe even if demand for recycled fabric disappoints. It also preserves member control of the cooperative: no bank can attach conditions to how the $300,000 is used, so the democratic leadership can respond to the 67% of members who value recycled fabric and the 62% who would pay $2.00 more. Retaining the $180,000 also demonstrates financial strength when negotiating with suppliers whose deliveries currently take 12 days.

However, RJC sells online as well as through two outlets and needs volume close to 28,000 units a year, so a regional newspaper has limited reach and cannot show the texture and colour of recycled fabric that 67% of members value.

Recommendation: RJC should choose social media advertising, supported by small in-store demonstrations. Social media gives national, measurable reach at controllable cost and can carry the recycled-fabric and $2.00-premium message to the 62% of members willing to pay more; in-store events alone are too local and costly per customer, and newspapers are rejected as static and regionally limited.     Question: RJC wants to reduce its 7.4% fabric waste and late supplier deliveries. Consider retraining cutters in quality control or introducing a supplier quality assurance programme. Which should RJC choose? Justify your decision.

Decision: RJC should introduce the supplier quality assurance programme first, with limited cutter retraining alongside it. A few $450 training places should still be funded so the 18 inspection failures fall, combining the two approaches rather than relying only on in-house fixes. The cooperative should review the 7.4% waste figure and the 12-day lead time each quarter so it can judge whether the $6,000 annual spend is delivering value.

  Q4(b) [12 marks]
    Question: Using Appendix 3, evaluate how the base interest rate rise to 6.0%, the 4.8% minimum wage increase and the 11.2% rise in organic cotton and recycled-fabric costs will affect RJC. Which change will have the greatest impact? Justify your answer.
    Answer: Interest rate rise (5.25% to 6.0%): If RJC's $300,000 bank loan is variable-rate, the annual interest cost increases by 0.75% of $300,000 = $2,250 a year (0.0075 × $300,000). This is small next to fixed costs of $210,000 a year, and if the loan is fixed there is no immediate extra charge. The cooperative can limit the risk by fixing the rate, so this is the least pressing of the three changes.

Minimum wage rise (4.8%, to $13.60 an hour): The insert gives a workforce of 52 but no hours worked or pay rates, so an annual wage total cannot be invented. Qualitatively, the rise increases the cost of running the two outlets and the returns hub and cannot be avoided. Because 7.4% of fabric is wasted and a $450 cutter retraining place is budgeted, any wage increase that is not matched by productivity will raise unit cost and narrow the $14.00 contribution, but the effect is spread across the cooperative rather than concentrated on one input.

Input cost inflation (11.2%): The insert gives a $11.00 variable cost per unit but does not decompose it. If all of it rose by 11.2%, the increase would be 0.112 × $11.00 = $1.23 per unit, and at 28,000 units that is $34,440 a year (28,000 × $1.23). Even a smaller rise would erode the $14.00 contribution on every garment sold; the $2.00 premium that 62% of members would accept can offset only part of it.

Conclusion: The 11.2% rise in fabric costs will have the greatest impact. It applies to every one of the 28,000 units, reaches a larger annual sum than the $2,250 interest change, and directly threatens the contribution that funds the $480,000 range. The interest rise is modest and can be fixed, and the wage effect cannot be quantified from the insert, so both rank lower; RJC should negotiate bulk fabric prices and introduce the premium gradually while monitoring the 7.4% waste figure.

--- MAIN STEM ---
Quill & Muse Boutique (QMB) is a sole trader business in the luxury online accessories sector, employing a workforce of 16. Founded in 2016 by Seraphina Quill in Paris, the business sells handmade scarves and bags through its own website and operates a hierarchical structure with autocratic leadership. QMB plans to invest $260,000 in a digital photography studio and an automated stock-control system, financed by a $150,000 bank loan and $110,000 of the owner's savings. It has fixed costs of $96,000 a year, a variable cost of $18.00 a unit and a selling price of $42.00, and sells 8,000 units a year. QMB faces two operational problems: the return rate has reached 12.1% because of sizing complaints and stock-outs are losing sales.

--- APPENDIX 1 — MARKETING/OPS ---
Market Research Summary — Q4 2026: A questionnaire of 300 online accessories buyers found 44% had returned an item for sizing reasons and 73% consult product photographs before purchase. The observed return rate in Q4 was 12.1%, up from 8.4%, and 52 complaints were logged about unclear product images. Stock-outs affected 9% of listed scarves. Focus groups of 24 shoppers found 68% would buy more if more angles were shown. Hiring a freelance photographer costs $12 per item, while training an existing employee in product photography costs $600 per person.

--- APPENDIX 2 — FINANCIAL DATA ---
Title: Extract from the Statement of Financial Position of Quill & Muse Boutique as at 31 March 2025 ($ '000)
Headers: ['Financial Metric', '2024', '2025']

Capital employed | 380 | 455

(2) The national minimum wage will rise 6.2% from $13.14 to $13.95 an hour from April 2027, affecting the cost of the 16-strong workforce. (3) Courier and packing material costs have increased 10.4% year-on-year, while consumer spending on luxury online accessories grew 4.2% in the same period.

The money not borrowed can instead fund the automated stock-control system, tackling the 9% of scarves affected by stock-outs, without increasing the burden of the $150,000 bank loan or forcing the $42.00 selling price higher.

Point 2: Owner savings carry no collateral or repossession risk, so Seraphina Quill's luxury accessories business is not exposed if the studio fails to reduce the 12.1% return rate. As a sole trader she also keeps full control: no lender can set conditions on how the website or photography is run, so decisions can be made quickly under the hierarchical structure. Committing her own savings also demonstrates personal commitment to suppliers and to the 16-strong workforce when the business invests $260,000 in new capacity. Keeping $110,000 of savings invested also reduces the risk that a fall in sales below the 4,000-unit break-even point leaves her unable to meet loan instalments.

    Question: Using Appendix 3, evaluate how the base interest rate rise to 5.5%, the 6.2% minimum wage increase and the 10.4% rise in courier and packing material costs will affect QMB. Which change will have the greatest impact? Justify your answer.
    Answer: Interest rate rise (4.75% to 5.5%): If QMB's $150,000 bank loan is variable-rate, the extra interest is 0.75% of $150,000 = $1,125 a year (0.0075 × $150,000). Minimum wage rise (6.2%, to $13.95 an hour): The insert gives a workforce of 16 but no hours or pay rates, so a defensible annual wage total cannot be calculated. --- MAIN STEM ---
Vale & Wren Xpress (VWX) is a public limited company in the fast-fashion e-commerce sector, employing a workforce of 240. Supplier assurance is not abandoned: it is deferred until inspection records show whether defects originate with suppliers, at which point prevention becomes the better long-term tool. --- MAIN STEM ---
Zephyr & Loom Fabrics (ZLF) is a partnership in the sustainable home-textile and fashion-fabric e-commerce sector, employing a workforce of 34. Founded in 2018 by partners Priya Loomis and Daniel Zephyr in Copenhagen, the business sells dyed fabrics online to craft and fashion makers through its own website and operates a flat structure with laissez-faire leadership. ZLF plans to invest $540,000 in a digital fabric-printing and online fulfilment hub, financed by a $320,000 bank loan and $220,000 retained profit. It has fixed costs of $240,000 a year, a variable cost of $9.00 a unit and a selling price of $21.00, and sells 36,000 units a year. ZLF faces two operational problems: dye waste has reached 6.8% and customer deliveries are running late.

--- APPENDIX 1 — MARKETING/OPS ---
Quality and Waste Report — Q4 2026: Dye waste ran at 6.8% of materials, down from 8.3%, and 27 fabric rolls were rejected for colour inconsistency out of 1,500 inspected. Customer returns were 310 units and 38 complaints concerned late delivery. Average order dispatch time was 6.2 days against a 4-day promise. A survey of 350 makers found 64% would pay $1.50 more for digitally printed fabric and 57% value faster delivery. Retraining a dye technician costs $520; a computer colour-matching system costs $28,000.

--- APPENDIX 2 — FINANCIAL DATA ---

Acid Test Ratio 2024 = 0.70 : 1

Detailed workings: 2024 current assets = $90,000 + $75,000 + $30,000 = $195,000; 2025 current assets = $70,000 + $90,000 + $36,000 = $196,000. Dividing by current liabilities of $150,000 in 2024 and $140,000 in 2025 gives the first pair of figures. Removing stock leaves $105,000 in 2024 and $126,000 in 2025, and dividing those by the same liabilities gives the second pair.

Evaluation: Liquidity has improved. The first ratio rose from 1.30 to 1.40 because current liabilities fell from $150,000 to $140,000 while current assets edged up, giving more cover for the $540,000 printing hub commitments. The second ratio improved from 0.70 to 0.90, so ZLF relies less on selling its $70,000 of inventories to pay short-term debts, which is helpful when 6.8% dye waste and 27 rejected rolls can make stock harder to sell. However, trade receivables rose from $75,000 to $90,000 and cash from $30,000 to $36,000 only slightly, so much cash is tied up in customers; the $320,000 bank loan also brings interest obligations if rates rise.

Conclusion: ZLF's financial position has improved. Both measures are higher and the rise in the second measure shows the gain is not merely stock-driven. The residual risk is slower collection from makers, so the partners should tighten credit control before committing more of the $540,000 investment while 38 delivery complaints remain unresolved.
    Keywords: 1.30, 1.40, 0.70, 0.90, $195,000, $196,000
    Mark scheme: level_1_1_to_4: States financial figures or changes without accurate ratio calculations. | level_2_5_to_8: Accurately calculates the current ratio and acid test ratio for both years with contextual analysis of the trend. | level_3_9_to_12: Accurate calculations for both years with detailed evaluation of inventory, receivables and liabilities movements and a justified conclusion on whether ZLF's position improved.

  Q4(a) [8 marks]
    Question: ZLF is considering a $1.50 premium for digitally printed fabric. Explain one advantage and one disadvantage for ZLF of this decision.
    Answer: Advantage: The survey of 350 makers shows 64% would pay $1.50 more for digitally printed fabric and 57% value faster delivery, so the premium is evidence-based and would raise contribution per unit from $12.00 to $13.50. Across 36,000 units that is $54,000 a year (36,000 × $1.50), helping ZLF cover fixed costs of $240,000 and part of the $540,000 hub cost even with home-textile spending up only 2.6%.

Disadvantage: The 36% of makers who would not pay more may switch to plain fabric, and the 12.8% rise in dye and chemical input costs could absorb much of the $1.50 before it reaches profit. With dye waste at 6.8%, 27 rejected rolls and 38 late-delivery complaints, a higher price may raise expectations that ZLF currently struggles to meet. The partners should therefore trial the premium on one print range while checking that the $28,000 colour-matching system reduces rejects. They should compare orders from the 64% who welcome printing with the 36% who do not, so the premium does not hasten a fall in demand for plain dyed fabric.
    Keywords: $1.50, 64%, 12.8%, 6.8%, $540,000, $9.00
    Mark scheme: knowledge_max_2: 1 mark for a valid advantage and 1 mark for a valid disadvantage. | application_analysis_max_6: Up to 3 marks per point for detailed contextual development linked to ZLF's survey, costs and quality record.

  Q4(b) [12 marks]
    Question: Using Appendix 3, evaluate how the base interest rate rise to 5.75%, the 5.5% minimum wage increase and the 12.8% rise in dye and chemical input costs will affect ZLF. Which change will have the greatest impact? Justify your answer.
    Answer: Interest rate rise (5.0% to 5.75%): On the specified $320,000 bank loan, if the rate is variable the extra interest is 0.75% of $320,000 = $2,400 a year (0.0075 × $320,000). That is small beside fixed costs of $240,000 a year and can be removed by fixing the rate, so this is the least significant of the three changes; higher rates could still dampen the 2.6% growth in home-textile spending.

Minimum wage rise (5.5%, to $13.40 an hour): The insert gives 34 staff but no hours worked or pay rates, so an annual wage bill cannot be invented. Qualitatively the rise increases the cost of dispatching orders and cannot be avoided. Its effect depends on the 36,000 units sold and on whether laissez-faire leadership maintains productivity; with 38 delivery complaints and a 6.2-day dispatch time, extra wage costs may not translate into better service unless the 4-day promise is met more often.

Dye and chemical inflation (12.8%): The insert gives a $9.00 variable cost per unit but does not decompose it. The honest upper bound is 0.128 × $9.00 = $1.152 per unit, which over 36,000 units is $41,472 a year (36,000 × $1.152). Even a smaller increase reduces the $12.00 contribution on every metre sold, and the 6.8% dye waste makes the problem worse because material is already being lost before it becomes a sale.

Conclusion: The 12.8% rise in dye and chemical costs will have the greatest impact. It can add about $41,472 a year, far above the $2,400 interest change, and it can be bounded from the insert whereas the wage rise cannot be quantified. Unlike the interest rise, it cannot be eliminated by fixing a rate and it strikes every unit of the 36,000 sold. ZLF should renegotiate dye supply, use the $28,000 colour-matching system to cut the 27 rejected rolls, and trial the $1.50 premium to recover part of the increase.
    Keywords: 5.75%, 5.5%, 12.8%, $13.40, $320,000, 6.8%
    Mark scheme: level_1_1_to_4: Identifies the external factors with limited application to ZLF. | level_2_5_to_8: Analyses the impact of at least two external changes on ZLF's costs, revenue or financing in context. | level_3_9_to_12: Detailed evaluation of all three external changes in the context of ZLF with a well-justified judgement that dye cost inflation has the greatest impact and why the others are smaller.

--- MAIN STEM ---
Thorncliff Bay Resort (TBR) is a private limited company in the seaside hospitality and tourism sector on the south coast, employing a workforce of 90. Founded in 2011 by Priya Rathore, it operates a hierarchical structure with democratic leadership and sells 18,000 units a year, one unit being an occupied room-night at an average selling price of $160. TBR plans to invest $900,000 in a new sea-view wing and spa, financed by a $600,000 ten-year bank loan and $300,000 retained profit. It has fixed costs of $420,000 a year and a variable cost of $60 a unit. TBR faces rising labour turnover among housekeeping staff and guest complaints about slow check-in at peak weekends.

--- APPENDIX 1 — MARKETING/OPS ---
Guest and Operations Report, Q4 2025: TBR recorded 4,500 room-nights last quarter with 14 online service complaints, down from 26 a year earlier. Average check-in time was 8.4 minutes against a 5-minute target, and the housekeeping defect rate (rooms failing inspection) was 3.6%, down from 5.1%. A survey of 750 guests found that 68% would pay up to $12 more for a sea-view spa room and 57% choose hotels on sustainability credentials. Staff records show 31 of 90 employees have not yet completed on-the-job training on the new check-in system; off-the-job training at the local hotel college costs $480 per employee.

--- APPENDIX 2 — FINANCIAL DATA ---
Title: Extract from the Statement of Financial Position of Thorncliff Bay Resort as at 31 March 2025 ($ '000)
Headers: ['Financial Metric', '2024', '2025']

Trade receivables | 120 | 150
Cash and cash equivalents | 35 | 55
Current liabilities | 160 | 170
Non-current assets | 2,100 | 2,650
Capital employed | 2,600 | 2,800

--- APPENDIX 3 — EXTERNAL ENVIRONMENT ---
Economic and Tourism Bulletin (November 2026): (1) The central bank has raised the base interest rate from 3.75% to 4.5%, increasing debt-service costs for TBR's variable-rate $600,000 bank loan. (2) The national minimum wage will rise by 5.2% from $14.07 to $14.80 an hour from April 2026, affecting housekeeping and front-of-house rosters. (3) Inbound tourist arrivals are forecast to grow 8.3%, while hotel energy and food input costs have risen 9.6% and domestic holiday inflation is 6.4%.

  Q1(a) [8 marks]
    Question: TBR plans to fund part of its new sea-view wing and spa with a $600,000 bank loan. Explain two advantages for TBR of using the $300,000 retained profit instead of borrowing more.
    Answer: Point 1: Using the $300,000 retained profit avoids all interest and repayment charges on that portion of the $900,000 sea-view wing and spa, protecting TBR's cash flow at a time when it already carries fixed costs of $420,000 a year and faces a base-rate rise to 4.5%. Every dollar not paid to the lender can instead cover the 9.6% increase in hotel energy and food inputs or fund the new spa's launch, so the resort can hold its $160 selling price rather than passing costs to guests. Retained profit is also immediately available, with no loan-approval delay before the building work starts.

Point 2: Retained profit requires no collateral and no fixed monthly instalments, so Priya Rathore's resort is not exposed to repossession risk if the new wing attracts fewer bookings than forecast, which matters given the rising labour turnover among housekeeping staff. It also keeps ownership and control within the existing company: a larger loan would let the lender impose conditions on how the sea-view wing is run. Using the $300,000 first therefore reduces the $600,000 bank loan actually needed, cutting TBR's debt commitment while it tackles slow peak-weekend check-in and a 5.2% wage rise.
    Keywords: retained profit, $300,000, $600,000, $900,000, $420,000, sea-view
    Mark scheme: knowledge_max_2: 1 mark for each valid advantage identified (max 2). | application_analysis_max_6: Up to 3 marks per point for contextual explanation applied to TBR's wing investment, costs and borrowing.

  Q1(b) [12 marks]
    Question: TBR is promoting its new sea-view wing and spa. Consider a national television campaign, regional radio advertising, and social media travel influencers. Which should TBR choose? Justify your recommendation.
    Answer: National television campaign: A television advertisement would build awareness of the new sea-view wing and spa quickly across the south coast and beyond, reaching the 68% of surveyed guests who would pay $12 more for such a room and helping justify the $900,000 investment. However, airtime and production are expensive for a 90-employee resort already servicing a $600,000 bank loan, and much of the audience lives outside TBR's drive-to catchment, so a large share of the spend would be wasted.

Regional radio advertising: Local radio is far cheaper and can target drive-to weekend guests within the resort's catchment, with flexible short-notice messages about spa breaks. Its weakness is reach and format: radio cannot show the sea views or the refurbished spa, and it will not reach the corporate and tour guests who make up much of the 18,000 room-nights, so it is unlikely to fill a whole new wing on its own.

Social media travel influencers: Travel and wellness influencers can show the sea-view spa visually to exactly the segment identified in TBR's research — the 57% of 750 guests who choose hotels on sustainability credentials and the 68% willing to pay $12 more. Engagement is measurable, cost per reached guest is low, and user-generated content keeps promoting the wing after launch. Results build more slowly than television and depend on choosing credible influencers.

Recommendation: TBR should choose social media travel influencers, backed by modest local radio for last-minute weekend availability. Influencers give visual reach at a fraction of television's cost and directly target the guests whose stated preferences justify the $900,000 wing. Television is rejected as unaffordable and untargeted while TBR carries a $600,000 loan and $420,000 fixed costs; radio alone is rejected because it cannot display the spa or reach enough guests to fill 18,000 room-nights. The $300,000 retained profit can fund the campaign without new debt.
    Keywords: $900,000, sea-view, $420,000, 18,000, 68%, $600,000

  Q2(a) [8 marks]
    Question: TBR's labour turnover among housekeeping staff is rising and check-in complaints are high. Explain two benefits for TBR of using its democratic leadership style to address these problems.
    Answer: Point 1: Democratic leadership gives TBR's workforce of 90 a genuine voice in how housekeeping and reception are organised, which addresses the rising labour turnover directly. When staff help design room-allocation rotas or suggest ways to cut the 8.4-minute check-in time towards the 5-minute target, they develop ownership and job satisfaction (Herzberg's motivators), so they are more likely to stay. Retaining experienced housekeepers protects service quality while the new sea-view wing opens and avoids the disruption of repeatedly recruiting and inducting replacements.

Point 2: Consulting the employees who actually clean rooms and greet guests generates practical improvements that management may miss. Housekeeping suggestions can target the weaker areas behind guest complaints and the 3.6% inspection defect rate, while reception ideas can smooth peak-weekend check-in, reducing the 14 complaints. Involvement also raises morale and attendance, easing pressure on the team when the minimum wage rises 5.2% to $14.80 and TBR must protect its $100 contribution per room-night. Democratic leadership suits a resort that needs fast, local problem-solving rather than purely top-down instructions.

  Q2(b) [12 marks]
    Question: TBR must train 31 staff on the new check-in system. Consider on-the-job training and off-the-job training at the local hotel college. Which should TBR choose? Justify your decision.
    Answer: On-the-job training: Coaching the 31 untrained staff at the front desk uses TBR's own check-in system and real guest situations, so learning is directly transferable and employees stay productive during peak weekends. It also removes staff from the desk for several days, reducing capacity during busy periods, and generic course content may not match TBR's exact check-in software, so some on-site follow-up would still be needed after the course.

Decision: TBR should choose on-the-job training as the main method, backed by short college modules for senior receptionists. On-the-job training is cheaper, system-specific and keeps the desk staffed while complaints are reduced and labour turnover is high; full off-the-job training is rejected because losing 31 staff from the front desk at once would worsen the 8.4-minute check-in problem and add $14,880 for content that still needs on-site adaptation. College placements can be added for new recruits once the new wing opens.

    Question: Using Appendix 3, evaluate how the base interest rate rise to 4.5%, the 5.2% minimum wage increase and the 9.6% rise in energy and food input costs will affect TBR. Which change will have the greatest impact? Justify your answer.
    Answer: Interest rate rise (3.75% to 4.5%): If TBR's $600,000 bank loan tracks the base rate, the annual interest cost rises by 0.75% of $600,000 = $4,500 a year (0.0075 × $600,000). That is small against fixed costs of $420,000 and can be largely removed by fixing the loan rate. Minimum wage increase (5.2%, to $14.80 an hour): Housekeeping and front-of-house roles at TBR are hourly paid, so this rise feeds into the wage bill and is not optional. Energy and food input costs (9.6%): These apply to every one of the 18,000 room-nights. --- MAIN STEM ---
Marlowe City Hotels (MBH) is a public limited company in the boutique hospitality sector, employing a workforce of 160 across six city-centre properties. Founded in 2008 by Daniel Okafor, it has a flat organisational structure with laissez-faire leadership and sells 24,000 units a year, one unit being an occupied apartment-night at an average selling price of $170. MBH plans to invest $1,200,000 in refurbishing and rebranding its properties, financed by a $500,000 share issue and a $700,000 bank loan. It has fixed costs of $600,000 a year and a variable cost of $70 a unit. MBH's guest satisfaction score has fallen to 3.9 out of 5 and absence among reception staff has reached 7%.

--- APPENDIX 1 — MARKETING/OPS ---
Quality and Guest Report, Q4 2025: MBH logged 6,000 apartment-nights last quarter with 47 service complaints, up from 29 in the same quarter last year. The guest satisfaction score slipped to 3.9 out of 5 from 4.4, and 7% of reception shifts were uncovered through absence. Check-in averaged 6.8 minutes against a 4-minute promise. A survey of 820 past guests found 61% would pay $15 more for a refurbished suite and 54% book boutique hotels through review sites. Of 160 staff, 38 have not completed on-the-job refresher training; off-the-job customer-care courses at the city college cost $540 per employee.

--- APPENDIX 2 — FINANCIAL DATA ---
Title: Extract from the Statement of Financial Position of Marlowe City Hotels as at 31 March 2025 ($ '000)
Headers: ['Financial Metric', '2024', '2025']
Inventories | 40 | 55
Trade receivables | 90 | 130
Cash and cash equivalents | 95 | 60
Current liabilities | 150 | 190
Non-current assets | 3,000 | 3,150
Capital employed | 3,200 | 3,300

--- APPENDIX 3 — EXTERNAL ENVIRONMENT ---
Economic and City Tourism Bulletin (November 2026): (1) The central bank has raised the base interest rate from 4.0% to 4.75%, raising the cost of MBH's variable-rate $700,000 bank loan. (2) The national minimum wage will rise by 4.8% from $14.50 to $15.20 an hour from April 2026, increasing reception and housekeeping wage costs. (3) City business rates have risen 7.2%, while city visitor spending grew 4.1% and hotel energy costs rose 11.3% year-on-year.

--- QUESTIONS ---
  Q1(a) [8 marks]
    Question: MBH plans to fund part of its refurbishment with a $700,000 bank loan. Explain two advantages for MBH of using the $500,000 share issue instead of borrowing more.
    Answer: Point 1: A share issue raises permanent capital that carries no interest and no fixed repayment dates, so MBH can commit the $500,000 to refurbishing six city-centre properties without adding to the interest burden on its $700,000 bank loan, especially as the base rate has risen to 4.75%. With fixed costs already at $600,000 a year and energy costs up 11.3%, avoiding debt service protects the $100 contribution earned on each of the 24,000 apartment-nights and leaves more cash to reverse the falling 3.9 guest satisfaction score.

Point 2: Share capital does not require collateral, so the properties themselves are not put at risk if the rebrand fails to attract bookings — a real concern while 7% of reception shifts are uncovered. As a public limited company, MBH can access equity investors more easily than a smaller firm, and the extra capital strengthens the balance sheet before the $1,200,000 programme. The trade-off is dilution of existing shareholders including founder Daniel Okafor, but the avoided interest and repayment obligations make the share issue attractive for a long-life refurbishment that will earn returns over many years.
    Keywords: share issue, $500,000, $700,000, $1,200,000, refurbishing, $600,000
    Mark scheme: knowledge_max_2: 1 mark for each valid advantage identified (max 2). | application_analysis_max_6: Up to 3 marks per point for contextual explanation applied to MBH's funding and refurbishment.

  Q1(b) [12 marks]
    Question: MBH is relaunching its boutique brand after refurbishment. Consider print press advertising, sponsorship on hotel-booking platforms, and social media travel influencers. Which should MBH choose? Justify your recommendation.
    Answer: Print press advertising: Newspaper and magazine features can build credibility for a relaunched boutique brand and reach older, higher-spending city visitors. However, print has no direct booking link, its reach is hard to measure, and the cost of full-page colour adverts in national titles would be high for a business already funding a $1,200,000 refurbishment with a $700,000 bank loan. Much of the readership will not be in MBH's six cities, so wastage is significant.

Sponsorship on hotel-booking platforms: Paid placement on the sites where 54% of surveyed guests say they book boutique hotels would intercept customers at the moment of decision and drive measurable bookings for the refurbished suites. The downside is cost per click on competitive city keywords and dependence on a third-party platform that also lists rivals; MBH would be renting visibility rather than owning a direct relationship with guests, which weakens the brand it is trying to rebuild.

Social media travel influencers: Design, food and city-break influencers can showcase the refurbished suites visually to the 54% who book via review sites and the 61% who would pay $15 more for a refurbished suite. Content is shareable, targeting is precise and cost per engagement is lower than print, though results take time to build and depend on credible, well-matched influencers.

Recommendation: MBH should choose sponsorship on hotel-booking platforms as the primary channel, reinforced by a smaller influencer campaign. Platform sponsorship converts the 54% who already book through review sites at the decision point, which is what the $1,200,000 refurbishment needs to fill 24,000 apartment-nights. Print is rejected as unmeasurable and costly while MBH services a $700,000 loan and $600,000 fixed costs; influencers alone are rejected because they build awareness more slowly than booking-platform placement. The $500,000 share issue can fund the launch without more debt.
    Keywords: $1,200,000, refurbished suite, $15, 61%, review sites, $700,000
    Mark scheme: level_1_1_to_4: Limited description of the promotional options with minimal application to MBH. | level_2_5_to_8: Discussion of advantages and disadvantages of at least two options in the context of MBH with some judgement. | level_3_9_to_12: Detailed discussion of all three options in the context of MBH with a well-justified recommendation explaining why print and influencers are rejected.

  Q2(a) [8 marks]
    Question: MBH's guest satisfaction score has fallen and reception absence is high. Explain two benefits for MBH of its laissez-faire leadership style in improving this situation.
    Answer: Point 1: Laissez-faire leadership gives MBH's experienced reception teams freedom to solve guest problems immediately, which is valuable when satisfaction has slipped to 3.9 out of 5 and 47 service complaints were logged. Staff closest to the guest can offer an on-the-spot remedy rather than waiting for a manager, speeding up a response to the 6.8-minute check-in and helping lift the score back towards 4.4. Faster decisions improve the guest experience without adding management layers to a flat structure of 160 employees.

Point 2: Delegating decisions can raise motivation and reduce the 7% reception absence, because trusted employees feel ownership of their work rather than being closely supervised. Higher autonomy often improves job satisfaction, encouraging staff to protect their shifts and lowering the disruption caused by uncovered desks. That continuity supports the $1,200,000 rebrand, since consistent service is needed to justify the $15 premium that 61% of surveyed guests say they would pay. Laissez-faire leadership therefore attacks both the satisfaction decline and the absence problem through faster local decisions and greater staff commitment.

    Question: MBH needs to train 38 staff in customer care after the refurbishment. Consider on-the-job training and off-the-job training at the city college. Which should MBH choose? Justify your decision.

    Question: Using Appendix 2, evaluate MBH's liquidity by calculating the current ratio and the acid test ratio for 2024 and 2025. Has MBH's financial position improved? Justify your answer.

Current Ratio 2025 = 1.29 : 1
Acid Test Ratio 2024 = 1.23 : 1

The small rise in inventories to $55,000 offers little protection because stock is the least liquid current asset.

Conclusion: MBH's financial position has not improved. Both measures are lower in 2025 and the fall in the stock-excluding measure to 1.00 is the stronger evidence of weaker underlying liquidity. Minimum wage increase (4.8%, to $15.20 an hour): Reception and housekeeping at MBH are hourly paid, so the rise feeds directly into wage costs and cannot be avoided. --- MAIN STEM ---
Kestrel River Expeditions (KRE) is a partnership in the adventure tourism and outdoor leisure sector, employing a workforce of 70. Founded in 2013 by Sofia Almeida and two partners, it runs a hierarchical structure with autocratic leadership and sells 14,000 units a year, one unit being a paid rafting place at an average selling price of $120. KRE plans to invest $640,000 in new rafts and a riverside activity centre, financed by a $240,000 hire-purchase agreement and $400,000 retained profit. It has fixed costs of $280,000 a year and a variable cost of $40 a unit. A recent gear inspection found a 4.2% defect rate in safety equipment and guide absence has reached 8%.

--- APPENDIX 1 — MARKETING/OPS ---
Safety and Operations Log, Q3 2025: KRE ran 3,500 expedition places with 12 incident reports, down from 19 last season, and a 4.2% defect rate in inspected buoyancy aids and helmets. Guide absence affected 8% of scheduled trips. Feedback from 640 participants showed 72% rated safety briefings as clear and 66% would pay $9 more for upgraded wetsuit hire. Of 70 staff, 26 guides have not completed on-the-job safety refresher training; off-the-job swiftwater-rescue courses cost $620 per guide.

--- APPENDIX 2 — FINANCIAL DATA ---

Headers: ['Financial Metric', '2024', '2025']

Cash and cash equivalents | 25 | 65
Current liabilities | 100 | 110
Non-current assets | 900 | 1,180
Capital employed | 1,100 | 1,320

(2) The national minimum wage will rise by 6.1% from $13.53 to $14.35 an hour from April 2026, affecting seasonal guide pay. (3) Diesel and equipment input costs have risen 13.4%, adventure-tourism demand grew 5.8% and consumer inflation is running at 5.5%.

    Answer: Point 1: Using the $400,000 retained profit avoids the interest charges and fixed periodic instalments attached to the $240,000 hire-purchase agreement, which matters for a seasonal rafting business whose cash inflows are concentrated in summer. With fixed costs of $280,000 a year already committed and the base rate rising to 4.25%, every dollar of retained profit spent now is a dollar of finance cost avoided, protecting the $80 contribution earned on each of the 14,000 expedition places.

Point 2: Retained profit gives KRE immediate ownership of the new rafts and centre without a hire-purchase lender holding title until the final payment, so the partnership is not exposed to repossession if a poor season reduces bookings. It also preserves the partners' control: no finance company can impose conditions on how Sofia Almeida and her partners run the riverside operation. Drawing on the $400,000 first reduces the hire-purchase balance actually required, cutting KRE's fixed commitments while it deals with a 4.2% defect rate in safety gear and 8% guide absence.

Its limitation is that audio cannot show the rapids or the riverside setting, and the audience includes many people who will never book a rafting trip, so a share of the spend is wasted while KRE is funding a $640,000 investment.

Content is shareable and results are measurable, though it takes time to build and depends on choosing influencers with genuine credibility in adventure tourism.

Recommendation: KRE should choose social media adventure influencers as the main channel, supported by low-cost leaflets in tourist offices. Influencers demonstrate the experience visually and reach the safety-conscious, experience-seeking segment that underpins the $640,000 centre, at a cost controllable from the $400,000 retained profit. Local radio is rejected because it cannot display the activity and reaches too many non-customers; leaflets alone are rejected because their reach is too narrow to fill 14,000 places.
