--- MAIN STEM ---
Pinecrest Leisure Parks (PLP) is a public limited company in the leisure and visitor-attraction sector, employing a workforce of 225. Founded in 1996 by Grace Oyelaran, it operates a hierarchical structure with democratic leadership and sells 45,000 units a year, one unit being a park admission at an average selling price of $75. PLP plans to invest $1,500,000 in a new water-slide complex and splash zone, financed by a $900,000 bank loan and a $600,000 share issue. It has fixed costs of $750,000 a year and a variable cost of $25 a unit. Average queue times at three popular rides have reached 42 minutes and food-outlet waste has risen to 6.4% of purchases.

--- APPENDIX 1 — MARKETING/OPS ---
Operations and Quality Report, Q2 2025: PLP welcomed 11,250 admissions with 63 complaint logs, up from 41 last year, while average queue time at the three busiest rides reached 42 minutes against a 20-minute target. Food-outlet waste was 6.4% of purchases. A visitor survey of 1,050 families found 74% would pay $8 more for a fast-track water-slide ticket and 59% choose parks with short queues. Of 225 staff, 44 ride operators have not completed on-the-job queue-management training; off-the-job customer-service courses at the regional college cost $410 per employee.

--- APPENDIX 2 — FINANCIAL DATA ---
Title: Extract from the Statement of Financial Position of Pinecrest Leisure Parks as at 31 March 2025 ($ '000)
Headers: ['Financial Metric', '2024', '2025']
Inventories | 48 | 55
Trade receivables | 70 | 105
Cash and cash equivalents | 90 | 120
Current liabilities | 205 | 215
Non-current assets | 4,200 | 4,600
Capital employed | 4,500 | 4,900

--- APPENDIX 3 — EXTERNAL ENVIRONMENT ---
Economic and Family-Leisure Bulletin (November 2026): (1) The central bank has raised the base interest rate from 4.25% to 5.0%, increasing the cost of PLP's variable-rate $900,000 bank loan. (2) The national minimum wage will rise by 5.9% from $14.21 to $15.05 an hour from April 2026, affecting ride and catering staff. (3) Park energy costs have risen 10.8%, family day-trip spending grew 3.7% and consumer inflation is 5.1%.

--- QUESTIONS ---
  Q1(a) [8 marks]
    Question: PLP plans to fund part of its water-slide complex with a $900,000 bank loan. Explain two advantages for PLP of using the $600,000 share issue instead of borrowing more.
    Answer: Point 1: A share issue provides permanent capital with no interest charges and no fixed repayment dates, so PLP can commit the $600,000 to the water-slide complex without increasing the burden of its $900,000 bank loan at a time when the base rate has risen to 5.0%. With fixed costs of $750,000 a year and energy costs up 10.8%, avoiding extra debt service protects the $50 contribution earned on each of the 45,000 admissions and leaves cash to tackle the 42-minute queues.

Point 2: Equity does not require the park's land and rides to be offered as collateral, so the $1,500,000 development does not put existing assets at risk if the new attraction underperforms — a genuine concern while complaints have risen to 63 and 6.4% of food purchases are wasted. As a public limited company, PLP can raise the $600,000 from investors and strengthen its balance sheet before borrowing the remaining $900,000.     Question: Using Appendix 2, evaluate PLP's liquidity by calculating the current ratio and the acid test ratio for 2024 and 2025. Has PLP's financial position improved? Justify your answer.
    Answer: Calculations:

Current Ratio 2025 = 1.30 : 1
Acid Test Ratio 2024 = 0.78 : 1
Acid Test Ratio 2025 = 1.05 : 1

Detailed workings: 2024 current assets = $48,000 inventories + $70,000 trade receivables + $90,000 cash = $208,000; 2025 current assets = $55,000 + $105,000 + $120,000 = $280,000. Excluding stock: 2024 = ($208,000 − $48,000) ÷ $205,000 = $160,000 ÷ $205,000 = 0.78; 2025 = ($280,000 − $55,000) ÷ $215,000 = $225,000 ÷ $215,000 = 1.05.

The rise in receivables is the main caution: if tour operators and corporate bookings pay late, part of this apparent strength could reverse, so credit control should be watched.

Conclusion: PLP's financial position has improved. Both measures are higher in 2025, and the move from 0.78 to 1.05 in the stock-excluding measure is the stronger evidence of better underlying liquidity. PLP should keep an eye on receivables but can fund the water-slide complex from a healthier short-term position.

    Question: Explain one advantage and one disadvantage for PLP of introducing the $8 fast-track water-slide ticket backed by 74% of surveyed families.
    Answer: Advantage: An $8 fast-track ticket turns the 42-minute queue problem into a revenue opportunity: the 74% of 1,050 surveyed families who would pay $8 more lift contribution per admission from $50 towards $58, helping cover $750,000 fixed costs and the $900,000 loan. Disadvantage: A paid fast lane creates a two-tier experience in which standard ticket holders face relatively longer waits, which could raise complaints further if the 42-minute queues are not also tackled operationally.   Q4(b) [12 marks]
    Question: Using Appendix 3, evaluate how the base interest rate rise to 5.0%, the 5.9% minimum wage increase and the 10.8% rise in park energy costs will affect PLP. Which change will have the greatest impact? Justify your answer.
    Answer: Interest rate rise (4.25% to 5.0%): If PLP's $900,000 bank loan follows the base rate, the extra interest is 0.75% of $900,000 = $6,750 a year (0.0075 × $900,000). This is a small fraction of the $750,000 fixed costs and can be largely avoided by fixing the rate. Higher borrowing costs could raise the price of future finance for the $1,500,000 complex, but the direct annual effect is modest.

Minimum wage increase (5.9%, to $15.05 an hour): Ride and catering staff are hourly paid, so this rise increases PLP's wage bill across the workforce of 225 and cannot be avoided. The insert gives no hours worked or individual pay, so an annual total cannot be invented; the defensible judgement is qualitative against the given 200 admissions per employee and $50 contribution per unit. With queues at 42 minutes and waste at 6.4%, productivity must hold if the wage rise is to be absorbed without raising the $75 price.

Park energy costs (10.8%): These affect the whole park and every one of the 45,000 admissions. The insert does not break down the $25 variable cost, so only a bound can be calculated honestly: if the whole variable cost rose 10.8%, that is 10.8% × $25 = $2.70 a unit, or about $121,500 a year (45,000 × $2.70). Even a smaller rise would cut into the $50 contribution needed to repay the loan and fund the water-slide complex, with only partial recovery through the $8 fast-track ticket.

Conclusion: The 10.8% rise in park energy costs will have the greatest impact. It compounds across all 45,000 admissions and directly erodes the $50 contribution underpinning the $1,500,000 investment, whereas the interest rise is modest and can be hedged by fixing the loan rate, and the wage rise can be offset through productivity and pricing. Energy inflation therefore calls for the most urgent response, such as efficiency investment and longer-term supply contracts.

--- MAIN STEM ---
Cedar Grove Catering (CGC) is a cooperative in the hospitality and contract-catering sector, employing a workforce of 100. Founded in 2015 by Habiba Yusuf, it operates a flat organisational structure with democratic leadership and produces 20,000 units a year, one unit being a catered meal sold at an average selling price of $90. CGC plans to invest $520,000 in a new central production kitchen and chilled-delivery vans, financed by a $320,000 bank loan and $200,000 retained profit. It has fixed costs of $300,000 a year and a variable cost of $30 a unit. Food waste has reached 6.8% of meals prepared and client complaints have risen to 18 a month, up from 11 a month last year.

--- APPENDIX 1 — MARKETING/OPS ---
Quality and Waste Report, Q1 2025: CGC prepared 5,000 meals in the quarter with 18 written client complaints a month, up from 11 a month last year, and food waste of 6.8% of meals, up from 4.3%. Average delivery punctuality was 91% against a 98% target. A survey of 560 event organisers found 63% would pay $6 more for a low-waste menu and 58% choose caterers on sustainability. Of 100 staff, 29 kitchen hands have not completed on-the-job food-safety training; off-the-job hygiene courses at the technical college cost $390 per person.

--- APPENDIX 2 — FINANCIAL DATA ---
Title: Extract from the Statement of Financial Position of Cedar Grove Catering as at 31 March 2025 ($ '000)
Headers: ['Financial Metric', '2024', '2025']
Inventories | 40 | 62
Trade receivables | 75 | 88
Cash and cash equivalents | 30 | 28
Current liabilities | 145 | 150
Non-current assets | 780 | 860
Capital employed | 900 | 980

--- APPENDIX 3 — EXTERNAL ENVIRONMENT ---
Economic and Hospitality Bulletin (November 2026): (1) The central bank has raised the base interest rate from 3.25% to 4.0%, increasing the cost of CGC's $320,000 bank loan. (2) The national minimum wage will rise by 7.4% from $13.92 to $14.95 an hour from April 2026, affecting kitchen and delivery staff. (3) Food input-cost inflation has reached 12.8%, corporate event spending grew 2.9% and general inflation is 6.2%.

Every dollar of interest avoided can instead absorb the 12.8% food input-cost inflation or fund waste-reduction measures, protecting the $60 contribution earned on each of the 20,000 catered meals.

It also preserves member control: no lender can impose operating conditions on how Habiba Yusuf and the members run CGC. Using the $200,000 first reduces the $320,000 bank loan actually required, lowering CGC's fixed debt commitment at a time when delivery punctuality is only 91%.

--- MAIN STEM ---
Northern Rails Freight (NRF) is a private limited company in the rail freight and logistics sector, employing a workforce of 120. Founded in 2011 by Anika Northern, the business hauls bulk containers for manufacturers and operates a hierarchical structure with autocratic leadership. NRF plans to invest $1,200,000 in a new diesel-electric shunting fleet and a regional depot, financed by a $700,000 ten-year bank loan and $500,000 retained profit. It has fixed costs of $320,000 a year, a variable cost of $18 a unit and a selling price of $28, and handles 40,000 units of freight a year. NRF faces two problems: wagon turnaround delays have pushed late deliveries to 14%, and a diesel-maintenance skills gap is raising repair costs.

--- APPENDIX 1 — MARKETING/OPS ---
Operations Report, Q4 2025: NRF moved 10,400 container units last quarter, with a late-delivery rate of 14%, down from 18% a year earlier. Damage claims fell from 33 to 19 per month. Average wagon turnaround is 2.6 days. A survey of 400 manufacturing clients found 71% would pay a 5% premium for guaranteed overnight slots, and 48% rank reliability above price. A skills audit shows 26 of 120 drivers lack diesel-engine maintenance certification; accredited courses cost $1,100 per employee.

--- APPENDIX 2 — FINANCIAL DATA ---
Title: Extract from the Statement of Profit or Loss and Capital employed data of Northern Rails Freight for the year ended 31 March 2025 ($ '000)
Headers: ['Financial Metric', '2024', '2025']
Revenue | 8,000 | 9,000
Cost of sales | 5,000 | 5,400
Gross profit | 3,000 | 3,600
Operating profit | 1,000 | 1,350
Capital employed | 5,000 | 6,000
Interest payable | 120 | 150

--- APPENDIX 3 — EXTERNAL ENVIRONMENT ---
Economic and Business Bulletin (January 2026): (1) The central bank lifted the base rate from 4.25% to 5.0%, raising interest costs on NRF's $700,000 variable-rate loan. (2) The national minimum wage rises 5.8% from $13.00 to $13.75 an hour from April 2026, increasing the wage bill for NRF's 120 staff. (3) Diesel fuel input costs have risen 9.5% year-on-year while economy-wide inflation is 4.2%; freight contract rates in NRF's region grew only 2.1%.

--- QUESTIONS ---
  Q1(a) [8 marks]
    Question: Explain two advantages for NRF of financing its $1,200,000 depot expansion with retained profit instead of the $700,000 bank loan.
    Answer: Point 1: Using the $500,000 retained profit costs NRF no interest or capital repayment, which protects cash flow while the business already carries fixed costs of $320,000 a year and a $700,000 loan commitment. With late deliveries at 14% and repair costs rising because of the diesel-maintenance skills gap, keeping interest charges low leaves more cash to fund training and shunting-fleet reliability. Every dollar not paid to the lender supports the $28 selling price and the $10 contribution without passing costs on to the 400 manufacturing clients.

Point 2: Retained profit avoids the collateral and repossession risk attached to the ten-year bank loan, so the $1,200,000 depot and new shunting fleet are not jeopardised if freight demand falls short of the 40,000-unit target. It also preserves Anika Northern's ownership and control: no external lender can impose conditions on how the regional depot is run or on the guaranteed overnight-slot strategy. That freedom lets NRF respond quickly to the 71% of surveyed clients who would pay a premium for guaranteed slots, which a lender imposing repayment milestones might restrict.
    Keywords: retained profit, $500,000, $700,000, $1,200,000, $320,000, bank loan
    Mark scheme: knowledge_max_2: 1 mark for each valid advantage identified (max 2). | application_analysis_max_6: Up to 3 marks per point for detailed contextual explanation applied to NRF's expansion, costs and survey data.

  Q1(b) [12 marks]
    Question: NRF is promoting its new guaranteed overnight freight slots. Consider national rail trade press advertising, regional radio sponsorship, or a direct email campaign to its 400 surveyed manufacturing clients. Which should NRF choose? Justify your recommendation.
    Answer: National rail trade press advertising: A campaign in rail and logistics trade titles would build credibility with the manufacturers who already buy NRF's bulk container haulage, and print adverts can explain the technical detail of guaranteed overnight slots. The downside is slow response and high cost relative to a business with fixed costs of $320,000 a year and a $700,000 loan to service; readership is also national while NRF serves a regional depot catchment, so much of the spend would be wasted.

Regional radio sponsorship: Radio reaches local manufacturers cheaply and quickly, and repeated slogans suit a simple message about reliability, which matters because 48% of surveyed clients rank reliability above price. However, radio cannot demonstrate the overnight guarantee and its audience includes many listeners who never buy freight services, so the 71% of the 400 surveyed clients who would pay a premium are not efficiently isolated.

Direct email campaign: A targeted email to the 400 manufacturing clients in NRF's own database reaches exactly the buyers who already use its services, can quote the 5% premium finding back to them, and costs little per contact. It is measurable through opens and replies, and can be personalised by depot. Its limits are that it cannot win entirely new customers and inboxes are crowded, so the message must be sharp.

Recommendation: NRF should choose the direct email campaign. It targets the precise segment in its own research, costs far less than trade press, and reaches the 71% willing to pay a premium, while radio and press are rejected as untargeted and expensive for a business funding an $1,200,000 expansion. NRF should add small trade-press adverts later to build awareness.
    Keywords: 400, 71%, 5%, overnight, manufacturing clients, $1,200,000
    Mark scheme: level_1_1_to_4: Identifies promotional options with limited reference to NRF. | level_2_5_to_8: Discusses advantages and disadvantages of at least two options in the context of NRF with some judgement. | level_3_9_to_12: Evaluates all three options in context with a justified recommendation that explains why trade press and radio are rejected.

  Q2(a) [8 marks]
    Question: NRF's late deliveries have reached 14% and a diesel-maintenance skills gap is raising repair costs. Explain two benefits for NRF of using autocratic leadership to improve performance in its depot.
    Answer: Point 1: Autocratic leadership lets Anika Northern set clear, uniform turnaround procedures across the hierarchical structure, so crane and shunting crews follow one agreed routine rather than local shortcuts. With wagon turnaround currently 2.6 days and late deliveries at 14%, a single imposed standard and close supervision can cut delays quickly, protecting the 40,000-unit service commitment and the 400 manufacturing clients who value reliability.

Point 2: Decisive, top-down instructions speed up the response to the diesel-maintenance skills gap. The audit shows 26 of 120 drivers lack certification, and autocratic leadership can immediately allocate the $1,100-per-employee accredited courses and enforce attendance without lengthy consultation. Faster decisions also mean breakdowns are triaged quickly, repairing wagons before they worsen the 14% late-delivery figure and keeping repair costs from eroding the $10 contribution per unit. A consultative approach would slow these decisions, whereas a clear directive keeps the 400 manufacturing clients confident that NRF can recover from the 14% late-delivery problem quickly.
    Keywords: autocratic leadership, 14%, 26, $1,100, hierarchical, 120
    Mark scheme: knowledge_max_2: 1 mark for each valid benefit identified (max 2). | application_analysis_max_6: Up to 3 marks per point for detailed contextual explanation applied to NRF's delivery, skills and cost data.

  Q2(b) [12 marks]
    Question: NRF must close a diesel-engine maintenance skills gap among 26 of its 120 staff. Consider in-house on-the-job coaching or accredited off-the-job courses costing $1,100 per employee. Which should NRF choose? Justify your decision.
    Answer: In-house on-the-job coaching: Coaching in NRF's own depot uses the actual diesel-electric shunting fleet and maintenance routines, so skills transfer directly and staff keep working while they learn, which protects the 40,000-unit service and helps attack the 14% late-delivery rate. It avoids course fees and can be delivered by the most experienced fitters. Weaknesses are that it depends on those fitters' availability, can pass on bad habits, and gives no external certificate, which may matter if manufacturers audit NRF's maintenance standards.

Accredited off-the-job courses: Paying $1,100 per employee gives all 26 staff a recognised qualification and up-to-date diesel-engine knowledge. The total cost of 26 × $1,100 = $28,600 is small beside the $1,200,000 depot investment and could be met from the $500,000 retained profit. The drawback is that 26 of 120 staff are away from the depot during training, reducing capacity at a time when turnaround averages 2.6 days and late deliveries already stand at 14%; the generic syllabus may also need follow-up on NRF's own wagons.

Decision: NRF should choose accredited off-the-job courses, followed by short on-site coaching. The $28,600 cost is affordable and the certificate directly addresses the audit finding on 26 unqualified drivers, whereas on-the-job coaching alone is rejected because it would perpetuate existing habits and offer no proof of competence to clients. Capacity loss can be spread across shifts, so the short-term disruption is manageable. Phasing the courses across small groups would limit that loss further, and the certificate would help NRF demonstrate competence to the 400 manufacturing clients when they audit the regional depot.
    Keywords: $1,100, 26, 120, 14%, diesel-engine maintenance, accredited courses
    Mark scheme: level_1_1_to_4: Basic description of the two training options with limited application to NRF. | level_2_5_to_8: Detailed analysis of benefits and drawbacks of both options in NRF's context, with some cost awareness. | level_3_9_to_12: Full evaluation of both options using the 26 staff, $1,100 and $28,600 figures, with a justified decision explaining why the alternative is rejected.

  Q3(a) [8 marks]
    Question: Calculate and explain how NRF's management can use its cost, break-even and productivity data.
    Answer: (i) Break-even output = 32,000 units | (ii) Contribution per unit = $10 | (iii) Four contextual uses explained: margin of safety of 8,000 units against 40,000 output; premium pricing from the 71% survey finding; loan-service feasibility on the $700,000 borrowing; and unit-cost benchmarking at $26 to track maintenance costs.
    Keywords: 32,000, $10, 40,000, $320,000, $18, $28

  Q3(b) [12 marks]
    Question: Using Appendix 2, evaluate NRF's financial performance by calculating the gross profit margin, profit margin and ROCE for 2024 and 2025. Has NRF's profitability improved? Justify your answer.
    Answer: Calculations:
Gross Profit Margin 2024 = 37.5%
Gross Profit Margin 2025 = 40.0%
Profit Margin 2024 = 12.5%
Profit Margin 2025 = 15.0%
ROCE 2024 = 20.0%
ROCE 2025 = 22.5%

Detailed workings: 2024 gross profit of $3,000,000 divided by revenue of $8,000,000 gives 37.5%; 2025 gross profit of $3,600,000 divided by $9,000,000 gives 40.0%. Operating profit of $1,000,000 divided by 2024 revenue gives 12.5%; 2025 operating profit of $1,350,000 divided by $9,000,000 gives 15.0%. Return on capital employed of $1,000,000 on $5,000,000 capital gives 20.0%; 2025 return of $1,350,000 on $6,000,000 gives 22.5%. Revenue grew 12.5% while cost of sales grew only 8.0%, and operating profit rose 35% against a 20% rise in capital employed.

Evaluation: Both years show a clear upward trend. The gross margin widened from 37.5% to 40.0% because revenue outpaced cost of sales, suggesting better control over diesel and maintenance spending even as the 14% late-delivery problem persisted. Operating return rose from 12.5% to 15.0%, so overheads were absorbed more effectively. Returns on the expanded capital base also improved, from 20.0% to 22.5%, which is important because the $1,200,000 depot and shunting fleet must justify the $700,000 loan. Interest payable rose from $120,000 to $150,000, but operating profit still grew far faster, so borrowing to fund expansion did not dent returns. A caveat is that these figures are historic and do not capture the 9.5% diesel increase in Appendix 3.

Conclusion: NRF's profitability has improved on all three measures, and the improvement is genuine because it is not dependent on a one-off asset sale. The main risk is that rising diesel input costs could squeeze the 40.0% gross margin in the next year, so management should protect the $10 contribution per unit.
    Keywords: 37.5%, 40.0%, 12.5%, 15.0%, 20.0%, 22.5%, 8,000
    Mark scheme: level_1_1_to_4: States financial figures or trends with little or no accurate ratio calculation. | level_2_5_to_8: Calculates the three profitability ratios for both years with some relevant analysis of the trends. | level_3_9_to_12: Accurate ratio calculations for both years, detailed evaluation of revenue, cost, capital and interest movements, and a justified conclusion on whether profitability improved.

  Q4(a) [8 marks]
    Question: Explain one advantage and one disadvantage for NRF of offering guaranteed overnight freight slots to its manufacturing clients.
    Answer: Advantage: The survey of 400 manufacturing clients found that 71% would pay a 5% premium for guaranteed overnight slots and that 48% rank reliability above price, so NRF can raise its effective price above the $28 selling price and increase the $10 contribution per unit. This directly attacks the 14% late-delivery problem by making punctuality a sellable feature, helping win business from competitors and strengthening the case for the $1,200,000 depot investment.

Disadvantage: A genuine overnight guarantee demands extra wagons, drivers and tight wagon turnaround, pushing up the $320,000 fixed costs and possibly the $18 variable cost per unit through overtime or premium fuel. If NRF misses a slot, the 71% who paid the premium may claim compensation, damaging the reliability reputation the service is meant to build. With a $700,000 bank loan already being serviced, any extra operating cost could erase the gain from the 5% premium before the new shunting fleet is fully productive.
    Keywords: 71%, 5%, 48%, overnight, $700,000, 400
    Mark scheme: knowledge_max_2: 1 mark for a valid advantage and 1 mark for a valid disadvantage. | application_analysis_max_6: Up to 3 marks per point for detailed development using NRF's survey, cost and delivery data.

  Q4(b) [12 marks]
    Question: Using Appendix 3, evaluate how the base rate rise to 5.0%, the 5.8% minimum wage increase and the 9.5% diesel cost rise will affect NRF. Which change will have the greatest impact? Justify your answer.
    Answer: Base rate rise (4.25% to 5.0%): If NRF's $700,000 loan is variable-rate, the interest cost rises by 0.75 percentage points, shown as 0.0075 × $700,000 = $5,250 a year. That is modest against fixed costs of $320,000 and interest payable of $150,000 in the accounts, and it could be removed by fixing the loan rate. It may also make future borrowing dearer, but it is a one-off financing effect rather than a continuing hit on every unit.

Minimum wage increase (5.8% to $13.75): The insert states a workforce of 120 and output of 40,000 units, so labour productivity is 40,000 ÷ 120 = 333.3 units per worker. Hours worked and individual pay are not given, so a wage-bill total cannot be invented; the honest test is whether productivity holds near 333 units or output grows, otherwise unit labour cost rises and the $10 contribution shrinks. The effect is real but manageable if the 26 staff are trained and turnaround improves.

Diesel cost rise (9.5%): The insert does not split the $18 variable cost, so only a labelled upper bound is defensible: if all of it were fuel, 9.5% × $18 = $1.71 per unit, and at 40,000 units that is 40,000 × $1.71 = $68,400 a year. Even a smaller fuel share would cut the $10 contribution, and freight contract rates grew only 2.1%, so NRF cannot easily pass the rise on.

Conclusion: The 9.5% diesel increase will have the greatest impact. It compounds on every one of the 40,000 units, directly erodes the contribution that funds the $1,200,000 expansion, and is harder to neutralise than the $5,250 interest rise or a wage increase that productivity can offset. The wage rise is second because it is a large recurring cost, while the interest rise is smallest and can be hedged.
    Keywords: 5.0%, 5.8%, 9.5%, $18, 4.25%, $700,000
    Mark scheme: level_1_1_to_4: Identifies the external changes with limited application to NRF. | level_2_5_to_8: Analyses the impact of at least two changes on NRF's costs or financing using case figures. | level_3_9_to_12: Detailed evaluation of all three changes with shown arithmetic, a justified greatest-impact judgement on diesel costs, and reasons why the other two are smaller.

PAPER 2 — P2_SET_402
UNIT: Paper 2 Case Study

--- MAIN STEM ---
Harbourline Logistics (HLG) is a private limited company in the port and container logistics sector, employing a workforce of 95. Founded in 2007 by Ravi Harbour, the business unloads and forwards shipping containers and operates a flat structure with democratic leadership. HLG plans to invest $950,000 in an automated container-stacking yard and a new warehouse, financed by a $600,000 bank loan and $350,000 retained profit. It has fixed costs of $450,000 a year, a variable cost of $12 a unit and a selling price of $21, and handles 60,000 units a year. HLG faces two problems: a 6.2% container damage rate at the quay and rising labour turnover among crane operators.

--- APPENDIX 1 — MARKETING/OPS ---
Operations and Quality Report, Q4 2025: HLG handled 15,200 container units last quarter at a damage rate of 6.2%, down from 8.4% a year earlier. Customer claims fell from 44 to 27 per month. Average quay turnaround is 3.4 days. A survey of 350 shipping clients found 68% would pay a 4% premium for guaranteed two-day clearance, and 55% rank damage-free handling above price. A skills audit shows 22 of 95 crane operators lack stacking certification; external courses cost $1,250 per employee.

--- APPENDIX 2 — FINANCIAL DATA ---
Title: Extract from the Statement of Profit or Loss and Capital employed data of Harbourline Logistics for the year ended 31 March 2025 ($ '000)
Headers: ['Financial Metric', '2024', '2025']
Revenue | 7,500 | 8,400
Cost of sales | 5,250 | 5,460
Gross profit | 2,250 | 2,940
Operating profit | 900 | 1,260
Capital employed | 5,000 | 6,000
Interest payable | 150 | 180

--- APPENDIX 3 — EXTERNAL ENVIRONMENT ---
Economic and Business Bulletin (February 2026): (1) The central bank increased the base rate from 4.0% to 4.75%, lifting financing costs on HLG's $600,000 variable-rate loan. (2) The national minimum wage rises 4.9% to $14.20 an hour from April 2026, raising wage costs for HLG's 95 staff. (3) Container-handling equipment and diesel input costs rose 7.3% year-on-year while port logistics inflation reached 3.6% and warehouse rental costs climbed 6.1%.

--- QUESTIONS ---
  Q1(a) [8 marks]
    Question: Explain two advantages for HLG of financing its $950,000 stacking-yard expansion with a bank loan rather than a share issue.
    Answer: Point 1: A bank loan leaves ownership and control with Ravi Harbour and the existing shareholders. A share issue would bring in new shareholders who would vote at meetings and share future profits, whereas the $600,000 loan has no voting rights. For a private limited company with a flat structure and democratic leadership, keeping decision-making inside the existing team is especially valuable when handling a 6.2% container damage rate that needs quick, coordinated action.

Point 2: Borrowing does not permanently give away a slice of profit. Once the loan is repaid, HLG keeps all the earnings from the new yard, while equity holders would share those earnings every year. The loan also lets HLG preserve its $350,000 retained profit as working capital to pay the 44 damage claims a month and fund crane-operator training, rather than surrendering cash to investors. With fixed costs of $450,000 a year, retaining that buffer reduces the risk of a cash shortfall while the automated yard beds in.
    Keywords: $950,000, $600,000, bank loan, $350,000, $450,000, retained profit
    Mark scheme: knowledge_max_2: 1 mark for each valid advantage identified (max 2). | application_analysis_max_6: Up to 3 marks per point for detailed contextual explanation applied to HLG's financing choice and case data.

  Q1(b) [12 marks]
    Question: HLG is deciding how to expand its container handling capacity. Consider owning a new stacking yard, leasing yard space, or using a third-party depot. Which should HLG choose? Justify your recommendation.
    Answer: Owning a new stacking yard: Building and owning the facility gives HLG full control over layout, equipment and service standards, which matters because 55% of surveyed shipping clients rank damage-free handling above price and the current damage rate is 6.2%. Owning also builds an asset for the long term. The drawbacks are the large $950,000 commitment, the need to service a $600,000 loan out of fixed costs already at $450,000 a year, and the risk that demand falls short of the 60,000-unit volume.

Leasing yard space: Leasing avoids the huge upfront outlay and keeps debt lower, giving flexibility if container volumes change. It can be negotiated with maintenance included and frees the $350,000 retained profit for other uses. However, lease payments are a continuing fixed commitment without building an asset, the landlord controls improvements, and HLG may struggle to install the automated stacking equipment it plans if the site is not its own.

Using a third-party depot: Outsourcing needs almost no capital and converts fixed costs into variable payments, which is attractive while labour turnover among crane operators is a problem. Control of quality is weaker, though, so the 6.2% damage rate could worsen, and margins would be shared with the depot operator, reducing the $9 contribution on each of 60,000 units.

Recommendation: HLG should own the new stacking yard. Control of handling quality is essential to cut the 6.2% damage rate and meet the 68% of clients willing to pay a 4% premium for reliable two-day clearance, and the $9 contribution on 60,000 units can service the $600,000 loan. Leasing is rejected because it blocks the automated investment, and outsourcing is rejected because it sacrifices quality control and margin.
    Keywords: 6.2%, 350, 68%, 4%, two-day clearance, 60,000
    Mark scheme: level_1_1_to_4: Identifies capacity options with limited application to HLG. | level_2_5_to_8: Discusses advantages and disadvantages of at least two options in HLG's context with some judgement. | level_3_9_to_12: Evaluates all three options using case figures and gives a justified recommendation explaining why leasing and outsourcing are rejected.

  Q2(a) [8 marks]
    Question: HLG's container damage rate is 6.2% and labour turnover among crane operators is rising. Explain two benefits for HLG of using democratic leadership to improve performance at the quay.
    Answer: Point 1: Democratic leadership invites the 95 employees, especially crane operators, to suggest safer handling methods. Because the flat structure has few layers, their ideas about why 6.2% of containers are damaged can reach Ravi Harbour quickly and be tested in practice. Staff who help design the new stacking procedures are more likely to follow them, reducing the 44 monthly damage claims and protecting the $21 service price.

Point 2: Involvement raises job satisfaction and can reduce the rising labour turnover among crane operators. The audit shows 22 of 95 operators lack stacking certification, and consulting them about the $1,250 external courses makes training feel supportive rather than punitive. Lower turnover preserves experience at the quay, shortens the 3.4-day turnaround and protects the $9 contribution per unit from the extra recruitment and induction costs that high turnover would create. The same consultation helps HLG direct its $350,000 retained profit effectively, because operators who understand the new yard procedures waste less time and cause fewer damage claims.
    Keywords: democratic leadership, 6.2%, 22, $1,250, flat, 95
    Mark scheme: knowledge_max_2: 1 mark for each valid benefit identified (max 2). | application_analysis_max_6: Up to 3 marks per point for detailed contextual explanation applied to HLG's damage, turnover and training data.

  Q2(b) [12 marks]
    Question: HLG needs 22 crane operators to gain stacking certification. Consider promoting experienced internal staff or recruiting certified operators externally. Which should HLG choose? Justify your decision.
    Answer: Internal promotion: Promoting existing crane operators rewards loyalty and uses workers who already know HLG's quay routines, which helps cut the 6.2% damage rate without a long induction. It supports the flat, democratic culture and can be combined with the $1,250 external courses to certify 22 staff at a cost of 22 × $1,250 = $27,500, far below the $950,000 yard investment. The limitation is that internal candidates may lack formal stacking qualifications and need time to train, during which the 3.4-day turnaround could suffer, and the pool of willing staff may be small.

External recruitment: Hiring already certified operators brings proven skills immediately and could reduce the 44 monthly damage claims quickly. New recruits also bring practice from other ports. However, external hiring is expensive in advertising and selection, risks clashing with the existing team, and raises labour turnover if the newcomers leave; it also does nothing to motivate the 22 current staff who remain uncertified, and the insert gives no evidence that external candidates are available locally.

Decision: HLG should promote internal staff and fund the $1,250 courses for all 22. The $27,500 cost is modest against the $600,000 loan, and internal promotion preserves experience and morale at a time when turnover is rising. External recruitment is rejected because its costs and integration risk are not justified when the skills gap can be closed with training, though HLG should recruit externally later if 22 internal candidates cannot be found. Spreading the $1,250 courses over several intakes would keep the 3.4-day quay turnaround stable while all 22 operators qualify.
    Keywords: $1,250, 22, 95, 6.2%, crane operators, certification
    Mark scheme: level_1_1_to_4: Basic description of internal and external recruitment with limited application to HLG. | level_2_5_to_8: Detailed analysis of benefits and drawbacks of both options using HLG's 22 staff, $1,250 and damage data. | level_3_9_to_12: Full evaluation of both options with shown cost arithmetic and a justified decision explaining why the alternative is rejected.

    Question: Calculate and explain how HLG's management can use its cost, break-even and productivity data.

    Keywords: 50,000, $9, 60,000, $450,000, $12, $21

  Q3(b) [12 marks]
    Question: Using Appendix 2, evaluate HLG's financial performance by calculating the gross profit margin, profit margin and ROCE for 2024 and 2025. Has HLG's profitability improved? Justify your answer.
    Answer: Calculations:

  Q4(a) [8 marks]

HLG can therefore raise its effective price above the $21 unit price and increase the $9 contribution, while giving clients a clear reason to choose HLG over other ports. Faster clearance also reduces the 3.4-day quay turnaround, easing the congestion that contributes to the 6.2% container damage rate.

Disadvantage: A two-day guarantee requires more crane capacity and tighter scheduling, which pushes up the $450,000 fixed costs and may increase the $12 variable cost per unit through overtime or expedited handling.   Q4(b) [12 marks]
    Question: Using Appendix 3, evaluate how the base rate rise to 4.75%, the 4.9% minimum wage increase and the 7.3% rise in handling-equipment and diesel costs will affect HLG. Which change will have the greatest impact? Justify your answer.
    Answer: Base rate rise (4.0% to 4.75%): If HLG's $600,000 loan is variable-rate, the increase is 0.75 percentage points, so 0.0075 × $600,000 = $4,500 a year. Minimum wage increase (4.9% to $14.20): HLG has 95 staff and handles 60,000 units, so productivity is 60,000 ÷ 95 = 631.6 units per worker. Conclusion: The 7.3% rise in handling-equipment and diesel costs will have the greatest impact. It applies to every one of the 60,000 containers, directly erodes the contribution that services the $600,000 loan and funds the $950,000 yard, and is harder to hedge than a $4,500 interest change or a wage rise that higher productivity can absorb. --- MAIN STEM ---
Voltwave Energy (VWE) is a public limited company in the renewable energy sector, installing rooftop solar systems, and employs a workforce of 80. Founded in 2013 by Priya Volt, the business serves commercial buildings and operates a hierarchical structure with autocratic leadership. VWE plans to invest $1,500,000 in a battery-storage assembly line, financed by an $800,000 bank loan and a $700,000 share issue. It has fixed costs of $600,000 a year, a variable cost of $40 a unit and a selling price of $70, and produces 26,000 units a year. VWE faces two problems: a 4.5% defect rate in battery packs and a shortage of qualified electricians delaying new commercial installations.

--- APPENDIX 1 — MARKETING/OPS ---
Quality and Operations Report, Q4 2025: VWE assembled 6,500 battery units last quarter with a defect rate of 4.5%, down from 7.2% a year earlier. Installation rework jobs fell from 31 to 18 per month. Average install time is 5.6 days. A survey of 280 commercial property clients found 73% would pay a 6% premium for certified battery storage, and 61% value quick installation most. A skills audit shows 18 of 80 technicians lack electrical certification; accredited courses cost $1,400 per employee.

For a public limited company, equity is a natural source of long-term capital for a $1,500,000 assembly line whose returns may take several years to arrive.

Point 2: Equity requires no collateral and cannot be repossessed if installation delays persist, so the new line and the commercial installations are not put at risk. It also spreads the financing risk between shareholders and lenders. Although existing shareholders are diluted, no cash leaves the business to service the capital, leaving more of the $30 contribution per unit to reinvest in training the 18 technicians who lack certification and in cutting the 5.6-day installation time that clients care about.

--- MAIN STEM ---
Swiftroute Couriers (SRC) is a private limited company in the parcel delivery and express logistics sector, employing a workforce of 140. Founded in 2015 by Daniel Swift, the business delivers same-day parcels for retailers and operates a flat structure with democratic leadership. SRC plans to invest $780,000 in an electric van fleet and a sorting hub, financed by a $480,000 bank loan and $300,000 retained profit. It has fixed costs of $280,000 a year, a variable cost of $5 a unit and a selling price of $12, and delivers 50,000 units a year. SRC faces two problems: 8% of parcels arrive late and absenteeism among van drivers is rising during peak periods.

--- APPENDIX 1 — MARKETING/OPS ---
Operations and Quality Report, Q4 2025: SRC delivered 13,000 parcels last quarter with 8% arriving late, down from 12% a year earlier. Damage complaints fell from 51 to 29 per month. Average delivery time is 1.4 days. A survey of 500 online shoppers found 69% would pay $1.50 more for guaranteed same-day delivery, and 57% choose couriers on reliability. A skills audit shows 30 of 140 drivers lack electric-van training; courses cost $750 per employee.

--- APPENDIX 2 — FINANCIAL DATA ---
Title: Extract from the Statement of Profit or Loss and Capital employed data of Swiftroute Couriers for the year ended 31 March 2025 ($ '000)
Headers: ['Financial Metric', '2024', '2025']

Gross profit | 1,500 | 1,960
Operating profit | 600 | 910
Capital employed | 5,000 | 6,500
Interest payable | 100 | 120

--- APPENDIX 3 — EXTERNAL ENVIRONMENT ---
Economic and Business Bulletin (December 2025): (1) The central bank raised the base rate from 4.5% to 5.25%, increasing interest on SRC's $480,000 loan. (2) The national minimum wage rises 6.4% from $13.10 to $13.94 an hour, affecting SRC's 140 drivers and sorters. (3) Electric-van battery and charging costs rose 8.6% year-on-year while fuel duty increased 3.2% and consumer spending on delivery services grew 4.7%.

--- QUESTIONS ---
  Q1(a) [8 marks]
    Question: Explain two advantages for SRC of financing its $780,000 sorting-hub expansion with retained profit instead of the $480,000 bank loan.
    Answer: Point 1: Retained profit of $300,000 needs no interest or repayment, which protects cash flow while SRC already meets fixed costs of $280,000 a year and has a $480,000 loan commitment. With 8% of parcels late and absenteeism rising among van drivers, the cash saved from interest charges can fund the $750 training courses and extra sorting capacity, helping protect the $12 price and the 69% of shoppers who will pay $1.50 more for reliable same-day delivery.

Point 2: Using internal funds avoids collateral and repossession risk, so the $780,000 electric vans and sorting hub are safe even if parcel volumes fall short of the 50,000-unit target. It also keeps control with Daniel Swift and the existing team: no lender can attach conditions to how the flat, democratic business runs its routes. That freedom matters when responding quickly to the 57% of shoppers who choose a courier on reliability, since service improvements can be made without seeking a lender's approval.

    Answer: Sponsoring a city delivery event: A high-profile event builds brand visibility and lets SRC demonstrate vans and speed directly to the public. It suits a same-day service and can generate word of mouth. However, sponsorship is expensive for a business with fixed costs of $280,000 and a $480,000 loan, and the audience includes many people who never buy parcel delivery, so the spend is poorly targeted and results are hard to measure.

Local radio advertising: Radio is cheaper than sponsorship and can repeat a simple reliability message, which matters because 57% of the 500 surveyed shoppers choose a courier on reliability. Its weakness is that listeners are a broad local audience while SRC's customers are online retailers, and radio cannot convey the $1.50 same-day premium clearly or prove that parcels arrive on time.

Targeted email campaign: An email to SRC's retailer contacts reaches the exact businesses that buy same-day delivery, can quote the 69% finding that shoppers will pay $1.50 more, and is cheap and measurable through replies and conversions. It can be personalised by retailer and adjusted quickly. The limits are that it will not build broad consumer awareness and inboxes are crowded, so the offer must be clear and timely.

Recommendation: SRC should choose the targeted email campaign.     Question: SRC's late-delivery rate is 8% and absenteeism among van drivers is rising. Explain two benefits for SRC of using democratic leadership to improve performance.

  Q4(a) [8 marks]
    Question: Explain one advantage and one disadvantage for SRC of guaranteeing same-day delivery to online shoppers.
    Answer: Advantage: The survey of 500 shoppers found that 69% would pay $1.50 more for guaranteed same-day delivery and that 57% choose a courier on reliability. SRC can add $1.50 to the $12 price, raising the $7 contribution per parcel and helping service the $480,000 loan and the $780,000 hub investment.     Question: Using Appendix 3, evaluate how the base rate rise to 5.25%, the 6.4% minimum wage increase and the 8.6% rise in electric-van battery and charging costs will affect SRC. Which change will have the greatest impact? Justify your answer.
    Answer: Base rate rise (4.5% to 5.25%): If SRC's $480,000 loan is variable-rate, the interest increase is 0.75 percentage points, so 0.0075 × $480,000 = $3,600 a year. This is small against fixed costs of $280,000 and interest payable of $120,000, and can be removed by fixing the rate. It raises the cost of future borrowing for the $780,000 hub but is otherwise limited.

Electric-van charging cost rise (8.6%): The insert does not split the $5 variable cost, so only a labelled upper bound is valid: if all of it were energy, 8.6% × $5 = $0.43 per parcel, and at 50,000 parcels that is 50,000 × $0.43 = $21,500 a year. Any real effect is smaller because the variable cost also covers other items, and fuel duty up 3.2% partly offsets the switch to electric vans. The $7 contribution would shrink only modestly.

Minimum wage increase (6.4% to $13.94): SRC has 140 drivers and sorters and delivers 50,000 parcels, so productivity is 50,000 ÷ 140 = 357.1 parcels per worker. Hours and individual pay are not given, so an exact wage-bill total cannot be invented; the correct test is whether productivity holds near 357 parcels per worker. Unlike the interest change, this rise cannot be hedged, and unlike the energy upper bound it is not confined to the $5 variable cost: it applies to the whole workforce of a labour-intensive courier.

Conclusion: The 6.4% minimum wage increase will have the greatest impact. It affects all 140 staff, cannot be removed by fixing a loan rate, and is not limited to a fraction of the $5 variable cost as the 8.6% energy rise is; on the evidence available it poses the largest recurring cost pressure. The energy rise ranks second at up to $21,500, and the $3,600 interest rise ranks third.

--- MAIN STEM ---
Coldchain Haulage (CHX) is a private limited company in the refrigerated road transport sector, employing a workforce of 110. Founded in 2010 by Elena Cold, the business carries chilled and frozen food for supermarkets and operates a hierarchical structure with autocratic leadership. CHX plans to invest $1,100,000 in a fleet of refrigerated trucks and a temperature-monitoring system, financed by a $650,000 bank loan and $450,000 retained profit. It has fixed costs of $540,000 a year, a variable cost of $15 a unit and a selling price of $27, and carries 54,000 units a year. CHX faces two problems: a 3.8% spoilage rate from temperature excursions and high driver turnover on long routes.

--- APPENDIX 1 — MARKETING/OPS ---
Quality and Waste Report, Q4 2025: CHX carried 13,500 chilled loads last quarter with a spoilage rate of 3.8%, down from 5.6% a year earlier. Temperature-alarm incidents fell from 26 to 14 per month. Average journey time is 2.8 days. A survey of 320 supermarket suppliers found 66% would pay a 3.5% premium for verified temperature-controlled transport, and 59% rank spoilage-free delivery above price. A skills audit shows 24 of 110 drivers lack refrigerant-handling certification; courses cost $1,050 per employee.

With fixed costs of $540,000 a year, predictable loan repayments let Elena Cold plan the $1,100,000 fleet investment without fearing a sudden call on funds.

--- MAIN STEM ---
Northstar Software (NSD) is a private limited company in the software sector, employing a workforce of 60. Founded in 2011 by Priya Raman, it develops cloud accounting software for small firms and operates a flat structure with democratic leadership. NSD plans to invest $900,000 in a new cloud data centre with automated testing tools, financed by a $600,000 ten-year bank loan and $300,000 retained profit. It has fixed costs of $420,000 a year, a variable cost of $14.00 a unit and a selling price of $29.00, and currently produces 80,000 units a year. NSD faces two problems: labour turnover has reached 14% and a skills gap in cloud engineering is slowing product releases.

--- APPENDIX 1 — MARKETING/OPS ---
Quality and Operations Report — Q4 2025: NSD released 18,000 software licences last quarter; the test log recorded a defect rate of 2.4%, down from 4.6% a year earlier. Customer support tickets fell from 310 to 185 per month. Average resolution time is 6.5 hours. A survey of 450 business clients found 68% would pay 5% more for guaranteed 99.9% uptime, and 57% rate data security as their top purchasing criterion. A skills audit shows 22 of 60 staff have not completed training on the new cloud platform; specialist external training costs $1,200 per employee.

--- APPENDIX 2 — FINANCIAL DATA ---
Title: Extract from the Statement of Profit or Loss and Capital employed data of Northstar Software for the year ended 31 March 2025 ($ '000)
Headers: ['Financial Metric', '2024', '2025']
Revenue | 1,800 | 2,400
Cost of sales | 900 | 1,080
Gross profit | 900 | 1,320
Operating profit | 360 | 576
Capital employed | 2,000 | 2,400
Interest payable | 40 | 55

--- APPENDIX 3 — EXTERNAL ENVIRONMENT ---
Economic and Technology Bulletin (January 2026): (1) The central bank has raised the base interest rate from 4.25% to 5.0%, increasing borrowing costs for firms with variable-rate loans. (2) Average salaries for qualified software developers rose by 8.5%, pushing up wage bills across the technology sector. (3) Wholesale cloud-server and data-storage input costs rose 11.0% year-on-year, while business software spending grew 4.2% over the same period.

--- QUESTIONS ---
  Q1(a) [8 marks]
    Question: NSD plans to fund part of its $900,000 cloud data centre with a bank loan. Explain two advantages for NSD of using retained profit instead of the bank loan.
    Answer: Point 1: Using retained profit costs NSD no interest charges or repayments, protecting cash flow while it services a $600,000 bank loan and funds the $900,000 cloud data centre. Every dollar saved on interest can be spent on specialist training at $1,200 per employee to close the skills gap and reduce 14% labour turnover, or absorbed if cloud-server input costs rise 11.0%. Keeping the $300,000 in-house also means the 80,000-unit software licence output does not have to carry extra debt service.

Point 2: Retained profit carries no collateral risk. If the new data centre failed to attract customers, a lender could call in the $600,000 loan, whereas $300,000 of internal funds puts no company asset at risk and preserves Priya Raman's control. It also avoids lender conditions on how the automated testing tools are introduced, letting NSD respond flexibly to the 2.4% defect rate and the 68% of surveyed clients who want guaranteed uptime. Retained profit is therefore cheaper, safer and leaves decisions with the founder.
    Keywords: retained profit, $900,000, $600,000, $300,000, $420,000, bank loan
    Mark scheme: knowledge_max_2: 1 mark for each valid advantage identified (max 2). | application_analysis_max_6: Up to 3 marks per point for contextual explanation and analysis applied to NSD's financing decision, costs and expansion.

  Q1(b) [12 marks]
    Question: NSD is launching a new cloud accounting package. Consider advertising in the national business press, paid search and social media advertising, or sponsoring a technology trade conference. Which should NSD choose to promote the launch? Justify your recommendation.
    Answer: National business press advertising: Full-page ads in national business newspapers would build credibility and reach owners of small firms, the target market for NSD's cloud accounting software. However, airtime and design costs are high, much of the readership is outside the small-firm segment, and the message is one-way with no click-through data. For a 60-person company already committing $900,000 to a data centre and servicing a $600,000 loan, this broad, expensive reach would waste scarce cash.

Paid search and social media advertising: These channels reach people actively searching for accounting software and can be targeted at small-firm decision-makers, with measurable clicks and low entry cost. They suit a product whose 68% of surveyed clients already want 99.9% uptime and 57% rank data security first, because copy can highlight those features directly and be adjusted quickly using ticket data (310 down to 185 per month). The drawback is that costs rise with competition for keywords and results need skilled management NSD currently lacks given its cloud-engineering skills gap.

Technology trade conference sponsorship: This puts NSD in front of an audience of IT professionals and partners, generating high-quality leads and demonstration opportunities for automated testing. It is far cheaper than a national press campaign but reaches few small-firm buyers directly, so the 80,000-unit sales target would not be supported, and one event gives only a short-lived spike.

Recommendation: NSD should choose paid search and social media advertising. It is measurable, affordable and targets the exact clients in its 450-person research who value security and uptime. National press is rejected as expensive and untargeted; conference sponsorship is rejected as too narrow to drive 80,000 units. NSD should fund it from the $300,000 retained profit rather than adding debt.
    Keywords: $900,000, 80,000, 68%, 57%, 450, workforce of 60
    Mark scheme: level_1_1_to_4: Lists or describes promotional options with limited application to NSD. | level_2_5_to_8: Discusses advantages and disadvantages of at least two options in NSD's context with some judgement. | level_3_9_to_12: Evaluates all three options in NSD's context and gives a justified recommendation explaining why press advertising and conference sponsorship are rejected.

  Q2(a) [8 marks]
    Question: NSD's labour turnover has reached 14% and it has a skills gap in cloud engineering. Explain two benefits for NSD of using democratic leadership to improve staff motivation.
    Answer: Point 1: Democratic leadership gives NSD's 60 employees a voice in how the new cloud data centre and automated testing tools are introduced. Consulting the engineers who handle releases satisfies social and esteem needs (Maslow) and makes staff feel valued, which directly targets the 14% labour turnover. When developers help set testing routines, they are more likely to stay, keeping the knowledge needed to cut the 2.4% defect rate and maintain 99.9% uptime promised to 68% of surveyed clients.

Point 2: Involvement generates practical ideas from the staff closest to the product, helping close the cloud-engineering skills gap without paying $1,200 per employee for every course. Participation is a motivator (Herzberg) that raises commitment and reduces the disruption caused when 22 of 60 staff still need training. In a flat structure with only a short chain of command, democratic decisions can be implemented quickly, protecting output of 80,000 units while the $900,000 expansion beds in.
    Keywords: labour turnover, skills gap, workforce of 60, 22, $1,200, democratic leadership
    Mark scheme: knowledge_max_2: 1 mark for each valid benefit identified (max 2). | application_analysis_max_6: Up to 3 marks per point for detailed contextual development linked to NSD's turnover, skills gap and expansion.

  Q2(b) [12 marks]
    Question: NSD must train 22 staff who have not completed training on the new cloud platform. Consider on-the-job training or specialist external training at $1,200 per employee. Which should NSD choose? Justify your decision.
    Answer: On-the-job training: Coaching at the workstation is specific to NSD's own cloud platform and automated testing tools, costs no external fees, and keeps the 22 staff productive while they learn, protecting output of 80,000 units and the drive to cut the 2.4% defect rate. Supervisors can demonstrate the exact release routines needed for 99.9% uptime. The drawback is that the trainers are themselves developers whose work slows down, bad habits can be copied, and there is no certificate, which may matter to the 57% of clients who rank data security as their top criterion.

Specialist external training: A college or vendor course gives structured, up-to-date cloud-engineering skills and a recognised qualification. For the 22 untrained staff the fee is 22 × $1,200 = $26,400, an explicit calculation from the insert figures and affordable against the $300,000 retained profit. It removes staff from releases temporarily and the generic content may not match NSD's exact platform, so follow-up coaching would still be needed, and 14% labour turnover raises the risk of losing newly trained staff.

Decision: NSD should choose on-the-job training first, with short external courses for the most senior engineers. On-the-job training is cheaper, platform-specific and avoids the $26,400 fee and loss of 22 staff from live releases while labour turnover is 14%. Full external training is rejected because the $26,400 cost and absence from the line would slow releases and the skills gap could return if trained staff leave. With 14% labour turnover the risk of losing newly qualified staff is real, so this blended approach limits that exposure while keeping the platform running.
    Keywords: $1,200, 22, cloud platform, $900,000, 80,000, 2.4%
    Mark scheme: level_1_1_to_4: Basic description of the two training methods with limited application to NSD. | level_2_5_to_8: Detailed analysis of benefits and drawbacks of both methods in NSD's context. | level_3_9_to_12: Comprehensive evaluation of both methods with a justified decision covering cost, disruption and platform relevance, rejecting the alternative.

  Q3(a) [8 marks]

    Answer: Interest rate rise (4.25% to 5.0%): If NSD's $600,000 bank loan is variable-rate, the extra interest is 0.75% × $600,000 = $4,500 a year (0.0075 × $600,000). Developer salary rise (8.5%): NSD employs a workforce of 60 and the insert does not state how many are developers or their hours, so no annual wage total can be invented. Cloud-server input cost inflation (11.0%): The insert gives a variable cost of $14.00 a unit but does not decompose it. Even a partial pass-through would materially shrink the surplus covering $420,000 fixed costs.

Conclusion: The 11.0% input-cost rise will have the greatest impact. It compounds on every unit, can add up to $123,200 a year on the stated assumptions and directly erodes the contribution that services the loan; the interest rise is only $4,500 at most and the wage effect cannot be quantified from the insert and can be offset by productivity.

--- MAIN STEM ---
Digital Ledger Technologies (DLT) is a private limited company in the financial technology sector, employing a workforce of 55. Founded in 2013 by Daniel Okafor, it provides mobile-payment services to small merchants and operates a hierarchical structure with autocratic leadership. DLT plans to invest $720,000 in a new mobile-payment platform with biometric authentication, financed by a $420,000 share issue and a $300,000 bank loan. It has fixed costs of $350,000 a year, a variable cost of $10.00 a transaction and a selling price of $24.00, and currently produces 70,000 units a year. DLT faces two problems: a payment error rate of 3.2% and 18 of its 55 staff lacking cybersecurity certification.

--- APPENDIX 1 — MARKETING/OPS ---
Operations and Quality Log — Q2 2025: DLT processed 32,000 digital-payment transactions; the error rate was 3.2%, down from 5.1% a year earlier. Customer complaints fell from 96 to 54 per month. Average settlement time is 2.8 hours. A survey of 380 merchants found 61% would switch providers for faster settlement, and 49% cited security as their main concern. A skills audit shows 18 of 55 staff lack cybersecurity certification; an external certification course costs $950 per employee.

Crestline Technology Group (CTG) is a public limited company in the digital services sector, employing a workforce of 72 across its regional operations.   Q2(b) [12 marks]
    Question: CTG must close the cloud-security training gap for 30 staff. Consider on-the-job coaching or external certification at $1,050 per employee. Which should CTG choose? Justify your decision.
    Answer: On-the-job coaching: Coaching alongside CTG's own servers is directly relevant to its hosting platform, costs no course fees and keeps all 30 staff available to maintain 99.2% uptime and cut support tickets from 260 per month. Engineers can learn the exact response routines behind automated server monitoring. The drawback is that trainers may themselves lack certification, bad habits can spread and no recognised qualification is gained, which matters for the 58% of clients who value green, secure hosting.

External certification: An accredited course supplies up-to-date security skills and a formal credential that reassures the 720 surveyed clients. For 30 staff the fee is 30 × $1,050 = $31,500, an explicit calculation from the insert figures, affordable against the $500,000 share issue. Staff are absent from duties while training, risking downtime, and generic content may not fit CTG's platform, so follow-up coaching would be needed.

Decision: CTG should choose external certification. The $31,500 cost is small relative to the $750,000 investment, the qualification is credible with clients, and on-the-job coaching cannot certify 30 untrained staff. On-the-job coaching is rejected because CTG's own trainers may not be qualified and the risk of downtime during the data-centre transition is too high given the 66% of clients demanding 99.9% uptime. Because laissez-faire leadership leaves engineers to solve problems, formal certification gives them a common standard to work to. The $31,500 is a one-off cost rather than a permanent salary increase, and staggering the 30 staff through courses would keep 99.2% uptime protected during the transition.
    Keywords: $1,050, 30, cloud-security training, $750,000, 85,000, 99.2%

--- MAIN STEM ---
Apex Mobile Applications (APX) is a partnership in the mobile app development sector, employing a workforce of 40 across its product teams. Founded in 2015 by Marcus Bell, it designs productivity apps for small businesses and operates a hierarchical structure with democratic leadership that consults developers before each release. APX plans to invest $680,000 in a new app-testing laboratory with automated crash-reporting, financed by $400,000 hire purchase and $280,000 retained profit. It has fixed costs of $300,000 a year, a variable cost of $12.00 a unit and a selling price of $27.00, and currently produces 60,000 units a year. APX faces two problems: a 1.9% app crash rate after updates and 12 of 40 staff lacking mobile-security training.

--- APPENDIX 1 — MARKETING/OPS ---
App Performance Report — Q3 2025: APX released 9,600 app updates; the crash rate was 1.9%, down from 3.6% a year earlier, and user ratings averaged 4.2 out of 5. Daily active users rose from 42,000 to 58,000. A survey of 500 users found 71% value offline access and 63% would recommend the app. A skills audit shows 12 of 40 staff lack mobile-security training; a certification course costs $880 per employee.

    Question: APX plans to acquire part of its $680,000 app-testing laboratory through hire purchase. Explain two advantages for APX of using retained profit instead of hire purchase.

Cash saved can fund certification at $880 per employee for the 12 untrained staff and help reduce the 1.9% crash rate, protecting the $27.00 price.

Point 2: Using internal funds avoids the risk that the lab equipment is repossessed if repayments are missed, unlike hire purchase where ownership passes only at the end. It also preserves the partnership's decision-making independence, letting Marcus Bell change testing priorities as the 500-user survey (71% wanting offline access) evolves, without a finance company's conditions. Retained profit is therefore cheaper and lower-risk than hire purchase. With consumer app spending growing 4.8%, that freed cash can fund features the 71% of surveyed users want, such as offline access, rather than payments to a finance company.

PAPER 2 — P2_SET_410
UNIT: Paper 2 Case Study

--- MAIN STEM ---
Vantage Digital Platforms (VDP) is a cooperative in the e-commerce sector, employing a workforce of 65. Founded in 2012 by Aisha Bello, it runs an online marketplace for small retailers and operates a flat structure with autocratic leadership. VDP plans to invest $600,000 in a new automated fulfilment warehouse with digital stock control, financed by a $350,000 bank loan and $250,000 from the sale of assets. It has fixed costs of $390,000 a year, a variable cost of $13.00 a unit and a selling price of $28.00, and currently produces 75,000 units a year. VDP faces two problems: a 2.7% pick-error rate and 24 of 65 staff lacking digital stock-control training.

--- APPENDIX 1 — MARKETING/OPS ---
E-commerce Operations Log — Q4 2025: VDP fulfilled 28,000 online orders; the pick-error rate was 2.7%, down from 4.1% a year earlier. Customer complaints fell from 175 to 88 per month. Average delivery time is 2.6 days. A survey of 640 shoppers found 62% prefer free returns and 55% buy mainly on mobile. A skills audit shows 24 of 65 staff lack digital stock-control training; a training course costs $980 per employee.

--- APPENDIX 2 — FINANCIAL DATA ---
Title: Extract from the Statement of Profit or Loss and Capital employed data of Vantage Digital Platforms for the year ended 31 March 2025 ($ '000)
Headers: ['Financial Metric', '2024', '2025']
Revenue | 1,600 | 2,000
Cost of sales | 880 | 1,000
Gross profit | 720 | 1,000
Operating profit | 280 | 440
Capital employed | 2,000 | 2,200
Interest payable | 45 | 60

--- APPENDIX 3 — EXTERNAL ENVIRONMENT ---
Economic and Retail Bulletin (September 2026): (1) The base interest rate rose from 4.0% to 4.75%, increasing borrowing costs on variable-rate loans. (2) The national minimum wage increased by 6.9% to $13.45 an hour from April 2026. (3) Packaging and delivery input costs rose 9.4% year-on-year, while online retail sales grew 5.2% over the same period.

--- QUESTIONS ---
  Q1(a) [8 marks]
    Question: VDP plans to fund part of its $600,000 automated warehouse with a bank loan. Explain two advantages for VDP of using the bank loan rather than the sale of assets.
    Answer: Point 1: A bank loan lets VDP keep the assets it would otherwise sell, so the cooperative retains the resources needed to run its marketplace while investing $350,000 of the $600,000 in the automated warehouse. Selling assets would reduce the capacity serving 75,000 units, whereas the loan preserves the asset base that supports the 2.7% pick-error improvement programme.

Point 2: A loan provides the full sum immediately and can be repaid over time, while a sale of assets may take months and fetch less than expected in a downturn. This certainty helps Aisha Bello commit to digital stock control and training at $980 per employee for 24 staff without delaying the project. It leaves the 65-member cooperative in control of operations, provided the $390,000 fixed costs and interest can be met. With packaging and delivery costs expected to rise 9.4%, avoiding an asset sale also keeps the cooperative's earning assets in place to absorb that pressure.
    Keywords: bank loan, $600,000, $350,000, $250,000, $390,000, sale of assets
    Mark scheme: knowledge_max_2: 1 mark for each valid advantage identified (max 2). | application_analysis_max_6: Up to 3 marks per point for contextual explanation and analysis applied to VDP's financing choice, operations and warehouse investment.

  Q1(b) [12 marks]
    Question: VDP is promoting its marketplace to new shoppers. Consider paid social media advertising, email marketing to existing shoppers, or discount vouchers with influencers. Which should VDP choose? Justify your recommendation.
    Answer: Paid social media advertising: Social ads can reach many shoppers quickly and can target the 55% of the 640 surveyed who buy mainly on mobile. They are measurable but costs rise with competition and results depend on creative quality; for a cooperative committing $600,000 to a warehouse and servicing a $350,000 loan, unmeasured spend would be risky.

Email marketing to existing shoppers: Email is cheap, directly reaches known customers and can highlight the free returns wanted by 62% of respondents and faster delivery from the new warehouse. It is readily measurable through open and click rates. Its limitation is that it cannot reach new shoppers beyond the existing list, so it may not grow the 75,000-unit base on its own.

Discount vouchers with influencers: Influencer vouchers can create buzz and attract new, younger shoppers, and can be tied to 62% preferring free returns. However, discounts cut the $28.00 price and $15.00 contribution, influencer fees are uncertain, and a 65-person cooperative has little experience managing such campaigns.

Recommendation: VDP should choose email marketing to existing shoppers. It is low-cost, measurable and matches the research insight that 62% want free returns and 55% buy on mobile, with funds better kept for the $600,000 warehouse. Paid social is rejected as competitive and costly; influencer vouchers are rejected because discounts would erode contribution needed to cover $390,000 fixed costs and the bank loan. Email also suits a cooperative whose 65 members value direct communication, and it can promote free returns to the 62% who want them without discounting the $28.00 price.
    Keywords: $600,000, 75,000, 62%, 55%, 640, workforce of 65

    Answer: Interest rate rise (4.0% to 4.75%): If VDP's $350,000 bank loan is variable-rate, the extra interest is 0.75% × $350,000 = $2,625 a year (0.0075 × $350,000). Minimum wage increase (6.9% to $13.45): The insert gives a workforce of 65 but not the hours worked or the number of minimum-wage staff, so no annual wage bill can be invented. Packaging and delivery input inflation (9.4%): The insert gives a variable cost of $13.00 a unit without decomposing it. Conclusion: The 9.4% rise in packaging and delivery costs will have the greatest impact. It applies to every order, can add $91,650 a year on the stated assumption and directly erodes the $15.00 contribution funding the $600,000 warehouse; the interest rise is only $2,625 and the wage effect cannot be quantified from the insert and can be offset by maintaining productivity.

--- MAIN STEM ---
Pinecrest Dental Practice (PDP) is a private limited company in the healthcare sector, employing a workforce of 40. Founded in 2011 by Dr Amina Farouk, it provides general and cosmetic dentistry to local patients and operates a flat organisational structure with democratic leadership. PDP plans to invest $540,000 in a second surgery with digital imaging equipment, financed by a $300,000 ten-year bank loan and $240,000 retained profit. It has fixed costs of $480,000 a year, a variable cost of $35 a unit and a selling price of $95, and carries out 14,000 units of dental treatment a year. PDP faces two problems: staff absenteeism has reached 8% and patient complaints about appointment waiting times are rising.

--- APPENDIX 1 — MARKETING/OPS ---
Operations and Quality Report — Q3 2025: The practice completed 3,450 patient appointments last quarter; the did-not-attend rate was 12%, down from 15% a year ago. Patient complaints about waiting times rose from 18 to 29 per month. Average appointment turnaround was 26 minutes. A survey of 500 registered patients found that 68% would pay $8 more for evening appointments, and 57% wanted online booking; the local college charges $650 per staff member for a customer-care course.

--- APPENDIX 2 — FINANCIAL DATA ---
Title: Extract from the Statement of Profit or Loss and Capital employed data of Pinecrest Dental Practice for the year ended 31 March 2025 ($ '000)

Cost of sales | 1,200 | 1,320
Gross profit | 800 | 1,080
Operating profit | 250 | 360
Capital employed | 1,250 | 1,600
Interest payable | 30 | 35

--- APPENDIX 3 — EXTERNAL ENVIRONMENT ---
Economic and Business Bulletin (November 2026): (1) The central bank has raised the base interest rate from 4.25% to 4.9%, increasing borrowing costs for practices with variable-rate loans. (2) The national minimum wage will rise by 5.2% to $14.10 an hour from April 2026, raising wage bills for clinical and reception staff. (3) Private dental insurance reimbursement rates have been cut by 6.5% while demand for private treatment grew 2.8%; dental materials input costs have risen 9.3% year-on-year.

  Q1(a) [8 marks]
    Question: PDP plans to fund part of its new surgery with retained profit rather than the $300,000 bank loan. Explain two advantages for PDP of using retained profit to finance the expansion.
    Answer: Point 1: Using the $240,000 of retained profit costs PDP no interest payments or capital repayments, which protects its cash flow and its $480,000 a year fixed-cost base. Unlike the $300,000 ten-year bank loan, there is no monthly debt service to find from the 14,000 units of dental treatment, so every dollar earned can be ploughed back into the second surgery rather than paid to the lender. This matters while patient complaints about waiting times are rising and Dr Amina Farouk still needs cash to hire reception cover.

Point 2: Retained profit carries no collateral risk and keeps ownership with Dr Farouk. The $300,000 bank loan could require the practice's assets or the founder's guarantee as security, putting the existing surgery at risk if the digital imaging equipment fails to attract enough patients. Using $240,000 of past profits avoids that exposure, imposes no lender conditions on how the second surgery is run, and preserves the democratic leadership's freedom to respond to the 8% absenteeism problem without consulting an external bank.
    Keywords: retained profit, bank loan, $240,000, $300,000, $480,000, dental treatment

  Q1(b) [12 marks]
    Question: PDP wants to attract patients to its new second surgery. Consider local radio advertising, social media promotions, or referral links with nearby GP surgeries. Which should PDP choose? Justify your recommendation.
    Answer: Local radio advertising: Radio reaches commuters across the practice's local catchment cheaply and suits time-limited messages such as a new surgery opening. It is far less costly than television, so it will not strain a business already committing $540,000 to the expansion and servicing a $300,000 loan. However, radio is untargeted: many listeners do not need dentistry, and it cannot convey the digital imaging message visually, so the 3,450 patients already attending and the 500 surveyed patients are not specifically reached.

Social media promotions: Targeted posts can reach exactly the patients identified in the survey — the 68% who would pay $8 more for evening appointments and the 57% who want online booking — at low cost and with immediate measurement. Posts can show the new imaging equipment directly and drive online booking. The drawback is that results depend on constant content, and older patients who may need cosmetic work might be missed by a purely digital channel.

Referral links with GP surgeries: Formal links with nearby GP practices would deliver a steady stream of referred patients with high trust and low marketing cost, and would help fill the second surgery's appointment book quickly, reducing the 12% did-not-attend rate through personal recommendation. Referrals take time to establish and depend on GPs' willingness to cooperate, and volumes may be too slow to cover the $480,000 fixed costs in the first year.

Recommendation: PDP should choose social media promotions. They reach the precise, research-identified segment, are affordable alongside the $540,000 investment, and can be built around the 68% premium for evening appointments and 57% demand for online booking. Radio is rejected as untargeted and wasteful; GP referrals are rejected as too slow to fill capacity quickly, though they should be developed later as a supplement.
