--- MAIN STEM ---
Meridian Learning Centre (MLC) is a private limited company in the education sector, employing a workforce of 30. Founded in 2014 by Priya Raman, it delivers exam-preparation courses to school pupils across the region and operates a hierarchical organisational structure with autocratic leadership. MLC plans to invest $360,000 in a new e-learning recording studio, financed by a $200,000 share issue and $160,000 retained profit. It has fixed costs of $270,000 a year, a variable cost of $20 a unit and a selling price of $65, and delivers 11,000 units of tuition a year. MLC faces two problems: tutor absenteeism has reached 10% and complaints about misprinted workbooks are rising, threatening its 96% pass rate.

--- APPENDIX 1 — MARKETING/OPS ---
Market Research Summary — 2025: A survey of 800 parents found that 72% wanted weekend classes and 61% would pay $12 more for recorded lessons; average satisfaction was 4.3 out of 5. The centre logged 45 workbook complaints last term, up from 31, and printed 9,800 workbooks at a waste rate of 3%. Tutor marking took an average of 4.2 days. A local college offers a $580 certificate course in e-learning production.

--- APPENDIX 2 — FINANCIAL DATA ---
Title: Extract from the Statement of Profit or Loss and Capital employed data of Meridian Learning Centre for the year ended 31 March 2025 ($ '000)
Headers: ['Financial Metric', '2024', '2025']
Revenue | 1,600 | 2,000
Cost of sales | 880 | 1,000
Gross profit | 720 | 1,000
Operating profit | 200 | 300
Capital employed | 1,250 | 1,500
Interest payable | 20 | 25

--- APPENDIX 3 — EXTERNAL ENVIRONMENT ---
Economic and Business Bulletin (November 2026): (1) The central bank has raised the base interest rate from 3.9% to 4.4%, increasing the cost of business borrowing. (2) The national minimum wage will rise by 4.8% to $13.60 an hour from April 2026, raising wage costs for tutors and support staff. (3) Printing and paper input costs have risen 8.6% year-on-year, while household spending on private tutoring grew 3.1% and exam-board licence fees rose 5.5%.

--- QUESTIONS ---
  Q1(a) [8 marks]
    Question: MLC plans to fund its new recording studio with a $200,000 share issue rather than using its $160,000 retained profit. Explain two advantages for MLC of the share issue.
    Answer: Point 1: A $200,000 share issue raises more money than the $160,000 of retained profit and does not drain the cash balance MLC needs to cover fixed costs of $270,000 a year and the 10% tutor absenteeism disruption. New share capital gives Priya Raman the full $360,000 studio without sacrificing working capital, so the $160,000 retained profit stays available as a cushion if recorded lessons take longer than expected to attract the 61% of parents willing to pay $12 more.

Point 2: Share capital does not have to be repaid and requires no interest, unlike a loan, so it places no strain on the operating profit that supports MLC's 96% pass rate and its rising workbook-quality costs. Issuing shares to outside investors may also bring useful contacts or e-learning expertise, and because MLC is a private limited company it can pass them the risk of the $360,000 studio while keeping day-to-day control in the hierarchical structure.

--- MAIN STEM ---
Sunrise Homecare Services (SHS) is a cooperative in the healthcare sector, employing a workforce of 50. Founded in 2008 by Nadia Osei, it provides domiciliary care visits to elderly clients across the county and operates a flat organisational structure with laissez-faire leadership. SHS plans to invest $280,000 in electric care vans and mobile scheduling software, financed by a $180,000 bank loan and $100,000 retained profit. It has fixed costs of $204,000 a year, a variable cost of $18 a unit and a selling price of $52, and delivers 12,000 units of home visits a year. SHS faces two problems: labour turnover has reached 14% and quality complaints about late visits are rising.

--- APPENDIX 1 — MARKETING/OPS ---
Quality and Waste Report — June 2025: 2,900 home visits were delivered; 5% of visits were late, down from 9% a year ago. Complaints about late arrivals rose from 33 to 47 per month. Average travel time between visits was 22 minutes. A survey of 300 clients found 74% valued evening visits and 62% would pay $6 more for them; a refresher manual-handling course costs $420 per carer.

--- APPENDIX 2 — FINANCIAL DATA ---

Keeping the $100,000 retained profit as a cash reserve protects the cooperative against the disruption caused by 14% labour turnover and the 47 monthly late-visit complaints while the new vans are introduced.

Point 2: Borrowing leaves SHS's own cash available to cover fixed costs of $204,000 a year and the $420 per-carer training costs, so the 12,000 units of home visits can continue without a cash squeeze. A bank loan spreads the cost of the vans over the repayment period, matching the way the vehicles will generate revenue over several years, whereas spending all $100,000 of retained profit at once would weaken the financial cushion that the flat, self-managing teams rely on when rotas are short-staffed.

--- MAIN STEM ---
Oakridge Private Hospital (OPH) is a public limited company in the healthcare sector, employing a workforce of 85. Founded in 1998 by Dr Ravi Menon, it provides private surgical procedures for patients across the region and operates a hierarchical organisational structure with democratic leadership. OPH plans to invest $1,200,000 in a new imaging suite, financed by a $700,000 bank loan and a $500,000 share issue. It has fixed costs of $540,000 a year, a variable cost of $120 a unit and a selling price of $300, and carries out 8,500 units of patient procedures a year. OPH faces two problems: a 3% surgical instrument defect rate and staff absenteeism of 7%.

--- APPENDIX 1 — MARKETING/OPS ---

--- MAIN STEM ---
Bluewater Laundry & Linen Services (BLL) is a partnership in the consumer services sector, employing a workforce of 40. Founded in 2007 by Elena Vasquez, it washes and irons linen for hotel clients along the coast and operates a flat organisational structure with autocratic leadership. BLL plans to invest $420,000 in a high-efficiency industrial washer, financed by $250,000 hire purchase and $170,000 retained profit. It has fixed costs of $216,000 a year, a variable cost of $8 a unit and a selling price of $26, and processes 20,000 units of laundry a year. BLL faces two problems: a 4% re-wash defect rate, machine downtime of 8% and staff absenteeism of 6%.

--- APPENDIX 1 — MARKETING/OPS ---
Quality and Waste Report — March 2025: 4,800 laundry loads were processed; 4% needed re-washing, down from 7% a year ago. Customer complaints fell from 51 to 36 per month. Average machine downtime was 6 hours a week. A survey of 200 hotel clients found 70% wanted 24-hour turnaround and 55% would pay $3 more; an operator training session costs $350 per person.

--- APPENDIX 2 — FINANCIAL DATA ---

(3) Energy and detergent input costs have risen 9.7% year-on-year, while coastal hotel occupancy grew 3.9% and demand for commercial laundry services rose 2.6%.

That reserve is valuable while the 4% re-wash defect rate and 8% machine downtime disrupt the 20,000 units of laundry and the $216,000 fixed costs still have to be met.

Point 2: Hire purchase gives BLL immediate use of the high-efficiency washer while paying for it over time, so the new machine can start reducing the 6 hours a week of downtime straight away. Unlike spending all $170,000 of retained profit, the partnership keeps a cash buffer for the $350 per person operator training and for the 55% of 200 hotel clients who would pay $3 more for better service, letting Elena Vasquez invest in quality while protecting the 20,000 units of laundry at the same time.

It compounds across all 20,000 loads, directly erodes the $18 contribution that funds the $420,000 washer, and is amplified by the 4% re-wash rate. The interest-rate effect is small and largely fixed; the wage rise is manageable at 500 loads per employee, whereas energy inflation raises the cost of every single load and cannot be avoided.
    Keywords: 4.1%, 5.8%, $13.45, 9.7%, 3.9%, $250,000
    Mark scheme: level_1_1_to_4: Identifies the external changes with limited application to BLL. | level_2_5_to_8: Analyses the impact of at least two external changes on BLL's costs, revenue or financing in context. | level_3_9_to_12: Detailed evaluation of all three external changes in the context of BLL with a well-justified greatest-impact judgement and reasons for rejecting the others.

--- MAIN STEM ---
Quarry Ridge Materials (QRM) is a private limited company in the quarried aggregates sector, employing a workforce of 50 at its limestone extraction site. Founded in 2011 by Niamh Ridge, the business supplies crushed limestone to regional construction contractors and operates a flat organisational structure with democratic leadership. QRM plans to invest $920,000 in a mobile crushing and screening plant with dust-suppression technology, financed by a $600,000 ten-year bank loan and $320,000 retained profit. It has fixed costs of $360,000 a year, a variable cost of $8.50 a unit and a selling price of $14.50, and currently produces 100,000 units a year. QRM faces two operational problems: dust-related absenteeism has reached 8% and stone-dust complaints from nearby residents are rising.

--- APPENDIX 1 — MARKETING/OPS ---
Operations and Quality Report — Q4 2025: The crushing line produced 25,000 units last quarter at a defect rate of 2.4%, down from 3.8% a year ago. Customer complaints about stone dust fell from 31 to 14 per month. Average delivery lead time is 4.1 days. A survey of 450 construction customers found that 61% would pay up to $0.50 more per unit for low-dust eco-aggregate made with recycled stone fines, and 48% require suppliers to meet dust-emission standards. Training records show 18 of the 50 staff have not completed on-the-job training on the new screens; off-the-job certification courses at the technical college cost $950 per employee. The plant manager is comparing end-of-line quality control inspection with quality assurance based on prevention and team working.

--- APPENDIX 2 — FINANCIAL DATA ---
Title: Extract from the Statement of Profit or Loss and Capital employed data of Quarry Ridge Materials for the year ended 31 March 2025 ($ '000)
Headers: ['Financial Metric', '2024', '2025']
Revenue | 1,400 | 1,600
Cost of sales | 840 | 920
Gross profit | 560 | 680
Operating profit | 168 | 200
Capital employed | 1,200 | 1,250
Interest payable | 28 | 32

--- APPENDIX 3 — EXTERNAL ENVIRONMENT ---
Economic and Construction Bulletin (January 2026): (1) The central bank has raised the base interest rate from 4.50% to 5.25%, increasing borrowing costs for businesses with variable-rate loans. (2) The national minimum wage will rise by 5.8% from $13.00 to $13.75 per hour from April 2026, lifting wage bills at extraction sites. (3) Diesel and wear-part input costs have risen 9.6% year-on-year, while construction cost inflation is running at 6.2% and infrastructure spending grew 2.9% over the same period.

--- QUESTIONS ---
  Q1(a) [8 marks]
    Question: QRM is funding part of its $920,000 crushing plant with a $600,000 bank loan. Explain two advantages for QRM of using retained profit for the $320,000 portion instead of borrowing more.
    Answer: Point 1: Using retained profit for the $320,000 portion means QRM pays no interest or capital repayments on that money, which protects its cash flow while it already carries fixed costs of $360,000 a year and a $600,000 ten-year bank loan. The saving can be spent on dust-suppression technology and on replacing screens, so the flat-structure quarry can tackle dust-related absenteeism of 8% without adding another fixed commitment. Every dollar of interest avoided also supports the $6.00 contribution per unit on each of the 100,000 units it produces.

Point 2: Retained profit does not require collateral or a charge over QRM's quarry assets, so Niamh Ridge's private limited company keeps control of the mobile crushing and screening plant without a lender able to repossess it if construction contractors cut orders. It is also faster and more flexible than arranging additional debt: the $320,000 is already in the business and can be released as the plant is commissioned, whereas a new loan would need approval and would raise the risk that the 48% of customers demanding dust-emission standards are not served on time.
    Keywords: retained profit, bank loan, $320,000, $600,000, $920,000, $360,000
    Mark scheme: knowledge_max_2: 1 mark for each valid advantage of retained profit over borrowing identified (max 2). | application_analysis_max_6: Up to 3 marks per point for contextual explanation linked to QRM's $320,000 funding, its $600,000 loan and its quarry operations.

  Q1(b) [12 marks]
    Question: QRM is promoting its new low-dust eco-aggregate to construction contractors. Consider advertising in construction trade journals, a programme of free site demonstrations, or paid social-media campaigns. Which should QRM choose to win new customers? Justify your recommendation.
    Answer: Trade journal advertising: A trade journal would put QRM's low-dust eco-aggregate in front of the regional construction contractors it already supplies, and printed technical specifications suit a product where 48% of surveyed customers require dust-emission standards. It is relatively cheap for a 50-employee quarry, but readership is slow to convert and many readers are outside QRM's delivery radius; it also cannot demonstrate the dust-suppression plant actually working, which is the product's main selling point.

Free site demonstrations: Inviting contractors to the quarry lets them see the mobile crushing and screening plant and verify dust levels for themselves, directly addressing the 31 dust complaints a month that the report records. Technical staff can explain the recycled stone fines and close orders on site. The drawbacks are high staff time, travel costs for customers and limited reach: only a small number of the 450 surveyed construction customers could attend, so this cannot by itself fill the extra capacity of the $920,000 investment.

Paid social-media campaigns: Targeted posts can reach exactly the contractors who check dust-emission standards, show short videos of the suppression technology and generate measurable enquiries at low cost, complementing the 61% of respondents who would pay $0.50 more. However, social media is easily ignored in a busy feed, needs constant content, and does not give the technical reassurance a quarry product requires.

Recommendation: QRM should choose a programme of free site demonstrations, supported by low-cost social-media follow-up. Demonstrations are rejected by neither cost nor scale because they convert the 48% standards-driven buyers fastest and directly counter the dust complaints; trade journals are rejected as passive and untargeted, while social media alone is rejected because it lacks the physical proof that makes the $920,000 dust-suppression investment credible.
    Keywords: 61%, 450, $0.50, low-dust, 48%, construction customers
    Mark scheme: level_1_1_to_4: Identifies the promotional options with limited reference to QRM's product or customers. | level_2_5_to_8: Discusses advantages and disadvantages of at least two options in the context of QRM's quarry and survey evidence. | level_3_9_to_12: Evaluates all three options in context and gives a justified recommendation that explains why trade journals and social media are rejected.

  Q2(a) [8 marks]
    Question: QRM's dust-related absenteeism has reached 8%. Explain two benefits for QRM of using democratic leadership to motivate its extraction and crushing team.
    Answer: Point 1: Democratic leadership invites the 50 quarry workers to contribute ideas on how the mobile crushing and screening plant should be run, which helps satisfy esteem and social needs and raises job satisfaction. Operators who help set sieve-changing routines and dust-control practices are more likely to attend regularly, so the practice attacks the 8% dust-related absenteeism directly. It also fits QRM's flat organisational structure, where short communication channels let a suggestion from the screening line reach Niamh Ridge quickly rather than passing through several management layers.

Point 2: Consulting the team produces practical improvements that a manager away from the face may miss, such as better positioning of dust-suppression nozzles, helping the line hold its 2.4% defect rate and reduce the 31 monthly dust complaints. Higher involvement builds commitment and lowers labour turnover, protecting the 25,000 units produced each quarter and avoiding the $950 per employee cost of off-the-job certification for replacements. In a private limited company funding a $920,000 plant with a $600,000 loan, keeping experienced operators is cheaper than repeatedly recruiting and retraining them.
    Keywords: democratic leadership, absenteeism, 8%, workforce of 50, flat organisational structure, 25,000
    Mark scheme: knowledge_max_2: 1 mark for each valid benefit of democratic leadership identified (max 2). | application_analysis_max_6: Up to 3 marks per point for applied analysis of QRM's absenteeism, flat structure, defect rate and training costs.

  Q2(b) [12 marks]
    Question: QRM must reduce dust exposure around its new dust-suppression plant. Consider on-the-job training on the screens or off-the-job certification at the technical college. Which should QRM choose? Justify your decision.
    Answer: On-the-job training: Coaching the 18 untrained staff beside the actual screens teaches the exact dust-control routines QRM needs, costs no course fees and keeps those workers producing during the 25,000-unit quarter. It allows immediate correction by experienced operators and reinforces the team working needed to cut the 31 monthly dust complaints. Its weaknesses are that trainers are themselves production staff whose output suffers, that bad habits can spread, and that there is no external certificate for the 48% of customers who want evidence of dust-emission standards.

Off-the-job certification: The technical college course at $950 per employee would cost $17,100 for all 18 staff, a small fraction of the $920,000 investment, and gives a recognised qualification that supports QRM's claim to meet dust-emission standards. It removes 18 people from a workforce of 50 for the course period, however, risking output and raising dust-related pressure on those left behind while absenteeism is already 8%; the generic syllabus may also need site-specific follow-up.

Decision: QRM should choose on-the-job training first, followed by short college certification for a smaller group of senior operators. On-the-job training is rejected as a complete answer only because it lacks formal evidence, but it wins on cost, machine relevance and uninterrupted output; full off-the-job training is rejected now because losing 18 of 50 workers and spending $17,100 while dust absenteeism is 8% would disrupt the crushing line when QRM most needs steady output. A mixed approach also spreads the risk if college places are limited, and part of the fee can be reserved for the 48% of customers who want evidence of dust-emission standards.
    Keywords: on-the-job training, off-the-job, $950, 18, 8%, $920,000
    Mark scheme: level_1_1_to_4: Describes the two training methods with minimal application to QRM. | level_2_5_to_8: Analyses benefits and drawbacks of both methods using QRM's figures, with limited judgement. | level_3_9_to_12: Fully evaluates both methods in QRM's context and reaches a justified decision that rejects the alternative.

  Q3(b) [12 marks]
    Question: Using Appendix 2, evaluate QRM's profitability by calculating the gross profit margin, profit margin and ROCE for 2024 and 2025. Has QRM's profitability improved? Justify your answer.
    Answer: Calculations:
Gross Profit Margin 2024 = 40.0%
Gross Profit Margin 2025 = 42.5%
Profit Margin 2024 = 12.0%
Profit Margin 2025 = 12.5%
ROCE 2024 = 14.0%
ROCE 2025 = 16.0%

Detailed workings: 2024 gross profit = $1,400,000 revenue − $840,000 cost of sales = $560,000; 2025 gross profit = $1,600,000 − $920,000 = $680,000. For 2024, $560,000 ÷ $1,400,000 = 0.400; $168,000 operating profit ÷ $1,400,000 = 0.120; $168,000 ÷ $1,200,000 capital employed = 0.140. For 2025, $680,000 ÷ $1,600,000 = 0.425; $200,000 ÷ $1,600,000 = 0.125; $200,000 ÷ $1,250,000 = 0.160.

Evaluation: Revenue grew by ($1,600,000 − $1,400,000) ÷ $1,400,000 = 14.3%, while gross profit grew from $560,000 to $680,000, so the business kept more of each sales dollar after direct costs. Interest payable edged up from $28,000 to $32,000, so the $600,000 loan does reduce the profit left for the private limited company's shareholders, but the effect is small beside the $200,000 operating profit.

Conclusion: QRM's profitability has improved. All three measures moved favourably — gross margin 40.0% to 42.5%, operating margin 12.0% to 12.5% and ROCE 14.0% to 16.0% — and the ROCE gain was achieved while the asset base grew, so the $920,000 investment is already supporting stronger returns rather than diluting them.

  Q4(a) [8 marks]
    Question: Explain one advantage and one disadvantage for QRM of producing low-dust eco-aggregate made with recycled stone fines.
    Answer: Advantage: The survey of 450 construction customers found that 61% would pay up to $0.50 more per unit for low-dust eco-aggregate and that 48% already require suppliers to meet dust-emission standards. Disadvantage: Recycling stone fines into the product adds handling and screening work that could raise the $8.50 variable cost, so the $0.50 premium might be wholly absorbed and the 42.5% gross margin in Appendix 2 would slip back. If the recycled fines vary in quality, the line's 2.4% defect rate could rise and more output would be scrapped, while dust-related absenteeism of 8% would still need the $920,000 dust-suppression plant to deliver savings before the eco-aggregate can be sold at a genuine premium.

  Q4(b) [12 marks]
    Question: Using Appendix 3, evaluate how the interest rate rise to 5.25%, the 5.8% minimum wage increase and the 9.6% rise in diesel and wear-part costs will affect QRM. Which change will have the greatest impact? Justify your answer.
    Answer: Interest rate rise (4.50% to 5.25%): If QRM's $600,000 ten-year bank loan is on a variable rate, the increase of 0.75 percentage points adds 0.0075 × $600,000 = $4,500 a year, which is small against fixed costs of $360,000 and operating profit of $200,000. If the loan is fixed, the direct cost is zero. Higher rates may also make future borrowing for the $920,000 programme dearer, but QRM can reduce this risk by fixing the rate, so the effect is limited and manageable.

Minimum wage increase (5.8%, from $13.00 to $13.75 an hour): With a workforce of 50, a wage rise feeds into quarrying and screening labour costs and cannot be avoided. The insert gives no hours worked or individual pay, so no annual wage total can be calculated honestly. The defensible comparison is with the productivity the data do support: 100,000 units ÷ 50 workers = 2,000 units per worker. If that holds, the higher wage per hour is spread over 2,000 units each; if dust-related absenteeism of 8% pulls output down, unit labour cost rises and the $6.00 contribution per unit is squeezed. This is a real but controllable pressure.

Input-cost inflation (9.6% on diesel and wear parts): The insert states variable cost of $8.50 per unit but does not decompose it, so the only honest bound is to assume the whole variable cost is exposed: 9.6% × $8.50 = about $0.82 per unit, and at 100,000 units that is roughly $81,600 a year (100,000 × $0.816). Even a smaller exposed share would cut contribution materially below $6.00, and higher diesel costs also affect deliveries to the 450 surveyed customers. QRM can recover at most part of this through the $0.50 eco-aggregate premium found in the research.

Conclusion: The 9.6% rise in diesel and wear-part costs will have the greatest impact. It applies to every unit produced, can erode around $81,600 of contribution on the stated bound, and directly undermines the return on the $920,000 plant. The interest rise adds only $4,500 a year and can be fixed, while the wage rise can be offset by maintaining 2,000 units per worker, so neither matches the scale or persistence of input-cost inflation.
    Keywords: 5.25%, 5.8%, 9.6%, $13.75, $8.50, $600,000
    Mark scheme: level_1_1_to_4: Lists the three external changes with little application to QRM. | level_2_5_to_8: Analyses at least two changes with correct use of QRM's figures and some judgement. | level_3_9_to_12: Evaluates all three changes in QRM's context, uses only insert-derived arithmetic and reaches a justified greatest-impact conclusion.

--- MAIN STEM ---
Kestrel Eco-Materials (KEM) is a public limited company in the eco-building-materials sector, employing a workforce of 60 at its recycling plant near Bristol. Founded in 2008 by Priya Kestrel, the business supplies recycled insulation panels to housebuilders and operates a hierarchical organisational structure with autocratic leadership. KEM plans to invest $780,000 in a low-energy panel-pressing line using recycled glass fibre, financed by a $300,000 five-year bank loan and a $480,000 share issue. It has fixed costs of $270,000 a year, a variable cost of $9.20 a unit and a selling price of $15.20, and currently produces 90,000 units a year. KEM faces two problems: a defect rate of 4.6% on new panels and rising labour turnover among machine operators.

--- APPENDIX 1 — MARKETING/OPS ---
Quality and Operations Report — Q4 2025: The pressing line produced 22,500 insulation panels last quarter with a defect rate of 4.6%, down from 6.1% a year earlier. Customer complaints about panel warping fell from 44 to 19 per month. Average order delivery time is 5.2 days. A survey of 720 housebuilders found that 58% would pay up to $0.60 more for panels made from recycled glass, and 66% require environmental product declarations. Training records show 14 of the 60 operators have not yet had on-the-job training on the new presses; off-the-job certification courses at the technical college cost $1,100 per employee. The operations director is comparing end-of-line quality control inspection with quality assurance based on prevention and team working.

--- APPENDIX 2 — FINANCIAL DATA ---
Title: Extract from the Statement of Profit or Loss and Capital employed data of Kestrel Eco-Materials for the year ended 31 March 2025 ($ '000)
Headers: ['Financial Metric', '2024', '2025']

Cost of sales | 750 | 825
Gross profit | 500 | 675
Operating profit | 150 | 210
Capital employed | 1,000 | 1,200
Interest payable | 24 | 34

(2) The national minimum wage will increase by 7.2% from $13.20 to $14.15 per hour from April 2026, pushing up wage bills across the plant. (3) Recycled glass and textile-fibre input prices have risen 11.3% year-on-year, while green-building material inflation is 7.4% and social-housing construction spending has grown 3.8% over the period.

That protects cash flow while the firm carries fixed costs of $270,000 a year and is trying to bring a 4.6% defect rate under control. The money can be tied up in the low-energy panel-pressing line without creating a new monthly commitment that would strain the 90,000-unit operation.

Point 2: Equity also improves the borrowing position for the future: with $480,000 raised from shareholders rather than lenders, KEM has more funds of its own before it approaches a bank, so the balance between borrowed and owned money is less stretched. Priya Kestrel keeps the pressing line in operation even if housebuilders delay orders, because no lender can enforce repayment on the share capital. Although existing shareholders may be diluted, the share issue lets KEM expand into recycled glass fibre panels while the 58% of surveyed housebuilders willing to pay $0.60 more are still being won over.
    Keywords: share issue, bank loan, $480,000, $300,000, $780,000, public limited company

For 2024, $500,000 ÷ $1,250,000 = 0.400; $150,000 operating profit ÷ $1,250,000 = 0.120; $150,000 ÷ $1,000,000 capital employed = 0.150. For 2025, $675,000 ÷ $1,500,000 = 0.450; $210,000 ÷ $1,500,000 = 0.140; $210,000 ÷ $1,200,000 = 0.175.

Evaluation: Revenue rose by 20.0%, from $1,250,000 to $1,500,000, but cost of sales rose by only $75,000, so gross profit jumped from $500,000 to $675,000. This suggests the recycled glass fibre line is winning better prices from housebuilders, consistent with the 58% of surveyed buyers who would pay $0.60 more. Operating profit grew from $150,000 to $210,000, faster than revenue, indicating that the $270,000 fixed costs were absorbed more effectively despite the 4.6% defect rate. ROCE improved from 15.0% to 17.5% even though capital employed increased from $1,000,000 to $1,200,000 for the $780,000 investment, which is a strong signal for shareholders who provided the $480,000 share issue. Interest payable rose from $24,000 to $34,000, so the $300,000 bank loan does absorb some of the gain, but operating profit still comfortably covers it.

Conclusion: KEM's profitability has improved. Every measure moved in the right direction — gross margin 40.0% to 45.0%, operating margin 12.0% to 14.0% and ROCE 15.0% to 17.5% — and the returns rose while the asset base expanded, so the pressing-line investment is adding value rather than merely increasing the scale of the business.
    Keywords: 40.0%, 45.0%, 12.0%, 14.0%, 15.0%, 17.5%, $780,000
    Mark scheme: level_1_1_to_4: Quotes selected Appendix 2 figures with little accurate calculation. | level_2_5_to_8: Calculates the three ratios for both years and describes the trend with some KEM context. | level_3_9_to_12: Accurate calculations for all three ratios in both years plus evaluation of revenue, cost, capital and interest with a justified conclusion.

  Q4(a) [8 marks]
    Question: Explain one advantage and one disadvantage for KEM of using recycled glass fibre in its insulation panels.
    Answer: Advantage: The survey of 720 housebuilders found that 58% would pay up to $0.60 more for panels made from recycled glass and that 66% require environmental product declarations. KEM can therefore support a higher selling price than $15.20 and meet a stated procurement requirement, which helps win specifications from large housebuilders and underpins the $780,000 low-energy pressing line. Disadvantage: Recycled glass fibre varies in quality and needs sorting and cleaning, which could push the $9.20 variable cost up and erode the $6.00 contribution per unit if the $0.60 premium is not accepted across all 90,000 units.   Q4(b) [12 marks]
    Question: Using Appendix 3, evaluate how the interest rate rise to 5.00%, the 7.2% minimum wage increase and the 11.3% rise in recycled glass and textile-fibre costs will affect KEM. Which change will have the greatest impact? Justify your answer.
    Answer: Interest rate rise (4.25% to 5.00%): If the $300,000 five-year bank loan carries a variable rate, the 0.75 percentage point rise adds 0.0075 × $300,000 = $2,250 a year, a small sum beside $270,000 of fixed costs and $210,000 of operating profit. KEM can also fix the rate or repay part of the loan early using equity from the $480,000 share issue, so this is the least threatening of the three changes even though future borrowing would be dearer.

Minimum wage increase (7.2%, from $13.20 to $14.15 an hour): With a workforce of 60, higher hourly pay raises the plant's wage bill and is unavoidable for eligible staff. The insert supplies no hours worked or individual wage rates, so an annual wage total cannot be invented. The supported comparison is productivity: 90,000 units ÷ 60 workers = 1,500 units per worker. If turnover among machine operators is brought under control and that productivity holds, the cost increase is spread across 1,500 units per worker; if the 4.6% defect rate worsens, unit labour costs rise and the $6.00 contribution is squeezed. The effect is meaningful but can be managed through training and retention.

Input-cost inflation (11.3% on recycled glass and textile fibre): The insert gives $9.20 variable cost per unit but does not decompose it, so an honest upper bound assumes the entire variable cost is exposed: 11.3% × $9.20 = about $1.04 per unit, and on 90,000 units that is roughly $93,600 a year (90,000 × $1.039). Even if only part of the cost is exposed, the impact is large, and it strikes at the same panels whose 45.0% gross margin depends on the $0.60 premium. KEM can pass some of it on to the 58% of buyers willing to pay more, but a 66% requirement for declarations does not guarantee that they will accept a large price rise.

Conclusion: The 11.3% rise in recycled input costs will have the greatest impact. It touches every panel, can remove around $93,600 of annual contribution on the stated bound and directly threatens the margins that justify the $780,000 investment. The interest rise costs only $2,250 a year and can be fixed; the wage rise can be absorbed through 1,500 units per worker and lower turnover, so neither is as large or as persistent as input-cost inflation.

--- MAIN STEM ---
Varden Block Materials (VBM) is a partnership in the construction-materials sector, employing a workforce of 40 near Leeds. Founded in 2013 by partners Ellis Varden and Ruth Pike, the business makes concrete paving blocks for housebuilders and operates a flat structure with laissez-faire leadership. VBM plans to invest $720,000 in an automated block-moulding press with a water-recycling system, financed by a $420,000 hire purchase agreement and $300,000 retained profit. It has fixed costs of $240,000 a year, a variable cost of $7.40 a unit and a selling price of $12.40, and currently produces 80,000 units a year. VBM faces two problems: a waste rate of 6.8% from off-cut concrete and frequent quality complaints from builders.

--- APPENDIX 1 — MARKETING/OPS ---
Operations and Waste Report — Q4 2025: The moulding line produced 20,000 paving blocks last quarter; 6.8% were scrapped as off-cuts, down from 9.2% in the previous quarter. Builder complaints about chipped edges fell from 36 to 17 per month. Average delivery time is 3.8 days. A survey of 380 small builders found that 63% would pay up to $0.45 more for water-recycled blocks, and 55% check environmental credentials when choosing suppliers. Water use per 1,000 blocks is 4,800 litres. The plant manager is comparing end-of-line quality control inspection with quality assurance based on prevention and team working.

--- APPENDIX 2 — FINANCIAL DATA ---

(3) Cement and aggregate input costs have increased 10.5% year-on-year, while construction cost inflation is 5.9% and regional house-building output grew 2.6% over the same period.

    Question: VBM is funding its $720,000 block press through a $420,000 hire purchase agreement. Explain two advantages for VBM of using retained profit for the $300,000 portion instead of more hire purchase finance.
    Answer: Point 1: Retained profit does not add another fixed repayment obligation, so the partnership avoids increasing the instalments already due under the $420,000 hire purchase agreement. With fixed costs of $240,000 a year and a 6.8% waste rate to tackle, keeping more cash inside VBM helps the partners pay for raw materials and maintain the 80,000-unit output without asking Ellis Varden and Ruth Pike to inject further personal capital.

Point 2: Using $300,000 of money already earned keeps ownership and control with the two partners rather than tying more of the firm's future cash to a finance company for the automated block-moulding press. Unlike hire purchase, where the asset can be repossessed if instalments are missed, retained profit carries no such risk. That flexibility matters when 55% of surveyed builders check environmental credentials and demand for water-recycled blocks may change quickly; the partnership can redirect the saved cash into quality improvements instead of being locked into another fixed contract.
    Keywords: hire purchase, retained profit, $420,000, $300,000, $720,000, partnership

    Question: VBM wants to win more small-builder customers for its water-recycled blocks. Consider advertising in trade magazines, sponsorship with a builders' merchant, or search-engine advertising. Which should VBM choose? Justify your recommendation.
    Answer: Trade magazine advertising: A regional trade title would reach the small builders VBM already supplies and allow technical details of the water-recycling system to be shown, which matters because 55% of the 380 surveyed builders check environmental credentials. It is inexpensive for a 40-person partnership. However, readership is falling, response is slow and hard to measure, and many readers are outside the Leeds delivery area, so it cannot readily fill the capacity of the $720,000 press.

Builders' merchant sponsorship: Paying a merchant to display water-recycled blocks puts the product where builders buy materials and can drive immediate orders, helped by the 63% who would pay $0.45 more. The drawbacks are that the sponsor controls the display, the deal is a recurring cost alongside $240,000 of fixed costs, and chipped-edge complaints of 17 a month could damage trust if quality is not fixed first.

Search-engine advertising: Paid search reaches builders at the moment they look for paving blocks, can be targeted at Leeds and surrounding towns, and produces measurable clicks and enquiries at a controllable budget. It also promotes the 4,800 litres of water saved per 1,000 blocks. Its weakness is that clicks are cheap but loyalty is low, and many searchers are price-focused rather than attracted by environmental credentials.

Recommendation: VBM should choose search-engine advertising, supported later by a small merchant display. Search is rejected as a complete answer only because it builds little loyalty, but it wins now on cost, measurability and local targeting; trade magazines are rejected as slow and unfocused, and full merchant sponsorship is rejected as an ongoing expense that hands too much control to another business while the 6.8% waste rate is still being reduced.

    Question: VBM must cut its 6.8% waste rate. Consider end-of-line quality control inspection or quality assurance through prevention and team working. Which should VBM choose? Justify your decision.

It also suits the flat structure and laissez-faire leadership because operators can stop the press when settings drift. Its limitations are that it takes time to train staff, needs accurate records, and cannot replace a final check for every block during the first weeks of the new $720,000 press.

Decision: VBM should choose quality assurance through prevention and team working, retaining a light final check only during commissioning. Quality control is rejected as the main method because it detects rather than prevents the 6.8% waste and keeps paying for scrap; quality assurance wins because it removes the cause of complaints, protects the 4,800-litre water saving and makes better use of the workforce of 40 than a separate inspection team.

--- MAIN STEM ---
Minegate Minerals (MNG) is a private limited company in the industrial minerals sector, employing a workforce of 50 at its silica-sand purification plant. Founded in 2015 by Tomas Minegate, the business supplies low-iron silica sand to solar-glass makers and operates a hierarchical structure with autocratic leadership. MNG plans to invest $600,000 in a magnetic-separation plant to remove iron impurities, financed by a $250,000 bank overdraft facility and $350,000 retained profit. It has fixed costs of $315,000 a year, a variable cost of $10.00 a unit and a selling price of $17.00, and currently produces 75,000 units a year. MNG faces two problems: a skills gap in operating the new separators and an impurity-related rejection rate of 5.4%.

--- APPENDIX 1 — MARKETING/OPS ---
Quality and Operations Report — Q4 2025: The purification line processed 18,750 units last quarter, of which 5.4% were rejected for excess iron, down from 7.9% a year ago. Customer quality complaints fell from 29 to 12 per month. Average order lead time is 6.3 days. A survey of 540 solar-glass buyers found that 59% would pay up to $0.70 more for low-iron sand, and 71% require purity certificates. A skills audit shows 12 of the 50 operators lack experience with magnetic separators and have had no on-the-job training on the separators; off-the-job external courses cost $1,250 per employee. The operations manager is comparing end-of-line quality control inspection with quality assurance based on prevention and team working.

--- APPENDIX 2 — FINANCIAL DATA ---
Title: Extract from the Statement of Profit or Loss and Capital employed data of Minegate Minerals for the year ended 31 March 2025 ($ '000)
Headers: ['Financial Metric', '2024', '2025']
Revenue | 1,120 | 1,350
Cost of sales | 700 | 810
Gross profit | 420 | 540
Operating profit | 112 | 162
Capital employed | 800 | 900
Interest payable | 22 | 26

--- APPENDIX 3 — EXTERNAL ENVIRONMENT ---
Economic and Manufacturing Bulletin (January 2026): (1) The central bank has increased the base interest rate from 4.50% to 5.10%, raising the cost of short-term borrowing such as bank overdrafts. (2) The national minimum wage will rise by 6.9% from $13.10 to $14.00 per hour from April 2026, increasing wage costs at the plant. (3) Energy and separation-medium input costs have risen 12.8% year-on-year, while industrial-minerals inflation is 8.3% and solar-panel installation grew 4.1% over the same period.

--- QUESTIONS ---
  Q1(a) [8 marks]
    Question: MNG is using a $250,000 bank overdraft facility for part of its $600,000 separation plant. Explain two advantages for MNG of using retained profit for the $350,000 portion instead of a larger overdraft.
    Answer: Point 1: Retained profit carries no interest charge, whereas a bigger overdraft would add to the interest payable of $26,000 already shown in Appendix 2 and to the cost of servicing the $250,000 facility. With fixed costs of $315,000 a year and a 5.4% rejection rate to fix, keeping $350,000 inside the business protects cash flow and leaves more of the $7.00 contribution per unit available for operating the magnetic separators.

Point 2: An overdraft is repayable on demand, so relying more heavily on one would leave Tomas Minegate's private limited company exposed if the bank withdrew the facility while the $600,000 plant was only part-installed. Retained profit is permanent funding and gives MNG freedom to invest at its own pace. That stability matters when 71% of surveyed solar-glass buyers require purity certificates and the plant must reach consistent quality before those customers will place larger orders, especially as the overdraft carries interest while the $350,000 of retained profit does not.
    Keywords: overdraft, retained profit, $250,000, $350,000, $600,000, $315,000
    Mark scheme: knowledge_max_2: 1 mark for each valid advantage of retained profit over an overdraft identified (max 2). | application_analysis_max_6: Up to 3 marks per point for contextual analysis of MNG's $350,000 retained profit, overdraft and quality demands.

  Q1(b) [12 marks]
    Question: MNG is promoting its low-iron silica sand to solar-glass makers. Consider technical brochures at industry exhibitions, a dedicated sales team, or sponsored research with a glass institute. Which should MNG choose? Justify your recommendation.
    Answer: Technical brochures at exhibitions: Printed purity data would reach many solar-glass buyers in one place and suit a technical product where 71% of the 540 surveyed buyers require purity certificates. It is relatively cheap for a 50-employee plant. Nevertheless, exhibitions are occasional, stand costs and staff time add up, and many visitors are not serious buyers; brochures alone cannot demonstrate that the new magnetic-separation plant consistently meets the 5.4% rejection target.

Dedicated sales team: A salesperson can visit solar-glass makers, explain the separation process, negotiate contracts and handle the 12 monthly quality complaints personally. This builds long-term relationships and can justify the $0.70 premium that 59% of buyers might accept. The drawback is cost: salaries and travel add to fixed costs near $315,000 a year, and a new salesperson needs technical training during a period when there is already a skills gap with the separators.

Sponsored research with a glass institute: Joint research would test MNG's sand under real glass-making conditions and produce independent evidence of purity, which is powerful for the 71% requiring certificates. It could also improve the product and reduce the 5.4% rejection rate. It is slow, however, and a small private limited company spending $600,000 on plant may struggle to fund a long research programme with immediate returns uncertain.

Recommendation: MNG should choose a dedicated sales team, with technical brochures used as support. Sales effort is not rejected outright, but it must be rather small at first because of the cost; it wins over brochures because it converts the 59% premium segment and handles complaints, and it wins over sponsored research because it produces nearer-term orders. Brochures are rejected as passive and research as too slow and expensive while the $600,000 plant needs steady demand.
    Keywords: 59%, 540, $0.70, 71%, solar-glass, purity certificates
    Mark scheme: level_1_1_to_4: Names the options with little reference to MNG's buyers or product. | level_2_5_to_8: Discusses advantages and disadvantages of at least two options in MNG's context. | level_3_9_to_12: Evaluates all three options and recommends one with explicit reasons for rejecting the alternatives.

  Q2(a) [8 marks]
    Question: MNG has a skills gap and a 5.4% rejection rate. Explain two benefits for MNG of using autocratic leadership during the commissioning of its new magnetic separators.
    Answer: Point 1: Autocratic leadership lets Tomas Minegate make swift, firm decisions about separator settings and safety while the new $600,000 plant is commissioned, which matters when a skills gap means 12 of the 50 operators lack experience. Clear instructions from the top reduce the chance that inconsistent settings cause the 5.4% impurity-related rejection rate to rise, and the hierarchical structure makes it obvious who gives the orders and who carries them out.

Point 2: Tight control also helps impose uniform quality checks, so the 18,750 units processed each quarter are tested the same way and the 29 to 12 fall in monthly complaints can continue. For a private limited company relying on 71% of buyers who require purity certificates, consistent procedures protect the $350,000 retained profit invested in the plant. Decisions are fast, which suits a technical commissioning period, though the style may need to soften later if MNG wants operators to suggest improvements to the separation process.
    Keywords: autocratic, hierarchical, skills gap, 5.4%, workforce of 50, 18,750
    Mark scheme: knowledge_max_2: 1 mark for each valid benefit of autocratic leadership identified (max 2). | application_analysis_max_6: Up to 3 marks per point for analysis applied to MNG's skills gap, rejection rate, structure and certificates.

  Q2(b) [12 marks]
    Question: MNG must train 12 operators on the magnetic separators. Consider on-the-job training or off-the-job external courses at $1,250 per employee. Which should MNG choose? Justify your decision.

The problem is that 12 of 50 workers are away from the plant, risking the 18,750-unit quarterly output and potentially pushing complaints back toward 29 a month; generic course content may also need site-specific follow-up before it changes practice.

Decision: MNG should choose on-the-job training first and fund external courses for a smaller group of supervisors afterwards. On-the-job training wins on cost, relevance and uninterrupted output, and is only rejected as a complete solution because it lacks certification. Full off-the-job training for all 12 is rejected now because losing nearly a quarter of the workforce and spending $15,000 while a skills gap and 5.4% rejection rate already exist would disrupt the commissioning of the separators.

--- MAIN STEM ---
Zephyr Bio-Resources (ZBR) is a cooperative in the eco-packaging sector, employing a workforce of 35 at its moulded-fibre plant. Founded in 2012 by cooperative chair Ada Zephyr, the business supplies biodegradable trays to food retailers and operates a flat structure with democratic leadership. ZBR plans to invest $540,000 in a low-waste fibre-moulding line using crop residues, financed by a $240,000 bank loan and $300,000 from new member share contributions. It has fixed costs of $210,000 a year, a variable cost of $6.30 a unit and a selling price of $11.30, and currently produces 70,000 units a year. ZBR faces two problems: fibre-waste of 7.2% and irregular deliveries from seed suppliers.

--- APPENDIX 1 — MARKETING/OPS ---
Quality and Supply Report — Q4 2025: The moulding line produced 17,500 trays last quarter, with 7.2% scrapped because of uneven fibre, down from 10.1% previously. Retailer complaints about tray breakage fell from 33 to 15 per month. Average delivery time is 4.6 days. A survey of 620 shoppers found that 67% prefer biodegradable packaging and 54% would pay up to $0.35 more for it. Supplier deliveries arrived late 11 times last quarter, against a target of 3. The board is comparing end-of-line quality control inspection with quality assurance based on prevention and supplier partnerships, and is considering on-the-job training for 9 operators; off-the-job courses cost $880 per employee.

--- APPENDIX 2 — FINANCIAL DATA ---
Title: Extract from the Statement of Profit or Loss and Capital employed data of Zephyr Bio-Resources for the year ended 31 March 2025 ($ '000)
Headers: ['Financial Metric', '2024', '2025']
Revenue | 760 | 900
Cost of sales | 456 | 495
Gross profit | 304 | 405
Operating profit | 76 | 117
Capital employed | 800 | 900
Interest payable | 16 | 20

--- APPENDIX 3 — EXTERNAL ENVIRONMENT ---
Economic and Retail Bulletin (February 2026): (1) The central bank has raised the base interest rate from 4.25% to 4.90%, increasing borrowing costs on variable-rate loans. (2) The national minimum wage will rise by 6.1% from $13.15 to $13.95 per hour from April 2026, raising the cooperative's wage bill. (3) Crop-residue and transport input costs have risen 9.4% year-on-year, while food-packaging inflation is 5.6% and sales of biodegradable food trays grew 4.4% over the period.

  Q1(a) [8 marks]
    Question: ZBR is raising $300,000 from new member share contributions for its $540,000 moulding line. Explain two advantages for ZBR of using member shares rather than the $240,000 bank loan.
    Answer: Point 1: Member share contributions are equity, so the cooperative does not have to repay the $300,000 or pay interest on it, unlike the $240,000 bank loan. That protects cash flow while ZBR carries fixed costs of $210,000 a year and a 7.2% fibre-waste rate. More of the $5.00 contribution per unit can be spent on the low-waste fibre-moulding line and on solving the 11 late supplier deliveries rather than on debt service.

Point 2: Raising money from members strengthens the cooperative's own capital base and spreads the risk among the people who use and own it, instead of leaving a bank able to call in the loan. Ada Zephyr and the members keep control of decisions about biodegradable trays and the 620-shopper survey findings. Since 67% of shoppers prefer biodegradable packaging, the cooperative can reinvest any surplus in more capacity without first asking a lender's permission or meeting new repayment terms.
    Keywords: member share contributions, bank loan, $300,000, $240,000, $540,000, cooperative
    Mark scheme: knowledge_max_2: 1 mark for each valid advantage of member shares over a bank loan identified (max 2). | application_analysis_max_6: Up to 3 marks per point for contextual analysis of ZBR's $300,000 equity, loan and cooperative aims.

  Q1(b) [12 marks]
    Question: ZBR wants to grow sales of biodegradable trays to food retailers. Consider in-store shelf displays, food-retail trade fairs, or social-media campaigns. Which should ZBR choose? Justify your recommendation.
    Answer: In-store shelf displays: A display beside the trays in food retailers would reach shoppers at the moment of purchase and can carry the message that 67% of the 620 surveyed shoppers prefer biodegradable packaging. This suits a cooperative with a modest budget and supports the $0.35 premium that 54% might pay. The drawback is that shelf space is limited and controlled by retailers, and a display cannot explain why ZBR's fibre trays are less wasteful than plastic once the shopper has walked past.

Food-retail trade fairs: Meeting buyers face to face allows ZBR to show samples, discuss the 7.2% fibre-waste improvement and negotiate listings with several retailers at once. Samples let buyers judge tray strength against the 15 monthly breakage complaints. Trade fairs are expensive, however, for a 35-person cooperative funding a $540,000 line, and one event produces leads rather than guaranteed orders; follow-up is essential.

Social-media campaigns: Low-cost posts and short videos can reach the 54% of shoppers who would pay $0.35 more and build a brand story around crop-residue trays. Results can be measured and the campaign changed quickly. Its weaknesses are that engagement does not automatically become sales in food retailers, that rivals use the same channels, and that it does not persuade the retailers who decide whether to stock the trays.

Recommendation: ZBR should choose in-store shelf displays, supported by low-cost social media. Displays are rejected as the only channel because they depend on retailer goodwill, but they win on cost and because they reach the shopper at the point of sale where the 67% preference matters. Trade fairs are rejected as too expensive for the cooperative right now, and social media alone is rejected because it influences consumers but not the retailers who control listings.
    Keywords: 67%, 620, $0.35, 54%, biodegradable, food retailers

    Question: ZBR must reduce fibre-waste and late deliveries. Consider end-of-line quality control inspection or quality assurance through prevention and supplier partnerships. Which should ZBR choose? Justify your decision.

It also suits democratic leadership and team working because operators can stop the line when fibre quality drifts. It is slower to establish, needs training such as the $880 per employee courses for 9 operators, and cannot yet replace a final check on every tray.

Decision: ZBR should choose quality assurance through prevention and supplier partnerships, keeping a light final inspection during the first weeks of the $540,000 line. Quality control is rejected as the main answer because it detects waste after it occurs and cannot fix supplier lateness; quality assurance wins because it removes the causes of both problems, protects the 67% of shoppers who prefer biodegradable packaging and makes better use of the workforce of 35. It also lets the cooperative train the 9 operators with the $880 courses in relevant prevention skills rather than in simple sorting, so the $540,000 line can raise tray quality as well as output.
    Keywords: quality control, quality assurance, 7.2%, 10.1%, $540,000, supplier partnerships

--- MAIN STEM ---
Kestrel Brook Vineyards (KBV) is a private limited company in the wine and beverage sector, employing a workforce of 40. Founded in 2007 by Rowan Kestrel, it now supplies bottled wine to national supermarket chains and operates a flat organisational structure with democratic leadership. KBV plans to invest $720,000 in a new irrigation system and automated bottling line, financed by a $450,000 ten-year bank loan and $270,000 of retained profit. It has fixed costs of $245,000 a year, a variable cost of $9.20 a unit and a selling price of $16.20, and currently produces 60,000 units a year for its retail customers. KBV faces two operational problems: bottling-line defects of 2.4% and labour turnover of 9%.

--- APPENDIX 1 — MARKETING/OPS ---
Operations and Quality Report — Q3 2025: The vineyard bottled 15,000 units last quarter at a defect rate of 2.4%, down from 3.6% a year ago. Customer complaints fell from 31 to 17 a month. Average order fulfilment is 4.1 days. Market research of 500 shoppers found that 68% would pay up to $0.50 more for sustainably bottled wine and 47% check bottle recycling before buying. A training-needs analysis shows 12 of 40 staff have not completed on-the-job training on the new bottling machines; off-the-job training courses at the local college cost $800 per employee.

--- APPENDIX 2 — FINANCIAL DATA ---
Title: Extract from the Statement of Financial Position of Kestrel Brook Vineyards as at 31 March 2025 ($ '000)
Headers: ['Financial Metric', '2024', '2025']
Inventories | 150 | 132
Trade receivables | 110 | 128
Cash and cash equivalents | 38 | 55
Current liabilities | 210 | 200
Non-current assets | 1,900 | 2,350
Capital employed | 2,300 | 2,650

--- APPENDIX 3 — EXTERNAL ENVIRONMENT ---
Economic and Business Bulletin (November 2026): (1) The central bank has raised the base interest rate from 4.25% to 5.0%, increasing borrowing costs for businesses with variable-rate loans. (2) The national minimum wage will rise by 5.8% from $13.00 to $13.75 per hour from April 2026, raising total wage bills. (3) Glass and cork input costs have risen 9.3% year-on-year, beverage-price inflation is 6.4%, while consumer spending on premium wine grew 3.5% in the same period.

--- QUESTIONS ---
  Q1(a) [8 marks]
    Question: KBV plans to fund part of its bottling-line expansion with a ten-year bank loan. Explain two advantages for KBV of using retained profit instead of the bank loan.
    Answer: Point 1: Retained profit is internally generated, so KBV pays no interest or capital repayments on the $270,000 used for the new irrigation system and automated bottling line. With fixed costs of $245,000 a year and a $450,000 bank loan already outstanding, avoiding another debt-service charge protects cash flow and the $7.00 contribution earned on each of 60,000 bottles. Every dollar saved in interest can instead absorb the 9.3% rise in glass and cork input costs, helping KBV hold its $16.20 selling price for national supermarket chains.

Point 2: Using retained profit keeps ownership and control with founder Rowan Kestrel and the existing shareholders. A further bank loan could impose covenants and, if the 2.4% bottling defects persisted and sales slipped, the lender could demand repayment or secure company assets, putting the whole $720,000 investment at risk. Retained profit carries no such condition, so the flat, democratic management team can decide how to run the new line without external pressure, while the existing $450,000 facility stays available for working capital and the 9% labour-turnover problem can be addressed with training.
    Keywords: retained profit, bank loan, $270,000, $450,000, $245,000, bottling
    Mark scheme: knowledge_max_2: 1 mark for each valid advantage of retained profit over a bank loan (max 2). | application_analysis_max_6: Up to 3 marks per point for contextual explanation applied to KBV's $270,000 retained profit, $450,000 loan, costs and defects.

  Q1(b) [12 marks]
    Question: KBV is launching its new sustainably bottled wine range. Consider a national television campaign, local radio sponsorship, or social media influencer marketing. Which should KBV choose to promote the launch? Justify your recommendation.
    Answer: National television campaign: A nationwide TV campaign would build brand awareness quickly across all the supermarket chains stocking KBV's wine and could reach millions of buyers in one flight. The drawbacks are decisive for a 40-employee vineyard: airtime and production costs are very high relative to $245,000 fixed costs, and much of the audience drinks no premium wine or lives outside the distribution network, so spend is wasted. Funding it would also compete with the $450,000 bank loan repayments on the $720,000 bottling investment.

Local radio sponsorship: Regional radio is much cheaper, targets KBV's core local catchment and suits time-sensitive messages about a new launch. Its reach is narrow, however; KBV supplies national supermarket chains and needs volume to sell 60,000 units a year, so regional listeners alone cannot create the demand required. It also cannot showcase the visual story of sustainable bottling as well as digital media.

Social media influencer marketing: Food and lifestyle influencers can demonstrate the sustainable bottles directly to the 68% of 500 surveyed shoppers willing to pay up to $0.50 more and the 47% who check recycling, with measurable engagement at low cost per reached shopper and national reach. Results build more slowly than TV and depend on influencer credibility, but this option precisely matches the research evidence.

Recommendation: KBV should choose social media influencer marketing. It reaches the exact identified segment, costs far less than television, scales nationally unlike radio, and supports the premium price needed for a $7.00 contribution per unit. Television is rejected as unaffordable and untargeted; radio is rejected as too narrow for national supermarket distribution.
    Keywords: sustainably bottled, 68%, 47%, $0.50, 500, 60,000
    Mark scheme: level_1_1_to_4: Identifies promotional options with limited application to KBV. | level_2_5_to_8: Discusses advantages and disadvantages of at least two options in KBV's context with some judgement. | level_3_9_to_12: Evaluates all three options in context and recommends influencer marketing, explaining why television and radio are rejected.

  Q2(a) [8 marks]
    Question: KBV's bottling-line defects are 2.4% and its labour turnover is 9%. Explain two benefits for KBV of using democratic leadership to improve motivation in its production team.
    Answer: Point 1: Democratic leadership gives the 40 employees a real voice in how the new automated bottling line is run, which helps satisfy social and esteem needs and raises job satisfaction. Workers who help set sealing routines and shift patterns are more likely to attend consistently, directly attacking KBV's 9% labour turnover and reducing disruption to the 60,000-unit output plan. This suits the flat organisational structure and keeps decision-making close to the people handling the bottles.

Point 2: Consulting operators produces practical ideas for reducing the 2.4% defect rate, because those staff see the sealing machines daily. Involvement builds commitment, so fewer skilled workers leave and KBV avoids repeatedly spending $800 per employee on off-the-job courses for the 12 of 40 staff still needing training. Higher commitment also protects the $7.00 contribution per unit and the $720,000 investment by keeping quality stable while the new line beds in, rather than relying on autocratic instructions that can breed resentment.
    Keywords: democratic leadership, 2.4%, 9%, workforce of 40, 12 of 40, $800
    Mark scheme: knowledge_max_2: 1 mark for each valid benefit of democratic leadership (max 2). | application_analysis_max_6: Up to 3 marks per point for contextual explanation linked to KBV's 2.4% defects, 9% turnover and training costs.

  Q2(b) [12 marks]
    Question: KBV must upskill 12 production staff to operate the new bottling machines. Consider on-the-job training or off-the-job training at the local college. Which should KBV choose? Justify your decision.
    Answer: On-the-job training: Coaching at the bottling line is directly relevant to KBV's own machines and quality standards, costs no course fees and keeps the 12 staff productive while they learn. This protects the 15,000 units packed last quarter and the effort already made to cut defects from 3.6% to 2.4%. The weaknesses are that trainers are themselves production workers whose output suffers, bad habits may be passed on, and there is little formal certification, which could matter if supermarket auditors request records.

Off-the-job training: The local college course at $800 per employee costs $9,600 for all 12 staff — small beside the $720,000 investment — and provides structured, up-to-date skills with a recognised certificate. It also removes 12 of 40 workers from the line for a period, cutting short-term capacity and risking the 9% labour-turnover situation worsening; the generic content may not match KBV's exact machine settings, so follow-up coaching would still be needed.

Decision: KBV should choose on-the-job training for the initial rollout, with short college top-ups later for senior operators. It is cheaper, machine-specific and avoids further output loss while defects are still 2.4%. Full off-the-job training is rejected because paying $9,600 and withdrawing 12 staff from a 40-person workforce would disrupt supermarket deliveries; college sessions can be added once the line is stable.
    Keywords: on-the-job training, off-the-job training, $800, $720,000, 12 of 40, 2.4%

  Q3(b) [12 marks]
    Question: Using Appendix 2, evaluate KBV's liquidity by calculating the current ratio and the acid test ratio for 2024 and 2025. Has KBV's liquidity improved? Justify your answer.
    Answer: Calculations:
Current Ratio 2024 = 1.42 : 1
Current Ratio 2025 = 1.58 : 1
Acid Test Ratio 2024 = 0.70 : 1
Acid Test Ratio 2025 = 0.92 : 1

Detailed workings: 2024 current assets = $150,000 inventories + $110,000 trade receivables + $38,000 cash = $298,000; 2025 current assets = $132,000 + $128,000 + $55,000 = $315,000. The 2024 figure divided by $210,000 current liabilities gives 1.42, and the 2025 figure divided by $200,000 gives 1.58. Excluding inventories: 2024 = ($298,000 − $150,000) ÷ $210,000 = 0.70; 2025 = ($315,000 − $132,000) ÷ $200,000 = 0.92.

Evaluation: Liquidity has strengthened on both measures. The current ratio rose from 1.42 to 1.58 because current assets grew by $17,000 while current liabilities fell by $10,000, so short-term obligations are covered more comfortably. The acid test rose from 0.70 to 0.92, meaning KBV is less dependent on selling wine inventories to pay debts — important while it services a $450,000 bank loan and has committed $720,000 to new equipment. The stronger acid test is the more convincing evidence of real improvement because it excludes stock that may be slow to sell if bottling defects persist at 2.4%. However, trade receivables increased from $110,000 to $128,000, tying up cash with supermarket customers, and cash of $55,000 is still small relative to $200,000 liabilities, so a late payment could weaken the position quickly.

Conclusion: KBV's liquidity has improved. Both measures are higher and the improvement does not rely on inventories, though rising receivables mean management should tighten credit control before further borrowing.

    Question: Explain one advantage and one disadvantage for KBV of offering sustainably bottled wine.

Capturing that premium would lift revenue per bottle from $16.20 toward $16.70 and protect the $7.00 contribution per unit against the 9.3% rise in glass and cork input costs. It also differentiates KBV's wine on national supermarket shelves, supporting demand for the 60,000 units needed to justify the $720,000 bottling investment.

Disadvantage: Sustainable glass and closures can cost more than standard packaging, and the insert does not separate the $9.20 variable cost into components, so the exact increase cannot be quantified; if suppliers pass on higher charges, contribution would fall unless the $0.50 premium is accepted across the range. Any breakage or shorter shelf life would also aggravate the current 2.4% defect rate and raise waste before the new line stabilises, while the $450,000 bank loan still requires cash.

  Q4(b) [12 marks]
    Question: Using Appendix 3, evaluate how the interest rate rise to 5.0%, the 5.8% minimum wage increase and the 9.3% rise in glass and cork input costs will affect KBV. Which change will have the greatest impact? Justify your answer.
    Answer: Interest rate rise (4.25% to 5.0%): If KBV's $450,000 ten-year bank loan is variable-rate, the additional cost is 0.75% of $450,000 = $3,375 a year (0.0075 × $450,000). That is modest against $245,000 fixed costs, and if the loan is fixed-rate the immediate effect is nil. Higher rates may also make consumers more cautious about premium wine and raise the cost of any future borrowing, but KBV can largely control this by fixing the loan rate.

Minimum wage increase (5.8%, to $13.75 an hour): With a workforce of 40, a wage rise feeds into costs and cannot be avoided. The insert gives neither hours worked nor individual pay, so no annual wage total is defensible. The honest test is productivity: 60,000 units ÷ 40 staff = 1,500 units a worker, so the rise is affordable only if productivity holds or output grows; otherwise unit labour cost rises and the $7.00 contribution shrinks.

Input-cost inflation (9.3% glass and cork): The insert does not decompose the $9.20 variable cost, so only a bound can be shown: if the whole $9.20 rose 9.3% that adds $0.86 a unit (0.093 × $9.20), or about $51,000 a year at 60,000 units. Even a smaller pass-through would cut contribution materially, though the $0.50 eco-premium and retailer negotiations can recover part of it.

Conclusion: The 9.3% input-cost rise will have the greatest impact: it applies to every one of the 60,000 bottles and directly erodes the $7.00 contribution that underpins the $720,000 investment, whereas the interest rise is quantifiable and small and the wage effect depends on unstated hours. It is also harder for KBV to offset than the other two changes.
    Keywords: 5.0%, 5.8%, 9.3%, 6.4%, $13.75, $9.20, $450,000
    Mark scheme: level_1_1_to_4: Identifies the external changes with limited application to KBV. | level_2_5_to_8: Analyses the impact of at least two changes on KBV's costs, revenue or finance in context. | level_3_9_to_12: Evaluates all three changes in context, concludes input-cost inflation is greatest and explains why the others are smaller.

--- MAIN STEM ---
Thornfield Dairy Produce (TDP) is a cooperative in the dairy-processing sector, employing a workforce of 65. Founded in 1998 by Marta Thornfield, it supplies cheese and yoghurt to regional supermarket chains and operates a hierarchical structure with autocratic leadership. TDP plans to invest $960,000 in a new cheese-making and cold-storage facility on its existing site, financed by a $600,000 ten-year bank loan and $360,000 of retained profit. It has fixed costs of $360,000 a year, a variable cost of $8.00 a unit and a selling price of $14.00, and currently produces 90,000 units a year for its retail customers. TDP faces two operational problems: milk-spoilage waste of 4.1% and absenteeism of 8% among production staff.

--- APPENDIX 1 — MARKETING/OPS ---
Quality and Waste Report — Q3 2025: The dairy packed 24,000 units last quarter at a spoilage rate of 4.1%, down from 5.6% a year ago. Customer complaints fell from 44 to 26 a month. Average delivery time is 2.8 days. A survey of 750 shoppers found that 61% would pay up to $0.35 more for farm-assured cheese and 55% check animal-welfare labels. Training records show 18 of 65 staff have not completed on-the-job training on the new pasteuriser; off-the-job training courses at the local college cost $950 per employee.

Because TDP has autocratic leadership in a hierarchical structure, using internally generated funds lets Marta Thornfield and the committee control the $960,000 project without external interference, and no extra interest exposure arises if the 8% absenteeism rate temporarily reduces output. --- MAIN STEM ---
Sunridge Citrus Ranch (SCR) is a partnership in the citrus-growing and fresh-produce sector, employing a workforce of 30. Founded in 2011 by Elena Sunridge, it supplies fresh citrus to national fruit wholesalers and operates a flat structure with laissez-faire leadership. SCR plans to invest $540,000 in a new packing and cold-storage shed, financed by a $300,000 ten-year bank loan and $240,000 of retained profit. It has fixed costs of $180,000 a year, a variable cost of $5.00 a unit and a selling price of $11.00, and currently produces 50,000 units a year for its wholesalers. SCR faces two problems: a blemish defect rate of 3.3% and labour turnover of 11%.

--- APPENDIX 1 — MARKETING/OPS ---
Quality and Market Report — Q3 2025: The ranch packed 12,500 units last quarter at a blemish rate of 3.3%, down from 4.8% a year ago. Customer complaints fell from 29 to 15 a month.     Question: Using Appendix 2, evaluate SCR's liquidity by calculating the current ratio and the acid test ratio for 2024 and 2025. Has SCR's liquidity improved? Justify your answer.

Current Ratio 2025 = 1.70 : 1
Acid Test Ratio 2024 = 0.73 : 1
Acid Test Ratio 2025 = 1.06 : 1

The caveat is that trade receivables grew from $70,000 to $88,000, so cash is tied up with wholesalers, and a late payment would quickly weaken the ratios.

Conclusion: SCR's liquidity has clearly improved, and crucially the acid test now exceeds 1, so short-term debts can be met without relying on selling fruit stock.     Question: Using Appendix 3, evaluate how the interest rate rise to 4.75%, the 7.1% minimum wage increase and the 10.2% rise in fertiliser and packaging input costs will affect SCR. Which change will have the greatest impact? Justify your answer.
    Answer: Interest rate rise (4.0% to 4.75%): If the $300,000 ten-year bank loan is variable-rate, the extra cost is 0.75% × $300,000 = $2,250 a year (0.0075 × $300,000). That is small against $180,000 fixed costs and nil if the rate is fixed, though future borrowing for the $540,000 shed becomes dearer and consumers may reduce discretionary fruit spending. Fixing the rate would largely remove this risk.

Minimum wage increase (7.1%, to $13.71 an hour): With a workforce of 30 this raises costs in packing and grading and cannot be avoided. The insert gives no hours or wage levels, so a valid annual total cannot be invented. The appropriate measure is productivity: 50,000 units ÷ 30 staff = about 1,667 units a worker, so the rise is bearable only if that productivity holds or output rises, otherwise unit labour cost eats into the $6.00 contribution.

Input-cost inflation (10.2% fertiliser and packaging): The $5.00 variable cost is not decomposed, so only a bound can be computed: if all of it rose 10.2%, that is $0.51 a unit (0.102 × $5.00), or roughly $25,500 a year at 50,000 units. Even partial pass-through reduces contribution, but the $0.30 locally grown premium and 3.2% demand growth can offset part of it.

Conclusion: The 10.2% rise in fertiliser and packaging costs will have the greatest impact because it applies to every unit and directly reduces the $6.00 contribution that supports the $540,000 investment. The interest charge is a known $2,250, and the wage effect depends on unstated hours, while input inflation is broad and persistent and cannot be fixed by a single contract change.

--- MAIN STEM ---
Millgrove Grain Kitchens (MGK) is a sole trader in the cereal and grain-milling sector, employing a workforce of 55. Founded in 2003 by Owen Millgrove, it supplies breakfast cereals to regional food retailers and operates a hierarchical structure with democratic leadership. MGK plans to invest $840,000 in a new grain mill and packaging line, financed by a $520,000 ten-year bank loan and $320,000 of retained profit. It has fixed costs of $300,000 a year, a variable cost of $6.25 a unit and a selling price of $12.25, and currently produces 75,000 units a year for its regional retail customers. --- MAIN STEM ---
Kestrel Tooling Industries (KTI) is a private limited company in the precision engineering sector, employing a workforce of 40. Founded in 2011 by Eleanor Kestrel, the firm manufactures tungsten-carbide cutting tools for aerospace and automotive clients across the region and operates a flat organisational structure with democratic leadership. KTI plans to invest $820,000 in a new CNC tool-grinding cell, financed by a $450,000 ten-year bank loan and $370,000 retained profit. It has fixed costs of $264,000 a year, a variable cost of $7.50 a unit and a selling price of $13.50, and currently produces 80,000 units a year. KTI faces two operational problems: defect rates on the old grinders have reached 2.2% and labour turnover is rising, while a shortage of skilled operators is slowing output.

--- APPENDIX 1 — MARKETING/OPS ---
Operations and Quality Report — Q3 2025: The grinding cell machined 19,200 cutting tools last quarter at a defect rate of 2.2%, down from 3.6% a year earlier. Customer complaints fell from 31 to 17 a month. Average order fulfilment is 4.1 days. A survey of 450 industrial buyers found 58% would pay up to $0.50 more for precision-ground tools and 47% check supplier accreditation before ordering. Training records show 14 of the 40 operators have not completed on-the-job training on the CNC grinders; external certification courses at the technical college cost $780 per employee.

--- APPENDIX 2 — FINANCIAL DATA ---

Minimum wage increase (5.5%, to $13.72 an hour): KTI employs 40 operators and the wage rise feeds into its wage bill, but the insert gives no hours worked or pay rates, so no annual total can be invented honestly. The defensible test is productivity: 80,000 units ÷ 40 staff = 2,000 units per worker, so a higher wage is affordable only if productivity holds at that level or output grows; otherwise unit labour cost erodes the $6.00 contribution per unit.

Input cost inflation (9.8% tungsten and cobalt): The $7.50 variable cost is not decomposed in the insert, so only a bound is honest — if the whole variable cost rose 9.8% it would add 0.098 × $7.50 = $0.735 a unit, or about 80,000 × $0.735 = $58,800 a year. Even a smaller rise cuts contribution and threatens the 44,000-unit break-even, though the $0.50 premium accepted by 58% of buyers offers partial recovery.

Conclusion: The 9.8% input-cost rise will have the greatest impact. It compounds across all 80,000 units and directly erodes the $6.00 contribution that justifies the $820,000 cell, and it cannot be removed by fixing a loan rate. The interest-rate effect is a bounded $3,375 at most, and the wage effect depends on productivity, so both are smaller and more manageable than pervasive input inflation.
    Keywords: 5.0%, 5.5%, 9.8%, interest rate, $450,000, $7.50, $13.72
    Mark scheme: level_1_1_to_4: Identifies the three external changes with limited application to KTI. | level_2_5_to_8: Analyses the impact of at least two changes on KTI's costs, revenue or financing in context. | level_3_9_to_12: Evaluates all three changes in the context of KTI and justifies why input-cost inflation has the greatest impact while the other two are smaller.
