--- MAIN STEM ---
Rothermere Marine Instruments (RMI) is a partnership in the marine electronics sector, employing a workforce of 50. Founded in 2008 by senior partner Innes Rothermere, the firm produces navigation displays and depth gauges for commercial fishing and leisure boats, and operates a hierarchical structure with autocratic leadership. RMI plans to invest $760,000 in a new display-assembly line, financed by $360,000 retained profit and $400,000 through hire purchase. It has fixed costs of $245,000 a year, a variable cost of $8.00 a unit and a selling price of $15.00, and currently produces 70,000 units a year. RMI faces two operational problems: a defect rate of 3.4% on assembled displays and longer delivery times, with labour turnover rising among test technicians.

--- APPENDIX 1 — MARKETING/OPS ---
Operations Log — Q3 2025: The assembly line built 16,800 marine displays last quarter at a defect rate of 3.4%, up from 2.1% a year earlier. Customer complaints rose from 22 to 39 a month and average delivery time stretched from 3.0 to 5.6 days. A survey of 520 boat owners found 61% would pay up to $0.60 more for a waterproof display and 44% check warranty terms before buying. Records show 12 of 50 technicians have not completed on-the-job training on the new test rigs; external certification courses cost $640 per employee.

  Q1(a) [8 marks]
    Question: RMI plans to finance $400,000 of its $760,000 display-assembly line through hire purchase rather than retained profit. Explain one advantage and one disadvantage for RMI of using hire purchase.
    Answer: Advantage: Hire purchase spreads the $400,000 cost of the new display-assembly line into manageable instalments, so RMI can install the equipment now and begin producing displays rather than waiting to build up cash. This preserves the $360,000 retained profit for working capital and helps a 50-person partnership protect its $15.00 selling price and the $7.00 contribution on each of 70,000 units while it tackles the 3.4% defect rate.

Disadvantage: Hire purchase is more expensive overall than paying cash because interest is built into the instalments, raising the true cost of the $760,000 investment and adding a fixed commitment alongside $245,000 a year of fixed costs. If delivery times lengthen and cash is tied up in the 16,800 displays built last quarter, missed instalments could put the equipment at risk, reducing Innes Rothermere's control over the new line.

The partnership can therefore keep the $7.00 contribution on 70,000 displays intact while it fixes the 3.4% defect rate, rather than spending part of each sale on hire-purchase interest.
    Keywords: hire purchase, $760,000, $400,000, $360,000, retained profit, $245,000, 4.75%

    Question: RMI must strengthen its testing team to cut the 3.4% defect rate. Consider internal recruitment or external recruitment. Which should RMI choose? Justify your decision.

Decision: RMI should choose external recruitment for the specialist testing roles. RMI should still use internal promotion for supervisory positions to keep morale high.

RMI should also set a probation period with a practical test on the new rigs so the 3.4% defect rate is actually reduced, and combine it with the $640 certification courses for existing staff. Without such checks, hiring an outsider would raise costs without fixing the 5.6-day delivery problem, and the partnership would gain little from the decision.

--- MAIN STEM ---
Portview Valves & Fittings (PVF) is a public limited company in the industrial fluid-control sector, employing a workforce of 60. Founded in 1999 by Jonas Portview, who remains chief executive, it makes brass valves and pipe fittings for water utilities and chemical plants, and operates a flat structure with laissez-faire leadership. PVF plans to invest $1,100,000 in an automated valve-testing facility, financed by a $700,000 new share issue and $400,000 retained profit. It has fixed costs of $360,000 a year, a variable cost of $12.00 a unit and a selling price of $20.00, and currently produces 90,000 units a year. PVF faces two operational problems: a defect rate of 2.8% in pressure testing and rising complaints about delivery reliability from utility clients.

--- APPENDIX 1 — MARKETING/OPS ---
Quality and Operations Report — Q3 2025: The test facility checked 21,600 valves last quarter at a defect rate of 2.8%, down from 4.0% a year ago. Late deliveries fell from 48 to 26 a month, and average lead time is 6.2 days. A survey of 380 procurement managers found 66% would pay up to $0.80 more for certified pressure-tested valves and 55% require test certificates before ordering. Training records show 16 of 60 assembly workers have not completed on-the-job training on the new test benches; external accreditation courses cost $920 per employee.

--- APPENDIX 2 — FINANCIAL DATA ---
Title: Extract from the Statement of Financial Position of Portview Valves & Fittings as at 31 March 2025 ($ '000)
Headers: ['Financial Metric', '2024', '2025']

Cash and cash equivalents | 70 | 95

Capital employed | 2,900 | 3,300

--- APPENDIX 3 — EXTERNAL ENVIRONMENT ---

(2) The national minimum wage will rise by 6.0% from $13.49 to $14.30 an hour from April 2026. (3) Brass and stainless-steel input costs have risen 10.5% year-on-year, energy price inflation is 7.2%, and European industrial production expanded 2.1% over the same period.

    Answer: Point 1: A share issue brings in $700,000 of permanent capital with no interest charges or compulsory repayments, so PVF does not add debt service to its $360,000 a year fixed costs while it equips the $1,100,000 testing facility. That protects the $8.00 contribution on each of 90,000 valves and leaves the $400,000 retained profit free for working capital as utility clients demand more reliable deliveries.

Point 2: Because PVF is a public limited company, a share issue can raise a large sum from many investors and spread the risk of the new facility beyond Jonas Portview's existing shareholders. Unlike borrowing, there is no collateral to pledge and no lender covenants, giving management freedom to set testing standards and respond to the 2.8% defect rate, while the 66% of surveyed buyers willing to pay $0.80 more for certified valves offer a return that can justify the new investment.

Shareholders also expect a return through dividends or rising value, so PVF must earn that $8.00 contribution on enough of its 90,000 units to keep the share price stable.

The concern is trade receivables rising from $240,000 to $265,000; if utility clients pay slowly, the stronger position could weaken, and lower inventories of $180,000 may need watching given 6.2-day lead times.

Conclusion: PVF's financial position has improved. Both the 2024–2025 measures (1.49 to 1.64 and 0.89 to 1.09) rose and the gain does not rely on stock. The residual risk is higher receivables, so tighter credit control should accompany the new investment.

With $540,000 of current assets against $330,000 of current liabilities, PVF has enough headroom to absorb a short dip in utility receipts while the testing facility is commissioned.

Minimum wage increase (6.0%, to $14.30 an hour): PVF employs 60 workers and the rise lifts its wage bill, but the insert gives no hours worked or pay rates, so a total cannot be calculated honestly. --- MAIN STEM ---
Solstice Battery Systems (SBS) is a private limited company in the rechargeable battery manufacturing sector, employing a workforce of 50. Founded in 2014 by Priya Solstice, it builds lithium-ion battery packs for forklifts and grid-storage units and operates a hierarchical structure with democratic leadership. It has fixed costs of $320,000 a year, a variable cost of $10.00 a unit and a selling price of $18.00, and currently produces 80,000 units a year. A survey of 410 industrial buyers found 63% would pay up to $0.70 more for recyclable battery packs and 49% check environmental credentials before ordering. Records show 13 of 50 assembly staff have not completed on-the-job training on the welding rigs; recycling-technician courses cost $860 per employee.

That protects the $8.00 contribution on 80,000 battery packs while the 3.1% welding defect rate is being reduced.

That matters because the 3.1% welding defect rate on 18,400 packs a quarter already wastes materials, and debt service would reduce the cash available for recycling-technician courses at $860 each.

--- MAIN STEM ---
Nordic Precision Bearings (NPB) is a worker cooperative in the precision engineering sector, employing a workforce of 48. Founded in 2007 by Anders Nord, it manufactures sealed ball bearings for wind turbines and machine tools and operates a hierarchical structure with laissez-faire leadership. NPB plans to invest $880,000 in a robotic bearing-grinding line, financed by a $480,000 bank loan and $400,000 of member share capital. It has fixed costs of $288,000 a year, a variable cost of $6.00 a unit and a selling price of $12.00, and currently produces 96,000 units a year. NPB faces two operational problems: a defect rate of 2.6% in grinding and rising waste of steel alloy, with delivery times lengthening.

--- APPENDIX 1 — MARKETING/OPS ---
Operations and Quality Log — Q3 2025: The grinding line finished 23,200 bearings last quarter at a defect rate of 2.6%, down from 3.9% a year earlier. Alloy waste fell from 41 to 28 tonnes a month, while average delivery time stretched from 3.4 to 5.1 days. A survey of 470 equipment buyers found 59% would pay up to $0.45 more for sealed long-life bearings and 51% check supplier reliability before ordering. Records show 11 of 48 members have not completed on-the-job training on the grinding robots; robotics courses cost $710 per employee.

--- APPENDIX 2 — FINANCIAL DATA ---
Title: Extract from the Statement of Financial Position of Nordic Precision Bearings as at 31 March 2025 ($ '000)
Headers: ['Financial Metric', '2024', '2025']
Inventories | 130 | 180
Trade receivables | 170 | 180
Cash and cash equivalents | 60 | 45
Current liabilities | 220 | 250
Non-current assets | 1,700 | 2,000
Capital employed | 1,850 | 2,150

--- APPENDIX 3 — EXTERNAL ENVIRONMENT ---
Economic and Business Bulletin (November 2026): (1) The central bank has raised the base interest rate from 4.1% to 4.9%, increasing borrowing costs. (2) The national minimum wage will rise by 5.2% from $13.10 to $13.78 an hour from April 2026. (3) Bearing-steel and alloy input costs have risen 8.7% year-on-year, freight and energy inflation is 4.9%, while wind-turbine component demand grew 3.6% over the same period.

--- QUESTIONS ---
  Q1(a) [8 marks]
    Question: NPB plans to raise $480,000 through a bank loan for its $880,000 grinding line. Explain two disadvantages for NPB of using a bank loan rather than member share capital.
    Answer: Point 1: A bank loan requires interest and capital repayments, so at a base rate raised to 4.9% the $480,000 borrowing adds a fixed financial burden on top of $288,000 a year operating costs. That drains cash which could otherwise cover the $6.00 contribution on 96,000 bearings and fund on-the-job training for the 11 of 48 members still learning the grinding robots.

Point 2: Lenders commonly require collateral and impose conditions, which can reduce the autonomy of a worker cooperative and put its assets at risk if the 2.6% defect rate delays returns from the $880,000 line. Member share capital of $400,000 carries no such fixed claim and keeps decision-making inside the cooperative, whereas a lender may restrict further borrowing or demand priority repayment, limiting NPB's flexibility on quality investment and the $710 robotics courses.

Interest on the $480,000 loan would also compete with the $710 robotics courses needed for the 11 of 48 members still in training, so member share capital, despite diluting ownership, better fits a cooperative's long-term aims.
    Keywords: bank loan, $480,000, $880,000, member share capital, $288,000, $400,000, worker cooperative
    Mark scheme: knowledge_max_2: 1 mark for each valid disadvantage of a bank loan (max 2).; 1 mark for each valid disadvantage of a bank loan (max 2). | application_analysis_max_6: Up to 3 marks per point for contextual explanation applied to NPB's interest cost, training and contribution.; Up to 3 marks per point for contextual explanation applied to NPB's collateral, control and cooperative status.

    Question: NPB is promoting its new sealed long-life bearings. Consider advertising in engineering trade journals, sponsoring a wind-energy exhibition, or e-commerce and digital marketing. Which should NPB choose? Justify your recommendation.

Yet circulation is narrow, insertions must be repeated, and print cannot demonstrate the reliability checked by 51% of buyers, so returns are weak for a 48-member cooperative funding an $880,000 line.

    Question: NPB's 2.6% defect rate and lengthening delivery times are a concern. Explain two benefits for NPB of introducing job rotation in its grinding team.

  Q2(b) [12 marks]
    Question: NPB must improve quality on its new grinding robots. Consider quality control inspection or quality assurance. Which should NPB choose? Justify your decision.
    Answer: Quality control inspection: Checking finished bearings at the end of the line can catch the 2.6% defect rate before they reach wind-turbine clients and is simple to introduce with the 23,200 bearings made last quarter. However, inspection finds faults only after alloy and labour have been used, so the 41 tonnes of waste a month continue, and it does not prevent the 5.1-day delivery delays caused by rework.

Quality assurance: Building quality into each grinding stage through prevention, worker involvement and the $710 robotics courses for the 11 of 48 members still training addresses the cause of defects and cuts waste from 41 to 28 tonnes. It suits a worker cooperative where members can own quality, but it takes longer to embed and needs on-the-job training before results appear.

Decision: NPB should choose quality assurance as its main approach. Prevention removes the root cause of the 2.6% defect rate and reduces waste, protecting the $6.00 contribution on 96,000 units. Pure inspection is rejected because it detects but does not stop defects and leaves rework delaying the 5.1-day deliveries; NPB should keep limited final sampling as a safety net while prevention becomes established.

NPB should begin with a small pilot on the grinding robots, recording defect counts on the 23,200 bearings before and after prevention measures, and use the $710 courses for the 11 of 48 members still training. Members should be rewarded for suggesting improvements, which fits the cooperative tradition and keeps waste falling from 41 to 28 tonnes. Only once defects are sustainably lower should routine final inspection be reduced, otherwise the 5.1-day delivery record could suffer and the $6.00 contribution on 96,000 units be put at risk.
    Keywords: 2.6%, 41, 28, $710, 23,200, on-the-job training
    Mark scheme: level_1_1_to_4: Describes quality control and quality assurance with limited application to NPB. | level_2_5_to_8: Analyses benefits and drawbacks of one or both approaches in the context of NPB. | level_3_9_to_12: Evaluates both approaches in the context of NPB and makes a justified decision that rejects pure inspection, covering waste, prevention and training.

  Q3(a) [8 marks]

  Q3(b) [12 marks]
    Question: Using Appendix 2, evaluate NPB's financial position by calculating the current ratio and the acid test ratio for 2024 and 2025. Has NPB's financial position improved? Justify your answer.
    Answer: Calculations:
Current Ratio 2024 = 1.64 : 1
Current Ratio 2025 = 1.62 : 1
Acid Test Ratio 2024 = 1.05 : 1
Acid Test Ratio 2025 = 0.90 : 1

Detailed workings: In 2024 current assets were $130,000 inventories + $170,000 trade receivables + $60,000 cash = $360,000, and $360,000 ÷ $220,000 current liabilities gives the 2024 measure. In 2025 the corresponding assets were $180,000 + $180,000 + $45,000 = $405,000, and $405,000 ÷ $250,000 gives the 2025 measure. NPB should run down excess inventory and tighten credit control before adding to its borrowing.

With $480,000 of bank-loan commitments, NPB should prioritise rebuilding its cash balance before further borrowing, because the current position leaves little room for a delay in receiving the $180,000 owed by customers.

    Question: Using Appendix 3, evaluate how the rise in the base interest rate to 4.9%, the 5.2% minimum wage increase and the 8.7% rise in bearing-steel input costs will affect NPB. Which change will have the greatest impact? Justify your answer.
    Answer: Interest rate rise (4.1% to 4.9%): NPB has a $480,000 bank loan, but the insert does not state whether it is variable-rate, so any direct figure is only an illustrative bound: a full 0.8 percentage-point rise on $480,000 is 0.008 × $480,000 = $3,840 a year. That is modest next to $288,000 fixed costs, and if the loan is fixed the effect is zero; higher rates may still slow wind-turbine investment.

Minimum wage increase (5.2%, to $13.78 an hour): The cooperative employs 48 members and the rise lifts wage costs, but the insert gives no hours worked or pay rates, so an annual total cannot be invented. The defensible test is productivity: 96,000 units ÷ 48 members = 2,000 units per worker. A higher wage is affordable only if productivity holds; otherwise unit labour cost erodes the $6.00 contribution.

Bearing-steel cost inflation (8.7%): The $6.00 variable cost is not decomposed, so only a bound is possible — if the whole variable cost rose 8.7% it would add 0.087 × $6.00 = $0.522 a unit, or 96,000 × $0.522 = $50,112 a year. Even a partial rise raises the 48,000-unit break-even, though the $0.45 premium accepted by 59% of buyers offers some recovery.

Conclusion: The 8.7% rise in bearing-steel costs will have the greatest impact. It applies to all 96,000 units and directly erodes the $6.00 contribution needed to service the $880,000 grinding line. The interest effect is at most a bounded $3,840 and the wage effect depends on productivity, so neither matches the reach of material inflation.

--- MAIN STEM ---
Zephyr Quay Fashion (ZQF) is a private limited company in the online fashion retail sector, employing a workforce of 40. Founded in 2013 by Nadia Zephyr, the business sells apparel through its own e-commerce site and operates a flat organisational structure with democratic leadership. ZQF plans to invest $720,000 in an automated e-commerce fulfilment and returns-processing centre, financed by a $420,000 ten-year bank loan and $300,000 retained profit. It has fixed costs of $216,000 a year, a variable cost of $8.20 a unit and a selling price of $15.20, and produces 72,000 units a year. ZQF faces two problems: its online return rate has climbed to 18% and picking errors are rising, while late deliveries are damaging customer ratings.

--- APPENDIX 1 — MARKETING/OPS ---
E-commerce Operations Extract — Q4 2025: The online store fulfilled 18,400 orders last quarter, with a picking error rate of 2.1% and an online return rate of 18%, up from 13% a year earlier. Average delivery time is 3.8 days. Customer complaints rose from 46 to 71 per month. Market research of 500 online shoppers found that 68% value fast delivery and 57% would pay more for free returns. Returns-processing training for the 40 staff costs $650 per employee.

--- APPENDIX 2 — FINANCIAL DATA ---
Title: Extract from the Statement of Financial Position of Zephyr Quay Fashion as at 31 March 2025 ($ '000)

Trade receivables | 140 | 165
Cash and cash equivalents | 55 | 48
Current liabilities | 200 | 210
Non-current assets | 900 | 1,150
Capital employed | 1,400 | 1,650

--- APPENDIX 3 — EXTERNAL ENVIRONMENT ---
Economic and Business Bulletin (November 2026): (1) The central bank has raised the base interest rate from 4.25% to 5.0%, increasing borrowing costs for firms with variable-rate loans. (2) The national minimum wage will rise by 5.8% from $12.40 to $13.10 per hour from April 2026, raising total wage bills. (3) Wholesale fabric and freight input costs have risen 9.6% year-on-year, while consumer spending on online fashion grew 2.4% over the same period.

  Q1(a) [8 marks]
    Question: ZQF plans to fund part of its $720,000 fulfilment-centre expansion with a $420,000 ten-year bank loan. Explain two advantages for ZQF of using its $300,000 retained profit instead of that loan.
    Answer: Point 1: Using the $300,000 retained profit costs ZQF no interest or capital repayments, so its cash flow is protected while it already carries $216,000 of fixed costs and an 18% return rate that ties up working capital. Every dollar not paid as loan interest stays inside the business to fund the picking-accuracy fixes needed after the 2.1% picking error rate and the rise in complaints from 46 to 71 a month. That protects the $7.00 contribution per unit earned on 72,000 units sold at $15.20 each, which is the cash the $720,000 expansion depends on.

Point 2: Retained profit carries no collateral or repossession risk. If the new automated returns-processing centre fails to cut the 18% return rate, a lender could still demand repayment of the $420,000 bank loan, putting the jobs of the 40 staff and Nadia Zephyr's control at risk. Internal funding imposes no lender conditions and leaves the loan facility untouched as a reserve for a sudden spike in returns or the late-delivery problem. It also signals to staff that growth is being paid for out of trading success rather than debt, which supports morale in a flat structure where democratic leadership relies on trust.
    Keywords: retained profit, $720,000, $420,000, $300,000, 18%, $216,000

  Q1(b) [12 marks]
    Question: ZQF is launching a faster-delivery service for its online fashion range. Consider national television advertising, paid search advertising, or social media influencer marketing. Which should ZQF choose to promote the launch? Justify your recommendation.
    Answer: National television advertising: A TV campaign would build mass awareness of the faster-delivery promise across the whole country, which could help ZQF win shoppers beyond its current customer base. However, airtime and production are extremely expensive for a 40-person e-commerce business already funding a $720,000 expansion with a $420,000 loan, and much of the audience does not buy online fashion. Given that market research of 500 shoppers found 68% value fast delivery, a broad TV message would waste spend on the 32% who do not, and it cannot demonstrate the 3.8-day delivery claim credibly.

Paid search advertising: Buying search terms such as 'next-day fashion delivery' reaches shoppers at the moment they are ready to buy, and spend can be capped and measured against orders. It directly targets the 68% who value fast delivery and can be switched off if the 18% return rate makes sales unprofitable. Its weakness is that it only reaches people already searching, so it does little to build the brand or explain why ZQF's delivery is better, and competition for popular terms can push the cost per click up sharply.

Social media influencer marketing: Fashion influencers can demonstrate the faster-delivery service and the new apparel range to a targeted audience, generating engagement and trust that a search advert cannot. It speaks directly to the 57% of surveyed shoppers who would pay more for better service, and it can show real parcels arriving in 3.8 days. The drawback is slower, less predictable volume and a dependence on influencer credibility, but cost per reached shopper is low and content can be reused across the site.

Recommendation: ZQF should choose paid search advertising as the primary launch channel, supported by a small influencer campaign. Search captures buyers at the point of purchase and is measurable against the 2.1% picking-error and return concerns; influencers supplement it with proof. Television is rejected as unaffordable and untargeted for a firm with $216,000 fixed costs and a $420,000 loan, and pure influencer marketing is rejected because its results are too slow to fill the new fulfilment centre.

Because the people handling the orders know where the 2.1% picking errors occur, their suggestions can be more practical than top-down rules, and involvement raises job satisfaction and commitment under Maslow's social and esteem needs. Higher engagement should reduce the mistakes that feed the 18% return rate and help cut the 71 monthly complaints, protecting the $15.20 selling price and the $7.00 contribution per unit.

That steadier attendance protects output of 72,000 units a year and makes the $650 per employee training spend more effective, since motivated workers apply what they learn.   Q2(b) [12 marks]
    Question: ZQF must improve picking accuracy among its 40 staff. Consider on-the-job training or off-the-job training at a local college. Which should ZQF choose? Justify your decision.

Decision: ZQF should choose on-the-job training for all 40 staff, with short college top-ups for the senior pickers. It is machine-and-process specific, avoids losing output at a time when complaints have risen from 46 to 71 a month, and spends nothing on the $650 fee. Full off-the-job training is rejected because withdrawing the whole team would endanger 72,000-unit output and the delivery promise, and the $26,000 fee is better reserved for the automated centre; the certificate gap can be closed later by sending a few supervisors to college.

--- MAIN STEM ---
Kestrel Bay Outfitters (KBO) is a public limited company in the outdoor clothing retail and e-commerce sector, employing a workforce of 48. Operations and Quality Report, Q3 2025: KBO's distribution centre packed 17,500 orders last quarter with a picking error rate of 3.2%, down from 5.0% last year. Market research of 520 shoppers found 63% would pay up to $2.00 more for responsibly sourced materials, and 49% compare delivery speeds before ordering. (2) The national minimum wage rises by 4.9% from $13.80 to $14.48 an hour from April 2026. (3) Wholesale textile and freight input costs have risen 11.2% year on year, while consumer spending on outdoor clothing grew 3.1%.

--- QUESTIONS ---
  Q1(a) [8 marks]
    Question: KBO plans to fund part of its warehouse expansion with a ten-year bank loan. Explain two advantages for KBO of using a share issue to finance the expansion instead of the bank loan.
    Answer: Point 1: A share issue raises $300,000 of equity that never has to be repaid and carries no compulsory interest, unlike the $600,000 bank loan. With fixed costs of $324,000 a year and an 11.2% rise in textile and freight costs, avoiding debt service protects KBO's cash flow and leaves more of the $30 selling price available to absorb cost increases.

Point 2: Equity does not require collateral, so the $900,000 automated distribution warehouse is not at risk of repossession if sales disappoint. It also strengthens the balance sheet ahead of future borrowing, which matters for a public limited company answerable to shareholders. The 63% of 520 surveyed shoppers who would pay $2.00 more for responsible materials give a growth opportunity that can be pursued without the lender conditions attached to a bank loan.
    Keywords: share issue, bank loan, $300,000, $600,000, $324,000, $900,000
    Mark scheme: knowledge_max_2: 1 mark for each valid advantage of a share issue identified (max 2). | application_analysis_max_6: Up to 3 marks per point for contextual explanation applied to KBO's costs, expansion finance and market evidence.

  Q1(b) [12 marks]
    Question: KBO is launching a new responsibly sourced outdoor jacket range. Consider a national television campaign, search-engine advertising, or outdoor influencer marketing. Which should KBO choose to promote the launch? Justify your recommendation.
    Answer: Television campaign: A national TV advert could quickly build awareness of KBO's waterproof jackets across all six countries and support its high-street stores. However, airtime and production are very costly for a business already funding a $900,000 warehouse, and the mass audience includes many non-buyers, so spend would be poorly targeted.

Search-engine advertising: Paid search reaches buyers at the moment they look for hiking gear, is measurable and can be capped to a budget, protecting cash flow alongside the $600,000 loan. Its limitation is that it captures only existing demand and does little to build the responsible-sourcing message that 63% of 520 shoppers value, while clicks in competitive outdoor categories are costly.

Outdoor influencer marketing: Walking and climbing influencers can demonstrate the jackets in real conditions and explain responsible sourcing to an audience that already buys outdoor clothing, matching the 49% of shoppers who compare delivery speeds and care about purchase details. Credibility is high and spend is targeted, although results depend on the influencer's reputation and may build slowly.

Recommendation: KBO should choose outdoor influencer marketing with a small search budget. It demonstrates product performance, reaches the specific outdoor segment and supports the $2.00 responsible-sourcing premium. Television is rejected as too expensive and untargeted; search alone is rejected because it cannot create the brand pull needed for a new jacket range.
    Keywords: 63%, 520, $2.00, website, 49%, $900,000
    Mark scheme: level_1_1_to_4: Limited description of promotional methods with minimal reference to KBO. | level_2_5_to_8: Discussion of advantages and disadvantages of at least two methods applied to KBO's retail and online business. | level_3_9_to_12: Detailed evaluation of all three methods with a justified recommendation that rejects television and explains the limits of search advertising.

  Q2(a) [8 marks]
    Question: KBO's absenteeism is rising and warehouse picking errors have increased. Explain two benefits for KBO of using autocratic leadership to improve performance in its distribution centre.

    Answer: Calculations:

Current Ratio 2025 = 1.80 : 1
Acid Test Ratio 2024 = 0.87 : 1
Acid Test Ratio 2025 = 0.85 : 1

For 2024, $366,000 ÷ $180,000 = 2.03; for 2025, $352,000 ÷ $196,000 = 1.80. Excluding stock: 2024 ($366,000 − $210,000) ÷ $180,000 = $156,000 ÷ $180,000 = 0.87; 2025 ($352,000 − $186,000) ÷ $196,000 = $166,000 ÷ $196,000 = 0.85.

Cash fell from $62,000 to $48,000 and inventories from $210,000 to $186,000; receivables rose to $118,000, tying up cash. The buffer at 1.80 is still adequate, so the position is not critical.

Conclusion: KBO's financial position has not improved. Both measures fell and the stock-excluding measure also weakened, so the decline is not explained by inventory alone. KBO should tighten credit control over the higher receivables and rebuild cash before drawing further on debt.

    Question: Using Appendix 3, evaluate how the interest rate rise to 4.8%, the 4.9% minimum wage increase and the 11.2% rise in textile and freight costs will affect KBO. Which change will have the greatest impact? Justify your answer.
    Answer: Interest rate rise (4.0% to 4.8%): If KBO's $600,000 ten-year bank loan is variable-rate, the annual interest cost rises by 0.8% of $600,000 = $4,800 a year (0.008 × $600,000). This is small relative to fixed costs of $324,000, and if the loan is fixed-rate the direct effect is zero. Higher rates could dampen outdoor-clothing spending and raise future borrowing costs, but the risk is manageable and can be hedged by fixing the rate.

Minimum wage increase (4.9%, to $14.48 an hour): With a workforce of 48, higher hourly pay raises KBO's wage bill and cannot be avoided. The insert gives no hours worked or individual wages, so an annual total cannot be invented; the defensible benchmark is productivity of 70,000 ÷ 48 = 1,458.3 units per worker. If productivity holds, the rise is absorbable; if it falls, the $12.00 contribution per unit is eroded.

Textile and freight inflation (11.2%): The $18 variable cost per unit is exposed, but the insert does not decompose it, so only an illustrative bound is honest: if the whole variable cost rose 11.2%, that adds 11.2% × $18 = $2.02 per unit, about $141,000 a year at 70,000 units. The $2.00 premium 63% of shoppers accept can offset part of this.

Conclusion: The 11.2% rise in textile and freight costs has the greatest impact. It applies to every unit sold, directly threatens the $12.00 contribution that supports the $900,000 expansion, and is only partly recovered through pricing; the interest effect is modest and the wage effect turns on unstated hours.

--- MAIN STEM ---
Quay Street Marketplace (QSM) is a private limited company in the online retail and e-commerce sector, employing a workforce of 26. Founded in 2016 by Nadia Quay, the platform sells its own craft giftware range through a website and mobile app alongside independent sellers and runs a flat structure with laissez-faire leadership. QSM plans to invest $520,000 in an automated stock-control and dispatch system, financed by a $320,000 five-year bank loan and $200,000 retained profit. It has fixed costs of $150,000 a year, a variable cost of $9 a unit and a selling price of $17, and currently produces 55,000 units a year. QSM faces two problems: staff turnover is rising and dispatch errors have increased.

--- APPENDIX 1 — MARKETING/OPS ---
Market Research and Operations Summary, Q3 2025: QSM processed 13,200 orders last quarter with a dispatch error rate of 1.9%, down from 3.6% last year. Complaints about late delivery fell from 47 to 22 per month. Average order dispatch time is 2.8 days. A survey of 380 marketplace buyers found 71% value fast delivery most, and 46% would pay up to $0.90 more for carbon-neutral shipping. Records show 9 of 26 staff have not completed on-the-job training on the new stock-control system; off-the-job training courses at the local college cost $680 per employee.

--- APPENDIX 2 — FINANCIAL DATA ---

Headers: ['Financial Metric', '2024', '2025']

(2) The national minimum wage rises by 6.1% from $13.10 to $13.90 an hour from April 2026. (3) Packaging and shipping input costs have risen 8.7% year on year, while online marketplace spending grew 5.4%.

Cash saved can absorb the 8.7% rise in packaging and shipping costs without raising the $17 selling price for the 71% of surveyed buyers who value fast delivery.

Point 2: Using $200,000 retained profit avoids the collateral and covenants of a bank loan, so the $520,000 stock-control and dispatch system is not endangered if sales fall short. It also preserves Nadia Quay's control of the platform instead of handing influence to lenders, letting QSM respond quickly to the 46% of buyers who would pay $0.90 more for carbon-neutral shipping. Faster decisions suit a small 26-employee e-commerce firm.

--- MAIN STEM ---
Juniper Row Collective (JRC) is a cooperative in the ethical fashion retail sector, employing a workforce of 36. Founded in 2011 by Iris Juniper, the business sells fair-trade clothing through a chain of boutiques across five cities and an online shop, and operates a hierarchical structure with democratic leadership. JRC plans to invest $760,000 in a new central distribution hub, financed by a $460,000 ten-year bank loan and $300,000 from the sale of assets. It has fixed costs of $266,000 a year, a variable cost of $20 a unit and a selling price of $34, and currently produces 48,000 units a year. JRC faces two problems: labour turnover is rising and garment return rates have increased.

--- APPENDIX 1 — MARKETING/OPS ---
Quality and Marketing Report, Q3 2025: JRC's boutiques and online shop sold 11,400 garments last quarter with a returns rate of 4.3%, down from 6.2% last year. Customer complaints fell from 33 to 19 per month. Average stock replenishment time is 6.4 days. A survey of 410 shoppers found 66% would pay up to $2.50 more for ethically made clothing, and 58% check labour practices before buying. Records show 11 of 36 staff still need induction on the new stock-control tablets; off-the-job training courses at the local college cost $820 per employee, while on-the-job training is provided in each boutique.

--- APPENDIX 2 — FINANCIAL DATA ---
Title: Extract from the Statement of Financial Position of Juniper Row Collective as at 31 March 2025 ($ '000)
Headers: ['Financial Metric', '2024', '2025']
Inventories | 132 | 118
Trade receivables | 40 | 52
Cash and cash equivalents | 28 | 44
Current liabilities | 112 | 106
Non-current assets | 1,340 | 1,690
Capital employed | 1,620 | 1,940

--- APPENDIX 3 — EXTERNAL ENVIRONMENT ---
Economic and Business Bulletin (November 2026): (1) The central bank raised the base interest rate from 4.5% to 5.25%, raising borrowing costs on variable-rate loans. (2) The national minimum wage rises by 5.8% from $13.40 to $14.18 an hour from April 2026. (3) Wholesale fabric and import costs have risen 10.4% year on year, while spending on ethical fashion grew 4.2%.

--- QUESTIONS ---
  Q1(a) [8 marks]
    Question: JRC plans to fund part of its distribution hub with a ten-year bank loan. Explain two advantages for JRC of using the sale of assets to finance the expansion instead of the bank loan.
    Answer: Point 1: Selling assets raises $300,000 immediately without interest or repayment, so JRC avoids adding debt to the $460,000 bank loan already planned. With fixed costs of $266,000 a year and fabric and import costs up 10.4%, preserving cash protects the $34 selling price and the 66% of surveyed shoppers who value ethical clothing.

Point 2: The sale of assets does not dilute the cooperative's ownership or give lenders control, so Iris Juniper and the members keep decision-making over the $760,000 hub. Freeing cash tied up in unused assets also improves liquidity, which matters given the 58% of 410 shoppers who check labour practices before buying and expect JRC to honour its ethical claims.
    Keywords: sale of assets, bank loan, $300,000, $460,000, $266,000, $760,000
    Mark scheme: knowledge_max_2: 1 mark for each valid advantage of the sale of assets identified (max 2). | application_analysis_max_6: Up to 3 marks per point for contextual explanation applied to JRC's costs, finance and survey evidence.

  Q1(b) [12 marks]
    Question: JRC is launching a new ethically made clothing range online. Consider a national television campaign, search-engine advertising, or fashion influencer marketing. Which should JRC choose to promote the launch? Justify your recommendation.
    Answer: Television campaign: A national TV advert could raise awareness of JRC's ethical range across all five cities and beyond, but airtime is very expensive for a 36-employee cooperative funding a $760,000 hub. Much of the mass audience would not buy fair-trade clothing online, so the spend would be poorly targeted.

Search-engine advertising: Paid search reaches shoppers looking for ethical fashion and can be capped to a budget, protecting cash alongside the $460,000 loan. Its weakness is that it captures only existing demand and cannot tell the labour-practices story that 58% of 410 shoppers check, while clicks in fashion categories are costly.

Fashion influencer marketing: Ethical-fashion influencers can demonstrate the garments and explain the fair-trade credentials to an audience that already cares, matching the 66% of shoppers who would pay $2.50 more. Current Ratio 2025 = 2.02 : 1
Acid Test Ratio 2024 = 0.61 : 1

    Question: Using Appendix 3, evaluate how the interest rate rise to 5.25%, the 5.8% minimum wage increase and the 10.4% rise in fabric and import costs will affect JRC. Which change will have the greatest impact? Justify your answer.
    Answer: Interest rate rise (4.5% to 5.25%): If JRC's $460,000 ten-year bank loan is variable-rate, the annual interest cost rises by 0.75% of $460,000 = $3,450 a year (0.0075 × $460,000). Minimum wage increase (5.8%, to $14.18 an hour): With a workforce of 36, higher hourly pay increases JRC's wage bill and cannot be avoided. The insert states no hours worked or individual wages, so an annual total cannot be invented; the defensible benchmark is productivity of 48,000 ÷ 36 = 1,333.3 units per worker. If productivity holds, the rise is absorbable; if it falls, the $14.00 contribution per unit is eroded.

Fabric and import inflation (10.4%): The $20 variable cost per unit is exposed, but the insert does not decompose it, so only an illustrative bound is honest: if the whole variable cost rose 10.4%, that adds 10.4% × $20 = $2.08 per unit, about $99,800 a year at 48,000 units. The $2.50 premium 66% of shoppers accept can recover part of this.

Conclusion: The 10.4% rise in fabric and import costs has the greatest impact. It applies to every garment, directly threatens the $14.00 contribution that justifies the $760,000 hub, and is only partly offset by higher prices; the interest effect is modest and the wage effect depends on hours not given in the insert.

--- MAIN STEM ---
Xanadu Parcel Company (XPC) is a public limited company in the online gift retailing and e-commerce fulfilment sector, employing a workforce of 40. XPC plans to invest $810,000 in a new automated gift-wrapping and dispatch line, financed by a $510,000 ten-year bank loan and a $300,000 share issue. It has fixed costs of $216,000 a year, a variable cost of $12 a unit and a selling price of $21, and currently produces 66,000 units a year. XPC faces two problems: absenteeism is rising and gift-wrapping quality complaints have increased.

--- APPENDIX 1 — MARKETING/OPS ---
Operations and Marketing Report, Q3 2025: XPC packed 16,800 gift orders last quarter with a packing error rate of 2.7%, down from 4.4% last year. Customer complaints fell from 44 to 26 per month. Average dispatch time is 3.6 days. A survey of 500 online gift buyers found 62% would pay up to $1.20 more for recyclable packaging, and 55% check delivery speed before ordering. Records show 13 of 40 staff still need on-the-job training on the new wrapping line; off-the-job training courses at the local college cost $720 per employee.

--- APPENDIX 2 — FINANCIAL DATA ---

Point 2: Equity requires no collateral, so the $810,000 wrapping and dispatch line is not at risk of repossession if gift demand falls. It also strengthens the balance sheet of a public limited company answerable to shareholders before further borrowing. The 62% of 500 buyers who would pay $1.20 more for recyclable packaging give a growth chance that can be pursued without lender conditions.

--- MAIN STEM ---
Harbour Leisure Tours (HLT) is a private limited company in the tourism and leisure sector, operating whale-watching and harbour cruises from a coastal marina and employing a workforce of 38. Founded in 2011 by Sofia Marais, HLT runs a flat organisational structure with democratic leadership, so skippers and crew help shape sailing schedules. It plans to invest $420,000 in a new catamaran and an online booking platform, financed by a $250,000 ten-year bank loan and $170,000 retained profit. HLT has fixed costs of $180,000 a year, a variable cost of $16.00 a unit and a selling price of $28.00, and currently produces 22,000 units a year, each unit being one passenger cruise. Recently labour turnover has reached 14% and complaints about boarding delays have grown, threatening the reputation Sofia built.

--- APPENDIX 1 — MARKETING/OPS ---
Customer and Operations Extract — Q3 2025: HLT sold 5,600 cruise tickets last quarter at an average price of $28.00, with 94% of departures running on time. Boarding complaints fell from 46 to 19 per month after a new queue system. Safety checks found 2.1% of life jackets failing inspection, down from 3.4% a year earlier. A survey of 500 tourists found 68% would book again if online booking were offered and 57% chose HLT for its eco-credentials. Retraining each crew member in customer care costs $480 at the local maritime college.

--- APPENDIX 2 — FINANCIAL DATA ---
Title: Extract from the Statement of Financial Position of Harbour Leisure Tours as at 31 March 2025 ($ '000)
Headers: ['Financial Metric', '2024', '2025']
Inventories | 60 | 50
Trade receivables | 90 | 110
Cash and cash equivalents | 30 | 55
Current liabilities | 120 | 110
Non-current assets | 900 | 1,150
Capital employed | 1,300 | 1,500

--- APPENDIX 3 — EXTERNAL ENVIRONMENT ---
Economic and Tourism Bulletin (November 2026): (1) The central bank raised the base interest rate from 4.25% to 5.0%, increasing borrowing costs for HLT's $250,000 variable-rate loan. (2) The national minimum wage will rise by 5.8% from $13.00 to $13.75 per hour from April 2026, raising the crew wage bill. (3) Marine fuel and insurance input costs have risen 9.6% year-on-year while tourism inflation is 6.3%, and inbound visitor arrivals grew 4.2%.

--- QUESTIONS ---
  Q1(a) [8 marks]
    Question: HLT plans to fund part of its new catamaran with a ten-year bank loan. Explain two advantages for HLT of using retained profit instead of the bank loan.
    Answer: Point 1: Using the $170,000 of retained profit costs HLT no interest or capital repayments, which protects cash flow while the company already carries fixed costs of $180,000 a year and a $250,000 bank loan. Every dollar not paid as interest can be spent on crew training at $480 per person to tackle the 14% labour turnover, or on marketing the $28.00 cruises, keeping more of the $12.00 earned on each passenger unit.

Point 2: Retained profit avoids the collateral and repossession risk of a bank loan, so the $420,000 catamaran and booking platform cannot be seized if visitor numbers disappoint. Sofia Marais also keeps full ownership and control of the flat structure and democratic leadership she built, because no lender can impose conditions on sailing schedules or on how the new online platform is run. With 38 staff depending on the business, avoiding extra debt commitments makes the expansion safer and steadier. Even allowing for the roughly $1,875 a year that the 0.75-point rise to 5.0% would add on a variable-rate $250,000 loan, the retained-profit route keeps more of the $12.00 contribution inside HLT to reinvest in the 22,000-unit cruise operation and in the $480 crew retraining that should ease the 14% turnover.
    Keywords: retained profit, $250,000, $170,000, $420,000, $180,000, workforce of 38
    Mark scheme: knowledge_max_2: 1 mark for each valid advantage identified (max 2). | application_analysis_max_6: Up to 3 marks per point for contextual explanation and analysis applied to HLT, its loan, its retained profit and its tourism operations.

  Q1(b) [12 marks]
    Question: HLT is promoting its new cruise schedule. Consider national television advertising, local radio sponsorship, or social media influencer marketing. Which should HLT choose to promote the launch? Justify your recommendation.
    Answer: National television advertising: A national TV campaign would build awareness of whale-watching cruises quickly across the whole country and could attract tourists who have never heard of HLT. However, airtime and production are extremely expensive for a private limited company with only 38 staff and a $420,000 expansion already funded by debt, and much of the audience lives far from the coastal marina and cannot book a $28.00 trip, so spend wastage would be high.

Local radio sponsorship: Local radio is much cheaper and reaches precisely the coastal catchment and day-trippers who can visit the marina, and it suits urgent messages about the new catamaran schedule. Its weakness is narrow reach: the survey of 500 tourists showed demand from visitors beyond the immediate area, and radio cannot reach them, limiting ticket sales growth.

Social media influencer marketing: Travel and lifestyle influencers can target the 68% of surveyed tourists who said they would rebook with online booking and the 57% drawn by eco-credentials, with measurable engagement at low cost and national reach. Results build more slowly than television, but the content can showcase the whale-watching experience directly.

Recommendation: HLT should choose social media influencer marketing. It reaches the exact segments in the research, costs far less than television and reaches further than local radio, and it drives the online booking platform. Television is rejected as unaffordable and wasteful; radio is rejected as too local; influencers are the best fit for a 38-staff operator. Reinvesting the marketing saving in the $480 crew training would also help cut the 14% turnover that forces repeated recruitment, so the campaign and the training budget can be planned together. Low-cost digital promotion leaves more cash to honour the eco-credentials that 57% of tourists value.
    Keywords: $420,000, 68%, 57%, 500, whale-watching, $28.00

  Q2(a) [8 marks]

--- MAIN STEM ---
Trek River Voyages (TRV) is a partnership in the tourism and leisure sector, running white-water rafting and river expedition holidays from a mountain basecamp and employing a workforce of 46. Founded in 2014 by Aisha Bhatt, TRV operates a hierarchical structure with autocratic leadership so safety decisions are made quickly by experienced leaders. It plans to invest $560,000 in a new riverside basecamp and certified safety equipment, financed by a $300,000 five-year bank loan and $260,000 retained profit. TRV has fixed costs of $210,000 a year, a variable cost of $25.00 a unit and a selling price of $40.00, and currently produces 24,000 units a year, each unit being one paid rafting place. A recent audit found a 4.5% defect rate in safety-kit checks and guide absenteeism is rising, raising concerns.

--- APPENDIX 1 — MARKETING/OPS ---
Operations and Quality Report — Q3 2025: TRV guided 6,200 rafting places last quarter at $40.00 each, with a 4.5% defect rate in pre-trip safety-kit checks, up from 2.8% a year ago. Guide absenteeism averaged 7 days a month across the team. Customer complaints rose from 12 to 27 per month. A survey of 450 adventure tourists found 61% rated safety as their top concern and 54% would pay $3.00 more for certified gear. Replacing a safety kit costs $75.

--- APPENDIX 2 — FINANCIAL DATA ---

Headers: ['Financial Metric', '2024', '2025']

Trade receivables | 100 | 130
Cash and cash equivalents | 60 | 25
Current liabilities | 140 | 180
Non-current assets | 1,100 | 1,320
Capital employed | 1,450 | 1,600

(2) The national minimum wage will rise by 7.2% from $12.80 to $13.72 per hour from April 2026, increasing the guide wage bill. (3) Specialised raft and safety-equipment input costs have risen 11.3% year-on-year while tourism inflation is 5.9%, and adventure-holiday bookings grew 3.1%.

Every dollar saved on interest can fund the $75 safety-kit replacements needed to cut the 4.5% defect rate, or support the 46-strong team, keeping more of the $15.00 contribution from each rafting place.

Point 2: Retained profit carries no collateral or repossession risk, so the $560,000 basecamp and certified equipment cannot be seized if bookings fall. Aisha Bhatt and the partners also keep full control of the hierarchical structure and autocratic safety decisions without a lender imposing conditions. With guide absenteeism rising and complaints up to 27 a month, avoiding another fixed debt commitment gives TRV breathing room to put its safety record right before the new basecamp opens. The 1.25-point rise to 5.25% would add about $3,750 a year in interest on a variable-rate $300,000 loan, so avoiding that charge releases funds for the $75 safety-kit replacements and the 4.5% defect-rate campaign. It also gives the partnership more flexibility if the 11.3% equipment inflation persists.

--- MAIN STEM ---
Lakeside Escape Inns (LEI) is a public limited company in the hospitality and hotel sector, running boutique inns and lakeside cabins and employing a workforce of 52. LEI has fixed costs of $240,000 a year, a variable cost of $30.00 a unit and a selling price of $55.00, and currently produces 18,000 units a year, each unit being one guest-room night. Recently cleanliness complaints have risen to 34 a month and housekeeping staff turnover is high, worrying managers.

--- APPENDIX 1 — MARKETING/OPS ---
Guest and Quality Report — Q3 2025: LEI sold 4,800 room-nights at $55.00 each, with an occupancy rate of 78%. Cleanliness complaints rose from 18 to 34 per month, and the 2025 guest survey found 72% of 380 respondents would return and 63% rated the lakeside location as the main reason for booking. Average check-in time is 12 minutes. Retraining a housekeeping employee costs $540.

--- APPENDIX 2 — FINANCIAL DATA ---
Title: Extract from the Statement of Financial Position of Lakeside Escape Inns as at 31 March 2025 ($ '000)
Headers: ['Financial Metric', '2024', '2025']

Trade receivables | 75 | 90
Cash and cash equivalents | 25 | 70

--- APPENDIX 3 — EXTERNAL ENVIRONMENT ---
Economic and Hospitality Bulletin (November 2026): (1) The central bank raised the base interest rate from 4.5% to 5.75%, increasing costs on LEI's $320,000 variable-rate loan. (2) The national minimum wage will rise by 6.4% from $13.20 to $14.04 per hour from April 2026, raising the housekeeping wage bill. (3) Energy and laundry input costs have risen 10.2% year-on-year while hospitality inflation is 5.6%, and domestic weekend breaks grew 4.8%.

    Question: Using Appendix 2, evaluate LEI's financial position by calculating the current ratio and the acid test ratio for 2024 and 2025. Has LEI's financial position improved? Justify your answer.
    Answer: Calculations:
Current Ratio 2024 = 1.45 : 1
Current Ratio 2025 = 1.90 : 1
Acid Test Ratio 2024 = 1.00 : 1
Acid Test Ratio 2025 = 1.52 : 1

Detailed workings: 2024 current assets = $45,000 inventories + $75,000 trade receivables + $25,000 cash = $145,000; 2025 current assets = $40,000 + $90,000 + $70,000 = $200,000. Dividing by current liabilities gives 2024 = $145,000 ÷ $100,000 = 1.45 and 2025 = $200,000 ÷ $105,000 = 1.90. Excluding inventories, 2024 = ($145,000 − $45,000) ÷ $100,000 = 1.00 and 2025 = ($200,000 − $40,000) ÷ $105,000 = 1.52.

Evaluation: Liquidity has strengthened. The 2024 figure of 1.45 rose to 1.90 as cash nearly tripled from $25,000 to $70,000 while current liabilities edged up only from $100,000 to $105,000. The stricter measure, which removes inventories, improved from 1.00 to 1.52, so LEI can meet short-term debts without relying on stock — helpful while it services a $320,000 loan and spends $720,000 on cabins and a spa. However, trade receivables rose from $75,000 to $90,000, tying up cash, so the stronger position depends partly on guests and agents paying on time.

Conclusion: LEI's financial position has improved. Both measures rose (1.45 to 1.90 and 1.00 to 1.52) and the cash build means the improvement is not inventory-driven. The residual risk is growing receivables, so LEI should keep tight credit control while funding the expansion. The stronger position gives LEI capacity to absorb the 10.2% energy and laundry inflation without delaying the $720,000 build. Continued cash discipline on the $90,000 of receivables will help keep both measures above their 1.45 and 1.00 starting levels.
    Keywords: 1.45, 1.90, 1.00, $320,000, $720,000, $70,000

--- MAIN STEM ---
Riverbend Eco Stays (RES) is a cooperative in the tourism and hospitality sector, running sustainable forest eco-lodges and employing a workforce of 34. Founded in 2013 by Tariq Ndiaye, RES is member-led with a flat structure and democratic leadership, so workers share decisions on sustainability. It plans to invest $420,000 in solar-powered cabins and a recycling facility, financed by $240,000 of member share capital and a $180,000 bank loan. RES has fixed costs of $144,000 a year, a variable cost of $20.00 a unit and a selling price of $38.00, and currently produces 16,000 units a year, each unit being one guest-night. Food-waste levels have risen to 11% of purchases and guest complaints are growing, concerning the founder.

--- APPENDIX 1 — MARKETING/OPS ---
Sustainability and Guest Report — Q3 2025: RES recorded 3,900 guest-nights at $38.00 each with 85% occupancy. Food waste rose to 11% of purchases from 7% a year ago, and guest complaints climbed from 15 to 29 a month. A survey of 320 eco-tourists found 66% chose RES for its green credentials and 59% would pay $2.50 more for solar-powered cabins. Installing solar panels costs $600 per cabin. Average energy use is 18 kWh per guest-night.

--- APPENDIX 2 — FINANCIAL DATA ---
Title: Extract from the Statement of Financial Position of Riverbend Eco Stays as at 31 March 2025 ($ '000)
Headers: ['Financial Metric', '2024', '2025']
Inventories | 55 | 60
Trade receivables | 85 | 105
Cash and cash equivalents | 20 | 45
Current liabilities | 125 | 130
Non-current assets | 800 | 1,050
Capital employed | 1,100 | 1,300

--- APPENDIX 3 — EXTERNAL ENVIRONMENT ---
Economic and Tourism Bulletin (November 2026): (1) The central bank raised the base interest rate from 3.75% to 4.5%, increasing costs on RES's $180,000 variable-rate loan. (2) The national minimum wage will rise by 5.5% from $13.40 to $14.14 per hour from April 2026, increasing the housekeeping wage bill. (3) Renewable equipment and organic food input costs have risen 8.7% year-on-year while tourism inflation is 4.9%, and eco-tourism bookings grew 5.4%.

    Question: RES is funding its new solar cabins partly with a bank loan. Explain two advantages for RES of using member share capital instead of the bank loan.
    Answer: Point 1: The $240,000 of member share capital needs no interest or repayment, protecting cash flow while the cooperative already has fixed costs of $144,000 a year and a $180,000 loan. Money not spent on interest can fund the $600-per-cabin solar panels and cut the 11% food waste, preserving the $18.00 earned on each $38.00 guest-night.

Point 2: Member share capital is not secured on RES's assets, so the solar cabins and recycling facility cannot be repossessed if eco-tourism demand slips. As a cooperative, the 34 members also keep democratic control of sustainability decisions without a lender's conditions, and dividends can be waived in a poor year, giving flexibility while the $420,000 investment gets underway. Although member share capital means profits are shared among the cooperative, it avoids the extra interest that the 0.75-point rise to 4.5% would add on a $180,000 loan, leaving more of the $18.00 contribution for the 34 members. It also fits the democratic culture Tariq Ndiaye established at the eco-lodges.

Acid Test Ratio 2024 = 1.08 : 1

--- MAIN STEM ---
Zephyr Transport Routes (ZTR) is a private limited company in the road freight and logistics sector, employing a workforce of 50. Founded in 2011 by Ravi Patel, the business moves palletised goods for manufacturers and operates a hierarchical structure with autocratic leadership. ZTR plans to invest $720,000 in an automated freight-sorting hub, financed by a $450,000 ten-year bank loan and $270,000 retained profit. It has fixed costs of $300,000 a year, a variable cost of $12.00 a unit and a selling price of $18.00, and currently handles 68,000 units a year. ZTR faces two operational problems: driver absenteeism has reached 8% and delivery defects are rising, with damaged consignments attracting complaints from manufacturing clients.

--- APPENDIX 1 — MARKETING/OPS ---
Operations and Quality Report — Q4 2025: The sorting hub handled 17,200 consignments last quarter at a damage/defect rate of 2.4%, down from 4.1% a year earlier. Customer complaints fell from 44 to 26 per month. Average delivery time is 2.8 days. A survey of 500 manufacturing clients found that 71% would pay up to $0.50 more for guaranteed undamaged deliveries, and 58% rate on-time reliability as their top criterion. A training needs analysis shows 18 of 50 drivers have not completed on-the-job training on the new sorting systems; off-the-job training at the local college costs $750 per driver.

--- APPENDIX 2 — FINANCIAL DATA ---

    Answer: Advantage: The client survey found 71% of 500 manufacturers would pay up to $0.50 more for guaranteed undamaged deliveries, so ZTR can add a premium that protects its $6.00 contribution per unit even as diesel and energy costs rise 9.5%. It also matches the 58% of clients who rank on-time reliability first, strengthening ZTR's chance of winning contracts for the new $720,000 sorting hub.

Disadvantage: Guaranteeing no damage requires better packing, careful handling and inspection, which would raise the $12.00 variable cost per unit and squeeze margins unless the full $0.50 premium is accepted across all 68,000 units. Any failure would trigger compensation claims and damage the reputation ZTR is trying to build, and the current 2.4% defect rate shows damage is not yet eliminated. With a $450,000 loan to service, ZTR has limited room to absorb a costly guarantee that clients may demand without paying extra. The 8% absenteeism also makes consistently undamaged, on-time service harder to guarantee.
    Keywords: 71%, 500, $0.50, 58%, $720,000, 2.4%, 9.5%
    Mark scheme: knowledge_max_2: 1 mark for a valid advantage and 1 mark for a valid disadvantage. | application_analysis_max_6: Up to 3 marks per point for detailed contextual development linked to ZTR's survey data, costs and investment.

  Q4(b) [12 marks]
    Question: Using Appendix 3, evaluate how the interest rate rise to 5.00%, the 5.5% minimum wage increase and the 9.5% rise in diesel and energy input costs will affect ZTR. Which change will have the greatest impact? Justify your answer.
    Answer: Interest rate rise (4.25% to 5.00%): If ZTR's $450,000 bank loan is variable-rate, the annual interest cost rises by 0.75% of $450,000 = $3,375 a year (0.0075 × $450,000). That is small beside fixed costs of $300,000, and if the loan is fixed-rate the increase is zero. Higher rates may also make clients cautious and raise the cost of any future borrowing, but ZTR can largely neutralise this by fixing the loan rate.

Minimum wage increase (5.5%, to $13.72 per hour): ZTR employs a workforce of 50, many in driving and handling roles, so a wage rise feeds into its cost base and is not optional. The insert gives no hours worked or individual pay, so no defensible annual wage total can be invented; the honest test is productivity — 68,000 units ÷ 50 staff = 1,360 units per worker. If productivity holds, the rise is affordable; if absenteeism at 8% lowers it, unit labour cost rises and the $6.00 contribution per unit is squeezed.

Diesel and energy inputs (9.5%): ZTR's variable cost of $12.00 per unit will be affected, but the insert does not decompose it, so only a bound is honest: if the whole variable cost rose 9.5% it would add 9.5% × $12.00 = $1.14 per unit, and at 68,000 units that is about $77,500 a year (68,000 × $1.14). Even a smaller pass-through cuts the $6.00 contribution materially. ZTR can offset part through the $0.50 undamaged-delivery premium found in the survey.

Conclusion: The 9.5% diesel and energy rise will have the greatest impact because it compounds across all 68,000 consignments and directly erodes the $6.00 contribution that justifies the $720,000 hub. The wage rise is second because it can be managed through productivity; the interest-rate effect is smallest and can be fixed. ZTR should pursue the $0.50 premium and fuel-efficient routing to protect its margins.
    Keywords: 5.00%, 5.5%, 9.5%, $13.72, $12.00, $450,000, 68,000
    Mark scheme: level_1_1_to_4: Identifies the external factors with limited application to ZTR. | level_2_5_to_8: Analyses the impact of at least two external changes on ZTR's costs, revenue or financing in context. | level_3_9_to_12: Detailed evaluation of all three external changes in the context of ZTR with a well-justified judgment that energy costs have the greatest impact and why the other two are smaller.

--- MAIN STEM ---
Fleetline Logistics Express (FLE) is a private limited company in the courier and parcel-delivery sector, employing a workforce of 40. Founded in 2014 by Sofia Marin, the business delivers parcels for online retailers and operates a flat organisational structure with democratic leadership. FLE plans to invest $560,000 in a fleet of electric delivery vans, financed by a $360,000 five-year bank loan and $200,000 retained profit. It has fixed costs of $180,000 a year, a variable cost of $4.50 a unit and a selling price of $9.00, and currently delivers 52,000 units a year. FLE faces two operational problems: labour turnover has reached 14% and parcel mis-sorts are rising, creating complaints from retailers about damaged or late items.

--- APPENDIX 1 — MARKETING/OPS ---
Operations and Quality Report — Q4 2025: The depot sorted 13,400 parcels last month with a mis-sort rate of 2.9%, down from 4.6% a year before. Customer complaints fell from 61 to 33 per month. Average delivery time is 1.9 days. A survey of 400 online retailers found that 68% would pay up to $0.30 more for carbon-neutral delivery, and 55% rank delivery speed as their top criterion. A training needs analysis shows 12 of 40 couriers lack electric-van handling skills; on-the-job training is available at the depot, while off-the-job training at the local college costs $620 per courier.

--- APPENDIX 2 — FINANCIAL DATA ---

Gross profit | 720 | 945
Operating profit | 216 | 294
Capital employed | 1,200 | 1,400
Interest payable | 24 | 35

Economic and Business Bulletin (November 2026): (1) The central bank raised the base interest rate from 3.75% to 4.50%, raising borrowing costs on variable-rate loans. (2) The national minimum wage will rise by 5.5% from $13.00 to $13.72 per hour from April 2026, increasing wage bills across the courier sector. (3) Electricity and fuel input costs rose 11.2% year-on-year, e-commerce parcel volumes grew 7.4%, and consumer spending fell 1.2% as households tightened budgets.

Spread over five years, repayments are predictable and can be matched to the $9.00 selling price and 52,000-parcel volume, so the fleet can start reducing the 2.9% mis-sort rate without delay.

Point 2: Using the loan leaves FLE's $200,000 retained profit free as a cash buffer for the 11.2% rise in electricity and fuel costs and for the $620 per courier training bill. Sofia Marin also keeps full ownership and control of the private limited company, since the lender has no equity claim, and the loan can be serviced from the gross profit shown in Appendix 2 without diluting future returns or surrendering a share of the growing parcel business. With revenue of $1,800,000 in 2024 shown in Appendix 2, the $360,000 facility is comfortably within FLE's capacity to service.

Television is rejected as unaffordable and untargeted for a firm with a $360,000 loan; local newspapers are rejected as too narrow and poorly matched to commercial buyers, though a small local press test could support the partnership campaign. --- MAIN STEM ---
Westline Logistics Xpress (WLX) is a public limited company in the warehousing and distribution sector, employing a workforce of 60. Founded in 2008 by Daniel Okafor, the business stores and distributes fast-moving consumer goods for retailers and operates a hierarchical structure with autocratic leadership. WLX plans to invest $900,000 in automated racking and computer stock control, financed by a $600,000 bank loan and a $300,000 share issue. It has fixed costs of $420,000 a year, a variable cost of $9.00 a unit and a selling price of $16.00, and currently handles 74,000 units a year. WLX faces two operational problems: stock damage has reached 3.6% of units handled and warehouse absenteeism is rising, causing complaints from retailers about inaccurate orders.

Operations and Quality Report — Q4 2025: The warehouse picked 18,600 orders last month with a damage rate of 3.6%, down from 5.2% a year earlier. Customer complaints fell from 72 to 41 per month. A training needs analysis shows 21 of 60 warehouse staff lack computer stock-control skills; on-the-job training is offered, while off-the-job training at the local college costs $880 per employee.

--- APPENDIX 2 — FINANCIAL DATA ---

    Question: Using Appendix 3, evaluate how the interest rate rise to 4.75%, the 6.0% minimum wage increase and the 10.5% rise in energy and packaging input costs will affect WLX. Which change will have the greatest impact? Justify your answer.
    Answer: Interest rate rise (4.00% to 4.75%): If WLX's $600,000 bank loan is variable-rate, the annual interest cost rises by 0.75% of $600,000 = $4,500 a year (0.0075 × $600,000). That is modest beside fixed costs of $420,000, and if the loan is fixed-rate the increase is zero. Higher rates may also caution retailers and raise the cost of future borrowing, but WLX can largely remove this risk by fixing the loan rate.

Minimum wage increase (6.0%, to $13.78 per hour): WLX employs a workforce of 60 in warehousing, so a wage rise feeds into its cost base and is not optional. The insert gives no hours worked or individual pay, so no defensible annual wage total can be invented; the honest test is productivity — 74,000 units ÷ 60 staff = about 1,233 units per worker. If productivity holds, the rise is affordable; if absenteeism lowers it, unit labour cost rises and the $7.00 contribution per unit is squeezed.

Energy and packaging inputs (10.5%): WLX's variable cost of $9.00 per unit will be affected, but the insert does not decompose it, so only a bound is honest: if the whole variable cost rose 10.5% it would add 10.5% × $9.00 = $0.95 per unit, and at 74,000 units that is about $70,000 a year (74,000 × $0.95). Even a smaller pass-through cuts the $7.00 contribution materially. WLX can offset part through the $0.60 error-free premium in the survey.

Conclusion: The 10.5% energy and packaging rise will have the greatest impact because it compounds across all 74,000 units handled and directly erodes the $7.00 contribution that supports the $900,000 automation. The wage rise is second because it can be managed through productivity; the interest-rate effect is smallest and can be fixed. WLX should secure the $0.60 premium and improve energy efficiency to protect margins.

--- MAIN STEM ---
Solstice Off-grid Lighting (SOL) is a private limited company in the renewable-energy sector, employing a workforce of 30. Founded in 2016 by Amara Nwosu, the business manufactures and installs rooftop solar lighting units and operates a flat structure with laissez-faire leadership. SOL plans to invest $1,200,000 in an automated panel-assembly line, financed by an $800,000 bank loan and a $400,000 share issue. It has fixed costs of $240,000 a year, a variable cost of $15.00 a unit and a selling price of $30.00, and currently produces 22,000 units a year. SOL faces two operational problems: a unit defect rate of 3.5% is above the industry norm and a skills gap in automated assembly is slowing output and quality.

--- APPENDIX 1 — MARKETING/OPS ---
Quality and Waste Report — Q4 2025: The assembly line produced 5,600 lighting units last quarter with a defect rate of 3.5%, down from 5.8% a year earlier. Customer complaints fell from 29 to 16 per month. Average installation time is 4.1 days. A survey of 350 installers and builders found that 60% would pay up to $1.00 more for units with a 25-year warranty, and 54% check product certification before specifying a supplier. A training needs analysis shows 9 of 30 technicians lack automated-assembly skills; on-the-job training is available, while off-the-job training at the local college costs $1,100 per technician.

--- APPENDIX 2 — FINANCIAL DATA ---

(3) Polysilicon and glass input costs rose 13.5% year-on-year, renewable-energy investment grew 9.2%, and construction activity slowed 1.8%.

As the business grows on the back of the $1,200,000 line and 9.2% renewable-energy investment, a larger share of the profits would leave the company rather than being retained.

Point 2: Share issue costs and the need to satisfy new shareholders can be significant, and unlike the $800,000 bank loan there is no tax-efficient interest charge; dividends are paid from profit after tax. With fixed costs of $240,000 and a 3.5% defect rate still to fix, diverting cash to dividends reduces the money available for the $1,100 per technician training and for absorbing the 13.5% polysilicon and glass rise. Issuing shares when the share price is weak can also raise less than the $400,000 needed. With 2025 revenue of $2,500,000 in Appendix 2, the dilution must be weighed against the growth the new line should deliver.

UNIT: Paper 2 Case Study

--- MAIN STEM ---
Harbourline Urban Lines (HUL) is a private limited company in the passenger transport sector, employing a workforce of 45. Founded in 2005 by Grace Mensah, the business runs coastal coach services for commuters and tourists and operates a hierarchical structure with democratic leadership. HUL plans to invest $960,000 in a fleet of low-emission coaches, financed by a $650,000 bank loan and $310,000 retained profit. It has fixed costs of $360,000 a year, a variable cost of $7.50 a unit and a selling price of $15.00, and currently carries 62,000 units a year. HUL faces two operational problems: driver absenteeism has reached 11% and rising vehicle defects are causing punctuality complaints from passengers.

--- APPENDIX 1 — MARKETING/OPS ---
Operations and Quality Report — Q4 2025: The coach fleet completed 15,800 journeys last month with a defect-related delay rate of 4.4%, down from 6.1% a year earlier. Passenger complaints fell from 85 to 49 per month. Average journey delay is 6.2 minutes. A survey of 700 passengers found that 64% would pay up to $0.40 more for guaranteed on-time, low-emission travel, and 59% check an operator's environmental record before booking. A training needs analysis shows 16 of 45 drivers lack low-emission vehicle skills; on-the-job training is available, while off-the-job training at the local college costs $780 per driver.

--- APPENDIX 2 — FINANCIAL DATA ---
Title: Extract from the Statement of Profit or Loss and Capital employed data of Harbourline Urban Lines for the year ended 31 March 2025 ($ '000)
Headers: ['Financial Metric', '2024', '2025']
Revenue | 2,600 | 3,000
Cost of sales | 1,560 | 1,680
Gross profit | 1,040 | 1,320
Operating profit | 312 | 420
Capital employed | 1,950 | 2,400
Interest payable | 42 | 58

--- APPENDIX 3 — EXTERNAL ENVIRONMENT ---
Economic and Business Bulletin (November 2026): (1) The central bank raised the base interest rate from 4.00% to 5.00%, increasing borrowing costs on variable-rate loans. (2) The national minimum wage will rise by 5.8% from $13.00 to $13.75 per hour from April 2026, raising driver wage bills. (3) Diesel and energy input costs rose 10.8% year-on-year, tourism bookings grew 5.6%, and household consumer spending fell 0.9%.

--- QUESTIONS ---
  Q1(a) [8 marks]
    Question: HUL plans to fund part of its $960,000 low-emission coach fleet with $310,000 retained profit. Explain two advantages for HUL of using retained profit rather than increasing its $650,000 bank loan.
    Answer: Point 1: Retained profit carries no interest charge or capital repayment, so using the $310,000 protects HUL's cash flow while it already services a $650,000 bank loan and faces fixed costs of $360,000 a year. Every dollar not paid as interest can absorb the 10.8% rise in diesel and energy costs, helping HUL hold its $15.00 fare and remain competitive with other coastal operators.

Point 2: Retaining profit avoids further collateral and the risk of coaches being repossessed if tourism bookings fall, and it preserves Grace Mensah's control of the private limited company. No lender can impose conditions on how the $960,000 fleet is deployed, so management can respond flexibly to the 11% driver absenteeism and the 4.4% defect-related delay rate without seeking a bank's approval. With 2024 revenue of $2,600,000 in Appendix 2, HUL has a solid profit base to release $310,000 internally. The $310,000 also reduces reliance on external finance as the 5.00% base rate rises.
    Keywords: $310,000, $960,000, $650,000, 11%, $780, 62,000
    Mark scheme: knowledge_max_2: 1 mark for each valid advantage identified (max 2). | application_analysis_max_6: Up to 3 marks per point for contextual explanation and analysis applied to HUL and its coach-fleet financing decision.

  Q1(b) [12 marks]
    Question: HUL is promoting its guaranteed on-time, low-emission coach travel. Consider a national television campaign, local radio advertising, or partnerships with tourism and commuter organisations. Which should HUL choose to promote the service? Justify your recommendation.
    Answer: Television campaign: A national TV campaign would build rapid, broad awareness of low-emission travel, but airtime and production costs are very high and most viewers are not potential coastal passengers. For a 45-employee operator funding a $960,000 fleet and a $650,000 loan, most of the spend would be wasted and few of the 700 surveyed passengers would be reached.

Local radio advertising: Local radio is much cheaper and can target the coastal communities HUL serves, carrying a simple punctuality message to drivers near its routes. However, its reach is limited to one region and cannot build a wider brand; the 64% of surveyed passengers willing to pay $0.40 more for on-time, low-emission travel include tourists from beyond the local area.

Partnerships with tourism and commuter organisations: Working with tourist boards, employers and commuter groups targets exactly the passengers who value reliable, low-emission travel, using the $0.40 premium in joint offers and measuring take-up through bookings. The 59% who check an operator's environmental record can be shown the new fleet's credentials directly, at low cost.

Recommendation: HUL should choose partnerships with tourism and commuter organisations. This reaches the precise segments in the survey, costs far less than television and delivers measurable bookings. Television is rejected as unaffordable and untargeted given the $650,000 loan; local radio is rejected as too narrow for a service that attracts tourists from outside the region, though short radio bursts can support the partnerships. HUL can also publicise the new low-emission fleet alongside the 5.6% growth in tourism bookings.
    Keywords: low-emission, 64%, 700, $0.40, 59%, $650,000
    Mark scheme: level_1_1_to_4: Limited knowledge or outline of the promotional options with minimal context. | level_2_5_to_8: Detailed discussion of the advantages and disadvantages of at least two options in the context of HUL with some judgement. | level_3_9_to_12: Detailed discussion of all three options in the context of HUL with a well-justified recommendation explaining why television and radio are rejected.

  Q2(a) [8 marks]
    Question: HUL's driver absenteeism has reached 11% and it uses democratic leadership. Explain two benefits for HUL of democratic leadership in reducing absenteeism among its drivers.
    Answer: Point 1: Democratic leadership gives HUL's workforce of 45 a genuine voice in how the new low-emission coach fleet and duty rosters are organised, satisfying social and esteem needs and raising job satisfaction. Drivers who help design schedules and rest arrangements are more likely to attend consistently, directly reducing the 11% absenteeism that disrupts the 62,000-unit service.
