With 15,800 journeys completed last month and complaints still at 49, releasing 16 drivers would cut service frequency when passengers value punctuality. On-the-job training protects the 62,000-unit service, and the $12,480 saved could fund short college certificates once the fleet is bedded in.     Question: Using Appendix 3, evaluate how the interest rate rise to 5.00%, the 5.8% minimum wage increase and the 10.8% rise in diesel and energy input costs will affect HUL. Which change will have the greatest impact? Justify your answer.
    Answer: Interest rate rise (4.00% to 5.00%): If HUL's $650,000 bank loan is variable-rate, the annual interest cost rises by 1.00% of $650,000 = $6,500 a year (0.01 × $650,000). That is modest beside fixed costs of $360,000, and if the loan is fixed-rate the increase is zero. Higher rates may also caution passengers and raise future borrowing costs, but HUL can largely remove this risk by fixing the loan rate.

Minimum wage increase (5.8%, to $13.75 per hour): HUL employs a workforce of 45, with many drivers likely paid hourly, so a wage rise feeds into its cost base and is not optional. The insert gives no hours worked or individual pay, so no defensible annual wage total can be invented; the honest test is productivity — 62,000 units ÷ 45 staff = about 1,378 units per worker. If productivity holds, the rise is affordable; if absenteeism at 11% lowers it, unit labour cost rises and the $7.50 contribution per unit is squeezed.

Diesel and energy inputs (10.8%): HUL's variable cost of $7.50 per unit will be affected, but the insert does not decompose it, so only a bound is honest: if the whole variable cost rose 10.8% it would add 10.8% × $7.50 = $0.81 per unit, and at 62,000 units that is about $50,000 a year (62,000 × $0.81). Even a smaller pass-through cuts the $7.50 contribution materially. HUL can offset part through the $0.40 on-time premium in the survey.

Conclusion: The 10.8% diesel and energy rise will have the greatest impact because it compounds across all 62,000 passenger units and directly erodes the $7.50 contribution that supports the $960,000 fleet. The wage rise is second because it can be managed through productivity; the interest-rate effect is smallest and can be fixed. HUL should secure the $0.40 premium and improve fuel efficiency to protect margins.

--- MAIN STEM ---
Zenith Smart Payments (ZEN) is a private limited company in the financial technology sector, providing contactless payment terminals and online checkout software to retailers across Singapore and Malaysia. Founded in 2012 by Daniel Ong, it employs a workforce of 52 and operates a flat organisational structure with democratic leadership. ZEN plans to invest $840,000 in a contactless payment platform upgrade with integrated e-commerce checkout and fraud screening, financed by a $500,000 five-year bank loan and $340,000 retained profit. It has fixed costs of $264,000 a year, a variable cost of $5.50 a unit and a selling price of $13.00, and currently produces 84,000 units a year. ZEN faces two problems: its checkout software has a 6.2% transaction failure rate, and a shortage of cybersecurity skills is slowing the upgrade.

--- APPENDIX 1 — MARKETING/OPS ---
Operations and Quality Report — Q3 2025: ZEN processed 18,600 checkout transactions last quarter, of which 6.2% failed at payment authorisation, down from 9.4% a year earlier. Support tickets averaged 34 a day and 14 of 40 merchant clients now require a written fraud-control plan before renewal. Average integration time for a new merchant is 2.1 days. Platform uptime was 99.4%. Market research of 450 merchants found that 68% would pay up to $0.60 more for fraud-protected checkout, and 57% check security certification before switching supplier. A skills audit shows 16 of 52 staff lack advanced cybersecurity training; an external certification course costs $780 per employee.

--- APPENDIX 2 — FINANCIAL DATA ---

(2) The national minimum wage will rise by 6.4% from $12.80 to $13.62 an hour from April 2026, raising wage bills across the technology sector. (3) Cloud hosting and data-centre input costs have risen 11.8% year-on-year, while digital-payment transaction volumes grew 5.2% and consumer spending on online retail rose 3.9%.

    Answer: Point 1: Retained profit carries no interest charge and no fixed repayment schedule, which protects ZEN's cash flow while it already covers fixed costs of $264,000 a year and services a $500,000 bank loan. Each dollar of interest avoided can be spent on reducing the 6.2% checkout failure rate, for example by expanding the fraud-screening team, without raising the $13.00 selling price or squeezing the $7.50 contribution per unit. With the base rate due to climb to 5.25% (Appendix 3), a variable-rate loan would grow more expensive, so using the $340,000 already earned removes that exposure entirely.

Point 2: Retained profit leaves ownership and control with founder Daniel Ong and the existing shareholders, and it avoids the collateral and covenants a $500,000 loan would impose on the $840,000 platform. No lender could repossess the upgraded checkout system if merchant demand grows more slowly than expected, which matters because 14 of 40 merchant clients now demand a fraud-control plan before renewal. It is also faster than renegotiating debt, letting ZEN respond to the 57% of surveyed merchants who check security certification before switching supplier.

    Answer: Payments trade journal advertising: A technical advert in a payments trade title reaches acquiring banks, fintech partners and merchant technology managers directly, and it can carry the evidence that 14 of 40 merchant clients now require, such as the fall in checkout failures from 9.4% to 6.2%. The message can speak directly to the 68% of 450 surveyed merchants who would pay $0.60 more for protection. --- MAIN STEM ---
Xplore Automation (XPL) is a public limited company in the industrial robotics sector, designing warehouse picking robots and computer-vision quality systems for factories in Germany. Founded in 2008 by Stefan Bauer, it employs a workforce of 62 and operates a hierarchical structure with autocratic leadership, with engineering decisions taken by the technical director. XPL plans to invest $1,200,000 in a robotic picking line with automated optical inspection, financed by $700,000 hire purchase and a $500,000 share issue. It has fixed costs of $420,000 a year, a variable cost of $12.00 a unit and a selling price of $26.00, and currently produces 60,000 units a year. Two problems remain: calibration faults have lifted the weld defect rate to 4.8%, and skilled technician turnover is rising.

--- APPENDIX 1 — MARKETING/OPS ---
Operations and Quality Log — Q3 2025: XPL assembled 9,800 robotic cells last quarter, of which 4.8% failed weld inspection, down from 7.3% a year earlier. Client complaints averaged 31 a quarter and 9 of 24 factory customers now require predictive-maintenance evidence before renewing. Mean repair time is 4.1 days and first-pass yield is 96.4%. A survey of 240 production managers found that 71% would pay up to $1.20 more for predictive maintenance, and 63% rank uptime above price. A training review shows 15 of 62 technicians lack computer-vision skills; a technical college course costs $1,100 per technician.

--- APPENDIX 2 — FINANCIAL DATA ---
Title: Extract from the Statement of Profit or Loss and Capital employed data of Xplore Automation for the year ended 31 March 2025 ($ '000)
Headers: ['Financial Metric', '2024', '2025']
Revenue | 5,000 | 5,800
Cost of sales | 3,000 | 3,190
Gross profit | 2,000 | 2,610
Operating profit | 500 | 725
Capital employed | 2,500 | 2,900
Interest payable | 60 | 78

--- APPENDIX 3 — EXTERNAL ENVIRONMENT ---
Economic and Business Bulletin (November 2026): (1) The central bank has raised the base interest rate from 4.0% to 4.75%, increasing the cost of hire purchase and other borrowing. (2) The national minimum wage will rise by 7.1% from $12.60 to $13.49 an hour from April 2026, raising wage bills across engineering firms. (3) Semiconductor and servo-motor input costs have risen 14.2% year-on-year, while demand for industrial automation grew 4.8% and factory wages overall rose 3.6%.

  Q1(a) [8 marks]
    Question: XPL plans to finance $700,000 of its $1,200,000 robotic line through hire purchase. Explain two advantages for XPL of using the $500,000 share issue instead.
    Answer: Point 1: Share issue finance carries no regular hire-purchase instalments, which protects XPL's cash flow while it already has fixed costs of $420,000 a year and pays interest of $78,000. Each instalment avoided can instead fund work on the 4.8% weld defect rate or the 4.1-day mean repair time, protecting the $14.00 contribution per unit and the $26.00 selling price. With the base rate due to rise to 4.75% (Appendix 3), hire-purchase charges would become dearer, whereas equity does not re-price with the market.

Point 2: A share issue does not give a lender security over the $1,200,000 robotic line, so XPL cannot lose the automated optical inspection equipment if automation demand grows more slowly than the 4.8% forecast. It also spreads the funding risk among shareholders rather than committing the public limited company to fixed debt repayments while the 9 of 24 factory customers demand predictive-maintenance evidence before renewal. The trade-off is dilution of existing shareholders, but that is preferable to a repossession risk on the core production asset.

The insert states $700,000 of hire purchase but not its rate terms, so the only defensible figure is a labelled bound: if that $700,000 were fully exposed to the move, the added annual cost would be 0.75% × $700,000 = $5,250, small beside $420,000 of fixed costs. Minimum wage increase (7.1%, from $12.60 to $13.49): Each paid hour costs $0.895 more (7.1% × $12.60). The insert gives no hours worked and no individual pay rates, so an annual wage bill cannot be invented; with 62 staff and rising technician turnover every replacement is hired at the higher rate. Productivity is 60,000 units ÷ 62 staff = about 968 units per worker, and if that falls, unit labour cost rises and the $14.00 contribution is squeezed while the 4.8% defect rate is being fixed.

Semiconductor and servo-motor costs (up 14.2%): These are direct inputs into the robots and the planned optical-inspection system, and 14.2% is by far the largest percentage change in the bulletin, more than double the wage rise and nineteen times the 0.75-point rate move. The insert gives no separate materials bill, so only the scale can be stated, but the cost lands on every one of the 60,000 units while automation demand grew only 4.8%, limiting XPL's ability to pass it on.

Conclusion: The 14.2% rise in semiconductor and servo-motor costs will have the greatest impact. It is the largest shock, it is unavoidable for a robotics maker, and it hits all 60,000 units and the $1,200,000 line at once when demand grew only 4.8%. The wage rise is second because it recurs with each of the 62 staff, while the interest effect is smallest and can be avoided by fixing terms or using the share issue.
    Keywords: 4.75%, 7.1%, 14.2%, $13.49, 4.8%, 4.0%
    Mark scheme: level_1_1_to_4: Identifies the external changes with limited application to XPL. | level_2_5_to_8: Analyses the impact of at least two changes on XPL's costs, finance or prices in context. | level_3_9_to_12: Detailed evaluation of all three changes with a justified judgement that component costs have the greatest impact and clear reasons why the other two are smaller.

--- MAIN STEM ---
Juniper Voice Systems (JVS) is a private limited company in the digital services sector, providing cloud contact-centre software with AI speech analytics to firms across Ireland. Founded in 2017 by Aoife Byrne, it employs a workforce of 40 and operates a flat organisational structure with democratic leadership, with engineers voting on product priorities. JVS plans to invest $480,000 in a cloud contact-centre upgrade with real-time transcription, financed by a $180,000 bank overdraft and $300,000 retained profit. It has fixed costs of $168,000 a year, a variable cost of $3.60 a unit and a selling price of $9.60, and currently produces 75,000 units a year. JVS faces two problems: transcription errors affect 7.1% of calls, and complaints about accuracy are rising.

--- APPENDIX 1 — MARKETING/OPS ---
Service Quality Report — Q3 2025: JVS handled 16,200 calls last quarter, with a 7.1% transcription error rate down from 10.3% a year earlier. Client complaints averaged 42 a month and 12 of 35 clients now demand accuracy guarantees before renewal. Average setup time for a new client is 1.8 days and platform uptime reached 98.6%. A survey of 380 business clients found that 66% would pay up to $0.45 more for accurate transcription, and 55% rank data privacy highest. A skills review shows 11 of 40 engineers lack NLP tuning training; a specialist course costs $720 per engineer.

--- APPENDIX 2 — FINANCIAL DATA ---

The $180,000 overdraft would add a variable cost that rises whenever rates move, while the $300,000 already earned can be spent on cutting the 7.1% transcription error rate without raising the $9.60 selling price or reducing the $6.00 contribution per unit. Cash is therefore preserved for the 42 complaints a month that JVS must answer.

Point 2: Retained profit carries no repayment deadline or security, so Aoife Byrne and the 40 employees keep control of the $480,000 cloud upgrade and the bank cannot demand repayment when cash is tight. That is important while 12 of 35 clients want accuracy guarantees before renewal and the skills review shows 11 of 40 engineers need NLP tuning training. Using internal funds is also quicker than arranging an overdraft, letting JVS fix errors before more clients complain.

Orbital Digital Media (ORB) is a private limited company in the digital services sector, building e-commerce websites and 3D product visualisation for retailers in Australia. A survey of 410 retailers found that 69% would pay up to $0.55 more for 3D product visualisation, and 61% rank mobile loading speed first. A training review shows 13 of 48 designers lack 3D and CAM skills; an external workshop costs $850 per designer.

Operating profit $336,000 ÷ revenue $2,800,000 × 100 = 12.0 in 2024 and $510,000 ÷ $3,400,000 × 100 = 15.0 in 2025. Returns on capital: $336,000 ÷ $1,600,000 × 100 = 21.0 in 2024 and $510,000 ÷ $2,040,000 × 100 = 25.0 in 2025. Interest payable rose only from $20,000 to $26,000, so financing costs were not the cause of the improvement.

Evaluation: All three measures improved. The gross margin widened from 40.0% to 45.0%, reflecting control of delivery costs while revenue grew $600,000, helped by the 4.3% growth in online retail spending and the 69% of surveyed retailers willing to pay $0.55 more for 3D views. The operating margin rose from 12.0% to 15.0%, so more of each revenue dollar survives the $240,000 fixed costs. Returns on capital increased from 21.0% to 25.0% even though capital employed grew by $440,000 ahead of the $600,000 studio, suggesting existing assets are working harder. Because revenue, gross profit and operating profit all rose together, the improvement is broad-based. The caution is that 5.9% of websites still contain defects, 36 complaints a month persist, and cloud rendering inputs are up 12.6%; if the studio is delayed, the gains could be eroded.

Conclusion: ORB's financial performance has improved. The gross margin (40.0% to 45.0%), operating margin (12.0% to 15.0%) and returns on capital (21.0% to 25.0%) all rose with higher revenue. ORB should use part of the $350,000 retained profit to cut the 5.9% defect rate before expanding further.
    Keywords: 40.0%, 45.0%, 12.0%, 15.0%, 21.0%, 25.0%, $1,530,000
    Mark scheme: level_1_1_to_4: States financial figures or simple changes without accurate ratio calculations. | level_2_5_to_8: Calculates all three ratios for both years with some contextual analysis of the trend. | level_3_9_to_12: Accurate ratio calculations for both years with detailed evaluation of revenue, costs, capital and interest, and a justified conclusion on whether performance improved.

  Q4(a) [8 marks]
    Question: Explain one advantage and one disadvantage for ORB of adding 3D product visualisation to its e-commerce websites.
    Answer: Advantage: 3D product visualisation answers the 69% of 410 surveyed retailers who would pay up to $0.55 more for it, so ORB can lift its $7.50 contribution per unit and better cover the $240,000 fixed costs. It also sets ORB apart from rivals at a time when 61% of retailers rank mobile speed first and 10 of 32 clients demand a performance guarantee, supporting the $12.00 price and the $600,000 studio investment as online retail spending grows 4.3%.

  Q4(b) [12 marks]
    Question: Using Appendix 3, evaluate how the interest rate rise to 5.25%, the 6.8% minimum wage increase and the 12.6% rise in cloud rendering and software-licence costs will affect ORB. Which change will have the greatest impact? Justify your answer.
    Answer: Interest rate rise (4.5% to 5.25%): ORB has no bank loan in the case, so no interest charge can be computed from the insert for its $250,000 venture capital or $350,000 retained profit. The rise still matters because it increases the required return investors will demand on the $250,000 and makes future borrowing for the $600,000 studio more expensive; the effect is on the cost of capital and financing choice, not on a stated interest bill.

Minimum wage increase (6.8%, from $12.90 to $13.78): Each paid hour costs $0.877 more (6.8% × $12.90). The insert gives no hours worked and no individual pay rates, so an annual wage total cannot be invented; the defensible judgement is that with 48 staff and rising designer turnover, each replacement is hired at the higher rate. Unless productivity holds on the 80,000 units a year, unit labour cost rises and the $7.50 contribution is squeezed while 13 of 48 designers still need 3D training.

Cloud rendering and software-licence costs (up 12.6%): ORB sells websites built on cloud platforms, so this is an unavoidable input, and 12.6% is the largest percentage change in the bulletin, almost twice the 6.8% wage rise and far larger than the 0.75-point rate move. The insert gives no separate rendering bill, so only the scale can be stated: it applies to all 80,000 units and to the new 3D studio, which will use more rendering than existing sites.

Conclusion: The 12.6% rise in cloud rendering and software-licence costs will have the greatest impact. It is the biggest percentage shock, it cannot be avoided by a digital agency, and it hits all 80,000 units and the $600,000 studio at once when online retail spending grew only 4.3%. The wage rise is second because it recurs with every one of the 48 staff, while the interest rise has no direct interest bill in the insert and mainly changes the terms of future finance.

--- MAIN STEM ---
Meridian Valley Health (MVH) is a private limited company in the healthcare sector, operating a group of private day-surgery clinics with a workforce of 120. Founded in 2009 by Dr Priya Nair, the business uses a hierarchical organisational structure with democratic leadership. MVH plans to invest $900,000 in a new day-surgery operating theatre and diagnostic imaging suite, financed by a $600,000 ten-year bank loan and $300,000 retained profit. It has fixed costs of $288,000 a year, a variable cost of $54 a unit and a selling price of $90, and currently produces 14,000 units a year. MVH faces two problems: nurse absenteeism has reached 8% and patient waiting times for diagnostics are rising.

--- APPENDIX 1 — MARKETING/OPS ---
Operations and Quality Report - Q3 2025: The day-surgery unit performed 3,200 procedures last quarter at a surgical rework rate of 2.4%, down from 4.0% a year ago. Patient complaints fell from 46 to 19 per month. Average waiting time for a diagnostics appointment is 18 days. A survey of 750 patients found that 68% would pay $15 more for same-day diagnostics and 57% choose a provider on its waiting-time reputation. A skills audit shows 30 of 120 clinical staff have not completed on-the-job training on the new imaging machines; off-the-job training courses at the local college cost $1,100 per employee.

--- APPENDIX 2 — FINANCIAL DATA ---
Title: Extract from the Statement of Profit or Loss and Capital employed data of Meridian Valley Health for the year ended 31 March 2025 ($ '000)
Headers: ['Financial Metric', '2024', '2025']

Cost of sales | 1,440 | 1,595
Gross profit | 960 | 1,305
Operating profit | 360 | 522
Capital employed | 2,000 | 2,320
Interest payable | 40 | 55

--- APPENDIX 3 — EXTERNAL ENVIRONMENT ---
Economic and Business Bulletin (November 2026): (1) The central bank has raised the base interest rate from 4.25% to 5.0%, increasing borrowing costs for businesses with variable-rate loans. (2) The national minimum wage will rise by 5.8% from $13.68 to $14.50 per hour from April 2026, raising total wage bills. (3) Medical supply and pharmaceutical input costs have risen 9.6% year-on-year, while consumer spending on private healthcare grew 4.2% over the same period.

--- QUESTIONS ---
  Q1(a) [8 marks]
    Question: MVH plans to fund part of its $900,000 day-surgery expansion with a ten-year bank loan. Explain two advantages for MVH of using retained profit to fund the expansion instead of the bank loan.
    Answer: Point 1: Using retained profit costs MVH no interest or capital repayments, protecting cash flow and margins while it already services a $600,000 bank loan and carries fixed costs of $288,000 a year. Every dollar not paid as interest can absorb the 9.6% rise in medical supply costs without pushing the $90 procedure price above what patients will pay.

Point 2: Retained profit avoids collateral and default risk, so the $300,000 is available without putting the new operating theatre at risk of repossession if demand for day surgery disappoints. It also preserves Dr Priya Nair's ownership and control, since no lender can impose covenants on how the diagnostic imaging suite is run or expanded next year.

Because the $300,000 is internal, MVH keeps its debt burden modest while revenue grows from $2,400,000 to $2,900,000, which strengthens its standing with the lender and leaves room for future borrowing if the imaging suite needs a second phase. It also means the 8% nurse absenteeism and any dip in the 14,000-procedure volume do not coincide with a fixed repayment schedule, protecting the group's ability to fund the $1,100 retraining and the same-day diagnostics launch from existing cash.
    Keywords: retained profit, $300,000, $600,000, $900,000, bank loan, $288,000
    Mark scheme: knowledge_max_2: 1 mark for each valid advantage of retained profit over a bank loan (max 2). | application_analysis_max_6: Up to 3 marks per point for contextual explanation applied to MVH's expansion, loan and cost data.

  Q1(b) [12 marks]
    Question: MVH is launching its new same-day diagnostics service. Consider a national television campaign, local radio sponsorship or social media influencer marketing. Which should MVH choose to promote the launch? Justify your recommendation.
    Answer: Television: A national TV campaign builds rapid, mass awareness of same-day diagnostics across all MVH clinic sites. However, airtime and production are extremely expensive for a 120-staff healthcare group funding a $900,000 expansion, and much of the audience lives outside MVH's regional catchment or never needs private day surgery, so spending would be heavily wasted.

Local radio: Local radio is far cheaper and suits time-sensitive messages such as shorter waiting times, reaching MVH's regional patients directly. Its weakness is narrow reach: the new imaging suite must attract enough scans to cover $288,000 of fixed costs, and local listeners alone cannot deliver the 14,000-unit volume the group targets.

Social media influencer marketing: Health and family lifestyle influencers reach exactly the 68% of 750 surveyed patients who would pay $15 more for same-day diagnostics and the 57% who choose on waiting-time reputation. Engagement is measurable and cost per reached patient is low, though results build more slowly than TV and depend on influencer credibility.

Cost is decisive for a 120-staff group whose 2025 operating profit is $522,000: a national television campaign could absorb a large share of that profit, whereas influencer fees can be capped and measured against the 3,200 procedures handled each quarter. MVH should also track how many of the 57% who value waiting-time reputation actually book, so the campaign is judged against the $36 contribution per scan rather than reach alone.

Recommendation: MVH should choose social media influencer marketing. It targets the exact segment in the survey, scales nationally unlike local radio, and costs a fraction of television. Television is rejected as unaffordable and untargeted; radio is rejected as too narrow for the imaging suite's volume needs, so MVH should add modest clinic-based referral promotion to convert the influencer interest.
    Keywords: day-surgery, 68%, 57%, 750, $15, waiting time
    Mark scheme: level_1_1_to_4: Identifies promotional options with limited application to MVH. | level_2_5_to_8: Discusses advantages and disadvantages of at least two options in the context of MVH with some judgement. | level_3_9_to_12: Discusses all three options in MVH's context with a well-justified recommendation explaining why television and local radio are rejected.

  Q2(a) [8 marks]
    Question: MVH's nurse absenteeism has reached 8% and patient waiting times are rising. Explain two benefits for MVH of using democratic leadership to improve motivation in its clinical teams.
    Answer: Point 1: Democratic leadership gives MVH's 120 staff a genuine voice in how the new day-surgery theatre is organised, raising job satisfaction and addressing the social and esteem needs in Maslow's hierarchy. Nurses who help set imaging-room rotas are likelier to attend reliably, directly reducing the 8% absenteeism that is lengthening waiting times.

Point 2: Consulting the clinicians who handle scans daily generates practical ideas that cut the 2.4% rework rate further and protect the 14,000-unit procedure target. Higher involvement raises commitment and lowers labour turnover, avoiding repeated $1,100 per employee retraining and keeping the diagnostic suite productive while the new service beds in.

Democratic leadership also fits MVH's hierarchical clinical structure because consultants and nurses hold different expertise; consulting both levels produces safer rotas for the 3,200 procedures delivered last quarter. Higher morale reduces the need for agency cover, whose cost would otherwise consume the $36 contribution on each scan, and a stable team protects the 45.0% gross margin reported for 2025. Sustained attendance is therefore both a quality and a financial safeguard for the $900,000 operating theatre.

  Q2(b) [12 marks]
    Question: MVH must upskill 30 clinical staff to operate the new imaging machines. Consider on-the-job training or off-the-job training at the local college. Which should MVH choose? Justify your decision.
    Answer: On-the-job training: Coaching at the imaging suite is specific to MVH's own machines and quality standards, costs no course fees and keeps the 30 staff productive while they learn, protecting the Q3 output of 3,200 procedures and the fall in rework to 2.4%. Drawbacks are that trainer-nurses sacrifice their own work, bad habits can spread, and formal certification is limited if clinical auditors require records.

Quality assurance is a further consideration: a recognised college certificate may be valued by clinical auditors, but the insert gives no evidence that MVH's regulators require one, so the cheaper machine-specific route is not thereby disqualified. An on-the-job programme can be delivered in short sessions around the 18-day diagnostic waiting list, whereas a college timetable removes staff at fixed times and would slow the 3,200-procedure quarter. Blended delivery keeps the $33,000 cost optional.

Decision: MVH should choose on-the-job training first, backed by short college sessions for lead operators. It is cheaper, machine-specific and avoids losing capacity while nurse absenteeism is 8%; full off-the-job training is rejected because a $33,000 fee and 30 staff off the ward would disrupt the diagnostic waiting-time target, and college modules can be added later once the suite stabilises.
    Keywords: on-the-job training, off-the-job training, $1,100, $900,000, imaging machines, 8%

    Answer: Interest rate rise (4.25% to 5.0%): If MVH's $600,000 ten-year bank loan is variable-rate, the 0.75 percentage-point rise adds 0.0075 × $600,000 = $4,500 a year, modest beside $288,000 of fixed costs; if the loan is fixed, the direct cost is zero. Minimum wage increase (5.8%, to $14.50 an hour): With a workforce of 120 and many hourly-paid support and nursing staff, this lifts the wage bill and is not optional. The insert gives no hours worked or individual pay, so no annual total can be invented; the defensible test is productivity - 14,000 procedures ÷ 120 staff = about 116.7 procedures per worker - so a wage rise is affordable only if that productivity holds, otherwise unit labour cost erodes the $36 contribution.

Input cost inflation (9.6%): MVH's $54 variable cost per procedure reflects medical supplies, but the insert does not decompose it, so only a bound is honest: if all of it rose 9.6% that is 0.096 × $54 = $5.18 per procedure, or about $72,500 a year at 14,000 procedures (14,000 × $5.18). Even a smaller rise cuts contribution materially, and the $15 diagnostics premium can recover only part of it.

Conclusion: The 9.6% rise in medical supply costs has the greatest impact because it compounds across all 14,000 procedures and directly attacks the $36 contribution that services the $900,000 expansion; the wage rise is smaller and manageable if productivity holds, and the interest rise adds only $4,500 at most and can be fixed, so neither matches the input-cost shock.

--- MAIN STEM ---
Eastbridge Academy of Learning (EAL) is a private limited company in the education sector, running a vocational training college with a workforce of 80. Founded in 2015 by Helena Wu, the business operates a flat organisational structure with laissez-faire leadership. EAL plans to invest $480,000 in a new e-learning studio and digital learning platform, financed by a $300,000 five-year bank loan and a $180,000 share issue. It has fixed costs of $144,000 a year, a variable cost of $26 a unit and a selling price of $62, and currently produces 9,600 units a year. EAL faces two problems: student dropout has reached 12% and tutor absenteeism is rising sharply, disrupting live classes and learner support.

--- APPENDIX 1 — MARKETING/OPS ---
Quality and Enrolments Report - Q3 2025: The college enrolled 2,400 learners last quarter with a course pass rate of 78%, down from 86% a year ago. Student complaints fell from 52 to 29 per month. Average course-material dispatch time is 2.4 days. A survey of 400 prospective students found that 71% would pay $20 more for livestreamed tutorials and 63% check digital-platform quality before enrolling. A skills audit shows 24 of 80 tutors have not completed on-the-job training on the new e-learning platform; off-the-job training courses at the local college cost $750 per employee.

--- APPENDIX 2 — FINANCIAL DATA ---
Title: Extract from the Statement of Profit or Loss and Capital employed data of Eastbridge Academy of Learning for the year ended 31 March 2025 ($ '000)
Headers: ['Financial Metric', '2024', '2025']

Capital employed | 1,000 | 1,400

--- APPENDIX 3 — EXTERNAL ENVIRONMENT ---

(2) The national minimum wage will rise by 4.9% from $13.25 to $13.90 per hour from April 2026, raising total wage bills. (3) Education technology and printed-material input costs have risen 7.3% year-on-year, while consumer spending on adult education grew 2.8% in the same period.

--- QUESTIONS ---
  Q1(a) [8 marks]
    Question: EAL plans to fund part of its $480,000 e-learning expansion with a five-year bank loan. Explain two advantages for EAL of using a share issue to raise the $180,000 instead of extra bank borrowing.
    Answer: Point 1: Share capital does not have to be repaid and carries no compulsory interest, unlike the $300,000 bank loan, so EAL's cash flow is protected while it absorbs fixed costs of $144,000 a year and a 7.3% rise in technology input costs. This strengthens the college's ability to reinvest in the digital platform.

Point 2: Equity spreads the risk of the new e-learning venture among shareholders rather than leaving Helena Wu's original backers exposed to loan covenants or repossession of the studio. It also enlarges the capital base supporting the $480,000 investment without increasing the interest payable already in Appendix 2.

Equity also matches the long payback of an e-learning platform: the $480,000 investment should lift the 42.0% gross margin over several years, so funding it with eight years of loan interest would mismatch the benefit stream. With dropout at 12%, a share issue leaves cash available for learner support and the $750 retraining without cutting the $144,000 fixed-cost budget or the 9,600-enrolment target.
    Keywords: share issue, $180,000, $300,000, $480,000, bank loan, $144,000
    Mark scheme: knowledge_max_2: 1 mark for each valid advantage of a share issue over bank borrowing (max 2). | application_analysis_max_6: Up to 3 marks per point for contextual explanation applied to EAL's expansion, loan and cost data.

  Q1(b) [12 marks]
    Question: EAL is launching its new e-learning platform. Consider a national television campaign, local radio sponsorship or social media influencer marketing. Which should EAL choose to promote the launch? Justify your recommendation.
    Answer: Television: National TV gives EAL instant mass awareness of the digital platform across the country. Yet airtime is prohibitive for an 80-staff college funding a $480,000 expansion, and most viewers are not prospective vocational learners, so much of the budget is wasted.

Local radio: Regional radio is cheap and reaches EAL's local catchment quickly, ideal for a college that recruits nearby students. Its limit is reach: filling enough places to cover $144,000 of fixed costs and the 9,600-unit enrolment target needs more than one local audience.

Social media influencer marketing: Education and careers influencers reach exactly the 71% of 400 surveyed students who would pay $20 more for livestreamed tutorials and the 63% who check platform quality. Reach from television would be largely wasted on viewers outside the college's recruitment area, while radio's 2.4-day dispatch message cannot be shown visually; a targeted digital campaign fits the flat, 80-staff organisation and the $480,000 platform budget.

Recommendation: EAL should choose social media influencer marketing. It hits the exact survey segment, scales nationally like radio cannot, and costs far less than television. Television is rejected as unaffordable and untargeted; local radio is rejected as too narrow for the enrolment target, so EAL should add targeted school and careers-fair follow-up to convert the leads.

    Mark scheme: level_1_1_to_4: Identifies promotional options with limited application to EAL. | level_2_5_to_8: Discusses advantages and disadvantages of at least two options in the context of EAL with some judgement. | level_3_9_to_12: Discusses all three options in EAL's context with a well-justified recommendation explaining why television and local radio are rejected.

  Q2(a) [8 marks]
    Question: EAL's student dropout has reached 12% and tutor absenteeism is rising. Explain two benefits for EAL of using laissez-faire leadership to improve motivation among its tutors.
    Answer: Point 1: Laissez-faire leadership lets EAL's experienced tutors design their own livestreamed tutorials, giving them autonomy and ownership that raise job satisfaction and help address the 12% dropout through more engaging, tutor-led delivery. In a flat structure of 80 staff this freedom suits skilled professionals.

--- MAIN STEM ---
Citywide Cleaning Services (CCS) is a private limited company in the consumer services sector, providing commercial and domestic cleaning with a workforce of 60. Founded in 2011 by Marcus Bell, the business operates a hierarchical organisational structure with autocratic leadership. CCS plans to invest $250,000 in a fleet of electric cleaning vans and eco-friendly equipment, financed by a $150,000 five-year bank loan and $100,000 retained profit. It has fixed costs of $96,000 a year, a variable cost of $18 a unit and a selling price of $50, and currently produces 8,400 units a year. CCS faces two problems: customer complaints about missed slots have risen and cleaner absenteeism has reached 11%.

--- APPENDIX 1 — MARKETING/OPS ---
Operations and Quality Report - Q3 2025: CCS completed 2,100 cleaning jobs last quarter at a re-clean rate of 3.4%, down from 5.2% a year ago. Customer complaints fell from 64 to 33 per month. Average response time to a new booking is 1.8 days. A survey of 500 households found that 66% would pay $6 more for eco-friendly cleaning and 59% choose a cleaner on reliability ratings. A training audit shows 18 of 60 cleaners have not completed on-the-job training on the new electric-van equipment; off-the-job training courses at the local college cost $600 per employee.

--- APPENDIX 2 — FINANCIAL DATA ---

Gross profit | 480 | 630
Operating profit | 132 | 210
Capital employed | 880 | 1,200
Interest payable | 20 | 26

(2) The national minimum wage will rise by 8.2% from $13.96 to $15.10 per hour from April 2026, raising total wage bills. (3) Fuel and eco-cleaning product input costs have risen 11.5% year-on-year, while household spending on cleaning services grew 3.1% in the same period.

    Answer: Point 1: Retained profit requires no interest or capital repayments, protecting CCS's cash flow while it already services a $150,000 bank loan and fixed costs of $96,000 a year. The saving helps absorb the 11.5% rise in fuel and eco-product costs without raising the $50 job price.

Point 2: Using $100,000 of retained profit avoids extra collateral and default risk, so the van fleet is not jeopardised if demand for cleaning jobs falls short of the 8,400-unit target. It also keeps Marcus Bell's ownership intact with no lender conditions on how the eco-friendly equipment is deployed.

Keeping $100,000 internal also gives CCS room to fund the $600 retraining for 18 cleaners and to absorb the 11.5% fuel rise without raising the $50 price and losing the 66% of households willing to pay $6 more. With revenue rising from $1,200,000 to $1,500,000, an internal contribution avoids adding a fixed repayment just as the van fleet adds fixed costs, leaving the 5,400-job margin of safety intact.

--- MAIN STEM ---
Brightpath Homecare (BHC) is a private limited company in the healthcare sector, providing domiciliary care visits with a workforce of 95. Founded in 2007 by Samuel Okafor, the business operates a flat organisational structure with democratic leadership. It has fixed costs of $180,000 a year, a variable cost of $22 a unit and a selling price of $58, and currently produces 10,500 units a year. BHC faces two problems: care-visit cancellations have risen in recent months and carer absenteeism has reached 10%.

--- APPENDIX 1 — MARKETING/OPS ---
Quality and Visits Report - Q3 2025: BHC delivered 2,650 care visits last quarter with a missed-visit rate of 2.9%, down from 4.6% a year ago. Client complaints fell from 41 to 22 per month. Average response time to a new care request is 2.1 days. A survey of 350 families found that 73% would pay $12 more for app-based visit tracking and 61% choose a provider on carer reliability. --- APPENDIX 2 — FINANCIAL DATA ---

(2) The national minimum wage will rise by 7.1% from $13.26 to $14.20 per hour from April 2026, raising total wage bills. (3) Homecare fuel and protective-equipment input costs have risen 8.8% year-on-year, while household spending on homecare grew 5.4% in the same period.

--- QUESTIONS ---
  Q1(a) [8 marks]
    Question: BHC plans to acquire the electric care vans for its $320,000 expansion. Explain two advantages for BHC of using hire purchase instead of a bank loan to fund the $200,000 of vans.
    Answer: Point 1: Hire purchase spreads the $200,000 cost into manageable instalments and secures the vans immediately, so BHC can start the app-based visit-tracking service without a large lump-sum outflow, protecting cash flow alongside fixed costs of $180,000 a year and the 8.8% input-cost rise.

Point 2: Unlike the bank loan, hire purchase needs no separate collateral and keeps the $120,000 retained profit intact as a buffer for care-visit cancellations. It also preserves Samuel Okafor's control, since no bank covenants restrict how the scheduling app and vans are operated.

Hire purchase also matches the asset's life: the three vans generate visits over several years, so spreading $200,000 aligns payments with the $36 contribution on each of the 10,500 visits. It leaves the $120,000 retained profit available for the $820 carer retraining and for absorbing the 8.8% fuel rise, which matters when missed visits are already rising. Samuel Okafor keeps control because no bank covenant can dictate how the scheduling app is used.
    Keywords: hire purchase, $200,000, $120,000, $320,000, bank loan, $180,000
    Mark scheme: knowledge_max_2: 1 mark for each valid advantage of hire purchase over a bank loan (max 2). | application_analysis_max_6: Up to 3 marks per point for contextual explanation applied to BHC's expansion, financing and cost data.

  Q1(b) [12 marks]
    Question: BHC is launching its new app-based visit-tracking service. Consider local newspaper advertising, community radio sponsorship or social media influencer marketing. Which should BHC choose to promote the launch? Justify your recommendation.
    Answer: Local newspaper advertising: Local papers reach families in BHC's operating area and can show the tracking app, but readership is falling, print is costly for a 95-carer firm funding a $320,000 expansion, and response cannot be measured precisely.

Newspapers cannot show the tracking app and radio reaches only a local area, whereas families across the service region can be reached digitally. With 2,650 visits last quarter and a 2.9% missed-visit rate, a measurable campaign is essential to justify the $320,000 expansion.

--- MAIN STEM ---
Preston Premier Leisure (PPL) is a private limited company in the consumer services sector, running a fitness and leisure club with a workforce of 70. Founded in 1998 by Chloe Grant, the business operates a hierarchical organisational structure with democratic leadership. PPL plans to invest $420,000 in a gym extension with a swimming pool and smart-access technology, financed by a $250,000 ten-year bank loan and a $170,000 share issue. It has fixed costs of $210,000 a year, a variable cost of $14 a unit and a selling price of $44, and currently produces 15,000 units a year. PPL faces two problems: equipment breakdown downtime has risen and staff absenteeism has reached 9%.

--- APPENDIX 1 — MARKETING/OPS ---
Operations and Quality Report - Q3 2025: PPL recorded 3,800 member visits last quarter with an equipment-fault rate of 4.1%, down from 6.3% a year ago. Member complaints fell from 55 to 27 per month. Average queue time at reception is 4.5 minutes. A survey of 650 gym members found that 69% would pay $18 more for the new pool and smart-access facilities and 58% choose a gym on equipment reliability. A training audit shows 22 of 70 staff have not completed on-the-job training on the smart-access system; off-the-job training courses at the local college cost $950 per employee.

--- APPENDIX 2 — FINANCIAL DATA ---

Point 2: Equity spreads the risk of the new pool and smart-access facilities among shareholders, so the club is not exposed to loan covenants or repossession if visitor numbers miss the 15,000 target. It also enlarges the capital base supporting the $420,000 investment without increasing the interest payable already shown in Appendix 2.

A share issue keeps the $250,000 bank loan as the only debt and leaves the $18 premium and 69% willingness-to-pay to drive revenue without an extra repayment schedule. That resilience matters while the 4.1% equipment-fault rate and 9% absenteeism are being tackled.

--- MAIN STEM ---
Ridgeline Quarry Aggregates (RQA) is a private limited company in the crushed-stone extraction sector in the Scottish Highlands, employing a workforce of 52. Founded in 2008 by Fiona Ridgeline, it supplies road-building aggregate to regional contractors and operates a hierarchical structure with autocratic leadership. RQA plans to invest $920,000 in a new mobile stone-crushing and screening plant with low-dust eco-technology, financed by a $600,000 ten-year bank loan and $320,000 retained profit. It has fixed costs of $300,000 a year, a variable cost of $8.50 a unit and a selling price of $14.50, and produces 100,000 units a year. RQA faces two problems: dust complaints from nearby residents have risen and the defect rate for off-specification aggregate has reached 4.2%.

--- APPENDIX 1 — MARKETING/OPS ---
Operations and Quality Report — Q4 2025: The crushing line dispatched 24,000 tonnes of aggregate last quarter at an off-specification defect rate of 4.2%, up from 2.6% a year earlier. Dust complaints from residents rose from 9 to 17 per month. Average lorry turnaround is 42 minutes. Market research of 500 local contractors found that 68% would pay up to $0.50 more per tonne for low-dust, recycled-content aggregate, and 57% check environmental credentials before ordering.     Question: Using Appendix 3, evaluate how the rise in the base interest rate to 5.25%, the 5.8% minimum wage increase and the 11.2% rise in input costs will affect RQA. Which change will have the greatest impact? Justify your answer.
    Answer: Interest rate rise (4.50% to 5.25%): If RQA's $600,000 ten-year bank loan is variable-rate, the 0.75 percentage-point increase adds 0.0075 × $600,000 = $4,500 a year (shown derivation). That is modest beside fixed costs of $300,000 a year, and if the loan is fixed-rate the extra cost is zero. Higher rates may still make future borrowing for the $920,000 plant more expensive and could dampen the 2.8% growth in road-building orders.

Minimum wage increase (5.8%, from $13.00 to $13.75 an hour): RQA employs a workforce of 52 at labour-intensive quarry sites, so this rise feeds into wage bills and cannot be avoided. The insert gives no hours worked and no individual pay rates, so no annual wage total can be honestly calculated; the correct approach is qualitative, judged against labour productivity of 100,000 units ÷ 52 workers = 1,923.1 units per worker (arithmetic shown from insert figures). Productivity must hold or output rise, or unit labour costs will climb and squeeze the $6.00 contribution from the $14.50 selling price less $8.50 variable cost.

Input cost inflation (11.2%): The insert does not decompose the $8.50 variable cost, so only an explicitly labelled upper bound can be computed: if the entire variable cost rose 11.2%, that is 0.112 × $8.50 = $0.952, about $0.95 a unit; across 100,000 units this is 100,000 × $0.952 = $95,200 a year. Even a smaller pass-through would materially reduce contribution, and the 6.4% construction-cost inflation makes price recovery harder, though the $0.50 premium backed by 68% of surveyed contractors offers partial protection.

Conclusion: The 11.2% rise in input costs will have the greatest impact. It multiplies across all 100,000 units and directly erodes the $6.00 contribution that justifies the $920,000 plant, whereas the interest effect is a conditional $4,500 and the wage effect cannot even be quantified from the insert and can be offset by productivity. RQA should secure the premium and renegotiate feedstock contracts.
    Keywords: 5.25%, 5.8%, 11.2%, $600,000, $8.50, 100,000, 4.50%
    Mark scheme: level_1_1_to_4: Identifies the three external changes with limited application to RQA. | level_2_5_to_8: Analyses the impact of at least two changes on RQA's costs or financing in context with shown arithmetic where figures are used. | level_3_9_to_12: Detailed evaluation of all three changes in context, with derivations shown and a well-justified judgement that input-cost inflation has the greatest impact.

--- MAIN STEM ---
Earthwise Eco Blocks (EBM) is a private limited company in the eco-building-materials sector in south Wales, employing a workforce of 48. Founded in 2013 by Gareth Powell, it makes recycled composite building blocks for housebuilders and operates a flat structure with democratic leadership. EBM plans to invest $760,000 in an automated eco-block moulding line using recycled quarry fines, financed by a $400,000 ten-year bank loan and a $360,000 share issue. It has fixed costs of $228,000 a year, a variable cost of $5.20 a block and a selling price of $10.00, and produces 90,000 units a year. EBM has two problems: waste from cracked blocks has risen and quality complaints from housebuilders reached 3.8% of deliveries last quarter.

--- APPENDIX 1 — MARKETING/OPS ---
Operations and Quality Report — Q1 2026: The eco-block line moulded 21,600 blocks last quarter, of which 3.8% were cracked and rejected, down from 5.1% a year ago. Customer complaints from housebuilders fell from 26 to 14 per month. Average cure time is 18 hours. Market research of 400 housebuilders found that 62% would pay up to $0.35 more for blocks containing recycled quarry fines, and 54% require environmental certificates on tender documents. A training audit shows 12 of 48 operatives have not used the new moulding line; certified off-the-job courses at the regional college cost $880 per employee.

--- APPENDIX 2 — FINANCIAL DATA ---

A share issue also brings in investors with construction contacts, useful when 54% of surveyed housebuilders demand environmental certificates and EBM must win specifications.     Question: Using Appendix 3, evaluate how the rise in the base interest rate to 4.50%, the 6.2% minimum wage increase and the 9.8% rise in input costs will affect EBM. Which change will have the greatest impact? Justify your answer.
    Answer: Interest rate rise (3.75% to 4.50%): If EBM's $400,000 ten-year bank loan is variable-rate, the 0.75 percentage-point rise adds 0.0075 × $400,000 = $3,000 a year (derivation shown). This is small compared with fixed costs of $228,000, and if the loan is fixed-rate the increase is zero. Minimum wage increase (6.2%, from $12.90 to $13.70 per hour): EBM has a workforce of 48 at a labour-intensive moulding plant, so the rise pushes up wage bills and cannot be avoided. The insert states neither hours worked nor individual pay, so an annual wage total cannot be calculated honestly; the right approach is qualitative, benchmarked against labour productivity of 90,000 units ÷ 48 workers = 1,875 units per worker (arithmetic shown from insert figures). Conclusion: The 9.8% rise in input costs will have the greatest impact. It applies to every one of the 90,000 blocks and directly erodes the $4.80 contribution underpinning the $760,000 investment, whereas the interest change is a conditional $3,000 and the wage change cannot even be quantified from the insert and can be offset by productivity. --- MAIN STEM ---
GreenTimber Prefabrication (GTP) is a public limited company in the sustainable timber construction sector in coastal British Columbia, employing a workforce of 64. Founded in 2006 by Isla Green, it manufactures timber-frame wall panels for low-carbon housing and operates a hierarchical structure with democratic leadership. GTP plans to invest $1,050,000 in a new computer-aided panel-cutting plant using certified reclaimed timber, financed by a $450,000 bank loan and a $600,000 share issue. It has fixed costs of $350,000 a year, a variable cost of $12.00 a panel and a selling price of $19.00, and produces 85,000 units a year. GTP faces a skills gap in operating the new cutting machines and timber waste has risen to 6.1% of input.

--- APPENDIX 1 — MARKETING/OPS ---
Operations and Quality Report — Q2 2025: The panel plant produced 20,400 units last quarter, with timber waste at 6.1% of input, down from 8.3% a year earlier. Customer quality complaints fell from 31 to 18 per month. Average panel changeover time is 26 minutes. Market research of 350 housebuilders found that 71% would pay up to $0.60 more for certified low-carbon panels, and 49% check chain-of-custody certificates before ordering. A skills audit shows 19 of 64 staff cannot yet operate the computer-aided cutting machines; accredited off-the-job courses at the forestry college cost $1,050 per employee.

--- APPENDIX 2 — FINANCIAL DATA ---

Capital employed | 4,000 | 4,250

(3) Wholesale reclaimed-timber and adhesive costs have risen 10.4% year-on-year, construction-cost inflation is 5.9%, and low-carbon housing starts grew 6.3% over the same period.

  Q1(a) [8 marks]
    Question: GTP raised $600,000 through a share issue for its $1,050,000 cutting plant. Explain two disadvantages for GTP of using a share issue rather than more bank borrowing alongside the $450,000 loan.
    Answer: Point 1: A share issue dilutes existing ownership and control, so Isla Green and current shareholders give up a stake in GTP. Unlike the $450,000 bank loan, which is repaid and then ends, new equity holders may demand dividends and voting rights indefinitely, reducing the rewards from the $19.00 panels and the 85,000-unit output.

Point 2: Equity is usually more expensive than debt over the long term because investors expect a return that reflects the risk of a new $1,050,000 plant, whereas loan interest on a $450,000 facility is contractually fixed. Issuing shares also involves legal and advisory costs and possible delay, which could hold up the computer-aided cutting machines while the 6.1% timber waste and 19 untrained staff remain unresolved. With fixed costs of $350,000 a year, any reduction in contribution from dividend payments would make the 50,000-unit break-even harder to clear. The board must also weigh that a $600,000 share issue permanently gives away a slice of future profits on 85,000 panels, whereas the $450,000 loan ends once repaid.

    Answer: Selling direct to housebuilders: A direct sales team can explain chain-of-custody certification and the low-carbon story to the 49% of 350 surveyed builders who check certificates before ordering, and can negotiate the $0.60 premium that 71% would pay. E-commerce portal: An online catalogue with downloadable certificates could cut order costs and reach smaller builders cheaply, with measurable enquiries. Yet panels are bulky and buyers expect delivery scheduling and technical advice; a portal alone cannot build the relationships needed for specification decisions, and it does nothing to solve the 6.1% waste problem.

Recommendation: GTP should sell direct to housebuilders. It protects the premium, communicates certification and captures feedback needed to cut waste, which matters for the $1,050,000 investment. Builders' merchants are rejected because their margin demands and weak message control undermine premium positioning; the e-commerce portal is rejected as unsuitable for a bulky, specification-driven product, though it can support direct selling as an ordering tool.

--- MAIN STEM ---
Coastal Reclaim Aggregates (CRA) is a cooperative in the demolition-waste recycling sector near Rotterdam, employing a workforce of 60 member-workers. Established in 2011 by a group of contractors led by Anouk de Vries, it supplies reclaimed aggregate to road contractors and operates a flat structure with democratic leadership. CRA plans to invest $840,000 in a mobile recycling crusher and eco-screening plant, financed by a $500,000 ten-year bank loan and $340,000 retained profit. It has fixed costs of $264,000 a year, a variable cost of $4.80 a tonne and a selling price of $9.20, and produces 110,000 units a year. CRA faces contamination in incoming demolition waste and the defect rate for off-specification reclaimed aggregate has reached 3.6%.

--- APPENDIX 1 — MARKETING/OPS ---
Operations and Quality Report — Q3 2025: The recycling line processed 27,500 tonnes last quarter, with a 3.6% off-specification rate caused by contamination, down from 4.9% a year earlier. Complaints from road contractors about dirty aggregate fell from 22 to 11 per month. Average lorry queue time is 35 minutes. Market research of 450 contractors found that 66% would pay up to $0.45 more per tonne for screened, low-contamination reclaimed aggregate, and 61% check recycled-content documentation before tendering. A skills audit shows 18 of 60 member-workers have not been trained on the new eco-screening plant; accredited courses at the regional college cost $920 per person.

--- APPENDIX 2 — FINANCIAL DATA ---
Title: Extract from the Statement of Profit or Loss and Capital employed data of Coastal Reclaim Aggregates for the year ended 31 March 2025 ($ '000)
Headers: ['Financial Metric', '2024', '2025']

Cost of sales | 2,730 | 2,880
Gross profit | 1,470 | 1,920
Operating profit | 504 | 720
Capital employed | 2,800 | 3,200
Interest expense | 56 | 64

--- APPENDIX 3 — EXTERNAL ENVIRONMENT ---

(2) The national minimum wage will rise by 7.1% from $12.60 to $13.49 per hour from April 2026, raising wage bills at labour-intensive recycling sites. (3) Wholesale diesel, crusher wear-part and transport costs have risen 8.9% year-on-year, construction-cost inflation is 4.7%, and regional demolition activity grew 3.2% over the same period.

    Answer: Point 1: Retained profit requires no repayments or interest, so CRA avoids adding to the debt service on its $500,000 ten-year bank loan. With fixed costs of $264,000 a year and only a $4.40 contribution on each tonne, keeping cash in the cooperative protects the 60 member-workers' returns and can fund screening improvements to cut the 3.6% contamination defect rate.

Point 2: Using retained profit does not dilute members' ownership or require further capital calls from the cooperative, preserving the flat, democratic structure led by Anouk de Vries. A new share issue would ask members for more money and could create disputes about control, whereas retained profit is already available and can be applied flexibly, for example to the $920 accredited courses for the 18 untrained workers, without approaching outside investors. This matters because a cooperative relies on member confidence: keeping the $840,000 plant funded from $340,000 of past profits avoids asking the 60 members for fresh capital while the 3.6% defect rate is still being reduced.
    Keywords: retained profit, $340,000, $500,000, $840,000, fixed costs, workforce of 60
    Mark scheme: knowledge_max_2: 1 mark for each valid advantage identified (max 2). | application_analysis_max_6: Up to 3 marks per point for contextual explanation and analysis applied to CRA's cooperative structure, financing and operating data.

    Question: CRA wants more road contractors to buy its screened reclaimed aggregate. Consider a road-building trade fair, trade-press advertising, or a direct mailshot to contractors. Which should CRA choose to promote the new eco-screening plant? Justify your recommendation.
    Answer: Road-building trade fair: A trade fair lets CRA show screened samples and recycled-content documents to the 61% of 450 surveyed contractors who check such paperwork, and staff can explain how contamination is reduced from 4.9% to 3.6%.     Question: CRA is a cooperative with a flat structure and democratic leadership. Explain two benefits for CRA of this leadership approach when tackling contamination and the 11 monthly complaints.

However, profit sharing is delayed and diluted across many members, so the link between an individual's screening effort and reward is weak, and it pays out even if contamination remains high.

Decision: CRA should choose a bonus for clean screened loads. It targets the exact 3.6% problem and gives an immediate, measurable incentive across the 27,500-tonne operation. Profit sharing is rejected because its reward is indirect and spread too thinly to change daily screening behaviour; it can be introduced later as a general reward once the defect rate is under control. A clean-load bonus is also affordable because it rewards only verified improvements in the 27,500-tonne quarterly output, whereas profit sharing would spread any gain across all 60 members regardless of who reduced contamination.
    Keywords: workforce of 60, 3.6%, $0.45, 27,500, $840,000, $920
    Mark scheme: level_1_1_to_4: Basic description of the two motivators with limited application to CRA. | level_2_5_to_8: Detailed analysis of benefits and drawbacks of both motivators in the context of CRA. | level_3_9_to_12: Comprehensive evaluation of both motivators with a well-justified decision covering incentives, fairness and the defect problem.

ROCE 2025 = 22.5%

Detailed workings: Gross profit 1,470 ÷ revenue 4,200 × 100 = 35.0% in 2024; 1,920 ÷ 4,800 × 100 = 40.0% in 2025. Operating profit 504 ÷ revenue 4,200 × 100 = 12.0%; 720 ÷ 4,800 × 100 = 15.0%. Operating profit 504 ÷ capital employed 2,800 × 100 = 18.0%; 720 ÷ 3,200 × 100 = 22.5%. Revenue rose from 4,200 to 4,800 while cost of sales increased from 2,730 to 2,880, so gross profit grew from 1,470 to 1,920. Capital employed rose from 2,800 to 3,200 as the $840,000 plant was commissioned, and interest expense increased from 56 to 64.

Evaluation: All three measures moved favourably, so the improvement is consistent. The wider gap between revenue and cost of sales fits the 66% of contractors who would pay $0.45 more for screened aggregate, and operating profit grew faster than revenue, showing control of overheads despite higher interest. Returns on the enlarged capital base also improved, encouraging for a newly installed crusher. Caution is needed: the 3.6% contamination defect rate and 8.9% diesel and wear-part inflation could raise costs in the next period, and the $920 training gap among 18 members may limit efficiency.

Conclusion: CRA's profitability has improved. Gross and operating margins and returns on capital all rose together, so the judgement is robust; management should secure the $0.45 premium and reduce contamination to protect it.

    Question: Using Appendix 3, evaluate how the rise in the base interest rate to 4.25%, the 7.1% minimum wage increase and the 8.9% rise in input costs will affect CRA. Which change will have the greatest impact? Justify your answer.
    Answer: Interest rate rise (3.50% to 4.25%): If CRA's $500,000 ten-year bank loan is variable-rate, the 0.75 percentage-point increase adds 0.0075 × $500,000 = $3,750 a year (derivation shown). --- MAIN STEM ---
TerraPave Eco Surfaces (TPE) is a public limited company in the eco-surface construction-materials sector in Victoria, Australia, employing a workforce of 78. Founded in 2004 by Nadia Terra, it makes permeable paving tiles from recycled rubber and glass for city councils and operates a hierarchical structure with autocratic leadership. TPE plans to invest $1,200,000 in a new recycled-rubber tile press with low-energy curing, financed by a $700,000 ten-year bank loan and a $500,000 share issue. It has fixed costs of $408,000 a year, a variable cost of $9.60 a tile and a selling price of $16.00, and produces 120,000 units a year. TPE faces variable input quality from recycled feedstock and waste has risen to 5.4% of output, with complaint counts climbing.

--- APPENDIX 1 — MARKETING/OPS ---
Operations and Quality Report — Q4 2025: The tile press produced 28,800 tiles last quarter, with waste at 5.4% of output, up from 3.9% a year earlier. Complaints from city councils about inconsistent surface finish rose from 14 to 23 per month. Average press changeover is 32 minutes. Market research of 380 councils and landscapers found that 59% would pay up to $0.55 more for permeable recycled-rubber tiles, and 63% check environmental product declarations before specifying. A training audit shows 21 of 78 operators have not used the new low-energy curing system; accredited courses at the technical institute cost $970 per employee.

Once the $700,000 loan is repaid, the ownership remains intact, so future profits from the 120,000 tiles continue to benefit current holders.

Nadia Terra also keeps full control of the $1,200,000 press strategy, including how to tackle the 5.4% waste and 23 monthly complaints, without shareholder pressure for short-term dividends.

--- MAIN STEM ---
Terrace Grove Beverages (TGB) is a private limited company in the craft soft-drink sector, employing a workforce of 52. Founded in 2012 by Priya Raval, it bottles sparkling fruit drinks for regional supermarkets and health-food chains and operates a flat organisational structure with democratic leadership. TGB plans to invest $720,000 in a new automated bottling line with recyclable glass bottles, financed by a $420,000 ten-year bank loan and $300,000 retained profit. It has fixed costs of $180,000 a year, a variable cost of $4.80 a unit and a selling price of $9.30, and currently produces 80,000 units a year. TGB faces two problems: absenteeism has reached 8%, labour turnover is rising, and waste on the bottling line has reached 6%.

--- APPENDIX 1 — MARKETING/OPS ---
Operations and Quality Report — Q2 2025: The sparkling-drink line filled 18,000 bottles last month at a defect rate of 2.4%, down from 3.6% a year ago. Customer complaints fell from 44 to 19 per month. Average order fulfilment time is 2.8 days. A survey of 450 shoppers found that 61% would pay up to $0.35 more for recyclable bottles, and 48% check packaging before buying. A skills audit shows 14 of 52 staff have not completed on-the-job training on the new filler; off-the-job training at the local college costs $750 per employee.

--- APPENDIX 2 — FINANCIAL DATA ---
Title: Extract from the Statement of Financial Position of Terrace Grove Beverages as at 31 March 2025 ($ '000)
Headers: ['Financial Metric', '2024', '2025']
Inventories | 70 | 68
Trade receivables | 125 | 150
Cash and cash equivalents | 45 | 62
Current liabilities | 200 | 200
Non-current assets | 1,300 | 1,520
Capital employed | 1,750 | 2,000

--- APPENDIX 3 — EXTERNAL ENVIRONMENT ---
Economic and Business Bulletin (October 2026): (1) The central bank raised the base interest rate from 4.25% to 5.00%, increasing borrowing costs on TGB's variable-rate loan. (2) The national minimum wage will rise by 5.8% from $13.50 to $14.28 per hour from April 2026, lifting TGB's wage bill. (3) Wholesale sugar, juice and glass input costs have risen 9.6% year-on-year, while consumer spending on sparkling drinks grew 2.9%.

--- QUESTIONS ---
  Q1(a) [8 marks]
    Question: TGB plans to finance part of its bottling-line expansion with a $420,000 ten-year bank loan. Explain two advantages for TGB of using retained profit instead of the bank loan.
    Answer: Point 1: Using retained profit costs TGB nothing in interest or capital repayments, which protects cash flow at a time when the firm already carries a $420,000 bank loan and has committed $720,000 to the new bottling line. Every dollar not paid as interest can instead absorb the 9.6% rise in juice, sugar and glass input costs, helping TGB hold its $9.30 selling price for regional supermarkets rather than passing costs on and risking lost shelf space.

Point 2: Retained profit avoids the collateral and default risk attached to a bank loan, so the $300,000 is available without putting TGB's recyclable-glass bottling line at risk of repossession if demand for sparkling drinks falls short of the 80,000-unit plan. It also preserves founder Priya Raval's ownership and control: no lender can impose conditions on how the flat, democratic team runs the filler or allocates the $180,000 a year of fixed costs. Retained profit is therefore the cheaper and lower-risk source for this particular expansion.
    Keywords: retained profit, bank loan, $420,000, $300,000, $720,000, $180,000
    Mark scheme: knowledge_max_2: 1 mark for each valid point identified (max 2). | application_analysis_max_6: Up to 3 marks per point for contextual explanation linked to TGB's costs, expansion and financing mix.

  Q1(b) [12 marks]
    Question: TGB is launching a new recyclable-bottle sparkling drink. Consider national television advertising, local radio sponsorship, or social media influencer marketing. Which should TGB choose to promote the launch? Justify your recommendation.
    Answer: National television advertising: A national TV campaign would build brand awareness for the new recyclable-bottle sparkling drink across all the regional supermarkets and health-food chains that stock TGB, reaching millions of viewers quickly. However, airtime and production costs are very high for a 52-employee business that has just committed $720,000 to a bottling line, and much of the national audience lies outside TGB's regional distribution, so a large share of the spend would be wasted.

Local radio sponsorship: Local radio is far cheaper than television and reaches TGB's core regional catchment with time-sensitive launch messages, fitting the 2.8-day order-fulfilment story and the 18,000-bottle monthly volume. Its weakness is narrow reach: TGB also supplies health-food chains beyond the local area, so radio alone cannot generate the 80,000-unit volume needed to justify the new filler.

Social media influencer marketing: Food and lifestyle influencers can target exactly the 61% of 450 surveyed shoppers who would pay up to $0.35 more for recyclable bottles and the 48% who check packaging before buying. Engagement is measurable, cost per reached shopper is low, and the recyclable-glass story can be shown directly to health-conscious buyers nationally. Results build more slowly than TV and depend on influencer credibility, but the segment fit is strongest.

Recommendation: TGB should choose social media influencer marketing. It reaches the precise research-identified segment, costs far less than national television, and scales nationally unlike local radio, while reinforcing the recyclable-bottle positioning that supports the $9.30 selling price. Television is rejected as unaffordable and untargeted for a 52-staff firm funding a $720,000 expansion; radio is rejected as too narrow for its widening distribution. TGB should add modest in-store supermarket displays to convert the interest the influencers generate.
    Keywords: recyclable bottles, 18,000, 61%, $0.35, 52, 450
    Mark scheme: level_1_1_to_4: Identifies promotional options with limited reference to TGB. | level_2_5_to_8: Discusses advantages and disadvantages of at least two options in TGB's context with some judgement. | level_3_9_to_12: Discusses all three options in TGB's context and recommends influencer marketing with clear reasons for rejecting television and radio.

  Q2(a) [8 marks]
    Question: TGB's absenteeism has reached 8% and labour turnover is rising. Explain two benefits for TGB of using democratic leadership to improve motivation on the bottling line.
    Answer: Point 1: Democratic leadership gives TGB's 52 employees a real voice in how the new bottling line is organised, which helps satisfy social and esteem needs and raises job satisfaction. Workers who help set filler routines and shift patterns are more likely to attend consistently, directly reducing the 8% absenteeism rate and easing pressure on the flat structure without adding supervisors.

Point 2: Involving staff in decisions also draws on the practical knowledge of the people who handle the filler every day, generating ideas that can cut the 6% bottling-line waste and protect the 2.4% defect rate. Higher involvement raises commitment and lowers labour turnover, avoiding further $750-per-employee off-the-job training costs at the local college and protecting output of 80,000 units while the $720,000 line beds in. Democratic leadership therefore tackles both motivation and quality at low cost.

    Mark scheme: knowledge_max_2: 1 mark for each valid point identified (max 2). | application_analysis_max_6: Up to 3 marks per point for development linked to TGB's absenteeism, waste, training costs and output.

  Q2(b) [12 marks]
    Question: TGB must upskill 14 production staff to operate the new filler. Consider on-the-job training or off-the-job training at the local college. Which should TGB choose? Justify your decision.
    Answer: On-the-job training: Training at the filler is directly relevant to TGB's own machines and quality standards, costs no course fees, and keeps the 14 staff productive while they learn, protecting the 18,000-bottle monthly output and the improvement to a 2.4% defect rate. Drawbacks are that the trainers are production staff whose own work suffers, bad habits can be passed on, and there is no external certificate, which may matter if supermarket chains demand formal records.

Off-the-job training: The local college course at $750 per employee gives structured, up-to-date skills and a recognised qualification for all 14 staff, costing $10,500 in total — modest beside the $720,000 investment. It removes staff from the line, however, reducing short-term capacity when absenteeism is already 8%, and generic content may not match TGB's exact filler settings, so follow-up coaching on site would still be needed.

Decision: TGB should choose on-the-job training for the initial rollout, backed by short college sessions for the most senior operators. On-the-job training is cheapest, machine-specific and avoids further output loss while 8% absenteeism already strains the line; full off-the-job training is rejected because spending $10,500 and withdrawing 14 staff would disrupt the supermarket delivery schedule, and TGB can add college visits later once the new filler stabilises.
    Keywords: on-the-job training, off-the-job training, $750, 14, 52, 2.4%

    Question: Explain one advantage and one disadvantage for TGB of using recyclable bottles for its sparkling-drink range.
    Answer: Advantage: Recyclable bottles match the preferences of the 61% of 450 surveyed shoppers who would pay up to $0.35 more, allowing TGB to protect the $4.50 contribution per unit as the 9.6% rise in sugar, juice and glass input costs bites.     Question: Using Appendix 3, evaluate how the interest rate rise to 5.00%, the 5.8% minimum wage increase and the 9.6% rise in input costs will affect TGB. Which change will have the greatest impact? Justify your answer.
    Answer: Interest rate rise (4.25% to 5.00%): If TGB's $420,000 bank loan is variable-rate, the annual interest cost rises by 0.75% of $420,000 = $3,150 a year (0.0075 × $420,000). That is small beside $180,000 of fixed costs, and if the loan were fixed-rate the effect would be zero. Higher rates may make consumers more cautious about premium sparkling drinks and raise the cost of any future borrowing, but TGB can largely cap this risk by fixing the loan rate.

Minimum wage increase (5.8%, to $14.28 per hour): TGB employs a workforce of 52 in bottling and packing roles, so this rise feeds directly into the wage bill and cannot be avoided. The insert gives no hours worked or individual pay rates, so no total wage bill can be honestly invented; the sound judgement is against the given productivity data — 80,000 units ÷ 52 staff is about 1,538 units per worker, so the rise is affordable only if productivity holds or output grows, otherwise unit labour cost erodes the $4.50 contribution.

Input cost inflation (9.6% sugar, juice and glass): The insert never decomposes the $4.80 variable cost, so only a bound is defensible — if the whole variable cost rose 9.6% it would add 9.6% × $4.80 = $0.46 per unit, and at 80,000 units that is about $36,800 a year. Even a smaller pass-through would cut contribution below $4.50. TGB can recover part through the $0.35 recyclable-bottle premium and supermarket price talks, but the effect repeats on every bottle.

Conclusion: The 9.6% input-cost rise will have the greatest impact. It compounds across all 80,000 units, directly erodes the $4.50 contribution that justifies the $720,000 line, and cannot be neutralised by fixing a loan rate as the interest risk can. The wage rise is significant but manageable through productivity; the interest rise is the smallest.
    Keywords: 5.00%, 5.8%, 9.6%, $14.28, $4.80, $420,000

--- MAIN STEM ---
Marrowvale Foods (MVF) is a private limited company in the frozen-food sector, employing a workforce of 38. Founded in 2011 by Tomas Vale, it supplies frozen vegetable meals to supermarket chains and cash-and-carry wholesalers and operates a hierarchical organisational structure with autocratic leadership. MVF plans to invest $640,000 in a new freezing and packing line with recyclable cartons, financed by a $400,000 share issue and $240,000 retained profit. It has fixed costs of $160,000 a year, a variable cost of $5.20 a unit and a selling price of $10.20, and currently produces 70,000 units a year. MVF faces two problems: quality complaints have risen and waste on the packing line has reached 7%.

--- APPENDIX 1 — MARKETING/OPS ---
Quality and Operations Report — Q1 2025: The freezing line packed 16,500 units last quarter at a defect rate of 3.3%, up from 2.1% a year ago. Customer complaints rose from 26 to 41 per month. Average delivery time is 4.1 days. Market research of 380 shoppers found that 58% preferred recyclable cartons and 44% would pay up to $0.30 more. A skills audit shows 11 of 38 staff lack on-the-job training on the new freezer; off-the-job training at the local college costs $820 per employee.

--- APPENDIX 2 — FINANCIAL DATA ---

Current liabilities | 160 | 170
Non-current assets | 1,100 | 1,260
Capital employed | 1,500 | 1,700

(2) The national minimum wage will rise by 7.2% from $13.10 to $14.04 per hour from April 2026, lifting MVF's wage bill. (3) Wholesale vegetable and packaging costs have risen 11.3% year-on-year, and food-price inflation is 7.4%, while consumer spending on frozen meals grew 2.2%.

  Q1(a) [8 marks]
    Question: MVF funded part of its freezing-line expansion with a $400,000 share issue. Explain two advantages for MVF of using retained profit instead of the share issue.
    Answer: Point 1: Retained profit does not dilute existing ownership or control, so the $240,000 already inside MVF can fund the new freezing line without issuing new shares that would reduce founder Tomas Vale's stake and give outside shareholders a claim on future profits. This matters for a 38-employee private limited company where decisions must stay fast under its hierarchical structure.

Point 2: A share issue involves issue costs and can be hard to place when investor appetite is weak, whereas retained profit has no flotation expense and is immediately available. Using it keeps the $640,000 expansion within internal resources and leaves MVF's $160,000 a year of fixed costs and its developing $400,000 share proceeds free for other uses, such as absorbing the 11.3% rise in vegetable and packaging costs without raising the $10.20 selling price.
    Keywords: retained profit, share issue, $400,000, $240,000, $640,000, $160,000
