  Q1(b) [12 marks]
    Question: MVF is launching frozen meals in recyclable cartons. Consider national television advertising, trade fairs and exhibitions, or social media influencer marketing. Which should MVF choose? Justify your recommendation.
    Answer: National television advertising: A TV campaign would create rapid brand awareness for the new recyclable-carton meals across the supermarket chains that stock MVF. However, airtime is extremely expensive for a 38-staff frozen-food firm that has just committed $640,000 to a freezing line, and much of the audience would never see the product in the cash-and-carry wholesalers it supplies, so spending would be poorly targeted.

Trade fairs and exhibitions: These let MVF demonstrate the cartons directly to supermarket buyers and wholesale customers, generate firm orders and gather feedback on the 3.3% defect-rate concerns. They are far cheaper than television and fit a business-to-business selling model. The limits are narrow reach to the trade rather than final shoppers, high staff time, and only occasional timing, which may not sustain a launch across 16,500 units a quarter.

Social media influencer marketing: Recipe and family-food influencers can show the frozen meals being cooked and reach precisely the 58% of 380 surveyed shoppers who prefer recyclable cartons and the 44% who would pay up to $0.30 more. Engagement is measurable, cost per contact is low, and the message can run continuously. Results depend on influencer credibility and build more slowly than TV, but the fit with the research segment is strong.

Recommendation: MVF should choose social media influencer marketing. It targets the research-identified shoppers who value recyclable cartons, costs far less than television, and reaches final buyers that trade fairs cannot, while supporting the $10.20 price. Television is rejected as unaffordable and untargeted for a 38-person business funding a $640,000 line; trade fairs are rejected as too narrow and occasional to sustain volume. MVF should complement influencers with a small presence at key trade fairs to win listings.
    Keywords: recyclable cartons, 16,500, 3.3%, 58%, $0.30, 380

--- MAIN STEM ---
Bramblewick Creamery (BRW) is a cooperative in the dairy-processing sector, employing a workforce of 64. Founded in 2003 by farmer Nora Bramblewick, it produces yoghurts and fresh cream for supermarkets and independent delis and operates a flat organisational structure with laissez-faire leadership. BRW plans to invest $910,000 in a new yoghurt filling line with returnable glass jars, financed by a $560,000 ten-year bank loan and $350,000 hire purchase. It has fixed costs of $242,000 a year, a variable cost of $6.80 a unit and a selling price of $12.30, and currently produces 95,000 units a year. BRW faces two problems: labour turnover is rising and product waste has reached 5%.

--- APPENDIX 1 — MARKETING/OPS ---
Quality and Waste Report — Q4 2025: The filling line produced 24,000 pots last month at a defect rate of 2.7%, down from 4.0% a year ago. Customer complaints fell from 52 to 30 per month. Average delivery time is 3.6 days. A survey of 520 shoppers found that 66% preferred returnable glass jars and 57% would pay up to $0.45 more for them. A training review shows 18 of 64 staff need on-the-job training on the new filler; an off-the-job course at the college costs $780 per employee.

--- APPENDIX 2 — FINANCIAL DATA ---
Title: Extract from the Statement of Financial Position of Bramblewick Creamery as at 31 March 2025 ($ '000)
Headers: ['Financial Metric', '2024', '2025']
Inventories | 90 | 80
Trade receivables | 125 | 136
Cash and cash equivalents | 45 | 50
Current liabilities | 200 | 190
Non-current assets | 1,650 | 1,880
Capital employed | 2,100 | 2,350

--- APPENDIX 3 — EXTERNAL ENVIRONMENT ---
Economic and Business Bulletin (January 2027): (1) The central bank cut the base interest rate from 5.25% to 4.75%, reducing borrowing costs on BRW's variable-rate loan. (2) The national minimum wage will rise by 6.1% from $13.80 to $14.64 per hour from April 2026, raising wage costs. (3) Wholesale milk and glass input costs have risen 10.5% year-on-year, and dairy-product inflation is 6.8%, while consumer spending on yoghurt grew 3.1%.

--- QUESTIONS ---
  Q1(a) [8 marks]
    Question: BRW funds part of its filling-line expansion with a $560,000 bank loan. Explain two advantages for BRW of using hire purchase instead of the bank loan.
    Answer: Point 1: Hire purchase spreads the cost of the $350,000 filling equipment over regular payments, so BRW does not need to service the full $560,000 bank loan immediately and preserves cash for the cooperative's 64 members and its $242,000 a year of fixed costs. The equipment is used to generate output while it is paid for, helping fund the 95,000-unit plan.

Point 2: Hire purchase is secured on the specific asset, so it can be easier to arrange than a large unsecured loan and does not require BRW to pledge other dairy assets. With the base rate having fallen to 4.75%, financing costs are also contained. This leaves more of the cooperative's resources free to absorb the 10.5% rise in milk and glass input costs without immediately raising the $12.30 selling price for supermarkets and delis.
    Keywords: hire purchase, bank loan, $560,000, $350,000, $910,000, $242,000
    Mark scheme: knowledge_max_2: 1 mark for each valid point identified (max 2). | application_analysis_max_6: Up to 3 marks per point for contextual explanation linked to BRW's financing, costs and output.

  Q1(b) [12 marks]
    Question: BRW is relaunching its yoghurt range in returnable glass jars. Consider national television advertising, in-store supermarket demonstrations, or social media influencer marketing. Which should BRW choose? Justify your recommendation.
    Answer: National television advertising: TV would build awareness of the returnable-glass-jar yoghurts across all the supermarkets stocking BRW. However, airtime is costly for a 64-member cooperative funding a $910,000 filling line, and much of the audience is outside the deli and supermarket catchment, so the spend would be poorly converted into pots sold.

In-store supermarket demonstrations: Tastings let shoppers try the product and learn how returnable glass jars work, directly reaching buyers at the point of purchase and supporting the 24,000 pots produced monthly. They can also explain the 2.7% defect-rate improvement. Drawbacks are high staff time, limited geographic coverage and dependence on supermarket permission, which may be hard to secure across every chain.

Social media influencer marketing: Food and family influencers can target precisely the 66% of 520 surveyed shoppers who prefer returnable glass jars and the 57% who would pay up to $0.45 more, showing the jars and the return process in short videos. Engagement is measurable and cost per contact low. Results build more slowly than TV and rely on influencer credibility, but the research fit is strongest and the message scales nationally.

Recommendation: BRW should choose social media influencer marketing. It reaches the research-identified shoppers who value returnable glass jars, costs far less than television and scales beyond the few stores covered by demonstrations, while supporting the $12.30 price. Television is rejected as expensive and untargeted for a cooperative spending $910,000; in-store demonstrations are rejected as labour-intensive and too narrow, though a few can be used to support the launch.

    Mark scheme: level_1_1_to_4: Identifies promotional options with limited reference to BRW. | level_2_5_to_8: Discusses advantages and disadvantages of at least two options in BRW's context with some judgement. | level_3_9_to_12: Discusses all three options in BRW's context and recommends influencer marketing with clear reasons for rejecting television and demonstrations.

  Q2(a) [8 marks]
    Question: BRW's labour turnover is rising and product waste has reached 5%. Explain two benefits for BRW of using laissez-faire leadership to improve motivation on the filling line.
    Answer: Point 1: Laissez-faire leadership gives BRW's 64 cooperative members and experienced filler operators freedom to decide how to organise their work, which can raise intrinsic motivation and job satisfaction. In a flat structure this suits skilled staff who want autonomy, helping to slow the rising labour turnover without adding management layers.

Point 2: Allowing operators to suggest and implement their own improvements can reduce the 5% product waste and sustain the 2.7% defect rate, because the people closest to the filler understand the causes better than distant managers.     Mark scheme: knowledge_max_2: 1 mark for each valid point identified (max 2). | application_analysis_max_6: Up to 3 marks per point for development linked to BRW's turnover, waste, defect rate and training.

  Q2(b) [12 marks]
    Question: BRW must train 18 staff on the new filler. Consider on-the-job training or off-the-job training at the college. Which should BRW choose? Justify your decision.

    Question: Using Appendix 3, evaluate how the interest rate cut to 4.75%, the 6.1% minimum wage increase and the 10.5% rise in input costs will affect BRW. Which change will have the greatest impact? Justify your answer.
    Answer: Interest rate cut (5.25% to 4.75%): This is beneficial for BRW because the insert records a $560,000 variable-rate bank loan. If that loan tracks the base rate, a 0.50% fall saves 0.50% × $560,000 = $2,800 a year (0.005 × $560,000), easing the burden alongside $242,000 of fixed costs. It also makes the $350,000 hire purchase or future borrowing cheaper and may support consumer spending on yoghurt, but the saving is modest and depends on the loan actually being variable-rate.

Minimum wage increase (6.1%, to $14.64 per hour): With a workforce of 64 in filling and packing, this raises BRW's wage bill and cannot be avoided. The insert gives no hours worked or individual pay, so no annual total can be invented; the defensible comparison is productivity — 95,000 units ÷ 64 staff is about 1,484 units per worker, so the rise is bearable only if that productivity holds or output grows, otherwise unit labour cost erodes the $5.50 contribution.

Input cost inflation (10.5% milk and glass): The insert never decomposes the $6.80 variable cost, so only a bound is honest — if the whole variable cost rose 10.5% it would add 10.5% × $6.80 = $0.71 per unit, and at 95,000 units that is about $67,900 a year. Even a partial pass-through would cut contribution, and 6.8% dairy-product inflation may limit BRW's ability to raise price to supermarkets.

Conclusion: The 10.5% input-cost rise will have the greatest impact. It repeats on every one of the 95,000 units and directly erodes the contribution behind the $910,000 line, while the interest cut is a benefit worth only about $2,800 and the wage rise can partly be offset by productivity.

--- MAIN STEM ---
Sable Ridge Agribusiness (SRA) is a public limited company in the grain-milling sector, employing a workforce of 74. Founded in 1998 by Isobel Ridge, it supplies flour and animal feed to bakeries and farms and operates a hierarchical organisational structure with autocratic leadership. SRA plans to invest $1,200,000 in a new silo and automated milling line with biodegradable packaging, financed by a $700,000 bank loan and a $500,000 share issue. It has fixed costs of $330,000 a year, a variable cost of $7.40 a unit and a selling price of $13.40, and currently produces 120,000 units a year. SRA faces two problems: a skills gap on the new mill and grain waste has reached 4%.

--- APPENDIX 1 — MARKETING/OPS ---
Operations and Waste Report — Q2 2025: The mill processed 30,000 sacks last quarter at a defect rate of 2.2%, down from 3.5% a year ago. Customer complaints fell from 33 to 17 per month. Average delivery time is 5.2 days. A survey of 610 buyers found that 63% preferred biodegradable packaging and 49% would pay up to $0.55 more. A skills audit shows 22 of 74 staff need on-the-job training on the new mill; off-the-job training at the college costs $950 per employee.

--- APPENDIX 2 — FINANCIAL DATA ---
Title: Extract from the Statement of Financial Position of Sable Ridge Agribusiness as at 31 March 2025 ($ '000)
Headers: ['Financial Metric', '2024', '2025']

Current liabilities | 280 | 260

Capital employed | 3,000 | 3,400

(2) The national minimum wage will rise by 5.5% from $13.40 to $14.14 per hour from April 2026, increasing the wage bill. (3) Wholesale fertiliser, fuel and packaging costs have risen 13.2% year-on-year, and food-input inflation is 8.3%, while consumer spending on bakery products grew 2.6%.

--- QUESTIONS ---
  Q1(a) [8 marks]
    Question: SRA plans to fund part of its milling expansion with a $700,000 bank loan. Explain two advantages for SRA of using a share issue rather than the bank loan.
    Answer: Point 1: A share issue, here $500,000, raises equity that does not have to be repaid and carries no compulsory interest, unlike the $700,000 bank loan. For a public limited company with $330,000 of fixed costs, this lowers the risk of default if grain demand weakens and leaves cash flow freer while the $1,200,000 mill is commissioned.

Point 2: Equity from shareholders can fund a larger, long-term asset such as the new silo without the collateral and covenants a bank would demand, and it strengthens the balance sheet. The newly issued shares also spread ownership beyond founder Isobel Ridge, giving SRA access to more capital for future expansion, which is useful as it faces a 5.5% wage rise and 13.2% input inflation at the same time.
    Keywords: share issue, bank loan, $500,000, $700,000, $1,200,000, $330,000

  Q1(b) [12 marks]
    Question: SRA is launching biodegradable packaging for its flour range. Consider national television advertising, trade fairs and exhibitions, or social media influencer marketing. Which should SRA choose? Justify your recommendation.
    Answer: National television advertising: TV would quickly build awareness of the biodegradable packaging among all buyers of flour and animal feed. However, airtime is very expensive for a 74-employee plc already funding a $1,200,000 mill, and much of the mass audience buys neither flour nor feed, so most of the spend would miss SRA's industrial and bakery customers.

Trade fairs and exhibitions: These put SRA's flour and feed directly in front of bakery and farm buyers, allowing demonstrations of the biodegradable packaging and immediate order-taking — a strong fit for business-to-business sales of 30,000 sacks a quarter. They are cheaper than television and provide competitor intelligence. Social media influencer marketing: Food and baking influencers could reach the 63% of 610 surveyed buyers who prefer biodegradable packaging and the 49% who would pay up to $0.55 more, with measurable engagement at low cost per contact. The content can run continuously and nationally. It depends on influencer credibility and reaches final consumers more than the bakeries and farms that actually place the orders, so conversion may be slower.

Recommendation: SRA should choose trade fairs and exhibitions as the primary channel. They reach the exact business buyers who place the 30,000-sack quarterly orders and suit a 74-staff agribusiness funding a $1,200,000 expansion; television is rejected as costly and untargeted at mass consumers, and influencer marketing is rejected as better suited to end buyers than to the bakery and farm customers SRA supplies. SRA can use social media as a low-cost supplement.

--- MAIN STEM ---
Harlow Valley Cooperative (HVC) is a cooperative in the confectionery sector, employing a workforce of 56. Founded in 2015 by chef Rowan Harlow, it makes organic chocolate bars for health-food shops and online customers and operates a flat organisational structure with democratic leadership. HVC plans to invest $780,000 in a new moulding line with compostable wrappers, financed by a $480,000 bank loan and $300,000 retained profit. It has fixed costs of $209,000 a year, a variable cost of $5.60 a unit and a selling price of $11.10, and currently produces 85,000 units a year. HVC faces two problems: labour turnover is rising and wrapper waste at the moulding line has reached 6%.

--- APPENDIX 1 — MARKETING/OPS ---
Quality and Waste Report — Q3 2025: The moulding line produced 21,000 bars last month at a defect rate of 2.9%, down from 4.2% a year ago. Customer complaints fell from 37 to 20 per month. Average delivery time is 3.0 days. A survey of 490 shoppers found that 69% preferred compostable wrappers and 54% would pay up to $0.40 more. A skills audit shows 16 of 56 staff need on-the-job training on the new moulder; off-the-job training at the local college costs $700 per employee.

--- APPENDIX 2 — FINANCIAL DATA ---
Title: Extract from the Statement of Financial Position of Harlow Valley Cooperative as at 31 March 2025 ($ '000)
Headers: ['Financial Metric', '2024', '2025']
Inventories | 72 | 60
Trade receivables | 120 | 145
Cash and cash equivalents | 42 | 50
Current liabilities | 180 | 170
Non-current assets | 1,200 | 1,430
Capital employed | 1,600 | 1,850

--- APPENDIX 3 — EXTERNAL ENVIRONMENT ---
Economic and Business Bulletin (November 2026): (1) The central bank raised the base interest rate from 4.50% to 5.25%, increasing borrowing costs on HVC's variable-rate loan. (2) The national minimum wage will rise by 6.4% from $13.25 to $14.10 per hour from April 2026, lifting the cooperative's wage bill. (3) Wholesale cocoa, sugar and wrapper costs have risen 12.7% year-on-year, and confectionery inflation is 7.9%, while consumer spending on organic chocolate grew 3.4%.

--- QUESTIONS ---
  Q1(a) [8 marks]

    Answer: Point 1: Retained profit costs HVC no interest or repayment, protecting cash flow while the cooperative services its other commitments and has committed $780,000 to the new moulding line. Every dollar not paid as interest can help absorb the 12.7% rise in cocoa, sugar and wrapper costs, allowing HVC to hold the $11.10 selling price for health-food shops and online buyers.

Point 2: Retained profit avoids the collateral and default risk of a $480,000 bank loan, so the $300,000 can fund compostable wrappers without risking the moulder's repossession if demand for organic chocolate falls short of 85,000 units. It also keeps decision-making inside the cooperative and its 56 members, avoiding lender conditions on how the flat, democratic team operates, which suits HVC's member-owned structure and its $209,000 a year of fixed costs.
    Keywords: retained profit, bank loan, $480,000, $300,000, $780,000, $209,000

    Question: HVC is relaunching its chocolate bars in compostable wrappers. Consider national television advertising, in-store health-food shop demonstrations, or social media influencer marketing. Which should HVC choose? Justify your recommendation.
    Answer: National television advertising: TV would create fast awareness of the compostable-wrapper bars among all chocolate buyers. However, airtime is very expensive for a 56-member cooperative funding a $780,000 moulding line, and much of the mass audience does not shop in health-food stores, so the spend would be poorly targeted and difficult to afford.

Recommendation: HVC should choose social media influencer marketing. It reaches the research-identified shoppers who value compostable wrappers, costs far less than television and scales beyond the few shops covered by demonstrations, while supporting the $11.10 price and online sales.   Q2(a) [8 marks]
    Question: HVC's labour turnover is rising and wrapper waste has reached 6%. Explain two benefits for HVC of using democratic leadership to improve motivation and reduce waste.
    Answer: Point 1: Democratic leadership gives HVC's 56 members a say in how the new moulder is run, raising job satisfaction and intrinsic motivation in a flat cooperative where members expect involvement.     Mark scheme: knowledge_max_2: 1 mark for each valid point identified (max 2). | application_analysis_max_6: Up to 3 marks per point for development linked to HVC's turnover, waste, defect rate and training.

    Question: HVC must train 16 staff on the new moulder. Consider on-the-job training or off-the-job training at the local college. Which should HVC choose? Justify your decision.
    Answer: On-the-job training: Coaching at the moulder is tailored to HVC's own machines and quality checks, costs no course fees, and keeps the 16 staff productive while they learn, protecting the 21,000-bar monthly output and the improvement to a 2.9% defect rate. However, it takes staff away from the line when wrapper waste is already 6%, reducing capacity, and generic content may not match HVC's moulder, so on-site follow-up would still be needed.

Decision: HVC should choose on-the-job training first, then send a few senior operators for the college certificate. It is cheaper, machine-specific and avoids output loss while waste is 6% and turnover rising; full off-the-job training is rejected because $11,200 and sixteen absences would disrupt shop and online orders, and the course can be added once the moulder is stable.
    Keywords: on-the-job training, off-the-job training, $700, 16, 56, 2.9%
    Mark scheme: level_1_1_to_4: Describes the two training methods with limited application to HVC. | level_2_5_to_8: Analyses benefits and drawbacks of one or both methods in HVC's context. | level_3_9_to_12: Evaluates both methods in HVC's context with a justified decision covering cost, disruption and machine relevance.

    Answer: Interest rate rise (4.50% to 5.25%): HVC has a $480,000 bank loan, and if it is variable-rate the annual interest cost rises by 0.75% × $480,000 = $3,600 (0.0075 × $480,000). Minimum wage increase (6.4%, to $14.10 per hour): HVC has a workforce of 56 in moulding and packing, so this raises its wage bill and cannot be avoided. Input cost inflation (12.7% cocoa, sugar and wrappers): The insert never decomposes the $5.60 variable cost, so only a bound is honest — if the whole variable cost rose 12.7% it would add 12.7% × $5.60 = $0.71 per unit, and at 85,000 units that is about $60,400 a year. Even a smaller pass-through would cut contribution, and 7.9% confectionery inflation may limit HVC's ability to pass costs on to shops and online buyers.

Conclusion: The 12.7% input-cost rise will have the greatest impact. It repeats on every one of the 85,000 bars and directly erodes the $5.50 contribution behind the $780,000 moulder, whereas the interest rise costs at most about $3,600 and the wage rise can partly be offset by productivity.

--- MAIN STEM ---
Briarcliffe Flow Valves (BFV) is a private limited company in the industrial valve manufacturing sector on Clydeside, employing a workforce of 48. Founded in 2011 by Eleanor Briarcliffe, the firm makes precision control valves for water and chemical plants and operates a flat structure with democratic leadership. BFV plans to invest $720,000 in a new CNC valve-machining cell, financed by a $420,000 ten-year bank loan and $300,000 retained profit. It has fixed costs of $216,000 a year, a variable cost of $8.50 a unit and a selling price of $14.50, and currently produces 60,000 units a year. BFV faces two problems: the seal-defect rate has reached 4.2% and labour turnover is rising among skilled machinists.

--- APPENDIX 1 — MARKETING/OPS ---
Operations and Quality Report — Q4 2025: The Clydeside plant machined 15,200 valves last quarter at a seal-defect rate of 4.2%, up from 2.6% a year ago. Customer quality complaints rose from 14 to 31 per month. Average delivery lead time extended to 11 days from 7 days. Market research of 400 plant buyers found that 58% would pay up to $0.50 more for certified leak-free valves, and 47% rank on-time delivery first. A skills audit shows 18 of 48 staff lack CNC programming training; on-the-job coaching is available, while off-the-job college courses cost $750 per employee.

--- APPENDIX 2 — FINANCIAL DATA ---
Title: Extract from the Statement of Financial Position of Briarcliffe Flow Valves as at 31 March 2025 ($ '000)
Headers: ['Financial Metric', '2024', '2025']
Inventories | 90 | 78
Trade receivables | 140 | 165
Cash and cash equivalents | 35 | 52
Current liabilities | 175 | 170
Non-current assets | 1,200 | 1,620
Capital employed | 1,500 | 1,850

--- APPENDIX 3 — EXTERNAL ENVIRONMENT ---
Economic and Business Bulletin (November 2026): (1) The central bank has raised the base interest rate from 4.50% to 5.25%, increasing borrowing costs for firms with variable-rate loans. (2) The national minimum wage will rise by 5.9% from $13.50 to $14.30 per hour from April 2026, raising wage bills across engineering. (3) Stainless steel and brass input costs have risen 9.8% year-on-year, while industrial valve demand across water and chemical plants grew 2.7%.

  Q1(a) [8 marks]
    Question: BFV plans to fund part of its $720,000 CNC cell with a ten-year bank loan. Explain two advantages for BFV of using the $300,000 retained profit instead of the bank loan.
    Answer: Point 1: Using retained profit commits BFV to no interest payments or capital repayments, which protects cash flow while the firm already carries fixed costs of $216,000 a year and a $420,000 bank loan on the rest of the $720,000 CNC cell. Every dollar of interest avoided can be spent on tackling the 4.2% seal-defect rate or on the $750 per employee training, so the machining cell can bed in without squeezing the $6.00 contribution earned on each valve.

Point 2: Retained profit brings no external lender conditions or security, so Eleanor Briarcliffe and the existing shareholders keep full control of how the new CNC cell is run. Unlike the bank loan, there is no risk of the plant being used as collateral if demand from water and chemical plants disappoints, and the $300,000 can be deployed flexibly alongside the $420,000 borrowing rather than being tied to a fixed repayment schedule.
    Keywords: retained profit, $300,000, $420,000, $720,000, bank loan, $216,000
    Mark scheme: knowledge_max_2: 1 mark for each valid advantage identified (max 2). | application_analysis_max_6: Up to 3 marks per point for contextual explanation and analysis applied to BFV, its $720,000 expansion and its finance mix.

  Q1(b) [12 marks]
    Question: BFV is launching its certified leak-free valve range. Consider a national trade-press advertising campaign, sponsorship of an industry exhibition, or social media targeting plant buyers. Which should BFV choose to promote the launch? Justify your recommendation.
    Answer: National trade-press advertising: A campaign in engineering journals would reach plant managers across water and chemical plants and lend credibility to a certified leak-free claim. However, print airtime is costly and hard to measure, and much of the readership will not be in BFV's Clydeside selling area or buying industrial valves, so a 48-employee firm funding a $720,000 cell would waste part of the budget.

Industry exhibition sponsorship: A stand at a process-engineering exhibition puts BFV's valves directly in front of buyers who specify equipment, allowing engineers to inspect seal quality and discuss the 4.2% defect-rate fix face to face. It suits the 39% of surveyed buyers who would pay up to $0.80 more for certified heat-treated drives in the related market. The drawback is high stand and travel cost and a short event window, so leads must be followed up quickly.

Social media targeting plant buyers: LinkedIn-style targeting can reach the 400 surveyed plant buyers and the 58% who would pay $0.50 more for leak-free valves, with precise job-title filters and measurable enquiries at low cost. It builds awareness fast but lacks the physical demonstration that technical buyers of a $14.50 valve may want before switching supplier.

Recommendation: BFV should choose industry exhibition sponsorship as the primary launch channel, supported by low-cost social media follow-up. Face-to-face inspection best overcomes concern about the 4.2% seal-defect rate and reaches specifiers directly. Trade press is rejected as untargeted and unmeasurable for a small manufacturer; social media alone is rejected because technical plant buyers want to see the certified valve before committing, so it should support rather than replace the exhibition.

  Q2(a) [8 marks]
    Question: BFV's seal-defect rate has reached 4.2% and labour turnover is rising. Explain two benefits for BFV of using democratic leadership to improve motivation among its machinists.

Machinists who help set sealing routines and shift patterns are likelier to take care over their work and attend consistently, directly attacking the 4.2% seal-defect rate and the rising labour turnover in BFV's flat structure. In Maslow's terms, being consulted meets higher-order needs that pay alone cannot, so motivation and attendance improve while the new cell is introduced.

Point 2: Consulting the machinists who run the machines generates practical improvements to seal fitting that managers on their own would miss, so quality can be raised without more capital spending on the $720,000 cell. Herzberg would treat the extra responsibility as a motivator, encouraging pride in the certified leak-free valves. Higher involvement builds commitment and reduces the need to replace skilled staff, saving the $750 per employee college cost and protecting output of 60,000 valves. However, staff leave the line, reducing short-term capacity, and generic content may not match BFV's exact machine settings, so follow-up coaching on site would still be required.

Decision: BFV should choose on-the-job coaching for the initial rollout, adding short college modules later for the most experienced machinists. Coaching is cheaper, machine-specific and avoids losing output while the defect rate is 4.2% and absence pressures the schedule.     Question: Using Appendix 2, evaluate BFV's liquidity by calculating the current ratio and the acid test ratio for 2024 and 2025. Has BFV's financial position improved? Justify your answer.

    Answer: Interest rate rise (4.50% to 5.25%): If BFV's $420,000 ten-year bank loan is variable-rate, the annual interest cost rises by the 0.75 percentage-point rise × $420,000 = $3,150 a year (0.0075 × $420,000). That is modest beside fixed costs of $216,000, and if the loan is fixed-rate the effect is zero. Minimum wage increase (5.9%, to $14.30 an hour): The insert gives a workforce of 48 but does not state hours worked, pay rates or how many machinists are on the minimum, so no defensible annual wage total can be invented. What can be derived from the insert is productivity: 60,000 valves ÷ 48 staff = 1,250 valves per worker. If output per worker holds at that level the rise is absorbable; if absence or the 4.2% defect rate cuts output, unit labour cost rises and the $6.00 contribution per valve is squeezed. The effect is therefore real but cannot be precisely quantified from the data given.

Input cost inflation (9.8% on steel and brass): The insert does not decompose the $8.50 variable cost, so only a clearly labelled upper bound is honest: if every dollar of that $8.50 rose 9.8%, it would add 9.8% × $8.50 = $0.83 a valve, and at 60,000 valves a year that is $49,800 (60,000 × $0.83). Even a smaller rise would compound across all 60,000 valves and cut contribution below $6.00. BFV can offset part through the $0.50 leak-free premium found in its research.

Conclusion: The 9.8% input-cost rise will have the greatest impact. It applies to every one of the 60,000 valves and directly erodes the $6.00 contribution that underpins the $720,000 cell, and the $49,800 bound is larger than the $3,150 interest effect. The interest rise is smaller and can be hedged by fixing the rate, while the wage rise cannot be quantified from the insert and can be offset by productivity of 1,250 valves per worker.
    Keywords: 5.25%, 5.9%, 9.8%, $13.50, $14.30, $8.50

--- MAIN STEM ---
Castlewick Chain Drives (CCD) is a public limited company in the industrial power-transmission sector near Wolverhampton, employing a workforce of 120. Founded in 1998 by Marcus Castlewick, it manufactures chain, sprocket and coupling drives for factory conveyor systems throughout the region and uses a hierarchical structure with autocratic leadership. CCD plans to invest $1,200,000 in an automated heat-treatment line, financed by a $700,000 share issue and a $500,000 bank loan. It has fixed costs of $480,000 a year, a variable cost of $12.00 a unit and a selling price of $20.00, and currently produces 120,000 units a year. CCD faces rising absenteeism, now 8%, and growing metal waste in its heat-treatment process.

--- APPENDIX 1 — MARKETING/OPS ---
Operations and Quality Log — Q4 2025: The Wolverhampton plant heat-treated 28,400 chain and sprocket units last quarter, with a recorded metal-waste rate of 6.4%, down from 8.1% a year earlier. Absenteeism reached 8% of shifts. Delivery lead time averaged 9 days against a 6-day target. A survey of 350 factory procurement managers found that 61% rank reliable delivery above price and 39% would pay up to $0.80 more for certified heat-treated drives. A training audit shows 26 of 120 staff need coupling-assembly retraining; in-house coaching is offered, while external courses cost $620 per employee.

--- APPENDIX 2 — FINANCIAL DATA ---
Title: Extract from the Statement of Financial Position of Castlewick Chain Drives as at 31 March 2025 ($ '000)
Headers: ['Financial Metric', '2024', '2025']
Inventories | 210 | 190
Trade receivables | 260 | 310
Cash and cash equivalents | 80 | 55
Current liabilities | 300 | 320
Non-current assets | 2,100 | 2,950
Capital employed | 2,600 | 3,300

--- APPENDIX 3 — EXTERNAL ENVIRONMENT ---
Economic and Business Bulletin (November 2026): (1) The central bank has raised the base interest rate from 4.25% to 5.00%, raising borrowing costs for firms with variable-rate loans. (2) The national minimum wage will rise by 6.2% from $13.10 to $13.91 per hour from April 2026, lifting wage bills across engineering. (3) Steel alloy and energy input costs have risen 11.3% year-on-year, while factory conveyor investment grew 3.1%.

--- QUESTIONS ---
  Q1(a) [8 marks]
    Question: CCD plans to fund part of its $1,200,000 heat-treatment line with a $500,000 bank loan. Explain two advantages for CCD of financing it through the $700,000 share issue instead.
    Answer: Point 1: A share issue raises $700,000 with no interest charge and no fixed repayment dates, so CCD avoids adding debt service on top of fixed costs of $480,000 a year. That protects cash flow while the automated heat-treatment line is commissioned and helps absorb the 6.2% minimum wage rise and the 11.3% rise in alloy and energy inputs without raising the $20.00 selling price. Retained earnings are not committed to lenders, so more cash stays inside the business.

Point 2: Equity does not have to be secured against the Wolverhampton plant, so the $2,950,000 of non-current assets are not exposed to repossession if factory conveyor demand weakens. For a public limited company, a share issue also broadens the shareholder base and supports a larger capital structure for future expansion, whereas the $500,000 bank loan would add fixed interest and repayment pressure on a business already employing 120 staff with 8% absenteeism. The $700,000 can therefore fund the $1,200,000 line without competing with the $480,000 fixed costs for cash.
    Keywords: share issue, $700,000, $500,000, $1,200,000, bank loan, $480,000
    Mark scheme: knowledge_max_2: 1 mark for each valid advantage identified (max 2). | application_analysis_max_6: Up to 3 marks per point for contextual explanation and analysis applied to CCD and its $1,200,000 financing decision.

  Q1(b) [12 marks]
    Question: CCD is launching its certified heat-treated drive range. Consider national trade-press advertising, sponsorship of a factory-automation exhibition, or a direct sales team calling on conveyor manufacturers. Which should CCD choose to promote the launch? Justify your recommendation.
    Answer: National trade-press advertising: Placing adverts in engineering journals would reach procurement managers across factory conveyor firms and support the claim of certified heat treatment. However, print campaigns are expensive, hard to measure and largely untargeted, so a firm already committing $1,200,000 to a new line and $480,000 a year in fixed costs would waste much of the spend on readers who do not buy drives.

Factory-automation exhibition sponsorship: An exhibition stand lets engineers inspect the heat-treated chains and sprockets and question CCD's team about the 6.4% waste rate and quality controls. It matches the 61% of surveyed managers who rank reliable delivery above price, since face-to-face discussion can reassure them. The disadvantages are the cost of the stand and the short window for follow-up, so leads must be converted quickly.

Direct sales team: A dedicated team calling on conveyor manufacturers could build long-term relationships and explain the $0.80 premium for certified drives to the 39% of buyers who would pay more. It gives full control of the message and fast feedback, but recruiting and funding a team for a 120-employee firm with 8% absenteeism adds significant fixed cost and takes time to produce results.

--- MAIN STEM ---
Ellersby Industrial Pumps (EIP) is a workers' cooperative in the industrial pump manufacturing sector in West Yorkshire, employing a workforce of 64. Founded in 2007 by Fatima Ellersby, it makes centrifugal pumps for water treatment and process plants and operates a flat structure with democratic leadership. EIP plans to invest $540,000 in a new pump-testing facility, financed by a $300,000 retained surplus and a $240,000 bank loan. It has fixed costs of $180,000 a year, a variable cost of $7.00 a unit and a selling price of $13.00, and currently produces 90,000 units a year. EIP faces a quality problem: customer complaints about pump seals have risen and the defect rate is 3.5%.

--- APPENDIX 1 — MARKETING/OPS ---
Quality and Market Research Summary — Q4 2025: The plant tested 12,600 pumps last quarter at a seal-defect rate of 3.5%, up from 2.1% a year ago. Customer complaints rose from 17 to 34 per month. Average fulfilment time lengthened to 8 days from 5 days. Research among 300 water-treatment buyers found that 55% would pay up to $0.60 more for a certified leak-free pump, and 44% check service records before ordering. A skills audit shows 14 of 64 members lack pump-test certification; on-the-job mentoring is available, while off-the-job college courses cost $680 per member.

--- APPENDIX 2 — FINANCIAL DATA ---
Title: Extract from the Statement of Financial Position of Ellersby Industrial Pumps as at 31 March 2025 ($ '000)
Headers: ['Financial Metric', '2024', '2025']
Inventories | 60 | 70
Trade receivables | 95 | 88
Cash and cash equivalents | 40 | 62
Current liabilities | 130 | 132
Non-current assets | 900 | 1,180
Capital employed | 1,100 | 1,400

--- APPENDIX 3 — EXTERNAL ENVIRONMENT ---
Economic and Business Bulletin (November 2026): (1) The central bank has raised the base interest rate from 4.50% to 5.25%, increasing borrowing costs for firms with variable-rate loans. (2) The national minimum wage will rise by 6.5% from $13.40 to $14.27 per hour from April 2026, raising engineering wage bills. (3) Cast iron and motor input costs have risen 8.9% year-on-year, while water-treatment plant spending grew 4.2%.

    Question: EIP plans to fund part of its $540,000 testing facility with a $240,000 bank loan. Explain two advantages for EIP of using the $300,000 retained surplus instead of the bank loan.
    Answer: Point 1: The retained surplus carries no interest or capital repayments, so EIP avoids new debt service on top of fixed costs of $180,000 a year. That protects the cooperative's cash flow while the $540,000 pump-testing facility is built and helps absorb the 6.5% minimum wage rise and the 8.9% rise in cast iron and motor costs without raising the $13.00 price. Cash not paid to a lender stays available for the 14 members needing certification training.

Point 2: Using the retained surplus keeps decision-making inside the cooperative, so the 64 member-workers control how the testing facility is run without a lender imposing repayment conditions or taking security over the plant. Unlike the $240,000 bank loan, there is no repossession risk if water-treatment orders slip, and the surplus can be combined flexibly with the borrowing rather than locked into a fixed schedule. This matters when the 3.5% defect rate is already pushing complaints up from 17 to 34 a month.

    Answer: Advertising in water-industry journals: Print adverts would reach procurement staff at water-treatment firms and give credibility to the certified leak-free claim. The drawback is cost and poor targeting: many readers will not buy centrifugal pumps, and a cooperative with fixed costs of $180,000 a year and a $540,000 testing facility cannot afford much wasted spend, nor can it easily measure enquiries.

Recommendation: EIP should choose the environmental technology exhibition as the primary channel, supported by low-cost social media.     Answer: Interest rate rise (4.75% to 5.50%): FPM's $260,000 hire-purchase agreement is the relevant commitment. Input cost inflation (10.6% on steel and resin): The insert does not split the $9.00 variable cost, so only an explicitly labelled upper bound is honest: if the whole $9.00 rose 10.6%, it adds 10.6% × $9.00 = $0.95 per component, and at 50,000 components a year that is $47,500 (50,000 × $0.95). Even a partial rise compounds across all output and cuts contribution below $7.00, although the $0.70 faster-tooling premium could recover some of it.

Conclusion: The 10.6% rise in tool steel and resin will have the greatest impact. Its $47,500 bound is far larger than the illustrative $1,950 interest effect, it applies to every one of the 50,000 components, and it directly erodes the $7.00 contribution that must cover $196,000 fixed costs and the $260,000 hire-purchase commitment. The interest effect is small and based on an illustrative calculation; the wage effect cannot be quantified from the insert and can be partly offset through productivity of 1,250 components per worker.

--- MAIN STEM ---
Garrow Turbine Components (GTB) is a partnership in the precision turbine-casting sector in South Wales, employing a workforce of 72. Founded in 2003 by Gwen Garrow, it casts turbine blades and hot-section components for energy and aerospace clients and operates a hierarchical structure with autocratic leadership. GTB plans to invest $880,000 in a new vacuum-casting furnace, financed by a $480,000 bank loan and $400,000 retained profit. It has fixed costs of $260,000 a year, a variable cost of $10.00 a unit and a selling price of $18.00, and currently produces 70,000 units a year. GTB faces an operational problem: the casting defect rate has reached 5.1% and skilled-worker absence is rising.

--- APPENDIX 1 — MARKETING/OPS ---
Operations and Quality Report — Q4 2025: The South Wales foundry poured 9,800 turbine-casting units last quarter at a defect rate of 5.1%, up from 3.2% a year earlier. Customer quality complaints rose from 19 to 37 per month. Average delivery time lengthened to 16 days from 10 days. A survey of 220 energy and aerospace buyers found that 59% would pay up to $1.10 more for certified low-defect castings, and 46% rank quality assurance first. A skills audit shows 21 of 72 staff need furnace-control retraining; on-the-job mentoring is offered, external courses cost $940 per employee.

--- APPENDIX 2 — FINANCIAL DATA ---
Title: Extract from the Statement of Financial Position of Garrow Turbine Components as at 31 March 2025 ($ '000)
Headers: ['Financial Metric', '2024', '2025']

Trade receivables | 180 | 205
Cash and cash equivalents | 55 | 78
Current liabilities | 200 | 195
Non-current assets | 1,400 | 1,960
Capital employed | 1,750 | 2,180

--- APPENDIX 3 — EXTERNAL ENVIRONMENT ---

(2) The national minimum wage will rise by 6.1% from $13.20 to $14.01 per hour from April 2026, raising wage bills. (3) Nickel alloy and cobalt input costs have risen 12.7% year-on-year, while turbine component demand grew 3.4%.

Input cost inflation (12.7% on nickel and cobalt): The insert does not decompose the $10.00 variable cost, so only an explicitly labelled upper bound is honest: if the whole $10.00 rose 12.7%, it adds 12.7% × $10.00 = $1.27 per casting, and across 70,000 castings a year that is $88,900 (70,000 × $1.27). Even a partial rise compounds over all output and cuts contribution below $8.00, though the $1.10 certified low-defect premium found in the survey could recover part of it.

Conclusion: The 12.7% rise in nickel and cobalt inputs will have the greatest impact. Its $88,900 bound far exceeds the $3,600 interest effect, it applies to every one of the 70,000 castings, and it directly erodes the $8.00 contribution needed to cover $260,000 fixed costs and service the $480,000 loan. The interest rise is small and hedgeable by fixing the rate; the wage rise cannot be quantified from the insert and can be partly offset through productivity of 972.22 castings per worker.
    Keywords: 5.00%, 6.1%, 12.7%, $13.20, $14.01, $10.00
    Mark scheme: level_1_1_to_4: Identifies the external changes with limited application to GTB. | level_2_5_to_8: Analyses the impact of at least two external changes on GTB with shown calculations where data allow. | level_3_9_to_12: Detailed evaluation of all three changes in the context of GTB using only shown derivations from insert figures and a well-justified greatest-impact judgment.

--- MAIN STEM ---
Pine Ridge Textiles (PRT) is a private limited company in the textile manufacturing sector, employing a workforce of 60. Founded in 2011 by Elowen Penrose, the firm weaves recycled-fibre fabrics for clothing brands and runs a hierarchical structure with autocratic leadership. PRT plans to invest $720,000 in an automated weaving loom, financed by a $420,000 ten-year bank loan and $300,000 from a new share issue. It has fixed costs of $216,000 a year, a variable cost of $5.20 a unit and a selling price of $9.70, and currently produces 80,000 units a year. PRT faces a rising defect rate of 2.4% on the new loom and skilled-operator absenteeism, which threatens its delivery schedules to clothing brands.

--- APPENDIX 1 — MARKETING/OPS ---
Operations and Quality Report — Q3 2025: The weaving line produced 18,400 metres of cloth last quarter at a defect rate of 2.4%, down from 4.0% a year earlier. Customer returns fell from 52 to 28 per month and average order lead time is 5.6 days. A survey of 450 clothing buyers found that 61% prefer fabrics made with recycled fibre and 48% will pay up to $0.50 more. A skills audit shows 16 of 60 operators have not received on-the-job training on the new looms; external machine-training courses cost $750 per worker.

(3) Wholesale cotton and dye input costs have risen 9.6% year-on-year, while clothing retail spending grew 2.9%.

Unlike the $420,000 bank loan, it does not add to PRT's interest burden, so the rise in the base rate from 4.25% to 5.00% cannot increase the cost of this part of the $720,000 loom. With fixed costs of $216,000 a year already to cover, avoiding extra interest protects the $4.50 contribution earned on each of the 80,000 units and leaves more cash to tackle the 2.4% defect rate.

Point 2: Equity does not have to be secured against PRT's assets, so the weaving business is not exposed to repossession if the new loom takes time to bed in. A larger bank loan would require collateral and covenants that could constrain Elowen Penrose's decisions as the firm expands. The new shareholders also supply $300,000 that can be spent on the loom immediately, speeding the shift to recycled-fibre fabrics that 61% of the 450 surveyed buyers prefer, which supports the $9.70 selling price and helps win more clothing-brand orders.

    Answer: Fashion trade fair sponsorship: A trade fair puts PRT's recycled-fibre fabrics directly in front of clothing-brand buyers and design teams, allowing the 18,400 metres of cloth to be inspected, which matters when the defect rate is 2.4% and buyers worry about consistency. Direct mail to clothing brands: Targeted letters and fabric samples reach decision-makers cheaply and can be followed up personally, which suits a private limited company selling to a small number of known accounts. Response rates are usually low, however, and mail cannot build the consumer awareness that makes brands request PRT by name; it also misses the 48% premium segment entirely.

The trade fair is rejected as expensive and too small for a 60-employee firm funding a $720,000 loom; direct mail is rejected as low-response and unable to build the awareness needed to sell 80,000 units. Current Ratio 2025 = 1.65 : 1
Acid Test Ratio 2024 = 0.75 : 1

    Question: Using Appendix 3, evaluate how the rise in the base interest rate to 5.00%, the 5.8% minimum wage increase and the 9.6% rise in cotton and dye input costs will affect PRT. Which change will have the greatest impact? Justify your answer.
    Answer: Interest rate rise (4.25% to 5.00%): If PRT's $420,000 bank loan is variable-rate, the annual interest cost rises by 0.75% of $420,000 = $3,150 a year (0.0075 × $420,000). That is modest beside fixed costs of $216,000 a year, and if the loan is fixed-rate the effect is zero. Higher rates may make clothing brands cautious and raise the cost of future borrowing, but PRT can reduce this risk by fixing the rate.

Minimum wage increase (5.8%, to $13.54 an hour): Much of the workforce of 60 is likely to be hourly-paid, so wage costs rise and cannot be avoided. The insert does not state hours worked or each worker's pay, so an annual wage total cannot be invented. The defensible test is productivity: 80,000 units ÷ 60 workers = about 1,333 units per worker. If the $720,000 loom lifts output per worker the higher wage is affordable; if absenteeism and the 2.4% defect rate hold productivity down, unit labour cost rises and the $4.50 contribution shrinks.

Cotton and dye input costs (9.6%): These feed the $5.20 variable cost per unit, but the insert never splits that cost, so only a labelled bound is honest: if the whole variable cost rose 9.6%, that is 9.6% × $5.20 = about $0.50 per unit; across 80,000 units that is roughly $40,000 a year (80,000 × $0.50). The 48% of buyers willing to pay $0.50 more and the 61% preferring recycled fibre give some pricing room, but clothing retail spending grew only 2.9%, so passing on the full rise may lose orders.

Conclusion: The 9.6% input-cost rise will have the greatest impact. It compounds on every one of the 80,000 units and directly erodes the $4.50 contribution that justifies the $720,000 loom; the interest rise is at most a known $3,150, and the wage rise can be offset by the productivity gains the new loom is meant to deliver.

--- MAIN STEM ---
Harbourline Seafoods (HSL) is a private limited company in the seafood processing sector, employing a workforce of 50. Founded in 2008 by Tomas Vale near the coast, it supplies frozen fish to restaurant chains and uses a flat structure with democratic leadership. HSL plans to invest $640,000 in a cold-storage and flash-freezing plant, financed by a $400,000 bank loan and $240,000 retained profit, with an overdraft also available. It has fixed costs of $180,000 a year, a variable cost of $4.10 a unit and a selling price of $8.10, and currently produces 70,000 units a year. HSL faces spoilage waste of 3.4% and a hygiene certification skills gap among its plant workers.

--- APPENDIX 1 — MARKETING/OPS ---
Operations and Quality Log — Q3 2025: The flash-freezing line packed 15,200 cartons last quarter at a defect rate of 1.5%, down from 2.8% last year. Spoilage waste fell from 6.2% to 3.4% of throughput and delivery to restaurants averages 2.1 days. Market research of 380 chefs found 67% value sustainably sourced fish and 55% would pay $0.35 more per carton. A training review shows 14 of 50 plant workers lack hygiene certification; college certification courses cost $620 per employee.

--- APPENDIX 2 — FINANCIAL DATA ---
Title: Extract from the Statement of Financial Position of Harbourline Seafoods as at 31 March 2025 ($ '000)
Headers: ['Financial Metric', '2024', '2025']
Inventories | 80 | 100
Trade receivables | 60 | 70
Cash and cash equivalents | 30 | 55
Current liabilities | 100 | 125
Non-current assets | 900 | 1,350
Capital employed | 1,100 | 1,550

(2) The national minimum wage increases by 6.2% from $12.90 to $13.70 per hour from April 2026. (3) Wholesale fish feed and packaging input costs rose 11.3% year-on-year, while restaurant demand for frozen seafood grew 4.1%.

    Question: HSL plans to fund its $640,000 plant with a $400,000 bank loan and $240,000 retained profit. Explain two advantages for HSL of using retained profit rather than an overdraft to fund the $240,000 portion.
    Answer: Point 1: Retained profit is internal cash, so HSL pays no interest and faces no repayable-on-demand clause, unlike an overdraft whose rate would rise with the base rate from 3.90% to 4.65%. With fixed costs of $180,000 a year and a $400,000 bank loan already committed, avoiding overdraft interest protects the $4.00 contribution on each of the 70,000 cartons and gives Tomas Vale steadier cash flow while the freezing plant is built.

Point 2: Retained profit needs no security and no bank approval, so the $240,000 can be spent quickly on the plant without risking HSL's assets. An overdraft is a short-term facility that the bank could withdraw, leaving the $640,000 project half-finished. Using past profits also keeps control with the existing owners and signals to the bank that the firm is generating enough profit to support its $400,000 loan, which may help when HSL next needs finance.

Costs are low and engagement rises. Results are gradual, and the 14 workers without hygiene certification may lack the knowledge to contribute fully at first.

Recommendation: HSL should choose supplier quality agreements. Spoilage originates in the delivered fish, so prevention at source is more effective than end-of-line inspection, which only finds waste after it is created; quality circles are valuable but slower and limited by the certification gap. Supplier agreements can be backed later by quality circles once the 14 workers are certified. The higher purchase cost is justified because it protects the $4.00 contribution on 70,000 units and the $640,000 investment.

    Question: Using Appendix 3, evaluate how the rise in the base interest rate to 4.65%, the 6.2% minimum wage increase and the 11.3% rise in fish feed and packaging costs will affect HSL. Which change will have the greatest impact? Justify your answer.
    Answer: Interest rate rise (3.90% to 4.65%): If HSL's $400,000 bank loan is variable-rate, the annual interest cost rises by 0.75% of $400,000 = $3,000 a year (0.0075 × $400,000). Minimum wage increase (6.2%, to $13.70 an hour): Some of the workforce of 50 is likely hourly-paid, so wage costs rise. The 55% of chefs willing to pay $0.35 more and 67% valuing sustainable sourcing offer some recovery, but restaurant demand grew only 4.1%, so full pass-through may cost sales.

Conclusion: The 11.3% input-cost rise will have the greatest impact. It hits every one of the 70,000 units and directly erodes the $4.00 contribution supporting the $640,000 plant; the interest rise is a known $3,000 at most, and the wage rise can be offset by productivity gains from the new plant.

--- MAIN STEM ---
Cedar Grove Furniture (CGF) is a partnership in the furniture manufacturing sector, employing a workforce of 35. Founded in 2013 by the cabinet maker Ingrid Solberg, it makes solid-wood cabinets for independent retailers and operates a flat structure with laissez-faire leadership. CGF plans to invest $560,000 in CNC cutting machinery, financed by $360,000 of hire purchase and $200,000 retained profit. It has fixed costs of $165,000 a year, a variable cost of $7.50 a unit and a selling price of $13.00, and currently produces 40,000 units a year. CGF is battling timber waste of 8.5% and a shortage of CNC-trained cabinet makers that threatens delivery targets to independent retailers across the country.

--- APPENDIX 1 — MARKETING/OPS ---
Operations and Quality Report — Q3 2025: The assembly shop finished 9,600 units last quarter at a defect rate of 3.3%, down from 5.1% a year ago. Customer complaints about finish fell from 44 to 19 per month and timber waste was 8.5% of material input. Average delivery time is 7.4 days. A survey of 320 homeowners found 58% prefer FSC-certified timber and 46% would pay $12 more per item. A skills check shows 11 of 35 cabinet makers need CNC training; external CNC courses cost $1,100 per person.

  Q1(a) [8 marks]

With fixed costs of $165,000 a year already to meet, smoother payments protect the $5.50 contribution on each of the 40,000 units and make the $560,000 machinery affordable for a partnership of 35.

Point 2: The machinery itself serves as security for the hire-purchase agreement, so CGF may find finance easier to obtain than an unsecured bank loan of the same size, and ownership passes once payments finish. Factory outlet: A shop at the workshop sells Seconds and excess stock directly, useful for reducing the 8.5% timber waste and the 3.3% defect rate by recovering some value from imperfect units. It is limited by location, attracts bargain hunters rather than buyers willing to pay a $12 premium, and needs staff to run it when 11 cabinet makers already need CNC training.

    Question: Using Appendix 2, evaluate CGF's financial position by calculating the current ratio and the acid test ratio for 2024 and 2025. Has CGF's financial position improved? Justify your answer.
    Answer: Calculations:
Current Ratio 2024 = 1.50 : 1
Current Ratio 2025 = 1.47 : 1
Acid Test Ratio 2024 = 0.77 : 1
Acid Test Ratio 2025 = 0.64 : 1

Detailed workings: 2024 current assets = $110,000 inventories + $70,000 trade receivables + $45,000 cash = $225,000; 2025 current assets = $150,000 + $95,000 + $20,000 = $265,000. The stock-excluding measure for 2024 is ($225,000 − $110,000) ÷ $150,000 = $115,000 ÷ $150,000 = 0.77; for 2025 it is ($265,000 − $150,000) ÷ $180,000 = $115,000 ÷ $180,000 = 0.64.

Evaluation: Liquidity has weakened. Current assets rose from $225,000 to $265,000, but current liabilities grew faster, from $150,000 to $180,000, so the 2024 figure of 1.50 slipped to 1.47 in 2025. More seriously, the stock-excluding measure fell from 0.77 to 0.64 because cash dropped from $45,000 to $20,000 while inventories climbed from $110,000 to $150,000 and receivables from $70,000 to $95,000. That means CGF is increasingly relying on selling timber stock to meet bills, which is risky while it has a $360,000 hire-purchase commitment and $560,000 of new machinery. The 8.5% timber waste makes the growing inventory especially worrying: some stock may be slow to turn into cash. Still-rising receivables also suggest independent retailers are paying more slowly.

Conclusion: CGF's financial position has not improved; it has worsened. Both measures fell (1.50 to 1.47 and 0.77 to 0.64), and the decline in the stock-excluding position shows the problem is not just inventory. CGF should cut the 8.5% waste, chase the $95,000 of receivables and rebuild cash before taking on more hire purchase.

--- MAIN STEM ---
Meridian Print Works (MPW) is a public limited company in the commercial printing sector, employing a workforce of 90. Founded in 1998 by the printer Rowan Ashworth, it prints packaging and marketing material for national clients and runs a hierarchical structure with autocratic leadership. MPW plans to invest $900,000 in a digital printing press, financed by a $600,000 share issue and a $300,000 bank loan. It has fixed costs of $300,000 a year, a variable cost of $3.80 a unit and a selling price of $7.30, and currently produces 120,000 units a year. MPW faces paper waste of 5.4% and reprint complaints that have strained its quality control with national clients.

--- APPENDIX 1 — MARKETING/OPS ---
Operations and Quality Report — Q3 2025: The print hall delivered 28,500 jobs last quarter with a defect rate of 2.0%, down from 3.6% a year earlier. Reprint complaints fell from 63 to 30 per month and paper waste was 5.4% of sheets used. Average turnaround is 4.3 days. A survey of 520 marketing managers found 71% value fast digital turnaround and 57% would pay $0.25 more per unit. A skills audit shows 22 of 90 press operators need digital-press training; courses cost $480 per employee.

--- APPENDIX 2 — FINANCIAL DATA ---
Title: Extract from the Statement of Financial Position of Meridian Print Works as at 31 March 2025 ($ '000)
Headers: ['Financial Metric', '2024', '2025']
Inventories | 200 | 180
Trade receivables | 140 | 165

Capital employed | 2,400 | 3,100

(2) The national minimum wage increases by 6.0% from $12.60 to $13.36 per hour from April 2026. (3) Wholesale paper and ink input costs rose 10.2% year-on-year, while commercial printing demand grew 3.3%.

    Question: MPW plans to raise $600,000 through a share issue for its $900,000 press. Explain two advantages for MPW of a share issue over increasing its $300,000 bank loan.
    Answer: Point 1: A share issue raises $600,000 of permanent capital with no interest charge and no fixed repayment schedule, unlike the $300,000 bank loan. With fixed costs of $300,000 a year, avoiding extra interest protects the $3.50 contribution on each of the 120,000 units and leaves cash to tackle the 5.4% paper waste. A rise in the base rate from 4.00% to 4.80% also cannot increase the cost of equity.

Point 2: Equity is not secured on MPW's assets, so the press cannot be repossessed if digital demand disappoints, and a public limited company can reach many investors. The $600,000 arrives in one amount, letting Rowan Ashworth install the $900,000 press at once to meet the 71% of 520 managers who value fast digital turnaround, rather than waiting for further loan tranches that a bank might refuse.

Detailed workings: 2024 current assets = $200,000 inventories + $140,000 trade receivables + $35,000 cash = $375,000; 2025 current assets = $180,000 + $165,000 + $95,000 = $440,000. The 2024 liquidity comparison is $375,000 ÷ $250,000 = 1.50; the 2025 comparison is $440,000 ÷ $240,000 = 1.83. The stock-excluding measure for 2024 is ($375,000 − $200,000) ÷ $250,000 = $175,000 ÷ $250,000 = 0.70; for 2025 it is ($440,000 − $180,000) ÷ $240,000 = $260,000 ÷ $240,000 = 1.08.

Evaluation: Liquidity has improved strongly. Current assets rose from $375,000 to $440,000 while current liabilities fell from $250,000 to $240,000, lifting the 2024 figure of 1.50 to 1.83 in 2025. The stock-excluding measure rose from 0.70 to 1.08, so MPW can now cover its short-term debts without selling the $180,000 of inventories — valuable while it services a $300,000 bank loan and has just raised $600,000 for the $900,000 press. Cash more than doubled from $35,000 to $95,000, a genuine improvement in headroom. Receivables did rise from $140,000 to $165,000, so some customers are slower to pay, but the cash increase more than offsets this. The 5.4% paper waste tied up in inventories is a smaller concern while stock is falling.

Conclusion: MPW's financial position has improved. Both measures (1.50 to 1.83 and 0.70 to 1.08) are higher, and the rise in cash confirms the gain is real rather than stock-driven. MPW should keep control of the $165,000 of receivables as the $900,000 press beds in.

  Q4(a) [8 marks]
    Question: Explain one advantage and one disadvantage for MPW of installing the new digital printing press.
    Answer: Advantage: The research shows 71% of 520 managers value fast digital turnaround and 57% would pay $0.25 more per unit, so MPW can shorten its 4.3-day turnaround and protect the $3.50 contribution per unit despite a 10.2% rise in paper and ink costs.     Question: Using Appendix 3, evaluate how the rise in the base interest rate to 4.80%, the 6.0% minimum wage increase and the 10.2% rise in paper and ink costs will affect MPW. Which change will have the greatest impact? Justify your answer.
    Answer: Interest rate rise (4.00% to 4.80%): If MPW's $300,000 bank loan is variable-rate, the annual interest cost rises by 0.80% of $300,000 = $2,400 a year (0.008 × $300,000). Minimum wage increase (6.0%, to $13.36 an hour): Some of the workforce of 90 is likely hourly-paid, so wage costs rise. Paper and ink input costs (10.2%): These feed the $3.80 variable cost per unit, but the insert does not split it, so only a labelled bound is defensible: if the whole variable cost rose 10.2%, that is 10.2% × $3.80 = about $0.39 per unit; across 120,000 units that is roughly $46,800 a year (120,000 × $0.39). The 57% of managers who would pay $0.25 more offer partial recovery, but printing demand grew only 3.3%, so a full price rise may lose jobs.

Conclusion: The 10.2% paper and ink rise will have the greatest impact. --- MAIN STEM ---
Orchard Vale Dairy (OVD) is a cooperative in the dairy processing sector, employing a workforce of 40. Founded in 2016 by the cheesemaker Gwenllian Price, it matures farmhouse cheese for specialist shops and uses a flat structure with democratic leadership and member involvement. It has fixed costs of $135,000 a year, a variable cost of $5.50 a unit and a selling price of $10.00, and currently produces 50,000 units a year. OVD faces milk waste of 4.8% and a maturation skills gap that limits how much cheese it can age for specialist shops.

Operations and Quality Log — Q3 2025: The cellars matured 11,800 wheels last quarter at a defect rate of 2.2%, down from 3.9% a year ago. A survey of 410 shoppers found 66% prefer farmhouse cheese and 53% would pay $1.50 more per wheel. With fixed costs of $135,000 a year, saving interest protects the $4.50 contribution on each of the 50,000 wheels and gives the cooperative steadier cash flow while it services the $300,000 loan.

PAPER 2 — P2_SET_476

--- MAIN STEM ---
Wave Ridge Hotels (WRH) is a private limited company in the hospitality sector, operating boutique coastal hotels and employing a workforce of 30. Founded in 2012 by Nadia Okoro, WRH runs a flat organisational structure with democratic leadership, giving reception and housekeeping teams a say in service routines. WRH plans to invest $720,000 in a new 60-room boutique wing with energy-efficient fittings, financed by a $450,000 ten-year bank loan and $270,000 retained profit. It has fixed costs of $180,000 a year, a variable cost of $25 a unit and a selling price of $85, and currently produces 12,000 units a year, each a booked room-night. WRH faces two problems: labour turnover has reached 18% among housekeeping staff and guest complaints about room cleanliness are rising.

--- APPENDIX 1 — MARKETING/OPS ---
Guest Services Report — Q3 2025: WRH recorded 3,000 room-nights last quarter at an average occupancy of 78%, down from 84% a year earlier. Room-cleanliness complaints rose to 46 per month from 29. Online review score fell to 4.1 from 4.5 out of 5. Average check-in time is 6.4 minutes. A survey of 500 guests found that 68% would pay up to $6 more for a certified eco-friendly room, and 57% choose hotels using renewable energy. Staff records show 11 of 30 employees have not completed on-the-job training in hygiene; off-the-job training refresher courses at the local college cost $260 per employee.

--- APPENDIX 2 — FINANCIAL DATA ---
Title: Extract from the Statement of Financial Position of Wave Ridge Hotels as at 31 March 2025 ($ '000)
Headers: ['Financial Metric', '2024', '2025']
Inventories | 30 | 25
Trade receivables | 90 | 120
Cash and cash equivalents | 20 | 45
Current liabilities | 100 | 110
Non-current assets | 1,400 | 1,950
Capital employed | 1,900 | 2,400

--- APPENDIX 3 — EXTERNAL ENVIRONMENT ---
Economic and Tourism Bulletin (October 2026): (1) The central bank lifted the base interest rate from 4.25% to 5.00%, raising borrowing costs on WRH's variable-rate bank loan. (2) The national minimum wage will rise by 5.8% from $12.50 to $13.23 per hour, increasing the wage bill for WRH's 30 housekeeping and reception staff. (3) Hotel energy and laundry input costs have risen 9.5% year-on-year, while domestic tourism spending grew 4.2% and local room occupancy rose 2.0 percentage points.

--- QUESTIONS ---
  Q1(a) [8 marks]
    Question: Explain two advantages for WRH of funding the new 60-room wing with a $450,000 bank loan rather than using only retained profit.
    Answer: Point 1: A $450,000 ten-year bank loan lets WRH complete the $720,000 wing now rather than waiting years to accumulate that sum from 12,000 room-nights a year at $85. Opening the 60 rooms sooner brings forward revenue that helps absorb fixed costs of $180,000 a year, and the loan is repaid over the same years the rooms earn. Keeping the $270,000 retained profit untouched also preserves cash for the rising trade receivables and inventories seen in Appendix 2, instead of locking every dollar into non-current assets.

Point 2: Borrowing matches the cost of the wing to the stream of room-night income it creates. With a contribution of $60 a room-night and break-even of only 3,000 room-nights, WRH has a margin of safety of 9,000 room-nights over its current 12,000, so the loan is comfortably serviceable. Holding $270,000 retained profit back gives a reserve if labour turnover of 18% forces extra recruitment or hygiene training at $260 per employee. A bank loan therefore accelerates growth while retained profit cushions the very operational problems WRH currently faces.
    Keywords: $720,000, $450,000, $270,000, bank loan, retained profit, workforce of 30
    Mark scheme: knowledge_max_2: 1 mark for each valid advantage of a bank loan over retained profit identified (max 2). | application_analysis_max_6: Up to 3 marks per point for contextual explanation applied to WRH's $720,000 wing, room-night economics and operational problems.

  Q1(b) [12 marks]
    Question: WRH is launching its new 60-room wing. Consider national television advertising, local radio sponsorship, or social media influencer marketing. Which should WRH choose to promote the launch? Justify your recommendation.
    Answer: National television advertising: A TV campaign reaches a mass audience quickly and could build awareness of the 60-room wing across the whole country. For a boutique coastal hotel group, however, most viewers live far from WRH's properties and cannot easily book, so much of the spend is wasted. Production and airtime costs would also be severe for a business with fixed costs of $180,000 a year and a $450,000 loan to service.

Local radio sponsorship: Radio is far cheaper and can target listeners near WRH's coastal hotels with time-sensitive launch messages. Its weakness is reach: WRH's 68% of 500 surveyed guests willing to pay $6 more for eco-friendly rooms are not confined to one local radio area, and a 30-employee operator needs bookings from across the country to fill 12,000 room-nights a year.

Social media influencer marketing: Travel and lifestyle influencers can show the energy-efficient rooms directly to the 57% of surveyed guests who choose hotels using renewable energy, with measurable engagement at a fraction of TV cost. Results build more slowly than television and depend on influencer credibility, but the message can be tracked and targeted nationally.

Recommendation: WRH should choose social media influencer marketing. It reaches the exact eco-conscious segment in the survey, scales nationally unlike local radio, and costs far less than television while reinforcing the $6 premium positioning. Television is rejected as unaffordable and untargeted, and radio is rejected as too geographically narrow for a group seeking to raise occupancy from 78%. The campaign can also be paused quickly if bookings do not rise.
    Keywords: 60-room, 78%, 500, 68%, 57%, $6
    Mark scheme: level_1_1_to_4: Limited outline of the three promotional options with minimal reference to WRH. | level_2_5_to_8: Discussion of advantages and disadvantages of at least two options with some application to WRH's launch. | level_3_9_to_12: Detailed evaluation of all three options in WRH's context with a justified recommendation that explains why television and radio are rejected.

  Q2(a) [8 marks]
    Question: WRH's labour turnover has reached 18% and cleanliness complaints are rising. Explain two benefits for WRH of using democratic leadership to improve staff motivation.
    Answer: Point 1: Democratic leadership gives WRH's 30 reception and housekeeping employees a real voice in how rooms are cleaned and inspected, which supports their social and esteem needs and raises job satisfaction. Staff who help design cleaning checklists are more likely to take pride in the work, directly tackling the 46 cleanliness complaints a month and protecting the 4.1 review score. In a flat structure, ideas reach Nadia Okoro quickly, so improvements can be made without delay.

Point 2: Consulting the team improves the quality of decisions because the people cleaning the rooms know which areas need more time or better equipment. Greater involvement builds commitment and should reduce the 18% labour turnover, saving the recruitment and $260 per employee hygiene-training costs. Stable staff also protect the 12,000 room-nights a year and the $60 contribution on each, making the $450,000 loan easier to service while the 60-room wing beds in.
    Keywords: democratic leadership, labour turnover, 18%, workforce of 30, 46, $260
    Mark scheme: knowledge_max_2: 1 mark for each valid benefit of democratic leadership identified (max 2). | application_analysis_max_6: Up to 3 marks per point for contextual development linked to WRH's turnover, complaints and training costs.

  Q2(b) [12 marks]
    Question: WRH must train 11 housekeeping staff in new hygiene procedures. Consider on-the-job training or off-the-job training at the local college. Which should WRH choose? Justify your decision.
    Answer: On-the-job training: Training beside experienced housekeepers is directly relevant to WRH's own rooms and cleanliness standards, costs no course fees and keeps all 11 staff productive while they learn. This protects the 3,000 room-nights handled last quarter and attacks the 46 monthly complaints at source. The drawbacks are that trainers are themselves working staff, so service can slow, and bad habits may be passed on unless supervisors inspect carefully; formal certification is also limited if guests demand proof of hygiene standards.

Off-the-job training: The local college course at $260 per employee gives structured, up-to-date hygiene knowledge and a recognised certificate for all 11 staff, costing $2,860 in total — small beside the $720,000 investment. It removes staff from the floor, however, reducing short-term room availability when occupancy is already 78%, and generic content may not match WRH's exact room-turnover routines, so follow-up coaching would still be needed.

Decision: WRH should choose on-the-job training first, with short college refresher sessions later. Managers should monitor the 46 complaints and 4.1 review score weekly, and supervisors should inspect rooms daily so bad habits cannot spread. If complaints do not fall after four weeks, a short college certificate course for the 11 staff should be funded from retained profit rather than delaying the $720,000 wing.

    Question: Using Appendix 3, evaluate how the interest rate rise to 5.00%, the 5.8% minimum wage increase and the 9.5% rise in energy and laundry input costs will affect WRH. Which change will have the greatest impact? Justify your answer.
    Answer: Interest rate rise (4.25% to 5.00%): If WRH's $450,000 bank loan is variable-rate, the annual interest cost rises by 0.75% of $450,000 = $3,375 a year (0.0075 × $450,000). That is modest beside fixed costs of $180,000 a year, and if the loan is fixed-rate the increase is zero. Higher rates could also make guests more cautious about discretionary coastal breaks and raise the cost of future borrowing, but WRH can limit this by fixing the rate.

Minimum wage increase (5.8%, to $13.23 per hour): With a workforce of 30 in housekeeping and reception, the rise feeds directly into the wage bill and cannot be avoided. The insert gives no hours worked or individual pay, so no honest annual total can be invented; the defensible test is productivity: 12,000 room-nights ÷ 30 staff = 400 room-nights per worker. If productivity holds, the extra wage cost is spread across more output; if labour turnover of 18% disrupts service, unit labour cost rises and the $60 contribution shrinks.

Input cost inflation (9.5% energy and laundry): The $25 variable cost per room-night is not decomposed in the insert, so only a bound is defensible: if the entire $25 rose 9.5%, that is 0.095 × $25 = $2.38 a room-night, and at 12,000 room-nights about $28,560 a year. Even a smaller increase compounds on every room-night sold and directly erodes the $60 contribution that justifies the $720,000 wing. The $6 eco-friendly premium can recover part of it, but not all.

Conclusion: The 9.5% rise in energy and laundry costs will have the greatest impact. It applies to all 12,000 room-nights and strikes at the $60 contribution that services the loan, whereas the rate rise adds a bounded $3,375 a year and the wage rise can be offset if the 400 room-nights per worker productivity is maintained.

--- MAIN STEM ---
Grandview River Tours (GRT) is a private limited company in the tourism and leisure sector, running scenic river cruises and employing a workforce of 24. Founded in 2015 by Ellis Mbeki, GRT uses a flat organisational structure with laissez-faire leadership, letting experienced skippers plan their own routes and commentary. GRT plans to invest $560,000 in two new electric river cruisers, financed by a $360,000 ten-year bank loan and $200,000 retained profit. It has fixed costs of $132,000 a year, a variable cost of $18 a unit and a selling price of $62, and currently produces 16,000 units a year, each a booked passenger-trip. GRT faces two problems: sickness absence has reached 8% and customer complaints about crowded cruises are rising.

--- APPENDIX 1 — MARKETING/OPS ---
Operations and Quality Report — Q2 2025: GRT ran 4,000 passenger-trips last quarter at an average load factor of 71%, down from 79% a year earlier. Complaints about overcrowding rose to 34 per month from 19. Customer satisfaction fell from 4.6 to 4.2 out of 5. Average boarding delay is 11 minutes. A survey of 400 tourists found that 61% would pay $5 more for a small-group eco-cruise, and 49% book their tours through social media. Training records show 9 of 24 crew have not completed on-the-job training in customer care; off-the-job training workshops cost $310 per crew member.

--- APPENDIX 2 — FINANCIAL DATA ---

Current liabilities | 80 | 95
Non-current assets | 980 | 1,420
Capital employed | 1,250 | 1,650

(2) The national minimum wage will increase by 6.2% from $12.80 to $13.59 per hour, raising crew wage costs. (3) Marine diesel prices have risen 11.3% year-on-year, while inbound tourism arrivals grew 5.4% and average household spending on leisure trips rose 2.8%.
