Bringing the boats forward raises revenue sooner to cover fixed costs of $132,000 a year and spreads repayment over ten years, matching the years the cruisers will operate. Keeping the $200,000 retained profit available gives a reserve for the rising trade receivables and lower cash shown in Appendix 2.

Point 2: Borrowing leaves ownership and control with founder Ellis Mbeki; no outside investor gains a claim on GRT or a share of future profit. With a contribution of $44 a passenger-trip and break-even of 3,000 trips, GRT has a margin of safety of 13,000 trips, so the loan is well covered. Retaining $200,000 also cushions the 8% sickness absence and the customer-care training bill of $310 per crew member, so expansion does not starve the existing cruises of working capital.
    Keywords: $560,000, $360,000, $200,000, bank loan, retained profit, workforce of 24

--- MAIN STEM ---
Sunfield Retreats (SFR) is a public limited company in the leisure and hospitality sector, running wellness resorts and glamping sites and employing a workforce of 42. Founded in 2008 by Priya Raman, SFR uses a hierarchical organisational structure with democratic leadership, so area managers consult resort teams before changing guest services. SFR plans to invest $1,200,000 in a new wellness spa and 40-unit glamping site, financed by a $700,000 ten-year bank loan, a $300,000 share issue and $200,000 retained profit. It has fixed costs of $240,000 a year, a variable cost of $30 a unit and a selling price of $110, and currently produces 14,000 units a year, each a booked guest-night. SFR faces two problems: staff turnover has reached 14% and maintenance complaints about the cabins are rising.

--- APPENDIX 1 — MARKETING/OPS ---
Quality and Operations Report — Q1 2025: SFR hosted 3,500 guest-nights in the quarter at an occupancy of 69%, down from 76% a year ago. Maintenance complaints rose to 52 per month from 31. Review score fell to 3.9 from 4.4 out of 5. Average check-in wait is 9 minutes. A survey of 700 guests found that 66% would pay up to $12 more for a wellness package and 58% prefer eco-friendly cabins. Records show 15 of 42 staff have not completed on-the-job training in cabin maintenance; off-the-job training certification costs $340 per employee.

--- APPENDIX 2 — FINANCIAL DATA ---
Title: Extract from the Statement of Financial Position of Sunfield Retreats as at 31 March 2025 ($ '000)
Headers: ['Financial Metric', '2024', '2025']

Non-current assets | 2,100 | 2,950
Capital employed | 2,600 | 3,400

--- APPENDIX 3 — EXTERNAL ENVIRONMENT ---
Economic and Leisure Bulletin (August 2026): (1) The central bank raised the base interest rate from 3.75% to 4.50%, raising finance costs on SFR's variable-rate loan. (2) The national minimum wage will rise by 7.1% from $13.00 to $13.92 per hour, lifting the wage bill for SFR's 42 staff. (3) Resort energy and maintenance input costs have risen 10.6% year-on-year, while staycation spending grew 3.9% and regional tourist arrivals rose 4.6%.

--- QUESTIONS ---
  Q1(a) [8 marks]
    Question: Explain two advantages for SFR of raising the $300,000 through a share issue rather than increasing the bank loan.
    Answer: Point 1: A $300,000 share issue brings in equity that carries no interest or repayment schedule, so SFR avoids adding to the interest burden on its $700,000 loan while developing the $1,200,000 spa and glamping site. With fixed costs of $240,000 a year already to cover, avoiding extra debt service protects cash flow. The new shareholders also share the risk: if the 40 glamping units are slow to fill, SFR is not obliged to find fixed loan instalments.

Point 2: Equity can be a larger and more flexible source than borrowing, allowing SFR to proceed with the whole development now rather than delaying it. The $200,000 retained profit stays available for working capital, which matters because trade receivables have risen to $130,000 in Appendix 2. As a public limited company SFR can access investors more easily, and keeping the loan at $700,000 leaves room to borrow later if the 14% staff turnover demands extra spending on recruitment.
    Keywords: $1,200,000, $300,000, $700,000, share issue, bank loan, workforce of 42
    Mark scheme: knowledge_max_2: 1 mark for each valid advantage of a share issue over more debt identified (max 2). | application_analysis_max_6: Up to 3 marks per point for contextual explanation applied to SFR's $1,200,000 development, debt and cash position.

  Q1(b) [12 marks]
    Question: SFR is launching the new wellness spa and glamping site. Consider national television advertising, regional press advertising, or social media influencer marketing. Which should SFR choose to promote the launch? Justify your recommendation.
    Answer: National television advertising: TV would give the spa and glamping launch huge reach and could quickly build brand recognition for SFR as a public limited company. The production and airtime costs, however, are very high for a business servicing a $700,000 loan, and most viewers are too far away to book a stay. With occupancy at 69%, SFR needs cost-effective bookings rather than broad awareness.

Regional press advertising: Newspapers and magazines in SFR's regions are cheaper and can target nearby staycationers, with scope for detailed pictures of the 40 glamping units. Their reach is limited and print readership is falling, so they cannot by themselves generate the 14,000 guest-nights a year needed, and the message lacks the visual impact of video.

Social media influencer marketing: Wellness and travel influencers can demonstrate the spa and eco-friendly cabins to the 58% of 700 surveyed guests who prefer such cabins, and the 66% who would pay $12 more for a wellness package. Engagement is measurable and can be targeted nationally. It builds results more slowly than TV and depends on influencer fit, but cost per booking is low.

It reaches the exact segments in the survey, supports the $12 premium and scales beyond regional press at a fraction of television cost.   Q2(a) [8 marks]
    Question: SFR's staff turnover has reached 14% and maintenance complaints are rising. Explain two benefits for SFR of using democratic leadership to improve staff motivation.
    Answer: Point 1: Democratic leadership invites SFR's 42 resort employees to contribute ideas on cabin maintenance and guest services, which satisfies social and esteem needs and raises job satisfaction. Staff who help set maintenance routines are more likely to spot faults early, directly attacking the 52 complaints a month and protecting the 3.9 review score. Conclusion: The 10.6% rise in energy and maintenance costs will have the greatest impact. It compounds across all 14,000 guest-nights and erodes the $80 contribution, whereas the interest rise is a bounded $5,250 and the wage rise can be absorbed if 333.33 guest-nights per worker is sustained.

--- MAIN STEM ---
Bayharbour Hotels (BHR) is a partnership in the hospitality sector, running a waterside hotel and rooftop restaurant and employing a workforce of 36. Founded in 2010 by Tomas Lindqvist, BHR uses a hierarchical organisational structure with autocratic leadership, so the senior partners set service standards for reception and kitchen teams. BHR plans to invest $880,000 in a 45-room extension with a rooftop restaurant, financed by a $580,000 ten-year bank loan and $300,000 retained profit. It has fixed costs of $200,000 a year, a variable cost of $28 a unit and a selling price of $92, and currently produces 13,000 units a year, each a booked room-night. BHR faces two problems: absenteeism has reached 10% and food waste in the restaurant is rising.

--- APPENDIX 1 — MARKETING/OPS ---
Operations and Waste Report — Q4 2025: BHR served 3,250 room-nights last quarter at 74% occupancy, down from 81% a year earlier. Kitchen food waste rose to 88 kg per week from 54 kg. Complaints about breakfast quality rose to 27 per month from 16. Guest rating fell from 4.5 to 4.1 out of 5. A survey of 550 guests found that 64% would pay up to $7 more for locally sourced breakfasts and 53% value active waste reduction. Records show 12 of 36 staff have not completed on-the-job training in food hygiene; off-the-job training courses cost $280 per employee.

--- APPENDIX 2 — FINANCIAL DATA ---
Title: Extract from the Statement of Financial Position of Bayharbour Hotels as at 31 March 2025 ($ '000)

Trade receivables | 60 | 95

Capital employed | 2,150 | 2,800

(2) The national minimum wage will rise by 6.5% from $12.60 to $13.42 per hour, raising wages for BHR's 36 staff. (3) Food and beverage input costs have risen 8.9% year-on-year, while domestic hotel demand grew 3.1% and business travel spending rose 2.4%.

With fixed costs of $200,000 a year already to meet, a smaller debt service protects the cash needed to run the rooftop restaurant while the 45 new rooms are filling.

Point 2: Retained profit is immediately available and carries no lender conditions, letting Tomas Lindqvist and the partners proceed without a further credit application or collateral. It also keeps decision-making inside the partnership. Holding $300,000 back from external finance leaves BHR better placed to absorb the 10% absenteeism and the $280 per employee hygiene-training costs, so the existing hotel is not starved of funds while the extension is built. As a partnership, BHR also avoids the market scrutiny that a public listing would bring.

--- MAIN STEM ---
Coastway Travel Holidays (CTH) is a cooperative in the tourism sector, selling coastal package holidays and employing a workforce of 28. Founded in 2011 by Grace Osei, CTH uses a flat organisational structure with democratic leadership, letting member teams vote on customer-service changes. CTH plans to invest $640,000 in a new online booking platform and three coastal tour hubs, financed by a $400,000 ten-year bank loan and $240,000 retained profit. It has fixed costs of $168,000 a year, a variable cost of $22 a unit and a selling price of $78, and currently produces 15,000 units a year, each a booked holiday. CTH faces two problems: staff turnover has reached 12% and customer complaints about booking errors are rising.

--- APPENDIX 1 — MARKETING/OPS ---
Customer Operations Report — Q2 2025: CTH handled 3,750 holiday bookings last quarter at an average booking value of $78. Online booking errors rose to 41 per month from 23. Customer complaints rose to 38 per month from 22. Satisfaction fell from 4.3 to 3.8 out of 5. Average response time is 14 minutes. A survey of 650 travellers found that 63% would pay $4 more for instant confirmation and 55% book by mobile. Records show 8 of 28 staff have not completed on-the-job training on the digital system; off-the-job training courses cost $230 per employee.

--- APPENDIX 2 — FINANCIAL DATA ---
Title: Extract from the Statement of Financial Position of Coastway Travel Holidays as at 31 March 2025 ($ '000)
Headers: ['Financial Metric', '2024', '2025']
Inventories | 12 | 15
Trade receivables | 65 | 96
Cash and cash equivalents | 28 | 15
Current liabilities | 70 | 90
Non-current assets | 820 | 1,300
Capital employed | 1,100 | 1,550

--- APPENDIX 3 — EXTERNAL ENVIRONMENT ---
Economic and Tourism Bulletin (June 2026): (1) The central bank raised the base interest rate from 4.00% to 4.60%, increasing borrowing costs on CTH's variable-rate loan. (2) The national minimum wage will rise by 5.5% from $12.20 to $12.87 per hour, raising the wage bill for CTH's 28 staff. (3) Travel fuel and commission costs have risen 9.8% year-on-year, while consumer spending on domestic holidays grew 3.3% and online bookings rose 6.1%.

--- QUESTIONS ---
  Q1(a) [8 marks]
    Question: Explain two advantages for CTH of using $240,000 retained profit alongside the $400,000 bank loan to fund the booking platform.
    Answer: Point 1: Combining $240,000 retained profit with the $400,000 bank loan reduces the amount CTH must borrow for the $640,000 platform, lowering interest and repayments. With fixed costs of $168,000 a year and a $56 contribution on each of 15,000 bookings, keeping debt smaller leaves more cash to run the three tour hubs. The retained profit is immediately available, so the platform can be launched without waiting for further credit approval.

Point 2: Using internal funds keeps control with the cooperative's members rather than a lender, and no collateral is tied up beyond the loan already agreed. It also leaves a reserve for the 12% staff turnover and the $230 per employee digital-training cost, so the existing service is not neglected while the new system is built. The mix therefore balances expansion with the working capital needed to cut the 38 monthly complaints. A cooperative keeps those savings available to its 28 member teams.
    Keywords: $640,000, $400,000, $240,000, retained profit, bank loan, workforce of 28
    Mark scheme: knowledge_max_2: 1 mark for each valid advantage of combining retained profit with debt identified (max 2). | application_analysis_max_6: Up to 3 marks per point for contextual explanation applied to CTH's $640,000 platform, booking economics and staffing.

  Q1(b) [12 marks]
    Question: CTH is launching its new online booking platform. Consider television advertising, direct mail, or social media influencer marketing. Which should CTH choose to promote the launch? Justify your recommendation.
    Answer: Television advertising: TV gives very wide reach and could quickly make travellers aware of the new platform, but airtime is expensive for a cooperative with a $400,000 loan and $168,000 fixed costs. Many viewers do not book coastal holidays, so much of the spend is wasted, and a 28-employee business cannot afford a national campaign.

Direct mail: Sending offers to existing customer lists is cheap and targeted, and could help recover satisfaction from 3.8 to 4.3. Response rates are low, printing and postage add up, and it will not reach the 55% of 650 surveyed travellers who book by mobile, limiting its ability to drive use of the new platform.

Social media influencer marketing: Travel influencers can demonstrate instant confirmation directly to mobile-first travellers and to the 63% of surveyed travellers willing to pay $4 more for it. Engagement is trackable and costs less than television. Results take time and depend on choosing credible influencers, but targeting is precise.

Recommendation: CTH should choose social media influencer marketing. It reaches the mobile booking segment in the survey, supports the $4 instant-confirmation premium and is far cheaper than television. Television is rejected as unaffordable and untargeted, and direct mail as too slow and narrow to promote a digital platform, so a small email follow-up to existing customers should supplement it. Conclusion: The 9.8% rise in fuel and commission costs will have the greatest impact because it compounds across all 15,000 bookings and erodes the $56 contribution, while the interest rise is a bounded $2,400 and the wage rise can be absorbed if 535.71 bookings per worker is maintained.

--- MAIN STEM ---
Harbour Reach Logistics (HRL) is a private limited company in the container freight and port logistics sector, employing a workforce of 50. Founded in 2007 by Alan Truscott, it moves imported goods for national retailers and operates a hierarchical structure with autocratic leadership. HRL plans to invest $1,200,000 in an automated container-handling crane system, financed by an $800,000 ten-year bank loan and $400,000 retained profit. It has fixed costs of $320,000 a year, a variable cost of $24 a unit and a selling price of $32, and currently produces 60,000 units a year, each unit a billable container consignment. HRL faces a growing skills gap: 18 of its 50 drivers and crane operators are not certified on the new automated system, and defect complaints at the terminal are rising.

--- APPENDIX 1 — MARKETING/OPS ---
Operations and Quality Report — Q3 2025: The container terminal handled 15,000 consignments last quarter at a damage defect rate of 2.2%, down from 3.6% a year ago. Customer complaints fell from 44 to 26 per month. Average truck turnaround time is 4.5 hours. A survey of 500 freight clients found that 68% would pay a 3% premium for guaranteed two-day delivery, and 57% rate on-time reliability as their top criterion. A skills audit shows 18 of 50 staff are not certified on the new automated crane; external certification courses cost $750 per employee.

--- APPENDIX 2 — FINANCIAL DATA ---

(3) Diesel fuel prices have risen 9.0% year-on-year and port handling charges are up 4.0%, while demand for container freight grew 2.5%.

    Answer: Point 1: Retained profit of $400,000 carries no interest charges or capital repayments, so it protects HRL's cash flow while the business already services an $800,000 bank loan and carries fixed costs of $320,000 a year. Every dollar saved in interest can be spent on the new automated container-handling crane without raising the $32 selling price, helping HRL win the 68% of surveyed freight clients who would pay a premium for reliable two-day delivery.

Point 2: Using retained profit keeps control with founder Alan Truscott and avoids the collateral conditions attached to the $800,000 loan, so the $1,200,000 expansion cannot be repossessed if freight demand disappoints. It also lets HRL act quickly on the skills gap among 18 uncertified staff by funding training from internal funds rather than seeking further bank approval, protecting the contribution earned on each of 60,000 container consignments and leaving the loan available for future working capital.
    Keywords: retained profit, $400,000, $800,000, $320,000, bank loan, $1,200,000

    Question: HRL is promoting its guaranteed two-day container delivery service. Consider national trade-journal advertising, social media marketing, or direct sales calls to freight clients. Which should HRL choose to promote the service? Justify your recommendation.
    Answer: National trade-journal advertising: A campaign in freight and logistics journals would reach many retail supply managers at once and build HRL's reputation as a reliable container carrier, supporting the premium two-day service. However, a full-page national campaign is expensive for a 50-employee firm already funding an $800,000 loan, and much of the readership lies outside the coastal catchment HRL actually serves, so a large share of the spend is wasted.

Direct sales calls to freight clients: A sales team can call the 500 surveyed clients and national retailers individually, demonstrate the two-day offer and negotiate the 3% premium that 68% said they would accept. This builds on existing relationships, gives immediate feedback on the 26 monthly complaints and targets the highest-volume accounts. It is slower to build broad awareness than print and uses staff time, but conversion per contact is high and it directly fills the 60,000-unit capacity.

Recommendation: HRL should choose direct sales calls as its main method, supported by low-cost social media. Direct calls turn the finding that 68% of 500 clients would pay a 3% premium into real bookings and handle complaints personally, which a journal campaign cannot do. Trade-journal advertising is rejected as too costly and untargeted for a 50-staff company servicing a loan; social media alone is rejected because its audience is too diffuse for specialist container freight.

--- MAIN STEM ---
Quayline West Transit (QWT) is a public limited company in the regional bus and coach transport sector, employing a workforce of 70. Founded in 1998 by Priya Raman, it runs services along the western coast and operates a flat structure with democratic leadership. QWT plans to invest $900,000 in a fleet of electric buses and charging depots, financed by a $600,000 ten-year bank loan and $300,000 share issue. It has fixed costs of $450,000 a year, a variable cost of $9 a unit and a selling price of $18, and currently produces 70,000 units a year, each unit one paying passenger journey. QWT faces rising labour turnover among drivers and a defect rate of 3.5% in vehicle maintenance checks.

--- APPENDIX 1 — MARKETING/OPS ---
Operations and Quality Report — Q3 2025: The western network ran 18,000 bus services last quarter with a maintenance defect rate of 3.5%, down from 5.2% a year earlier. Passenger complaints fell from 62 to 34 per month. Average punctuality is 88.0% of services running on time. A survey of 700 commuters found that 61% would switch to electric buses if fares stayed the same, and 49% cite reliability as the main reason for choosing QWT. A driver audit shows 22 of 70 drivers need retraining on electric vehicle systems; certification courses cost $650 per driver.

--- APPENDIX 2 — FINANCIAL DATA ---
Title: Extract from the Statement of Profit or Loss and Capital employed data of Quayline West Transit for the year ended 31 March 2025 ($ '000)
Headers: ['Financial Metric', '2024', '2025']

Operating profit | 216 | 315

Interest payable | 24 | 30

--- APPENDIX 3 — EXTERNAL ENVIRONMENT ---
Economic and Business Bulletin (November 2026): (1) The central bank has raised the base interest rate from 4.0% to 4.8%, increasing the cost of QWT's $600,000 bank loan. (2) The national minimum wage will rise by 6.0% from $12.50 to $13.25 per hour from April 2026, raising the wage bill for its 70 drivers and staff. (3) Diesel and electricity costs for the fleet have risen 11.0% year-on-year, while passenger fare revenue grew only 2.0% and regional bus usage fell 1.5%.

--- QUESTIONS ---
  Q1(a) [8 marks]
    Question: QWT financed its $900,000 electric bus fleet with a $600,000 bank loan and a $300,000 share issue. Explain two advantages for QWT of using the share issue rather than more bank borrowing for this expansion.
    Answer: Point 1: The $300,000 raised by a share issue does not have to be repaid and carries no interest, so it eases the cash flow burden on QWT, which already pays interest on a $600,000 bank loan and bears fixed costs of $450,000 a year. That saving helps hold the $18 fare steady while fleet energy costs rise, keeping the service attractive to the 61% of surveyed commuters who would switch to electric buses.

Point 2: Equity strengthens QWT's balance sheet because the $300,000 increases capital Employed without adding a creditor who could demand repayment or seize buses if passenger revenue falls. As a public limited company, QWT can issue shares to existing holders or new investors, preserving borrowing capacity for the charging depots and allowing founder Priya Raman to keep the $900,000 project on schedule despite rising labour turnover among drivers.

  Q4(b) [12 marks]
    Question: Using Appendix 3, evaluate how the base interest rate rise to 4.8%, the 6.0% minimum wage increase and the 11.0% rise in fleet energy costs will affect QWT. Which change will have the greatest impact? Justify your answer.
    Answer: Interest rate rise (4.0% to 4.8%): If QWT's $600,000 bank loan is variable-rate, the increase is 0.8 percentage points (4.8% − 4.0%), so extra annual interest is 0.8% × $600,000 = $4,800 a year. That is modest against fixed costs of $450,000, and if the loan is fixed the direct cost is nil. The larger risk is indirect: higher rates may suppress consumer spending, but QWT can hedge by fixing the rate.

Minimum wage increase (6.0%, to $13.25 per hour): With a workforce of 70, driving and depot roles are largely hourly-paid, so the rise lifts the wage bill and cannot be avoided. The insert gives no hours worked or individual pay, so a total wage cost cannot be honestly invented; the defensible test is productivity of 70,000 journeys ÷ 70 staff = 1,000 journeys per worker. If productivity holds, the rise is absorbable; if labour turnover pushes it down, the $9 contribution per journey is squeezed.

Fleet energy costs (11.0% rise in diesel and electricity): These feed into the $9 variable cost on each of 70,000 journeys. The insert does not split that cost, so only a bound can be shown: if the whole $9 were energy and it rose 11.0%, that would be 11.0% × $9 = $0.99 per journey, or up to $69,300 a year at 70,000 journeys — but energy is only part of variable cost, so the true figure is lower and cannot be stated exactly from the insert. Because fares grew only 2.0% and usage fell 1.5%, QWT cannot easily pass this on.

Conclusion: The 11.0% rise in fleet energy costs will have the greatest impact. It touches every journey, far exceeds the $4,800 interest effect, and is harder to offset than wages because fares are growing only 2.0% while demand is falling. The interest rise is the smallest and can be fixed; the wage rise is significant but manageable at 1,000 journeys per worker. Energy inflation directly erodes the $9 contribution that underpins the $900,000 fleet investment, so it matters most.
    Keywords: 4.8%, 6.0%, 11.0%, $600,000, 4.0%, $13.25
    Mark scheme: level_1_1_to_4: Identifies the external factors with limited application to QWT. | level_2_5_to_8: Analyses the impact of at least two external changes on QWT's costs, revenue or financing in context. | level_3_9_to_12: Detailed evaluation of all three external changes in the context of QWT with a well-justified judgment that fleet energy inflation has the greatest impact and why the other two are smaller.

--- MAIN STEM ---
Zenith Power Limited (ZPL) is a private limited company in the renewable energy equipment sector, employing a workforce of 90. Founded in 2012 by Nadia Okafor, it manufactures photovoltaic panels for commercial solar farms and operates a hierarchical structure with autocratic leadership. ZPL plans to invest $2,400,000 in an automated solar-cell assembly line, financed by a $1,500,000 ten-year bank loan and $900,000 retained profit. It has fixed costs of $900,000 a year, a variable cost of $84 a unit and a selling price of $120, and currently produces 45,000 units a year, each unit one photovoltaic panel. ZPL faces a quality control problem, with a defect rate of 4.1% on finished panels and rising waste levels in the assembly hall.

--- APPENDIX 1 — MARKETING/OPS ---
Quality and Waste Report — Q3 2025: The assembly line produced 11,000 panels last quarter with a defect rate of 4.1%, up from 2.6% a year earlier. Customer warranty claims rose from 19 to 37 per month. Average material waste is 6.4% of input. A survey of 400 solar installers found that 72% would pay a 4% premium for panels with a longer warranty, and 55% rank product reliability as their top purchase factor. A training audit shows 24 of 90 assembly workers lack training on the new automated cell handlers; external courses cost $820 per worker.

--- APPENDIX 2 — FINANCIAL DATA ---

The interest saved can fund the $820 training courses for 24 workers, improving the quality control problem without raising the $120 selling price or cutting the $36 contribution on each panel.

Point 2: Using internal funds keeps decision-making with founder Nadia Okafor and avoids the security conditions attached to the $1,500,000 loan, so the $2,400,000 assembly line is not at risk of repossession if solar subsidies are cut. It also allows ZPL to act quickly on the 4.1% defect rate and rising waste, since no lender approval is needed to spend the $900,000 on rectifying the automated cell handlers.

    Answer: Interest rate rise (4.5% to 5.25%): If KET's $600,000 bank loan is variable-rate, the rise is 0.75 percentage points (5.25% − 4.5%), so extra annual interest is 0.75% × $600,000 = $4,500 a year. That is small against fixed costs of $480,000 and can be removed entirely by fixing the loan rate. Higher base rates may slow consumer spending, but parcel volumes are still forecast to grow 8.0%.

Minimum wage increase (7.0%, to $12.84 per hour): With a workforce of 80, warehouse and driving roles are largely hourly-paid, so the rise raises the wage bill and cannot be avoided. The insert gives no hours worked or pay rates, so a total cannot be honestly invented; the defensible test is productivity of 120,000 parcels ÷ 80 staff = 1,500 parcels per worker. If productivity holds, the rise is absorbable, but with 8% absenteeism and 16 untrained staff the $6 contribution per parcel could be squeezed.

Fuel and packaging costs (10.0% rise): These feed the $8 variable cost on every one of 120,000 parcels. The insert does not split that cost, so only a bound can be shown: if all $8 were affected, 10.0% × $8 = $0.80 per parcel, which at 120,000 parcels is about $96,000 a year — but fuel and packaging are only part of variable cost, so the true figure is lower and cannot be stated from the insert. With the average delivery price falling 1.0%, KET cannot easily pass this on despite the $0.50 premium that 66% would accept.

Conclusion: The 10.0% rise in fuel and packaging costs will have the greatest impact. It applies to every parcel, dwarfs the $4,500 interest effect, and is harder to offset than wages because the average price is falling 1.0%. The interest rise is the smallest and hedgeable; the wage rise is serious but manageable at 1,500 parcels per worker if absenteeism is tackled. Input inflation directly attacks the $8 variable cost behind the $6 contribution, so it matters most.

    Mark scheme: level_1_1_to_4: Identifies the external factors with limited application to KET. | level_2_5_to_8: Analyses the impact of at least two external changes on KET's costs, revenue or financing in context. | level_3_9_to_12: Detailed evaluation of all three external changes in the context of KET with a well-justified judgment that fuel and packaging inflation has the greatest impact and why the other two are smaller.

Founded in 2015 by Priya Raman, NEXA employs a workforce of 60 and operates a flat organisational structure with democratic leadership. NEXA plans to invest $960,000 in a contactless payment platform and merchant mobile app, financed by a $600,000 ten-year bank loan and $360,000 retained profit. It has fixed costs of $600,000 a year, a variable cost of $145 a unit and a selling price of $245, and currently produces 12,000 units a year. NEXA faces an operational problem: 11% of transactions last quarter were failed or delayed and merchant installers show skills gaps on the new platform.

--- APPENDIX 1 — MARKETING/OPS ---
Market Research Summary — October 2026: A survey of 640 small Ontario retailers found 73% now accept contactless payments in store (up from 51% three years ago) and 61% would switch their payment provider for faster settlement. NEXA's current app takes 4.2 days to settle merchant funds; 11% of transactions last quarter were flagged as failed or delayed. Average merchant onboarding takes 5.5 days. Rival fintechs charge 2.4% per transaction while NEXA charges 2.8%. Referrals from existing merchants deliver 38% of new sign-ups; a support audit found a 1.9% repeat-contact rate on installation issues.

    Question: NEXA plans to fund part of its new contactless payment platform with $360,000 of retained profit. Explain two advantages for NEXA of using retained profit instead of borrowing the full $960,000 externally.
    Answer: Point 1: Retained profit is internally generated cash, so NEXA pays no interest or capital repayments on the $360,000, protecting the cash flow that must already absorb fixed costs of $600,000 a year. Every dollar saved on interest can fund the rollout of the $960,000 contactless platform and help cover the 9.2% rise in cloud processing costs without pushing the $245 selling price above what the 640 surveyed Ontario retailers will bear, especially as rivals already charge 2.4% per transaction against NEXA's 2.8%.

Point 2: Using retained profit leaves the $600,000 ten-year bank loan as the only external claim, so Priya Raman's existing shareholders keep full ownership and control, and no lender can impose conditions on how the merchant app is built or priced. With 11% of transactions failing or delayed, NEXA needs freedom to redirect spending into fixing settlement times rather than satisfying bank covenants. Funding growth from its own trading success also signals confidence to the 61% of surveyed retailers who would switch for faster settlement, while avoiding a larger debt burden on a 60-person business.

It lets NEXA answer the 2.4% rival price objection with the faster-settlement message of the 61% switch segment. Costs can be capped daily, protecting cash flow.

Recommendation: NEXA should choose search-engine advertising. It captures high-intent demand at controllable cost and can be scaled with the $960,000 rollout. Profit Margin 2025 = 20.6%

ROCE 2025 = 20.0%

  Q4(b) [12 marks]
    Question: Using Appendix 3, evaluate how the rise in the policy rate to 5.00%, the 5.8% minimum wage increase and the 9.2% rise in cloud processing costs will affect NEXA. Which change will have the greatest impact? Justify your answer.
    Answer: Policy rate rise to 5.00%: NEXA carries a $600,000 ten-year bank loan. If it is variable-rate, the 0.75 percentage-point rise adds 0.75% of $600,000 = $4,500 a year (0.0075 × $600,000). That is modest beside fixed costs of $600,000 and 2025 interest payable of $76,000; if the loan is fixed-rate the direct cost is nil. Higher rates may also cool Ontario small-retailer spending on new payment systems, but NEXA can largely neutralise the financing risk by fixing the rate.

Minimum wage rise of 5.8% to $17.46 per hour: The insert does not state hours worked or how many of the 60 staff are hourly-paid, so no defensible annual wage total can be invented. The honest test is productivity computed from the insert: 12,000 units ÷ 60 staff = 200 units per worker. If output per worker holds, the rise is absorbable within a 45.0% share of revenue retained as gross profit; if installation delays reduce that productivity, unit labour costs climb and the $100 contribution per unit shrinks. NEXA can also pass part of it on given the 61% switch-intent segment.

Cloud processing cost inflation of 9.2%: This strikes every unit. The insert does not decompose the $145 variable cost, so only an explicitly labelled upper bound is honest: if the entire variable cost rose 9.2%, it would add 9.2% × $145 = $13.34 per unit, and at 12,000 units that is roughly $160,000 a year (12,000 × $13.34). Even a fraction of that erodes the contribution underpinning the $960,000 platform, and it cannot easily be passed on to retailers already comparing 2.4% rates.

Conclusion: The 9.2% rise in cloud processing costs will have the greatest impact. It compounds across all 12,000 units and attacks the $100 contribution that justifies the $960,000 investment; by contrast the rate rise is at most $4,500 and the wage effect cannot be quantified without invented assumptions. NEXA should lock cloud contracts and fix the loan rate.
    Keywords: 5.00%, 5.8%, 9.2%, $17.46, $600,000, $145
    Mark scheme: level_1_1_to_4: Identifies the external factors with limited application to NEXA. | level_2_5_to_8: Analyses the impact of at least two external changes on NEXA's costs, demand or financing in context. | level_3_9_to_12: Detailed evaluation of all three external changes in the context of NEXA with a well-justified judgment that cloud processing cost inflation has the greatest impact and why the other two are smaller.

--- MAIN STEM ---
Qubit Smart Systems (QBIT) is a public limited company in the smart-home technology sector, making connected hubs and voice-control devices for Singapore households. Founded in 2011 by Mei Lin Chua, QBIT employs a workforce of 70 and operates a hierarchical structure with autocratic leadership. QBIT plans to invest $1,400,000 in a next-generation smart-home hub and voice-assistant app, financed by an $800,000 ten-year bank loan, a $300,000 share issue and $300,000 retained profit. It has fixed costs of $900,000 a year, a variable cost of $210 a unit and a selling price of $390, and currently produces 14,000 units a year. QBIT faces a quality problem: 2.4% of hubs assembled last quarter were defective and 1.6% of installations suffered firmware-update failures.

--- APPENDIX 1 — MARKETING/OPS ---
Operations and Quality Log — Q4 2026: The smart-home hub line assembled 3,600 units last quarter at a defect rate of 2.4%, down from 4.0% a year earlier. Customer returns fell from 62 to 34 per month. Average firmware-update failure rate is 1.6% of installations. Delivery lead time averages 6.2 days. A survey of 720 Singapore homeowners found 68% want voice-control compatibility and 57% would pay a 10% premium for faster setup. Technician audit shows 24 of 70 field staff have not completed on-the-job training on the new hub; off-the-job certification costs $1,100 per technician.

--- APPENDIX 2 — FINANCIAL DATA ---
Title: Extract from the Statement of Profit or Loss and Capital employed data of Qubit Smart Systems for the year ended 31 March 2025 ($ '000)
Headers: ['Financial Metric', '2024', '2025']
Revenue | 4,000 | 4,800
Cost of sales | 2,600 | 2,784
Gross profit | 1,400 | 2,016
Operating profit | 560 | 864
Capital employed | 3,200 | 4,600
Interest payable | 90 | 150

--- APPENDIX 3 — EXTERNAL ENVIRONMENT ---
Economic and Technology Bulletin (November 2026): (1) Singapore's central bank has tightened policy, lifting the three-month interbank rate from 3.30% to 4.05% and raising borrowing costs on variable-rate business loans. (2) The national minimum wage will rise 5.5% from $15.00 to $15.83 per hour from July 2027, increasing wage costs for field and support staff. (3) Semiconductor and sensor input costs rose 11.3% year-on-year as global chip demand recovers, while Singapore smart-home device sales grew 8.6% over the same period.

  Q1(a) [8 marks]
    Question: QBIT plans to raise $300,000 for its new smart-home hub through a share issue. Explain two advantages for QBIT of using the share issue rather than borrowing the whole $1,400,000 from banks.
    Answer: Point 1: A share issue brings permanent equity with no repayment schedule or interest charge, so QBIT avoids piling further debt on top of its $800,000 ten-year bank loan and shields fixed costs of $900,000 a year from extra interest. The $300,000 can fund the voice-assistant app and absorb the 11.3% rise in sensor costs, helping hold the $390 selling price for the 57% of surveyed homeowners who would pay a 10% premium for faster setup rather than passing costs on.

Point 2: Equity does not require collateral or covenants, so Mei Lin Chua's expanded shareholder base faces no lender pressure if the hub launch is delayed by the 2.4% defect rate or 1.6% firmware failures. Unlike the bank, shareholders share the risk of a 14,000-unit sales target without demanding early repayment. A larger capital base also improves credibility with Smart Nation partners and retail chains, supporting the 68% of homeowners who want voice-control compatibility and the wider $1,400,000 platform rollout.
    Keywords: share issue, bank loan, $300,000, $800,000, $1,400,000, fixed costs
    Mark scheme: knowledge_max_2: 1 mark for each valid advantage identified (max 2). | application_analysis_max_6: Up to 3 marks per point for contextual explanation and analysis applied to Qubit Smart Systems and its expansion decision.

    Answer: Electronics retail chains: Stores would let shoppers see and try voice-control features, important when 68% of surveyed homeowners want compatibility and 57% would pay more for faster setup. Staff can demonstrate the hub and handle the 6.2-day delivery question face to face. However, chains demand generous margins and shelf fees, which would squeeze the $390 price and the contribution available to repay the $800,000 loan, and QBIT would lose control of how the product is presented.

Direct online store: Selling directly captures the full margin, builds first-party customer data and lets QBIT explain the 10% premium for fast setup in detailed product pages. It suits the 720 surveyed homeowners comfortable with technology. The drawback is that customers cannot test voice control before buying, returns could rise above the current 34 per month, and QBIT must fund its own marketing and a delivery network, stretching a 70-person firm already managing a $1,400,000 expansion.

Telecommunications provider partnerships: Telcos already visit homes and bundle devices with broadband, so they can install the hub while solving the 1.6% firmware-failure risk and reach households at scale. Partner branding reassures buyers. The downside is that telcos take a share of revenue and may favour their own hardware, and QBIT becomes dependent on a few large partners.

Recommendation: QBIT should choose direct online sales as the primary channel. It protects margin on the 14,000-unit plan, owns the customer relationship and lets QBIT communicate the 57% speed premium. Retail chains are rejected because shelf fees and lost control erode returns; telco partnerships are rejected as the main route because revenue sharing and partner dependence weaken the $1,400,000 investment case. QBIT can add one telco partner later for installation support.

Strong reviews should also cut customer returns, already down from 62 to 34 a month.

Disadvantage: Smart-home hardware is unforgiving: the 2.4% defect rate and 1.6% firmware-failure rate could multiply across a high-profile launch, turning the 57% premium segment into dissatisfied buyers and raising returns above 34 a month. The 24 untrained field staff may struggle to install the new hub within the 6.2-day lead time, and rising 11.3% sensor costs could force QBIT to absorb margin or raise the $390 price beyond what the 720 surveyed homeowners accept.

  Q4(b) [12 marks]
    Question: Using Appendix 3, evaluate how the rise in the interbank rate to 4.05%, the 5.5% minimum wage increase and the 11.3% rise in sensor costs will affect QBIT. Which change will have the greatest impact? Justify your answer.
    Answer: Interbank rate rise to 4.05%: QBIT has an $800,000 ten-year bank loan. If it is variable-rate, the 0.75 percentage-point rise adds 0.75% of $800,000 = $6,000 a year (0.0075 × $800,000). That is modest next to fixed costs of $900,000 and 2025 interest payable of $150,000, and if the loan is fixed-rate the direct cost is nil. Higher rates could also dampen Singapore household spending on smart-home devices, but QBIT can largely remove the financing risk by fixing the rate.

Minimum wage rise of 5.5% to $15.83 per hour: The insert does not state hours worked or how many of the 70 staff are hourly-paid, so no defensible annual wage total can be invented. The sound test is productivity computed from the insert: 14,000 units ÷ 70 staff = 200 units per worker. If that holds, the rise is absorbable within a 42.0% share of revenue retained as gross profit; if the 2.4% defect and 1.6% firmware problems cut output per worker, unit labour costs rise and the $180 contribution per unit shrinks. QBIT can offset part of it via the 57% premium segment.

Sensor input cost inflation of 11.3%: This hits every unit. The insert does not decompose the $210 variable cost, so only an explicitly labelled upper bound is honest: if the whole variable cost rose 11.3%, it would add 11.3% × $210 = $23.73 per unit, and at 14,000 units that is roughly $332,000 a year (14,000 × $23.73). Even a fraction of that erodes the contribution financing the $1,400,000 hub, and it cannot easily be passed on to price-conscious homeowners.

Conclusion: The 11.3% rise in sensor costs will have the greatest impact. It recurs on all 14,000 units and directly attacks the $180 contribution that justifies the hub investment, whereas the rate rise is at most $6,000 and the wage effect cannot be quantified without invented assumptions. QBIT should lock chip contracts and fix the loan rate.

    Mark scheme: level_1_1_to_4: Identifies the external factors with limited application to QBIT. | level_2_5_to_8: Analyses the impact of at least two external changes on QBIT's costs, demand or financing in context. | level_3_9_to_12: Detailed evaluation of all three external changes in the context of QBIT with a well-justified judgment that sensor cost inflation has the greatest impact and why the other two are smaller.

--- MAIN STEM ---
Jestron Software Services (JSTS) is a private limited company in the business software sector, providing cloud accounting and payroll systems to trade firms across Dublin. Founded in 2017 by Ciara O'Donnell, JSTS employs a workforce of 50 and operates a flat organisational structure with laissez-faire leadership. JSTS plans to invest $720,000 in an automated invoicing and payroll platform, financed by a $450,000 ten-year bank loan and a $270,000 share issue. It has fixed costs of $720,000 a year, a variable cost of $120 a unit and a selling price of $300, and currently produces 10,000 units a year. JSTS faces a quality problem: 9% of invoices issued last quarter needed manual correction and a code audit found a 2.6% defect rate in released updates.

--- APPENDIX 1 — MARKETING/OPS ---
Market Research Summary — August 2026: A survey of 560 Irish trade firms found 66% still issue paper invoices and 59% would switch accounting software for automated payroll. Jestron's platform currently takes 3.8 days to process a payroll run; 9% of invoices last quarter required manual correction. Average customer support response is 7.1 hours. Competitors charge $19 per user per month while Jestron charges $23. Word-of-mouth referrals generate 41% of new subscribers; a code audit found a 2.6% defect rate in released updates.

--- MAIN STEM ---
Xentric Cloud Hosting (XNTR) is a private limited company in the cloud infrastructure sector, providing renewable-powered website hosting to small firms across Auckland. XNTR plans to invest $1,080,000 in a green data centre with automated server provisioning, financed by a $640,000 ten-year bank loan and $440,000 retained profit. It has fixed costs of $1,080,000 a year, a variable cost of $90 a unit and a selling price of $270, and currently produces 13,000 units a year. XNTR faces an operational problem: 1.7% of server set-ups were defective last quarter and unplanned downtime reached 26 incidents a month.

--- APPENDIX 1 — MARKETING/OPS ---
Operations Log — Q3 2026: XNTR provisioned 4,200 hosting accounts last quarter with a server-setup defect rate of 1.7%, down from 3.3% a year earlier. Unplanned downtime incidents fell from 48 to 26 per month. Average provisioning time is 2.9 hours. A survey of 840 New Zealand small firms found 62% now require renewable-powered hosting and 54% would switch providers for a greener option. Rivals charge $18 per month for entry hosting while XNTR charges $21. Engineering audit shows 18 of 65 engineers have not completed on-the-job training on the new provisioning system; off-the-job cloud certification costs $1,250 per engineer.

    Question: Using Appendix 3, evaluate how the rise in the official cash rate to 5.25%, the 5.2% minimum wage increase and the 9.7% rise in electricity costs will affect XNTR. Which change will have the greatest impact? Justify your answer.
    Answer: Official cash rate rise to 5.25%: XNTR carries a $640,000 ten-year bank loan. If it is variable-rate, the 0.75 percentage-point rise adds 0.75% of $640,000 = $4,800 a year (0.0075 × $640,000). That is modest beside fixed costs of $1,080,000 and 2025 interest payable of $118,000, and if the loan is fixed-rate the direct cost is nil. Higher rates could slow New Zealand small-firm spending on hosting, but XNTR can largely remove the financing risk by fixing the rate.

Minimum wage rise of 5.2% to $18.94 per hour: The insert does not state hours worked or how many of the 65 staff are hourly-paid, so no defensible annual wage total can be invented. The sound test is productivity computed from the insert: 13,000 units ÷ 65 staff = 200 units per worker. If that holds, the rise is absorbable within a 37.5% share of revenue retained as gross profit; if 26 downtime incidents and 1.7% defects cut output per worker, unit labour costs rise and the $180 contribution per unit shrinks. XNTR can pass part on to the 54% green-switch segment.

Electricity and cooling cost inflation of 9.7%: This reaches every unit. The insert does not decompose the $90 variable cost, so only an explicitly labelled upper bound is honest: if the whole variable cost rose 9.7%, it would add 9.7% of $90 = $8.73 per unit, and at 13,000 units that is roughly $113,000 a year (13,000 × $8.73). Even a fraction of that erodes the contribution funding the $1,080,000 centre, and with rivals at $18 it cannot easily be passed to small firms.

Conclusion: The 9.7% rise in electricity and cooling costs will have the greatest impact. It recurs on all 13,000 units and attacks the $180 contribution behind the $1,080,000 centre, whereas the rate rise is at most $4,800 and the wage effect cannot be quantified without invented assumptions. XNTR should lock energy contracts and fix the loan rate.

--- MAIN STEM ---
Zyra Warehouse Robotics (ZYRA) is a private limited company in the industrial automation sector, supplying robotic picking systems to distribution centres in Rotterdam. It has fixed costs of $1,200,000 a year, a variable cost of $250 a unit and a selling price of $550, and currently produces 10,000 units a year. ZYRA faces a quality problem: the pick-error rate reached 1.5% last quarter and customer damage complaints remain at 39 a month.

--- APPENDIX 1 — MARKETING/OPS ---

A survey of 760 Dutch warehouse managers found 64% plan to automate picking within two years and 56% would switch integrators for faster installation. Rivals charge $22 per hour for robotic-as-a-service while ZYRA charges $26. Technician logs show 16 of 50 field engineers have not completed on-the-job training on the new fleet software; off-the-job certification costs $1,400 per engineer.

PAPER 2 — P2_SET_491
UNIT: Paper 2 Case Study

--- MAIN STEM ---
Meridian Health Partners (MHP) is a private limited company in the private healthcare sector, based in the Dublin region and running day-case surgery clinics, employing a workforce of 80. Founded in 2012 by Dr Aisha Rahman, it receives referrals from local GP practices and operates a hierarchical structure with democratic leadership. MHP plans to invest $1,200,000 in a new endoscopic day-surgery suite with sterile single-use procedure packs, financed by a $750,000 ten-year bank loan and $450,000 retained profit. It has fixed costs of $480,000 a year, a variable cost of $18 a unit and a selling price of $42, and produces 60,000 units a year. MHP faces a rising instrument reprocessing defect rate of 3.4% and nurse absenteeism of 11%.

--- APPENDIX 1 — MARKETING/OPS ---
Quality and Operations Log — Q4 2025: The day-surgery suite completed 14,500 procedure packs last quarter at a reprocessing defect rate of 3.4%, up from 1.9% a year earlier. Patient complaint letters rose from 18 to 31 a month. Average pre-op waiting time is 6.4 days. A survey of 500 patients found 68% would pay $15 more for a private same-day slot, and 57% choose clinics with published infection-control rates. A skills audit shows 24 of 80 clinical staff have not completed on-the-job training on the new endoscope reprocessors; off-the-job training courses in infection control at the regional college cost $620 per employee.

--- APPENDIX 2 — FINANCIAL DATA ---
Title: Extract from the Statement of Profit or Loss and Capital employed data of Meridian Health Partners for the year ended 31 March 2025 ($ '000)
Headers: ['Financial Metric', '2024', '2025']
Revenue | 3,000 | 3,600
Cost of sales | 1,800 | 2,016
Gross profit | 1,200 | 1,584
Operating profit | 420 | 576
Capital employed | 2,800 | 3,200
Interest payable | 60 | 75

--- APPENDIX 3 — EXTERNAL ENVIRONMENT ---
Economic and Healthcare Bulletin (November 2026): (1) The central bank raised the base interest rate from 4.25% to 5.00%, increasing borrowing costs for businesses with variable-rate loans. (2) The national minimum wage will rise by 5.8% from $13.80 to $14.60 per hour from April 2026, lifting payroll costs for clinical support staff. (3) Sterile-pack and disposable-kit input costs have risen 9.6% year-on-year, while patient demand for same-day surgery slots grew 3.2%.

--- QUESTIONS ---
  Q1(a) [8 marks]
    Question: MHP is funding part of its $1,200,000 day-surgery suite with a $750,000 ten-year bank loan. Explain two advantages for MHP of using the $450,000 retained profit instead of borrowing more.
    Answer: Point 1: Retained profit has no interest charge or compulsory repayment, so MHP keeps the cash flow needed to meet fixed costs of $480,000 a year while it services the $750,000 loan. Every dollar not handed to the bank can absorb the 9.6% rise in sterile-pack costs, helping MHP hold its $42 selling price and keep the day-surgery suite competitive for the local GP practices that refer patients.

Point 2: Using $450,000 retained profit avoids further collateral and protects Dr Aisha Rahman's ownership. The $1,200,000 suite cannot be repossessed if demand for the 60,000 units falls short, and the survey finding that 68% of 500 patients would pay $15 more for a same-day slot gives MHP confidence to fund the launch from internal resources rather than increase debt. With nurse absenteeism at 11% and a 3.4% reprocessing defect rate already raising costs, that flexibility matters because loan interest must be paid however many procedure packs are actually delivered. Internal funds also avoid lender conditions on how the suite is run.
    Keywords: retained profit, bank loan, $750,000, $450,000, $1,200,000, day-surgery
    Mark scheme: knowledge_max_2: 1 mark for each valid advantage identified (max 2). | application_analysis_max_6: Up to 3 marks per point for contextual explanation and analysis applied to MHP's financing decision and its day-surgery operations.

  Q1(b) [12 marks]
    Question: MHP is promoting its new endoscopic day-surgery suite. Consider national television advertising, partnerships with local GP practices, or social media campaigns. Which should MHP choose? Justify your recommendation.
    Answer: National television advertising: TV would build rapid, mass awareness of the new $1,200,000 suite across the Dublin region and make the same-day slot offer familiar to thousands of viewers. The drawback is cost and waste: airtime and production are expensive for a business with fixed costs of $480,000 and a $750,000 loan, and most viewers are outside MHP's referral network of local GP practices, so the spend would not convert into the 14,500 procedure packs delivered last quarter.

Partnerships with local GP practices: GPs already refer patients to MHP, so formal links, shared leaflets and short practice presentations would reach precisely the people who need day-case surgery. This route is cheap, uses the 68% of 500 surveyed patients who would pay $15 more for a same-day slot, and can highlight the published infection-control rates that 57% of respondents check. It is slower to build than a TV campaign and depends on GPs' willingness to promote one provider, but it fits MHP's hierarchical referral relationships.

Social media campaigns: Targeted adverts can show the new suite, display infection-control data and drive direct bookings, with measurable clicks against the 6.4-day pre-op waiting time. They are cheaper than television and reach younger patients, but clinical choices are trust-heavy and online leads are less credible than a GP recommendation, so conversion may be low and the message competes with many other providers.

Recommendation: MHP should choose partnerships with local GP practices, supported by a small social media campaign for appointment reminders. This is the cheapest option, builds on existing referrals and matches the 57% who check infection-control rates. Television is rejected as unaffordable and untargeted for an 80-staff clinic servicing a $750,000 loan; social media alone is rejected because it lacks the clinical trust that a GP endorsement supplies.
    Keywords: GP practices, 68%, 57%, 500, 14,500, $1,200,000, 6.4 days
    Mark scheme: level_1_1_to_4: Limited outline of the promotional options with minimal application to MHP. | level_2_5_to_8: Discussion of advantages and disadvantages of at least two options in the context of MHP with some judgement. | level_3_9_to_12: Detailed discussion of all three options in the context of MHP with a well-justified recommendation explaining why television and social media are rejected.

  Q2(a) [8 marks]
    Question: MHP's instrument reprocessing defect rate has risen to 3.4% and nurse absenteeism to 11%. Explain two benefits for MHP of using democratic leadership with its workforce of 80.
    Answer: Point 1: Democratic leadership invites the 80 staff to suggest how the new endoscope reprocessors should be run, raising ownership of infection-control routines. Operators who help set reprocessing checks are more likely to follow them consistently, directly attacking the 3.4% defect rate that has risen from 1.9% and protecting the 14,500 procedure packs completed last quarter; this matters inside MHP's hierarchical structure, where front-line views can otherwise be lost.

Point 2: Involvement raises job satisfaction and reduces the 11% nurse absenteeism, because staff who are consulted are more committed to their shifts. Inside a hierarchical structure this upward flow of ideas is especially useful because it brings front-line detail to managers who may not see every reprocessing cycle, so the $620 college course becomes a backup rather than an immediate cost.

  Q2(b) [12 marks]
    Question: MHP must train 24 of 80 clinical staff who have not completed on-the-job training on the new endoscope reprocessors. Consider on-the-job training or off-the-job training at the regional college. Which should MHP choose? Justify your decision.

    Question: Using Appendix 2, evaluate MHP's financial performance by calculating the gross profit margin, profit margin and ROCE for 2024 and 2025. Has MHP's financial performance improved? Justify your answer.
    Answer: Calculations:
Gross Profit Margin 2024 = 40.0%
Gross Profit Margin 2025 = 44.0%
Profit Margin 2024 = 14.0%
Profit Margin 2025 = 16.0%
ROCE 2024 = 15.0%
ROCE 2025 = 18.0%

In 2025, $3,600,000 revenue less $2,016,000 cost of sales gives $1,584,000, so $1,584,000 ÷ $3,600,000 × 100 = 44.0. Operating profit of $420,000 in 2024 and $576,000 in 2025 divided by revenue gives $420,000 ÷ $3,000,000 × 100 = 14.0 and $576,000 ÷ $3,600,000 × 100 = 16.0. Returns on capital were $420,000 ÷ $2,800,000 × 100 = 15.0 in 2024 and $576,000 ÷ $3,200,000 × 100 = 18.0 in 2025. The caution is that the 3.4% reprocessing defect rate and 11% absenteeism could push costs up and reverse the trend if the $1,200,000 suite is not managed well.

Conclusion: MHP's financial performance has improved.     Question: MHP is considering extending sterile single-use packs across all its day-surgery clinics. Explain one advantage and one disadvantage for MHP of this decision.

    Question: Using Appendix 3, evaluate how the base interest rate rise to 5.00%, the 5.8% minimum wage increase to $14.60 and the 9.6% rise in sterile-pack input costs will affect MHP. Which change will have the greatest impact? Justify your answer.
    Answer: Interest rate rise (4.25% to 5.00%): The increase is 0.75 of a percentage point, so if MHP's $750,000 ten-year loan is variable-rate the extra cost is 0.75% × $750,000 = $5,625 a year (0.0075 × $750,000). That is modest beside fixed costs of $480,000, and a fixed-rate loan would avoid it entirely. Higher rates could also make future borrowing for the $1,200,000 suite dearer and slightly dampen the 3.2% growth in demand for same-day slots.

Minimum wage increase (5.8%, to $14.60 an hour): MHP's workforce of 80 includes hourly-paid clinical support staff, so payroll costs rise and cannot be avoided. The insert states neither hours worked nor individual pay, so an annual wage total would be invented and is not given. The defensible test is productivity: 60,000 units ÷ 80 staff = 750 units per worker, so the higher wage is affordable only if that rate holds or improves; cutting 11% absenteeism and the 3.4% defect rate and training the 24 untrained staff can help sustain it.

Input cost inflation (9.6%): Sterile packs and disposable kits feed the $18 variable cost on every procedure. The insert does not decompose that cost, so only a bound is honest: if the whole $18 were exposed, 9.6% × $18 = $1.728 per unit, and at 60,000 units that is 60,000 × $1.728 = $103,680 a year. Even a smaller exposed share would erode the $24 contribution on every pack sold.

Conclusion: The 9.6% rise in sterile-pack input costs will have the greatest impact. It repeats across all 60,000 units and directly attacks the $24 contribution that services the $750,000 loan and funds the $1,200,000 suite, whereas the interest rise costs $5,625 a year and the wage effect can be offset by sustaining 750 units per worker. MHP should cut the 3.4% defect rate and seek the $15 same-day premium rather than absorb the full increase.
    Keywords: 5.00%, 5.8%, 9.6%, $14.60, $750,000, $18

--- MAIN STEM ---
Northbridge Learning Group (NLG) is a private limited company in the private education sector, based in the Melbourne area and running tutorial colleges, employing a workforce of 55. Founded in 2015 by Elena Vasquez, it works with local schools and operates a flat structure with laissez-faire leadership. NLG plans to invest $640,000 in a new digital learning studio with tablet-based courses, financed by a $400,000 ten-year bank loan, $200,000 retained profit and a $40,000 overdraft. It has fixed costs of $216,000 a year, a variable cost of $10 a unit and a selling price of $28, and produces 50,000 units a year. NLG faces an online-course content error rate of 4.1% and tutor absenteeism of 9%.

--- APPENDIX 1 — MARKETING/OPS ---
Quality and Operations Log — Q4 2025: The studio delivered 11,200 course places last quarter with a content error rate of 4.1%, up from 2.3% a year earlier. Student complaints rose from 22 to 40 a month. Average marker feedback time is 5.6 days. A survey of 400 parents found 72% would pay $20 more for small-group digital tutoring, and 60% check pass rates before enrolling. A skills audit shows 18 of 55 tutors have not completed on-the-job training on the new learning platform; off-the-job training courses at the city college cost $540 per tutor.

--- APPENDIX 2 — FINANCIAL DATA ---

(2) The national minimum wage will rise by 6.2% from $13.80 to $14.66 per hour from April 2026, lifting tutor support payroll costs. (3) Tablet and cloud-licence input costs have risen 8.4% year-on-year, while demand for digital tutoring grew 5.1%.

Every dollar not paid to the bank can absorb the 8.4% rise in tablet and cloud-licence costs, helping NLG hold its $28 selling price and keep the studio attractive to the local schools that refer students.

Point 2: Using $200,000 retained profit keeps Elena Vasquez's ownership intact and avoids more collateral risk. The $640,000 studio cannot be repossessed if enrolments fall short of the 50,000 units target, and the survey showing 72% of 400 parents would pay $20 more for small-group tutoring gives NLG confidence to fund the launch internally rather than increase its bank debt. With a 4.1% content error rate and 9% tutor absence already threatening the 11,200 course places, cash kept inside the business can be redirected to rework and cover without asking the bank; it also avoids lender conditions on studio operations.

The drawback is cost and wastage: airtime is expensive for a business with fixed costs of $216,000, a $400,000 loan and a $40,000 overdraft, and most viewers are not parents of the 11,200 course places delivered last quarter, so conversion would be weak and the message poorly targeted.

Recommendation: NLG should choose partnerships with local schools, backed by a modest social media presence for enquiries. This is the cheapest route, uses existing links and matches the 60% who check pass rates.     Question: Using Appendix 3, evaluate how the base interest rate rise to 4.75%, the 7.1% minimum wage increase to $14.35 and the 10.2% rise in medical consumables and dementia equipment costs will affect CCH. Which change will have the greatest impact? Justify your answer.
    Answer: Interest rate rise (4.00% to 4.75%): The increase is 0.75 of a percentage point, so if CCH's $900,000 ten-year loan is variable-rate the extra cost is 0.75% × $900,000 = $6,750 a year (0.0075 × $900,000). That is small beside fixed costs of $700,000, and a fixed-rate loan would avoid it. Higher rates could also make future borrowing for the $1,500,000 wing dearer and slightly dampen the 4.6% growth in demand for dementia places.

Minimum wage increase (7.1%, to $14.35 an hour): CCH's workforce of 120 includes hourly-paid care workers, so payroll costs rise and cannot be avoided. The insert gives neither hours worked nor individual pay, so an annual wage total would be invented. The defensible test is productivity: 90,000 units ÷ 120 staff = 750 resident-days per worker, so the higher wage is affordable only if that rate holds or improves; cutting 12% absence and the 2.8% error rate and training the 30 untrained workers can help sustain it.

Input cost inflation (10.2%): Medical consumables feed the $22 variable cost on every resident-day. The insert does not decompose that cost, so only a bound is honest: if the whole $22 were exposed, 10.2% × $22 = $2.244 per unit, and at 90,000 units that is 90,000 × $2.244 = $201,960 a year. Even a smaller exposed share would erode the $28 contribution on every resident-day sold.

Conclusion: The 10.2% rise in medical consumables and dementia equipment costs will have the greatest impact. It repeats across all 90,000 units and directly attacks the $28 contribution that services the $900,000 loan and funds the $1,500,000 wing, whereas the interest rise costs $6,750 a year and the wage effect can be offset by sustaining 750 resident-days per worker. CCH should cut the 2.8% error rate and seek the $25 premium rather than absorb the whole increase.

--- MAIN STEM ---
Brightpath Dental Clinics (BDC) is a private limited company in the private dentistry sector, based in the Auckland region and running dental practices, employing a workforce of 40. Founded in 2017 by Dr Samuel Okafor, it receives referrals from local GP practices and operates a flat structure with democratic leadership. BDC plans to invest $520,000 in a new digital scanning and same-day crown unit with recyclable impression trays, financed by a $300,000 ten-year bank loan and $220,000 retained profit. It has fixed costs of $180,000 a year, a variable cost of $14 a unit and a selling price of $38, and produces 40,000 units a year. BDC faces a crown remake rate of 5.2% and dental nurse absenteeism of 10%.

--- APPENDIX 1 — MARKETING/OPS ---
Quality and Operations Log — Q4 2025: The clinic fitted 9,800 crowns last quarter at a remake rate of 5.2%, down from 7.0% a year earlier. Patient complaints fell from 33 to 19 a month. Average appointment waiting time is 9.5 days. A survey of 450 patients found 74% would pay $30 more for a same-day crown, and 63% choose clinics offering digital scanning. A skills audit shows 12 of 40 staff have not completed on-the-job training on the new intraoral scanners; off-the-job training courses at the dental college cost $860 per employee.

--- APPENDIX 2 — FINANCIAL DATA ---
Title: Extract from the Statement of Profit or Loss and Capital employed data of Brightpath Dental Clinics for the year ended 31 March 2025 ($ '000)

(2) The national minimum wage will rise by 6.4% from $13.90 to $14.79 per hour from April 2026, lifting dental-nurse payroll costs. (3) Impression material and scanning consumable costs have risen 8.9% year-on-year, while demand for same-day crowns grew 4.8%.

That is modest beside fixed costs of $180,000, and a fixed-rate loan would avoid it entirely. Higher rates could make future borrowing for the $520,000 unit dearer and slightly dampen the 4.8% growth in demand for same-day crowns.

Minimum wage increase (6.4%, to $14.79 an hour): BDC's workforce of 40 includes hourly-paid dental nurses, so payroll costs rise and cannot be avoided. The insert gives neither hours worked nor individual pay, so an annual wage total would be invented. The defensible test is productivity: 40,000 units ÷ 40 staff = 1,000 crowns per worker, so the higher wage is affordable only if that rate holds or improves; cutting 10% absence and the 5.2% remake rate and training the 12 untrained staff can help sustain it.

Input cost inflation (8.9%): Impression materials and scanning consumables feed the $14 variable cost on every crown. The insert does not decompose that cost, so only a bound is honest: if the whole $14 were exposed, 8.9% × $14 = $1.246 per unit, and at 40,000 units that is 40,000 × $1.246 = $49,840 a year. Even a smaller exposed share would erode the $24 contribution on every crown sold.

Conclusion: The 8.9% rise in impression material and scanning consumable costs will have the greatest impact. It repeats across all 40,000 crowns and directly attacks the $24 contribution that services the $300,000 loan and funds the $520,000 unit, whereas the interest rise costs $2,250 a year and the wage effect can be offset by sustaining 1,000 crowns per worker. BDC should cut the 5.2% remake rate and seek the $30 premium rather than absorb the whole increase.
    Keywords: 5.00%, 6.4%, 8.9%, $14.79, $300,000, $14
    Mark scheme: level_1_1_to_4: Identifies the external changes with limited application to BDC. | level_2_5_to_8: Analyses the impact of at least two external changes on BDC's costs, revenue or financing in context. | level_3_9_to_12: Detailed evaluation of all three changes in context with a well-justified judgment that input-cost inflation has the greatest impact and why the others are smaller.

--- MAIN STEM ---
Willowbrook Early Learning (WEL) is a private limited company in the early-years childcare sector, based in the Toronto region and running nursery centres, employing a workforce of 65. Founded in 2013 by Nadia Farouk, it works with local parent groups and operates a hierarchical structure with democratic leadership. WEL plans to invest $780,000 in a new nursery wing with outdoor learning areas and recycled-fibre play equipment, financed by a $480,000 ten-year bank loan, $250,000 retained profit and a $50,000 overdraft. It has fixed costs of $288,000 a year, a variable cost of $12 a unit and a selling price of $30, and produces 45,000 units a year. WEL faces an attendance-recording error rate of 6.8% and nursery-worker absenteeism of 13%.

--- APPENDIX 1 — MARKETING/OPS ---
Quality and Operations Log — Q4 2025: The nurseries recorded 10,500 child-place weeks last quarter with an attendance-recording error rate of 6.8%, down from 9.1% a year earlier. Parent complaints fell from 52 to 28 a month. Average settling-in period is 12.4 days. A survey of 380 parents found 79% would pay $18 more a week for outdoor learning, and 68% check staff-to-child ratios before enrolling. A skills audit shows 22 of 65 nursery workers have not completed on-the-job training on the new safeguarding app; off-the-job training courses in childcare at the city college cost $580 per worker.

Every dollar not paid to the bank can absorb the 9.3% rise in outdoor-equipment costs, helping WEL hold its $30 selling price for the local parent groups it works with.

Point 2: Using $250,000 retained profit keeps Nadia Farouk's ownership intact and avoids further collateral risk. The $780,000 wing cannot be repossessed if enrolments fall short of the 45,000 units, and the survey showing 79% of 380 parents would pay $18 more a week for outdoor learning gives WEL grounds to fund the launch from its own resources rather than increase borrowing. With 13% absence and a 6.8% recording error rate already straining the nurseries, keeping cash free of interest matters more than adding another fixed repayment; it also leaves the $50,000 overdraft as a short-term buffer rather than permanent debt.

--- MAIN STEM ---
Northgate Ceramic Works (NCWK) is a private limited company in the eco-friendly building materials sector, employing a workforce of 50. Founded in 2011 by Priya Nandakumar, the business supplies recycled-content ceramic tiles to builders' merchants and operates a flat organisational structure with democratic leadership. NCWK plans to invest $720,000 in a new low-emission kiln for recycled-content eco-tiles, financed by a $420,000 ten-year bank loan and $300,000 retained profit. It has fixed costs of $360,000 a year, a variable cost of $8.00 a unit and a selling price of $14.00, and currently produces 100,000 units a year. NCWK faces two problems: the glazing defect rate has reached 4.2% and kiln energy waste is rising.

--- APPENDIX 1 — MARKETING/OPS ---
Quality and Waste Report — Q3 2025: The eco-tile line fired 25,000 tiles last quarter at a glazing defect rate of 4.2%, down from 6.1% a year ago. Customer complaints about chipped tiles fell from 44 to 19 per month. Average order fulfilment time is 5.6 days. Kiln waste currently runs at 7.5% of output. A survey of 400 builders' merchants found that 68% would pay up to $0.50 more per tile for recycled-content eco-tiles, and 57% check environmental credentials before ordering. A training audit shows 18 of 50 production staff have not completed on-the-job training on the new kiln controls; off-the-job certification courses at the local college cost $750 per employee.

--- APPENDIX 2 — FINANCIAL DATA ---
Title: Extract from the Statement of Profit or Loss and Capital employed data of Northgate Ceramic Works for the year ended 31 March 2025 ($ '000)
Headers: ['Financial Metric', '2024', '2025']
Revenue | 2,400 | 2,800
Cost of sales | 1,560 | 1,680
Gross profit | 840 | 1,120
Operating profit | 288 | 448
Capital employed | 1,600 | 2,000
Interest payable | 36 | 48

--- APPENDIX 3 — EXTERNAL ENVIRONMENT ---
Economic and Business Bulletin (November 2026): (1) The central bank has raised the base interest rate from 4.5% to 5.25%, increasing borrowing costs for firms with variable-rate loans. (2) The national minimum wage will rise by 5.9% from $13.10 to $13.87 an hour from April 2026, lifting wage bills across the construction supply chain. (3) Wholesale clay and energy input costs have risen 9.8% year-on-year, while building-material inflation is 6.4% and spending on new housing starts grew 2.9%.

--- QUESTIONS ---
  Q1(a) [8 marks]
    Question: NCWK plans to fund part of its $720,000 low-emission kiln with a $420,000 bank loan. Explain two advantages for NCWK of using the $300,000 retained profit instead of borrowing that amount.
    Answer: Point 1: Using the $300,000 retained profit means NCWK pays no interest or capital repayments on that portion of the $720,000 kiln, protecting cash flow while the business already carries fixed costs of $360,000 a year. Every dollar not paid to the lender can absorb the 9.8% rise in clay and energy input costs, so the $14.00 selling price need not be raised and the 4.2% defect-rate problem can be tackled without extra debt pressure.

Point 2: Retained profit keeps control with Priya Nandakumar and the existing shareholders. A bank loan can impose covenants and require collateral, putting the new kiln at risk if demand for recycled-content eco-tiles disappoints; using internally generated funds avoids that risk and preserves the flat, democratic structure, since no outside lender can dictate how the 50-strong workforce is managed or how the $420,000 loan itself is serviced.

The owner-managed culture also means the decision can be taken quickly by Priya Nandakumar without waiting for lender approval, helping NCWK respond to the 9.8% input-cost rise.
    Keywords: retained profit, $300,000, $420,000, $720,000, $360,000, bank loan

  Q1(b) [12 marks]
    Question: NCWK is launching recycled-content eco-tiles. Consider advertising in trade magazines, sponsoring a builders' trade exhibition, or running targeted social media campaigns. Which should NCWK choose to promote the launch? Justify your recommendation.

Trade magazines are rejected as slow, untargeted and expensive for a business servicing a $420,000 loan; exhibitions are rejected because the cost of a single stand is high relative to the 4.2% defect-rate fix and the 100,000-unit output target still needs steady year-round demand.

    Question: NCWK's glazing defect rate has reached 4.2% and kiln energy waste is rising. Explain two benefits for NCWK of its democratic leadership style in addressing these problems.

--- MAIN STEM ---
Ridgeview Timber Products (RTPL) is a worker cooperative in the sustainable construction materials sector, employing a workforce of 36. Founded in 2008 by Tomas Berg, the business supplies reclaimed timber flooring to decorators and operates a hierarchical structure with laissez-faire leadership. RTPL plans to invest $640,000 in a reclaimed-timber grading and drying line, financed by a $240,000 bank loan and $400,000 from a share issue of member shares. It has fixed costs of $280,000 a year, a variable cost of $12.00 a unit and a selling price of $20.00, and currently produces 80,000 units a year. RTPL faces two problems: labour turnover has reached 14% and timber waste is rising.

--- APPENDIX 1 — MARKETING/OPS ---
Operations Log — Q3 2025: The reclaimed-timber line processed 19,000 board metres last quarter at a defect rate of 3.4%, down from 5.0% a year ago. Customer complaints about warped boards fell from 31 to 14 per month. Average delivery lead time is 6.2 days. Timber waste is currently 8.8% of input. A survey of 350 decorators found that 62% would pay $0.75 more for certified reclaimed flooring, and 49% check sustainability labels before ordering. A skills audit shows 14 of 36 operatives have not completed on-the-job training on the new grading saw; off-the-job courses at the training centre cost $620 per person.

--- APPENDIX 2 — FINANCIAL DATA ---

The $240,000 bank loan can then be serviced from contribution of $8.00 a unit without the extra burden of a second loan.

Point 2: Issuing member shares strengthens the cooperative's own capital base and keeps ownership with the 36 worker-members, supporting the laissez-faire culture and long-term commitment. A bank would require security and covenants over the new grading saw; member equity has no such conditions, so the 11.2% rise in timber and transport costs can be absorbed without breaching lending terms or risking the reclaimed-timber line.

Because the cooperative already has a $240,000 loan, keeping the new capital as member equity avoids pushing interest costs higher and preserves the improving gross margin trend in Appendix 2 while the grading line beds in.

    Question: RTPL wants to grow sales of its certified reclaimed flooring. Consider selling only through decorators' merchants, launching an e-commerce website, or supplying national DIY chains. Which should RTPL choose? Justify your recommendation.
    Answer: Decorators' merchants only: This keeps distribution simple and uses existing relationships with the 350 decorators surveyed, giving predictable orders and low selling costs for a cooperative of 36. It caps reach, however: relying on one channel leaves RTPL exposed if merchants cut stock, and the 62% who would pay $0.75 more may never see the product, wasting the $640,000 grading-line investment.

Recommendation: RTPL should launch an e-commerce website, retaining merchant sales as a base. PAPER 2 — P2_SET_498
UNIT: Paper 2 Case Study
